title: St. Michaels Reorganizes Police, OKs Raises
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
St. Michaels reorganizes police, OKs raises

 August 11, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: A5 | Section: News 
 
 282
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS - The Commissioners of St. Michaels voted unanimously Wednesday to revise job descriptions in the town's police department and approve raises in light of the new organizational structure.The need to restructure the small police department came about earlier this summer after former Chief Anthony Smith retired on June 30. Newly appointed Chief Jeffrey Oswald was sworn in the same day, leaving his former position as the department's captain unfilled.Instead of attempting to locate a new officer to serve as captain, with a salary ranging from $85,000 to $100,000, Oswald suggested restructuring the department through restructuring and promoting two of his officers to sergeants.The department's old structure included a chief, a captain and two corporals, each with two officers under them. The newly proposed and now-approved structure includes the chief and two sergeants, each with two officers under them.A memo in the town's meeting agenda packet indicated that both sergeants will be able to fulfill each other's roles, but each will have a separate primary focus in assisting the chief: one to help handle patrol responsibilities and one to aid in administrative tasks.Oswald said he previously handled the responsibilities of the captain position for 12 years while ranked as a sergeant and lieutenant and wanted to provide his officers with the same opportunities for advancement.The new structure will have a minimal budgetary impact, as the total base salary impact for the restructuring is $7,200.The promoted sergeants will receive mandatory first line administrator training and will be recognized by the Police Training Commission to take command in Oswald's absence. The positions come with a two year probationary period.

The St. Michaels Police Department is located at 100 S. Fremont St.

title: Talbot Board of Ed Adds Makeup Day for Snow; Approves 2025-26 Calendar
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot Board of Ed adds makeup day for snow; approves 2025-26 calendar

 January 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 580
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — During Wednesday's meeting, the Talbot County Board of Education added a day onto the end of this year's school calendar following last week's snowstorm.Talbot County Public Schools was closed Monday through Friday last week due to snow that blanketed the Mid-Shore. However, the 2024-2025 school calendar only had four inclement weather days built in, meaning an additional day was needed to comply with the state's 180-day requirement.
Helga Einhorn, assistant superintendent of school leadership and student success, recommended that a day be added in June, moving the last day of school for students to Friday, June 13.
The last day for teachers would be Monday, June 16. Einhorn said that historically, most teachers complete mandated training that affords them with not having to come in on the last day.
The board unanimously passed the adjusted calendar for this year.
2025-26 CALENDAROn Wednesday, the board also chose the district's calendar for the 2025-2026 school year.
At last month's meeting, Einhorn presented a draft calendar with two days off in March and a five-day spring break, which was the recommendation of the calendar committee. Board President Emily Jackson, however, expressed frustration there weren't multiple options posed.
This month, Einhorn returned with three draft calendars. The first was similar to what the board saw in December, with a four-day weekend in March and the shorter spring break. The second draft removed the off days in March and had an eight-day spring break.
A third draft included both the March break and an eight-day spring break, pushing the last student day back to June 10, 2026.
All three drafts included the typical days off in November for Easton's Waterfowl Festival, as well as a winter break from Dec. 20, 2025, to Jan. 4, 2026.
"There is no calendar that we're going to create that is best for every single person," Jackson said.
Jackson said it's clear — based on previous polling and community input — that most families favor the extended spring break. Board Vice President Amy Dodson suggested the board move forward with the second or third calendars.
Board member Karla Wieland-Cherry said she preferred the first calendar with the shorter spring break.
"You're losing a lot of school time for eight days off for students," Wieland-Cherry said. "You're losing a lot of momentum. And plus you're concerned with providing day care. Not all employers are going to allow that. That's quite a long time to take off of work and find day care and so forth."
She added that not all families are looking for a longer spring break.
"My only concern is that if 59% of our students are at the poverty level, we're really talking about more of a smaller group who are really going to financially be able to afford an Easter holiday," Wieland-Cherry said. "… You really could possibly potentially be causing more hardship for something that's more an elitist type thing, quite honestly."
Jackson said while she agrees with Wieland-Cherry's point, she has "to go with what the community is saying."
"We have asked again and again, and the majority of the respondents to any time we've asked this have said they like that spring break," Jackson said.
Following board discussion, Jackson motioned for approval of the third calendar featuring two off days in March and five days for spring break. Her motion included an amendment to the calendar that the March days off serve as two of four inclement weather days for the district.
By a 6-1 vote, with only Wieland-Cherry voting against, the board approved the 2025-2026 school year calendar.

title: Talbot Council, Eastern Shore Legislators Share Heartburn Over State Mandates
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot council, Eastern Shore legislators share heartburn over state mandates

 October 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 599
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — There's still more than two months until the 2026 Maryland General Assembly kicks off, but on Tuesday, local officials struck a chord of financial concern over the state's propensity to push down costs on county governments.The heartburn was shared during a joint meeting between the Talbot County Council and three elected officials in the General Assembly — Dels. Chris Adams and Tom Hutchinson and Sen. Johnny Mautz, all Republicans who represent multiple Mid-Shore counties.
At one point, council member Dave Stepp asked the legislators which additional cost burdens the state may place on counties heading into fiscal year 2027.
"Name it," Adams responded.
"I think that the assumption that there'll be additional burdens and additional costs is probably a safe assumption," Mautz said.
County Council Vice President Pete Lesher pointed out the state legislature's choice last fiscal year to require counties pick up a portion of teachers' pensions payments, which are run through a state program. Talbot's share was $440,000, which prompted an increase, albeit slight, in the property tax rate for residents.
Lesher said if the state wants counties to increase financial responsibilities for the pensions, counties should be granted authority over the program, too.
"We're just being handed the bill," Lesher said. "And if they want to share this responsibility, share the authority. But obviously there's no interest in doing that."
It's unclear exactly which cost shifts could be at play with session still weeks away, but the Republican legislators and county officials spent much time during Tuesday's meeting discussing The Blueprint, Maryland's expansive funding and improvement plan for education.
In fiscal year 2026, the county was required by the Blueprint to include $55 million in education funding in its budget. That share will sharply increase in future years, according to reports from the state Department of Legislative Services as of the spring.
In Talbot County, the required funding mark could hit $90 million by fiscal year 2034, a hike school officials described as "sobering."
On Tuesday, Talbot County Finance Director Martha Sparks shared concerns with discrepancies state agencies have had when calculating the minimum funding marks counties must dole out to areas such as education and health departments.
Sparks said in the past, "core funding" required by the Maryland Department of Health to go to local health departments was off by around $250,000. The discrepancies have put other counties in more of a bind, she acknowledged, but still impact Talbot since the notice of changes from the state agencies come after the county has already significantly completed or passed its budget.
"These differences in funding have been small, relatively so," Sparks said. "They're still large for us. We want our budget to be right."
HOTEL TAX COLLECTION
Sparks and the Eastern Shore legislators opened Tuesday's meeting with a short discussion on Senate Bill 979, a law which will soon require the Comptroller's Office to collect certain accommodations tax information from companies such as Airbnb and Vrbo. Currently, counties are the collectors.
Hutchinson said while the bill gained support from some jurisdictions, it could actually hurt Talbot County since the finance office has a "terrific" collection system.
"In Talbot County, the bill was a negative to them," he said. "To other counties … where they don't really have a process in place, they were somewhat supportive of it."
Lesher said if the state assumes the collection duties, Talbot County could lose timely access to important tourism and rental data. Legislators were optimistic that Comptroller Brooke Lierman (D) is open to allowing an opt-out to the bill mandating the state take over collection.
"I think it'd be helpful if the council would say, 'We don't want the state to collect this,'" Mautz said.

title: Oxford Tackles Short-Term Rental Compliance Issues
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Oxford tackles short-term rental compliance issues

 October 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 339
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — Oxford currently has somewhere between 35 and 44 short-term rentals, but according to Town Commissioner Dave Donovan, only five are licensed.Donovan proposed an ordinance at Monday's Town Commission meeting amending town code to hold operators liable for non-compliance and gather accurate data on the number, location and rental frequency of short-term rentals in town.
The information will help commissioner make better-informed policy decisions, Donovan said.
He believes the primary issue with short-term rental compliance is operators forgetting or neglecting to register.
"I suspect that the real problem with compliance, at least in the last couple years, is that people in town just forgot," Donovan said. "And, obviously that's not okay, but also, you got to do something to make sure they remember."
The town's current short-term rental rules fine operators that are not licensed $100 to $200 every day they remain unlicensed. Donovan said this is difficult to enforce, especially considering unlicensed rentals are hard to track because they advertise online without physical signs.
The proposed ordinance would fine short-term rental operators who do not comply a flat fine of $1,000 a month, which Donovan said will likely be more effective. It would also make the act of advertising a short-term rental property without a license a violation, requiring owners to remove listings if not properly registered.
"The agents are the ones that really should, and most likely do, understand the requirements of the local ordinances, whether it's here, or Easton, or Trappe, or St. Michaels or the county. And so, there's really no excuse," Donovan said.
The current ordinance restricts licenses to "natural persons," which prevents corporations and investment groups from buying multiple properties for short-term rentals.
"I think it's very clever. It really provides a tremendous disincentive to the true out-of-towners, the true real estate investment companies that just want to come into a town like ours and buy up chunks of it and run a short-term rental business, because they can't," Donovan said.
There will be a public hearing on this proposed ordinance at the Oxford Town Commissioners meeting on Oct. 28.

title: Workshops Held During Oxford Commission Meeting
author: Lily Tierney ltierney@chespub.com
content:
Workshops held during Oxford Commission Meeting

 September 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: LILY TIERNEY ltierney@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 510
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Commissioners of Oxford held several work sessions during the town's Sept. 29 meeting. These included:Town electionsCommissioners discussed the possibility of creating a supplemental municipal voter list in addition to the county's list.
They plan to discuss the matter further at a workshop on Oct. 8 and are actively seeking the public's feedback.
Ethics ordinance recommendations from the Ethics CommissionCommissioners considered revising the ethics ordinance after the Ethics Commission said the current version is confusing from years of edits.
Additional proposals included adding an alternate member, staggering terms for continuity, and clarifying the distinction between the Ethics and Town commissions.
Members of the Ethics Commission suggested narrowing financial disclosure rules, which currently require candidates to report all global property and business interests, to instead focus on conflicts of interest within Maryland.
The Ethics Commission also discussed separate disclosure standards for elected officials, appointed members and staff, and agreed to add a campaign finance section requiring filings at candidacy, election and post-election.
The updates are slated for completion by February ahead of the next election cycle.
Economic development prioritiesThe Oxford Business Association pressed town leaders for clear economic development priorities to guide its work, particularly on tourism and use of accommodation tax revenues, now at historic lows.
Commissioners asked for detailed budgets and proof of return on investment before committing tax dollars, moving away from funding with "no strings attached."
The association's representative said they must consult members before releasing past financials. They agreed performance metrics, like website analytics, which are currently hindered by technical issues, will be needed once town priorities are defined.
Short-term rental permitting processCommissioners considered adopting a software called Granicus to crack down on unlicensed short-term rentals, estimating 35 to 44 units operate in town but only five hold permits.
The program, already in use by Talbot County, would cost Oxford $2,000 a year.
The software would also help enforce a proposed rule requiring license numbers in rental ads, which officials say are easier to track than actual bookings.
Breezeline franchise agreementCommissioners are reviewing their franchise agreement with Breezeline, weighing whether to stay with the old terms or adopt a new template that covers only cable.
The draft also drops the 2% public, educational and government funding, meaning the town would need to add a franchise fee of up to 5% to recoup costs.
Commissioners said they'll hold a public hearing, likely after the holidays, to gather resident feedback on service quality before entering negotiations.
Utility payment processingCommissioners are exploring new approaches to utilities and services, including an online portal for utility bill payments that would allow credit card use but carry a 1.5% to 3.5% transaction fee which will likely be passed on to residents rather than absorbed by the town.
An Automated Clearing House payment option through Shore United Bank is also being considered, with specific cost proposals to be discussed at a future meeting.
Electric fees paid by the townThe Electric Vehicle Institute has offered to replace the current chargers with faster, pay-as-you-go chargers that would eliminate the current expense of $600.
Commissioners will also separately review electricity costs tied to the watermen's boat slips, citing the town's commitment to its working waterfront.

title: Easton Council Members to Host Ward Town Halls for Residents
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton council members to host ward town halls for residents

 September 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 459
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Beginning Monday, Easton council members will host ward-specific town halls in hopes of increasing transparency and engaging with constituents.Maureen Curry (Ward 1), Robert Rankin (Ward 2), David Montgomery (Ward 3) and the Rev. Elmer Davis (Ward 4) will each host town halls open to their constituents at the Easton Volunteer Fire Department in the coming weeks.
The town halls were mentioned during Easton's recent election, including by Don Abbatiello, now council president and then Ward 2 representative.
Abbatiello said he aims to attend all four town halls.
"We wanted to make sure that we left no stone unturned when it came to sharing information," Abbatiello said.
Rankin will kick off the meetings with Ward 2 residents on Monday. Montgomery will host Ward 3's discussion on Oct. 9. Davis will lead Ward 4's on Oct. 23, and Curry will wrap it up with Ward 1's meeting on Oct. 27. All four meetings will be held at the Easton fire hall from 7 to 8 p.m.
Abbatiello said the idea to host semi-regular ward town halls birthed from discussions on the campaign trail, with some residents feeling like they didn't have enough access to town information or couldn't attend town meetings, which are typically twice a month at 5:30 p.m.
The council president said the town's done a good job in improving its communication to residents since he joined the council in 2019, especially on its website and social media platforms. The new town halls are a continuation of that effort, he said.
Council members will provide brief presentations to residents at the meetings, updating them on recent projects in town and their respective wards. Then, the sessions will open up for feedback and questions from the public.
"We want residents to be informed and know what's going on," Rankin said. " ... The more we can hear from folks … that really helps us a lot."
Housing, growth and traffic are expected to be major points of discussion, council leaders said.
"The central topic, for me at least, will be growth," Montgomery said. "And I think that's a topic that concerns everybody of Ward 3 because of how residents have to tend to traffic."
Rankin said he expects his discussion to touch on recent development projects and the town's comprehensive plan, which is in the process of being updated for the first time since 2010 and will lay out a vision for the town's growth over the next decade.
Davis said that in addition to growth and development, he expects to field questions on the Easton Police Department and resident concerns about safety.
The Ward 4 representative highlighted the town halls as another avenue to be open with the public.
"Everybody can be included and get some questions answered," Davis said. "Our main goal is to show transparency to the community."

title: MACo Leaders Meet with Talbot Officials to Discuss 2026 General Assembly
author: Konner Metz
content:
MACo leaders meet with Talbot officials to discuss 2026 General Assembly

 September 25, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 536
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Leaders from the Maryland Association of Counties shared predictions for a calmer legislative session in 2026 during a meeting with the Talbot County Council on Tuesday.Michael Sanderson, MACo's executive director, and Jack Wilson, the association's president and current Queen Anne's County commissioner, met for an annual check-in with Talbot officials.
Sanderson reminded the council members of last year's volatile General Assembly session, during which legislators and Gov. Wes Moore (D) had to reckon with closing a $3 billion gap in the state's fiscal year 2026 budget.
Some savings came through cost shifts placing more burden on county governments, the MACo leaders said. But they added that the upcoming 2026 session, and the fiscal year 2027 budget that goes along with it, likely won't be as dire.
"Relatively calm, probably not a big crisis," Sanderson said of his projection for this year's session, which officially kicks off Jan. 14 in Annapolis.
He said the large budgetary concerns are likely to reappear in 2027 as legislators put together a plan for fiscal year 2028.
"The story from last year is gonna repeat itself, but with a year off," Sanderson predicted.
Specifically, the executive director said Maryland's expansive education funding formula, The Blueprint, will influence the 2027 session. And in the short-term, some counties are already coming to grips with increasing cost shares for education.
"Every county is either in the midst or a year or two away from seeing a year where the increase in school spending required under Blueprint requires all the money or even more money than your county's likely to gain in revenue for that year," Sanderson said. "It's an obvious squeeze at the local level."
Talbot County's fiscal year 2026 budget included $55 million in education funding required by The Blueprint's formulas. On top of that, the council approved an additional $600,000 in funding to fill new positions.
That mark had been scaled back twice from the original ask the Talbot Board of Education made of the council — first requesting $5.5 million in supplementary funds, then $1.1 million.
County Council Vice President Pete Lesher, who supported the district's $1.1 million request earlier this year, said it was "short-sighted" for the county to only fund the district's request partially, given that Blueprint requirements are only set to increase in future years. But other council members opted to hold back on dedicating the full request as the county aimed to even out its spending hikes seen in years prior.
Sanderson said on Tuesday that housing legislation will be at the forefront this winter. Recently, Moore signed an executive order that aims to speed up the permitting and building of affordable housing projects.
"I anticipate that being a big fight," Sanderson said. "Whether it's a big fight in the more rural jurisdictions is yet to be seen."
Council Member Lynn Mielke asked how Easton fits into state plans to tackle the housing issue.
Sanderson said there's an opportunity for MACo to advocate for provisions so a potential housing package doesn't "overwhelm" local jurisdictions. He said the association can help push for certain changes to help counties and towns that lack authority in certain areas, such as the variation of impact fees on developers.
"At the same time, we generally want to keep land use decisions local," he added.

title: Members of Oxford Historic District Commission Removed
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Members of Oxford Historic District Commission removed

 September 11, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 494
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — With a unanimous vote last month, Oxford commissioners removed three of the the five members from the town's Historic District Commission.At the Aug. 19 town meeting, Commission President Katrina Greer announced that the Commissioners of Oxford unanimously voted in closed session to change the makeup of the commission. Greer said in a statement at the meeting that this decision reflects the best interest of the town.
Jennifer Stanley, Jim Wilcox and Justin Werner were removed from their roles on the commission. Their terms were not set to expire until 2026 and 2027. A fourth member of the commission, Terry Sullivan, whose term expires Saturday, has not been confirmed of a reappointment.
The commission's fifth and final member, Margaret Morris, is listed on the town's website as an "alternate member." Two new members were appointed at the August meeting.
The Oxford Town Historic Commission is a volunteer body appointed by town commissioners and has five members who have three year terms. The commission provides current and prospective property owners with guidance on how historical properties should be handled in the town.
Oxford Town Commissioner Dave Donovan said the commission will not discuss details of their decision beyond confirming unanimity of the vote and saying it was taken in the "best interest of the community."
"I think that's really all we're willing to discuss on that topic," Donovan said.
Stanley, one of the three Historic District Commissioners who was removed, said she was told about the decision in person prior to the meeting by a commissioner, who cited that she "wasn't efficient enough." Stanley did not disclose which commissioner gave her this news. She said she was never given advice on how to be more efficient.
Stanley, who has lived in the town for 45 years, said she had seen behavior like this before from town officials and expected something like this to happen. "I don't think this is an issue of transparency. I think this is an issue of control," she said.
Greer said that the decision was made in the best interest of the town, noting that the commissioners' top priority is serving all residents. She also expressed gratitude to the many volunteers on boards and commissions who help carry that commitment forward.
Stanley does not agree that this decision is in its best interest. "It's unfortunate for the town," she said.
Moving forward
Barbara Ranson and Will Cawley were appointed to the Historic District Commission at the Aug. 19 meeting. According to Town Manager Holly Wahl, there are two additional spots that need to be filled. She said town commissioners held interviews Sept. 2.
"Commissioners recently implemented a new process for the town where they are reviewing applicants for all boards and commissions in public so that there's a transparent review of how members are appointed," Wahl said. "And so after an interviewing process, members are now appointed to boards and commissions by a vote of all commissioners."
Appointments for the open two spots are planned for the Sept. 29 regular commission meeting.

title: Easton Council Debates How to Move Forward with Food Trucks
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton council debates how to move forward with food trucks

 August 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 632
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — After uproar from food truck owners and residents, the Easton Town Council is considering changes to its restrictions on food trucks.On Monday, the council discussed potentially revising a 2011 ordinance that limits food trucks to only operating during special events like festivals.
"I think that should be something we should take on as soon as we can," said Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis.
All five council members acknowledged they must keep in mind the town's existing restaurants when making any relaxations to food truck rules.
"2011 was a long time ago, and things change," Ward 1 Councilmember Maureen Curry said. "But we have to be mindful of our brick-and-mortar restaurants. We don't want to do anything unnecessarily to compete with them."
In the last two weeks, pushback against Easton's food truck rules has been widespread online. A petition garnered over 3,000 signatures.
The outcry came after town code enforcement began to more closely enforce the 2011 rules, prohibiting food trucks from operating in the parking lot of the town's hospital.
The council and attorney Sharon VanEmburgh agreed Monday to look at amending the ordinance by next spring. Then, they focused discussion on a short-term solution.
PILOT PROGRAM
Much of the food truck debate has centered on vendors that had been setting up outside the Shore Medical Center hospital on South Washington Street. Curry said the council received "tremendous" feedback from hospital employees who relied on the food trucks during lunch breaks.
"It's literally impossible to even go pick up a sandwich sometimes with the traffic in our wonderful, little town and get back to the desk within 30 minutes," Curry said.
Curry asked if the town could include the hospital in a short-term fix, such as a pilot program floated Monday. The program would likely be created through a resolution, VanEmburgh said, allowing certain businesses to invite food trucks to their properties.
Easton's program, if approved, would likely include a setback rule from nearby restaurants. VanEmburgh said the best mark may be around 300 feet.
Town Council members debated various provisions that could be included in a resolution to establish the pilot program.
Davis said any pilot program introduced would need to apply to other businesses in town.
"If we're gonna do it for the hospital, we got to be fair across the board to other people," Davis said. "I get the hospital has a need, but you can't just arbitrarily give them favor."
Ward 4's David Montgomery pushed back, saying a pilot program is meant to try out "in a specific time and place." He said the hospital should have "first crack" at a food truck pilot program.
Davis raised the concern that certain food trucks could be excluded from the pilot, providing an example.
"If there's a food truck that specializes in African American food that is not served at the hospital, what do we do in those instances to be fair?" Davis asked.
Montgomery replied, "It just seems to me that you're being obstructionist in these comments.
" ... The hospital has chosen in the past what food truck to invite on their private property," he added. "I think that's their right to do it."
The council also touched on transient license fees that food trucks pay when setting up at permitted festivals or events. Vendors pay $500 for the first two days and $150 for each day after up to 30 days.
"I would not be opposed to waiving that right now while we're in the pilot program," Curry said. "Because you can't expect a food truck to pay $500 to sit outside a hospital or a store or anywhere. Because they'll never recoup."
VanEmburgh said it makes sense to reduce that fee for the pilot program, though she said there probably should still be some fee.
The Town Council is expected to consider a pilot program proposal at a future meeting, potentially on Sept. 2.

title: Easton's Food Truck Rules Come Under Scrutiny
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton's food truck rules come under scrutiny

 August 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 677
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Residents and food truck owners are speaking out against Easton's rules on food trucks as the town has begun enforcing restrictions more closely.Trisha Wright and Daniel Reyes, owners of the Korean BBQ food truck T & D Fusions, say they had been setting up next to places like the Shore Medical Center and Kohl's before the crackdown this month.
Wright organized an online petition this week for the town to reconsider its limits on food trucks. As of Friday, it received over 3,000 signatures and widespread attention on social media.
"I just feel like we're being shafted because we're mobile," Wright said.
An ordinance on food trucks has been in effect since 2011. It states that mobile food businesses must operate in conjunction with an approved temporary use, such as a permitted festival or parade. Other town rules include:
Food trucks can operate on property owned by the food truck establishment itself, said Town Council President Don Abbatiello in an interview.Food trucks serving crews at active construction sites are exempt, per the 2011 ordinance.Food trucks can acquire a "transient business" license, per the
town charter
. Fees for the first two days are $500 each, and $150 for each day after up to a maximum 30 days.
Discourse online has especially centered on food trucks that had been setting up during lunch hours outside the hospital.
Food truck operators say they've heard from hospital employees who are upset the trucks are no longer there. Employees relied on them as an easy, accessible lunch option, said Mary Jo Flatten, owner of the lemonade bus Bravanson's Main Squeeze.
"They take care of us, so we should turn around and take care of them," Flatten said.
Shore Regional Health spokesperson Trena Williamson said in a statement the hospital complies with town zoning rules.
"We appreciate the interest from food truck vendors; the Town of Easton determines where they may operate and what zoning and permitting requirements they must follow," Williamson wrote.
The food truck debate is expected to come up at Monday's Town Council meeting. President Don Abbatiello said the council is considering both short- and long-term solutions.
"What we're gonna try to do is try to come up with something at the very least that would allow for food trucks to go back to the hospital area," Abbatiello said.
Further out, he believes there's a "desire on the council to have a real conversation" on the ordinance. Any major proposals will include ample time for public input, he said.
"We got to be fair to the restaurants and businesses that actually employ the folks that live here in town and pay taxes to help support town initiatives," Abbatiello said.
Abbatiello said he's unsure of exactly how consistently the town has enforced the 2011 ordinance. This summer, a restaurant raised the concern of food trucks operating in town limits, Abbatiello said. Town leaders declined to name the restaurant.
The recent enforcement has followed the "ordinance as it is written," Abbatiello said.
Wright said other areas have been more welcoming, such as Caroline County and Cambridge. But local food trucks are still pushing for change in Easton's regulations, she said.
"It does take effect on all of us, so we have to become one," Wright said. "We have to become stronger together."
As council members prepare to discuss the matter on Monday and food truck supporters organize to come out to the meeting, one local business is stepping in to fill the void.
KustomScapes & Pools owners Karen Glass and Jon Glass Sr. are scheduling a lineup of food trucks outside their business next week. The pool business sits off of Easton Parkway at the end of Route 662. Despite being surrounded by town land on all sides, the property itself is county land and not bound by Easton's food truck ordinance.
Karen Glass said they wanted to pull together as a community after hearing about the food truck controversy. They have trucks slated for almost every day next week and a coffee truck every other Friday, she said.
"This is what our community was built on," Jon Glass said. "The community supporting each other and small businesses supporting small businesses."

title: Easton Moves Forward with Campaign Finance Ordinance
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton moves forward with campaign finance ordinance

 August 6, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 431
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Three months after a heated municipal election, Easton leaders are advancing legislation to limit campaign contributions and add a number of new reporting measures for candidates.The Town Council has ironed out a drafted campaign finance ordinance. Council members wrapped up their proposed edits to the legislation Monday during the second of two workshops on the matter.
Ward 3 representative David Montgomery, who sponsored the ordinance alongside Mayor Megan Cook during the lead-up to May's election, says he's pleased with its status.
"I think there have been some very valuable comments," Montgomery said in an interview Tuesday. "So I'm very happy where the draft stands now."
Easton doesn't currently have any campaign finance-related laws in place, and financial disclosures submitted by candidates around the dates they file for candidacy don't offer specific details into campaign contributions. The matter raised debate during the election cycle in May, especially between current Council President Don Abbatiello and his predecessor, Frank Gunsallus.
The council is expected to decide on a public hearing date for the ordinance at its next meeting Aug. 18. That hearing will allow for more resident input before the legislation is eligible for a vote.
On Monday, Ward 4 representative the Rev. Elmer Davis asked for the council to take its time with the legislation.
"I don't want to rush into anything when we have time on our side," Davis said.
Here's a look at some of the specific rules candidates would have to follow if the ordinance passes:
Campaign contributions, except from spouses or domestic partners, would be limited to $1,000. Council increased the mark from $250 as originally proposed.Contributions from political committees and organizations would be prohibited. (Town elections are nonpartisan, though May's election raised questionsabout political party influence.)All candidates would need a treasurer.Treasurers would be required to submit regular campaign reports to the town office, beginning no later than two months prior to the election date.Campaign materials would have to include authority lines unless the town's election supervisor grants exemption.Candidates would not be allowed to accept more than $2,500 in loans during an election cycle.As drafted, the ordinance would also require persons, organizations and political committees to report election-related spending, even if independent of any candidates. Expenditures under $100 would not need to be reported to the town.On Monday, the council agreed to increase a 48-hour deadline for the reporting of independent expenditures to one week.Also at Monday's workshop, council amended the draft legislation to require that election winners pay any fines related to the campaign finance rules before being sworn in. A violation of the campaign finance ordinance would result in a $500 fine.

title: Talbot County Considering New Cannabis Legislation
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot County considering new cannabis legislation

 July 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 523
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Talbot County is reviewing regulations on cannabis operations, but drafted legislation drew concerns from prospective business owners at a recent meeting.As drafted, legislation would bar cannabis growing and processing operations from locating within 500 feet of residential properties. That mark could be reduced for a specific project only if all property owners within that radius agree.
At a County Council meeting on July 8, a public hearing on the legislation was opened, during which two state license holders raised concerns. Discussion centered on changing the 500-foot setback to 200 feet.
Dave Ferraris, winner of a cannabis-processing license from the Maryland Cannabis Administration, which are awarded via a lottery, said the proposed restrictions would be "detrimental."
"It's not the wild west," Ferraris said of cannabis operations. "It's agriculture with oversight."
Easton resident Lori Yates received a license for cultivation. She said on July 8 that passage of the county legislation would hinder her progress toward acquiring a property in Cordova, the now-closed Triple Creek Winery.
"It really would pull the rug out from us trying to work with the current owners," Yates said.
On the prospect of a 200-foot setback, Yates said she feels it would still allow for proper space "to have it off of the public access road."
Brennan Tarleton, the county's planning and zoning director, noted that in the original draft legislation, there's already a written-in opportunity to reduce the setback to 200 feet if the affected property owners agree. But he said moving the starting point down from 500 feet is a possibility.
"Two hundred feet isn't a pie-in-the-sky idea for a setback," Tarleton said.
If passed, the legislation would require processors and growers to obtain site plan approval from the county and operate on a lot of at least 20 acres. Additionally, operators must procure professional testimony that cannabis odor is not "detectible from adjacent properties or public rights-of-way."
Ferraris voiced opposition to the "no odors" regulation, citing it is too extreme of a rule.
"Talbot County will realistically and effectively be disqualified from participating in cannabis processing and growing endeavors," Ferraris said.
He added that prospective cannabis operators aren't looking to exploit the county. "We're not asking for a blank check. We're just asking for a fair chance," he said.
Tarleton noted the county mostly mirrored Easton's cannabis ordinance in regard to the odor requirement. He said Easton restricted to just indoor growing operations, though. Tarleton said council could consider exempting open-air growing operations from the "no odors" rule.
Talbot's draft cannabis legislation also lays out standards for cannabis dispensaries to follow, largely falling in line with the state's recent legislation effective in July, 2024.
Dispensaries cannot be located within 500 feet of schools, child care centers, playgrounds, recreation centers, libraries, public parks or places of worship. They also can't locate within 1,000 feet of one another; that standard is present in Easton town limits, too, and in one case created competition between businesses.
While Talbot County's potential regulations stick with the state, local jurisdictions are permitted under state law to change those distance requirements.
The county's cannabis legislation wasn't eligible for a vote on July 8. It may return to the council at its July 22 meeting or later in August.

title: When Easton Needed Him, Alan Lowrey Stepped Up as Interim Town Manager
author: Konner Metz
content:
When Easton needed him, Alan Lowrey stepped up as interim town manager

 July 11, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 861
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — It was shaping up to be a normal council meeting early last August for Easton Police Chief Alan Lowrey, until the mayor suddenly asked him a big question before the meeting started.The town had parted ways with former Town Manager Don Richardson on Aug. 5, 2024, and a stand-in was needed while the town conducted a search to find a permanent replacement. Mayor Megan Cook asked Lowrey if he would step in.
Back in his police uniform in his office on Thursday, Lowrey recalled knowing that if he assumed the interim role, it wouldn't just be a transition for the town and the police department. Things would change at home, too, with the high demands of both roles.
Lowrey talked to his wife, Michelle, before agreeing to become interim town manager. They have four kids, ages 15 to 19. Their love and respect for Easton — where they've lived since 2011 — played a role in saying yes.
"The town is really important to us," Lowrey said.
In the 11 months since, Lowrey was Easton's acting town manager, trading out his uniform for a suit and tie at council meetings. And even as new Town Manager Andy Kitzrow, who started Monday, takes over, Lowrey's helping with the transition process.
The police chief said it's been humbling to learn so much from the town's different departments. Whether it was absorbing new knowledge about stormwater management or crafting a $28 million budget, Lowrey said the job allowed him to grow closer with the department heads who carry out the town's important duties.
"We all want the same thing, a great Town of Easton," Lowrey said. "And to do that, it's helpful when we all pull together."
'TRUE PUBLIC SERVANT'
Easton's government has had its fair share of hot-button topics since last August. The town had to obligate its remaining pandemic-era funds by the end of 2024; a debate between a seafood processor and neighboring residents persisted for months; and Easton residents elected a new council president in a heated and politically contentious election cycle.
Cook said Lowrey was the perfect person for the interim role during such a busy time. She said he's capable of working with anyone.
"He's so calm," the mayor said in an interview last month. "He's genuine, he's sincere, he's easygoing. I can't say enough good things about him."
One of the most challenging tasks, Lowrey said, was creating a budget, a six-month process. He and Finance Officer Carol Callahan spearheaded efforts to execute the mayor's vision in creating the town's fiscal year 2026 budget.
The budget, touted by town leaders as "lean" amid the culmination of pandemic-era federal funding, was nearly even with the previous year, and it didn't raise property tax rates. Council unanimously approved the budget in May.
"It was a huge commitment. I know it took a toll on the police department, his family," Cook said of Lowrey. "It was a true sacrifice. What a public servant. True public servant."
EPD FORGES AHEAD
As Lowrey took on new responsibilities, so too did Deputy Chief Greg Wright, who became Easton's acting police chief as Lowrey shifted his focus to town government.
Wright had already served as interim chief for two months between former Chief David Spencer's retirement and Lowrey's appointment in 2022.
"I've always felt comfortable making the decisions that need to be made," said Wright, a nearly 40-year veteran of the department.
For Lowrey, since joining the Easton force as chief in 2022, Wright hasn't just been his deputy chief but a mentor and trusted colleague. Lowrey said the confidence in Wright to lead the police department made it easier to accept the temporary town manager job.
Wright, who began to sit in on town meetings as EPD's lead contact, said he now has a greater appreciation for town operations and the hard work of department heads and town employees. The solid relationship between the Town of Easton and the police department is better off, too, he noted.
"I think it makes us stronger," Wright said.
Cook said that when asking Lowrey to step in, she knew the strong leadership of Wright and other officers would come in handy.
"(Lowrey) has tremendous staff in the police department that would help carry the load of the department in his absence," Cook said.
"They both knew that it was for the betterment of the town," Town Council President Don Abbatiello said of the two police leaders. "... The town owes a debt of gratitude to the both of them."
Easton Town Council members thanked Lowrey on Monday for stepping up when the town needed it.
"You have just done an absolutely spectacular job, as well as keeping on top of your police force," Ward 3 representative David Montgomery said.
Abbatiello said in an interview Friday that Lowrey's leadership abilities were key.
"He's phenomenal at bringing people together to tackle challenges," Abbatiello said.
The town will be in good hands with Kitzrow, Lowrey said, emphasizing that the former Salisbury city administrator brings a "fresh perspective" that can be beneficial.
"He knows more about being a town manager than I will ever know," Lowrey said.
And for Lowrey himself, he's excited to be back at the Easton Police Department full-time, surrounded by the police officers and staff he loves.
"This is where my heart is," Lowrey said.

title: Oxford Commissioners Test the Dignity Index
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Oxford commissioners test the dignity index

 July 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 266
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — Oxford Town Commissioners are discussing implementing a new system of dignity and respect among the council members called the Dignity Index.The Dignity Index is a scale from 1-8 that aims to ease divisions, prevent violence and solve problems, according to the website.
One is the lowest end of the dignity scale and states: "they're not even human. It's our moral duty to destroy them before they destroy us." Eight is the highest end and states: "each of us is born with inherent worth, so we treat everyone with dignity — no matter what."
The index was introduced to commissioners at the Maryland Municipal League summer conference in mid June.
"Holly, Katrina and I heard about it at MML, and all three of us said, 'That's a ... good idea,'" Commissioner Norm Bell said.
The goal of the index is to build better communication skills and maintain respect during disagreements. To build these skills and go from a one to an eight, the index provides ways to have "dignified disagreements."
To have dignified disagreements, the index suggests the following:
To build up rather than tear down.Acknowledge others' points.To challenge ideas without attacking people.By listening to understand rather than listening to respond.By regulating your emotions before a debate.To approach disagreements with curiosity and language that opens dialogue.
"Norm and I want to talk about doing what Holly does, which is treating everyone with dignity and explaining things," Commission President Katrina Greer said.
Bell said commissioners are discussing implementing the system among themselves first, and if that is successful, they will implement it with town staff as well.
"And then maybe beyond that," Bell said.

title: 'Proven Leader': Easton Will Soon Welcome Kitzrow as New Town Manager
author: Konner Metz
content:
'Proven leader': Easton will soon welcome Kitzrow as new town manager

 June 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 740
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — After nearly a year without a permanent town manager, Easton will welcome Andy Kitzrow next month.Kitzrow, the current Salisbury city administrator, was tapped by Mayor Megan Cook to assume the post from Police Chief Alan Lowrey, the interim town manager since August. Kitzrow begins July 7.
During an interview in Salisbury last week, Kitzrow said he instantly noticed opportunity in Easton.
"The more I looked at Easton, the more I started to fall in love with where they're going," Kitzrow said.
The new town manager is Cook's most major appointment in her two years as mayor. Kitzrow will oversee town operations, lead department heads and town staff, and be a point of contact with the mayor and Town Council members.
After whittling down a list of around 12 semifinalists, the town conducted full-day interviews with four finalists. It was an intensive but worthwhile process, Cook said.
She felt Kitzrow rose above the others, as he was up to speed on what's happening in Easton and meshed well with her and with town employees.
"(Staff) really thought of the candidates, he could get up and running the fastest because he had the background of Maryland politics," Cook said.
Kitzrow, 42, served as Wicomico County recreation superintendent before becoming Salisbury's deputy city administrator in 2017 and city administrator in 2023.
In Salisbury, Kitzrow worked under three different mayors, including Jake Day, now the Department of Housing and Community Development secretary. Day noted Kitzrow's oversight of city permit and procurement operations as especially impactful.
"It's not easy work, but he's a proven leader," Day said of Kitzrow. "Somebody who can do it."
Cook says while the Day connection didn't factor into her decision, it will benefit Easton as the town tackles its own housing challenges and initiatives.
"Having that relationship, I think, is great. It's key," Kitzrow said. "A lot of this is about relationships, whether they are elected officials or state officials."
A BETTER FIT
Working under three different mayors, Kitzrow says he's experienced three very different visions.
In early 2023, Day left Salisbury with then-city administrator Julia Glanz to head up the state's housing and community development efforts. Jack Heath served as mayor until current Mayor Randy Taylor won an election later that year.
During Day's tenure, Salisbury undertook a number of efforts to redevelop its downtown through programs providing tax incentives to developers, such as "Here is Home" and HORIZON — the latter aimed at bringing multifamily residential and hotel units, an initiative which Kitzrow championed.
"(He was) the mastermind behind the HORIZON legislation that we passed locally," Glanz said.
Taylor and developers have clashed in recent months over the stalling of downtown projects, some of which were approved by former mayors and councils. In April, DelmarvaNow.com reported that developers of a downtown project filed a $40 million lawsuit against Salisbury and Taylor.
While Kitzrow believes the change in vision is OK and can be solved through compromise, he acknowledges it factored into his choice to accept the Easton post. Neither Taylor nor Heath could be reached for an interview.
"Professionally and personally, the town that Megan wants to run and her goals align more with what I value and what I want to be part of," Kitzrow said.
GOALS IN EASTON
Salisbury's population is nearly double Easton's, but Kitzrow sees similar challenges and opportunities in the two areas.
He said he wants to "move projects forward in a smart way." In Salisbury, he's dealt with a housing pipeline of around 5,000 units and led a focus on building "from the inside out." Easton's pipeline has recently hovered around 1,000 units.
Kitzrow is hoping to bring a focus to Easton's Rails to Trails network, given his parks and recreation background, as well as get "under the hood" in the human resources department.
Cook said she's excited to bring on a consistent leader during what she says has been a year full of change in town. "I'm looking forward to a steady ship ... and some calm seas ahead," Cook said.
Working for the mayor, Kitzrow emphasized that strong relationships with the Town Council will be crucial in completing the work that will make Easton a better place.
"We are working together, not against each other, and I think that's important," Kitzrow said.
Kitzrow will remain living in Salisbury with his wife and kids. He owns Escape Salisbury, a downtown escape room business.
But he's looking to learn as much about Easton as possible. He said he's especially excited to meet business owners, nonprofit leaders and community members in his first 60 days on the job.

title: Easton Council Maintains Seafood Odor Ordinance, Rejects Amendment
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton council maintains seafood odor ordinance, rejects amendment

 June 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 678
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Easton Town Council on Monday rejected a proposal to relax language in a seafood odor ordinance that has been a topic of contention between residents and a local business for much of the last year.In a 4-1 decision, with council member Maureen Curry the lone yes, the council voted down an amendment proposed to change the wording of the odor law that takes effect July 1.
The town's ordinance, passed back in December, is meant to address resident complaints of odor from Chesapeake Brand Seafood on Maryland Avenue, a crab processing facility near many homes. Per the ordinance, the business must install odor control technology and do so "in such a manner that no odor ... can be detected."
While attorney Zach Smith said Monday that an odor control system was recently installed, he appealed to the council to accept the amendment. Smith and Chesapeake Brand Seafood owner Mitch Hughes have said the "no odor" standard is unachievable, citing industry experts. They've expressed concern that once the ordinance goes into effect, further complaints could leave them out of compliance and force them to close the business.
Ward 2 representative Robert Rankin visited the business last week and said on one hand, he's "optimistic and hopeful" the new odor system will address the residents' complaints.
"On the other hand, it just being installed over the weekend, it doesn't give a lot of time to measure success," Rankin said.
Ward 4 representative the Rev. Elmer Davis said it's a "wait-and-see" approach. "We may have to look at our (original ordinance) and make sure that it has teeth," he said.
Ward 3's David Montgomery said he wished there was a more obvious correct decision. He said the focus will turn to town code enforcement on how future complaints or violations are dealt with.
During more than 40 minutes of public comment on the topic, multiple residents said the smell hasn't gone away since the system was installed. A Chesapeake Brand employee noted the system may take some time to be fully dialed in.
Those who spoke included family and friends of Hughes or local watermen. Some criticized the town for issuing the restrictions targeted toward Chesapeake Brand, a business that was legally permitted by the town and opened in 2019.
"There's been a negative portrayal of my cousin in the paper and on social media when in fact it should be the town that is to blame for all of this drama," said Kim Gibbons-Neff, Hughes' cousin.
"The town should have nipped this in the bud after the initial complaints and told the residents that the business is in compliance and they are doing nothing wrong," she added.
Local business owner Donna Bramble said the town could be losing trust with small businesses.
"As a business owner, how can small businesses trust the Town of Easton if you issue a permit, they put the expense in of starting their business, and then because there's a complaint, you force them to move?" Bramble asked. "And that's really what's happening. You're going to force Mitch to close up and move."
Peter Maloney, one of the residents who's led calls for reduced odor from the business, said residents don't have anything against Hughes or small businesses.
"They got a legal permit to be there. And that is a question you all need to ask, as to why that legal permit was given," Maloney said toward the council. "But that doesn't mean that they should be there."
Smith, the attorney, warned the council that its "authority here is not limitless."
"While the town can certainly adopt new standards to some extent, you can't adopt standards that are going to preclude him from continuing to operate his business," Smith said.
Following the public hearing and vote, council President Don Abbatiello said people on both sides made valid points and that it wasn't an easy decision to reject the business' amendment.
"But at the end, at least for myself, it's responsibility to represent the residents," Abbatiello said. "And my hope is that going forward, this mitigation process will work, and the facility will be able to stay there and be successful."

title: St. Michaels Suspends Zoom Meetings After 2nd Security Incident This Year
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
St. Michaels suspends Zoom meetings after 2nd security incident this year

 June 10, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 341
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — St. Michaels commissioners announced live Zoom meetings for the town government would be "discontinued for the foreseeable future" after second security incident in 2025.Both incidents involved disruptions caused by meeting attendees, town officials said.
"Both the February and June incidents were the same or similar with intentions of disrupting the open format forum," Town Manager Don Richardson said in a email to the Star Democrat on Tuesday. "A Zoom attendee took control of the screen and displaying an indecent video clip along with hate text. They also took control of audio playing loud sounds and noises. Staff caught this quickly, shut down the online display, and the Historic District Commission completed the meeting as schedule.
"On Friday, the town issued the Constant Contact to notify the public that meeting participation would be changing to keep our town meeting safe and accessible."
The announcement came after the June 5 meeting, where the Zoom feed was interrupted. Commissioners President Alfred Mercier described the contents of the video displayed by the person disrupting the meeting as "propaganda associated with foreign countries and explicit graphic presentations of individuals."
"This came with a lot of thought because we certainly want full transparency in what we present and how we present to the town, and we certainly want to be cognizant of the fact that everything that we present and the information that we display out there needs to be communicated effectively to our to our residents," Mercier said to the Star Democrat on Tuesday.
St. Michaels is not the only town that have stopped Zoom meetings, the Town of Greensboro also stopped recording meetings via Zoom after an incident in February.
"These graphic obscenities that have have been occurring not only in St. Michaels, but in many towns throughout the U.S., have presented a challenge for a lot of these towns," Mercier said.
St. Michaels plans to record the meetings as they occur and to have a question and answer session for residents to ask questions. Town officials are currently looking for more secure softwares to conduct town meetings.

title: Talbot County Removes DEI Statement Amid Funding Concerns for Airport
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot County removes DEI statement amid funding concerns for airport

 June 10, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 752
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Talbot County Council voted Tuesday to remove the diversity, equity and inclusion statement from the county's employee handbook, reversing course from March, when the council upheld the diversity statement.Tuesday's decision came amid concerns for millions of dollars in federal funding for an ongoing Easton Airport project. Those worries stem from an April directive from U.S. Department of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy outlining the Trump administration's view that DEI programs violate federal law.
Council Vice President Pete Lesher and council member Dave Stepp sponsored Tuesday's resolution, which passed 4-1 with council member Keasha Haythe opposing. Haythe, Lesher and council member Lynn Mielke had voted down Stepp's attempt to remove the DEI statement in March.
Lesher, a Democrat, said it was a difficult decision, noting he changed his tune on the measure due to a "vindictive and maleficent federal administration."
"The risk is that some incompetent political appointee will read only the title of our statement, misconstrue it as an illegal policy and deny a federal grant on that basis," Lesher said. "In an event like that, even if we win on appeal, it could leave us in a state of construction limbo for an unacceptably long time."
Lesher added, "We simply need to ensure that we are using none of the language that could trigger some snowflake in Washington."
Mielke, a Republican, said she agreed with Lesher and that Talbot County has always been a merit-based employer.
Stepp, a Republican, said council members "fell short" and put the county in a vulnerable spot when they rejected his original proposal in March.
"It's very frustrating that we even need to be discussing this here today. It should've been dealt with months ago," Stepp said. "This matter has been highly politicized and turned into something it is not."
"Today's action is fiscal in nature," he added.
Council President Chuck Callahan, a Republican, voted to remove the statement in March and did so again Tuesday. He said the controversial topic — which garnered strong resident opposition and led to two heated meetings — has been "tough on council."
"I know we all have our own beliefs, one way or the other with the DEI stuff," Callahan said. "But at this time I think we've made the right decision and the right statement."
Haythe, the council's only non-white member and a Democrat, asked county attorney Patrick Thomas about an opinion letter he provided on the DEI statement and Duffy's directive. Duffy's directive to all DOT funding recipients referenced the U.S. Supreme Court's 2023 rejection of affirmative action programs at Harvard University.
"I do not believe that the statement is discriminatory, and I do not believe that the Supreme Court (case) being referenced in the secretary of transportation letter applies to that statement," Thomas said.
Tuesday's resolution, effectively immediately, voids Talbot County's DEI statement. Two 2020 diversity resolutions are also "of no further force and effect," according to the newly approved resolution.
Those resolutions had facilitated the creation of the diversity statement and required the county manager to provide an annual diversity training report to the council, respectively.
The new resolution states nothing in it "shall be construed as a repudiation of the intent and desire" of the county to ensure a "welcoming workplace" in which employees are treated fairly based on race, sex, national origin, etc.
Lesher asked county staff to work on a "replacement welcoming statement" for the county's employee handbook.
AIRPORT PROJECT
Easton Airport's ongoing modernization project — which will relocate and expand the airport's main runway — is 90% funded by the Federal Aviation Administration, an organization within the Department of Transportation. The airport is owned and operated by Talbot County.
Airport Manager Micah Risher said he consulted with county staff after the April DOT letter. In an interview Tuesday, Risher said he has "absolute faith" in the council's support of the airport. Risher added that the airport ensures it is always abiding by federal and state laws.
"To have Easton Airport have any sort of funding at jeopardy, it's a bigger deal than the average person may think," Risher said, citing the airport's large economic impact on the community.
According to Risher, the airport received around $17 million from the FAA for the first two phases of the project. Estimates on the remaining federal funding for the rest of the project aren't available since bids are out, he said, but over $30 million of work remains.
"We're up here against our greatest milestone that is really going to ensure that we have a viable airport, and this great economic engine, succeed here in Talbot County for another 80-plus years," he said.

title: Talbot County to Revisit Removing DEI Statement with Airport's Federal Funding at Risk
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot County to revisit removing DEI statement with airport's federal funding at risk

 June 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 635
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Talbot County Council will revisit the prospect of removing its diversity, equity and inclusion statement amid concerns for Easton Airport's federal funding.Though voted down in March, a resolution to remove the diversity statement found in the county's employee handbook is on the agenda for Tuesday's council meeting. Its reappearance is fueled by a directive from U.S. Department of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy that could put millions of dollars for an ongoing Easton Airport project at risk, council members say.
The diversity statement — created after the passage of a 2020 resolution — defines diversity, equity and inclusion, explains its purpose and details the county's approach to ensuring diversity. It also outlines how employees can report discrimination.
In an April 24 letter, Duffy outlined the department's interpretation of federal law, including regarding DEI.
"Whether or not described in neutral terms, any policy, program, or activity that is premised on a prohibited classification, including discriminatory policies or practices designed to achieve socalled 'diversity, equity, and inclusion,' or 'DEI,' goals, presumptively violates Federal law," Duffy wrote.
Duffy wrote that noncompliance with federal law or "failure to cooperate" with federal agencies "could lead to a loss of Federal funding from DOT."
Easton Airport's ongoing modernization project — which will relocate and expand the airport's main runway — is 90% funded by the Federal Aviation Administration, an organization within DOT. The airport is owned and operated by Talbot County.
The resolution to remove Talbot County's DEI statement was initially proposed by council member Dave Stepp in February. It elicited strong resident opposition, stirred two heated council meetings and split the five-member council.
The council rejected the statement's removal in March by a 3-2 vote: President Chuck Callahan joined Stepp, while Vice President Pete Lesher and council members Keasha Haythe and Lynn Mielke opposed.
But now, Stepp and Lesher are sponsoring the resolution's reappearance after working together to tweak it given the recent DOT directive. Lesher said he supports it "without enthusiasm."
"The two of us came together, knowing that we are coming at this from different points of view," Lesher said in an interview Monday.
They both say passing the resolution will protect essential federal funds for the Easton Airport's modernization project. Stepp said $46.8 million is at risk.
"I think that folks didn't think this was real prior," Stepp said of the funding risks. "And they certainly will now."
Lesher said he's confident the county isn't violating what the Trump administration and DOT are targeting. But merely having the DEI statement, he said, could lead to blowback from what he called a "capriciously" acting administration.
"Does this feel like extortion? Yes," Lesher said. "We have to choose our battles. And I believe that what we are giving up here is important for appearances, but it is not substantive. We are not changing any policies in Talbot County by issuing this new administrative resolution."
The two sponsors of Tuesday's resolution offered slightly different interpretations of what it will do if passed.
Lesher said it would supersede the 2020 resolution and either lead to the removal or revision of the DEI statement so that it doesn't "presumptively violate" Duffy's directive.
Council can't "un-direct" staff to create the statement, Lesher said. Instead, he said, the resolution serves as "fresh direction."
Stepp, meanwhile, indicated the measure would completely repeal the 2020 resolution and remove the DEI statement, which is how the resolution was initially presented when it failed.
"It was fiscal responsibility then, and it's fiscal responsibility now," Stepp said.
The updated resolution will be read aloud Tuesday and potentially voted on. Lesher and Stepp both say they expect it to pass.
"We cannot afford to put the airport funding at risk," Lesher said. "It just would leave us in the middle of a project. It would really leave us in a lurch."
The Talbot County Council meets at 5 p.m. Tuesday in the Talbot County Courthouse Bradley Meeting Room.

title: Easton Council Members Hesitant to Change Seafood Odor Ordinance
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton council members hesitant to change seafood odor ordinance

 June 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 642
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Easton Town Council members indicated Monday that they were leaning toward rejecting a debated amendment to the town's seafood odor ordinance, though there was no vote to put the issue to bed.The council's final vote on the amendment could take place at its June 16 meeting, ending months of discussion on the matter.
Passed by the Easton Town Council in December, the ordinance came after repeated odor complaints from residents living near Chesapeake Brand Seafood, a wholesale crab processor on Maryland Avenue. The law is set to take effect July 1.
The legislation requires that the business install odor control technology and do so "in such a manner that no odor ... can be detected" — or, in other words, "effectively eliminate outdoor odors."
Chesapeake Brand Seafood owner Mitch Hughes and his attorney requested the amendment to the ordinance, citing the "no odor" requirement as unachievable per industry experts.
Last month, the Planning Commission voted against Chesapeake Brand's proposed amendment. But the commission wasn't sold on the council's original ordinance, either. In a formal recommendation, commission members advised the council to find a more enforceable and achievable standard.
On Monday, the Town Council discussed but didn't take official action on that recommendation. Council members largely leaned away from changing the soon-to-be effective ordinance.
"If we move this to something else, then we're not going to get anything resolved," said Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis.
Davis represents many of the neighboring residents and has consistently advocated for the placement of odor requirements on the business. He said Monday the issue "needs to be dealt with yesterday."
Ward 2 representative Robert Rankin said he understands Chesapeake Brand — which opened in 2019 under a town permit — is simply a business trying to operate. But he said it's "unclear" if the business is ready to address its odor issue.
"I don't see a reason to change what's in place at this point," Rankin said.
Hughes has said he's ready to install odor control technology but is holding off since he doesn't want to foot monthly costs if the odor system won't end up meeting the ordinance's requirements.
"They all said we can install a system and get your odor down," Hughes said in an interview last month. "But there's no way you can reach zero odor."
The Planning Commission specifically recommended the Town Council alter language in the ordinance so it requires the business to "effectively mitigate" odors instead of "effectively eliminate" them. Town planners say it's consistent with odor reduction language used by the Environmental Protection Agency.
Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery said he didn't like the proposed change to "mitigate."
"It simply introduces a more ambiguous word for a clear one," he said.
The ordinance has brought mixed public reaction. A handful of residents and some seafood industry leaders spoke at the recent Planning Commission meeting, urging the town not to drive Chesapeake Brand away.
"Mitch got a permit," Donna Bramble said May 15. "He did not hide what kind of business he was having. He told you what it was going to be. It's a signed, legal document, and now the town is trying to take that away."
Meanwhile, neighbors concerned with the odors appealed Monday for the council to retain the legislation as passed.
"This is law," Peter Maloney said, adding concerns about the proposed amendment. "Are we allowing businesses to write law for us? That whole piece of this irks me."
After public comment, Ward 1 representative Maureen Curry said the council won't leave residents hanging.
"You guys (are) worth a lot more to us than Chesapeake Brand," Curry said. "And you've been there longer, and all we want is for him to be a good neighbor. And we're going to hold his feet to the fire."
Though the Planning Commission recommended against the seafood odor amendment, the council still has final say. A public hearing will take place before the potential vote June 16.

title: St. Michaels Commissioners Pass Ordinance on Leaf Blowers
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
St. Michaels commissioners pass ordinance on leaf blowers

 April 25, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 323
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — After a five-year discussion on leaf blowers, the Commissioners of St. Michaels passed an ordinance limiting contractors' use of leaf blowers to certain times and days.Contractors can use leaf blowers from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Mondays through Fridays. The use of leaf blowers on Saturdays, Sundays and federal holidays is now prohibited for contractors.
The ordinance does not apply to residents of St. Michaels. Homeowners working on their own property are allowed to use leaf blowers and other loud equipment from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. Monday through Friday and 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. Saturday and Sunday under town code.
"I'm really happy that the commercial contractors as well as the residents were able to come up with the resolution," Alfred Mercier, commission president, said.
The discussion around leaf blowers has reared its head several times since 2020. It was brought up for consideration in 2023 and again on Jan. 22 of this year.
The discussion Jan. 22 was about whether the town should only allow electric leaf blowers, which make less noise than gasoline-powered leaf blowers. The commissioners ultimately decided not to include language on gas or electric leaf blowers in the ordinance passed Wednesday.
Contractors and St. Michaels public works officials argued gas leaf blowers make their jobs easier. Electric or battery-powered leaf blowers must be charged, which takes time. They also argued that gas-powered leaf blowers are more powerful and help them accomplish their jobs faster.
"We thought it was a very tremendous burden for contractors to go totally out to electric leaf blowers," Mercier said. "So instead of doing that, we put time limitations and also the fact that they will not be able to do any work on weekends now.
"During the week, we lessened the time by an hour each day," he continued. "So we're hoping that will appease a lot of the residents and obviously create a more quiet neighborhood for them, especially on the weekends."
