title: Easton Council Rejects Gunsallus' Proposal to Delay Introduction of Campaign Finance Law
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton council rejects Gunsallus' proposal to delay introduction of campaign finance law

 April 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 784
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Town Council members held a heated discussion Monday on a proposed ordinance mandating campaign finance reporting in town elections.Before the opening Pledge of Allegiance and prayer, council President Frank Gunsallus moved to remove the campaign finance law's introduction from Monday's meeting agenda.
Gunsallus said the law shouldn't be introduced due to current conflicts of interest existing with the town's upcoming election.
Mayor Megan Cook and Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery announced their sponsorship of the ordinance last week. It comes as the town's May 6 election nears, with Gunsallus facing off against current Ward 2 representative Don Abbatiello in an increasingly heated race. Montgomery, along with Ward 1's Maureen Curry, have publicly endorsed Abbatiello.
On Monday, Gunsallus read a letter he sent to the Attorney General's Office, requesting guidance for how to proceed with the ordinance that he called "retroactive."
Montgomery and town attorney Sharon VanEmburgh, who drafted the ordinance, said the ordinance would not retroactively apply to the May 6 election.
"This won't apply to this election," VanEmburgh said. "If you're thinking about a conflict, there will always be a conflict for all five of you because you will all at some point potentially be running for reelection. This is for a future election."
Gunsallus said he didn't feel comfortable discussing the ordinance without clarification from the attorney general. VanEmburgh said the attorney general has no authority over the town election, later adding it's unlikely the attorney general will offer an official opinion to Gunsallus' request.
When Gunsallus said he would not entertain the ordinance as an agenda item, Montgomery moved to overrule him and was joined by the remaining three council members.
"All we're saying is that we want to move forward with (the ordinance) at a first reading," Curry said.
THE ORDINANCE
As drafted, the ordinance would require candidates to have a treasurer file campaign contribution reports to the town before and after the election. It would also set a maximum $250 contribution limit for all individuals, businesses and organizations, excluding the candidate and their spouse or partner.
Councilmembers shared mixed thoughts.
Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis said it's a "good starting point" but emphasized it needs to use "inclusive language."
Curry said, "not everyone has a spouse" and asked if the limits would apply to other family members. VanEmburgh said as written, other family members would need to adhere to the $250 cap.
Council members agreed to further discuss the ordinance at a workshop May 19. Residents, though, were more steadfast in their concerns during a heated public comment session.
Resident Daniel McBride said the $250 limit "seems a bit arbitrary" and "serves as a barrier to free expression of town voters." McBride and other residents said it would put grassroots or less wealthy candidates at a disadvantage.
Residents also questioned Montgomery and Cook for introducing the ordinance so soon before next month's election, with some labeling it election interference and an attack on Gunsallus' campaign.
"I believe it was done to try to destroy one of the members of the council," Catherine Nobles said.
CAMPAIGN DONATIONS
At the onset of Monday's meeting, Gunsallus asked the council to "follow my lead by disclosing your campaign finances ... with the state." He has been reporting online through the Maryland Campaign Reporting Information System each January since he was elected.
In the system, the most recent filing from the Friends of Frank Gunsallus shows campaign finances from Jan. 11, 2024 through Jan. 8, 2025.
Montgomery encouraged Gunsallus to report finances from his ongoing campaign.
"I do not understand how you can claim that you have revealed your campaign expenditures in the state when there's nothing there," Montgomery said.
Gunsallus said Monday that transparency is "paramount" and he will continue reporting through the state next January. Tuesday, Gunsallus told The Star Democrat that he's received approximately $16,000 in campaign contributions from 34 donors.
Abbatiello sent a log of campaign donations to the town office Monday.
From Dec. 29, 2024, through Monday, Abbatiello has brought in just over $13,000. More than 70 individual donors are listed, though Abbatiello said he's not releasing their specific donation amounts since "many people donated believing their names and donations would not end up on a list or scrutinized by the public."
"I also think that what's more important than the dollar amount, is that with only a few exceptions, the donors live in Easton," Abbatiello wrote in an email to The Star Democrat. "I'm also not taking any money from a political party or any group with a special interest in town."
In an interview with The Star Democrat's editorial board Tuesday, Gunsallus said the proposed campaign finance ordinance is "nonsensical" and that the town could instead fall in line with state law regarding campaign finance disclosures.
"We don't have to have political theater as we witnessed last night," Gunsallus said.

title: Frank Gunsallus
author: Konner Metz
content:
Frank Gunsallus

 April 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Frank Gunsallus

 Read News Document

 Email: fgunsallus@eastonmd.govAge: 36
Family: Wife, Iryna, and daughter, Maria.
Education: Salisbury University and Easton High School
Occupation: Account Manager
Previous political experience: Current Easton Town Council President since 2023. Served on the Talbot County Chamber of Commerce Government Affairs Committee and Mid-Shore Board of Realtors Government Affairs Committee
1. Why are you running for Easton Town Council president?
My core reason for seeking reelection as Easton Town Council president is my inherent and unwavering dedication to serving the community. I believe service to one's fellow citizens is an exceptionally important calling and a fundamental responsibility to make a positive difference.
I am running for reelection because Easton is at a critical point. We are facing serious decisions about housing, growth, infrastructure and public safety that will impact our town's future. I've served the council with a focus on results, not rhetoric. I will continue to provide steady, common-sense leadership that respects the taxpayer, protects our neighborhoods and moves Easton forward.
2. What issues will you prioritize if elected?
I will prioritize four primary issues: defeating the proposed inclusionary zoning ordinance, enhancing public safety, improving infrastructure and increasing government transparency.
The inclusionary zoning ordinance would drive up costs for home builders, discourage investment in our community and negatively impact home values.
I will ensure the police and fire departments receive the necessary funding and support to effectively serve the community.
As we see more development, we need to consider investing in areas like roads, utilities and stormwater management to improve infrastructure.
We must ensure Easton's residents have an in-depth understanding of issues and proposals and why decisions are reached. I will strongly encourage more direct community engagement.
3. While the town has grown, affordable housing remains a challenge for residents. How should the town build more housing, in particular affordable housing?
Inclusionary zoning is not the answer. It restricts supply and raises costs for builders and homebuyers through the redistribution of losses imposed on market-rate units to offset the cost of below-market rate requirements.
Over time this type of legislation can create a deflationary effect, reducing the market value of comparable homes. The town should instead encourage workforce housing by streamlining permitting, offering targeted incentives and considering the removal or deferral of upfront costs when specific housing products are being delivered. I served on the Attainable Housing Task Force, and there are more effective ways to expand workforce housing by collaborating with private and nonprofit partners — without penalizing those who already live here.
4. The town has seen increased development in its downtown core as well as on Route 50. How should the town prepare for the impacts of such growth?
We need to get ahead of the growth, not react to it after the fact. That starts with infrastructure: roads, traffic flow, sewer capacity and stormwater systems all need investment. We also need to be clear-eyed about the fiscal impact of development and make sure projects pay their fair share toward the infrastructure they require. Growth must be managed, which includes enforcing our comprehensive plan and making sure development fits the character and capacity of the area.
5. What are your plans for public safety in Easton? What can be improved?
Public safety is non-negotiable. As Easton grows, the demands on our police and volunteer fire departments grow too. We need to ensure these departments are fully staffed, have modern equipment and receive the training they need. I support data-driven policing and community-based approaches, but that only works if the departments are adequately resourced.
I will lead efforts to explore various options to support our first responders financially, including improving retirement benefits for our public safety personnel by increasing contribution percentages or by exploring enrollment in alternative programs such as Law Enforcement Officers' Pension System, which could strengthen lateral recruitment efforts.
6. What have you accomplished during your time on the council thus far? How will you seek to continue those efforts?
I've supported freedom, family values, public safety, key infrastructure investments and capital improvements. I've worked to improve communication between the town and residents. I've advocated for fiscal responsibility and accountability. I led the effort for the council to formally oppose a bill that would restrict the abilities of law enforcement agencies. I testified publicly in Annapolis against tax increases. I took the initiative to rewrite the council's rules and procedures.
I'll continue asking questions, doing research and making decisions based on what's best for Easton. My primary focus remains on the four items I have prioritized herein and on delivering the best results for the people of Easton.

title: DON ABBATIELLO
author: Konner Metz
content:
DON ABBATIELLO

Education: Bachelor's degree in education from Salisbury University, masters degree in history from Salisbury University
Occupation: Public school teacher for 27 years
Previous political experience: Six years as Easton Town Council Ward 2 representative
1. Why are you running for Easton Town Council president?
I'm running for council president because elections should be about options, not just be a coronation. It's important to offer voters a choice.
I want to bring a collaborative, consensus-building leadership style to the council and to be a leader who listens. Good leadership is about teamwork — no matter how strong your ideas are, they won't move forward without support from your fellow council members. I believe I can lead with respect and cooperation to help guide thoughtful decisions that reflect the needs of our residents.
2. What issues will you prioritize if elected?
My priorities are smart development, public safety and fiscal responsibility. Easton is growing fast, and we need to manage that growth and avoid unnecessary development.
I support limiting annexation until we ensure infrastructure can support our current development. For large redevelopment projects, the Town Council needs to be included in the decision making.
I'll prioritize support for our police and fire departments — funding, staffing and equipment must be maintained to support first-class service. Health care access is another major concern. I want to work with medical partners to attract more doctors.
I will ensure we continue balanced budgets, prioritizing services residents rely on without wasting taxpayers' money.
3. While the town has grown, affordable housing remains a challenge for residents. How should the town build more housing, in particular affordable housing?
There's no one-size-fits-all solution to affordable housing, but we must be proactive. I'd work closely with partners like the Affordable Housing Board and Habitat for Humanity to explore opportunities for creating starter homes. Zoning tools, incentives for developers and creative use of town-owned properties could also play a role. We need to support a mix of housing types to serve working families, young professionals and seniors. It's important to balance affordability with quality in the community.
4. The town has seen increased development in its downtown core as well as on Route 50. How should the town prepare for the impacts of such growth?
To prepare for Easton's growth, we need a strong, forward-thinking plan that addresses traffic, infrastructure and public services. New development should not outpace our ability to support it. Council members must be actively involved in major project decisions, particularly those with large impacts. Developers should be responsible for mitigating traffic and parking issues their projects may cause. Infrastructure improvements should be timed with development, not after. Transparency, community input and smart land-use policies are key to guiding growth in a way that keeps Easton a livable, vibrant town and preserves our way of life.
5. What are your plans for public safety in Easton? What can be improved?
Strong public safety services are essential to maintaining Easton as a safe and welcoming place for families, businesses and visitors.
I support increasing the presence of police on the rail trails, in parks and at community events to ensure safety and visibility. I support expanding our public camera system to deter crime and aid investigations. Our police need competitive benefits, including improved pensions, to attract and retain top talent.
Our volunteer fire department needs to be supported with the best equipment. I'm incredibly proud of the Easton Volunteer Fire Department's regional training campus that will better prepare our emergency responders and reduce training costs.
6. What have you accomplished during your time on the council thus far? How will you seek to continue those efforts?
During my time on the council, I've supported initiatives that improve quality of life and promote responsible government. I've worked to expand walkability, including sidewalk and crosswalk improvements. I've brought new playgrounds and improved old ones in my ward. We've passed balanced budgets every year without raising the property tax rate. I helped implement the take-home car program for Easton Police, an important recruitment and retention tool. I've focused on community-based policies that are practical and sustainable.

After the end of my terms of service on the Easton Town Council, residents of our community continued to call upon me to help resolve issues. In February, I was called because tenants had been unceremoniously evicted from their rental home without a shred of due process under law. I was more than bothered. Address lack of housing for all ages and income brackets.Reexamine the criteria for infill development, including provisions for green space.Work on economic development, particularly on bringing in jobs and business opportunities that are sustainable in this community. Young people need a good wage earning opportunity to consider living here long term.Conduct a feasibility study to determine if the existing hospital campus on Washington Street can be refurbished for veterans.Conduct a feasibility study for the former health department site for use as heritage tourism attraction.Explore how the town can prepare to help citizens impacted by potential shortfalls in Medicare and social security, as well as food insecurity.

title: Commissioners of Oxford Table Voting Resolution
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Commissioners of Oxford table voting resolution

 March 13, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 426
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — Although at the start of a Commissioners of Oxford discussion Tuesday Commission President Norm Bell recommended the commissioners vote that evening on a resolution to clarify the town's voting registration requirements, the commissioners tabled the resolution in a two to one vote."In order to get this right, I think we need more time," Commissioner Katrina Greer said. "I think it would be better to do nothing and write some rules for the election committee, which we can do without a charter change."
The now tabled resolution would amend the town's charter to clarify a person must register with the Talbot County Board of Elections to qualify as a voter in the town. This means a resident would not be able to vote in Oxford town elections if they aren't registered with the county board.
Before the vote was taken, Bell expressed concern that if the resolution is not voted on at the meeting, it could be delayed to the point where, if the resolution is passed, it is not in effect for the town's upcoming election in June when Commissioner Tom Costigan's term is set to expire.
But Bell, who ultimately voted in favor of tabling the resolution, acknowledged the commissioners should not rush into making amendments to the charter regarding voting.
At a public hearing for the resolution Feb. 25, residents shared thoughts on who should and shouldn't be considered eligible to vote in town elections. The discussion, which opened the doors to potential additional charter amendments, led commissioners to hold a work session March 5.
Greer said the work session brought a lot of input, and she said there were still a lot of questions.
"I do not want to pass this in a rush tonight," she said Tuesday.
Costigan, the only commissioner to vote against tabling the resolution, said he felt the resolution addressed a "flaw" in the charter's verbiage.
"All that it did was recognize that the Talbot County system was the most logical way to assure that people are eligible and can vote," he said, adding that the concerns around who is eligible to vote would need to be addressed in another section of the charter.
After the resolution was tabled, Town Attorney Lyndsey Ryan suggested the commissioners write rules for the Oxford Election Board regarding registration, absentee ballots and poll watching.
"The last election we had a livestream for individuals to watch," she said. "If you're going to follow that process again, we should have something established."
Greer said they should hold a work session on the matter, and Bell agreed that a work session should be scheduled.

title: After Heated Meeting, Talbot County Retains DEI Statement by 3-2 Vote
author: Konner Metz
content:
After heated meeting, Talbot County retains DEI statement by 3-2 vote

 March 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 995
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — During a charged meeting that saw council members exchange remarks and three members of the public asked to leave for speaking out of turn, the Talbot County Council rejected a resolution to repeal the county's DEI statement.Although tensions eased by the meeting's end Tuesday night, council members had heated back-and-forth before voting 3-2 against the resolution sponsored by Dave Stepp.
Council President Chuck Callahan joined Stepp in favoring the resolution. Vice President Pete Lesher and council members Keasha Haythe and Lynn Mielke opposed.
Stepp contends the resolution will protect Talbot County's federal funding after a Jan. 20 executive order from the Trump administration to end all diversity, equity and inclusion policies and programs in the federal government.
Stepp said he's heard from many county employees that want the diversity statement repealed. He called it a "political stunt" for the measure to be voted down.
"You simply choose to go against the oath of office you took when you took this office," Stepp said of the three council members who voted against.
Haythe, Lesher and Mielke contested Stepp's claims.
"We really were not going to go there tonight because all five of us have agreed to sit here and tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth," Haythe said. "And in some of those statements, the truth was not told."
She said she hasn't heard from any county employees who want the statement removed.
"What we are not going to do as this council is stand here and accept the lies that are pushed down from the federal government to our local community," Haythe said. "We are not doing that."
The failed resolution would have repealed two 2020 resolutions — the first developed the county's diversity statement found in the employee handbook, and the second implemented an annual report of diversity training offered to staff.
Stepp said that an email to the council from Talbot County Sheriff Joe Gamble, a Republican, stated a grant for police work in Trappe is at risk due to the county's DEI statement.
Lesher disagreed, stating that Trump's executive order "does not deprive federal funds for our airport modernization, for rural development or for policing."
"Those funds are not in peril," Lesher said.
"So you're saying the sheriff is lying?" Stepp responded.
Prior to the vote, Haythe added her support for diversity training, saying it helps people identify their underlying biases, including herself.
"Council members should go through diversity training as well," Haythe said. "We all should, because there is bias. There's bias on this council. I've received it."
SPLIT PUBLIC
At the council's Feb. 26 meeting during which the matter was tabled, more than 100 residents attended, most speaking against Stepp's resolution. Tuesday, public opinion was split.
At one point, Stepp motioned to move public comment so it occurred before the council's vote. Callahan seconded, but the rest of the council disagreed.
Some residents expressed displeasure the vote would be held before their comments. Stepp said "the three council members didn't want those to speak in the audience."
Haythe responded, pointing out that the council did not move up public comment at its last meeting.
"We had public comment in the same order at our last meeting, and we did not move anything to the front," Haythe said.
Many residents opposing DEI attended Tuesday's meeting. Lori Stepp, chair of the Talbot County Republican Central Committee and Dave Stepp's wife, said the DEI statement including equity and inclusion doesn't line up with the original 2020 resolution that only mentioned diversity in its text.
"That's not what the original council voted on," she said in an interview. "So unfortunately, I'm not sure how the equity and inclusion piece got thrown in there for the county employees."
Easton resident Brandi Whiting said DEI is "here for a reason" and that she's seen it make a positive impact in her experiences hiring for different companies.
"If you want to sell your morals for money, you go right ahead," Whiting said during public comment. "But I'm glad that at least three of our council people did not."
Resident Shari Wilcoxon called out Haythe, Lesher and Mielke for voting against Stepp's resolution.
"If we do indeed lose these funds that you have now put in jeopardy, it is on the three of you ... who rolled the dice for all Talbot County citizens," Wilcoxon said.
Following her comments, Wilcoxon and another resident expressed disagreement from their seats with Haythe while Callahan and a third resident went back and forth. "You've been a problem all night," Callahan told the third resident.
After Callahan initially requested only the third resident leave the room, Haythe said to him that the others who spoke from their seats out of turn should be asked to leave as well.
Callahan then asked the other two residents to leave. While deputies escorted the third resident out, the other two left on their own.
MOVING ON
Rhetoric toned down once public comment closed, as council members ensured they will continue to work together in the future.
"I don't think any minds got changed, but I appreciate the public engagement," Lesher said.
Stepp said he still wished public comment was moved up. "But I thank those who did stick around to make sure that those comments, you were able to get them out," he said.
Haythe and Callahan said the council will move on as a unified group.
"Once we take a vote, we're done and we move on. That's it," Haythe said. "And we still continue to be friends."
Callahan thanked county staff for supporting the council during the controversial last two weeks and expressed appreciation for fellow council members.
"I really appreciate you putting your thoughts together," Callahan told Stepp. "It takes a lot of bravery to do that. It really, really does. And Keasha, the same way with you.
"But at the end of the day, it's over, we've made a decision and we all move on."
This story has been updated to clarify that three residents were asked to leave during the public comment portion of the meeting for speaking out of turn. Police escorted one person while the other two left on their own.

title: St. Michaels Discuss Ordinance for Leaf Blowers
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
St. Michaels discuss ordinance for leaf blowers

 February 28, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 340
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — On Wednesday, St. Michaels officials held their third discussion of Noise Ordnance 567, which deals with gasoline-powered leaf blowers.Residents have voiced their concerns about gas leaf blowers being very loud and being used at especially early or late hours, concerns the new ordinance aims to address.
"So I think the main challenge from a policy standpoint is the impacts on local commercial lawn care companies by requiring electric leaf blowers," Town Administrator Rob Straebel said. "But for non commercial users such as residents and property owners, this could be a fairly easy transition."
The conversation surrounding limiting leaf blowers was first brought up on Oct. 25, 2023 but stopped after commercial landscape operators said they couldn't do their job properly with electric leaf blowers. The conversation was brought back up on Jan. 22, this time aimed at just gas-powered leaf blowers, which are usually noisier.
The commissioners would take into the consideration that residents would need to purchase electric leaf blowers, they said, by ensuring it does not go into effect for another year or two. Noise levels for electric or battery leaf blowers will have to be limited to 65 decibels.
Contractors and St. Michaels public works officials argued that gas leaf blowers makes their jobs easier. Electric or battery powered leaf blowers must be charged, which takes time. They also argued that gas-powered leaf blowers are more powerful and help them accomplish their jobs faster.
Commissioner Alex Roiter argued that the contractors and workers are wasting time by just blowing a couple of leafs with the gas blower.
Public Works Operational Manager Brian Thompson pushed back and explained that "most contractors are not going to waste time. They want to get in and get out because it's money flow."
Thompson said he is not against electric leaf blowers but that there are certain times when gas-powered equipment is needed.
After back-and-forth, the officials decided the ordinance needed some work because it did not properly explain what equipment can be used and by whom.
The commissioners decided to table the conversation for another meeting.

title: Easton OKs Outdoor Party at Hummingbird Inn for Pride Festival Weekend
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton OKs outdoor party at Hummingbird Inn for Pride Festival weekend

 February 20, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 627
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Town Council approved its first extension of Easton's new noise ordinance, granting the Hummingbird Inn permission to host an outdoor dance party the night after the Delmarva Pride Festival this summer.A zoning certificate was passed by councilmembers in a 3-1 vote during a Monday meeting. Ward 1 Councilmember Maureen Curry was absent from the meeting.
The exception will allow the Hummingbird Inn to host a party June 14 until 11:30 p.m., a 90-minute extension of the town's normal limit for outdoor music.
The 10 p.m. cutoff was established last July following resident concerns of music at night. The council instituted a noise ordinance, which required businesses or groups seek special approval to play amplified outdoor music past 10 p.m.
Eric Levinson, owner of the Hummingbird Inn, said he was happy and relieved when the council approved the inn's zoning certificate.
"What I appreciated was the fact that they didn't just assume it was going to be a problem and deny it," Levinson said in an interview, "and that they said, 'Let's see how it goes. And then if there's a problem, then we'll deal with it at that time.'"
Before Monday's Town Council meeting, Levinson gained signatures from surrounding neighbors in support of the extended dance party. Last year, around 70 people attended. Easton police noted no complaints were made.
Levinson expects 100 to 120 people at the event this year. The later end time will allow for a better atmosphere, he said.
"The problem was at that time of year it doesn't really get dark until later, so we had people hanging around and stuff, but nobody was actually doing anything until it was dark," Levinson said of 2024's party. "It just didn't set the right mood."
Monday, councilmembers thanked Levinson for reaching out to neighbors well in advance. However, Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery voted against the extension.
Montgomery said approving the request would set a "very dangerous precedent," and that there are many other one-time events that could seek similar exemptions.
"I don't see how to differentiate this request for a special exemption from one that might come from the Tidewater Inn if they have a couple with 100 guests, a man and woman who are being married and they want to have Christian gospel music until 11:30 at night," Montgomery said. "I think we would have to approve that request equally well."
Ward 2 Councilmember Don Abbatiello, who voted in favor, acknowledged Montgomery's concerns as valid. But he said the dance party being an annual event versus a weekly one made a difference in his opinion.
"I was going to give them the benefit of the doubt with the idea that if there are complaints … then I'm fine with not approving it in the future," Abbatiello added.
Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis said he's not "overly concerned," though this approval will set a precedent and that the town will be monitoring if complaints are made.
Levinson said Town Council President Frank Gunsallus helped the business navigate the request for the extension, a first for the town as well. Gunsallus made the motion for its approval Monday.
"Given everything that you've done to go through this the right way and do your due diligence, and the fact that this is a once-a-year thing, I think that it is completely acceptable," Gunsallus said.
Considering tense discussions and split votes surrounding the Delmarva Pride Festival and its place in Easton in recent years, Levinson says he's glad the town is following through on its promises to be both inclusive and neighborly.
"It is good to see that they're following that, standing by that, and putting their own personal preferences or opinions aside," Levinson said. "Because that's the way it should be. It's not based on what they like or dislike. It's what's good for the community."

title: As New Oxford Town Manager, Holly Wahl Wants to Focus on People
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
As new Oxford town manager, Holly Wahl wants to focus on people

 February 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 627
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — For Oxford Town Manager Holly Wahl, it's all about ensuring the success of town staff and making sure residents have the information and clarity they need."My first goal is people," Wahl said in an interview with The Star Democrat Tuesday.
Wahl — who has been in the position for nearly a month — wants to make sure town employees, whose jobs have a direct impact on citizens, have the resources they need to be successful.
Staff redundancy, or making sure more than one person has the training and licensure to do a job, has been a focus. For example, Wahl said the town's nutrient removal treatment plant only has one licensed operator, who also serves as the plant's superintendent. She said the town is working on getting additional training so there is more than one licensed operator in town.
Along with supporting staff, Wahl is also focused on government transparency and streamlining communication for residents. She sees upping the town's communication game as a way to build residents' trust in Oxford town government, which has been a concern over the past two years.
During the most recent Commissioners of Oxford meeting on Jan. 28, the commissioners approved a contract with a company to develop an updated website that includes a direct resident messaging platform. Wahl said updating the website was a priority for her because it will streamline communications and address residents' frustrations with not being able to find information.
Commissioner Katrina Greer said the new website will include a searchable town code so that residents won't have to "wade through an out of date PDF" to find what they're looking for.
Wahl is also trying to address concerns about the town's budget by sharing updated fiscal information at town meetings.
"There've been a lot of comments about budgeting and making sure citizens can understand the budget, understand what's within the budget," she said. "So (we're) working on providing clarity in that."
The town's record system is another area Wahl is setting her sights on improving. Currently, the town has a paper record system. She would like to digitize it so that individual records can be found more easily and the town can respond more efficiently to public information requests.
As she settles into the Oxford Town Office, Wahl is working on obtaining a doctorate in public administration and public policy from George Washington University. She is currently finishing up her dissertation, which focuses on how town managers respond in the complexities of local government.
"It's really centered on how we can be more inclusive (and) engage further so that, ultimately, we're solving problems with better decision making models," Wahl said.
All three Commissioners of Oxford agree that Wahl is a great fit for the job.
"She seems to have picked everything up without missing a step," Commissioner Tom Costigan said.
Greer and Commission President Norm Bell both noted Wahl's significant experience and qualifications. Greer said Wahl is the ideal person for the job.
"What you want for this job is someone who's committed to the profession of public administration," Greer said.
A month into the job, Wahl is looking for housing on the Eastern Shore and getting used to the pace of things on this side of the Bay Bridge. Although she hasn't had much time in the last few years, she would love to get back into doing water sports, like kayaking and paddle boarding. She is excited to explore all the Eastern Shore has to offer.
Looking to the future, Wahl hopes that 10 years from now, Oxford will have "more avenues for engagement" so more perspectives are brought to the table.
"I think everyone should feel comfortable giving their feedback," she said. "They might not want to do it in a town meeting, but there might be other ways that we provide them opportunities to do that."

title: Easton Leaders Split on Property Tax Breaks for First Responders, Veterans
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton leaders split on property tax breaks for first responders, veterans

 January 25, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 559
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — During Tuesday's meeting, Town Council President Frank Gunsallus suggested the town should consider property tax breaks — and potential removals — for emergency responders and veterans."One idea to explore is the reduction or removal of property taxes for our emergency responders, as well as for our active duty military (and) veterans," Gunsallus said immediately before the meeting adjourned. "Such an initiative could help us attract more volunteers to our fire department, ensuring it remains a volunteer-driven organization."
Gunsallus encouraged the council to consider his proposal. Councilmembers have offered mixed opinions.
Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery said while an "immense debt" is owed to all veterans, he thinks "broad-based" tax relief for veterans is likely not the way to go.
"I could not see offering property tax reductions to all veterans," Montgomery said in an interview. "I don't think we could afford it. I think there are other ways that we can express our appreciation."
At the state level, disabled veterans and surviving spouses can apply for property tax exemptions.
According to Easton's budget ordinance from last year's budget cycle, it was estimated the town would bring in $13.4 million in revenue from real property taxes.
'the town's current property tax rate is 0.52 cents per assessed $100 of value. Last year, the council voted unanimously to keep it at that rate, a mark that hasn't been increased in nearly two decades.
Ward 2 Councilmember Don Abbatiello, who is running against Gunsallus to be council president, said property tax removals for all veterans would create a budget shortfall and impact the town's funding toward its police, fire and public works departments.
"As a result residents will either do with reduced services in town or other residents will have to pay higher taxes to make up for the loss of revenue," Abbatiello wrote in an emailed statement.
In an email, Gunsallus stated he hopes to explore the possibility of property tax breaks this budget season. He emphasized any consideration of property tax relief should be balanced with fiscal responsibility.
"I fully appreciate, understand, and share the concerns regarding potential impacts on our budget," Gunsallus wrote. "My ardor for this initiative is tempered by financial stewardship."
Ward 1 Councilmember Maureen Curry said in an interview that she would rather see the council look toward assisting first responders in buying homes, noting the town's affordable housing shortage.
"It's really not our property taxes that are the problem, it's the cost of buying a home that's a problem," Curry said.
Abbatiello, a member of the Easton Volunteer Fire Department, added that former Mayor Bob Willey spearheaded a tax relief program for Easton firefighters that is still in place. Life members or volunteers who go on at least 100 calls in a year receive a $500 tax incentive, he said.
Abbatiello, who announced his campaign for Town Council president earlier this month, alluded to the town's upcoming election in his statement.
"Volunteer Firefighters and Veterans have not been asking for a tax cut," Abbatiello wrote. "But they do expect responsible government. Proposing a massive change to the tax base without truly examining its effects because it's an election year is not being fiscally responsible."
Gunsallus says he's heard from first responders and veterans regarding potential tax reductions.
"Through numerous conversations, I've gathered that there is interest for this form of financial relief," Gunsallus wrote. "While these requests have not been formal, the sentiment is clear and merits our attention."

title: Commissioners of Oxford Swear in New Town Manager
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Commissioners of Oxford swear in new town manager

 January 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 499
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — New Town Manager Holly Wahl was sworn into office in an uncharacteristically short Commissioners of Oxford meeting Tuesday, bringing hope for calmer seas after half a year of rough water in the town."I think I speak for the three of us. It gives us great, incredible pleasure to swear Holly in," Commission President Norm Bell said before giving Wahl the oath of office in front of a full audience that included Wahl's parents.
Wahl was previously the town administrator for Chesapeake Beach, a town on the western shore. Her arrival marks the end of a nearly six-month period in Oxford where there was no town manager.
In late June, Michael Calvert — a former city administrator in Liberty, South Carolina — was hired to fill the role of town manager, which former Town Manager Cheryl Lewis was retiring from. But just three days after the commissioners announced the hire, they announced the town and Calvert had "mutually agreed to part ways."
The commission never commented on why the decision was made. Former Liberty City Council Member Peggy Edwards said that when Calvert was in his position in Liberty, there was a lack of transparency and mismanagement of money.
The situation led to Oxford's commissioners choosing a search firm to assist in its search for the next town manager, which led to Wahl's hiring.
After getting sworn in Tuesday evening, Wahl told residents that it's "great" to be in Oxford and said they should feel free to stop by the town office or reach out to her with any questions or concerns.
"It's been a wonderful start coming here in a major snow storm and watching commissioners climb through a treatment plant and truly be engaged to understand what staff needs," she said.
In the 30 minute meeting, from the swearing in to conversations about updating the town's website and creating a searchable town code in an effort to increase transparency, no disagreement was voiced aloud from residents nor commissioners.
In an interview with The Star Democrat, Bell said there hasn't been any contention at the "last several meetings."
Many Oxford residents have said that since former Oxford Police Chief Patrick Maxwell's abrupt retirement in February 2023 — for which the town never provided a reason — community involvement in town government has heightened. This has led to some tense meetings with significant debate.
Bell said he hopes that with Wahl's entrance, Oxford is entering a new chapter. But he said time will determine if this change in meeting culture is a "definite trend."
He said there is a lot the town can accomplish with Wahl and he is excited for the town.
At the end of the meeting on Tuesday, Commissioner Katrina Greer said the commissioners are "delighted" to have Wahl in Oxford.
"And we look forward to a smooth process and great business management," Greer said.
On Thursday evening, the town will host a meet and greet with Wahl from 5:30 to 7:00 p.m. at the Oxford Community Center.
This report has been updated to include comment from Norm Bell.

title: Talbot County Establishes Commission for Country's 250th Anniversary
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot County establishes commission for country's 250th anniversary

 January 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 304

 EASTON — Talbot County now has its own commission to prepare for the United States' 250th anniversary in 2026.At Tuesday's Talbot County Council meeting, the Talbot 250 Commission was unanimously approved. Vice President Pete Lesher — who serves on the Maryland 250 Commission — expressed his excitement that Talbot County will have its own dedicated version of the group.
"The state has been encouraging local jurisdictions — municipalities and counties — to similarly establish local commissions to do a local coordinating effort," Lesher said.
Lesher said many of his colleagues at the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum are looking forward to getting involved. He thanked Sarah Kilmon, the county's communications coordinator, for her efforts in organizing the commission's creation.
"This legislation has been a long time coming," Kilmon told the council. "I believe (Maryland 250 Commission Director Michele Johnson) was asking us about a year ago when our commission was coming. And so I'm excited that we've got it up and running today with your approval."
Kilmon says the commission will promote local events and celebrations around the semiquincentennial, as well as engaging with the community and bringing other organizations to the table.
"As we approach America's 250th anniversary, this is a moment to reflect on our shared history and envision the future we want to build together," Kilmon added in a press release. "We are thrilled to bring our community together through this commission to create meaningful and memorable celebrations honoring our past, present, and future."
On Jan. 21 at 6 p.m., Talbot 250 will host an interest meeting at the Talbot County Free Library. The meeting will provide insight into commission's goals and show attendees how they can get involved.
For more information about Talbot 250 or to RSVP for the interest meeting, email talbot250@talbotcountymd.gov or visit talbot250.org. Talbot 250 can be found on Facebook and Instagram at @Talbot250.

title: Oxford's Next Town Manager Faces Controversies on Western Shore
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford's next town manager faces controversies on western shore

 December 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 835
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — As Oxford prepares to welcome Holly Wahl as its next town manager, controversy is swirling in the town where she was previously employed.Wahl announced her resignation as Chesapeake Beach's town administrator on Dec. 4, amid some turmoil in the western shore town.
Bruce Wahl, who had served as mayor of Chesapeake Beach from 2008 to 2016, ran for the position again earlier this year and was elected mayor on Nov. 5.
Prior to Election Day, in social media posts, Bruce Wahl said that if elected, the "persecution of town citizens" by "the current town administration will completely cease."
His comments were related to complaints from residents who claimed their water and sewer bills have recently risen dramatically.
Holly Wahl and Bruce Wahl are not related.
In interviews with the Star Democrat on Friday, the Commissioners of Oxford said they were aware of and not concerned about the controversy in Chesapeake Beach.
"We're confident that we hired the right person," Oxford Commission President Norm Bell said. "We were delighted to talk to her. We're very comfortable in her experiences and how they can help the town. And that's what we based the decision (on)."
Bell said his understanding of the water and sewer bill issue is that people weren't paying annual water and sewer bill connection fees. He said that when Wahl took on her position in Chesapeake Beach, she saw that as a problem and made sure the town started collecting that money.
During a Chesapeake Beach Town Council work session in early September, Wahl said audits revealed "significant underpayment of connection fees" by commercial properties and said the delinquent payments amounted to a $6 million loss to the town.
In an email, Wahl told the Star Democrat: "My record of contributions to the Town of Chesapeake Beach, MD, is publicly available on the Town's website, along with meeting minutes and recordings. I am very much looking forward to working with the Commissioners, staff, citizens, and businesses of the Town of Oxford."
Oxford Commissioner Katrina Greer said Friday that Wahl is a "highly qualified and ethical manager" who was "wringing out corruption" in the connection fees issue.
"And it only made me feel stronger about hiring her," Greer said.
Oxford Commissioner Tom Costigan said Wahl was carefully vetted by the hiring search firm Baker Tilly. He said the information coming out about Wahl is not something the commissioners are worried about.
"We interviewed a lot of candidates," he said. "We narrowed it down to four. She was by far the strongest of the four, and we are optimistic about her future performance here in Oxford."
Oxford hired Baker Tilly to do the search after the town announced the hire of — and then three days later announced they would be parting ways with — Michael Calvert as the next town manager.
Shortly after the news of Calvert's hire, some Oxford residents expressed concerns about the town's candidate vetting process. The week the town announced the decision to part ways with Calvert, Peggy Edwards, a former council member from the town where Calvert was previously employed, told the Star Democrat she resigned from the council due to issues with Calvert and the city's mayor. She said that when Calvert was in the position, there was a lack of transparency and mismanagement of money.
SEVERANCE PACKAGE CONCERNS
On the same day Wahl announced her resignation, the outgoing mayor and the Chesapeake Beach Town Council met for what was labeled an "emergency meeting" to consider for approval of an "emergency ordinance" approving a severance package for Wahl. The town's previous Mayor Pat "Irish" Mahoney said the severance package was reasonable.
The ordinance, which was unanimously approved by the current council, gives Wahl a severance of six months' salary and all accrued vacation time. Southern Maryland News, which is owned and operated by the same company as the Star Democrat, has filed a Freedom of Information Act request for the dollar amount of Wahl's compensation package.
The approved ordinance states that Wahl will receive the compensation "in a lump sum with one payment paid prior to Dec. 18, 2024, based upon her wage rate on the date of her resignation."
In addition to the compensation, the ordinance stipulates that "the town agrees to hold Holly Wahl harmless in any future actions including all indemnification and attorneys' fees for any action that may be pursued against her."
During the public comment portion of the Dec. 4 meeting, a few citizens spoke out against the pending action. Daniel Duvall, who lost the race for a Chesapeake Beach Town Council seat by three votes, said approving a severance package "is not an emergency" and was "a questionable use of taxpayer funds."
Another Chesapeake Beach resident, Deborah Buckingham, reiterated the ordinance did not "meet the criteria of an emergency." She added, "Holly Wahl doesn't deserve any severance."
There was plenty of praise for the town administrator at the meeting, too.
"She's fantastic. I've never seen so much communication in the last eight years," Randy Getman, the town's election administrator, said. "I have no issue with Bruce Wahl wanting to pick his own town administrator."

title: St. Michaels commissioners approve updates to docking infractions
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
St. Michaels commissioners approve updates to docking infractions

 December 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 359
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — On Wednesday evening, the Commissioners of St. Michaels voted to give police authority to cite docking infractions and approve bids for trash and recycling services.Amendments were made to town Boats and Boating code regarding town-owned slips. A public discussion was held on a proposed amendment to provide police authority to cite docking infractions, as well as measures to correct grammar errors, change language for uniformity and remove a "problematic provision" that references judgment liens of personal prosperity.
The amendments were unanimously approved.
PROPERTY MAINTENANCEA proposed amendment to a town ordinance concerning property maintenance and littering was brought before the commissioners. The requested amendment would remove duplicative language, increase penalties for littering and provide certain authorities to cite for littering and weed control violations.
Prior to the amendment, the ordinance stated that "no owner of property within the town" can cause, permit or maintain the existence of weeds higher than 12 inches on the property. The new amendment it added "or occupant" to provide accountability on rentals as well.
Additionally, it adds that a violation of this article is subject to a fine of $200 for first offense and that the property owner and occupant of the property may each be separately cited. Repeat violations would be subject to a fine of $300.
The amendment was unanimously approved by the commissioners.
TRASH COLLECTION SERVICESA bid was approved for a three-year contract with Republic Services for trash and recycling services. The proposed contract states costs for the town would be $239,001.91. In comparison, during fiscal year 2023 the town spent $191,000 for recycling and trash collection.
St. Michaels' staff reached out to other trash and recycle businesses for new bids but only Republic Services sent in a bid. Ultimately, the commissioners approved the three year contract with Republic Services.
TOWN MANAGER RECRUITMENTFinally, a bid was approved for the Mercer Group Associates as the firm to lead recruitment of the next Town Administrator. The firm's bid was for $24,000 to provide services including position analysis, recruitment process, resume review, candidate screening and interview process.
Mercer Group will also assist in the negotiation of an employment contract after completing the roughly 100-day recruitment process.
Commissioners unanimously approved the bid.

title: Legislators Hear Cambridge's Priorities Before General Assembly Session Begins
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Legislators hear Cambridge's priorities before General Assembly session begins

 December 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 580
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Before the regularly scheduled Cambridge City Council meeting on Dec. 9, the council and city staff shared their priorities with state legislators, who are preparing to go back to Annapolis for the 447th session of the Maryland General Assembly.During the legislative delegation work session, Cambridge City Manager Glenn Steckman acknowledged getting state funding this year will be difficult and asked that the Lower Shore delegation notify the city if they come across anything during session that could benefit Cambridge.
Steckman said the city doesn't have a list of laws or law changes that it wants enacted by the General Assembly.
"We're not here to try to make laws and recommend the law changes, but to show you what the issues that the elected leadership here is dealing with and the appointed staff is dealing with," he said. "We're looking for your help and guidance on the legislative level."
The six priorities — which Steckman detailed during the meeting and said are in no particular order — are to:
Preserve and renovate Cambridge's historic City Hall on Gay Street.Continue to move the Cambridge Harbor project forward.Improve housing and revitalize the Pine Street neighborhood.Make enhancements and improvements to city youth services.Update and improve the city's water and sewer infrastructure.Provide local workforce development programs and opportunities.
Steckman said when it comes to workforce development, it can be difficult for residents without transportation who are seeking employment or training opportunities in other counties.
"Obviously, if we want to grow the industrial part of the economy or (the) commercial (part), we need more job training to prepare, not only our existing workforce, but our workforce coming up through the school system," he said.
After Steckman discussed the city's priorities, Del. Tom Hutchinson (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico), Del. Sheree Sample-Hughes (D-Dorchester, Wicomico), Del. Chris Adams (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) and Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) all chimed in.
Hutchinson said he sees improving youth services as a very important priority, referencing a local teen who had been detained by the Department of Juvenile Services for stealing a car.
"This is a really serious issue," Hutchinson said. "If we have children who are saying, 'I'm bored and it's fine,' then we really need to work on that and correct that."
Sample-Hughes said that some of the bills on rentals and housing that didn't get passed during last year's session could come back to the General Assembly this year. She said it would be useful for the city to keep in touch as the legislators hear these bills brought back.
"I think your on the ground insight is very beneficial to what we have to do when it comes to the policy work and not only just the financial side of things," she said.
Adams told the council this year will be a "budget year." The state faces a predicted $2.7 billion budget deficit in fiscal year 2026.
"We know that this is going to be a tough year," Adams said. "So legislative requests that revolve around funding capital projects are going to be tough. There is always bond money, and we as a delegation will surely do our part ... in submitting those requests."
Mautz asked that the council stay in touch with the Lower Shore delegation throughout the upcoming legislative session. He said that when the governor's budget comes out, the city should make sure there aren't cuts that will negatively affect the city.
"If there's an actual cut that's going to affect something in the City of Cambridge, somebody needs to call (us)," he said.

title: St. Michaels Raises Penalties for 6 Town Code Violations
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
St. Michaels raises penalties for 6 town code violations

 December 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 290
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — Significant increases in fines for various violations of town codes were approved by the St. Michaels commissions on Wednesday evening.The increases were made on six different town codes and included including raises in fines for short-term rental, transient vendors and leash animal control violations. The fines for some infractions increased by more than 10 times.
Violation fines for short-term rentals operating without permission from the town doubled from $250 to $500.
Condemnation, otherwise known as "housing standards," increased from a steady $100 to $250 for a first violation, $300 for a second violation and $500 for a third violation.
Addressing non-compliance currently has a violation fine of $25. It has been increased to $150. This means that any owner of a building or premises that is not posted with the official street number within 30 days after said owner receives notice of the official street number shall be punishable by a fine of $150. Each day that the owner fails to display the official street number will constitute a separate offense.
Fines for violations relating to transient vendors, or vendors who sell produce or seafood at a roadside or a temporary location, were increased from $25 to $250.
Public urination fines were increased from $25 to $250, and public defecation fines went from $50 to $500.
Finally, leash animal control violation fines doubled from $50 to $100.
Commissioner David Wojciechowski asked if code enforcement officers would issue a warning first prior to issuing fines on the violations. Officer Jeffrey Oswald said on most of the violations there will be warnings prior to the penalties. This would not be the case for public urination and defecation.
After Commissioner Alfred Mercier opened a quiet public hearing on the increases, the commission unanimously approved the fine raises.

title: Some Oxford Residents Call for Change, Creating Rift in Town
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Some Oxford residents call for change, creating rift in town

 October 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 1820
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — When Tom Costigan was first elected to the Commissioners of Oxford in 2022, somewhere between six and 10 people would sit in the audience during most town meetings."Including my wife," he said.
Today, getting a seat at Oxford's meetings, held every other Tuesday evening, can be a challenge.
Usually by the 6 p.m. start time, most, if not all of the seats, are filled. Sometimes, it's standing room only. In late July, the town office learned that a resident had reported town meetings to the Office of the State Fire Marshal for being overcrowded.
Many residents say the community's heightened involvement in Oxford's government started with former Police Chief Patrick Maxwell's abrupt retirement in February 2023, for which the town never provided a reason.
Since then, residents have continued to show up for meetings. Many of them seek more transparency from the town's government, which some residents think is more of a concern than others.
Town Commissioner Katrina Greer said she thinks Maxwell's departure was a wake-up call for the town.
"There were things that came to light about salaries and jobs and things that were not completely transparent to the public," Greer said. "And so that's when I decided to run for office, that March."
At the Feb. 28, 2023, town meeting, over 100 residents packed the Oxford Community Center, many voicing concerns about the circumstances of Maxwell's retirement and transparency in the town's government.
Commission President Norm Bell said Maxwell's departure resulted in "contentious meetings."
"My belief is that the tension was always under the surface," he said about residents' concerns. "This opened it up and let it explode."
CHANGE IN ATMOSPHEREWhen Costigan and his wife bought their house in Oxford in 2000, there were multiple things he loved about the town. He loved the many volunteer opportunities, the "tremendous sense of community" and the normalcy of saying hello to a passing stranger on the street.
"It just seemed like Valhalla," he said.
Twenty-four years later, Costigan thinks the town is different, but the "important vestiges" of what he loved still remain.
He said he's noticed a change in the atmosphere at town meetings.
"When you've got people sitting there that you know are just waiting to pounce on you, it's really hard to do a meeting like that," he said.
Bell characterized town meetings these days as vocal and, to some extent, tense.
Recently, the town passed — and then repealed and replaced — a resolution establishing general rules and procedures regarding public participation at town meetings. When Bell introduced the original resolution in early September, he said it was developed as a result of "disruptive behavior" at a previous town meeting in August.
During that August meeting, yelling broke out after resident Scott Rensberger asked to sit down with Bell at a later date to discuss a public letter Bell wrote in April. The letter mentioned videos made by Rensberger about government transparency in Oxford. One of the videos detailed concerns with decisions made by former Town Manager Cheryl Lewis.
In the time since Maxwell's departure from the police department, residents have brought up concerns with some of the town practices and asked for more transparency regarding town finances, salaries and hiring practices.
Before Lewis — who some of the transparency concerns were directed toward — retired in June, the town announced her role would be filled by Michael Calvert, who was previously a city administrator in Liberty, South Carolina.
Just three days after the announcement, it was announced that the town and Calvert had "mutually agreed to part ways."
The commission did not comment on why the decision was made. Former Liberty City Council member Peggy Edwards said she resigned from the council due to issues with Calvert and the city's mayor. She said that when Calvert was in the position, there was a lack of transparency and mismanagement of money.
Rensberger said it didn't take him long to find out that "there were a lot of problems" in Liberty and took the information he found to Oxford's town attorney.
SPECTRUM OF VIEWSThe yelling incident at the August meeting caused resident Tom Campbell to say that he has a hard time recognizing the town anymore.
"This can't be every town meeting," Campbell said. "We're getting nowhere, and it's making it hard for me to cheer on my community anymore."
Rensberger said in an email that he thinks town meetings are "just fine." He said people are entitled to their opinions and should raise their hands to speak. He said he is against interruptions and name calling.
Greer said there have been very few incidents during town meetings that were "even a small problem." She said sharing different viewpoints is essential to coming to the best possible decision.
"You'll have people in the same room that are ultra-conservative, and you'll have people that worked for Nancy Pelosi," she said. "And they're ignited, and they care about open government and professionalism and having things be transparent."
Greer said this is what makes commissioners better. She said commissioners shouldn't necessarily agree all the time, either. "It should not be a rubber stamp of ideas," she said.
Not every resident in town is on the same page about whether what is happening at town meetings is for the better.
Deborah Pulzone, who has lived in Oxford for almost 30 years, said things have gotten "too divisive and ugly" in the last year. She said she is trying to maintain a "center ground."
"There have been so many times I've bitten my tongue, I almost have a hole in it," she said.
For Pulzone, division in Oxford is a microcosm of what's happening in the country.
"There is a lot of divide in the country," she said. "And people are seeing it and hearing it, and they're feeling it here."
Resident Karen Wayland, who moved to Oxford two years ago, but grew up in a small town, said there might be some division in the town, but it's no different from other places.
"I just think it's uncomfortable for people who have had a certain way of doing things and now are being asked to justify their decisions more than they had to in the past," she said.
Wayland said that's what being in government is all about. "Being able to articulate why you're doing something to everyone who has a right to know," she said.
Greer thinks the sustained involvement and interest in town government from residents is amazing. She sees it as a reflection of the post-COVID-19 world.
"People are paying attention," she said. "We have a particularly engaged and intelligent citizen community that often works together on many different nonprofits and commissions. And so they're paying attention."
TAKING STEPS FORWARDRuss Gray, who has lived in Oxford for almost 22 years, said everyone in town wants the same thing: faith and trust in their government and open communication with their government.
He thinks there is a faction of the town that "is pretty much talking about everything that's wrong with Oxford."
To overcome division, Gray thinks the Oxford community needs to figure out how to get back to engaging in a friendly way and listening to each other, even when they disagree.
"Everyone needs to put effort in it," he said. "We cannot pick sides. Period."
Rensberger, who bought a home in Oxford eight years ago, said the town is "completely torn apart." He said on one side, there are the people who control the town and its various boards and commissions, and on the other, there are people with no control.
"Right now, the two commissioners that run the town are doing their best to keep my side from even asking questions," he said in an email.
Rensberger called Oxford the least transparent town he's ever seen. He thinks a forensic audit would bring clarity to multiple issues, but said he doesn't think all of the commissioners want that.
"Oxford's only about 40 simple questions away from becoming the perfect town," he said.
Gray said there is a need for transparency, "but not where you think it would be."
At a town meeting on Sept. 24, Gray brought up an informal meeting Greer held days before for residents to share their thoughts on the process for interacting with commissioners and qualities they want in a town manager.
The email, which the Star Democrat obtained, was sent to a list of undisclosed recipients. One of those recipients was Commission President Bell. If Bell had attended, it could have been considered a quorum, the minimum number of commissioners needed to conduct business.
At a town meeting on Oct. 8, Town Attorney Lyndsey Ryan said that if two commissioners had been present at the informal meeting, it could have been a violation of the Maryland Open Meetings Act, but since Bell was not there, it was not a violation.
In an interview, Gray said Greer's actions could have resulted in an Open Meetings Act violation and said there are ways to get word out to the entire public, not just to select residents.
Greer said meeting individually with residents is one of the best things you can do as a commissioner. She said the email did go to Bell, but Bell and Costigan are "smart enough to know" what they can and can't do when it comes to the Open Meetings Act.
Greer said she didn't send the email to everyone because she doesn't have everyone's email. She said she doesn't normally post on social media.
Wayland said improving public notice and getting better at sharing public documents are important steps toward improving residents' transparency concerns.
"If you operate with a commitment to transparency, people are more likely to take your word for what you say rather than trying to FOIA everything," she said. "I think, unfortunately, there's a lot of mistrust in the town and it's going to take a real commitment to openness and transparency before the commissioners are going to get a lot of breathing room."
Greer said there are many things she thinks the commissioners will need to address, but for right now, they need to address staffing issues.
Oxford's town office is currently without a town manager or a planning and zoning coordinator. At the end of the month, it will also be without an assistant clerk. Costigan said he thinks the shelf life of employees is getting shorter, not just in Oxford, but all over.
As they address staffing, Greer said the commissioners need to move toward a more transparent government.
Bell said he thinks there are people in town that are satisfied with the transparency of town government and those that want more of it.
"I'm not arguing with that," he said about those who want more transparency. "They're right."
Bell said the commissioners are taking those steps toward increased transparency, it's just a matter of how they go about it and timing.
Greer said there are some people who have been involved with Oxford's government for many years that have had difficulty accepting change.
"And I'm sensitive to that," she said. "But it doesn't mean, as an organization, that we shouldn't inspect ourselves and try to be better. It's not a criticism of the past, it is a wish for the future."

title: Changes Made to St. Michaels Tourism Advisory Board
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Changes made to St. Michaels Tourism Advisory Board

 October 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 534
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — The Commissioners of St. Michaels have made changes to the controversial Tourism Advisory Board, including additional members and updated language.According to Commissioner David Wojciechowski at a Wednesday meeting, the ordinance establishing the board was "re-drafted" to take into consideration comments from the commissioners and the public.
The idea of a tourism board was brought forth during the town election last May. Wojciechowski, Alexis Roiter and Jay Hudson, who were all later elected as commissioners, said during their campaigns that they would work with business owners to make the town more friendly to their needs.
The purpose of the board, according to a town memo, would be to assist the town in its efforts to encourage businesses to locate or remain in the town and to make recommendations to the commissioners. The board would also "work closely with the Talbot County Tourism Board on a unified, regional marketing approach."
During an August commission meeting, the proposed tourism board was met with pushback from residents, who raised an array of concerns about potential conflicts of interest and a lack of data supporting the board's creation.
A major change to the ordinance Wojciechowski pointed out was a change in language. For the purpose of the board, language was changed to "manage, promote and stabilize the economic health of the town's tourism economy."
"One of the objectives here is to stabilize tourism, to make it to the right size, if you will. Not too large for the town, not too small, but to manage tourism doesn't get out of hand," Wojciechowski said.
Additionally, there were changes to the amount of members on the board. Originally, the board would comprise seven members serving four-year terms, all appointed by the commissioners. Membership would include a resident not associated with a business and representatives from the lodging, eating/drinking, retail or service, marinas, museums and nonprofit sectors.
There was outcry by residents over the low number of residents on the board. Now membership has been changed to include two town residents.
Public CommentDuring public comment, resident Daniel Spiegel, who in the past has shared concerns over the establishment of the tourism board, said he and other residents have marked issues with what he describes as a "seriously flawed ordinance."
Spiegel's main concerns involved potential conflicts of interest and the town's level of involvement in private business operations and gathering data. He stressed there are already small business associations, such as the lodging association, which could gather the necessary information that the tourism board would gather.
According to Spiegel, by creating a government board rather than an advisory board outside of the town's legal boundaries, it will create conflict of interests where the business owners on the board could propose budgetary expenditures that could directly benefit them.
"There's nothing wrong with promoting tourism," Spiegel said. "The question is whether the town wants to be deeply engaged in the way that this ordinance is. Which for a town of (this) size, is really surprising. We're not a county, we're not a big city, we're a small town, and I think you will regret that you've set it up this way."
After public comment, the board unanimously approved moving the ordinance toward a public hearing. The hearing will be held on Nov. 13.

title: Oxford Commissioners Repeal and Replace Meeting Procedures Resolution
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford commissioners repeal and replace meeting procedures resolution

 October 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 360
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — After a workshop last week and additional discussion at a town meeting Tuesday, the Commissioners of Oxford have come to an agreement on how to amend the wording of a recently passed resolution establishing town meeting procedures.The original resolution, passed Sept. 24, establishes general rules and procedures regarding public participation at town meetings, including when and for how long public commenters can speak. When Commission President Norm Bell introduced the resolution in early September, he said it was developed as a result of "disruptive behavior" at a previous town meeting in August.
At the town meeting on Sept. 24, some residents expressed concerns with the resolution's limitations on public comment, as well as the way in which the resolution was passed.
On Tuesday, the commissioners unanimously voted to repeal and replace the current resolution with one that adjusts the wording regarding public comment. Specifically, it states that commissioners shall invite public questions and comments before a vote is taken on a resolution or an ordinance.
Town Attorney Lyndsey Ryan said the commissioners also would have the discretion to open up other agenda items for public comment. She said that because ordinances already require public hearings, this resolution would essentially add the requirement of holding public comment before voting on resolutions.
One of the main discussions during a workshop Oct. 2 was whether the resolution should say that commissioners "may" invite public comment on agenda items or "shall" invite public comment on agenda items. The former would give commissioners discretion on which items should be opened up for public comment.
Toward the end of the workshop, the commissioners agreed to use "shall" instead of "may" in a new draft resolution, which they could vote on following discussion at the town meeting Tuesday.
The vote to repeal and replace the resolution on Tuesday garnered applause from residents in the audience.
Before the commissioners came to a decision, they heard from residents. The majority of residents who spoke shared that they think "shall" should be used.
Resident Jane McCarthy said she didn't think the commissioners had the right to use the word "may" in the resolution.
"We are the people," she said. "We are the taxpayers in this town."
