title: Talbot County Council Discusses Election Judges, Route 50 Housing Project
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot County Council discusses election judges, Route 50 housing project

 October 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 566
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — During Tuesday's public meeting, members of the Talbot County Council revisited the ongoing dialogue surrounding the partisan breakdown of election judges in Talbot County for the upcoming election.Council Member Dave Stepp originally raised concerns at a Sept. 24 council meeting regarding an imbalance of election judges selected by the Talbot County Board of Elections to work polling places this November. At the time, the board's breakdown of judges was 62 Democratic, 50 Republican and 11 unaffiliated.
At Tuesday's meeting, Stepp said the difference between Democratic and Republican judges had lowered to seven. "I ask that we keep up that work," Stepp said.
He also thanked Talbot County Sheriff Joe Gamble for sending a letter to the Board of Elections and Election Director Tammy Stafford last week. In that letter, Gamble "strongly" urged the board to follow state election law.
Council Member Lynn Mielke, as she did on Sept. 24, disagreed with Stepp. She brought up a letter written by Attorney General Anthony Brown that was sent to Gamble on Monday.
In that letter, Brown addressed the "limited role of local law enforcement … in the electoral process." While not an official opinion of the attorney general, Brown said achieving "exact party balance" isn't always possible for local election boards due to volunteer rates, training and no-shows on Election Day.
"My Office has consistently advised that opening a polling place, even if the number of judges from each party is not exactly equal, is preferable to closing the polling place and disenfranchising all the voters who would have voted there," Brown wrote in his letter.
Mielke said Tuesday, "We have rulings from the attorney general that the procedure that was started by (Council Member) Stepp and others, were overruled … And that there was nothing found … that the local board of elections have done wrong."
ZONING WAIVERCouncil members unanimously approved a zoning change waiver for around 17 acres of land off of U.S. Route 50 that developers aim to use for an affordable multifamily housing project in Easton.
The development on the east side of Ocean Gateway is planned by developers Corrigan & Trippe Ventures. Easton Town Council approved the annexation of the land in July.
The resolution passed Tuesday approves a waiver that will allow a proposed zoning change to take immediate effect without a five-year hold. The area will be rezoned from the county's town conservation zoning to the town's residential zoning, providing developers with a higher approved density.
"They would essentially be locked into the uses that are permitted under the county's TC zoning now for a period of five years," County Attorney Patrick Thomas said if the waiver was not passed.
Zach Smith, an attorney representing the developers, said the maximum density under the town's residential zoning is 3.5 units per acre, along with a 5-unit-per-acre mark permitted by the town's multifamily housing special exception.
If developers plan to exceed those marks, they will have to come before the Easton Town Council for a planned unit development approval. Smith noted developers would then need to revisit the County Council for a supplemental waiver.
Smith emphasized to council members that while developers are obligated within the annexation agreement to reach a 50% mark of affordable units, the goal is for 100% of the units to be affordable.
"This housing is not necessarily housing designed to attract new folks to our community, it's really to serve folks that are already in our community," Smith said.

title: Trappe Council Discusses Procurement Policy Changes
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Trappe council discusses procurement policy changes

 October 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 284
 Words 

 Read News Document

 TRAPPE — On Wednesday evening, the Trappe Town Council discussed making revisions and updating current procurement policy in an effort to save money and more swiftly receive needed services.The current procurement policy requires the town to make a request for proposal for any services or item. Requests for proposals are a form of reverse auction that solicits a business proposal by an organization interested in the procurement of a service or product from potential suppliers.
According to Lyndsey Ryan, Trappe's attorney, towns on the Eastern Shore, including Queenstown, have recently made similar changes.
Ryan said last year leaders of Queenstown we're finding it difficult to go through the formal advertising and drafting process every time they wanted to make a purchase.
Queenstown developed a tiered system so any purchase under $10,000 wouldn't require requests for proposals to be sent out. Purchases between $10,000 to $25,000 would require staff to reach out to firms and seek quotes for purchases.
Any purchase over $25,000 would have the advertised proposal process, where a formal request for proposal would be required.
Ryan said these revisions would help cut costs. When going through the procurement policy, costs are driven up by having to pay attorneys, engineering firms or other experts to draft the full requests for proposals and then have to pay $400 to advertise it in the newspaper.
"As time progresses, things get more expensive," Ryan said. "You just to keep increasing that number, because it becomes too burdensome. When you get to the $25,000 (mark), that's a substantial amount of money. So you want that public competitive procurement process."
Trappe Commissioners unanimously decided to have a draft of the revised policy ready for consideration for the next council meeting on Nov. 6.

title: Oxford Commissioners Discuss Amending Meeting Procedures Resolution at Workshop
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford commissioners discuss amending meeting procedures resolution at workshop

 October 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 590
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — During a Commissioners of Oxford workshop Wednesday morning, the three town commissioners presented their recommendations for amending a recently passed resolution establishing town meeting procedures.By the end of the workshop, the commissioners agreed to have an amended resolution drafted for the next town meeting on Oct. 8. The commissioners also agreed to continue the discussion at that meeting before taking a vote.
The current resolution in place, passed on Sept. 24, establishes general rules and procedures regarding public participation at town meetings. Specifically, it limits when and for how long public commenters can speak and prohibits heckling, defamatory comments and profanity.
When Commission President Norm Bell introduced the resolution in early September, he said the resolution was developed as a result of "disruptive behavior" at a previous town meeting in August.
At the meeting on Sept. 24, some residents expressed concerns with the limitations on public comment in the resolution, as well as the way in which the resolution was passed.
During the workshop, each commissioner brought their own approach to allaying those concerns.
Bell proposed an amendment to make it more explicit that residents can speak before a vote on an agenda item — not including ordinances, as ordinances require public hearings — at the discretion of the commissioners.
"From time to time, the Commissioners of Oxford may expressly invite public testimony, questions, comments or other forms of public participation during specifically-designated agenda items," Bell read from his draft of the amended resolution.
Bell said his draft amendment would also change the language so commissioners "may" respond to comments and questions from residents during public comment periods, and will answer all questions after the meeting "as quickly" as they can. The resolution passed last week states comments and questions will receive written responses after the meeting is over.
Working off Bell's new draft, Commissioner Katrina Greer said when it comes to public participation during agenda item discussions, the word "may" in Bell's draft should be changed to the word "shall." This change would make it so that public comment must be offered for each agenda item.
Greer said the commissioners don't always know what issues residents will want to speak on.
"Sometimes we're surprised by what's important to the public," she said. "We can't know that until we take the temperature of the room."
Commissioner Tom Costigan proposed having a public comment section at the beginning and end of every meeting like St. Michaels does. He said residents would be able to address any agenda items before they are voted on at the opening of the meeting and ask questions or give comments on any issue before the end of the meeting.
"This structure allows the commission to conduct the town's business without constant interruptions," he said. "It also affords the opportunity for more citizen comment in a constructive and respectful manner."
Greer said she thinks it would be better to limit public comment to each agenda item before a vote is taken because it would better inform the commissioners' vote.
The commissioners agreed to use "shall" instead of "may" in a new draft resolution based on Bell's draft, which they can vote on following discussion at the next town meeting.
At the end of the workshop, residents shared their views. Some said they favored Greer's suggestion of using "shall" and a few said they favored Bell's use of the word "may."
Resident Jim Wilcox suggested that instead of the commissioners choosing between "shall" and "may," they amend the resolution to say that at least one commissioner needs to request public comment on a specific agenda item for it to be added.

title: Oxford Commissioners Pass Meeting Policy, Residents Express Concerns
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford Commissioners pass meeting policy, residents express concerns

 September 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 651
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — Gasps, sighs and exclamations could be heard throughout a Commissioners of Oxford discussion on Tuesday evening that ended in a 2-1 vote to pass a resolution establishing town meeting procedures.The resolution, introduced by Commission President Norm Bell at a town meeting on Sept. 10, establishes general rules and procedures regarding public participation at town meetings. During the Sept. 10 meeting, Bell said the purpose of the policy "is to create an atmosphere where the elected officials, staff and members of the public can attend to business efficiently, fairly and with full participation."
Specifically, the policy limits when and for how long public commenters can speak and prohibits heckling, defamatory comments and profanity. The resolution also makes it so commissioners do not have to answer questions residents ask during public comment.
The different limitations, as well as the way in which the resolution was passed, drew concern from residents.
Both Bell and Commissioner Tom Costigan said during the discussion that the commissioners had been receiving responses from residents regarding Bell's proposed resolution since the previous town meeting when it was introduced.
Commissioner Katrina Greer — who voted against passing the resolution — brought up the town's charter, which says, "the rules of the commissioners shall provide that residents of the town shall have a reasonable opportunity to be heard at any meeting in regard to any municipal question."
Greer said she is proposing a different resolution, which hadn't yet been posted on the town website prior to Tuesday's meeting. Greer said she wanted to schedule a workshop, gather input and put together one merged resolution to vote on.
"There is a need, and most towns have it, for a little bit of rules," she said. "But this is something that the town needs to participate in and see the documents."
Greer said that unlike Bell's proposal that restricts public comment to the end of a meeting, hers would allow for public comment before actionable items, or items that are voted on.
"Letting people talk at the end of the meeting about something that has already been voted on is useless and does not satisfy the requirement for a reasonable opportunity to be heard at the meeting," she said. "It is also dismissive of the right of citizens to participate."
Tensions rose throughout the discussion, which public comment was not allowed during. At one point, one resident asked the commissioners, "Are you really not going to allow public comment on this?"
Bell responded that the commissioners had received feedback prior meeting. When another resident spoke up, Bell said, "Excuse me, there will not be back talk. Please."
At another point, when resident Susan Kordell started to make a comment, Bell banged his gavel and told her to "sit down, please."
At the end of the meeting, Bell said he acted "quickly" to try to stop commenters due to concerns about the commissioners' time to discuss the matter at hand.
Although Greer felt the commissioners should not vote on meeting procedures Tuesday evening, both Costigan and Bell said they were ready to vote.
"It's a resolution, and if there are any amendments to it, we can certainly address them in the two weeks, and we (can) vote on any amendments or changes or adoption of one over the other," Bell said.
Along with approving Bell's proposed resolution, Bell and Costigan agreed to schedule a workshop on the topic for next week so at the next town meeting, the commissioners can consider any amendments that might be suggested.
At the end of the meeting, resident Emilie Knud-Hansen said she though thought the procedure around the resolution at the meeting was unfair.
"We deserve to find out what you're voting on before you say, 'We'll vote on this resolution and then we'll deal with amendments,'" she said. "I think that's really backwards."
Resident Dave Donovan said at the end of the meeting that there was irony in the fact that a resolution on public comment "was itself enacted without public comment."

title: Easton Retains 10-Cent Paper Bag Fee Following Public Hearing
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Easton retains 10-cent paper bag fee following public hearing

 September 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 738
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — After a lengthy public hearing during Monday's meeting, a divided Easton Town Council voted against an ordinance that would have removed a 10-cent fee on paper bags used by retailers after the council last year banned plastic bags.Council President Frank Gunsallus and Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery were in the minority, voting in favor of removing the fee. Public opinion was varied, though most residents spoke in support of keeping the fee in place.
In September 2022, the council passed an ordinance prohibiting retailers from giving customers single-use plastic bags. The law, which went into effect in April of 2023, required retailers to charge customers a fee of at least 10 cents for each paper bag used, encouraging shoppers to bring reusable bags.
On Monday, many residents pointed to the environmental benefits of the 10-cent fee, saying it trains shoppers to bring reusable bags. Some highlighted the effectiveness of a paper bag fee in other towns.
"The law works. The fee is proven effective nationwide," said Marion Arnold, a member of Plastic-Free Easton. "Our law is not a one-off experiment. Millions of plastic bags were never circulated as a result."
Speaking on behalf of the Maryland Retailers Alliance, Sarah Price said grocery stores would make paper bags free to stay competitive with other businesses if the 10-cent fee requirement is waived. One clothing department in another store Price talked to saw an increase in bag costs from $7,000 to $30,000 when the required fee was not present.
Alan Girard, advocacy director at the Chesapeake Bay Foundation, encouraged council to reject the ordinance.
"Compared to plastic bags, paper bags produce two times the solid waste, three times the greenhouse gasses and four times the water consumption of plastic bags," Girard said.
Supporters of the ordinance, including Gunsallus, argued that the 10-cent fee is a burden on low-income residents.
Resident Shari Wilcoxon spoke for more than nine minutes during the public hearing in opposition to the fee. She said she helped collect more than 850 petition signatures from those who want to see the fee requirement removed.
"We are not for bringing back plastic bags," Wilcoxon said. "We are for allowing the merchants the freedom to decide for themselves to charge or not for their customers' bags."
Nearly seven minutes into Wilcoxon's comment, Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis said, "I think time has expired," referring to the time allowed for individuals to comment.
"It has not," Gunsallus replied, stating the extended comment is "permissible" per the town charter.
Public comment has typically been limited to three minutes for individuals and five minutes for organizations. At previous meetings, Gunsallus has asked those who went over the three-minute mark to cede the podium and return after others have spoken.
"We do not have the right to cap speech," Gunsallus said Monday, adding that speakers to follow would receive the additional time afforded to Wilcoxon. " … Anything in this meeting that goes over that, now has to be afforded to every single other speaker. That is the rules that we have. If you want to come back up and speak, you are more than welcome to."
Once the public hearing ended, Gunsallus emphasized that the goal of the ordinance was to remove just the 10-cent paper bag fee and not the plastic bag ban entirely.
Prior to the vote, Montgomery expressed his reasoning for wanting the fee requirement eliminated. He disagreed with claims that the 10-cent fee is manageable for residents.
"It's not trivial to the business community, so we cannot claim that it is trivial to the people who have to pay that fee," Montgomery said.
Davis looked for the council to move past the topic.
"I think we've used an enormous amount of time to discuss this matter, when I have far more things in Ward 4 that I should be dealing with," Davis said. "(I) can't deal with those because we are dealing with this issue."
Davis called for the vote. He joined Ward 1 Councilmember Maureen Curry and Ward 2 Councilmember Don Abbatiello in voting no on the ordinance.
Abbatiello said if the fee requirement proves ineffective moving forward, he's willing to take a second look at removing it "down the road."
"If people are not doing the right thing and recycling and reusing their bags, then this will not work," Abbatiello said. "I'm putting my faith in the folks in Easton and the folks in Talbot County and the folks that come here to shop, that they're going to do the right thing."

title: Oxford Commissioners Mull Meeting Procedures After 'Disruptive Behavior' at August Meeting
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford commissioners mull meeting procedures after 'disruptive behavior' at August meeting

 September 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 579
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — The Commissioners of Oxford will be considering a resolution to establish meeting procedures at its next meeting on Sept. 24.At a regular meeting on Tuesday evening, the commissioners agreed to table the proposed resolution, which would establish general rules and procedures regarding public participation at town meetings.
Commission President Norm Bell, who read the proposed resolution and rules aloud, said the purpose of the policy "is to create an atmosphere where the elected officials, staff and members of the public can attend to business efficiently, fairly and with full participation."
Before reading the resolution, Bell said the proposed rules and procedures were developed as a result of "disruptive behavior" at the previous town meeting on Aug. 27.
During the public comment portion of that meeting, yelling broke out between residents after resident Scott Rensberger asked to sit down with Bell at a later date to discuss a public letter Bell wrote in April. The letter mentioned videos made by Rensberger about government transparency in Oxford.
The incident caused resident Tom Campbell to say that he has a hard time recognizing Oxford anymore.
"This can't be every town meeting," Campbell said Aug. 27. "We're getting nowhere. And it's making it hard for me to cheer on my community anymore."
If the resolution is passed, unless there is a public hearing, public comment would not be permitted until the end of the meeting. Public comments would need to be related to public business, and commenters would not be allowed to ask questions.
"This part of the meeting is not a question-and-answer period," Bell read from the policy. "If a question is asked, it will not be answered."
The policy would limit public comment to three minutes and would allow the commissioners to limit the total time of the public comment period.
The policy would prohibit cheering, booing, interrupting and any other forms of heckling. Defamatory comments, profanity and obscenities will also not be tolerated.
The proposed policy states anyone who wants to record the meeting must do so from a "designated area" in the meeting room and cannot walk around to move equipment during the meeting.
On Tuesday, Bell said it's important that the commissioners conduct business in an environment "where everyone feels safe (and) no one feels threatened, bullied or harassed."
After Bell read the proposed policy, commissioners Katrina Greer and Tom Costigan shared their thoughts on it.
Greer said that she thinks there should be a meeting policy in place, but she didn't want to vote on it on Tuesday and asked that they postpone the vote until the Sept. 24 meeting.
"Anything that we vote on that's as important as public comment should be posted for the public to see five or six days in advance so they get a chance to comment on it," she said.
Greer said she did not like that public comment would only come at the end of the meeting. She said there should be an opportunity for the public to speak before the commissioners take a vote on something. Greer also asked that the policy be amended to take out the part about public comment not being a question and answer period.
"If people ask a question, we should, if we can, answer that question," she said.
Costigan said he agreed with everything in the resolution. But he said he didn't have a problem waiting to vote on it until the next meeting.
"I think that we should put either a thumbs up or a thumbs down on this at our meeting on the 24th," he said.

title: Easton Looking into Using AI, Safeguarding Against Dangers
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Easton looking into using AI, safeguarding against dangers

 September 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 599
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — As artificial intelligence extends its reach, the town of Easton is having preliminary discussions on how AI can be a tool in its daily operations.Easton Town Council President Frank Gunsallus believes there are practical uses in which AI can help governments operate more efficiently, such as sifting through data sets so employees can dedicate more time elsewhere.
"It's as big as the internet or the printing press when you look at humanity, really, the history of it and innovative technologies that come about," Gunsallus said. "In my opinion, this is one of those that has a way to systemically change the way the world functions and commerce transacts."
While Gunsallus said its benefits are exciting, he noted that it's not "something to rush into." At a town workshop on Sept. 3, councilmembers hosted a discussion regarding AI and how the town can move forward in using it responsibly.
One of the major action items was to look into developing an acceptable use policy so employees understand proper usages of artificial intelligence in a town setting. One of the distinctions brought up during the workshop was free programs, such as ChatGPT, versus paid programs and whether information is more at risk when free programs are used.
Scott Messick, the town's IT director, worked with AI in creating the town's parking application that reads license plates and detects activity in parking lots. He emphasized one's purpose when using the technology is of the utmost importance when it comes to security.
"It's not so much the tool you use, but what you're doing with it," Messick said on Sept. 3. He said if an employee is putting personal information into an artificial intelligence tool, "then that is not appropriate."
Easton Utilities, a not-for-profit utility and telecommunications company, provides electric, natural gas, water, internet and more to residents. The company has begun to embrace AI.
Easton Utilities uses a paid program to maintain cybersecurity. Chief Information Officer Fred Christie said it has worked AI into its acceptable use policy.
"The knowledge base or the data store that it's using is where all of the risk is," Christie said in an interview. " … It's very important to make sure that you have an acceptable use policy that tells your employees how they should use it and how they should not use it, and that's where the town of Easton is right now."
Christie noted the cybersecurity defense is an example of predictive AI, in which a program detects "anomalies" and learns on its own what is normal and what isn't. Easton Utilities also uses generative AI, whether it's for internal communication or marketing.
Though not used at Easton Utilities, some companies use predictive AI programs for vegetation management to protect infrastructure or prepare in the case of a hurricane.
"AI is not rocket science, it really isn't," Christie said. "It is essentially a very sophisticated, math-based, statistical-based search base."
Christie said training and educating employees is key to managing the technology effectively and responsibly. While it increases efficiency, AI is not replacing any positions at the company. "It's just going to make us do our job better," he said.
Gunsallus, whose day-to-day job is at an IT service provider in Easton, was happy the town held a workshop so the public knows the town is exploring both the potential benefits and risks of AI programs.
"The good it could do is make things more efficient," Gunsallus said. "It (helps with) savings of time and money. When you're handling other people's money, in my opinion, it is paramount that you are doing just exactly that — being efficient and prudent stewards of the town's finances."

title: Easton Town Council Divided Over Proposal to Remove 10-Cent Paper Bag Fee
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Easton Town Council divided over proposal to remove 10-cent paper bag fee

 September 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 789
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A proposal to remove a 10-cent fee on paper bags in town was brought to the Easton Town Council Tuesday night, drawing mixed opinions from council members and residents.In September 2022, the council passed an ordinance prohibiting retailers from giving customers single-use plastic bags. The law, which went into effect in April of 2023, required retailers to charge customers a fee of at least 10 cents for each paper bag used, encouraging shoppers to bring reusable bags.
Ordinance 829, introduced at Tuesday's meeting, would alter the original ordinance and allow businesses to provide paper bags free of charge.
"The reason for the proposal to remove this fee comes directly from the voices of many Easton residents who are feeling its impact," said Council President Frank Gunsallus, "especially those in lower-income brackets who are already stretching every dollar to make ends meet."
Gunsallus and Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery both said they've talked to residents who do not support the current 10-cent fee. The rest of the council, though, stated otherwise.
"I have heard from many people the exact opposite, that the ban is working and that the 10 cents is not onerous in any way, shape or form," Ward 1 Councilmember Maureen Curry said.
Ward 2 Councilmember Don Abbatiello and Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis stated the fee has incentivized people to bring their own reusable bags. Abbatiello said, "the reason for that (fee) is because paper bags pollute just as much as plastic bags do."
"I'm just not quite sure why we're even diving into all of this," Davis said, asking that the paper bag fee remain in place. "It blows my mind."
Gunsallus asked that a public hearing on the ordinance be added to the council's agenda for the next meeting so residents affected by the paper bag fee have the time to "plan ahead" and attend.
Davis asked that the discussion not be extended to a future meeting, pointing out the large crowd in attendance, most of whom were in support of keeping the 10-cent fee.
"So you're saying you want to hold this over because there's some people that need to be here?" Davis asked Gunsallus.
"(They) should be able to voice their concerns over the public hearing," Gunsallus responded. "That is a routine part of the process."
"Not everyone is privileged enough to have a salary where 10 cents is a negligible fee," Gunsallus later said, after Curry asked audience members in support of the fee to raise their hands.
Abbatiello stated that while he will vote against the proposed ordinance to remove the fee, he's willing to have the issue go to a public hearing.
"I still think that everybody should have an opportunity to speak," he said. "I think that's important. So if we hold this over until the next meeting, I'm fine with that."
Curry made a motion to dismiss the proposed ordinance and not discuss it at the town's next meeting. Davis seconded that motion, but it failed, as Abbatiello, Montgomery and Gunsallus voted against it. Gunsallus stated a public hearing on the paper bag fee ordinance will be held Sept. 16.
PUBLIC INPUTNearly all of the residents in attendance at Tuesday's meeting spoke in disapproval of the proposed ordinance to remove paper bag fees. Some brought reusable bags to display, and others brought signs that read, "KEEP THE 10 CENT FEE."
Many members of Plastic-Free Easton, a group that lobbied for the plastic bag ban in 2022, spoke on Tuesday.
"We didn't want to go from free plastic bags to free paper bags, effectively going from one type of environmental problem to another," member Elaine Tama said. "We need a more livable climate for our children and grandchildren's future."
Sarah Price spoke on behalf of the Maryland Retailers Alliance, indicating the group recommends council to maintain the original ordinance so that businesses aren't forced to drop the fee and subsequently increase grocery prices.
"If you remove the mandated fee, businesses will likely have to reduce or completely remove the fee to remain competitive with one another, and you will see your prices go up in all likelihood," Price said.
Easton resident Shari Wilcoxon held a different stance, questioning why the businesses are forced to charge the 10-cent fee.
"I don't know why people are afraid of freedom of choice," Wilcoxon said. "Why don't you let the merchants decide if they want to charge or not, what's wrong with that?"
Following a lengthy public comment section, Gunsallus emphasized the proposed ordinance is not meant to bring plastic bags back. He said it was brought to the table to address the struggles of "people who are having a hard time (making) ends meet."
"That is why this has been introduced, that's why it's being discussed, that's why it's being revisited," Gunsallus said. "However the pieces fall, so be it."

title: Oxford Tables Plastic Bag Ban Ordinance
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford tables plastic bag ban ordinance

 August 29, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 521
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — Following a nearly 30-minute public hearing, the Commissioners of Oxford tabled an ordinance that would ban retail establishments in town from giving out single-use, disposable plastic bags.At a town meeting on Aug. 27, Town Attorney Lyndsey Ryan said the ban would apply to retail establishments including grocery stores, convenience stores, shops, department stores and service stations. The ordinance would not apply to restaurants and food service establishments.
Ryan said while the ordinance would apply to the Oxford Market, it would not apply to the deli within the market.
"So the sandwiches, subs, things like that that would be wrapped in plastic would continue to be in plastic," she said.
During the public hearing, some local business owners and employees expressed their concerns with the proposed ordinance. Graham Norbury, the general manager at Safe Harbor Oxford, said that while this may be a national issue, he doesn't observe plastic bags being littered often in Oxford.
"Why is restricting a retailer's right to choose the best delivery mechanism for their products, why is that something that the commissioners feel necessary?" he asked.
Oxford Vintage & Trade owner Barbara Ranson said in her six years of being in business in Oxford, she has always used paper bags. She said she doesn't understand why the commissioners are looking at this legislation when "it may or may not target three very small businesses."
"So it seems to me (like) legislation looking for a problem, and I don't understand why we would spend one minute on this," she said, receiving some applause from residents in the audience.
Ranson also brought up a part of the ordinance that would require retail establishments to charge a 10 cent fee — which the retail establishment would keep — for each paper bag it hands out to customers. She said that having to charge and keep track of that would take up time and labor and would just be another thing that the town needs to enforce.
"And who's going to do that?" she asked. "Because we already have ordinances that are not enforced because we don't have anybody to do them."
Resident David Donovan, who is in support of the ordinance, acknowledged that it won't solve the global problem.
"But if every one of us in every little town stands up and does their share, you do solve a problem," he said.
Resident Rose Donovan said she considers this to be a "common sense ordinance." She said this is a way to stop using plastic bags "where we can."
Commissioner Katrina Greer said she feels passionately about banning plastic, but Oxford is facing a lot of other important issues now.
"So I would like to find a way forward with this. But perhaps just not now," she said, adding that there is more commissioners should consider regarding the ordinance.
Before the commissioners voted unanimously to table the ordinance, Ryan brought up the idea of giving retail establishments an incentive to not use plastic bags, rather than banning them. She said the commissioners could consider a tax incentive, among other possible incentives.
Commission President Norm Bell said they should bring all of these ideas to the table before they make a decision.

title: Proposed St. Michaels Tourism Board Met with Pushback
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Proposed St. Michaels tourism board met with pushback

 August 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 738
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — On Wednesday evening, St. Michaels commissioners were faced with outcry from residents regarding the town's proposed Tourism Advisory Board.Residents raised an array of concerns, including potential conflicts of interests and a lack of data supporting the board's creation.
An exact timeline for further creating the tourism board has not been established, according to Commissioner Jay Hudson. But commissioners voiced a desire to act quickly on the matter during Wednesday's meeting.
"There was a pushback on what we proposed towards the board, which was a little surprising, which means that we have to go back a little bit and get some modifications and see if we can't come to a resolution," Commissioner David Wojciechowski said. "In the end, we are running out of time."
The idea of a tourism board was brought forth during a commissioners candidate forum hosted by the St. Michaels Business Association last April, when representatives of the Business Associations stated a need for marketing assistance due to a decrease in revenues within the last year.
During that forum, David Wojciechowski, Alexis Roiter and Jay Hudson, who were all later elected as commissioners, said they would work with business owners to make the town more friendly to their needs.
The Tourism Advisory Board was again raised during a July 10 meeting while the town was hearing marketing bids. At the direction of the commissioners, an ordinance was pulled together to establish the board.
The purpose of the board, according to a town memo, would be to assist the town in its efforts to encourage businesses to locate or remain in the town and to make recommendations to the commissioners. The board would also "work closely with the Talbot County Tourism Board on a unified, regional marketing approach."
The board would comprise seven members serving four-year terms, all appointed by the commissioners. Membership would include residents not associated with a business and representatives from the lodging, eating/drinking, retail or service, marinas, museums and nonprofit sectors.
DATADuring the public hearing Wednesday, resident Daniel Spiegel said the establishment of the tourism board is based on anecdotal information provided by St. Michaels business owners and not on actual data.
"The major rationale for this board, according to the language of the ordinance, is to promote business and retain business in this town," Spiegel said. "And I'd like to know whether the commission has been presented (with data) other than anecdotal information?"
Wojciechowski said part of the purpose of the Tourism Advisory Board would be to obtain data. He said he felt the board would provide an incentive for businesses to volunteer their revenue data so the town can have a better understanding of the needs they may have.
David Breimhurst, a resident and former St. Michaels commissioner, said he appreciated Wojciechowski's words on data gathering, but he proposed other means of obtaining it.
"I would suggest an in-depth economic study by a first tier economic study group would be the first step, so that we understand the true nature of our economy," Breimhurst said. "… So the data is most important, and I don't see any data supporting the rationale for creating this board in the first place."
CONFLICT OF INTERESTThe secondary concern brought by residents was the "conflict of interest" this board would pose to the town.
"You are making these business people and using representatives part of the structure of this town," Spiegel said. "And you will defer to them in terms of their ideas and recommendations, and their ideas and recommendations are going to have a budgetary impact that are going to impact their own financial well being, and that is a conflict of interest that should be avoided."
Commissioner Alexis Roiter gave a brief comment emphasizing the tourism board would focus on advising. It would not be a governmental board, she said.
"You can call it anything you want," Spiegel said "This is a board you are appointing. This board, they are governed by the laws and the rules and the ordinances of this town. You aren't creating a business advisory committee that you meet with from time to time. You are creating a mechanism that has all of the attributes of the Planning Commission."
After a bit of back and forth, Roiter suggested the town may need a tourism task force rather than a tourism board — an idea residents seem to agree on.
Toward the end of discussion, commissioners agreed to bring the subject of the tourism board up for discussion again at the next meeting in September.

title: Oxford Adopts Administrative Guide, Clarifies Agenda Setting
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford adopts administrative guide, clarifies agenda setting

 August 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 344
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — On Tuesday, the Commissioners of Oxford approved a resolution to adopt an administrative guide for town employees and commissioners and to clarify the authority to set agendas for commissioners meetings.The resolution also makes it so that commission meeting agendas will now have a consent agenda, which groups agenda items to be voted on together. Department head reports will be placed on the consent agenda. Commissioner Katrina Greer said this will allow for more legislative time at meetings.
The resolution, effective immediately, permits the commissioners to develop and adopt administrative policies that "promote good governance and transparency."
Greer made the motion to pass the resolution at the commission meeting on Tuesday. The resolution was passed unanimously.
"We've been talking about how to best deal with each other and the staff and setting up some norms," Greer said before the vote.
When it comes to agenda setting, the resolution sets deadlines for when items can be submitted and states that the commissioners must approve the agenda.
The administrative guide will break down what commissioners must approve and be notified of and what decisions and tasks are under the authority of the town manager or clerk treasurer. The guide will also details that in the event there is not a town manager, those duties will be taken on by the clerk treasurer with guidance from the commissioners.
The town has been without a manager since the retirement of former Town Manager Cheryl Lewis at the end of June.
The commissioners' next open session meeting will be next Tuesday, Aug. 20 at 6 p.m.
Greer said the commissioners will also be holding a special closed meeting on Friday to discuss search firm contracts. The town is seeking a search firm to help in its search for the next town manager.
Commission President Norm Bell said the commissioners started with a list of seven search firms and have since narrowed it down to five. He said some due diligence is still needed before the commission can come to a decision, but if all goes well, the commissioners will vote on a search firm next Tuesday.

title: Easton, Town Manager Agree to 'Part Ways'
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Easton, town manager agree to 'part ways'

 August 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 576
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Town of Easton and Town Manager Donald "Don" Richardson have come to a "mutual agreement to part ways" effective Monday, according to a Tuesday press release from Mayor Megan Cook.Terms regarding the separation are still being considered by both parties.
"This difficult decision was made with the best interest and long-term health for the Town of Easton in mind, and the continued success and well-being of our employees and community as our top priority," Cook said in a statement. "Personally, I appreciate the work and support Don provided when I served on the council and again during my transition to the role of mayor."
In an interview with the Star Democrat, Cook said she couldn't say why the decision was made and probably would not give any detail in the future, but she reiterated it was a mutual decision. Cook was in charge of the decision, she said, as the mayor has the power to hire and fire the town manager.
Richardson began his career with the Town of Easton in 2007, serving as a code official. He was instrumental in helping the Town of Easton Building Department become Maryland's first International Accreditation Service accredited building department. Richardson was then appointed to town manager by Mayor Bob Willey in September 2016 and was instrumental in overseeing the administration, operations and budget of multiple department.
During his tenure, Richardson was involved as a leader on numerous major projects, including Mistletoe Hall Commerce and Business Park, Housing on the Hill, Rails to Trails, Easton Point Park and stream restorations.
Richardson was not present at the Easton Town Council meeting on Monday.
Cook said the process to hire a new town manager has not yet begun but will as soon as possible. She said the town will advertise the position through the Maryland Municipal League, the Maryland Association of Counties and "all other avenues" they have used in the past for hiring other positions. A committee will be tasked with going through resumes, she said.
Once interviews have been held and the list of candidates has been narrowed down, Cook will make a recommendation to the Easton Town Council. The council will then either approve or deny the request.
Cook anticipates it will take about three to five months to hire a new town manager.
In the meantime, Easton Police Chief Alan Lowrey will serve interim town manager. Town Council President Frank Gunsallus said the council voted unanimously to approve Lowrey as the interim town manager.
Lowrey said although he hasn't been a town manager before, and there's a lot for him to "come up to speed on," the Town of Easton already has a good team in place, which will make it easier to lead.
He said that while he is maintaining both roles of police chief and interim town manager, Deputy Chief Greg Wright is "well-capable" of keeping operations running at the police department.
Cook said she thinks Lowrey will be a good fit for the interim position.
"I really like his way of thinking," she said. "He has a very analytical mind and a good perspective."
Cook said that with Lowrey and Wright, the Easton Police Department has "two good leaders." She said she felt that "would offer an opportunity" for Lowrey to spend part of his time in the main office.
"I want to thank him for taking on this additional responsibility," Cook said in the news release. "Our focus is to ensure a smooth transition and maintain the excellent services we provide to our community."

title: Oxford Commissioners Interview Recruiting Firms for Open Town Manager Position
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Oxford commissioners interview recruiting firms for open town manager position

 August 2, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 530
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — In an effort to move past the town's recent fruitless town manager hire, the Commissioners of Oxford held workshops Wednesday to interview two recruiting firms.This workshop was held a month after the town passed resolution requiring the hiring of a search firm for the town manager position as a result of controversy concerning the former town manager hire, Michael Calvert.
Calvert — who was previously a city administrator for Liberty, South Carolina — had been slated to get sworn in as Oxford's next town manager in July. But just three days after announcing the hire on June 24, the Commissioners of Oxford announced the town and Calvert had "mutually agreed to part ways."
Shortly after the news of Calvert's hire, some community members expressed concerns about the town's candidate vetting process.
In an effort to move forward with finding a new candidate, Commissioner Katrina Greer introduced the resolution during a July 9 meeting, requiring the town to use a "professional search team that specializes in local government."
During the workshops Wednesday, separate interviews were held for the two firms, GovHRUSA and Berkley Group.
Each firm gave a presentation showing the goals, working timeline and outreach that could be done if they were hired. After each presentation, the commissioners asked questions of the firms.
Commissioner Katrina Greer requested a thorough understanding of the background checks each firm conducts on candidates.
Charlene Stevens, executive vice president for recruitment services at GovHRUSA, said her firm prides itself on ensuring well-researched candidates.
"We do media searches on candidates, to understand what is out there on them, as well as be able to have a conversation with them," Stevens said. "If there's media that is concerning, then … Mike (senior consultant) will review that information with you and make sure that you are comfortable moving forward with the candidate."
Kelsey Wong, chief operating officer for Berkley Group, said her firm uses a third-party background check to assess candidates but at the time could not remember the name of the company and said she could provide that information later.
Greer stated it was vital for the firm to come back with the company name since the background check was essential for hiring a new candidate.
"We had a problem with (background checks), and we would want criminal search to go back a number of years, do the credit check, do the civil check, etc. because people are handling money and purchases, etc.," Greer said. "And a national criminal check going back 23 years."
Each commissioner asked questions concerning issues of the timeline of hire, whether or not the firms have worked with communities with populations below 1,000, networking and how the firms involve the community in the hiring process.
Commissioner Tom Costigan said the workshop was informative and helpful for the process of finding a new town manager.
"It's important to us because we're basically doing our due diligence to find the best possible candidate for our town manager position," Costigan said.
A decision will be made in the "next couple of weeks," and a follow up meeting with Berkley Group was requested to be scheduled to meet the rest of the team and to have a better understanding of the firm's background check process, according to Greer.

title: 'Difficult and frustrating period for our town': Oxford hears from public after fruitless town manager hire
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
'Difficult and frustrating period for our town': Oxford hears from public after fruitless town manager hire

 July 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 734
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — In an effort to rebuild from controversy faced in the aftermath of a recent hire, Oxford hosted a public comment and passed a resolution to better vet future candidates.With the anticipated large turnout for the Commissioners of Oxford meeting Tuesday evening, the town opted to move the event from its regular location on Market Street to the Oxford Community Center.
More than 100 people were in attendance, with many people standing against the walls of the building when available seating was filled.
"This has been a difficult and frustrating period for our town and its leadership," Commissioner Tom Costigan said to the crowd. "... We thought we had secured the services of the best candidate possible using the information we had available. I'm disappointed to admit that we were wrong."
CONTROVERSEY
The center of controversy is Michael Calvert, the town's would-be-town manager.
Calvert — who was previously a city administrator for Liberty, South Carolina — had been slated to get sworn in as Oxford's next town manager at this meeting. But just three days after announcing the hire, the Commissioners of Oxford announced the town and Calvert had "mutually agreed to part ways."
According to a statement sent out June 27, the town and Calvert determined that "it was not a good fit."
Shortly after the news of Calvert's hire, some community members expressed concerns. Oxford resident Scott Rensberger said it was "shocking" the town didn't vet Calvert more because it took him a short time to find out "there were a lot of problems" in Liberty.
Former Liberty City Council member Peggy Edwards told the Star Democrat she resigned from the council due to issues with Calvert and the city's mayor. She said that when Calvert was in the position, there was a lack of transparency and mismanagement of money.
According to a November news release from the City of Liberty, Calvert resigned at the beginning of the year after nearly two and a half years in the position. He cited family relocation as the reason for his resignation.
MOVING FORWARD
Commissioner Katrina Greer said Tuesday it was essential to move forward with the hiring process methodically, thoughtfully and with more input.
"I move to make a resolution to have a search firm conduct the search for a town manager," Greer said. "... This process of finding the right firm and the right fit might take several weeks, and we will be looking for input, but we should tell the public that we have a plan that we are going to professional services."
Greer said this resolution would require the town to use a "professional search team that specializes in local government." Costigan seconded the resolution, and it was unanimously approved by the commission.
In March, the commissioners voted to place advertisements for Lewis' position and issue a request for proposal for a search firm in the event it is needed. On June 27, Costigan said the town did not end up using a search firm in the search that resulted in Calvert's hire.
In addition to the resolution, Greer said the town should not delay too long in moving forward with hiring a new candidate due to the pressure it would put on the staff.
PUBLIC COMMENT
During public comment, several people spoke their concerns to the commission.
Jane Greenhawk, an Oxford resident, said she appreciated that the town will be using a professional search firm but would like answers to how the town ended up in this position in the first place. She asked several questions of the commissioners, including whether or not a criminal background check was completed and who had completed the background check?
Lyndsey Ryan, Oxford Attorney, attempted to answer all of Greenhawk's questions. After a bit of back-and-forth, Ryan said the background investigation was done through an online firm by the prior town manager.
In a June 28 statement, the Commissioners of Oxford said that Calvert underwent a pre-employment background check but that the results could not be disclosed because they are "confidential personnel records."
Grace Nave, an Oxford native, advocated for hiring someone local to fill the position.
"I really am so proud of this town that I know there's a lot of hiccups in it," Nave said. "There's good, bad, ugly and sad, but I want us to try to maybe think about the possibility of hiring someone local. If you hire somebody professional, you might get the top notch, but if they're out of town, they don't love this town like we do."

title: Easton Town Council Passes Ordinance to Prohibit Outdoor Music at Night
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Easton Town Council passes ordinance to prohibit outdoor music at night

 July 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 384
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A new ordinance to prohibit outdoor music after 10 p.m. was passed by the Easton Town Council on Monday. It comes after residents expressed concerns about excessive noise coming from the Tidewater Inn on Dover Street.Ordinance 823 states that "amplified music from commercial establishments" is not allowed from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. Council members voted unanimously to approve the legislation after a short discussion.
Resident Helen Houseman lives on Goldsborough Street right behind the hotel and wedding business. She explained her concerns to council members Monday.
"I'd only moved in for a couple of months when the Tidewater hosted a wedding," Houseman said. "And that music was so loud that I couldn't hear my TV. I could make out every single lyric that was playing.
"It's all about the decibels. It is so incredibly loud … When they host an event in that tent, it is so irresponsibly loud that it's profoundly affecting my quality of life."
Enid McKitrick, Houseman's neighbor, agreed.
"It wasn't just the noise, it was the vibrations in the walls," McKitrick said. "It felt as if there was a band in my bedroom. It was so loud."
Resident Brandi Whiting felt the 10 p.m. cutoff was a bit early.
"I think cutting it off at 10 is a little drastic if you want to keep bringing in young people into this town," Whiting said. "There's not a lot to do after 9, not a lot to do after 8."
The ordinance defines amplified music as "any music that is played outside of enclosed structures and is amplified through speakers or other electronic means." It also states that if doors or windows are open for an "extended period," then music from indoors will be considered outdoor music and thus be prohibited.
"I do think that Tidewater and any other business should be good neighbors," Ward 4 Council Member the Rev. Elmer Davis said. "If they're having something outside, they should talk to the neighbors and make them aware of what's going on. It's about being neighborly."
Council President Frank Gunsallus noted that the ordinance does include the option for businesses to procure a permit to play outdoor music during the restricted hours. The ordinance also exempts "music played for government-sponsored events and ceremonies."
The ordinance will go into effect 20 days following approval from Easton Mayor Megan Cook.

title: Lengthy Public Comment Examines Council’s Stance on Pride
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Lengthy public comment examines council’s stance on Pride

 July 2, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 904
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — For the third consecutive meeting, Easton residents filled town council chambers to express opinions on council rhetoric regarding last month's Delmarva Pride Festival, Pride banners and the LGBTQ+ community.Council President Frank Gunsallus originally came under scrutiny for comments made at a May 20 council meeting. At that meeting, he said the Pride flag was "antithetical to America" and questioned whether town funds should support downtown Pride banners.
Richard Potter, the president of Talbot County's NAACP branch, told Gunsallus on Monday that his office will send the council vice president a letter requesting a meeting this week.
"We found the rhetoric from this council troublesome," Potter said. "We found the information resembling that of the Jim Crow era."
"That rhetoric when I heard it, coming from members of the council, it was disturbing," resident Rudy Reyes said Monday. "I did feel unsafe.
"I'm also scared. I think a lot of people, especially after the May 20 meeting, are scared. A lot of people don't want to come up here in front of the council to address some of the things that were said."
The June 3 meeting was the first of three highly-attended meetings in which residents pushed back on Gunsallus' comments. That is also when Ward 3 Council Member David Montgomery claimed there is a present "danger to our community from promotion of (the) transexual ideology."
At the subsequent June 17 meeting, Mayor Megan Cook, along with many residents, denounced Montgomery's comments.
On Monday, numerous residents spoke in support of Montgomery.
"I feel that we have devolved into a me against you and you against me," resident Anne Cerutti said. " … I saw nothing wrong with what Mr. Gunsallus and Mr. Montgomery had said."
Resident Judi Esola thanked Montgomery and Gunsallus for "being free." "I think we're afraid of being conservative," Esola added.
Montgomery said Monday's meeting was "a much more congenial atmosphere" than the June 17 meeting, in which one resident called on him and Gunsallus to resign.
"I appreciate those who have spoken on both sides, but in particular hearing the emphasis that these are opinions, these are points of view," Montgomery said.
FESTIVAL PERMIT
In January, Gunsallus and Montgomery each voted against a permit for this year's third annual Delmarva Pride Festival in downtown Easton. Kyle O'Donnell, chair of the Delmarva Pride Center, told council members Monday that he has filed for a public assembly permit for 2025.
He said the center is committed to continuing the "family-friendly event," adding that he would like to see the council return to the unanimous, bipartisan support for the permit it had in 2022 and 2023.
"If you cannot bring yourself to vote yes for this public assembly permit, to vote yes for freedom, consider casting a respectful abstention," O'Donnell said.
Residents on both sides spoke out during the public comment section.
"Nobody needs to go after our children," resident Catherine Nobles said. "We do not need them coached, we do not need them groomed, we do not need them telling their parents that they have no rights to what they want to do."
"I saw so many happy families, happy children," resident Brandi Whiting said of the festival. " … What I didn't see was scantily clad people, I didn't see people grooming anybody. … I saw businesses making money … and I saw dollar signs."
BIAS COMPLAINT
At the start of Monday's meeting, Gunsallus read aloud a statement from Talbot County Sheriff Joe Gamble regarding a hate bias complaint filed last month.
Tina Jones, a board member of the Delmarva Pride Center, filed the complaint June 7 to the attorney general's office in light of the previous council comments. The attorney general's office then directed her to reach out to Talbot County law enforcement.
She said she called the Talbot County Sheriff's Office to report the bias incident.
Jones told The Star Democrat that her main goal is to have open dialogue with council. Although Jones said she spoke with Gunsallus following a June meeting, she said neither Montgomery nor Gunsallus have reached out to her privately to discuss the matter.
"I'm trying to have a dialogue," Jones said. "And I have offered that up every time I've spoken."
The statement from Gamble said that after reviewing Easton Town Council video footage, the Talbot County State's Attorney's Office and the Office of the State Prosecutor determined that there was no hate crime committed at the meeting.
"However, since the Maryland law required police departments to take reports for bias incidents, our office generated a report and the incident was documented," the statement said. "This is not a criminal investigation."
Gamble told The Star Democrat he contacted the attorney general's office to obtain a legal definition for a hate bias incident, to which the office said there is no legal definition.
"My office does not weigh in on whether a bias incident occurred since there is no legal definition on what exactly a bias incident is," Gamble's statement read by Gunsallus said. "The Maryland legislature passed the law in 2019 requiring Maryland law enforcement to take these reports but failed miserably to give legal guidance."
Jones attended Monday's meeting but did not speak during public comment as she has in previous meetings.
"Clearly, I feel like I have a target on my back," Jones said. "It would've been very difficult for me to get up there last night and state on the record ... what my home address is. There's a level of fear."
This report has been updated to further clarify the history of discussions between Jones and Gunsallus.

title: Easton Town Council Hears Support, Pushback in Aftermath of Pride Festival
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Easton Town Council hears support, pushback in aftermath of Pride festival

 June 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 589
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — In the wake of the Delmarva Pride Center's third annual Pride festival last Saturday, the Easton Town Council saw a full chamber June 17.For a second consecutive meeting, many attendees spoke out in support of Pride initiatives and the festival, including Tina Jones, a board member of the Delmarva Pride Center.
"Those four days were a time of love and joy, of music and dance," Jones said of the festival. "Everyone could be themselves, love themselves and share their love with others."
The June 3 meeting saw significant pushback on council President Frank Gunsallus for questioning whether the town funds should support downtown Pride banners at a council meeting in May.
"I think it is safe to say that the economic return to the Town of Easton more than offset the cost of a few banners and a handful of street lights," Jones said on June 17.
Some who attended the festival thanked council members they saw Saturday, including Gunsallus, Curry and Davis.
Resident Jen Voshell spoke during public comment to Gunsallus, "wondering if (he) would consider retracting (his) previous opposition" and "support the permitting (of the festival) in 2025." In January, Gunsallus and Ward 3 council member David Montgomery voted against issuing the permit to hold the annual event.
At the end of Monday's meeting, Gunsallus said he "(appreciated) the meaningful conversations with members of the community" and was "glad that everyone had a good time" at the festival.
Others spoke to express displeasure with the council's approval of the festival's permit.
Resident Gary Judy called out the council members who approved the festival's permit in January by a 3-2 vote — Maureen Curry, Don Abbatiello and the Rev. Elmer Davis. "You three will be remembered for opening this door," he said, adding that other groups may now have the ability to obtain festival permits.
Shari Wilcoxon, who wrote to the council in the winter asking for the festival to be held on West Street instead of South Harrison Street, called Monday evening for the council to be "apolitical."
"Would you fully support … a Moms for Liberty parade?" Wilcoxon asked. "Would you pay for banners?"
MONTGOMERY COMMENTS
Meanwhile, other meeting attendees addressed Montgomery's comments from the June 3 meeting, which included a claim of "danger to our community from promotion of (the) transexual ideology."
"By saying that Pride, the Pride flag or any section of our LGBT community is merely an ideology overlooks what the essence of Pride is: a celebration of human rights and the recognition of inherent dignity of all individuals regardless of their (sexual) orientation or gender identity," Mayor Megan Cook said at the outset of Monday's meeting.
Montgomery responded, saying he "did not appreciate being chastised" by Cook. The mayor said they will likely not ever "see eye-to-eye on social issues," but that she hopes everyone can keep an "open mind."
"What I'm trying to do is to be helpful to those who are being misled by what I think is clearly an ideology, and it's demonstrated by the way my comments were received last month," Montgomery said. "Shouting someone down in an effort of de-platforming simply proves we are dealing with an ideology and a political movement."
Jen Wagner, a St. Michaels resident who owns a business in Easton, took to the podium to call for the resignation of Gunsallus and Montgomery, to which the Town Council president said "that's too far."
"I will not prolong this debate tonight on facts or their interpretation," Montgomery said at the meeting's end. "I will object to personal attacks, which exclusively came from the audience directed in this direction."

title: Gunsallus Scrutinized for Easton Pride Flag Comments
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Gunsallus scrutinized for Easton Pride flag comments

 June 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 840
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A packed chamber at Easton's June 3 Town Council meeting spoke out against Council President Frank Gunsallus for his remarks during a meeting last month concerning Pride flags and the LGBTQ+ community.At the May 20 meeting, Gunsallus said that the Pride flag is "antithetical to America" and questioned whether the town should use funds to support such flags and banners.
"I believe that it is a socialist endeavor parading beyond or behind the guise of a social movement," Gunsallus said May 20. "And I think that we should not be using taxpayer funds to support a cause that is antithetical to our country and our principles and our Constitution."
Many residents addressed those comments directly during Monday's Town Council.
"Council President Gunsallus, you, sir, have done the citizens of Easton a great service by revealing your personal bigotry," Easton resident Elizabeth Parks said. "We know not to vote for you ever. To say that LGBTQ people are antithetical to what America stands for, is to say that you would deny them the right to be who they are."
Parks and subsequent residents received loud applause for their words during the public comment section.
"The comments made at the previous meeting showed that the LGBTQ members of the Easton community cannot trust the council," resident Lauren Fierman said. "... Why are you pushing back so much on the LGBTQ community when Easton enthusiastically supports Juneteenth, Waterfowl Festival, St. Patrick's Day parades?"
"I do not believe that the leadership of the council was interested in saving money," resident Kelley Moran said. "I believe that the interest of the council leadership was in looking at a way to remove the Pride flags."
Resident Shari Wilcoxon was one of a few residents who spoke in support of the council president.
"This is not a topic about gay people. That's not what I heard," Wilcoxon said. "The topic that I heard was about fiscal responsibility of this Town Council. ... I'm thankful that (Gunsallus) is diligently looking out for the financial well-being of Easton."
After a lengthy public comment section, Gunsallus addressed his remarks from the previous meeting.
"I'd like to clear the air — the absolute truth is that I firmly believe all people are equal and should be treated as such," he said. "This is why I support every member of our community. While aiming to be cognizant of the challenges they face, as an elected official, I must be fiscally responsible and use hard-earned taxpayer dollars to support the town's operational needs. And that was the focus of my comments from the last meeting. I apologize if my intent was not clear."
In January, the council tackled a similar topic, with Gunsallus and Ward 3 Council Member David Montgomery voting against a public assembly permit for the Delmarva Pride Center's annual Pride festival, held June 13 to 16.
MONTGOMERY COMMENTS
Montgomery supported Gunsallus' statements about the flags May 20 and doubled down Monday evening.
"We were discussing first an issue about the town displaying Pride flags," Montgomery said. "…I do not believe it is the town's business to make everyone feel good about their identity."
Montgomery continued, stating the country is being "torn apart by identity politics." He went on to call out the transgender community's involvement in the LGBTQ+ movement specifically, which was met with boos and some attendees leaving the chamber.
"This is about the hijacking of the movement by a transexual ideology," he said.
"This country's being torn apart because of people like you," one attendee said out loud. Others called Montgomery "pathetic."
"I've listened to everyone here and I've noticed that every one of you misstated what Frank and I were talking about," Montgomery said, referencing the May 20 comments. "What I stated was that there is a danger to our community from promotion of this transexual ideology.
"...This town has no business putting up flags that promote the notion that you will feel better, you will solve your teenage problems if you decide that you should go out and demand your sex be changed," he continued. "That's what I object to, nothing about any individual."
OTHER COUNCIL COMMENTS
Following Tuesday's public comments, Ward 1 council member Maureen Curry stated her support for the residents and the LGBTQ+ community, with Ward 2 council member Don Abbatiello echoing her stance.
"I am fully supportive of the LGBTQ community and the Delmarva Pride Center, and I'm looking forward to celebrating with you this month," Curry said. "Words do matter. ... I'm on your side."
Ward 4 council member the Rev. Elmer Davis Jr. stated to the council and audience: "We should learn to love everybody. We're not all going to agree on things."
Prior to public comment, Easton Mayor Megan Cook denounced Gunsallus' original comments before the council, which was met with applause from a number of attendees.
"I feel those comments were dangerous, and they do foster a climate of intolerance and exclusion," Cook said. "Asserting that the Pride flag or support of our LGBTQ community is antithetical to our country or our Constitution is incorrect.
"When such divisive comments are made, it begins to tear at the fabric of our town."

title: Easton Town Attorney Brings Town Council Draft Amendment to Hospital Agreement
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Easton town attorney brings Town Council draft amendment to hospital agreement

 May 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 585
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Three weeks after attorneys for the Town of Easton, Talbot County and UM Shore Regional Health came before new regional medical center stakeholders to discuss possible upcoming amendments to the development rights and responsibilities agreement, Town Attorney Sharon VanEmburgh brought the Town Council a draft.The original agreement, which was signed in 2014, ensures that zoning will not change for the land that Shore Regional intends to build a new hospital on. Specifically, the agreement — which was negotiated by the town, the county and UM Shore Regional Health — vests Shore Regional in Easton's Regional Healthcare zoning district.
The regional medical center is planned to be built off Longwoods Road in Easton. According to previous Star Democrat reporting, construction on the medical center is anticipated to begin in spring 2025, with doors tentatively opening in summer 2028.
At the April 15 workshop, which brought together representatives from UM Shore Regional Health and the county and town governments, VanEmburgh mentioned changes in the construction industry, dates that are no longer realistic in today's climate and changes in the hospital's needs and utility requirements as some of the reasons for why an amendment is necessary.
At the Town Council meeting Monday, VanEmburgh said most of what the draft amendment does is take things out of the original DRRA to be put into a public works agreement with more specific information.
"Because that information is not available at this time as we are moving forward with the amendment to the DRRA," she said.
Items that would be taken out of the agreement include "several" utility specifics including completion dates and capacity needs at various points in the project.
VanEmburgh said the most substantive proposed change to the agreement is to expand the 30-year-term of the DRRA.
"It's been 10 years and no development has occurred yet," VanEmburgh said. "So Shore Health would like that term — because it's 30 years originally — to start from when we enter into this amendment."
Other proposed changes to the agreement include updates to the existing land use regulations to match ordinances that have passed since the agreement was made and updates to the ownership of land, as Shore Regional has taken title of the properties since entering into the agreement.
After VanEmburgh spoke, Ward 4 council member the Rev. Elmer Davis Jr. asked whether the amendment included the addition of a fire apparatus, which Ward 2 Council member Don Abbatiello asked about during the workshop on April 15. At the workshop, Abbatiello voiced support for adding that the Shore Regional include a fire apparatus in the project "to meet any needs that the hospital might have."
In response to Davis' question, UM Shore Regional Health Attorney Ryan Showalter said Shore Health is in the process of cutting things out of the project to make the budget work. He said adding a fire apparatus to the project is not consistent with those efforts, but they are open to continuing discussion.
Abbatiello said he understood money would be tight during construction and was hoping this could be agreed upon for later on, not during construction of the hospital.
"So it's a shame that that couldn't make it in (the drafted amendment)," he said. "Because ... the town and the (fire) department was hoping for some kind of commitment down the road."
VanEmburgh recommended the council set a public hearing and refer the amended DRA document to the Easton Planning Commission to review whether it is consistent with the town's comprehensive plan. A public hearing on the draft amendment is set for June 3.
