title: Local legislators reflect on General Assembly
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Local legislators reflect on General Assembly

 April 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 629
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG — On Wednesday morning, the Caroline County Chamber of Commerce hosted a Legislative Wrap-up Breakfast with Maryland senators and delegates from the Eastern Shore.The meeting provided a summary and discussion of the recent Maryland state legislative session, the General Assembly. Topics discussed included DAF residual legislation and solar energy.
Sens. Stephen Hershey (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, and Caroline) and Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico), along with Dels. Jay Jacobs (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, and Caroline), Steven Arentz (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, and Caroline), Christopher T. Adams (R-Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) and Jefferson Ghrist (R-36, Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, and Caroline), were in attendance.
Jacobs spoke on his work on the Environmental and Transportation Committee and the work both delegates and local leadership in Caroline County had on regulating dissolved air flotation, or DAF, residuals.
"I really do appreciate the fact that all three county commissioners and Caroline County were there because it had a huge impact on the committee in Annapolis," Jacobs said. "With an issue that meant that much to the county, all three county commissioners showed up and gave very compelling testimony as to the real problem."
DAF is a method for processing wastewater from food processing plants. The method leaves behind a sludge-like byproduct, or DAF residuals.
House Bill 991 and its pair, Senate Bill 1074, aim to establish a food processing residuals utilization permit authorizing the Department of Agriculture to issue the permits, develop a fee schedule and inspect any site where food processing residuals are utilized.
This bill is significant to the residents of Caroline County, who have raised concerns about the storage of dissolved air flotation residuals and other waste materials.
The Caroline County Commissioners introduced legislation on Feb. 6 to establish four moratoriums related to DAF residuals, vegetable processing wastewater and the storage of biosolids not permitted by the Department of the Environment.
Commission Vice President Larry Porter said he met with Del. Sara Love (D-Montgomery); Alan Girard, Eastern Shore director at the Chesapeake Bay Foundation; and a Caroline County Department of Planning and Codes representative to discuss the draft legislation.
The bill is awaiting final approval by Governor Wes Moore to sign into law.
SOLAR DEVELOPMENT
Delegates expressed concerns over legislation they said took away a vital part of the comprehensive solar development planning process, giving local communities less determination over solar expansion.
Jacobs spoke on Senate Bill 783, or the Brighter Tomorrow Act, which would lower the cost of developing Maryland solar projects and increase the value of solar energy for consumers across the state.
Commission Vice President Larry Porter, who was in attendance, argued that if counties are forced to have more solar, they should be able to negotiate and charge what they want from solar facilities. SB 783 attempted to limit taxes charged to commercial solar facilities.
"I made a comment in the committee: If solar was as good as we are told it's good … Why doesn't everybody in this room have it?" Arentz said. "We're pushing so hard for something we can do. And I think the General Assembly has to, at some point, wake up."
The state's Renewable Portfolio Standard had already established a nation-leading mandate to deploy solar that equals 14.5% of Maryland's electric demand by 2030. Maryland has fallen behind the pace to meet that goal, only meeting 55% of the policy's intermediate 2022 target.
After the delegates had reflected on this year's legislative session, Arentz expressed his appreciation to his fellow delegates for the work that was accomplished during the legislative session.
"I appreciate the time. You guys are wonderful. And as these guys said, this is kind of a love fest. We do it here. We do it up in Cecil County. And we're very, very lucky because we have a lot of like-minded people to communicate, we talk, and we work well together," he said.

title: Talbot Council Approves Resolution 338 and Its Amendment
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Talbot Council approves Resolution 338 and its amendment

 April 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 1051
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — On Tuesday evening, the Talbot County Council approved a resolution amending the Talbot County Comprehensive Water and Sewer Plan and requiring any future expansion of the new Lakeside wastewater treatment plant shall require an amendment to the comprehensive plan.Resolution 338's passage has been long awaited. The process of developing and approving it began over a year ago.
Patrick Thomas, Talbot County attorney, said prior to voting that if this resolution is approved, it will go to the Maryland Department of the Environment, and the MDE will have the ability to either approve it, modify it or revise it.
The MDE could deny the resolution. Thomas said that if that were to happen, there would be an opportunity to request a hearing before the MDE secretary.
The council had an opportunity to pass Resolution 353, a resolution already approved by the county planning commission, but chose to table the resolution for another time.
BackgroundLakeside is a residential development project that has been 20 years in the making. It has been a hot topic of discussion for residents of Trappe and throughout the county. Lakeside is a planned 2,501-unit development spanning more than 850 acres off of U.S. Route 50 in Trappe.
According to Erin Braband, Trappe's town clerk, 114 building permits have been issued, and 109 connections have been made to the town's existing wastewater treatment plant.
Trappe's existing plant accommodates wastewater from the development's first 120 homes. The flow will eventually be diverted to a new wastewater treatment plant serving the development. The plant is expected to be operational by the beginning of June, according to Ryan Showalter, an attorney representing Lakeside's developers who spoke to commissioners at an April 2 meeting.
Before the introduction of Resolution 338, attempts were made to amend Talbot County's comprehensive plan to reclassify certain portions of the development's property for immediate priority for water and sewer service. The resolution created was called Resolution 281.
The MDE approved the resolution in November 2020. But a month later, the agency sent a letter stating that Resolution 281 did not provide the number of equivalent dwelling units for the different phases of Lakeside's construction — information needed for further development.
Council member Lynn Mielke, who introduced Resolution 338 in February 2023, called 338 a "standalone resolution on a specific issue that the Maryland Department of the Environment has brought forth. The other issues have to deal with subsequent comments by MDE that they wanted answers to."
The legislation proposes amending the county's comprehensive plan to be consistent with the provisions of Lakeside's wastewater discharge permit. Any expansion to the new plant would require a change to the plan and a certification of consistency from the Planning Commission.
The amendment, approved alongside the resolution, states as a requirement that any amendment to the comprehensive water and sewer plan must include a certification by the Planning Commission that the amendment is consistent with the county's comprehensive plan.
The language to be incorporated from Resolution 338 proposes amending the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan to be consistent with the Maryland Department of the Environment's discharge permit for Lakeside's wastewater treatment plant.
The permit, issued in October 2022, is limited to the project's first phase and allows for an annual average flow of 100,000 gallons per day, or roughly 250 gallons per day per equivalent dwelling unit, allowing only 400 residential units to be built.
Amended Resolution 338 was found consistent with the county's comprehensive plan in December, with Planning Commission Chairman Chip Councell saying it would be the county's only chance for a review of potential expansion.
The council approved the resolution and its amendment with a 4-1 vote on April 9. Talbot County Council President Chuck Challahan voted against it.
The council voted to table discussion of Resolution 353, a resolution approved by the Planning Commission last week, until its May 14 meeting, along with two other resolutions relating to Lakeside, 347 and 348.
Resolution 353 "combines Resolutions 338, 347 and 348 into a single resolution," according to County Attorney Patrick Thomas.
On April 2, the Talbot County Commission found Resolution 353 to be consistent with the Talbot comprehensive plan and moved it toward approval by the County Council.
During their discussion of Resolution 353 April 9, County Council members raised questions relating to two changes in wording made to the resolution by the Planning Commission on April 2.
The Planning Commission decided to revise aspects of Resolution 353 before finding it consistent with the comprehensive plan, fixing wording to make it compatible throughout the resolution. The revision also includes the removal of language pertaining to the initial flow for the units.
Resolution 348 addresses incorrect water and sewer classifications shown in two exhibits — maps displaying updates to Trappe's proposed water and sewer service areas — to Resolution 281.
Resolution 347 provides the number of equivalent dwelling units across all six phases of the Lakeside development's construction. A later amendment to 347 incorporates wording from the still-pending 338.
Alone, Resolutions 347 and 348 were deemed by members of the Planning Commission to be confusing, and 348 and 347 were voted to be inconsistent with the Talbot County Comprehensive Plan at the April 2 meeting.
Public CommentDuring a public hearing before the vote, Brian Schmidt, Trappe Town Council president, opposed the proposed Lakeside resolutions and their amendments.
Schmidt said the county has been treating Trappe differently than other towns, hurting the growth of the municipality.
"We did not ask this council to intervene," Schmidt said. "MDE is the controlling authority in matters of wastewater discharge, not the county. Disguising growth legislation as wastewater discharge is not proper procedure is only impeding the town's authority to control its own growth. Passing any of these resolutions, not only will you then be making decisions for the county, but you will also be making them for Trappe as well."
In a press release by the Chesapeake Bay Foundation, Alan Girard, Maryland advocacy director, said in a statement that citizens, businesses and CBF members have long sought greater oversight for Lakeside and appreciate the county's decision.
"Lakeside is no longer being left up to chance," Girard said. "Talbot County Council's decision to conduct limited oversight of the project is a positive step to protect residents and the environment. The authority to periodically review Lakeside will give county officials an essential opportunity to evaluate the project's impacts on the environment and public investments like schools, roads and emergency services."

title: Possible Change to Exempt Status Would Affect a Dozen Town Employees
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Possible change to exempt status would affect a dozen town employees

 April 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 313
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Approximately 13 Town of Easton employees could receive exempt status in the new fiscal year.At an Easton Town Council workshop on exempt and non-exempt employment status Monday, the council discussed the possibility of switching some employee statuses from non-exempt to exempt.
During the workshop, Chief Human Resource Officer Rick Farr said all current town employees are non-exempt employees. This means they receive overtime pay. Exempt employees do not.
Easton Mayor Megan Cook said in an interview Wednesday that around 13 department heads are the only town employees whose status could be changed to exempt. At the workshop, Cook said that with the switch to exempt status, those employees would get a 3% pay increase. The employees also would be able to receive compensatory time or overtime hours that can go toward time off from work.
Ward 2 Council member Don Abbatiello said in a Wednesday interview that if this change is made, it would not affect other town employees, such as police officers.
"None of their overtime is going to be impacted by this change," he said. "What we're talking about is people at a more administrative or executive kind of role within the town."
Abbatiello said this possible change is tied in with the budget that Cook has proposed, and so it most likely would take effect on July 1 when the next fiscal year begins. The council will have its first budget hearing of the year on April 9 at 6 p.m.
Abbatiello said fiscal responsibility is the reason behind the idea to change the employee status for certain employees.
"Our goal is to try to be fiscally responsible and not have to, for example, raise property tax rates in order to cover that," he said. "So we're trying to figure out a way to be as fiscally responsible as possible, while at the same time supporting the hard work that the town employees do."

title: Easton Town Council Discusses Moving to Exempt Status for Employees
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Easton Town Council discusses moving to exempt status for employees

 April 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 391
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Easton Town Council discussed making the employment status of town employees exempt during a workshop that followed the council meeting Monday evening.Exempt status employees are employees that are paid a salary instead of an hourly wage, and are therefore not paid overtime.
During the workshop, Chief Human Resource Officer Rick Farr said all current town employees are non-exempt employees. This means they receive overtime pay.
Easton Mayor Megan Cook, who has worked with Farr and Town Manager Donald Richardson to look at removing overtime from departments that have requested it, said that with the switch to exempt status, all employees would get a 3% pay increase. Although overtime pay would be taken off the table, those employees would be able to receive compensatory time, or overtime hours that can go toward time off from work.
Farr said he thinks this move is in the best interest of the town.
"As far as managing payroll, being able to align, as I said before, the knowledge, skills and abilities of the staff that are going to those exempt statuses," he said.
Ward 2 Council member Don Abbatiello said this idea has been talked about for years. He told Cook that he appreciated her moving forward on it.
Abbatiello said he had two concerns with the plan. One of his concerns is with the increase in salaries for the employees that are already on the high end of salary ranges.
He asked about what happens to compensatory time when a person retires and whether those individuals would be paid out for compensatory time. Cook said those employees would not be paid out for compensatory time when they retire.
Ward 4 council member the Rev. Elmer Davis Jr. said exempt status employees should be given a fair market value salary and should not receive compensatory time.
"You can't have it both ways," he said.
Davis said exempt status will save the town money in the long term and said it is fiscally responsible.
Before the work session ended, Abbatiello said the council recognizes that there are a lot of town employees "who work their butts off."
"And I think that's important to point out," he said. "And we all realize that. We're not trying to take what they do for the town for granted in any way, shape or form. We are just trying to — as Rev. Davis said — be fiscally responsible."

title: St. Michaels Commission Apologizes for Oversight Regarding Makers Market
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
St. Michaels commission apologizes for oversight regarding Makers Market

 March 29, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 399
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — On Wednesday evening, the St. Michaels commissioners apologized to the Markers Market and the St. Michaels Business Association for a previous oversight during a March 13 meeting.At that meeting, the commissioners voted to permit the Makers Market to host a vendor event at Muskrat Park, though the town code prohibits for-profit use of the park.
"We apologize that it was an oversight previously," Commission President David Breimhurst said. "And I can tell you that the staff is well aware of what the issue was. These permits will be thoroughly vetted in the future before they come to us."
During the March 13 meeting, Trish Payne and Mark Montoya, members of Talbot County's local art community, requested the use of the park every other Saturday or every second Sunday starting in April for a local art vendors event.
There was vocal opposition by members of the St. Michaels Business Association, who said that the vendor event could bring harm to local businesses.
After a heated discussion by members of the public, the commissioners approved the event on a trial run to begin in April to assess impacts to the local community.
During public comment at the March 27 meeting, Eric Bridges, a resident of St. Michaels, said that the town code prohibits for-profit events at Muskrat Park. He added that the town code prohibits tents on the park's grass to preserve the integrity of the grass.
Joan McNamara, a St. Michaels resident, said the commission should apologize for the oversight regarding the approval of the Makers Market hosting vendor events at Muskrat Park.
"The fact that no tents being erected in Muskrat Park was already in the code," McNamara said. "I would think that a public apology to two organizations, yes SBA (St. Michaels Business Association) and the Maker's Market, would be appropriate because there were some hard feelings."
Along with Breimhurst's apology, Rob Straebel, town administrator, apologized to the public and privately apologized to the event organization the previous week.
"I also apologize to the SBA for the oversight," Staebel said. "We have some new staff members, and ultimately, the buck stops with me, so I take full responsibility for that oversight. It won't happen again."
OTHER ACTIONS
The commissioners unanimously approved permits for the following events: Seaglass Festival, Taste of St. Michaels and the Charm City Running Festival 2024.
The commissioners approved R.L. Ewing Contractors's bid for $26,248 for milling and paving work on Fremont Street.

title: Oxford Amends Floodplain Management Ordinance
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford amends floodplain management ordinance

 March 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 430
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — The Commissioners of Oxford unanimously passed an amendment at a meeting Tuesday that removes a section from an ordinance that deals with floodplain management.The section of the floodplain management ordinance that the commissioners voted to remove allows for certain equipment to be located below the elevation of the lowest floor of a building or structure if that equipment is designed and installed to prevent water from entering and "to resist hydrostatic and hydrodynamic loads and stresses," according to the ordinance.
Equipment listed in this section includes electrical systems, heating, ventilation, air conditioning, plumbing appliances and fixtures and duct systems.
By removing this section, the town will be able to maintain its Federal Emergency Management Agency Community Rating System classification of seven. If the commissioners had voted to keep the section in the ordinance, the town's classification would have changed to a nine.
Oxford Town Attorney Lyndsey Ryan said the increase to a classification of nine would mean a loss in certain insurance benefits to residents. According to the FEMA website, class seven communities, a part of the FEMA Community Rating System, receive a 15% percent premium reduction on floodplain insurance.
Oxford Planning and Zoning Coordinator Marilyn Williams said the town would eventually need to make this ordinance change anyway due to the state's updated floodplain regulations. She said the town is due for an audit regarding these regulations.
"It has been out of FEMA regulations and the state's floodplain regulations for some time," she said about the exemption. "So it's not just because of the CRS (Community Rating System) component."
This was not the only agenda item at the meeting Tuesday that dealt with flooding. Brent Jett, an engineer, certified floodplain manager and climate change professional with the architecture and engineering firm George, Miles and Buhr, presented an engineering study on stormwater and tidal water mitigation for the greater Tilghman Street and South Morris Street areas.
Jett talked about high tides and increases in rainfall, and how these things are affecting the town's "antiquated" water systems. He also talked about what could be coming down the pike in the next 100 years.
The engineering firm proposes the town put in two pump stations, put a small pump in the wetlands area, replace its current tide gates and replace its stormwater piping. Jett estimated the cost of these changes to be between $350,000 and $400,000 total.
He said these changes could help the town land an even better FEMA Community Rating System classification in the future.
"Maybe it's just a little help," he said. "The cherry on top, potentially, to get you to the six (classification)," he said.

title: Oxford Holds Workshop on Hiring Practices
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford holds workshop on hiring practices

 March 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 550
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — With Town Manager Cheryl Lewis set to retire at the end of June, Oxford residents packed the commissioners meeting room Tuesday evening to hear about hiring practices.The Commissioners of Oxford workshop was moderated by Carol Kachadoorian, an Oxford resident and executive director of dblTilde CORE, a nonprofit whose mission is to advance knowledge about and planning for sustainable mobility and wellness in communities.
Don Borut, former executive director of the National League of Cities, and David Deutsch, a former city manager, were invited to speak about the process of hiring a new town manager.
Borut said a search firm will work with a commission to identify the skill sets that it feels would be most beneficial to its community. He said there are things a search firm does that a town might not get from advertising and hiring for a job position on its own.
These benefits include having knowledge of candidates that would be interested as well as finding candidates that didn't apply but could be a good fit.
"Ultimately, this is about helping you," Borut said. "It's not about someone coming in and telling you what you should do. It's rather providing counsel, expertise and experience that you can draw on to the extent you want."
Deutsch — who is currently a senior associate at Mercer Group Associates, a company that does executive recruiting for local government — explained how this process works. He said this process is generally the same across search firms and said he was not at the workshop to promote his group.
In explaining the process, Deutsch said search firms will first hear from a commission on the qualities and traits they would like to see in a new town manager. From there, that search firm will create a brochure that describes the town government, community and position. Deutsch said this brochure is then used as the main advertising piece.
The value in using a search firm, he said, is that a firm will go beyond local advertising.
"I've had some luck, for example, advertising in the Virginia Municipal League and the Pennsylvania Municipal League for Maryland positions because of our geographic proximity," he said.
Along with this, Deutsch said, search firms have databases of potential candidates.
After Borut and Deutsch spoke, Commissioner Katrina Greer asked how a search firm might engage the public.
Deutsch said he would take guidance from the commission. He gave an example of one experience in another municipality where they held a community meeting.
Commission President Tom Costigan asked about the cost of these services.
Deutsch said most public sector recruitment firms have a fixed price contract that they negotiate at the start of the process. He estimated that most firms would charge somewhere in the mid-$20,000s.
Commissioner Susan Delean-Botkin asked Deutsch if he had an idea of the number of applicants they would provide the town with.
Deutsch said that for a national search, he would like to see 25 to 35 applicants.
Delean-Botkin also asked if they use any instruments, like the Hogan Values assessment, to evaluate candidates. Deutsch said there are methods of evaluating, and if the commission requested that, it would be an additional fee.
During the regular meeting that followed the workshop, Greer asked to discuss at the next meeting the possibility of using a recruiter to recruit the next town manager. Costigan said they can discuss that.

title: St. Michaels Commissioners Bid Farewell to DuPont, Approve Ordinances
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
St. Michaels Commissioners bid farewell to duPont, approve ordinances

 February 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 573
 Words 

 Read News Document

 At the Commissioners of St. Michaels meeting Wednesday evening, leaders discussed Commissioner Thomas "Tad" duPont's resignation. The board also approved an ordinance establishing zoning regulations for cannabis businesses and approved the proposed contract with International Computer Services Incorporated for IT work.DUPONT RESIGNATIONCommission President David Breimhurst announced the resignation of Commissioner Thomas "Tad" duPont. Breimhurst stated that duPont's resignation was due to health reasons.
DuPont submitted a letter of resignation on Feb. 6 that Breimhurst read to those at Wednesday's meeting. In the letter, duPont recounted the "challenging" three years and nine months the board had while he was in office. Among the challenges duPont listed were navigating the pandemic, creating budgets and many other efforts.
"It has been a pleasure to serve, and (I) wish all continued success," stated duPont's letter.
DuPont was most recently elected to serve as a town commissioner in July 2020. He first served as a commissioner from 2010 until resigning in August 2013 over concerns with an ethics ordinance, according to prior Star Democrat reporting.
The vacancy on the town commission came three months shy of the town's upcoming election. Three seats, including duPont's, will be up for grabs on May 6.
But because duPont's resignation came within 90 days of the next regular election, the vacancy will remain unfilled until the election, according to the town's charter.
When Breimhurst finished reading the letter, he added a personal note on how grateful he was to serve alongside duPont.
"I thank Tad for his dedication and devotion to the town of St. Michaels. His love for the town is never ending," Breimhurst said.
CANNABIS BUSINESSES ZONINGThe Commissioners unanimously approved an ordinance changing zoning regulations for cannabis businesses that would permit cannabis dispensaries and processing facilities as a special exception in St. Michaels' general commercial zoning districts.
These changes would allow the zoning board to review each application based on factors such as noise, parking and compatibility with the neighborhood.
A nine-month cannabis moratorium, which temporarily blocked applications, site plans, permits, construction, processing and approval for businesses looking to manufacture or sell recreational or medicinal cannabis in St. Michaels will run its course at the end of the month.
ICSI CONTRACTThe Commissioners voted to renew St. Michaels' contract with International Computer Services Incorporated to assist with the town's IT services. ICSI is the town's current IT consultant and is under contract for another year and a half.
Town Manager Rob Straubel recommended the approval of the ICSI proposal because it will avoid issues with having multiple service providers and separate maintenance contracts.
OTHER TOWN BUSINESSMike Bibb, a member of the Talbot County Police Accountability Board, presented an annual review of actions taken by the Accountability Board, established in January 2023.
This board comprises two parts — the Policy and Procedure Committee and the Accountability and Charging Committee.
The Accountability and Charging Committee reviewed 50 complaints filed, and Bidd stated that no cases were made against law enforcement from St. Michael's.
The challenges faced by the Police Accountability Board included police recruiting and retention and new juvenile justice laws that make it more difficult to charge juveniles for crimes, Bidd said. He advocated for improved police training and changing laws regarding the statute of limitations for police misconduct charges.
The commissioners then discussed reviewing the town's ethics code.
Straubel recommended developing a board to review the code. The board will comprise five people: one to be a commissioner and four to be community members. The commission will post an announcement to the general public in ConstantContact for volunteers.

title: Oxford Town Manager to Retire at End of June
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford town manager to retire at end of June

 February 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 710
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — Cheryl Lewis, Oxford's town manager of more than a decade, will be retiring June 30.Lewis, who has worked for the town since 2012, made the announcement at a Commissioners of Oxford meeting Tuesday.
Before making the announcement, Lewis discussed the town's progress in hiring four open positions in the town, including a planning and zoning coordinator, a clerk-treasurer and a police chief.
"As you can see, I'm kind of working through a transition of replacements," Lewis said.
Over the next several months, Lewis plans to get the town administration positions filled so that she can set up a "somewhat seamless" transition, where people have been hired and trained for their roles before she leaves.
ADMINISTRATIVE POSITIONS
During the meeting, Lewis said the planning and zoning coordinator position has been filled.
In an interview Wednesday, Lewis said Marilyn Williams from the Wicomico County Department of Planning, Zoning and Community Development has been hired for the job.
The position, which was previously held by Maria Brophy, Lewis' daughter, was posted on Dec. 28. Lewis said at the meeting Tuesday that Williams will begin working at the end of February.
The clerk-treasurer is a new position for the Town of Oxford.
At the meeting Tuesday, Lewis said she has recommended to the commissioners that the town try to hire clerk-treasurer by the end of February so that person can begin working by the end of March.
According to the job posting on the town's website, the new hire will be tasked with directing and managing the town's finances under the town manager's direction and implementing policy set by the Commissioners of Oxford. The clerk-treasurer will act as the chief financial officer of the town.
The creation of this position was talked about at a Jan. 11 Commissioners meeting, when Commissioner Katrina Greer said she wanted to discuss the possibility of hiring someone to take on the town's financial duties.
At the Jan. 11 meeting, Greer said this could address a material weakness detailed in the town's audit for the town's lack of internal controls. This has been a finding in town audits going back to 2016.
Once the town has brought in a planning and zoning coordinator and a clerk-treasurer, Lewis said she recommends the town advertise for a new town manager. At the meeting Tuesday, she said the town manager would "replace the remaining bits and pieces" of her job, which would be split up by having three town administration positions, not including an administrative assistant.
"I do believe, in order to seamlessly move forward, that you will need to bring in three people," she said. "You're going to have to disburse the workload. You can't just have a person come and replace me and pick up all three of these pieces."
Lewis said there have not been any discussions yet regarding the salary range for the town manager position, but she said it will be included in the job posting. According to the clerk-treasurer job posting, the estimated salary range for that position is $60,000 to $80,000 per year.
OTHER OPEN POSITIONS
The town is also in need of a new police chief and a new public works member.
Oxford Police Chief Eric Kellner stepped down from his position in January for "personal and professional reasons," but is staying with the police department as an officer. The department's Lieutenant Chris Phillips has stepped up as interim chief.
At the meeting Tuesday, Lewis said she planned to post the chief position online Wednesday and hopes the town can hire a new chief by mid-March so that person can begin working in April.
Mike McWilliams, will be leaving the town's Public Works Department. Public Works Wastewater Superintendent Matt Ozman said McWilliams came to work for Oxford from the City of Cambridge and is going back to the City of Cambridge.
Lewis said she hopes to get the job posting up for McWilliams' position in the next week or two.
Toward the end of the meeting, Greer thanked Lewis for the "well thought out" transition plans.
Commissioner Susan Delean-Botkin said she had worked with Lewis for 12 years now.
"I've worked for a lot of people in my 50 years of business," she said. "And I have never met anyone as confident and as caring as you are to this town. Thank you. Thank you for this transition."
After Delean-Botkin spoke, the room erupted in applause.

title: Tense Discussion Precedes Easton Town Council Approval for Pride Festival
author: Natalie Jones
content:
Tense discussion precedes Easton Town Council approval for Pride festival

 January 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Local News 
 
 1010
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A request to approve a public assembly permit for the Delmarva Pride Center's annual Pride festival, though approved in a 3-2 vote, elicited strong concerns from some Easton Town Council members.Though the Delmarva Pride Festival is heading into its third year in Easton, one council member's uneasiness with the contents of the festival stirred up a multi-pronged discussion on Town Council precedents and the council's responsibilities and scope in reviewing events meant to benefit the community good.
This year's Delmarva Pride Festival is set for Saturday, June 15, from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. It's planned as a celebration of the Delmarva LGBTQ+ community and its allies during Pride Month.
The previous two Pride festivals held in Easton featured a variety of food trucks, live music, local vendors and performances. Residents and pets alike donned rainbow clothing and accessories as they celebrated in the heart of downtown Easton.
Festival organizers expect about 2,000 people to attend the 2024 festival.
COUNCIL CONTENTIONS
After the introduction of the festival's public assembly permit at Tuesday's town council meeting, Ward 3 Council Member David Montgomery raised a flag about the festival's activities in previous years.
He cited a video he'd seen that reportedly showed "overtly sexualized performances and behavior" and voiced concern about harm to children exposed to those displays.
"For these reasons, I don't believe this event as it was constituted in the past serves the common good of our town," Montgomery said.
The Ward 3 council member said he wanted to see what could be done to find a "more appropriate" location and about festival organizers' efforts to prevent similar behavior, adding that the displays were "not ones that many people want to see in this town."
Montgomery suggested postponing Delmarva Pride Center's application to a later meeting for a more thorough discussion.
Town Council President Frank Gunsallus said the council should extend the privilege of waiting to Montgomery, citing the council's precedent of tabling discussions based on members seeking more information or a deeper understanding prior to voting.
Ward 4 council member the Rev. Elmer Davis Jr. disagreed, calling it "quite unfair" to change the Pride festival's location or timing.
"I respect my colleagues, but I don't respect their opinion on this issue and this concern," he said. "I think the date and time is here and available to us, and I think we should vote on it."
Davis honed in on Montgomery's mention of young children in the context of the event, pointing out that parents had brought them to the festival.
"We are not in a position to be parental guidance for anyone; that's the parents' responsibility. We don't have oversight," he said, eliciting some claps from residents in the gallery.
Montgomery countered, saying he thought the council did have a responsibility to look at the content of festivals proposed to occur in the town. He re-emphasized his concerns about opening the festival up to minors and potentially harmful content.
Easton Mayor Megan Cook pointed out the festival's success over the last two years and a lack of complaints.
"The only complaint I ever heard was that it was such a lovely event, and it's shared with Juneteenth — he wished it was actually extended into two weekends," she said before Gunsallus began speaking over her.
"We've had an outpouring of people raising concerns in the past week," he said.
"We've also had an outpouring of support on this," Cook said, being echoed by Ward 1 Council Member Maureen Curry.
"You're right, and that's fine," Gunsallus said. "But we also have to serve everyone that has voted and put us in this position as a broader community."
Montgomery's motion to table approving the festival's permit was put to a vote, with Gunsallus seconding it. But before a roll call could be taken, Ward 2 council member Don Abbatiello chimed in.
"While I wholeheartedly disagree with waiting, and I have every intention, when we do vote on this, to vote in favor of allowing the public assembly permit to go through — if there is a member of this council who would like to wait, even if I disagree with it ... then we should wait," he said.
Though Abbatiello supported waiting because of the precedent set by the council before, he emphasized strongly that he would be voting in favor of the assembly permit as soon as possible.
Curry and Davis also emphasized their intentions to support the permit's approval, but they said they would honor Montgomery's request to wait.
VIDEO
A video of a performer from a previous festival was shown at the meeting, though it was not the same video that put Montgomery on edge. That video reportedly involved children coming up to a dancer, watching the dancer's crotch and handing money to them, he said later.
Tina Jones, a co-founder and treasurer of Delmarva Pride Center, approached the podium to try to allay the concerns voiced by some council members, tackling the questions sparked by the video.
"These are dancers, these are performers — if you decided they're something else, that's the decision you're making, but these are professionals," she said. "They are no different than a ballet dancer or somebody in a musical, and I bet you would have no problem letting a child come up with them and present flowers."
No one was "scantily clothed" either, Jones said.
Montgomery said he only asked for assurances that there would be no exhibitions like the ones reportedly in the video he referred to.
"We are not trying to groom anybody, we are not trying to change anybody's mind about who they are or what they want to be," Jones said. "We're just trying to say to folks who feel different, who feel like they don't have a place, that they do have a place, and I would love for that place to be the place where I grew up."
Montgomery later conceded to the council moving to vote, saying he doubted the council would hear anything different.
Curry initiated the motion to approve the assembly permit for the Pride festival, which was supported with resounding "ayes" from Abbatiello and Davis.
Montgomery and Gunsallus voted against approving the permit for the Pride festival, resulting in a 3-2 approval.

title: County Council Approves Change to Alcohol Code Allowing for Possible Liquor Store in Trappe
author: Natalie Jones
content:
County council approves change to alcohol code allowing for possible liquor store in Trappe

 January 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Local News 
 
 239
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Talbot County Council on Tuesday approved a change to the county's alcoholic beverage code, paving the way for a liquor store to be considered and established in Trappe.The bill, first introduced in November, came after a request from several Trappe residents hoping to develop a liquor store within the town.
The existing county code included certain restrictions on the issuance of off-sale licenses, or licenses that allow the sale of alcohol for off-premises consumption.
According to Patrick Thomas, the county attorney, a formula limits the number of off-sale licenses that can be issued.
Thomas said Trappe does have some off-sales licenses, but the town does not have a Class E license, which is required to open a liquor store. It's the only municipality in Talbot County that does not have one.
"This would allow any municipality to have up to one Class E establishment, so that way, residents of Trappe would have the same access to a store that others in the county have," he said.
Town residents currently have to drive to Easton or Cambridge to shop at a liquor store.
Council Vice President Pete Lesher emphasized that the council does not issue liquor licenses — the county liquor board does — but the bill enables that the board to be able to review one for the town.
"Without this legislation, a new business would not be possible," he said. "So this is enabling legislation for sure."
The bill was approved unanimously.

title: Easton Town Council Approves Changes to Bicycle Code
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
Easton Town Council approves changes to bicycle code

 January 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 439
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - The Easton Town Council unanimously passed legislation Tuesday updating the town's code on bicycles, skateboards and scooters.Ordinance 802, first introduced in November, deletes outdated provisions of the town code relating to bicycles, skateboards and scooters and updates language on prohibited riding areas and enforcement.
The most significant change to this part of the town code concerns who is allowed to ride bicycles on sidewalks within town limits.
Under the existing code, all residents are prohibited from riding bicycles on the sidewalks. A newly added exception, which will go into effect within three weeks, allows children under 13 years old to ride on the sidewalk.
Prior to the ordinance passing, Heather Grant, the executive director of Talbot Thrive, a local nonprofit dedicated to promoting healthy and safe outdoor mobility within the county, requested a revision to allow for all those under 18 years old to ride on sidewalks.
"This age-appropriate exception allows schoolchildren to ride their bikes where they feel safest, whether on the sidewalk, a trail or a town street, and goes hand-in-hand with our organization's mission to get more kids on bikes and more kids riding them to school," she said.
An idea for a dismount district - an area where bike, skateboard and scooter riders would need to walk instead - in downtown Easton was initially floated around by Ward 1 Council Member Maureen Curry, but ultimately was not enacted.
Language on lawful bicycle riding was also updated in the new ordinance.
It includes provisions on maintaining safe operation and control of the bike, riders considering the safety of others, and yielding right of way to pedestrians.
The code update additionally makes riding skateboards and scooters on streets, sidewalks, parking lots and other public property lawful.
The use of both devices in those spaces was prohibited under a town ordinance passed in 1988.
Today, skaters can flex their skills at Easton's recently opened skate park and pump track in North Easton Park.
Language allowing roller skating was added to the code for the first time through the new ordinance.
Provisions of the bicycle ordinance will be enforced by the Easton Police Department. Violations are municipal infractions.
If police see a child operating a bicycle, skateboard or scooter in an unsafe or dangerous way, they can impound the vehicle, whether or not a citation is issued from the violation.
Grant called on police to also enforce existing laws, including the three-foot buffer between cyclists and cars and requiring cars to stop for pedestrians at all crosswalks.
Provisions on town bicycle inspections and licensing will be deleted through the new ordinance.

title: Changes Coming to Oxford Finance Committee Draft Resolution

 OXFORD - Before the Commissioners of Oxford decide whether they will create a Financial Advisory Committee, an Investment Advisory Committee or neither, at least one of the drafted resolutions will be receiving some changes.At the town meeting on Tuesday, Commissioner Katrina Greer said that she would like to make changes to the drafted resolution for a Financial Advisory Committee, which she introduced and first discussed in depth at a workshop Oct. 19.Greer's proposed Financial Advisory Committee would be tasked with providing recommendations to the commissioners on issues related to town finances and other financial topics. Specifically, the committee would give advice on short-term and long-term interest rates and types of investments.Commission President Tom Costigan's proposed Investment Advisory Committee would be tasked with reviewing the towns investments quarterly, providing recommendations to the commissioners on investment opportunities, responding to other commissioner requests, and annually reviewing and providing recommendations on the town's investment policy.The committee would receive a packet of documents, which are listed in the proposed resolution, by the town manager. In Greer's proposal, committee members would be able to request information related to town finances that is accessible via the Maryland Public Information Act.Greer's draft resolution will be reposted to the town website once changes have been made so that residents can share any thoughts they have on the proposals before commissioners are expected to vote on them at the Dec. 12 meeting.The first change Greer said she wants to make is to change the membership requirements "to be as inclusive as possible." She said she would like to make it so that voters, residents and property owners can be on the committee.At the Oct. 19 workshop, Costigan said that Greer's original proposed requirement that members must own real property in town was elitist and offensive to renters.In Costigan's proposal, committee members must be registered to vote in Oxford.Greer said she wanted to change another part of the language regarding qualifications."Tom's proposal asks for experience and training in investment policies and implementation," she said."My proposal is much more specific." Greer said she thought they could meet in the middle so that both proposals say: "The members shall have demonstrable, professional experience in finance, such as a financial certification or advanced degree in finance, economics or accounting." Greer also asked that they meet in the middle on the size of the committee.Greer's proposed committee is made up of five members, while Costigan's is made up of three members.Costigan did not say whether he would be amending any of the language in his proposed resolution, but told Town Manager Cheryl Lewis that if he decides to, he will do it as soon as possible.Both Costigan and Greer's drafts were posted online following the Oct. 24 meeting so that residents could compare them and voice their thoughts, either in writing or during the meeting Tuesday.At the meeting, Greer said that the commissioners received a lot of letters."Close to 100," she said. "And that didn't even include duplicate letters." Greer said that 66 of the letters were in support of her proposed committee, four were in support of Costigan's proposed committee and 28 were in support of having no committee at all. Of those 28 letters in support of no committee, Greer said that 15 of them stated that they preferred Costigan's resolution.Commissioner Susan Delean-Botkin reminded residents that neither of the committees need to be created. She said that, according to the town's investment policy, there are only five types of investments the town can make and there is a one year limit on the maximum term of maturity."Restrictions appropriately limit the investment opportunities," she said. "So there is a third option that we do not need other committees for investments or for financial oversight."

title: Easton Town Council Passes Six-Month Cannabis Moratorium
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
Easton Town Council passes six-month cannabis moratorium

 November 8, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: 4 | Section: News

 EASTON - After brief discussion Monday evening, the Easton Town Council passed a revised six-month moratorium for businesses looking to produce or sell cannabis within the town limits.The support for implementing the moratorium comes three weeks after a heated discussion ensued on a decision to delay the vote to wait for further input from the town's planning commission.The moratorium, originally introduced this summer as a nine-month ban on cannabis businesses, will place a pause on applications, approval, construction, expansion, processing or issuance of building permits for a business that grows, processes or sells cannabis within the Easton town limits.The legislation was originally slated for a vote in mid-September, but was postponed to mid-October so all five council members could be present to vote.It will also allow the town to consider and adopt a revised zoning ordinance.Easton's existing zoning ordinance already contains definitions and permitted zoning districts for medical cannabis dispensaries and growing and processing facilities, but does not include language on standards for recreational facilities.At its Oct. 19 meeting, the planning commission began discussing specific items to potentially be included in the zoning ordinance, said Town Attorney Sharon Van Emburgh.Following further discussions this month and in December, the planning commission expects to vote on a set of zoning amendments at its January meeting, according to a letter the commission's chair submitted to the council.The zoning amendments will then need to go through the town council's legislative process, which includes at least one public hearing.Van Emburgh estimated it would take about six months to fully pass the cannabis zoning legislation.That estimation prompted Council President Frank Gunsallus to propose an amendment to shorten the moratorium to six months, which was passed unanimously by the council. A unanimous vote on the amended moratorium followed.The planning commission will continue discussion on the zoning requirements for adult-use cannabis dispensaries at its Thursday, Nov. 16 meeting.

title: Oxford Passes Charter Amendments, Policies
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Oxford passes charter amendments, policies

 October 27, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 2 | Section: News 
 
 548
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD - The Commissioners of Oxford voted on two charter amendments, one policy update and one new policy at a meeting on Tuesday.CHARTER AMENDMENTSThe commissioners voted to pass two resolutions to amend the town charter.These resolutions address a recently enacted charter amendment that changes the way commission vacancies are filled - from appointment to special election.The first resolution that was passed removes references to "general" elections in the charter to make it clear that it is referring to all elections, not just general elections.The second resolution passed clarifies that a person filling a vacancy would serve the balance of the term they are filling, rather than serving until the next election.While the commissioners were supposed to vote on a third resolution to amend the charter, which would address the deadline for filing a certificate of nomination, Town Attorney Lyndsey Ryan said there was some confusion with what was posted online. The commissioners decided to postpone the public hearing for that resolution until their next meeting on Nov. 14.FINANCIAL INVESTMENT POLICYThe commissioners voted to repeal and replace the town's financial investment policy. The policy, which defines what the town can and cannot do regarding its financial investments, was originally passed in 1996.However, the town didn't know about its existence until recently.Commission President Tom Costigan said this update to the policy cleans up some references to outdated or no-longer-existing Maryland codes, gives the town an addition investment option of certificates of deposit account registry service, or CDARS, and allows the town to put money in the Maryland Local Government Investment Pool.The update also removes the word "substantial" from the section that states commissioners and the clerk treasurer must disclose "any substantial personal investment or management role in any financial institution which conducts business in Talbot County." "So we must now disclose any personal investment or management role in any financial institution which conducts business in Talbot County," Costigan said.EMPLOYEE HIRING POLICYThe commissioners voted to put in place a Town of Oxford Hiring Policy and Procedure Guideline. Costigan said that last March, he proposed that an ad hoc committee of citizens be formed to develop this policy. He said the ad hoc committee met multiple times to look at best hiring practices in other jurisdictions and create a policy for Oxford."I feel that their work product is fair, balanced and will meet the town's needs going forward," Costigan said.Commissioner Susan Delean-Botkin voiced her concern with a line in the policy that states applicants need to disclose any familial relationships with current town employees. She questioned whether that is legal to do.Ryan said that, because the town has an existing policy regarding conflicts of interest, she did not have any concerns with the line."I don't think the intent is that, when the applicant discloses (a familial relationship), they would be excluded from the application process," she said. "They're still involved in the application process." Ryan said the disclosure would allow those interviewing the candidate to understand that if there were a subordinate relationship, other revisions would need to be put in place."With that explanation, I think this is fine then," Delean-Botkin said before making the motion to approve the policy.

title: Oxford Financial Committee Decision Delayed Again - News
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Oxford financial committee decision delayed again - News

 October 26, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 3 | Section: News 
 
 811
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD - No decisions have been made on two proposed committees by the Commissioners of Oxford.Following a workshop last Thursday, Commissioner Katrina Greer and Commission President Tom Costigan each shared their proposals for a Financial Advisory Committee and an Investment Advisory Committee, respectively, at a Commissioners of Oxford meeting Tuesday evening.By the end of the meeting, it was decided that both proposals would be posted on the town website so that residents can compare them and voice their thoughts, either in writing or during the next Commissioners meeting on Nov. 14, before a decision is made."At the following meeting in December, more than likely, we will make a decision on this," Costigan said.The commissioners could decide to choose Greer's proposal, Costigan's proposal or they could chose to take no action at all, he said.At the meeting, Greer briefly read through her proposal first, which was shared in detail at the workshop last week.According to her proposal, the Financial Advisory Committee would be tasked with providing recommendations to the commissioners on issues related to town finances and other financial topics. Specifically, Greer said the committee would give advice on shortterm and long-term interest rates and types of investments."The committee recommends, the commissioners approve, the treasurer implements and manages and then the commissioners review" Greer said. "It is not auditing, it is not maintaining accounting systems, it is not collecting taxes or transferring money."After Greer spoke, Costigan shared his proposal for an Investment Advisory Committee that would be tasked with reviewing the towns investments quarterly, providing recommendations to the commissioners on investment opportunities, responding to other commissioner requests, and annually reviewing and providing recommendations on the town's investment policy.The committee would receive a packet of documents, which are listed in the proposed resolution, by the town manager. In Greer's proposal, committee members would be able to request information related to town finances that is accessible via the Maryland Public Information Act.Greer said she would vote in favor of Costigan's proposal pending three changes The first change would be to use the same language in the town's financial investment policy for the ethics requirement of committee members.The second change would be to include the word "demonstrable" to describe the experience that committee members must have.The third change would make it so that real property owners, along with those registered to vote in the Town of Oxford, can become committee members.Costigan's proposal makes it so that a committee member must be registered to vote in Oxford.This specific requirement ofwho can be a committee member was brought up multiple times during the meeting.When Greer shared her proposal, she said she wanted to include real property owners because no committee in Oxford is restricted to only voters and said it would be a shame to miss out on people with experience who are not registered to vote in Oxford.Town Manager Cheryl Lewis said that while there is no restriction within the charter, it has been the policy of the town that members on committees are fulltime residents that are registered to vote in Oxford.Greer gave an example of a chartered financial analyst who lives in another state but comes to Oxford regularly throughout the year to visit his mother."I think it's important to have stakeholders that are paying taxes, and therefore have a vested interest in the town, getting the most out of its investments safely," she said.At the workshop last Thursday, Costigan said Greer's committee proposal requirement that members must own real property in town was elitist and offensive to renters.During public comment, Russ Gray said a task force or ad hoc committee might be a better alternative to creating a formal committee."It requires a ton of work, it requires bureaucracy, which I think all of us are against," Gray said about forming a committee. "Based on what we're limited to investing in, are there going to be any hidden surprises in terms of dramatic changes over a period of time? Doubtful."Gail Rosenfeld spoke in favor of having a committee. She said it's always a good thing to have thoughtful people involved and added that having a committee is about transparency."We should know what's going on," she said.Rosenfeld added that she isn't a voter, but she is a resident."I adore this town," she said. "This matters to me greatly."After the meeting, former Commission President Jimmy Jaramillo said he supports Costigan's proposal because he thinks it's important that voters and full-time residents are the ones who can serve on the committee."They're invested, they're here all the time, they can make these meetings," he said. "Having someone that's not here full time, only three times a year, (and) lives in a different state - they're not invested."

title: Easton Town Council Vote on Cannabis Moratorium Delayed - Tabled Measure Leads to Heated Discussion Among Council Members
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
Easton Town Council vote on cannabis moratorium delayed - Tabled measure leads to heated discussion among council members

 October 18, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 710
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - A move by Easton Town Council President Frank Gunsallus to continue a hearing on a proposed cannabis moratorium drew strong reactions from other council members.A tense back-and-forth exchange between Gunsallus and Ward 3 Councilman David Montgomery toward the end of Monday's council meeting stemmed from the council president's executive decision to delay a vote on the moratorium for an additional three weeks.The nine-month moratorium on cannabis businesses, introduced this summer, was originally slated for a public hearing and vote at the council's Sept.18 meeting. The matter had been tabled until Monday so all five council members could be present to vote.The moratorium, if passed, would place a pause on applications, approval, construction, expansion, processing or issuance of building permits for a business that grows, processes or sells cannabis within the Easton town limits.The moratorium would also allow the town to consider and adopt a revised zoning ordinance.Easton's existing zoning ordinance already contains definitions and permitted zoning districts for medical cannabis dispensaries and growing and processing facilities, but does not include language on standards for recreational facilities.Montgomery strongly objected to Gunsallus' continuance, saying the council president did not have the authority to do so. Gunsallus affirmed that he did."Sir, you will contain yourself please," Gunsallus said, speaking over Montgomery, who started to make a comment.Gunsallus reaffirmed he had the power to continue discussion on the moratorium until the next meeting, explaining that he wanted to wait until the town's planning commission made an additional recommendation later in the week.However, in August, the commission unanimously gave a favorable recommendation to approve the ordinance.Montgomery called for a vote on the continuance, questioning Gunsallus' authority."The fact that four of us could reveal that we want to vote now means nothing to you, that you will override the wishes of the council because you are sitting there as the town council president," he said.Town Attorney Sharon Van Emburgh chimed in, saying the council can override the president's action. But in the past, the council has typically given members additional time to vote as a courtesy.Montgomery pointed out that the council had already given an additional month for consideration.Gunsallus reemphasized the upcoming planning commission meeting would provide more clarifying information."Excuse me, what information will that be?" Montgomery said."(The planning commission's) recommendations, as I've stated, so please contain yourself - you've already spoken more than permissible," Gunsallus said.Montgomery motioned to overrule Gunsallus and vote on the ordinance as presented.Ward 2 Councilman Don Abbatiello interjected, saying while he understood Montgomery and "definitely" disagreed with how the decision had been handled, he agreed that granting additional time to decide was in line with past council actions.Mayor Megan Cook, a former council president herself, interrupted the quarreling, calling for the councilmen to settle down."I agree that we are a group of five where you all are independent and you all have various opinions - absolutely.We must respect ourselves - the fighting, we need to" she said, trailing off and moving her arms to motion to calm down."Please." Ward 4 Councilman Rev.Elmer Davis Jr. initially seconded the motion, rescinding his vote just minutes later to agree with Abbatiello's stance on the council's precedent. He voiced worry with how the situation was handled."We have never had such a dialogue that we had tonight regarding issues and concerns," he said. "That dialogue - I'm quite concerned about things that have been said, I've never seen this on this council in all my days." The council will again table voting on the ordinance until its Monday, Nov. 6, meeting.Uncertainty still remains on the moratorium. During Monday's meeting, council members and town residents raised questions on the moratorium's duration, specifics on licensing for both recreational and medical facilities and zoning laws for both types of establishments.The Easton Planning Commission will discuss zoning requirements for adult-use cannabis dispensaries at its Thursday, Oct. 19, meeting.

title: Oxford Debates Wording of New Charter Changes
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Oxford debates wording of new charter changes

 September 15, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 547
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD - Following a work session to discuss a recently enacted charter amendment that changes the way commission vacancies are filled, Oxford commissioners asked Town Attorney Lyndsey Ryan to draft a proposed resolution to iron out language issues with the amendment.The charter amendment, which voters approved in July, makes it so that a midterm commission vacancy is filled via a special election rather than via appointment by commissioners.Earlier in July, before the amendment was approved, commissioners held a special meeting to discuss what language would need to be changed if residents voted in favor of passing the amendment. At that meeting, Ryan talked about language issues regarding length of term of the elected commissioner, when candidates need to file a certificate of nomination and the timing from a vacancy announcement to when the election would need to be held.At the work session Tuesday, Ryan gave the commissioners options for simple charter amendments that would address these language issues."[The changes] make it so that a special election this year or 10 years from now, or 15, are all operated in the same exact manner without interpretation," she said.Ryan said that when it comes to filing to be a candidate, the charter currently states you need to file by the third day of May, rather than by a certain number of days before the election."For instance, a 30-day time frame would allow you to file anytime throughout the year prior to either a regular or a special election," she said.Ryan brought up the importance of making it clear that a commissioner elected to fill a vacancy would serve the balance of the unexpired term.She also brought up the importance of including language that helps avoid having two elections."So that if a vacancy occurs within either 90 or 40 days prior to a regular election, that seat would go to the regular election rather than a special election and then a general election," she said.Resident Susan Kordell spoke during the meeting to give her thoughts on the changes that should be made. Kordell gave handouts of her proposal to meeting attendees.Kordell proposed making changes for clarity and simplicity. These changes include naming the elections (general election versus special election), naming the dates "associated with the elections" and using calendar days."We want to try to make this as simple as possible," she said before going through the list of specific changes in her proposal.Both Kordell and Ryan had similar ideas for what changes should be made."It's like we read each other's minds," Ryan said.At the regular commissioners meeting later that that evening, Ryan said the general consensus from the work session was to use calendar days, replace the word "appointed" with "elected," specify that a person elected to a vacant seat is to serve the rest of the unexpired term and possibly change the way notice of an election is provided."We don't have control over the publication of the newspaper," Kordell said during the work session. "In town owned and operated models like our website, like our town bulletin board, if we want to post it, we post it. No lag time."

title: Town Council President Candidates State Case
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
Town Council president candidates state case

 August 31, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: A1 | Section: News 
 
 1207
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - The four candidates vying to be the Easton Town Council's next president shared their thoughts on growth, development and health care in the town with community members at a town hall forum Tuesday evening.The candidate town hall, held at the Avalon Theatre and hosted jointly by the Talbot Spy and the Avalon Foundation, was moderated by Craig Fuller.Questions to the candidates centered on the role of the town council president, development and the community's health care needs.To former Easton Mayor Bob Willey, his decades of service to Easton, including a six-year stint as council president and experience managing a large workforce and millions of dollars in town budgets, set him apart as a candidate."I think there's a lot of things Easton has going for it, and I'd like to be part of keeping those things moving and getting them a little better, and (adding) a few more bells and whistles," he said.Experience is a key part of the campaign for former Ward 1 Councilman Al Silverstein, who said he'd learned a lot from others in his eight years on the council."It's a 20-month service, that's all we have left on this term, but I think it's 20 months of being able to move Easton in the right direction," he said in his opening statement. "I think we've gone a long way under Mayor Willey in the past, but it's time to move forward with new ideas and new challenges, so I look forward to the opportunity." For Frank Gunsallus, who ran a close race for the Ward 1 seat on the town council in May, his campaign for Town Council president is a way to capitalize on momentum and support from the previous election."I am here to focus on smart growth, attainable housing, better health care and fair representation for all citizens of Easton," he said.To Kevin Bateman, continuing to serve Easton residents in a new way and improving the town are key reasons for running."I'm a person that believes that everyone matters, no matter who you are, where you come from, what your religion is, what your ethnicity is - we all matter, we're human beings first," he said. "And keeping that in mind, that is why I've taken on this adventure: to try to make sure that every person in this town matters." Much of the town hall discussion focused on growth and development, issues that the public has frequently chimed in on in recent months.A Talbot County native, Willey recalled growing up in Easton in the 1940s and 1950s, when the town's population was under 6,000. But while the town's landscape has changed since then, some things have remained the same."I think we tend to soft pedal affordable housing; we think if we go ahead and build 100 houses, we're going to solve the problem - we aren't," he said."That problem's been around for years, it's going to be around for years to come." Willey said the town needs to look at including representation from all of the county's municipalities on the Talbot County Housing Commission, saying that all need to tackle the issue together. Having information on the types of homes available is key, too."Easton is not the one to solve the affordable housing issue; we'll do our part, but we don't do it all, and the others have got to chime in," he said.Also addressing development, Gunsallus spoke about ways to bring more connections to residents living on the east side of U.S. Route 50, where there isn't a place to safely cross."Finding ways to make bike-ability and walkability attainable for people who live across (Route) 50, who want to get downtown and not have to drive their car and worry about parking or traffic, are ways we should be looking to incorporate them into the fabric of our town," he said.Speaking on future development within the town, Bateman said that finding a suitable location for affordable housing for residents is the difficult part."It's a tough challenge to find the location that fits, that has the right space and the right mix," he said. "We want to grow, we want to see responsible, common sense growth, and that's going to take a lot of thought and a lot of planning." To Silverstein, getting broader community input on the town's future comprehensive plan and keeping the town's growth rate at 1% are keys in addressing development."I think we have to plan for some growth, but we have to be smart about it," he said.And as for addressing the critical need for workforce housing, Silverstein said the town needs to buy land and designate it as a planned workforce housing project.The town needs to look at the financial factors impacting future home buyers to develop a strategic plan moving forward, he said.The discussion then pivoted to health care and a shortage of medical professionals in the community.Gunsallus said the need for a new hospital in Easton is "long overdue," but it's only part of the problem. A shortage of primary care physicians and specialists greatly impacts many community members, and long wait times exacerbate the issue.To address the shortage in care, Gunsallus said the town could look into being designated as a health professional shortage area, which would open up state loan repayment programs for physicians to alleviate burdens for doctors trying to repay school debts.Tax incentives, along with state and federal grants and subsidies, are other things the town can look at utilizing to attract new physicians."Those are all things that we should be considering and trying to address in the short term, because those are also problems that a new hospital is not going to solve; that will only bring a new building here," he said, later adding: "There are many people here who should not have to wait that long, and we have more pressing concerns in the short term." Bringing the new hospital to Easton is a top priority for Silverstein in the next 20 months if elected president of the council. To him, community leaders and members need to be making noise about building the new regional medical center."I think we need to be engaged with them, just like the county is engaged with them, on an ongoing basis, on a weekly basis, to ask the question: 'What's going on?'" he said. "We should be up in Annapolis banging on the governor's door and banging on the University of Maryland's door in Baltimore saying, 'This is not acceptable.Our community and our region deserve better service.'" If elected, a top priority for Bateman is completing long-outstanding projects that have been postponed, ranging from the hospital to drainage issues."There's other communities in our town that have been they haven't been neglected, they just haven't had the attention that they should have," he said.In addition to the hospital, another priority for Willey, if elected, is addressing the comprehensive plan update."If that was in place, and we had our zoning rules up to date, if we had our needs for housing up to date, if we had the annexation requests up to date, and what we're going to need for public facilities, we wouldn't have had the fights that we were having over Poplar Hill and Maryland Health Club."
