title: Council Changes Direction on Updating Lakeside Information
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
Council changes direction on updating Lakeside information

 August 25, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: A1 | Section: News 
 
 381
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - The Talbot County Council voted 3-2 to address updated information on Lakeside's development phases and Trappe's water and sewer service maps as standalone resolutions, revising an earlier decision to submit the materials as part of the county's draft 2023 Report of the Review.The initial decision to submit the information as part of the draft report of the review was made at the council's Aug. 8 meeting. But at Tuesday's meeting, Council Member Lynn Mielke brought forward a motion to reconsider, saying she thought it would be better as a two-step process.In letters dated from April and May, the Maryland Department of the Environment requested that the information - updated water and sewer maps for Trappe and a request for the number of equivalent dwelling units for all phases of the Lakeside at Trappe development - be submitted to the agency.According to County Attorney Patrick Thomas, the requested information could be addressed as part of the county's draft 2023 Report of the Review or in standalone amendment resolutions. At the previous meeting, Thomas said including the information within the draft report would be the most straightforward approach.The council voted 4-1 at the Aug. 8 meeting to submit the information as part of the draft report, with Council Vice President Pete Lesher voting against it.Arguing in favor of reconsidering the previous decision, Mielke described including the requested information in the report as "putting the cart before the horse." While the council could address the information by introducing standalone resolutions, the legislation would need to go through the comprehensive water and sewer plan amendment process while MDE also reviews the draft report. Taking that action would mean two separate documents are sent to MDE, Thomas said.Council President Chuck Callahan said he felt more comfortable submitting the requested information to MDE in one package.After additional discussion, Lesher, Mielke and Council Member Keasha Haythe voted in favor of reconsidering the council's previous decision and directing the county attorney to draft the resolutions amending the comprehensive water and sewer plan. Callahan and Council Member Dave Stepp voted against both actions.The resolutions will be introduced at the council's Sept. 12 meeting.

Newly constructed houses built close together line Lakeside Boulevard, the main street entering the Lakeside at Trappe development.

title: Oxford Commissioners Introduce Charter Amendment
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Oxford commissioners introduce charter amendment

 August 11, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: A2 | Section: News 
 
 338
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD - At a town meeting Tuesday, the Commissioners of Oxford introduced a charter amendment that would increase the number of election judges on the town's Election Board.If the drafted resolution is passed, the number of election judges would increase from three to six.At Tuesday's meeting, Oxford Town Attorney Lyndsey Ryan said the amendment would address the increased hours of town elections. While elections used to be held from 2 p.m. to 7 p.m., they now begin at 8 a.m. and end at 8 p.m.Commissioners approved this change in election hours at an Aug. 23 meeting in 2022. The election in June of this year to fill previous Commission President Jimmy Jaramillo's seat was the first election where the increased hours were in effect.The drafted resolution would also change the start of term for election judges.Currently terms begin the first Monday in April of the year they are appointed by the commission."So essentially, if you're appointed in September, you're term had already started," Ryan said.The drafted resolution would make it so that election judges begin their term the day they are appointed. These terms would run for two years.A public hearing on the drafted resolution will be held Sept. 12 at 6 p.m. at 101 Market Street in Oxford.At Tuesday's meeting, commissioners also set a date to discuss language changes for the charter amendment that residents approved in a July 18 special election.The amendment, which goes into effect Aug. 17, changes how mid-term commission vacancies are filled. Instead of being appointed by the remaining commissioners, vacancies will be filled via special election.A work session to discuss possible adjustments to the language of this amendment will be held at 5 p.m. before the regular town meeting on Aug. 22.During a special meeting in July, Ryan discussed aspects of the amendment that might need to be changed including the length of the term of the elected commissioner, when candidates need to file a certificate of nomination and the timing from a vacancy announcement to when the election would need to be held.

title: St. Michaels Commissioners Discuss Comprehensive Plan
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
St. Michaels Commissioners discuss comprehensive plan

 October 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 359
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — St. Michaels commissioners dove into the process of renewing the town's comprehensive plan with a workshop meeting on Tuesday.One of the main topics discussed was the town's priorities for the updated plan, which is revised every 10 years.
While no firm decisions were made, the commissioners said existing passages in the current plan would be taken into consideration.
Commissioners President Jay Hudson said there will be a special meeting schedule to discuss the commissioners priorities.
"We have been discussing getting together with a special session to discuss what those priorities are," Hudson said. "As you know, we've just hired a new town manager as of April, and he's been busy getting himself acclimated to his role. Now it is time for us to sit down and kind of prioritize projects moving forward."
Hudson said that the commissioners would come back to the Nov. 5 comprehensive plan meeting with priorities mapped out. Hudson also mentioned that the priorities in already outlined in Chapter 14 of the comprehensive plan will be the road map.
During the meeting, commissioners brought up multiple concerns and items they wished were included within the plan. Commissioner Alexis Roiter mentioned demographics as a consideration. Hudson said that the Planning Commission plans to add all of those to the plan before the next meeting.
"Those are easy ones. Looking at a 10 year plan, it's definitely necessary to see what the demographics are when we're writing it," Hudson said.
With federal funding in question, to make sure all of St. Michaels plan can be completed, the town plans to strengthen its relationship with Talbot County.
"I think all the municipalities in Talbot County have a wonderful working relationship with the county," Hudson said. "I think now with grant funding running out and having a better idea of what we need moving forward, I think for us now it's imperative to strengthening the relationships with the county. It's more creating these programs so that these relationships can work."
The special meeting to discuss the commissioners' priorities for the comprehensive plan has not been scheduled yet, but the next comprehensive plan meeting will be Nov. 5 at 5 p.m. at 407 St. Mary's Square.

title: Easton Leans Away From Annexing New Land in Comprehensive Plan Update
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton leans away from annexing new land in comprehensive plan update

 September 10, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 728
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — As planners draft Easton's new comprehensive plan, the town's direction on annexing new land is becoming clear: slow down.At a workshop Monday, the Easton Planning Commission chose to retain language in the comprehensive plan update that discourages new annexations in the next 10 years.
As recently as last year, Easton annexed around 17 acres of county land east of U.S. Route 50 between the Royal Farms and Unitarian Universalist Fellowship. It's expected to become an affordable housing project, though the developer will still need town approval on an application.
Town Council members have indicated concerns about annexing additional land into town, especially as Easton deals with the question of whether it's maxing out on residential growth.
The comprehensive plan, last updated in 2010, is undergoing revisions before potential council approval later this year or early next year. It outlines how the town aims to grow in the next decade, touching on areas such as annexation, population growth and traffic.
On Monday and at a workshop last month, commission and council members noted that there may be exceptions to the no-annexation rule.
"I would have a hard time with being absolute about annexation, saying that that's not happening," Ward 2 Councilmember Robert Rankin said on Aug. 25. "Because there may be exceptions."
The main exception to completely halting annexation seems to be Easton Point, the development project that seeks to revitalize Port Street and the area around the Tred Avon River. The effort hasn't significantly progressed in recent years, council members say.
Ward 1 Councilmember Maureen Curry said at last month's meeting that Easton Point's redevelopment is "an enigma." She advocated that annexation of the county land in that area be excluded from any no-annexation directive in the new comprehensive plan.
"The Easton Point development project's been on the board for almost 20 years," Curry said. "We have to find a way to move that forward if we can."
Town leaders largely agreed that a project like Easton Point rises to the level of an "extraordinary" annexation that should be permitted under the comprehensive plan's guidance.
Still, the plan should emphasize that annexation generally is "not a priority for the town," said Planning Commission member Victoria McAndrews on Monday.
GROWTH RATE
Hesitation to approve future annexation requests stems, in part, from the town's growth. From 2000 to 2010, the town's population increased 36%, according to census data. In the next decade, growth slowed to 7%, bringing Easton's population from 15,945 to 17,101.
When commission and council members met for a joint workshop in August, the council maintained that the comprehensive plan should include a target growth rate for population. The 2010 version has a 1% annual growth rate, which for the most part hasn't been exceeded. Bumping it up to 1.75% was discussed.
Michael Ports, the commission's vice chair, said Monday that 1.75% "makes the most sense." But other commission members leaned toward a 1.14% annual growth rate, which is based off of historical trends.
Commission Chairperson Phil Toussaint agreed with the 1.14% rate, emphasizing that it needs to be at a mark so the Town Council feels comfortable approving the plan as a whole.
TRAFFIC
When housing projects come to the commission or Town Council for approval, they include traffic impact studies. Developers typically hire a traffic engineering firm to conduct the study of the development's potential impact on traffic backups.
Planning Commission members said moving forward, the comprehensive plan needs to demand more thorough traffic reviews. Klein said studies often choose a few intersections next to the project and ignore the town's main arteries, where traffic is already an issue.
Easton Planning and Zoning Director Miguel Salinas said the best way to expand the scope of a traffic impact study for a development is if town engineers or the State Highway Administration request a larger scope during meetings with the project's traffic engineer.
Town Engineer Rick Van Emburgh said he wants to continue requiring developers' traffic studies to include a percent change in traffic based on if the development were to be built.
Toussaint said he wants the studies to include more consideration on the impact to pedestrians, not just vehicles. He added that studies should be framed around the town's ongoing Complete Streets study, which is assessing Easton's roads on a large scale.
"What we've received in the past as a traffic impact study is going to be worthless for us going forward," Toussaint said. "It's propaganda at this point, prepared by the applicant's engineers."

title: How Much Growth Is Too Much for Easton? Balance Between Housing Needs, Infrastructure Unsettled
author: Konner Metz
content:
How much growth is too much for Easton? Balance between housing needs, infrastructure unsettled

 August 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 1988
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The predicament on the minds of many Easton residents and leaders continues to be just how much the town can afford to grow.Easton is under a period of significant residential growth with multiple large-scale housing projects under construction. In 2000, the town's population was 11,708, according to census data. Ten years later, it rose to 15,945, and since, it's grown at a slower pace to 17,101 in 2020.
The boom has raised a litany of concerns, from increased traffic to a change in the town's small-town complexion.
Some residents, and a few officials, think Easton should press the brake pedal. But local real estate agents contend that a halt to growth could box out lower- and middle-class buyers and renters.
Martha Witte Suss, an associate broker for Coldwell Banker Realty and Easton resident, said the housing market has been in a crunch since the pandemic. She said there's not enough reasonably priced homes or rentals to satisfy employees who commute from outside Talbot County.
"We have plenty of housing that they can't afford," Suss said. Residential growth, if it focuses on affordability, could cure that dry spell, she added.
Michael Ports, vice chair of the Easton Planning Commission, poses the town's conundrum like this: "What are the housing needs of the people currently, and can we achieve that in a way that doesn't compromise everyone's needs for services?"
It's a question town leaders are taking on, even if there's no easy answer.
This fall, 136 apartments on Elliott Road will begin opening. Two large communities are under construction east of Route 50, combining for over 450 projected single-family homes. Near Easton's downtown, a developer plans to transform two former Perdue AgriBusiness sites into housing projects, totaling 144 units.
In all, roughly 1,127 units are recently finished, under construction or approved by the town's public bodies, according to information from town planners and developers of the 17 listed projects.
The pipeline of projects has yielded varying opinions from town leaders. Some don't want any new large housing projects approved in the next few years. Others prefer a case-by-case approach.
Mayor Megan Cook said the right answer is "probably somewhere in between." The town should focus on the current projects but not be too quick to disregard new ones, she said.
The mayor said growth is a charged topic and especially complicated due to affordable housing needs. No solution is a "silver bullet," Cook and others have repeatedly said.
"It is a balancing act," Town Council President Don Abbatiello said. "There would have to be a project come along that would fit that need, that workforce housing, that affordable housing piece."
In interviews with The Star Democrat, Easton officials weighed in on the town's current list of housing developments. When asked about infrastructure, the most recognized concerns included roads, fire and police services and schools.
They offered thoughts on where the town should focus its residential growth. Most leaned toward building from the inside-out. Planning Commission Chairperson Phil Toussaint is of that opinion. He hopes the sprawling, single-family developments are coming to an end.
"We wouldn't really want to support any development on the outskirts at all," Toussaint said.
And broadly, the 1,127-unit mark can be misleading since some units aren't under construction and may not be for years, Toussaint and others said.
"(People) think they're gonna appear tomorrow," Toussaint said. "They're not."
Single-family home neighborhoods typically take years to build out, such as Easton Village off of St. Michaels Road, a project of around 250 homes first approved in 2003 and just now reaching completion. So far, the 200-home Gannon Range and 252-home Four Seasons projects only have 18 and 11 building permits, respectively, according to Easton planning and zoning director Miguel Salinas.
"It's a daunting number. It's hard to hear," said Cook, who as mayor doesn't have a vote on housing applications. "But at the same time, you look at some of the examples as a community, the neighborhoods that we've had. They're built out over 20 years."
THE PIPELINE
Since town planners prepared a list of Easton housing projects this winter, chatter of "the pipeline" has been frequent at Town Council and Planning Commission meetings. Those two bodies are responsible for approving most of the projects.
The commission is made up of volunteer members and often can only make a recommendation to the council, whose members are elected. But sometimes, the commission holds final say, such as when it approved the 116-apartment Easton Crossing complex on Brookletts Avenue this year.
The five members of the council and six members of the commission offer a range of opinions when it comes to the town's growth.
Town Council Ward 3 representative David Montgomery provided perhaps the most rigid perspective.
"I want to stop for at least five years before we add anything more to this backlog," Montgomery said. "I want to see how fast it actually grows, it's actually built out."
Others were less firm on completely stopping growth, though all council members interviewed for this story said, at the very least, the town needs to be mindful. Some prefer a project-by-project approach, such as Abbatiello, who said future housing proposals need to be the "right fit" for Easton.
"I think right now, there's enough in the pipeline for us to say, 'Let's see how the projects impact the town's resources before we go adding a lot more to that list,'" Abbatiello said.
Planning Commission members have mixed thoughts, too.
Ports, the commission's vice chair, said Easton is "missing a good bit" even with the current project inventory. He said the missing units largely fall between expensive single-family homes and for-rent apartments — a sphere urban planners call "the missing middle."
"The reality is that the median sale price of a home right now is almost twice what a family of four making the absolute average income here in Easton can afford," Ports said. According to Maryland Realtors, the July 2025 median sales price in Talbot County was $545,000, the third highest in the state.
Tom Klein was the commission's lone vote against the Easton Crossing project, citing traffic and parking concerns. He said the need for more affordable housing is clear. But Klein would prefer to have a target number. At times, it feels like Easton is "chasing something" it doesn't know, he said.
"How many more do we need? Do we just keep assuming we keep needing more?" Klein asked. "That, to me, is something I don't really know the answer to. I think it would be helpful to know that so we don't just blindly build."
'MORE AND MORE CROWDED'
Town planners and engineers have processes to gauge the impacts residential projects will have on the town, such as traffic and environmental studies or reviews by the town's nonprofit utility, sewer and water company, Easton Utilities.
Even with project-specific studies, many town leaders believe traffic is a top-of-list concern, along with other infrastructure matters.
Montgomery said town staff should be "much more skeptical about the traffic impact studies" submitted alongside housing proposals. Ward 4 representative the Rev. Elmer Davis said the traffic issue is obvious to the human eye.
"I don't need a traffic study to tell me that the traffic in Easton, periodically, is a problem at best," Davis said.
Handling traffic backups is a tricky matter, Cook said, since some roads are state-run, others are under county purview and many downtown are maintained by town engineers and public works employees.
Off of Route 328, or Matthewstown Road, 136 apartments are opening soon, while 200 single-family homes will be built just down the road. It's an area residents have flagged during council and state transportation meetings.
"(Route) 328 is going to become busier and busier, and folks, I fear, are going to have more and more challenges getting out to (Route) 50," said Councilmember Robert Rankin, who represents residents in the Route 328 area.
A State Highway Administration planning and environmental study is underway to assess pedestrian and traffic needs on the busy state road that funnels onto Ocean Gateway. Previously proposed concepts by the state include adding left-turn lanes on Matthewstown Road and adding a second through lane on Goldsborough Road as drivers cross Route 50.
Traffic has consistently been brought up as a reason to lean away from annexing land for residential growth outside of Easton's core. Nearly all commission and council members interviewed for this story said they prefer to keep growth within the area encircled by Route 50 and Easton Parkway (322).
The Planning Commission has especially expressed that preference during workshops updating the town's comprehensive plan, which lays out the town's vision for handling growth in the next decade.
In July, the commission rejected the Fox Chase Estates, a 365-unit, mixed-use development proposed near a warehouse and industrial park north of Easton Airport and near the under-construction Shore Regional Health hospital. Town Council members maintain final voting power on the project, though it's unclear when or if it will come before them.
The Planning Commission voted unanimously to recommend against the development, citing a lack of connectivity as a main reason. The vote lines up with the commission's recent direction as they draft the new comprehensive plan: build from the inside-out.
"We'd rather see infill," Klein said. "We want to see connected neighborhoods."
That line of thinking, shared by many Town Council members, still leaves Easton with infrastructure challenges, such as downtown streets, utilities and safety. The latter was emphasized by Cook and council members as a chief priority.
Funding for the Easton Police Department and Easton Volunteer Fire Department makes up around 40% of the town's general fund budget. Abbatiello, who volunteers for the fire company, wants to hold off a massive increase in the cost for fire services by maintaining the department's volunteer status for "as (long) as possible."
"The biggest tax increase residents of Easton are ever going to see is if the Town of Easton needs to go to a paid (fire) department," Abbatiello said.
Easton Utilities evaluates water demands annually. According to a statement from Doug Abbott, director of engineering and water/wastewater departments, the utility is using 60% of its water and wastewater capabilities, leaving 40% "to accommodate future growth."
And as for downtown traffic, some town leaders are worried infill will do more harm than good.
"Our streets are becoming more and more crowded, and I am concerned the more that we have infill development, the harder it is to maneuver around this town," Ward 1 Councilmember Maureen Curry said at a comprehensive plan workshop Aug. 25.
"I just don't accept that assumption," Toussaint, the commission chair, later said. He argued that concentrating growth downtown will take cars off town streets and improve walkability.
Overall, the Aug. 25 meeting yielded a key takeaway: the new comprehensive plan is likely to include a preferred annual population growth rate around 1.75%. Planners initially proposed not to mark an annual growth rate in the plan, a change from the 2010 version, which stamped the rate at 1%.
Town Planner Lynn Thomas said at the meeting that without a growth rate, the plan would use historic projections to determine if the town should consider adopting policies to remedy growth trends either "significantly lower or significantly higher" than expected.
But Town Council members said a rate should be clearly stated to keep the town honest.
"I do think it would be helpful to have at least something to point toward," Rankin said. The Planning Commission will adjust the drafted plan later this fall, likely reinstating an annual growth rate, before hosting a public hearing.
The town's Affordable Housing Board and Attainable Housing Task Force are other bodies taking cracks at addressing the housing-growth debate. The task force is currently producing a list of recommended housing policies for the Town Council to consider.
Cook acknowledged that while town boards and discussions are great, "actionable items" — such as the comprehensive plan and policies — are on the way and will bring true benefits to residents. But nevertheless, she's happy Easton is addressing its growth problem head-on.
"No one else around here is having these conversations, but the Town of Easton is," Cook said. "They're difficult conversations. They're polarizing conversations, they're very emotional conversations. But we're having them."

title: The 'Missing Middle': Why Some Town Leaders See a Gap in Easton's Housing Stock
author: Konner Metz
content:
The 'missing middle': Why some town leaders see a gap in Easton's housing stock

 August 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 712
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Often, the Town Council and Planning Commission are forced to consider projects like a large single-family development or a high-density apartment complex. But the in-between is being lost in the shuffle, some town leaders argue."Missing middle housing" is a phrase used by urban planners, typically referring to townhomes or duplexes, triplexes and fourplexes (buildings containing two, three and four units respectively).
In Easton, this housing has been a frequent topic of conversation as town officials grapple with how to fill affordable housing needs and balance the infrastructure concerns that come with significant growth.
Some town leaders see "missing middle" housing as a key rung in the ladder for residents working toward homeownership.
"It's a big step," Ward 2 Councilmember Robert Rankin said. "Owning a home is a tremendous responsibility, and it's a huge milestone in someone's life."
Local real estate agents are noticing the gap, too. Alex Archer, sales manager for The Gerdes Team and a Talbot County resident, said many residents don't have the ability currently to work their way up to buying a single-family home costing hundreds of thousands of dollars. More options in the middle could help that mobility, he said.
"Where's the step to get to that for a lot of blue-collar workers, or for the restaurant workers or for the people who aren't making $150,000 a year?" Archer asked.
Town Council President Don Abbatiello and his wife have experience climbing this ladder. The Abbatiellos first bought a townhome, he said. They later sold it and moved into a single-family home.
But a lot of Easton residents don't have that opportunity since there's not enough affordable housing units available for purchase, Abbatiello said.
"It seems like there's a big drive toward rentals," he said. "But the problem with rentals is you don't build equity."
Tom Klein, an Easton Planning Commission member, said the recently shot-down Fox Chase Estates project had an affordable ownership aspect that he liked. The 365-unit proposal included not just single-family homes, but three-story townhomes, too. It was voted down by Klein and the rest of the commission, though, largely due to connectivity concerns and its placement at the northernmost part of town.
Of affordable rentals, which have carved out notable space in the town's housing pipeline, Klein said: "It still doesn't give people an opportunity to build equity."
A recent draft report from the town's Attainable Housing Task Force takes aim at addressing the missing middle phenomenon in Easton.
Townhomes, duplexes and other missing middle units account for around 20% of the town's stock, according to the draft report, which is undergoing revisions before it is officially presented to the Town Council. The 18-member task force has held discussion on the matter and others as it prepares the report, which is being written by planning and zoning director Miguel Salinas.
The report, referencing census data, states that from 2000 to 2023, around 1,700 new single-family detached homes were built, compared to around 300 single-family attached homes or other middle housing types.
Single-family detached typically refers to a stand-alone house, while attached homes are often townhomes or duplexes.
Michael Ports, vice chair of the Planning Commission, said going straight from an apartment to a detached home can be difficult financially, especially after the pandemic drove up prices.
One potential missing middle housing recommendation the task force may make to the Town Council includes permitting duplexes or townhomes without requiring special approvals or exemptions to the zoning, according to the draft report. Such zoning changes could reduce permitting and time-based costs for developers.
Mayor Megan Cook said such housing types could be crucial for the town's senior population as well.
"We have seniors who have moved here," Cook said. "They maybe now have some health issues, they've lost a spouse or whatnot. They don't need a big home anymore. Maybe they're looking for a smaller footprint."
Gwen Eskridge, an associate broker for Coldwell Banker Chesapeake, lives in Easton. Her daughter and granddaughter both remain at home due to the high cost of homes and rentals in the area.
Development in the missing middle housing range could give them a path toward homeownership, Eskridge said.
"Workforce housing is so critical in this area," Eskridge said. "And I think we really need to start looking into … maybe low-density townhomes or duplexes that would be able to help individuals like my daughter who's living with us."

title: Here's where Easton leaders stand on growth
author: Konner Metz
content:
Here's where Easton leaders stand on growth

 August 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Headlines 
 
 309
 Words 

 Read News Document

 It's a classic debate: build more housing or curb growth?Since joining the The Star Democrat in June 2024, I've seen the housing-growth debate consistently occupy the minds of elected officials, town planners, developers and residents. If you ask a Town Council member or a longtime resident the number one issue that Easton faces, I'd venture to say the answer will be growth-related more times than not.
There's hundreds of housing units in the town's pipeline — 1,127, to be exact. But at the same time, it's well-documented that Easton and Talbot County have an affordability problem, leaving many employees to commute daily from Caroline or Dorchester counties.
So what are the plans to pare down already-heavy traffic and keep the Easton Volunteer Fire Department from transitioning to a paid agency? And at the same time, how can the town still pursue some level of reasonably-priced housing for those that need it most?
It's a complex set of questions I asked the town's top officials, from the mayor, to elected council members, to a surprisingly powerful, six-member volunteer planning board.
The answers aren't clear. Some say slam the brakes. Others believe letting off the gas here and there will do.
There is, however, an approach gaining steam: focus on building from the inside-out, rather than annexing more county land into town or approving sprawling, single-family home developments. Most officials I spoke with endorse that strategy.
No "silver bullet" has emerged or will emerge, many town leaders told me. But a combination of items on the horizon — including a comprehensive plan update, zoning reform and a pause on annexations — will work to manage the town's growth without forgetting about those that seek an affordable place to live.
To hear specifics from town officials, or to find out where Easton's 1,127 units in the pipeline are located, check out my story below.
Thanks for reading.
— Konner Metz

title: Easton Task Force Narrows List of Recommended Housing Solutions
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton task force narrows list of recommended housing solutions

 August 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 650
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — An 18-member group tasked with identifying solutions to address the Easton's affordable housing stock is honing in on which specific recommendations to send to Town Council.Last Thursday, 11 members of the Attainable Housing Task Force met to review a draft version of the task force's final report prepared by Miguel Salinas, the town's planning and zoning director.
They agreed on five main recommendations, which will be spelled out in an edited version of the draft and eventually presented to the Town Council at a joint workshop. Those recommendations include:
Zoning reform suggestions including removing limits for "missing middle" units such as townhomes, increasing maximum densities for some residential districts and adjusting dimensional standards and lot size requirements.A public-private partnership with a housing organization to build an affordable housing project on public land. Potential sites to include the old Talbot County Health Department and vacant county land near Magnolia Drive.Community education to help residents better understand the affordable housing issue.Make some fee exemptions for developers. A main recommendation is to create a Payment in Lieu of Taxes, or PILOT, program, which could provide a property tax break to developers building affordable units.Inclusionary zoning.
Many at the meeting said the task force's job is to lay out potential solutions to improve Easton's affordable housing conundrum. There is no "silver bullet" fix, said task force co-chair Michael Ports, also a member of the Planning Commission.
"These are all just little pieces to the puzzle," said Susie Hayward, director of government affairs for Mid-Shore Board of Realtors. "Not one area is gonna solve the problem. These are all just pieces to make it better."
DEBATE
Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery — who serves on the task force alongside Ward 2's Robert Rankin — raised most of the concerns on the recommendations.
Montgomery said the community outreach recommendation went out of bounds for town government duties. He asked for a "more neutral tone." The draft report indicated that the Town Council should consider a housing webpage and a "media initative to 'put a face' to the housing crisis."
"The part that I could never, ever support on this is a media campaign to provide a human face" to the issue of affordable housing, Montgomery said. " … I just don't think that's the role of government."
Others responded that it's needed to educate people on what exactly affordable housing is.
"It's important to define it for people to understand it because nobody does," task force member and realtor Jim Bent said.
Hayward added that people need to understand that affordable housing matters for "the survival of our businesses."
"They're surviving now without them," Montgomery responded. Hayward disagreed, citing a Talbot County Chamber of Commerce survey of business owners where they expressed concerns that "employees are tentative when they're living in other counties," she said.
At one point, Montgomery said the task force didn't have the proper time "to discuss the pros and cons" of the recommendations. It met 10 times in 2024, though draft recommendations weren't specifically discussed until the final five meetings.
Rankin suggested that when editing the report, Salinas include drawbacks to the recommendations. Ports said the pros and cons aspect was already written especially well by Salinas in the section recommending inclusionary zoning, which Ports believed "strengthened" the argument for inclusionary zoning.
Inclusionary zoning was a hot topic during the town's last election. A draft town ordinance requiring residential developers to allocate 15% of their units as affordable stalled out this winter.
Montgomery, a vocal opponent of the measure, said at the task force meeting that the body's recommendation should be less focused on the old draft ordinance and take a more general stance on inclusionary zoning.
Even if passed, Montgomery said, inclusionary zoning wouldn't immediately bring affordable housing units to Easton.
"That's right, that's why we should've passed it three years ago," Hayward responded. "That's why we gotta pass it today, for all the developments that are coming up in the next five years, 10 years."

title: Talbot County's Cannabis Bill Fails, Goes 'Back to the Drawing Board'
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot County's cannabis bill fails, goes 'back to the drawing board'

 August 13, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 802
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A zoning bill for cannabis facilities in Talbot County failed to pass Tuesday after months of consideration, sending the County Council back to square one.Since recreational cannabis was legalized in Maryland in 2023, local jurisdictions have been tasked with creating zoning regulations for different types of cannabis operations. Talbot County planners have worked nearly a year on drafting a cannabis processing and growing bill, outlining rules on setbacks from homes, odor mitigation and more.
On Tuesday, council members voted down two proposed amendments to the cannabis bill and, eventually, the bill itself. Opposition from council President Chuck Callahan and member Lynn Mielke, along with abstentions from Keasha Haythe (and, in one instance, Dave Stepp), combined to defeat the legislation. Vice President Pete Lesher and Stepp supported the amendments, while Lesher was the sole yes vote on the unamended bill.
Lesher told The Star Democrat that he didn't expect the bill to fail. He believes without it, the county in a tricky spot.
"I think we find ourselves in an interesting position figuring out what the course forward is on regulating cannabis," Lesher said during the meeting. "The state has told us that we must do so, and we now don't have a plan."
As drafted, the legislation would have required processors and growers to locate at least 500 feet away from residential lots, mitigate cannabis odors so nothing is "detectible from adjacent properties" and obtain site plan approval from the county.
Multiple state cannabis license holders had advocated for a reduced setback and lessened odor mitigation requirements, citing that they may not be able to successfully open in Talbot County without those changes. But those edits didn't appear in legislation on the table Tuesday.
Stepp offered an amendment to harden the 500-foot setback so it couldn't be reduced by way of an agreement between affected neighbors, though that failed with only Lesher's support.
Lesher offered an amendment to make permits for processors available only through special exception, as well as increase minimum lot size for growers and processors from 20 to 40 acres. Those changes were recommended by the county's Planning Commission, but only Stepp joined the vice president in supporting them.
Council members who voted no on the legislation cited varying reasons.
Haythe said in an interview after the meeting that she needs more information and has concerns about the effects of odor on children.
"We're gonna have to go back to the drawing board and come up with something," Haythe said. On Wednesday, Haythe said she's working with council and County Attorney Patrick Thomas on drafting a new bill.
In an interview, Stepp said there were "too many moving parts" with the legislation for it to pass. The residential setback should be closer to 1,000 feet, he said.
"I feel like it wasn't the best product that we could've put forward yet," Stepp said. While he still has "a hard time believing" recreational cannabis passed statewide, he acknowledged the county is in a position where it must create some sort of local zoning law.
Many residents have weighed in on the legislation. The matter gained traction in Cordova after a license holder said she was in talks to buy the now-closed Triple Creek Winery. Property owners haven't confirmed or denied if that's still a consideration.
Some residents raised worries that a cannabis business could locate too close to Chapel District Elementary School. Haythe echoed that sentiment.
"Children are a huge concern as it relates to the odor that's smelled, the air that's breathed in the areas where the growing and processing will be done," she said. "We just don't want that to affect the children at that school."
Callahan wrote to The Star Democrat that his concern is land value. "The community doesn't want this," he wrote on Wednesday.
WHAT'S NEXT
It's unclear exactly how soon legislation may return to the council's desk. Any significant changes may necessitate a return to the Planning Commission and potentially a council-commission work session. The council already met with commission members in September to draft the now-failed bill.
In the meantime, the county will operate without clear zoning on cannabis processing and growing facilities. At Tuesday's meeting, Lesher asked how staff will deal with potential permit applications from cannabis license holders looking to locate in Talbot County.
Bryce Yelton said he believes the county "might have to hold it" based on the fact that zoning legislation is under consideration. He deferred to Thomas, the county attorney, for a firmer answer.
Thomas said state law requires cannabis operations to comply with local zoning. Prospective cannabis operators may not be able to make progress in this current limbo period, he said.
"If the county were to take the position that cannabis does not fall under existing agricultural use, then it wouldn't be permitted as such under the zoning code," Thomas said. "So without this (bill), they wouldn't be able to go forward under that position."

title: Move-in Date for Doverbrook Apartments Uncertain Due to Snag with HUD
author: Konner Metz
content:
Move-in date for Doverbrook Apartments uncertain due to snag with HUD

 August 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 614
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Doverbrook Apartments, rebuilt and seemingly ready to welcome in residents, have spent all summer empty due to a snag between the Housing Commission of Talbot and the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development.Run by the housing commission, the 64-unit, voucher-based complex celebrated a renovation this spring, adding 14 apartments to accommodate more low-income tenants. It opened its doors to town, county and state officials for tours upon completion.
But move-in for residents has been delayed since May.
Easton Town Council members expressed concerns earlier this month about the delay, pointing out how it has and will continue to create confusion for residents.
"You're gonna have a lot of people who ride by those buildings, and say, 'What in the world is going on?'" said Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis, whose ward includes Doverbrook, at an Aug. 4 town meeting.
Don Bibb, the Housing Commission's executive director, fielded questions from the council on the matter.
Bibb said the mounting holdups stem from HUD's requirement that the complex's housing choice voucher plan undergo a 45-day public comment period and be advertised in a newspaper. The plan, available for public review in Easton's town office, outlines the complex's occupancy guidelines and priority and waitlist rules, among other things.
Bibb said the commission made slight changes to the plan, such as clarifying which residents are given priority. HUD determined the changes necessitated a reset of the 45-day comment period.
"We dispute that point," Bibb said at the Aug. 4 meeting. He said a waiver request has been submitted to the federal agency.
HUD did not respond to a request for comment Tuesday.
The apartments were closed in December 2023 for renovation. Returning residents, who have been temporarily housed by the commission in St. Michaels, will have priority. In April, 145 people applied to be put on the Doverbrook waitlist, Bibb said last week.
Davis said in an interview Tuesday that the situation is a "sad state of affairs."
The council member has spoken to residents who have sent in applications, and he said their excitement to move into the new apartments has dwindled with the significant delay.
Residents must meet income standards and qualify for the housing vouchers to have their applications approved for the voucher-based complex. Davis is concerned the holdup could put some at a disadvantage.
"What if a person was good in May and may not be good in August or September?" Davis said. "They won't be able to get an apartment, and I don't think that's fair."
Bibb said in an interview last month that rumors spurred by the delay, such as site contractors not getting paid, are false.
Amid swirling speculation, Bibb said the commission would like to get the ball rolling, but he maintained that the commission would continue to honor HUD's needs.
"We're losing revenue. That's not a good thing," Bibb said on July 25. "But it is what it is. Compliance with federal government is a critical point for any type of project like this."
At the time, Bibb said the hope was for most of the units to be occupied by the end of August. But at last week's Town Council meeting, it seemed that target would be moving back.
Bibb told the council that if the waiver request isn't approved, the updated housing choice voucher plan for Doverbrook Apartments was set to go live Aug. 7. That would make Sept. 21 or 22 the worst-case scenario dates for move-in to begin, he said.
Davis said he hopes such delays can be prevented in the future. He acknowledged that the renovated apartments themselves are impressive.
"I think (last week's) discussion brought a lot of enlightenment," Davis said on Tuesday. " ... There were still a lot of questions that were left on the table."

title: Planners Send Short-Term Rental Regs to County Council with Major Revisions
author: Konner Metz
content:
Planners send short-term rental regs to County Council with major revisions

 August 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 360
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — New short-term rental rules proposed by two Talbot County Council members this spring will soon return to the council's desk, though the controversial draft legislation has been significantly changed by the county's Planning Commission.On Wednesday, commission members voted 3-0 to recommend a much different version of short-term rental rules originally introduced by council members Lynn Mielke and Pete Lesher.
Mielke and Lesher's proposals aimed to address what some say is a proliferation of rentals in the county, hurting small communities and villages. Rental owners and agents, though, have said the proposals are an unnecessary example of government overreach.
According to county data from June, there are about 185 short-term rentals in operation. That's largely even with the past two years.
As currently set up, property owners obtain short-term rental licenses from a review board. Once an initial license is approved, they must obtain renewal from the board one year later, then every two years. Thirteen new licenses had been approved in 2025 as of early June, per county data.
Initially, Mielke and Lesher's proposed restrictions included mandatory landlines, more detailed stay logs for license renewals, a seven-night minimum stay for lease holders in residential and village districts, and a split of licenses into two classes based on if the property is the applicant's primary residence.
The Planning Commission gutted most of that.
Landlines, seven-night minimum stays, a class split for licenses and most of the stay log requirements were struck through by the commission in its recommendation.
In some areas, such as with a 60-day deadline for rental license holders to submit a renewal application, the commission is suggesting reduced regulation.
County staff prepared the edits that were presented Wednesday based on a lengthy discussion at the commission's July meeting. Commission member Chip Councell said the update was an accurate reflection of that meeting.
The County Council, though, will have final say on the matter and whether or not language struck by the commission is plugged back in. As of Friday, the short-term rental legislation isn't on the council's agenda for its Tuesday meeting.
"Of course, the ball's in the County Council's court," Councell said. "This is our recommendation. Obviously, they can do whatever they see fit."

title: Talbot's Cannabis Regulations Draw Mixed Reviews from Residents, Operators
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot's cannabis regulations draw mixed reviews from residents, operators

 August 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: News 
 
 678
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CORDOVA — Debate over how strict Talbot County should be on cannabis operations has peaked in recent weeks, especially among Cordova residents.Last month, the county began to consider draft cannabis legislation focused on growing and processing operations. As originally written, such businesses would be barred from locating within 500 feet of residential properties.
Two Talbot County residents who were awarded state licenses for cannabis operations spoke out against strict "no odor" requirements and the 500-foot mark in the draft rules. They asked the council to consider dropping the residential setback to 200 feet as they look to acquire property to locate their cannabis businesses, potentially in Cordova.
Many residents disagree.
"We knew we were going to have agricultural smells," Cordova resident Donna Albright said in an interview. "We were not expecting the continuous odor of marijuana."
Albright and others have lobbied the Talbot County Council to reject the 200-foot setback and keep the "no odor" requirement as initially drafted. Albright said at a county meeting last month that around 150 residents signed onto a petition against any amendments relaxing the setback.
Some have objected to cannabis operations as a whole.
"I have grandchildren that come over, and I would like them to not have to look at this," Cordova resident Perry Davidson said at a July 22 meeting. "So I would ask you not to let something like this happen in Talbot County. It's just not a great idea."
Recreational cannabis use was legalized in 2023 in Maryland. Talbot County's legislation comes as neighboring jurisdictions have enacted regulations on growing and processing operations. The County Council is eligible to vote on the cannabis legislation at its Aug. 12 meeting.
Discussion on cannabis among Cordova residents largely began online and at county meetings after a cultivation license holder, Lori Yates, said at a July 8 meeting that she was potentially working on acquiring the Triple Creek Winery property.
The winery, now closed, is located on Three Bridge Branch Road in Cordova. An owner of the property did not respond to a request for comment.
Yates said in an email Thursday that her entity, Hanson Street Partners LLC, prefers to locate somewhere in Talbot County and plans to acquire property by the end of the year.
She wrote that a 500-foot setback is "quite burdensome," citing the fact that other jurisdictions use 200-foot marks for cannabis operations.
Yates says her motivation to open a cannabis site comes from her experience as a cancer survivor. She pointed out cannabis' use by cancer patients.
"Recreational use has gained increasing cultural acceptance and has shown itself to be less dangerous than alcohol consumption," Yates wrote.
For the residents opposed, the location of Chapel District Elementary School in comparison to the winery raised qualms. Albright also shared worries about groundwater contamination due to high water use.
Albright said she's not against cannabis use, but that "our biggest thing is about processing in our front yard." Speaking to the County Council last month, Albright asked that the county keep the "no odor" language.
"We are deathly opposed to the continuous odor," she said.
Zac Hopkins, co-founder of Lady Grace LLC, the county's other license holder for processing, said he's reviewed more than 10 potential sites in Talbot County.
"Unfortunately, if the current draft cannabis legislation is enacted as written, every one of these properties would be deemed noncompliant; effectively preventing the production of this Maryland state-certified agricultural product within our county," Hopkins wrote in an email.
While over 100 people signed onto the petition against reducing the setback, some Cordova residents have expressed their support for vetted cannabis operations.
"I know that these facilities are run clean," longtime Cordova resident Sylvia Carroll said in an interview. "They don't destroy the environment."
Carroll acknowledged that "the further away from a residence, the better." But she added that she sees much of the opposition coming from misunderstandings about the prospective operations.
"I've lived through the chicken factory and I've lived through the manure spreading and chicken houses being emptied," Carroll said. "I think people just aren't really informed as to what it is. I think they think they're just going to be selling drugs out the back door."

title: Proposal for More Public Input in Easton Housing Projects Gains Traction
author: Konner Metz
content:
Proposal for more public input in Easton housing projects gains traction

 July 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: News 
 
 554
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A proposal to require more public involvement in the early planning stages for development projects is gaining traction in Easton.With hundreds of new housing units under construction or approved, some recent proposals by developers to add to Easton's housing stock have garnered pushback from residents.
Most projects, though, don't receive that public input until developers come before a town board like the Planning Commission. Resident Maury Schlesinger is looking for that to change.
"Most projects, the only way somebody's going to find out that they're more than half-baked is if they pay attention to the agendas for the Planning Commission," Schlesinger said.
He wrote a proposal to the commission last month asking for the town to require meetings between the developer and residents for large-scale residential projects and potentially some commercial uses. While there's no official drafted legislation yet, Schlesinger's proposal draws from similar rules in jurisdictions like Prince George's and Anne Arundel counties.
At its July meeting, the Planning Commission was receptive to Schlesinger's ask.
"I think that's fair to the communities to have a formal process to listen and be heard before it comes to us," said commission member Victoria McAndrews.
Commission Chair Philip Toussaint said the community meetings could benefit developers, too.
"I think developers could really use this as an advantage because they would be able to get new ideas for their projects," Toussaint said. "I think it could be a positive thing."
Toussaint noted that it's important for public input to occur before site plans are completed, since it then becomes hard for developers to reverse course on those plans while maintaining financial viability.
Developers for recently approved Easton Crossing project — a 116-unit mixed-use plan on Brookletts Avenue by nonprofit developer Fello — held multiple community meetings before a site plan was submitted to the commission. Schlesinger noted that those meetings made positive impacts to Fello's final designs, such as the massing and architecture of the buildings.
In his mind, the Easton Crossing process was especially effective compared to Silo Court, Fello's 28-unit townhouse project on Needwood Avenue. Neighboring residents felt it didn't include enough public input early in the process.
Ross Benincasa, vice president of community development for Fello, said in a statement that the Easton Crossing meetings also led to developers including lighting along walkways and areas for art in the project plan.
"Our goal in these meetings is to listen, answer questions, and be transparent about the project's possibilities and constraints, which can include factors like space, materials, and financial feasibility," Benincasa wrote.
Schlesinger compares community involvement in housing projects to test screenings for movies where revisions are made after gauging feedback.
"If you can get people involved earlier in the process, they may not get everything they want, but they nudge the project in a direction that's better overall," he said.
Planning Commission Vice Chair Michael Ports said in an interview that community meetings can also increase accessibility for residents who can't attend the monthly commission meetings.
"We want the developer to be meeting with the community, even if it's without us, to have earnest conversations about what they want," Ports said. "I think this is especially true for infill projects."
Town Planner Lynn Thomas said at the July meeting that he's met with Schlesinger on the community input proposal. Those discussions on how to implement the public input requirements will continue over the upcoming months, Schlesinger said.

 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Easton Planning Commission didn't budge Thursday on its staunch opposition to a proposed 365-unit housing development near the under-construction hospital and Easton Airport.The body unanimously agreed to send a negative recommendation to the Town Council on an application from developers looking to build the Fox Chase Estates on 112 acres of land off of Airport Road.
As they did last month, commission members cited the lack of connectivity, segregation between housing types and an already large pipeline of other housing projects as reasons for their disapproval.
Commission member Victoria McAndrews said OK'ing the Fox Chase homes would be a "hasty" decision. She said the town should let other projects build before adding more units to the pipeline.
"I'm feeling like it's the wrong place, wrong time," McAndrews said.
Easton Sunrise Partners LLC and Scott Wagner, a Talbot County businessman and a former Republican member of the Pennsylvania State Senate, are the developers. They previously aimed to build warehouses on the site but in recent years shifted to residential.
Wagner was seeking approval through Easton's planned unit development process, which would allow the homes to be built on the commercial-zoned land. It's near what will be Easton's new hospital on Longwoods Road, which is expected to open in 2028. University of Maryland Shore Regional Health President and CEO Ken Kozel has voiced support for the housing development, hoping it would help retain and attract health care workers.
Wagner's attorney Lawrence Scott defended the project on Thursday. He focused on the argument that Fox Chase meet the standards of Easton's comprehensive plan, which is the basis the commission uses when deciding whether to recommend a development.
"This land has been in the town for over 25 years," Scott said. "This is not an annexation to do residential building. This is not someone trying to grow the town."
But Scott's appeals didn't quell the commission's concerns nor the public's. Many residents spoke against the proposal during public comment.
"When I first saw this project, I had to reach for an oxygen bottle because it took my breath away," resident Bruce Harrington said.
Easton resident Barbara Lane shared concerns about the homes causing more traffic on Airport and Goldsborough Neck roads, as well as how far the development would be away from Easton's other residential areas.
"There's no connectivity to other neighborhoods," Lane said.
THURSDAY'S DEBATE
Developers on Thursday agreed to fixing a number of items flagged by town and county officials in June, including the lack of a second vehicle access point to the neighborhood. But largely, the site plan remained as originally submitted.
Of the 365 proposed units, 108 are single-family detached homes, 137 are three-story townhomes and 120 are multifamily units. Developers say 185 of the units will be affordably priced. Those units would enjoy the same access to the neighborhood's commercial buildings and open space, though they're largely grouped by type on the site plan.
Commission Vice Chair Michael Ports took issue with that aspect.
"We are making several different neighborhoods where it is very clear that there are different housing types and different income levels within them, and I don't believe that's in the spirit of the comp plan," Ports said.
Meanwhile, commission members echoed resident concerns that the development wouldn't be connected enough to the rest of town, citing that as a core tenet of Easton's current comprehensive plan.
Approved in 2010, the comprehensive plan is undergoing a major update. The Planning Commission and town staff are drafting an updated plan, which will lay out objectives for growth in town and may offer more clarity on what town planners envision for the northernmost part of town around the new hospital.
As the commission's negative views on the project became clear Thursday, Scott contested that some reasons for disapproval were "beyond the scope of what we're here today to do."
"Making us wait for the next comprehensive plan is not part of today's deliberation," Scott said.
"The alternative here is we go back to giant warehouses and the Amazons of the world and 1,000 trucks a day," he added. "At the end of the day, the property owner has a right to make use of his property."
Developers have said they've met multiple times with council members and Mayor Megan Cook to discuss the need for affordable housing, although it remains unclear where council members will land if the project goes to them for a vote. Council has final say as the commission is only a recommending body.
"We're here because we met with council members, and they said, 'We need for-sale, affordable homes,'" Scott said Thursday.
Commission Chair Philip Toussaint said his body's letter to the Town Council will lead with why the project isn't in line with the comprehensive plan. He noted the project brings about health worries and strays from the plan's future land use map, in addition to not meeting connectivity and integrated housing standards.
Some residents expressed worries the development would damage Easton's small-town character. McAndrews acknowledged the "anywhere USA" concerns.
"There's a lot of suburban sprawl outside Easton, and that's what we're trying to control," Toussaint said.

title: Fate of Talbot's Short-Term Rental Proposals Still Up in the Air
author: Konner Metz
content:
Fate of Talbot's short-term rental proposals still up in the air

 July 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 728
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The future of short-term rental legislation in Talbot County remains uncertain as the county's planning commission and elected officials have yet to find a middle ground.In an ongoing debate since May, Talbot County Council members Lynn Mielke and Pete Lesher are aiming to further regulate short-term rental properties in the county. But agents, owners and now county planners have indicated opposition to the proposals.
At its July 2 meeting, the Talbot County Planning Commission reviewed draft legislation line-by-line. Commission members delivered mixed thoughts on some of the rules, but for the most part, they provided negative reviews on changes they described as "onerous" and unnecessary.
And on a couple specifics, they discussed relaxing requirements instead of increasing them.
In an interview Tuesday, Mielke said it's clear the commission is "100% on the side of short-term rentals."
"Anybody who is affected negatively by short-term rentals doesn't have a voice," she said. "And those who are profiting from short-term rentals control."
The Planning Commission left written comment open on July 2, and it's unclear exactly when that body's amended version of the legislation will be officially sent to the council.
The commission's recommendation is likely to gut a number of the proposed regulations; however, the commission is only a recommending body in the matter, leaving the County Council with final say.
PROPOSED RULES
Proponents of the legislation, such as Mielke and some county residents, argue a proliferation of short-term rentals is hurting local communities, especially village zones. Opponents say the number of rentals hasn't significantly increased in the last few years and that changes aren't needed given a lack of formal complaints from neighbors.
As currently set up, property owners obtain short-term rental licenses from a review board. Once an initial license is approved, they must obtain renewal from the board one year later, then every two years.
Some of the new proposed restrictions include mandatory landlines, more detailed stay logs for license renewals, a seven-night minimum stay for lease holders in residential and village districts, and a split of licenses into two classes based on if the property is the applicant's primary residence.
As drafted, properties that aren't the applicant's primary residence would face new license limits: one license per 500 or 1,000 feet, depending on the zoning district.
Commission member Paul Spies said the class split is a "hard sell."
"I think the law as it is is fine," he said. "Two licenses, to me, doesn't make sense."
"It seems onerous on staff," Commission Chair James Corson said.
For renewal applicants, the proposed legislation lays out new logging requirements. Property owners would need to submit specific stay logs, including when the property was occupied by the owner or family members.
"I think that's a little bit too much of an overreach," Chip Councell said.
Mielke said the concerns around how much work will be put on staff and what would be asked of rental owners aren't totally valid. She said wording for the draft regulations was derived from Prince George's County.
"It had a basis," Mielke said, adding that for tax purposes, rental owners should already be documenting information that the new proposals would ask for.
The commission at times voiced that Talbot County's current short-term rental rules could be relaxed. Commission members said the council should make rental licenses transferable. Currently, new applications must be submitted if ownership of a property is transferred.
"The use hasn't changed. Zoning follows a land, it does not follow the owner," Councell said. "So it would seem to me that there would be a way that makes sense.
"I would say that a short-term rental license should be transferable" with conditions, he added.
Lesher and Mielke disagree.
"That's something that I don't support," Lesher said in an interview. "I think that who is running one of these matters, and that should not be automatic in the transfer and renewal."
Lesher said the council does pay attention to the commission's recommendation, and that with positive reviews of some smaller aspects of the proposals, there will be an update to the code no matter where some of the more major pieces land.
"I do think that something should pass here," Lesher said.
It's still unclear whether Mielke and Lesher's proposals will garner majority support from the council. Dave Stepp and Keasha Haythe both said they are waiting for the commission's official recommendation and further discussion.
Council President Chuck Callahan says he hopes to take the recommendations into account while coming "to a compromise" with all council members.

title: Remaining units at Easton Crossing receive OK from Planning Commission
author: Konner Metz
content:
Remaining units at Easton Crossing receive OK from Planning Commission

 June 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 507
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Easton Planning Commission on Tuesday approved the remaining portion of a residential project on Brookletts Avenue at the site of the former Perdue AgriBusiness operation.Developers from Fello, formerly The Arc Central Chesapeake Region, are aiming to build Easton Crossing, a mixed-use project with commercial space and significant open space in the center of the residential buildings.
In February, the commission OK'd 67 units but balked on Building 409, the project's largest structure, which was originally proposed to stand five stories tall and house 56 units.
Tuesday, developers returned with a smaller Building 409, down to four stories and 38 units. A previously approved building, Building 411, was increased in the adjusted site plan to account for some of those lost units. The entire project, though, is still down from its original 123-unit plan to 116.
Commission members were largely pleased with the new Building 409. Developers and architects moved the large structure to the north of the project site, creating a larger lawn in the middle of the buildings.
Chair Philip Toussaint said he needed to be "sold a little bit more about" the center lawn after the building's move.
Ross Benincasa, Fello's vice president of community development, said it will help address a lack of public open space between John Ford Park and Idlewild Park.
"We have to make this more of a focal point so that people know this is open for them to use," he said.
Commission member William Ryall said he was first unhappy with the decision to move the building but warmed up to the idea after hearing Benincasa's explanation.
Some of Tuesday's discussion involved concerns over the lack of a landscaping plan, which had been approved in February. Commission members felt like it should be resubmitted in more detail given the significant changes to the project.
"I think it's an incomplete submission if you haven't updated the landscape plan," Toussaint said.
"The landscape plan could mitigate a lot of the concerns people have about the project," commission member Victoria McAndrews said.
Despite those qualms, the commission — which applauded developers in February for an attractive project with proper community outreach — was on board with the revised plans.
In a 4-1 vote, the revised Easton Crossing site plan was approved with conditions, one of them being a return by developers to present a landscaping plan. The votes fell the same way as they did in February, with Tom Klein being the sole no vote.
Klein, who cited a lack of parking on site as a reason for voting down the project in February, did so again Tuesday. He said competition for nearby on-street parking spaces will occur once tenants move in.
"I like a lot about this project," he said. "But I still am not going to be able to vote yes because I'm still not comfortable with the off-street parking."
Apartments are expected to be available beginning in 2027. At least 30% of the rental units are planned to be affordably priced — between 30% to 80% of the area median income. Other units will be at workforce and market-rate levels.

title: Planners Not Sold on 365-Unit Development Near New Easton Hospital
author: Konner Metz
content:
Planners not sold on 365-unit development near new Easton hospital

 June 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 739
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — An application for a 365-unit residential development near the in-construction regional medical center in Easton has been submitted to the town's Planning Commission for review, though it's drawing criticism from some town and county officials.The project, Fox Chase Estates, is proposed on 112 acres of land off of Airport Road nestled within the Easton Technology Center. Developers are seeking town approval through Easton's planned unit development process, which would allow the homes to be built on the commercial-zoned land.
The developers are Easton Sunrise Partners LLC and Scott Wagner, a Talbot County businessman and a former Republican member of the Pennsylvania State Senate. They previously aimed to build warehouses on the site, but in recent years plans shifted to residential — an effort that Shore Regional Health President and CEO Ken Kozel supports, according to Wagner's attorney, Lawrence Scott.
"We are trying to build a residential community that meets the need of the hospital," Scott said Tuesday, noting that Wagner and Kozel have met to discuss the project.
In a statement Wednesday, Kozel said affordable housing availability is "essential" to recruit and retain health care workers in a rural community like Easton. The hospital is not legally or financially involved with the proposed development, Scott said.
At an hours long meeting Tuesday, Planning Commission members were nowhere near ready to provide a positive recommendation on the proposal.
"It feels like we're being the Planning Commission for the hospital and not for the town," said member William Ryall. "And that gives me a lot of concern."
Victoria McAndrews said the plans are "overwhelmingly suburban." Michael Ports, the commission's vice chair, said a lack of connectivity from the proposed development — which sits at the northernmost part of town limits — to Easton's core is a "non-starter."
Philip Toussaint, commission chair, said parts of the plan significantly fall short of meeting Easton's comprehensive plan, which sets the framework for how the town facilitates growth. That comprehensive plan is undergoing an update currently, and McAndrews said such a large project should wait for that update.
Scott said Tuesday that developers have met individually with Town Council members and Mayor Megan Cook multiple times and that the 365-unit project meets affordable housing needs that the town and its residents are asking for.
THE UNITS
Application documents show that developers are planning for a variety of units, including single-family homes, three-story townhomes and multifamily buildings, along with two commercial buildings.
The 365 units are broken down as follows: 108 single-family detached homes, 137 three-story townhomes and 120 multifamily units, the latter of which are contained in four four-story buildings.
The density is well below the maximum permitted by the town's planned unit development standards. According to developers, 185 of the 365 units would be affordably priced.
"We're doing that without even the statutory forcing of us to do it," Scott said, adding that developers have a "bidding war" from home building companies to take on the project. "The market is working on its own."
APPROVAL PROCESS
Fox Chase Estates still has a handful of steps before it is approved by Easton officials. With significant pushback already, it's likely to be a lengthy process.
In staff analysis of the application, concerns were raised about the site plan, which only includes one main vehicle access point to the 365-unit development. An emergency exit stretching west to Goldsborough Neck Road did not satisfy town staff. Scott said developers would prefer not to add that as a main access point but will consider it.
"We really want two access points to any project like this," said Town Engineer Rick Van Emburgh.
Talbot County Engineer Ray Clarke criticized the project and the lack of communication between developers and the county. Clarke said it'll put an undue stress on Airport and Goldsborough Neck Roads and added concerns that the homes will be in the runway protection zone for Easton Airport.
"We need to be very, very careful when we're looking at these types of development," Clarke said. "This was general commercial as originally planned. We were told three or four years ago it was going to be warehouses."
On Tuesday, the Planning Commission opted to place a pin in the matter and revisit it on July 17. Commission members may then provide a recommendation.
Once the commission makes its recommendation, council members will consider the application and hold a public hearing before any decision. While the council may take the commission's decision into account, the five council members have the final say, with a majority required for approval.
