title: Talbot council, planning commission weigh in on controversial short-term rental restrictions
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot council, planning commission weigh in on controversial short-term rental restrictions

 June 13, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 567
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Talbot County Planning Commission members are largely skeptical of proposals to increase regulations on short-term rentals in the county.During a joint workshop with the County Council on Tuesday, the commission reviewed legislation sponsored by council members Lynn Mielke and Pete Lesher. Planning Commission members said they struggled to understand why stricter rules for short-term rentals were necessary.
Commission Member Chip Councell said some of the proposed items are more of a "hindrance" than an improvement to the county's existing rules.
"I would almost support an easing of some of the restrictions more so than getting more stringent," Councell said. "I'm struggling to see this as a balance."
Mielke has previously said the legislation was drafted amid a "proliferation" of short-term rentals in Talbot County, noting her concerns for St. Michaels village communities such as Bentley Hay and Rio Vista.
Mielke said Tuesday that in village zones, some communities don't have covenants or restrictions on the temporary rentals. County attorney Patrick Thomas, who helped draft the legislation, noted it can be "tricky" to change covenants since many require 75 to 80% of homeowners to agree.
"They can be overwhelmed by short-term rentals, so the idea was to sort of make a distinction," Mielke said.
Mielke added that an increasing number of short-term rentals are "being scooped up by investors," which she says is hurting the county's affordable housing stock. Planning Commission members disagreed.
"I don't see where this is a proliferation," Councell said, citing that the number of licensed short-term rentals hasn't significantly increased or reached 200 in the last few years.
"They're taking them from subpar to show pieces for people to come down and enjoy," said commission chair James Corson. " … I don't think the majority of these are even in that range of affordable housing."
Some of the new restrictions if the legislation is passed would include: mandatory landlines; more detailed stay logs for license renewals; a seven-night minimum stay for lease holders in residential and village districts; and a split of licenses into two classes based on if the property is the applicant's primary residence.
As drafted, properties that aren't the applicant's primary residence would face new license limits: one license per 500 or 1,000 feet, depending on the zoning district.
The proposals have drawn support from a number of residents around the county but sharp criticism from short-term rental property agents and owners who view them as government overreach.
Property owners already must go through a review board to obtain or renew a license to operate a short-term rental. Most license requests are granted.
Corson raised qualms with how the proposed seven-night minimum stay could deter tourists from attending weekend events such as the Waterfowl Festival. Lesher acknowledged it's "largely a weekend business" and said he's comfortable keeping the current three-day minimum in place.
County Council member Dave Stepp weighed in against proposals for more detailed logs and required landlines.
"To have that legislation in there, it just doesn't make any sense," he said of the landlines.
No official changes were made to the draft regulations Tuesday. The commission will hold a public hearing and discuss the legislation at its July 2 meeting. A recommendation will then be made to the council, likely with significant revisions to the original proposals.
Planning Commission vice chair Michael Strannahan said the issue comes down to preserving the balance between economic benefits and maintaining the county's complexion.
"It's the old growth versus character thing we face all the time," Strannahan said.

title: Short-term Rentals Come Under Scrutiny in Talbot County with Proposed Regulations
author: Konner Metz
content:
Short-term rentals come under scrutiny in Talbot County with proposed regulations

 June 6, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 720
 Words 

 Read News Document

 As a proposal to increase regulations on short-term rentals in Talbot County draws sharp criticism from rental owners and companies, some residents are pushing back in support of the legislation.Leslie Steen, of Tilghman Island, says there are four short-term rental properties within 1,000 feet of her home. She's worried it'll become a domino effect for the "tight-knit" community if more rentals pop up.
"The more houses we lose, the less of a community we have," Steen said. "And that's not healthy."
Regulations proposed last month by County Council members Lynn Mielke and Pete Lesher would introduce stricter rules on short-term rental operations and the licenses they receive. The proposal elicited divided opinions at a county meeting last month, and there's no clear middle ground as county planners prepare to meet with the council Tuesday for a workshop on the legislation.
Property owners already must go through a review board to obtain or renew a license. Most license requests are granted.
Proposed are measures that some rental owners argue go too far, including a seven-night minimum stay for lease holders in residential and village districts, an increase from the current three-night requirement.
Lesher says the seven-day minimum isn't a huge change — he says short-term rentals are "by and large a weekend business."
"It's really, how often can it be rented?" Lesher added, saying an increase from three to seven days still leaves 52 weeks a year on the table.
Michelle Hoyle, owner of the rental company Tidewater Vacations, says renters won't be likely to pay for seven days if they can only stay for less than a week. She says shorter stays have become more common since many of her renters have gone back to in-person work in Washington, D.C.
"This will shut me down," Hoyle said. "Three-day is hard enough. We understand the three-day."
Hoyle says the possibility of the change is already leading her to seek out homes in nearby counties. Currently, Tidewater Vacations operates seven short-term properties, all in Talbot County.
"It's something I don't want to do because I truly do love this county," Hoyle said. "But I don't have an option."
ADDED RESTRICTIONS
Draft legislation would amend the county's current short-term rental rules, which property owners largely say they understand and accept.
Along with the seven-day stay requirement, some of the proposed rule additions that have received divided reactions include:
Licenses would split into two classes — one for properties that are the applicant's primary residence and the other for non-primary residences. The latter class would limit one license per 500 or 1,000 feet, depending on zoning district.Landlines would have to be installed in all short-term rentals.Short Term Rental Review Board members would only be eligible for one immediate reappointment.Renewal applications would require logs of when the rental was occupied by tenants, family members and the owner.
The ask to provide more detailed logging hasn't sat well with Easton residents Kevin and Angeline Hartmann, who often rent out a second home on the Miles River.
"To me, that's a total overreach," Kevin Hartmann said. "I still can't believe that lawmakers and the county attorney would put that in the legislation."
Keith Watts is chair of the review board and owns two short-term rental properties himself. He says the new restrictions would only add more stress on county planners tasked with reviewing and tracking licenses and applications.
"The amount of time that planning and zoning spends on short-term rentals is astronomical," Watts said.
Residents supportive of the regulations view them as an improvement from the current rules that they feel are "one size fits all." They hope the class distinction could help prevent clusters of short-term rentals from popping up in St. Michaels neighborhoods like Bentley Hay or on smaller residential roads in areas such as Tilghman Island.
"You may not need the same kind of restrictions for 10-acre lots as you do for houses that have 10-foot setbacks," St. Michaels resident Monica Otte said.
The revisions are still far from a potential vote. The commission and council will hold a joint workshop Tuesday at 2:30 p.m. Lesher said in an interview that he's listening to critics of the legislation, especially those who have specific objections.
Residents like Otte say they aren't looking for legislation to completely kill short-term rentals, but instead something to provide more balance.
"What we're looking for is a better balance, a more fair balance between Talbot residents and short-term rental owners," Otte said.

 EASTON — As Talbot County prepares to update its comprehensive plan, residents are asked to share their thoughts through an online survey.Bryce Yelton, the county's assistant planning officer, said Tuesday that updates to the actual comprehensive plan language haven't started. "I'd just like to give a shoutout to staff on this," Stamp said. "Council, you've really kind of created a mandate for staff to try to enhance our transparency and communication with the public."

 May 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 675
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — As summer nears, disagreement between a local seafood processor and neighboring residents over odor mitigation efforts is resurfacing.Residents in Ward 4 have long complained of odor emanating from Chesapeake Brand Seafood on Maryland Avenue during crab season.
It led to action by the Easton Town Council last December. The town passed an ordinance requiring seafood processing operations to install odor control technology "in such a manner that no odor" could be detected.
Per the ordinance, an odor control system must be installed by July 1. But Chesapeake Brand Seafood is now requesting an amendment to the ordinance, citing that industry experts say the "no odor" language is an unachievable goal.
Peter Maloney, who lives around 500 feet from the business, has been a vocal neighborhood leader for affected residents. He says the odor makes it hard for his kids to enjoy time outside.
"It's not something we signed up for," said Maloney, who moved to Easton around five years before the business opened in 2019.
He added that Chesapeake Brand Seafood isn't acting as a good neighbor with its attempt to amend the already-approved ordinance.
"They're kicking the can down the road," Maloney said.
At Monday's Town Council meeting, the amendment was introduced and referred to the Planning Commission for review at its May 15 meeting. Town Council will still have the final say.
If passed, the amendment will remove the requirement that odor control systems act "in such a manner that no odor from any product or by-product can be detected outside the building on the same property or on adjacent properties or public rights-of-way."
Replacing the deleted language is, in part, the requirement that engineers or industry experts confirm the installed odor control equipment uses "best control technologies and methods designed to mitigate odor before it leaves a building."
Owner Mitch Hughes says his business requested the amendment due to the "no odor" language. He's looking for clarity over whether that mandate would be based on odor detection or resident complaints.
"Zero odor means I'm done completely," Hughes said. "It's just not possible."
Hughes is ready to install the odor control technology, but he's holding off since he doesn't want to begin footing the $800 monthly cost if it won't end up meeting the ordinance.
"They all said we can install a system and get your odor down," he said. "But there's no way you can reach zero odor."
Maloney and other residents spoke in opposition to the proposed amendment Monday.
"I feel like I've earned my right to retire, and I don't want to have to do it inside my household," Carla Howell said.
"We are organized, and we are all very angry about this as you can hear," Emily Stone said. "And we will not be quiet until something is done."
Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis, who pushed for the ordinance to be passed last year, said he's against any amendment.
"I think the ordinance as it stands is an excellent ordinance," Davis said. "And the crab industry hasn't been a good neighbor."
Ward 1's Maureen Curry said Monday that Chesapeake Brand Seafood gave the council a "flat-out no" on the prospect of moving to a new location, likely one not in a residential area. Hughes, whose business was legally permitted by the town to locate on that property, says he's only against moving if he has to foot the full bill.
Hughes said the business has taken steps as requested by town code enforcement to reduce odor. Remaining complaints, he said, are due to the steaming process.
"It's kind of hard to fix the smell of steamed crabs," Hughes said. "That's just part of the process. That is our process."
But Maloney and other residents said Monday the proposed amendment feels like a stall tactic from Chesapeake Brand Seafood as the July 1 deadline nears.
Maloney said in an interview that the neighbors aren't looking to hurt a business. They are, however, fighting for what he calls a "well-worded" and effective ordinance to stand as originally approved.
"To loosen this at the expense of all property owners who have dealt with this for five years is unfair," Maloney said.

title: In Packed Meeting, Short-Term Rental Owners Speak Out Against Proposed Regulations
author: Konner Metz
content:
In packed meeting, short-term rental owners speak out against proposed regulations

 May 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 764
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Over 40 people filled the room for Wednesday's Talbot County Planning Commission meeting, an unusually large turnout for the 9 a.m. event.Many of those in the crowd were property owners who came to oppose potential new regulations on short-term rentals.
In legislation drafted by Talbot County Council members Lynn Mielke and Pete Lesher and subsequently referred to the Planning Commission, new restrictions would be placed on short-term rental operations and licenses.
Mielke says the proposed revisions come as there's a "proliferation" of short-term rentals that are hurting neighbors and communities. But owners argue some of the proposals will derail short-term rental businesses.
One change would mandate a seven-night minimum stay for short-term lease holders in some districts, while the other districts would maintain the current rule of a three-night minimum.
"That is absolutely a killer," said Bill Morrison, who operates a rental in St. Michaels. "It will drive business away."
Property owners called the potential revisions government overreach and a breach of privacy. Kathleen Schamel called the legislation a "non-starter."
Mielke, along with a handful of residents who spoke in support of the draft regulations, disagreed.
Tilghman Island resident Leslie Steen said short-term rentals "diminish the sense of community."
"Concentration is an issue," she said. "Four short-term rentals within 1,000 feet is too many. There's a domino effect. My neighbor goes short-term rental, I'm out of here. Then my house, guess what? It'll sell as a short-term rental."
THE LEGISLATION
In order to obtain a short-term rental license, property owners in Talbot County must go through the Short Term Rental Review Board. Most license requests are granted. The properties are often listed on sites such as Airbnb or Vrbo and leased out to tenants.
Once an initial license is approved, property owners must obtain renewal from the board one year later, and then every two years after the one-year mark.
Cindy Reichart, vice chair of the board, spoke in opposition to Mielke's proposed regulations Wednesday. Reichart noted the number of licenses hasn't significantly increased in recent years — there were 157 in 2018 and 164 in 2024, she said.
"I'm scratching my head trying to understand why all these changes are requested," Reichart said.
In addition to the seven-night minimum, the proposed revisions would:
Split licenses into two classes. Class A for properties that are the applicant's primary residence and Class B for properties that aren't the applicant's primary residence.
Limit Class B licenses to one per 500 feet or one per 1,000 feet, depending on the zoning district.
Require that short-term rentals install landlines.
Require that license renewal applications include detailed logs of when the rental was occupied by tenants, family members and the owner.
Some short-term rental owners said having to provide logs of when family or friends stay will infringe on privacy or become an extra burden.
"Our renewal process is already plenty burdensome," said Steve Goldberg.
Mielke noted that the purpose of the revisions is to "strike a balance between residents and short-term rental owners." She said many residents moved into communities such as Bentley Hay and Rio Vista not expecting much of the neighborhood to be flooded with short-term rental houses.
WHAT'S NEXT
The proposed revisions were introduced by the County Council April 18, then referred to the Planning Commission. A second version of the revisions — which added wording on the seven-night minimum stay — was created between April 18 and Wednesday's meeting.
Some property owners and representatives said the edited legislation should've never been reviewed by the commission since County Council didn't introduce it as edited.
"Councilwoman Mielke picked and chose what she wanted and presented it without council approval," said Martha Suss, a former Short Term Rental Review Board member.
The legislation would have to make its way back to the County Council's desk in order to be voted into law. Once the Planning Commission makes a recommendation on the revisions, they will likely appear on the council's agenda for approval.
The Planning Commission received over 70 written testimonies regarding the proposed changes. Wednesday, it held public comment for over 90 minutes, including remarks from commission member Ed Heikes, who recused himself from the dais to speak against the legislation.
Commission members agreed to leave written public comment open. The proposal will return when the commission and County Council host a joint workshop Tuesday, June 10, at 2:30 p.m.
Keith Watts, chair of the STR Review Board, said Wednesday the revisions shouldn't make it out of the commission.
"This should die a quiet and dignified death somewhere," Watts said.
But St. Michaels resident Monica Otte felt the proposal is an adequate effort to provide balance.
"Balance between the interests and rights of the short-term rental owners, and the neighbors, the full-time resident neighbors," Otte said.

title: Two Potential Dispensaries Compete to Open in Easton
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Two potential cannabis dispensaries are racing to secure final approvals from the Easton planners, but only one will be able to be built, at least in the location the business plans.Both potential locations sit near each other in the former bank locations near the Giant and Walmart on Elliott Road. State law will require one of the two dispensaries to find another spot.
"It was described at our hearing as something of a race to the finish at this point," said Lynn Thomas, town planner, in an interview. "The one issue that is at play for both of them is part of the state law requires minimum separation between other cannabis dispensaries.
"They obviously are right across the street from one another, so whoever gets their final approval first is going to prevent the other from opening at that location."
According to the Maryland Cannabis Administration, dispensaries are required to be 1,000 feet away from each other.
The applicant for 8223 Elliott Road is BGFY LLC and the applicant for 8171 Elliott Road is Driller Ventures LLC, Thomas said in an email.
Both business were approved for special exception by the town on different dates.
According to the town planner, BGFY LLC received its special exception on Dec. 17. A subdivision application for this property is currently under review, which would create a new parking lot surrounding the dispensary. Following the completion of the subdivision, the business will also need to submit applications for building permits.
According to Thomas, Driller Ventures LLC received a special exception on Jan. 25. The business' next step in the process is to apply for building permits.
The town planner states, "to my knowledge, we have not yet received any such applications."
The Star Democrat could not reach Driller Ventures LLC or BGFY LLC for comment.

title: Keefe, Rankin Discuss Growth, Businesses and More Ahead of Ward 2 Election
author: Konner Metz
content:
Keefe, Rankin discuss growth, businesses and more ahead of Ward 2 election

 May 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 564
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — May 6, residents in Easton's 2nd ward will head to the polls to choose a new representative. Current Ward 2 Councilmember Don Abbatiello is running for Town Council president.Lynn Keefe and Robert Rankin are running for the open seat. In interviews with The Star Democrat's editorial board last week, Keefe and Rankin discussed a need to control growth in Easton.
Keefe said the town's pipeline of approved projects — which recently included around 1,000 housing units — could negatively impacts schools and infrastructure.
"Apartments and apartments and apartments — lots of them coming, without really taking into consideration schooling, and roads and things like that that are really going to be affected," Keefe said.
Keefe said it is possible to address housing needs while managing growth. She worries the influx of apartment projects may result in a large number of unoccupied units.
"It's going to come back to bite you," she said.
In regards to the town's comprehensive plan, which lays out a vision for how the town should prioritize its growth, Rankin said he prefers "slower growth."
The current plan, which hasn't been updated since 2010, calls for 1% year-to-year growth. It is in the draft stages of being revised by the town's planning department and commission.
Rankin said he doesn't see annexation — which has been used by the town to facilitate future housing developments — as an "apparent" need.
"I am pretty comfortable with the footprint of Easton currently, and I think we have enough space within the town for redevelopment purposes, for refurbishing, to meet the needs of immediate future development," Rankin said.
BUSINESSES
Both candidates offered thoughts on how to support local businesses.
Keefe, who owned a small business in Virginia for 18 years, said Easton has less red tape than where she operated her business. But she says Easton can still reduce some obstacles to help business owners.
"We need to make it a little bit easier for people. So many hoops," she said.
Meanwhile, Rankin said it's important to improve pedestrian safety and prevent potential accidents in order for residents to feel comfortable walking to downtown businesses.
"I think there is an opportunity in Easton to have some more pedestrian-friendly interventions to make it easier for folks to feel comfortable walking around, and crossing streets and walking among traffic," Rankin said.
PROPERTY TAXES
While Easton's real property tax rate has remained even at 52 cents per $100 of assessed value since 2008, property values have significantly increased.
Easton Mayor Megan Cook proposed a fiscal year 2026 budget last month that would keep the property tax rate the same. The budget projects $13.6 million in real property tax revenue, slightly up from FY25.
Keefe and Rankin were asked their takes on the property tax dilemma.
Keefe said the town should keep spending under control and be cognizant of the potential impacts of tax hikes.
"You don't want to tax your people to death where they have to move," Keefe said. "I have an elderly couple at church, they're concerned. They're living on social security. They're concerned about if it gets too much higher, 'We're going to have to move.' And I think that's a travesty."
Rankin said due to this year's tight budget, a property tax increase is a "real topic" of conversation.
"While we don't want to just raise taxes unnecessarily, if we want to deliver the services that residents want and need, that is a serious consideration we're going to have to make," Rankin said.

title: Plan for Zaxbys in Easton Receives Partial Approval, Draws Design Concerns
author: Konner Metz
content:
Plan for Zaxbys in Easton receives partial approval, draws design concerns

 March 28, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 492
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A plan to build a Zaxbys restaurant at the site of the former Wendy's on Route 50 has been partially OK'd by the Easton Planning Commission, though it's a significant step away from receiving the full stamp of approval.On March 20, the commission approved landscaping waivers but tabled a decision on the architectural plans for the proposed fast-food chain. Commission members cited concerns about the bright red and blue colors in design renderings.
"I really would like (Route) 50 to start looking better," William Ryall said. "I don't think this improves the look of 50 at all."
Franchise co-owner Curtis Snyder presented the plans for a new 2,000-square-foot building to replace the old Wendy's at the site, which closed this year. The Zaxbys is projected to open in late 2025 or early 2026, Snyder told The Star Democrat Thursday.
Snyder, a local attorney and real estate developer, noted the Easton Zaxbys would be one of the chain's first locations to feature its new branding design.
"Compared to what's there existing today, this is an extreme improvement," Snyder said March 20. He added the corporation is "very hesitant to any sort of changes. It's such a new brand. There's one existing (restaurant with this new design concept) in the U.S. and a few in construction."
Commission chair Philip Toussaint suggested the colors be toned down in terms of brightness.
"If you can't do that, I think the fit probably isn't good between what you're proposing and Easton," Toussaint said. "That's not what Easton is about, and that's not what's in the (comprehensive) plan."
"That would be asking McDonald's to not be yellow," Snyder said.
Following further discussion, Snyder presented the commission with an alternative design — just approved by corporate that morning — which adds more brick around the building. Commission members were encouraged by the added brick but asked Snyder to return to them at a future date with colored renderings of the alternative design.
"We really want you to be in town, and we really want that lot to be developed," commission member Tom Klein said. "But I can't tell what this looks like from what you gave me. And I think it's going to look a lot better than what you have now, but I wouldn't feel comfortable giving you approval when I can't really envision what it looks like."
"If we make any changes that affect the brand negatively, that's going to reduce our return on investment," co-owner and Trappe businessman Tom Mitchell said.
The Planning Commission unanimously approved the landscaping waivers, and developers agreed to return in April with updated renderings.
In an interview Thursday, Snyder said with most of the landscaping waivers approved, site work preparation can begin. He said returning to the commission "doesn't help the timeline, but I don't see a huge delay."
Snyder said it's part of the process of "trying to balance town and corporate wants, and also our costs."
The Easton Planning Commission's next meeting is slated for April 17 at 1 p.m.

title: Easton Considers Tightening Zoning Regulations Amid Council Concerns
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton considers tightening zoning regulations amid council concerns

 March 4, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 522
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — At a workshop Monday, town planners presented potential changes to Easton's planned redevelopment overlay, a district which aims to facilitate revitalization of industrial areas or older, dilapidated parts of town.The discussion comes as the Easton Town Council is seeking more say in large housing projects, particularly following the approval last month of most of Easton Crossing, a 123-unit mixed-use development on Brookletts Avenue.
Since that project sits in the planned redevelopment overlay district, the Planning Commission granted final approval rather than the Town Council.
"If I'm going to be the head coach, I want to call the play," Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis said Monday. "Because the only person they get rid of is the head coach."
Town Planner Lynn Thomas brought two main options to give councilmembers more oversight. The overlay district could be deleted, sending projects through a planned unit development application (which requires Town Council approval). Or the town could introduce limits to what can be done through the planned redevelopment overlay district, such as a cap on the number of units or overall size of the project.
If limits were instituted, developers looking to build in the overlay district above those caps would go through the planned unit development process, and thus the council.
Thomas said town staff lean toward revising the planned redevelopment instead of eliminating it entirely. Councilmembers largely agreed.
Ward 2 Councilmember Don Abbatiello said his main concern lies with "large-scale projects" not coming before the council.
"I think the residents would probably appreciate another opportunity to speak up (at Town Council meetings) on a development of that size," Abbatiello added, referencing the Easton Crossing project.
Town Attorney Sharon VanEmburgh said based on council feedback, she and town staff will return at a later date with specific options for the limits that could be placed on the planned redevelopment overlay district.
Thomas, a longtime town employee, noted that since the redevelopment overlay was introduced in 1993, part of its intent has been to incentivize developers to locate in those parts of town. Results have been mixed, he said.
"I think we've seen some (reinvestment) but probably not as much as we envisioned when enacted," Thomas said.
The overlay district accounts for 155 acres, around 2% of the town's total area. Recent projects in the overlay include Easton Crossing, the 28-unit Silo Square project on Needwood Avenue, and Building African American Minds' new academic center on Jowite Street.
Other recommendations provided Monday included establishing regular planning and zoning reports to the council and holding joint workshops between the council and Planning Commission.
Council President Frank Gunsallus said a mix of those reports and workshops would be beneficial. Davis pushed on why those aren't already occurring.
"That's low-hanging fruit. Tell me why we're not doing that now," Davis asked Miguel Salinas, the town's planning and zoning director.
Salinas replied, "It is low-hanging fruit, and I think it's a good tool for communication."
Planning Commission Chair Philip Toussaint spoke at the end of Monday's workshop, expressing desire to work closely with the Town Council moving forward.
"I think any enhanced model of communication that we can put together, I'm all for that," Toussaint said. "I think that's a fantastic idea."

title: Planning Commission Approves Majority of 123-Unit Easton Crossing Development
author: Konner Metz
content:
Planning Commission approves majority of 123-unit Easton Crossing development

 February 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 641
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A mixed-use project on Brookletts Avenue at the site of the former Perdue AgriBusiness operation received a stamp of approval, though not a full one.The Easton Planning Commission voted Thursday to approve 67 of the 123 units planned for Easton Crossing, a joint commercial and residential development. But Building 409, the project's largest structure, and the 56 units that come along with it are still under consideration.
Commission members and residents alike expressed concerns about the five-story building that includes around 10,000 square feet of retail space. Developers from The Arc Central Chesapeake Region, the project's developer, agreed to work on alternative options for the unapproved building and return to the commission at a future date.
Largely, the commission applauded developers for their advanced outreach to the community, as well as what they called an attractive project aimed at addressing Easton's lack of affordable housing.
"I love the project," commission chair Philip Toussaint said. "I think the positive aspects of it far outweigh any negative aspects. We have to take that into account when we're making a decision."
Toussaint joined vice chair Michael Ports, William Ryall and Victoria McAndrews in approving the project with the exception of Building 409. Thomas Klein was the sole vote against, citing his concerns that the plan's 217 off-street parking spots won't suffice once the units are occupied and commercial tenants move in.
The proposal noted 49 on-street parking spaces along Brookletts Avenue are mostly unused right now and would provide additional parking once renters and businesses move into Easton Crossing.
Klein said only 217 dedicated spaces for a 229-bedroom development did not seem sufficient, particularly if the backup plan is parking on Brookletts.
"If people from the development start to go and park in those areas, the tenants that live there now are not going to have any place to park," Klein said.
Ross Benincasa, senior vice president of Chesapeake Community Development, presented the site plan at Thursday's meeting. It calls for 30% of the rental units to be affordably priced, with others at workforce and market-rate levels.
Demolition of the Perdue grain bins and storage buildings currently on the lot began this month. Apartments are expected to be available beginning in 2027.
Speaking to the commission Thursday, Benincasa said the nonprofit developers felt a "necessary duty" to make a dent in Easton's affordable housing crisis with the infill project.
"We really felt kind of a need to make sure that if this was going to be developed, that we thought of it more inclusively," Benincasa said, "and more geared around making sure there was housing provided for all income levels, including people with disabilities."
BLENDING INWhile many complimented the project's cohesion with the intersecting Rails to Trails, worries centered around the fact that the structures don't integrate into the neighboring historic community.
Talbot County Council Member Lynn Mielke, speaking for herself and not the council, said the project is "incompatible" and its architecture ignores the nearby residential buildings.
Toussaint pushed Benincasa on if it was appropriate for the project to face away from The Hill, one of the first free African American neighborhoods in the country. The commission chair said that's been a significant source of public input.
"It appears to me that you've turned your back on the existing community, The Hill district," Toussaint said. "And you focus on Rails to Trails, and did a wonderful job of that."
Benincasa said The Arc doesn't own a lot of land in The Hill community to be able to integrate with it and that he disagrees with sentiments that the project doesn't fit into the surrounding fabric.
"We are not necessarily in that community here, and I would go as far to say as I think that doing duplexes here or mimicking that in some way would kind of really negatively offset what we could do in terms of usable units," Benincasa said. "It's never been a serious consideration."

title: Easton Councilmembers Ask for More Say in Approving Housing Projects
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton councilmembers ask for more say in approving housing projects

 February 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 544
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — With 1,000 units in the town's residential pipeline, some Easton councilmembers are asking whether the Town Council should be granted a larger role in approving housing developments."Many people are pretty upset about the rate of growth we've been experiencing," Town Council President Frank Gunsallus said during a workshop Monday. "So I guess I'm just really trying to understand how we got here and why perhaps there aren't tighter checklists when things go in front of the Planning Commission."
According to numbers from Easton's planning and zoning department, 1,004 housing units are approved for construction by the town as of Feb. 3. While some are built or have permits, nearly 800 of those units are waiting to be permitted.
Most projects received a final thumbs up from the Planning Commission or Board of Zoning Appeals and never make it before the Town Council. The Town Council greenlit 369, or 36.8%, of the approved units.
Those 369 units make up three projects that went through a planned unit development application, requiring council permission. They are a 136-apartment complex on Elliott Road, a 200 single-family home development on Matthewstown Road and a 33-townhome project at the site of the former Safeway on North Washington Street.
Projects under the planned redevelopment overlay district are typically in industrial areas or older, dilapidated areas of town. They do not go in front of the council and instead seek final approval from the Planning Commission.
Recently, Silo Square, a 28-unit townhome development on Needwood Avenue, went through that process. Easton Crossing, a 123-unit mixed-income development at the site of former Perdue properties in town, is expected to be on the Planning Commission's Feb. 20 agenda.
Following a discussion regarding priority areas for annexation as the town aims to add to its housing stock, councilmembers chimed in on the projects that are proposed within town limits.
"I'm struggling with the fact that we're approving all of this stuff, and I feel like we're doing it sort of in a hole," Ward 1 Councilmember Maureen Curry said. "And we're not taking everything into the full picture."
Miguel Salinas, Easton's planning and zoning director, said Curry's concerns were fair. He said given council feedback, the town should look at whether the planned redevelopment process is appropriate given the town's current needs.
"Do we still need that for the Town of Easton? A lot of the redevelopment areas have now redeveloped," said Salinas. "And certainly other ones could come forward in the future. But is that really needed?"
Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery suggested the council eliminate the overlay district. In response, Salinas suggested the planning department could come back to the council with multiple options to consider.
"Any proposal we would provide you would include any potential changes to criteria the Planning Commission looks at," Salinas added.
At the end of the workshop, Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis said there's not enough communication between the Planning Commission and the Town Council.
"It goes to the Planning Commission, and we get phone calls like no tomorrow about things that went through the Planning Commission that we as elected officials really had no oversight over," Davis said.
Salinas said the commission could look at doing a couple joint workshops each year as well as an annual report to the Town Council detailing housing pipeline data.

title: Easton Leaders at Odds Over Affordable Housing Ordinance's Next Step
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton leaders at odds over affordable housing ordinance's next step

 February 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 602
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Town leaders held a tense discussion Monday regarding inclusionary zoning, debating how quickly the town should move forward with an ordinance meant to address affordable housing shortages.At Monday's meeting, the Town Council was asked to schedule a workshop to review the draft of an inclusionary zoning ordinance that's been in the works for two years.
In November, the Planning Commission approved the ordinance by a 4-1 vote. It would require residential developers to allocate 15% of their units as affordable.
Initially, Town Council President Frank Gunsallus made a motion for the town to seek out a firm and delay the workshop. The motion was immediately seconded by Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery, but a lengthy discussion followed before the motion was eventually rescinded.
"It's clear from studies in other jurisdictions that the impacts have varied but that they've included a serious slow down in building because this is essentially a tax on builders," Montgomery said of inclusionary zoning. "They've included higher housing costs to the extent that it's been possible to pass those on."
Gunsallus proposed the town find an independent firm to conduct a study "over the next nine to 12 months." The firm would provide "an objective analysis" of the positive and negative effects an inclusionary zoning ordinance may have, he said.
Montgomery said in his experience, the town could be "looking at $50,000 at a minimum" for such a study.
Mayor Megan Cook disagreed with the proposal to hire an outside firm for a long-term study. She emphasized that town planners, staff, and the Planning Commission have already spent a significant amount of time drafting the ordinance and considering its potential effects.
Town planners worked with an advisory firm, David Paul Rosen & Associates, to help revise the legislation last summer.
"What information are you looking to gain that has not already been looked at?" Cook asked Gunsallus. "And by the way, we don't have $50,000 in this year's budget."
"I beg to differ," Gunsallus responded. "I read the budget thoroughly, I would actually very much beg to differ on that."
Ward 1 Councilmember Maureen Curry said she'd like to "see the scope of work" before the town commits funds toward a study. Curry asked who would select the firm. Gunsallus said the council would be in charge.
"Why? Why would the council be choosing?" Cook asked.
"Because we're the ones tasked with needing to make a decision on this," Gunsallus said. "The town has already spent a significant amount of money into drafting it. Because the responsibility ends right here, that's why."
Gunsallus later added that based on studies he's read, there are "serious doubts" about whether inclusionary zoning will lead to the number of affordable units the town is seeking.
"But there's equal research out there that shows that it will," Cook said.
Councilmembers Don Abbatiello and the Rev. Elmer Davis said they'd like to have the workshop before making a decision on a study. Council agreed to a March 3 workshop for the Attainable Housing Task Force to provide a report related to the ordinance.
Gunsallus maintained that he appreciates the hard work of town staff. He said it's the council's "responsibility to carefully evaluate what has worked elsewhere before determining the best course of action for Easton."
"There is a serious housing issue with the Town of Easton," Cook said toward the end of the discussion. "We can't even employ a police officer, hire a new police officer, and have them be able to live in the town that they have been sworn to serve. That is a real issue."
"We are talking this to death," Cook added. "And that is inaction by constant conversation."
This story has been updated.

title: Easton Planners: Amid Affordable Housing Shortage, Inclusionary Zoning May Be Useful
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton planners: amid affordable housing shortage, inclusionary zoning may be useful

 January 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 1134
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Through her work at the Chesapeake Multicultural Resource Center, Daisy Aguilar interacts with many prospective first-time homebuyers. Of the many challenges they face, housing prices in Easton and Talbot County are at the top of the list."The houses, they're not affordable right now," Aguilar, the center's housing coordinator, said. "And most people that are buying, they're buying in Dorchester County because it's more affordable than it is in Talbot County."
An inclusionary zoning ordinance in the works could pave the way for more affordable homeownership and rental opportunities in Easton. It would require residential developers to allocate 15% of their units as affordable, defined separately for ownership and rental.
Inclusionary units in ownership developments would need to meet an affordable price for households making up to 100% of area median income, while rental developments would need to meet prices affordable for households making up to 60% of area median income.
According to Jim Bent, chair of the Affordable Housing Board, Easton's area median income was around $98,000 last year.
While similar legislation has faced hurdles in the past, town leaders and affordable housing proponents are hopeful the time is now for inclusionary zoning to be implemented.
EASTON'S WORKFORCEEaston Mayor Megan Cook is well aware of the fact many can't afford to live in town, including essential workers, town employees and police officers.
"When you're sworn to protect and serve a community, yet you can't even live in the community that you're dedicating your life to, that says something," Cook said. "That's not quite the message we should be sending people."
According to the draft ordinance, Census data shows that 42% of around 17,000 Talbot County workers commute into the county. Cook and others are hoping the ordinance can lower that percentage.
"A lot of the people who work in those fields earn wages where they have been priced out of the Easton market, and so their only option is to find housing in adjacent counties," said Miguel Salinas, Easton's director of planning and zoning.
For homebuyers, the local market is a significant challenge. According to the Mid-Shore Board of Realtors, the average home price in Talbot County in 2024 was $856,000.
Town staff's calculation of the maximum affordable home price for a family of four making the area median income is $292,000.
"There was a time, a couple years, not too long ago, that houses were affordable," Aguilar said. "I mean, they were selling fast, but they were affordable. And at least you had the possibility of actually getting a house."
THE ORDINANCESalinas, who has led the town's efforts to create the ordinance, recognizes it is just one piece of the puzzle. But it's a critical step, he said.
"This is one tool in the toolbox. And it's been discussed for 20-plus years," Salinas said.
Since it was initially presented in February 2023, Salinas said the ordinance has endured many revisions, along with being viewed by the town's Affordable Housing Board, Attainable Housing Task Force and an outside contractor.
Town planners looked at similar provisions in jurisdictions such as Queen Anne's County, Annapolis and Frederick when drafting the ordinance.
A draft version of the inclusionary housing ordinance was passed 4-1 by the town's Planning Commission last November.
Planning Commission member Michael Ports, speaking for himself and not the commission, said the inclusionary zoning ordinance would do two things particularly well. It would push the "cost burden predominantly away from existing residents" and incentivize developers to build inclusionary units.
In addition to the requirement that 15% of units fit the inclusionary definitions, the ordinance would grant developers that provide inclusionary units on the same site as market-rate units with a 20% density bonus.
Such aspects of the ordinance encourage mixed-income projects, which town leaders believe can help to reduce housing inequities.
"Housing segregation opens the door to other types of segregation, and you can certainly see that in many, many communities," Salinas said. "But not just racial and ethnic, but also age."
Tom Klein, the Planning Commission's sole vote against the ordinance, says he is a proponent of more affordable and workforce housing. He believes inclusionary zoning is not "necessary nor a cost-effective way" to achieve that goal.
"For the past two years that I have been on the Planning Commission, just about every new development proposal has come with a component of affordable/workforce housing," Klein wrote in an email.
Recent developments that provide the town with affordable housing include projects from The Arc Central Chesapeake Region, such as Port Street Commons, a multi-use property with nine affordable apartment units that opened in December, and Silo Square, a mixed-income housing project greenlit in October.
Revitalization of the Doverbrook Apartments complex in Easton is underway and will feature an additional 14 affordable units on top of 50 existing ones. On Elliott Road, more than 100 apartments are under construction, a portion of those affordable.
Last July, the town approved the annexation of 17 acres of land for a housing project on the east side of Route 50. In the annexation agreement, developers agreed at least 50% of the project's apartment units will be affordable.
Given the number of ongoing projects, Klein says he feels inclusionary zoning would not "provide a significant number" of additional affordable units.
But Ports believes the ordinance will ensure that the limited supply of undeveloped land in the town is being used properly.
"It's really the biggest asset any community has," Ports said. "If we want to allow someone to potentially change it forever, we need to make sure that they're investing in the community in some way."
REGULATIONAt the November Planning Commission meeting, Klein and other commission members expressed concerns of overregulation prior to voting on the ordinance.
"I think that the market's taking care of it," Klein said. "I think that we're putting a lot of regulation here. Like I said, I think there could be a lot of unintended consequences that come out of that and a lot of cost for what we get out of it."
Salinas and Bent both said the market hasn't been able to address ballooning home and rental costs in recent years.
Bent said he's heard from planning commissioners in the past that a "tool" is needed to point developers toward what the town wants in terms of affordability.
While proponents of inclusionary zoning are confident it can be this tool, they recognize the housing problem in Easton is complex.
"If we got into this hole of housing deficiency over the course of decades, it's impossible to fix that in one year, let alone even 10 years," Ports said. "It will be a game of playing catch-up."
Cook hopes Easton residents, along with the Town Council, see affordable housing as a top challenge to tackle.
"I do hope that they see the importance of this issue, and I also hope that the community itself sees the importance of the issue," Cook said. "For the longevity and the vibrancy of the Town of Easton, it's an important issue."

title: New Restrictions on Historic Vacation Cottages in St. Michaels
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
New restrictions on historic vacation cottages in St. Michaels

 January 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 394
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — On Wednesday evening, the St. Michaels commissioners unanimously approved an ordinance to permanently bar historic cottages from obtaining new short-term rental permits in historic districts.The ordinance focuses on homes in the R-2 District, which encompases areas within Chestnut Street and Mill Street including Water Street and St. Mary's Square.
Short-term rentals that have been lawfully operating as of Jan. 8 will be allowed to continue under the new ordinance, but no new rentals will be allowed to operate.
Rob Straebel, town administrator, said there are approximately 11 approved short term rentals in the assigned district that will be grandfathered into the new regulations.
Commissioners were presented with findings from the resolution that was passed in September.
During the public hearing, Commissioner David Wojciechowski asked logistical questions on the short-term rental permits that are grandfathered in, including whether or not short-term rental permits could be transferred with new ownership.
Straebel said as long as the new owners file proper paperwork for permits, the homes can continue to operate as short-term rentals.
"I think all of the areas that have approvals are within the area we would like to see them," Straebel said. "And if (short-term rental properties) do run with the land and the legal background on special exceptions are that they can continue with the change into the ownership as long as it's the same location."
The restrictions were first introduced as a resolution during a Sep. 18 commissioners meeting as a moratorium on new zoning permits or licenses for historic vacation cottages in the R-2 District for a period of six months.
The town's Planning Commission reviewed the regulations at a Nov. 7 meeting, where they supported the moratorium because "regulations have been successful in promoting historic preservation of older and smaller houses in the Historic District," according to an opinion the commission.
Additionally, the Planning Commission said the intention was to concentrate renovations in the Carpenter Street and Locust Street area and should not be promoted to expand this use elsewhere.
In the ordinance it states that a lawful vacation cottage used for short-term rentals in the R-2 District that existed as of Jan. 8, 2025 may be continued provided the use remains otherwise lawful and meets the provisions already embodied in town.
After a quiet public comment, the commissioners moved to vote on the ordinance. It was unanimously approved by all commissioners.
The ordinance will take effect Jan. 28.

title: Trappe Commission Approves Building Permit Process for New Lakeside Homes
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Trappe commission approves building permit process for new Lakeside homes

 December 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 528
 Words 

 Read News Document

 TRAPPE — On Tuesday evening, the Trappe Planning Commission heard and approved several new building plans for the further construction of the Lakeside at Trappe residential development.Representatives from Lennar and Brookfield, two separate construction companies, presented plans for new residential buildings to be added to the existing Lakeside development. including townhouses and more cost-effective single-family homes.
Kilber Arrington, product development manager for Lennar, said he manages all the architectural efforts for Lennar's Maryland division, which also spans into Delaware and parts of Pennsylvania. Arrington said the Lennar team looks forward to starting its new development plans with the town.
"We're excited to come down here to Trappe," Arrington said. "We've been looking for places to put our product in and let it get to market, and we think that this is a really good place for this product to succeed. What we introduced were a total of seven single-family homes and two townhomes."
In his presentation, Arrington said the single-family homes range in square footage from just under 1,400 square feet to just under 2,000 square feet. According to Arrington, this particular lineup is designed specifically for the "move down buyers." Arrington defined the "move down buyers" as those who want to downsize a bit from previous large homes.
Arrington said the designs also work for young families and couples who are moving out of townhomes and want to get an affordable single family home.
Next, Arrington presented the townhouses, which are three stories high and range between 1,600 square feet and 2,200 square feet. Arrington said these townhouses are designed for first-time buyers and young families.
After the presentation, the floor was open for questions and commissioners asked clarifying questions on design, color schemes and price ranges for the entry-level single family homes, which Arrington said he is reluctant to say because they are still being worked out.
Nick Higgins, production manager for Brookfield, presented designs next. He showed three product designs with two products that were "evolutions" of products already built in Lakeside. The idea of the two designs was to make them more cost effective.
Additionally, Higgins presented a third product that he described as a "huge success" for the company across the Washington, Maryland and Virginia area.
"We think it's a fantastic, esthetically very livable, and it's one of our also one of our most kind of cost-effective products that we built," Higgins said. "We thought these three products would fit really well into here to address some of the affordability concerns given the rates that have gone up significantly since the start of this project."
Commissioners asked similar questions about design of the products as they did of the other company's designs.
Robert Rauch, owner of Rauch Inc., Lakeside's developer, said his company has worked with Lennar and Brookfield to make sure that their designs and plans follow all regulations and requirements for the Lakeside properties.
"In our role, we prepare the actual building permit application package, and part of that is an extensive checklist that we go through to verify and confirm that the proposed plans are consistent with both the guidelines of the Lakeside and your (project management) plan," Rauch said.
The council unanimously approved the building permit processes for Lennar and Brookfields.

title: Developers Host 3Rd Community Meeting For Easton Crossing Project
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Developers host 3rd community meeting for Easton Crossing project

 December 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 591
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Developers and residents gathered Wednesday evening for a third community meeting concerning a planned mixed-use development on Brookletts Avenue.Chesapeake Community Development, a subsidiary of The Arc Central Chesapeake Region, hosted the meeting to update neighbors on its draft site plans and facilitate community feedback.
The Easton Crossing infill project is expected to add around 120 units where a former Perdue AgriBusiness operation used to sit. Additionally, there are significant plans for commercial use and open areas.
Renderings show six buildings planned for the 6.5-acre site. Ross Benincasa, senior vice president of community development at Chesapeake Community Development, said the first building, which will have 15 residential units, is projected to open in December 2027.
Benincasa emphasized the mixed-income aspect of the project on Wednesday. Some units will be at market rate, and others down to where people "will be paying $500 to $600 a month for a new apartment."
"Unlike most developers, we don't build affordable units and market-rate units," Benincasa said. "We build the same unit across the site, and we just have specific ratio goals that we hit for that site. If I'm living in an affordable unit and Joe is in a market-rate unit, and I go over to … Joe's apartment one night, I will have no idea who pays what."
Based on previous feedback, developers and architects are looking into using bricks that are darker in color to match surrounding buildings. They also touched on other topics that were raised at previous community meetings this year, such as lighting, open space and plantings.
"You're going to be seeing a mix of pedestrian (lights) and some larger lights in the areas of the parking lot," Benincasa said. "But those larger lights, from a sizing perspective, are going to feel more like downtown Easton."
There will be a focus on maintaining open space at the property, as well as around 70% native plantings. Benincasa added that once finished, there will be "around four to 10 shrubs or trees per 50 feet."
All parking spots will be screened, some by shrubs and trees and others by buildings. While Benincasa said South Street will be a "secondary" exit and entrance for residents, developers "fully anticipate" most drivers to use Brookletts Avenue.
"But we don't want them on Brookletts. That's the point," resident Harriett Page said.
Benincasa said a traffic study was completed by Lenart Traffic Consulting last week, which did not signify worries about the traffic increase around the site. An increase of around 20 cars during peak hour on Brookletts Avenue is projected.
Resident Joe Minarick said "with Brookletts being the main thoroughclear and the main import" for the site, those projections "(seemed) a little funny."
"Brookletts might be the front of the project, but it is not the only way that people are going to go in and out," Benincasa said. Those heading east toward Caroline County may use Kemp Lane to access Dover Road, he said.
As for the commercial aspect of the site, Benincasa said developers aren't expecting national businesses. In fact, Chesapeake Community Development is looking for local businesses "emotionally invested in their success."
Developers may also encourage businesses to hire people with disabilities, a segment of the population that The Arc strives to serve.
"We have had discussions about if a business wants to hire people with disabilities, then there would be, sort of, credits for that," said Jonathon Rondeau, president and CEO of The Arc. "Or for hiring local as well."
"That will be coming in 2026, 2027," he continued, "as we think about what those incentives are as we begin to market the commercial spaces."

title: Easton Town Council Hears Update on Seafood Odor Mitigation
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Easton Town Council hears update on seafood odor mitigation

 November 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 652
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Easton Town Council heard an update Monday evening from Chesapeake Brand Seafood, a business on Maryland Avenue that's drawn complaints from residents for its odor in recent months.At a Nov. 4 town meeting, councilmembers discussed a draft ordinance to limit seafood processing uses in business commercial zoning through special exception only.
That exception would require that seafood by-products are "stored within a closed or refrigerated vehicle," with operators required to install "odor control technology" so "no odor from any product or by-product can be detected outside the building."
Zach Smith, an attorney representing Chesapeake Brand Seafood owner/operator Mitchell Hughes, spoke Monday regarding the town's Nov. 4 discussion and how the potential legislation may impact Hughes' business. Smith said finding a new site for Chesapeake Brand Seafood, as was previously suggested by Ward 1 Councilmember Maureen Curry, is not his client's preferred course of action.
"I did speak to Mitchell about that, and that is not preferable," Smith said. " … He located there lawfully. He followed the town's rules. The town zoning still allows that use in that location. So he doesn't necessarily feel like he should have to relocate."
Smith said Hughes has invested around $200,000 in "fitting the space" for his operation. Additionally, many employees live within walking distance of the current site, the attorney said.
"While things are pretty good at the moment, you never know when fisheries are going to decline, when regulations are going to cause restrictions, and so he just doesn't know," Smith said. "The prospect of investing a large amount of money to relocate just doesn't seem reasonable to him at this time."
Hughes' attorney said the business owner is "committed" to addressing the odor and has looked into an odor mitigation solution that may be viable. "I think he would hope there could be some cost-sharing in that," Smith said.
The proposed ordinance, which would require existing businesses to comply by Jan. 1, 2026, was not voted on Monday, and the public hearing was left open.
Carla Howell, a resident on South Aurora Street, asked the council to consider a compliance deadline earlier than 2026.
"I was hoping we'd get some relief when the crab season was over, but we haven't," Howell said. " … I'm hoping you all will at least change the date, and we can go along with (Smith's) idea. I think it would be marvelous if they just put in some kind of a filter system."
Carolyn Johnson, an employee at Chesapeake Brand Seafood and Hughes' aunt, vouched for her nephew and his work as a local business owner.
"He has always wanted to be a good neighbor, and whenever we've had a situation, a complaint from the mayor's office or the town, we have addressed it," Johnson said. "He's taken care of it. And I feel that that shows what he is. He wants to be in business here in Easton. And he was allowed to be in business here in Easton. You guys, the town, gave him that permission."
Councilmembers offered limited perspective on the seafood legislation Monday, as it will likely be revisited at Town Council's Dec. 2 meeting. Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery said he's "pleased" that a solution for all parties is in the works.
Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis, who represents the area in which the business is located, spoke to his constituents and told them "their concerns have not been brushed aside."
In previous meetings, Davis pushed for a deadline sooner than Jan. 1, 2026. He also contended that seafood processing should not be allowed in business commercial zoning at all.
"If I have to stand by myself, I will," Davis said regarding a potential council vote on the matter. "I will represent the voices and the members of that community in such a fashion that they are heard and represented at the table whether they're there or not. So I want all of my colleagues to know that's where I stand."

title: Approved Silo Square housing project generates resident opposition
author: Konner Metz
content:
Approved Silo Square housing project generates resident opposition

 November 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 815
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Maury Schlesinger knows the town needs more housing, but when he takes the short walk from his home to 410 Needwood Ave, he can't quite envision the development that's being planned for the lot.A recently approved 28-unit townhouse development has garnered mixed opinions from the Easton community, particularly East End residents like Schlesinger.
The property is currently home to 10 unused grain bins from a former Perdue AgriBusiness operation. The Arc bought the 2.36-acre lot from Perdue and received approval from the Easton Planning Commission in October to move forward with developing the site into mixed-income housing.
While not immediately surrounded by residences, the lot is close to a number of single-family homes. Schlesinger, who's been outspoken at town meetings against the design of the project, says the project is "inappropriate" and "out of context" with the surrounding residential areas.
"You're putting a tear through the fabric of our town," Schlesinger said.
Schlesinger, along with other neighbors, say they support bringing more affordable and workforce housing to Easton, and even to the lot in question. Many of their concerns stem from the design of the townhomes and the process by which Silo Square was designed and approved.
"Most all folks ... are on record supporting housing at the site, simply not as proposed, and not in the manner that this has been done," said Matt Carberry, who lives within viewing distance of the grain bins.
DESIGN CONCERNS
Planning Commission members voiced split opinions on Silo Square designs during two hearings in September and October.
Commission Chairperson Philip Toussaint, Vice Chairperson Michael Ports and Chair Pro Tem William Ryall each complimented developers for how the townhomes looked in renderings. Commission members Victoria McAndrews and Thomas Klein were less receptive to the design, though both joined the other three in approving the project at the Oct. 17 meeting.
Residents who spoke during public comment were more unified in their opposition.
Ross Benincasa, senior vice president of community development at Chesapeake Community Development, said in an interview that developers want to use high-quality materials and avoid creating something that's a "faux representation of a different time period."
"We're not in downtown Easton," Benincasa said. "We didn't really like the idea of replicating just another kind of brick facade, or another kind of 1990s-looking townhome community. We want to make sure when people look back on it, they know that this was built in 2024."
Resident Loretta Hatzel-Geraci says her largest gripe with the design is that the townhomes face inwards on the lot.
"Inward-facing doesn't really promote community interaction," she said.
"I can appreciate the community's concerns around inward-facing," Benincasa said. "The reality with the site is that because we have no other homes around us, if we made it outward-facing, those homes are just going to face the back of industrial properties."
Benincasa said that of the 28 units, around 21 will start off at market-rate rent prices, with the other seven priced at workforce rates achievable for those making around $55,000 to $70,000 annually.
APPROVAL PROCESS
Since the project falls within the town's planned redevelopment overlay district, it did not require approval from the Easton Town Council. The Planning Commission could have approved it at a September meeting, though it asked developers to procure a traffic study and return one month later.
Between the two commission hearings, developers held a meeting with Silo District residents. Benincasa said two main topics were discussed: the design and entrances to the development, the latter of which was adjusted to move the main entrance onto Maryland Avenue.
Still, East End residents wish that public input played more of a role and that the process wasn't so quick.
"The public gets to see the project too late in the process," Schlesinger said. " … There's no opportunity for dialogue. There's only the opportunity to shout yay or nay."
Both Hatzel-Geraci and Carberry say they felt the approval was a done deal, whether the residents spoke out or not.
"Whatever observations or comments made by the community, if considered, were essentially dismissed by the Planning Commission," Carberry said. "The appearance was that the project's approval was basically pre-approved absent any community input."
Schlesinger says he wishes developers were required to reach out to the community before an application is sent to the town. He added that the process for Easton Crossing, The Arc's mixed-use project on Brookletts Avenue, included the level of community outreach he wishes Silo Square was afforded.
Benincasa said he's heard from community members that The Arc is held to a "higher standard," a challenge the organization welcomes.
"I would agree that I think moving forward, for our projects, we're going to try and make sure there's more community outreach well ahead of time," Benincasa said.
"The normal developer kind of builds, fills, and sells, that's how they make their money. We don't," he continued. "And so we go into a project with the attitude that we're going to be neighbors. We need to make sure that we have a good relationship."

title: Oxford Planning Commission Makes Decision That Could Affect Inn's Plans
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford Planning Commission makes decision that could affect inn's plans

 November 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 583
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — The Oxford Planning Commission has voted to not proceed with a draft ordinance that would allow apartments, townhomes and condos in the town's C-2 general commercial district by special exception.The Tuesday afternoon vote was of particular importance to David Snyder, owner of the Robert Morris Inn.
During a Planning Commission meeting on Oct. 1, Snyder requested a text amendment that would allow him to create luxury villas on the inn's property, which he believes will help make the business profitable. He said the inn has faced economic challenges since he took ownership this past year and he is losing over $30,000 every month.
At the outset of the Planning Commission meeting Tuesday, Commission Chair Lucy Garliauskas clarified the commission did not have any plans to take action on the draft ordinance. She said she asked for language to be drafted because the town's planning and zoning coordinator was leaving the position and the commission is currently working on a comprehensive long-range plan.
"But we are not dealing with anything related to any development or plans on Robert Morris Inn," she said.
Town Attorney Lyndsey Ryan said the draft ordinance — if pushed through and approved by the Commissioners of Oxford — would make apartments, townhomes and condos "presumptively permitted" in the C-2 general commercial district unless the particular location of the special exception request "would have an adverse effect above and beyond what it would have at a C-2-zoned property anywhere else in town."
Garliauskas said drafting the legislation might be considered "putting the cart before the horse," but offered a good opportunity for clarification. "And I think at this point, I think we're all in agreement that we're not going to pursue this ordinance," she said.
Commission member Steve Mroczek made the motion to not pursue the ordinance, which passed unanimously.
"The sense that we've gotten over the last month is that this is not something the community is very interested in," he said. "And like it or not, we try to reflect what the community's interested in doing."
During the meeting, Snyder interjected a few times to ask if he could speak. He was told it was not a public hearing and he cannot call out in the middle of a meeting. However, at one point, he did express his concerns.
"I spoke with the town attorney at the outset, and I was told I would have an opportunity to speak on the record," he said. "And I also need to make a motion to recuse, and I need clarity on this because I was blindsided by this. This is not what I expected out of this process."
Ryan said Snyder had not submitted a formal application or petition to the Planning Commission. Snyder said he had reached out to Ryan and hadn't gotten calls back for "weeks now."
"It is not my job to represent you as a property owner," Ryan replied. "I represent the town."
Snyder said he would have submitted the appropriate paperwork if he had known about it.
"I'm in a real bind," he said.
Ryan said she had told him in a past conversation that he could submit a petition to the town for a text amendment or the Planning Commission could make a change on its own volition. Ryan said she also told him the Planning Commission process would be faster.
"And so you said you were going to pursue that," she said to Snyder. "But you were made aware of the petition. If you would like to submit one, you have the right to do so."
