title: Easton Considers Ordinance to Crack Down on Seafood Processing Odors
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Easton considers ordinance to crack down on seafood processing odors

 November 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 811
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Amid resident concerns, the Easton Town Council is considering an ordinance to adjust zoning and place restrictions on seafood processors.The legislation, sent to the council for review following approval from the Planning Commission, was created in response to odor complaints from residents living near the business Chesapeake Brand Seafood on Maryland Avenue.
At Monday's Town Council meeting, councilmembers heard mixed reviews on the ordinance from residents and business owners, opting to leave the public hearing open and explore options such as moving the business out of a residential area.
Under the ordinance's proposed definition, seafood processing would be defined as "harvested seafood" being "cleaned, cut, eviscerated or otherwise prepared or cooked for sale in bulk, with a resulting by-product."
If approved, seafood processing would remain permitted in the industrial zoning district but only allowed in business commercial through a special exception. That exception would require that by-products are "stored within a closed or refrigerated vehicle," with operators required to install "odor control technology" so "no odor from any product or by-product can be detected outside the building."
Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis, who said he's heard the complaints from many of his constituents, took issue with the fact that the proposed ordinance requires existing businesses to comply by Jan. 1, 2026 instead of sooner.
"I don't think it's fair for the individuals who live in that area to have to go through another summer dealing with the odor," Davis said. "It's unfair. So I'm going to advocate that it be six months."
Davis added he doesn't think seafood processing should be allowed in business commercial zoning at all. Ward 2 Councilmember Don Abbatiello agreed with Davis' perspective but asked that the council consider the legislation's potential impacts on other seafood businesses.
"My only concern would be that we have several other seafood facilities in town who don't have these issues," Abbatiello said. "And I would hate to see them get caught up in a similar scenario, where they're getting, for lack of a better term, punished."
Council President Frank Gunsallus asked if the town had a plan to aid smaller seafood businesses if they're forced to comply with the costly odor mitigation requirements.
"If we're going to be potentially imposing regulations on businesses that have significant financial impact to the point which some have claimed would put them out of business, I think we should take pause with that," Gunsallus said.
"I'm not quite concerned about that, personally," Davis responded. "I'm more concerned about the constituents in the neighborhood. … What you're just saying (makes) it seem like it's a hardship on the business when they probably haven't even tried."
Zach Smith, attorney for Chesapeake Brand Seafood owner/operator Mitchell Hughes, provided a letter to the council to be read aloud during the public hearing on the ordinance.
If passed, the ordinance "will put Mitchell out of business and will cause significant economic harm to him, his families, his employees and the local watermen that he supports," Smith wrote.
The attorney said Hughes has taken "reasonable steps" to mitigate the impact on residents as they have brought up concerns. However, he says buying new equipment isn't doable.
"While Mitchell has tried to be a good neighbor, he cannot reasonably install equipment that prohibits any smell from being detected outside of his building," Smith wrote. "Mitchell has looked into what will be necessary to satisfy this proposed regulation, and such technology is not feasible and will be extremely cost prohibitive."
RESIDENT CONCERNSDuring the public hearing, many residents voiced impacts Hughes' business has had on their quality of life. Resident Philip Bernot said he's lived next to grain processors, metal fabricators and plumbers at the site since 2001, never before experiencing any issue that brought him to a town meeting.
"Not a single one of these businesses has ever brought me up here to complain," Bernot said. "Not a single one of these businesses has repeatedly caused a gut-wrenching stench to take over the neighborhood."
A representative for Sea Watch International said the business on Glebe Park Drive would be "swept up into new legislation." Bruce Cole, owner of Cole's Seafood House & Deli, echoed this, saying the ordinance would negatively impact his operation on North Washington Street.
"(The) impact that he has is going to impact me," Cole said, noting equipment may cost around $100,000. " … I don't have any complaints."
Following the public hearing, Ward 1 Councilmember Maureen Curry asked the council to pause on taking action. She emphasized the operation of the business under scrutiny is different from businesses like Cole's.
"They're not doing it for retail, they're doing it for wholesale and to push out a product," Curry said. The council left the public hearing open for the Nov. 18 meeting.
Curry added that she hopes the council can work toward a "best case scenario" in which Chesapeake Brand Seafood moves out of its current location to a more appropriate one away from residents.

title: ‘A gem’: State and Local Leaders Celebrate Port Street Commons Project
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
‘A gem’: State and local leaders celebrate Port Street Commons project

 November 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 596
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A multi-use property bringing affordable housing and behavioral health services to Easton is officially complete.Port Street Commons, a 24,000-square-foot project led by The Arc Central Chesapeake Region, celebrated the end of construction with a ribbon-cutting ceremony that included local and state officials. The space houses nine apartment units as well as a headquarters for The Arc, complete with offices and a behavioral health suite.
Speaking to more than 100 attendees Thursday morning, The Arc President and CEO Jonathon Rondeau said the organization is "building a future where equity and inclusion are the norm."
"There will be people whose lives change within these walls because of the services they receive, the connections they make, the housing they can afford," Rondeau said.
The $11 million project, financed through a capital campaign, received $2.5 million in investment from the state and $750,000 in federal funding, Rondeau said. Chesapeake Neighbors, a housing subsidiary of The Arc, held a lottery in September for potential tenants that fell within the income requirements, with more than 250 people entering.
There are seven two-bedroom units and two three-bedroom units, all of them featuring free Wi-Fi and appliances. Two of the first-floor units are tailored to accommodate tenants with disabilities.
Members of the Easton Town Council and Talbot County Council, along with Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) and Del. Tom Hutchinson (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico), attended Thursday's ceremony.
Easton Mayor Megan Cook said the project is a fit for the town's goal to revitalize the area next to the Tred Avon River. She noted Port Street Commons is the first project to fall under the town's mixed-use waterfront zoning.
"We're eager to encourage mixed-use facilities such as this, allowing for exciting new businesses in tandem with more affordable housing, both of which are critical for growth in our community," she said.
The site at 480 Port Street was identified in July 2021, and construction began just under two years later. In an interview, Rondeau said the quick timeline helps The Arc fulfill the community's immediate housing needs, adding that the town was a crucial partner.
"There's a lot of development happening here in Easton," Rondeau said. "It's a small town, only so many inspectors and things like that. The town has been great. They've really worked with us to help meet those timelines when we had a problem."
Rondeau said four families who were randomly drawn have been confirmed, with the first of those moving in Dec. 2. All nine apartments should be occupied by March, he said.
Julia Glanz, deputy secretary of the Maryland Department of Housing & Community Development, and Carol Beatty, secretary of the Maryland Department of Disabilities, both complimented the housing project during the ceremony.
Beatty said the apartments tackle "one of the most common concerns" she hears from Marylanders with disabilities — a lack of accessible housing that is also affordable.
Glanz was excited about the project and hopes it can be an example for other mixed-use housing endeavors.
"It is, I think, a gem across the state," Glanz said in an interview. " … From what I've seen in the last year and a half, this is very unique. And it's bringing so many different facets of life into one space."
The deputy secretary noted that the House Expansion and Affordability Act of 2024, which encourages higher-density affordable housing projects, reduces government barriers. However, Port Street Commons completed most of its three-and-a-half year turnaround before that act was passed.
"The Arc being able to do that without that legislation … is a testament to the community effort here in Easton and Talbot County, which we don't see everywhere," Glanz said.

title: Community Survey, Town Workshop Jumpstart Discussion on Health Department Lot in Easton
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Community survey, town workshop jumpstart discussion on health department lot in Easton

 November 2, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 552
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Around 200 county residents participated in a community-led survey regarding potential next steps for a one-acre lot in Easton that used to house the Talbot County Health Department.The department moved from 100 S Hanson St. to its new location, 510 Cadmus Ln., in July. Easton residents Greg Zimmerman and Joyce DeLaurentis created a survey intended to gather opinions from residents on what they would like to see replace the old Health Department building.
Zimmerman took time to analyze the results of the survey, which received 203 responses, some from residents that live near the building and others from county residents outside of town.
"For me, the two most revealing takeaways were that there was very strong support for the town to take a leadership role," Zimmerman said, "and that there was strong support for some type of green space and either indoor or outdoor gathering venue."
According to survey results, around 77% of respondents answered it was "important" the town "(coordinate) the redevelopment" of the property, with 6% answering that it was not. The property is currently owned by the county, which could choose to sell or transfer it to the town.
Nearly 50% of respondents answered in support of a community pocket park or gathering space, with around 24% in opposition. Many of the other alternatives posed in the survey — splitting the lot between housing and open space, renovating for small businesses and garden apartments — received similar levels of support and opposition.
A question asking if residents would support single-family homes at the lot had around 22% of respondents answer yes and 53% answer no.
Zimmerman said the survey served its purpose of getting residents involved and having their voices heard prior to a decision being made about the property.
"I think the survey is successful in revealing what people think so that there's better alignment between the public and policymakers," Zimmerman said.
The lot is included in Easton's East End Small Area Plan, an initiative to redevelop and improve a one-half square mile area in town.
Last week, town planners and consultants led a five-day workshop to move forward with that plan, including opportunities for public input. Seth Harry, principal architect for Frederick-based Seth & Harry Associates, said there was substantial feedback on the Health Department site.
At the workshop's final presentation on Oct. 28, Harry and Dave Ager, of Clarksville-based Townscape Design, presented five potential ways the lot could be used. Some would necessitate the removal of the building, while other options repurpose or resize the current building.
These alternatives included: a garden space, an outdoor pavilion with open space, open space on the perimeter with the existing building, adding onto the existing building and keeping green space, and a redesigned building with an outdoor event lawn.
"It was our goal and our direction to come up with ideas," Ager said. "These are ideas to be contemplated and discussed by the community."
Zimmerman believes the outreach done to the community has served as a "conduit" between residents and policymakers, as well as increasing public participation.
"In some cases, people even living … right around the health department property didn't even know that the Health Department was moving," Zimmerman said.
To view the survey results, send an email to eastoncommunitysurveys@gmail.com. To view the Town of Easton's East End presentation and the included alternatives for the health department lot, visit eastend.eastonmd.gov/charrette.

title: Easton Workshop Comes to Close as East End Plans Move Forward
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Easton workshop comes to close as East End plans move forward

 October 30, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 495
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — More than 50 residents and town employees gathered Monday night to get a closer look at the East End Small Area Plan being developed by the town's planning and zoning department.The town hosted a final presentation of its five-day interactive workshop at the Easton Church of God on Monday. Consultants presented renderings and potential redevelopment options for Easton's East End plan, which will update the town's current plan that dates back to 1997.
Planning and Zoning Director Miguel Salinas thanked attendees for participating in multiple public sessions over the weekend and stressed that the opportunity for public participation did not end Monday.
"This is not the final opportunity for public input," Salinas said, pointing out that the plan will go through refinement and then hit the desks of the town's Planning Commission and Town Council before final approval.
Seth Harry, principal architect of Frederick-based Seth Harry & Associates, and Dave Ager, principal of Clarksville-based Townscape Design, are each on the town's consultant team. They explained shared with residents some of the main goals in their East End designs: open space, walkability, connectivity and local employment opportunities.
A rendering of a redesigned Dover Street and Dover Road intersection was shown, with "civic open space" occupying the "triangle" formed when the two roads meet. Ager said the open space could be the "heart of the overall area."
"The entire Dover Road or Dover Street north side is really ideal for commercial, and the south side is really ideal for residential," Ager said.
"It was an opportunity hidden in plain sight, and we just needed to reveal that potential," Harry said.
East towards U.S. Route 50, Ager and Harry discussed adding on-street parking and "enhanced" pedestrian crossings to slow down traffic near the Doverbrook Apartments. They also detailed plans to extend Easton's downtown with small commercial opportunities.
"The incubator and commercial space works to change the character of the street," Harry said. "So the idea again is bringing more of the downtown core farther out."
"... It's essentially unfettered all the way to (Route) 50, and it doesn't feel like you're in a community or a … walkable neighborhood," he continued. "So, the drivers drive accordingly."
Resident Maury Schlesinger asked if the Dover Triangle and commercial plans would interfere with the success of the rest of the downtown. Harry said the downtown's primary competition comes from retail on Route 50.
"The retail here in Dover Triangle is positioned to complement and not compete with the downtown shopping," Harry said. "It should actually enhance your regional capture and make your downtown more of a destination."
During the weekend, town planners and consultants also worked to create renderings of small "pocket neighborhoods" that could address housing needs at the Brookletts Avenue and Rails to Trails intersection.
It was discussed that the area could provide workspaces for local artists as well.
The East End Area, according to the town, is just under one-half square mile and is home to more than 2,000 residents.
Residents can visit eastend.eastonmd.gov/charrette to view renderings and learn more.

title: Despite Split Opinions, Easton Planning Commission Approves Silo Square Townhomes
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Despite split opinions, Easton Planning Commission approves Silo Square townhomes

 October 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 656
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Amid resident pushback and design concerns, the Easton Planning Commission unanimously voted to approve a 28-unit townhouse development at the site of a former Perdue AgriBusiness operation in Easton.The Silo Square development is led by Chesapeake Community Development, a subsidiary of The Arc Central Chesapeake Region. It is a mixed-income housing project on a 2.36-acre lot at 410 Needwood Avenue, within the East End area that the town is aiming to revitalize.
An updated site plan was presented at Thursday's Planning Commission meeting, along with a traffic study that was requested when developers weren't granted approval last month. The project is set to include 16 three-story townhomes and 12 two-story townhomes.
The 10 grain bins currently on the lot, often referred to by community members as silos, would be demolished.
Residents that live near the site spoke during public comment on Thursday, largely in opposition to the design of the townhomes. Developers have stated the architecture is intended to "pay homage" to the Perdue site and fit in the surrounding industrial area.
"This is the core of Easton," resident Tom Ledvina said. "The code and the (comprehensive) plan say it has to look, it has to be compatible with that historic look that makes Easton special. And this just doesn't."
Zach Smith, an attorney representing the developers, asked that the commission look toward the town staff's review and analysis of the project, which noted it does fit within Easton's comprehensive plan.
"We don't have to get the consensus of the neighbors in order to move forward," Smith said. "What we have to do is to comply with the town's requirements."
Resident Maury Schlesinger spoke in disapproval of how the project faces inward toward the parking lot, with its back to the street. He said it will be "distinct" and "separate" compared to the nearby residential designs.
"Is this how we want our economically challenged people to live?" Schlesinger asked the commission. "Is this how we build an inclusive community? And is the desire to approve more housing right now so great that concern for (developers') budgets and timetable overcomes the need to protect the character of the town?
"I'm all for affordable housing, but it shouldn't look like this."
COMMISSION SPLITCommission members Victoria McAndrews and William Ryall, who were not present at the September meeting, expressed their own concerns about the project. McAndrews and fellow member Thomas Klein said they didn't like the design.
"This to me, has an incredibly suburban subdivision feel, as opposed to being an integrated part of the neighborhood," McAndrews said. "And I'm just wondering what is the rationale for not following the existing framework of how the neighborhood is laid out."
Commission Chairperson Philip Toussaint and Vice Chairperson Michael Ports complimented the design of the townhomes and pushed for approval.
Smith did the same, noting that developers fulfilled the requests made by the commission last month to include a traffic study — which revealed no significant impacts — and remove a section of fencing.
"We left this meeting last month with a clear direction that we needed to address the fence and we needed … a traffic study," Smith said. "We've done both of those things, and now we're at a point where we're facing having to come back yet again. This is how workforce housing projects die."
Ryall, who said he liked the design but was "torn" over whether it fit within the surrounding residential area, joined Toussaint and Ports in supporting approval.
"I don't want to let perfection get in the way of the good," Ryall said. "So I'm willing to vote in favor of it."
Ports moved for approval, seconded by Toussaint. All members voted yes, though McAndrews and Klein did so reluctantly, emphasizing their disagreement with the design.
Since the proposal came in the town's planned redevelopment overlay district, it will not require approval from the Easton Town Council. Thursday's vote was passed on the conditions that developers make minor adjustments to the site plan and approval is granted by town staff.

title: Second community meeting for Easton Crossing development
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Second community meeting for Easton Crossing development

 September 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 530
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Over a month after Chesapeake Community Development's initial community meeting for a planned mixed-use development on Brookletts Avenue, dozens of people once again gathered to learn more about the plans.The Sept. 18 meeting provided the opportunity for developers to show initial designs for Easton Crossing, a six-acre development in Easton, based on feedback received at a community meeting in July. Leaders of Chesapeake Community Development, the developer for the project, have made a point to work with local community members on the overall outcome of the development.
According to Ross Benincasa, vice president of Chesapeake Community Development, Wednesday's meeting showed attendees the initial site plan. The plan broke down the five buildings on the property, as well as open spaces and plans for parking, general traffic and pedestrian flow, all of which were concerns raised in July.
"It was extremely important, just from the standpoint of making sure that our residents had a chance to not only see what we were thinking, but then to give feedback again on that, to tell us kind of what we got right and maybe what we missed," Benincasa said.
Chris Wheedleton, consultant at Rivers and Roads, was hired on the project to lead in gathering feedback from the community. Wheedleton said the meeting provided a chance to answer any questions residents might still still have regarding the new site.
After a presentation of the site plan, people were separated into groups and were encouraged to answer two questions: "Would you like what you saw?" and "What would you like to see differently moving forward?"
Wheedleton said he received general positive feedback from the site plan. Major point raised by residents included diversity of housing options offered and making sure the development would integrate properly with the existing community.
An additional concern addressed was the potential for a grocery store to be built on the development. Benincasa took time to make clear that a grocery store was considered by developers but it would not be included in the project moving forward.
It was felt by Chesapeake Community Development that nearby local and international grocery stores are close enough to the project to meet the need of future residents.
Bob Porter, owner of the Sharper Graphics, said his business is next door to the planned Easton Crossing development. He attended the meeting on Sept. 18.
Porter said the piece of territory is important to him due to his 44-year history living near it. For Porter, he was excited to hear the development would serve all incomes in the community.
"The project is going to be made available at lower rates to to family, people that are working in the in the neighborhood and living in the neighborhood and making sure that they can afford to participate in the project without being in some kind of a federal or state project program," Porter said. "And that was very meaningful to me."
Wheedleton said there are still opportunities for people to weigh in and give their feedback and input into the project. A third meeting will take place sometime in December, details have yet to be released, this meeting will show development and further renderings of the project before it goes before all necessary approvals.

title: Talbot County Discusses Draft Legislation for Cannabis Operations
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Talbot County discusses draft legislation for cannabis operations

 September 25, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 587
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Talbot County Council and Planning Commission held a lengthy work session Monday to discuss draft legislation regarding cannabis zoning.On June 1, state legislation took effect providing local governments additional flexibility to change requirements for cannabis businesses.
Planning Commission members discussed potential zoning requirements for cannabis businesses that generally fall under three categories: dispensaries, growers and processors. They honed in on concerns about the odors that emanate from cannabis processing facilities and strategies for regulation.
Gary Nusinov, a former vice president at a cannabis cultivation business, spoke during the work session as a subject matter expert. Nusinov was awarded a lottery license for cultivation by the state this cycle.
"We know that many of the counties on the Eastern Shore have not really addressed the zoning," Nusinov said. " … Because the conditional licenses for most of these lottery winners happened in July, … we have a six-month period to prove our capitalization and that we are able to locate in a properly-zoned area."
State law regulates that dispensaries may not locate within 500 feet of schools, places of worship, playgrounds, libraries and public parks. Counties, though, may reduce that requirement. Counties are also permitted to increase the required 1,000 feet between dispensaries up to a half-mile, or decrease that 1,000-feet rule.
Under the new state law, local jurisdictions may not restrict licensed dispensaries more than alcoholic beverage retailers.
Nusinov explained that for dispensaries, most odor concern stems from a dispensary that has its own packaging operation. He suggested the county require treatment to ventilation so odors are decreased.
"When you are making formulated products such as a gummy or chocolate, the odor of that confection mixed with the smell of cannabis will emanate from the air," Nusinov said.
"The stigma of the past still exists for some, but for most, it's really not there," Nusinov added. "You don't want to have a noxious odor or constant smells. It can give some people an allergy or a headache."
PROCESSING FACILITIESPlanning Commission Vice Chairman Chip Councell emphasized the commission's main concern was with processing facilities and odors from those operations.
Tim Crosby, principal of Crosby & Associates, has experience with local and international cannabis projects. He suggested the processing facilities be limited to just light industrial zones or agriculture zones in order to avoid high-density, retail areas.
"It can be dealt with, but to say that there isn't an odor coming out of those, even the best of systems, I think that would be disingenuous," Crosby said.
He said a reasonable setback from residences for processing facilities would be at least 200 feet. Crosby also encouraged the council and commission to consider its restrictions on agricultural practices as a whole.
"Remember you're opening up a Pandora's box here," Crosby said. " … Processing cannabis is an agricultural practice, and I think the (cannabis) owners would come back to you and say, 'What are you doing about chicken houses?'"
Following the discussion, Councell and other commission members agreed that cannabis-processing facilities are best fit for agricultural areas. Brennan Tarleton, planning and zoning director, said the county could either put odor mitigation rules in the county code or require all processing facilities to go through a special exception use through the Board of Appeals.
The commission and council members came to two drafted requirements for processing facilities that may show up in future legislation: at least a 1,000-foot setback requirement from residences and a maximum building size of 10,000 square feet.
Before the County Council can introduce any cannabis zoning legislation, the Planning Commission will first have to go through review and approval.

title: Planning Commission OKs Apartment Project on North Washington Street
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Planning Commission OKs apartment project on North Washington Street

 September 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 625
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Last week, the Easton Planning Commission approved a proposed 16-unit, two-story residential apartment complex at the intersection of North Washington Street and Aurora Street.The application, which came from Lane Engineering and 350 N Washington Street Investments, was presented at Thursday's commission meeting. Developers sought approval for a plan that outlines a 27,000-square-foot complex consisting of four two-bedroom units and 12 one-bedroom units.
While still needing approval from the Easton Town Council, Thursday's thumbs up was a step forward for transforming the lot into multifamily housing. The lot is wedged in between commercial buildings on Aurora Street and homes on Washington Street.
Attorney Brendan Mullaney spoke on behalf of developers at Thursday's meeting.
"We believe that this is a use that is appropriate at the scale that it's proposed for this property, that doesn't create any undue impacts to traffic, congestion, or the health and safety of residents on the property, or property owners in the area," Mullaney said to the commission.
Mullaney said early estimates on rent rates for the apartments would be as follows: between $1,400 and $1,600 for the one-bedroom units, and between $1,800 and $2,000 for the two-bedroom units.
"(That's) pretty consistent with what's been called attainable or workforce housing for other projects in the town," Mullaney said.
Since the proposal comes in the town's commercial business zoning district, developers went to the Board of Zoning Appeals prior to the Planning Commission's meeting. That board unanimously gave special exception approval to the project after a lengthy review.
Designs have 27 total parking spaces, with 16 off-street and in the apartment lot and 11 on-street. One parking space was removed from initial site plans in order to avoid limiting sight lines on Washington Street. A 12-by-45-foot loading area was also added to the site plan.
Commission Member Thomas Klein appreciated developers for slightly changing those designs after hearing community feedback.
"I applaud the development team for listening to the public," Klein said. "You guys have made several adjustments to your original plan based on the letters and the comments that you received."
All three commission members present approved the application with the condition that developers work with town staff to adjust the originally proposed roofline elevations.
SAFETY CONCERNSMike Lenhart, president of Lenhart Traffic Consulting, told commission members that a traffic study revealed negligent impacts to the surrounding area if the complex is built. The study showed almost no increases in traffic delay at the intersection during the peak morning and evening hours, he said..
However, many nearby residents expressed reservations about the development due to the safety of the Aurora and Washington intersection.
Kevan Full, a member of Talbot Thrive, asked the commission to consider the area's difficult sight lines and lack of accessible sidewalk crossings, among other concerns.
"Before any construction gets started, let's get the intersection, roadways, sidewalks, crossings and bike lanes addressed," Full said. "Don't work backwards by installing an apartment complex first, as that leads to workaround solutions."
Sheila Lawson, who lives on Washington Street, said she's not against the apartment complex, but provided her worries about the intersection's safety.
"I won't even drive that intersection, I've almost been t-boned twice there," Lawson said. "I've seen five accidents in the three and a half years that I've been here. I'm just asking you guys to really think about that. It is a chance to improve it, and improve it in conjunction with what''s going on with the development there."
Town Engineer Rick Van Emburgh said the town is in the process of a "complete street study," along with taking a closer look at sidewalks and potential bike lanes to improve safety on North Washington Street.
As the town embarks on a traffic signal improvement project, the intersection will be one of the spots for a traffic consultant to analyze in the future, he added.

title: Planning Commission Tables Approval of Silo Square Housing Development
author: Konner Metz
content:
Planning commission tables approval of Silo Square housing development

 September 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 766
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The proposal for a 28-unit townhouse development at the site of a former Perdue AgriBusiness grain operation is drawing hesitation from community members as well as Easton's Planning Commission.At the commission's Thursday meeting, developers from Chesapeake Community Development, a subsidiary of The Arc Central Chesapeake Region, presented sketch plans for a mixed-income housing project at 410 Needwood Avenue.
As part of the Silo Square proposal, the 2.36-acre lot near downtown Easton would be converted into 16 three-story townhomes and 12 two-story townhomes.
The 10 grain bins currently on the lot, often referred to by community members as silos, would be demolished.
Zach Smith, an attorney representing the developers, said the proposal adheres to the town's comprehensive plan and fits what is sought for Easton's planned redevelopment overlay district.
"This is truly infill development in every sense of the word," Smith told the commission. "Not just within the town's boundaries, but within sort of our historic, central core. It's truly a walkable site. It's along the rail trail. But it's also connected to town."
Smith emphasized the project will "provide a greater variation of housing types" and partly create affordable housing. "Not all of the units will be rent control, some of them will be market rate," Smith said.
Ross Benincasa, vice president of community development at Chesapeake Community Development, said seven units would be set aside for workforce housing.
"What we're expecting to see here, frankly, is going to be an EPD officer and an instructional assistant at the high school," Benincasa said. "It's going to be a single mom that has three kids, potentially."
Commission members applauded that the design wasn't driven by cost, but they raised extensive concerns about the lack of a traffic study.
Town Engineer Rick Van Emburgh said that during the staff review period, there was no requirement for a traffic study, though the commission could request one. The 28-unit mark fell under what would've triggered a traffic study per town policy for planned redevelopment.
Many of Thursday's public comments came from residents who live in the surrounding "silo district," some of them concerned about increased traffic on narrow streets.
"The project will increase traffic on Maryland and Needwood Avenues as well as the very narrow Higgins and Davis Avenue," resident Maury Schlesinger said. "And (there are) no mitigations proposed."
Resident Matthew Carberry asked the commission to request a traffic mitigation study. He disputed the town staff's analysis of the sketch plan and proposal, which concluded there'd be no adverse effects on health or safety. "Of course it's going to be more hazardous," Carberry said.
Commission members brought up the option of having developers return at an October meeting for a final vote of approval so a traffic study could be included. Both Benincasa and Smith asked that the commission make a motion of approval contingent on the study's completion instead of delaying.
"Is there some reason why that isn't a good way to go?" commission Chairperson Philip Toussaint asked.
"There's a lot of things you make conditions on, and they're easy for the staff to confirm and verify, but a traffic study's a lot bigger deal and could have greater implications," Town Attorney Sharon VanEmburgh said.
"It relates to a finding you have to make," she continued. "And if you can't make that finding today, because you don't have a traffic study, then I don't think you can approve it with a condition."
The three commission members present at the meeting voted unanimously to table potential approval of the application until October's meeting, upon the completion of a traffic study, as well as the removal of a section of fencing in the design.
OPINIONS ON DESIGNThe design of the townhomes yielded mixed feedback on Thursday. Developers stated the design intended to "pay homage" to the Perdue site.
In the middle of the lot, there is a gazebo in the shape of a silo, meant to call back to Perdue's grain bins. Renderings show metal roofing on the townhomes, similar to the material of the silos.
"Is there anything we can do to dress them up a little bit with peaks, bricks or shutters or something?" Commission Member Thomas Klein asked. "It just seems really flat and plain to me."
On the other hand, commission Vice Chairperson Michael Ports said he appreciated the simple design.
Schlesinger, who met with neighbors in the silo district to discuss the site, presented worries about the lack of open space other than the gazebo. He added that he doesn't think the callbacks to the industrial history of the site will ring obvious.
"If the design attempt was to recall the former silos on the site, perhaps only a few will see that connection," Schlesinger said.

title: County Introduces Zoning Change Resolution for Potential Housing Project
author: Konner Metz
content:
County introduces zoning change resolution for potential housing project

 September 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 405
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Talbot County Council introduced a resolution Tuesday proposing a zoning change waiver for around 17 acres of land off of U.S. Route 50 for a potential affordable multifamily housing development project in Easton.The development on the east side of Ocean Gateway is planned by developers Corrigan & Trippe Ventures. Easton Town Council approved the annexation of the land back in July.
The resolution states that the proposed rezoning from the county's town conservation zoning to the town's residential zoning "will result in substantially different uses or substantially higher density" than would be allowed for proposed development under the county's zoning.
Thus, the town is requesting the zoning change along with a waiver on a five-year hold. That hold would restrict the ability to develop annexed land for five years after annexation for such uses that are either substantially different or of a substantially higher density.
The county's town conservation zoning, which the land is currently under, allows for one dwelling unit per acre, Talbot County Planning and Zoning Director Brennan Tarleton said. The town's residential zoning would allow for 3.5 dwelling units per acre, he added.
County Council President Chuck Callahan asked about the total number of units that could be proposed in that area if the zoning change is made. Tarleton said around 50 to 60.
"That's not an exact number because there are included environmental constraints," Tarleton said. "These properties are relatively heavily forested, so I'm sure there will be some environmental buffers included in that."
He noted that the property is expected to be proposed as a planned unit development to the town in the future, meaning "it could be proposed at a larger density permissible on these properties" than the town's residential zoning. Developers initially told the town a maximum density could be around 240, though town council feedback was mixed on whether that mark was excessive.
Council Vice President Pete Lesher brought up accessibility to the property, asking if there will be publicly accessible entrances other than U.S. Route 50.
"No, unfortunately it doesn't appear that there's any connectivity to any existing subdivisions within the town or within the county based on where these properties exist today," Tarleton responded. " … It's likely that the access for any future development on this property would come directly from Route 50."
"That's a nut for the town to crack," Lesher said.
The resolution was introduced Tuesday, and a public hearing will be held at the council's Oct. 8 meeting.

title: Parking in Easton garners mixed opinions
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Parking in Easton garners mixed opinions

 August 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 747
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — As Easton fields housing proposals, some residents and officials are questioning whether the town has adequate parking.At multiple town meetings, Ward 1 Council Member Maureen Curry has expressed a keenness to dig deeper into the town's parking systems and availability. Curry, who has served on the council from 2003 to 2008 and since 2023, believes a parking analysis should be completed.
"Twenty years ago, I was sitting in the same seat, talking about the same thing, that we need parking downtown," Curry said at a June 17 meeting. "But now it's critical."
While Curry and others have been adamant about needs to improve parking access and availability, a range of differing opinions have been raised regarding parking in Easton. And some believe the parking problem is sometimes more perceived than it is real.
'PERCEIVED' OR REAL?Since moving to Easton in 1997, resident and restaurant owner Steve Mangasarian is used to hearing calls for increased parking. When concerns were raised during discussions of housing proposals at Easton Town Council, he decided to take an inventory of spaces in town.
Mangasarian said he spent three weekdays earlier this summer assessing available parking, all at different times of the day. On average, he found anywhere from 180 to 250 empty spots, not counting street parking and dedicated spots for businesses.
"It's completely overblown," Mangasarian said of demands for additional parking.
Scott Messick, the town's IT director, has led efforts in the town's parking kiosks and mobile parking app, Easton Park Smart. As he attended parking conferences and learned about the industry, he developed a similar stance on parking in town.
"It is a perceived problem. And part of the perception is I want what I want, where I want it, when I want it," Messick said.
Messick said free on-street parking and low per-hour rates hurt the availability of premium parking near businesses, which is often what residents and visitors seek.
However, with more than 500 spots in lots across town, Messick argues additional parking isn't a dire need. Around 100 of those spots are 50 cents per hour and around 150 spots are 25 cents per hour, with more than 300 free of charge.
Curry's view is that as the town grows and adds new residents, those residents will need to be accommodated. On Aug. 19, the Easton Town Council passed proposal for a 33-unit housing development at the site of the former Safeway on North Washington Street.
Currently, the lot has around 50 parking spaces that are used, which will be taken away once construction begins. Curry says it's "incumbent upon us as the Town Council" to push for a parking study before that construction.
"We're not the same town center that we were 20-plus years ago," Curry said. "We're ever changing. We definitely need to take a look at it."
KIOSKS AND APPTwo downtown paid parking lots have kiosks where drivers can pay with credit or cash, Lot 1 at the corner of Glenwood Avenue and South Harrison Street, and Lot 5 between Washington Street and Harrison Street.
Holly DeKarske, executive director of the Easton Economic Development Corporation, says tourists often come to the Easton Visitor Center after struggling with the downtown parking kiosks.
"I'm frustrated about this kiosk parking," Curry said in an interview. "And I want to see a solution to that because I don't think that's working. … They're not user-friendly to begin with, in my opinion."
Messick said it's a "mixed bag" with drivers understanding the technology. "There are people who think it's the greatest thing since sliced bread, and there are people who want that meter back," he said.
The meters, though, aren't a viable option since parts are hard to find if one breaks and the price per hour cannot be changed, Messick noted.
The town's mobile parking app, Park Smart, allows users to register a vehicle and choose a payment method. The app will automatically draw from an initial balance so users can simply park and walk away.
Both Curry and Messick pointed out that parking enforcement is a challenge with only two meter enforcement officers in town. Thus, many hours during the week go without meter enforcement on duty.
Along with a lack of enforcement, education and expert help remain at the forefront of Curry's vision.
"We need a comprehensive parking solution. … I don't claim to have the answers, I just want to go find them," Curry said. "And I want to find somebody that can help us get to the next level so that we can be more welcoming to our citizens and our visitors."

title: Town Council Approves 33-Unit Housing Project at Former Safeway Site
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Town Council approves 33-unit housing project at former Safeway site

 August 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 620
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A proposal for a 33-unit housing development at the site of the former Safeway in downtown Easton was unanimously approved by the Easton Town Council on Monday evening.The proposal came from Lane Engineering on behalf of NAI Saturn Eastern and Safeway, along with Miller Development Corporation, the potential developers of the project. It includes 24 partially-connected townhomes and nine standalone units. The property, which has been vacant since 2017, sits at 139 N. Washington St.
The town's planning and historic district commissions reviewed the proposal before it landed on the Town Council's agenda this summer. On Monday, council members gave the green light to the project, which fell under the town's planned unit development infill subdistrict.
"I can assure you that we all thought long and hard about this," Ward 2 Councilmember Don Abbatiello said before the vote. "This was not a quick decision. … This is going to be a decision that is going to outlive our tenures on the council."
Town Attorney Sharon VanEmburgh discussed three conditions included in a findings of fact for the application prior to the vote.
The first condition requires developers to contribute $10,000 per unit to the town's affordable housing fund, with $5,000 due when the unit's building permit is issued and the other $5,000 due when the unit becomes occupied.
The second condition indicates the units "shall be privately maintained by a homeowners' association established for the community, which shall also provide private trash collection for all residences of the PUD District."
"They have to include that in their covenants," VanEmburgh said, "so there is notice to everyone who buys a piece of property there that it will be private trash pickup."
The final condition states if developers stray too much from the approved architecture of the homes, the project will have to return to the town's planning and historic district commissions for review.
While an Aug. 5 public hearing went by without resident input, many concerns were brought to the council at the project's previous public hearings in June and July. Abbatiello directly addressed those concerns prior to the vote Monday, including traffic, parking and the prospect of building a grocery store at the site.
"Traffic was another concern that was raised by many of my constituents," Abbatiello said, "and while the 33 units will add some traffic to the area, it will be significantly less than what was there when Safeway was open."
Abbatiello added that after following up on Town Council discussions about parking, he learned there are "over 550 parking spots, not including on-street parking, in the downtown area." Some residents' wishes that a grocery store replace Safeway "comes down to the fact that the current owner of the property is not going to sell it with the idea of developing another grocery store in that spot," he said.
Abbatiello's most difficult hurdle in fully supporting the project was the affordability aspect, he said.
"None of these units are going to be affordable," Abbatiello said. "We need housing for seniors, which was mentioned a lot. We need apartments that don't charge $1,600 for a one-bedroom. We do need those things. But when you look at the sale price for this property, there's no way a developer could purchase that and turn it into an affordable housing project."
Abbatiello thanked Robert Miller, the founder of Miller Development Corporation, for listening to council concerns and agreeing to "financially support an infrastructure project that's going to provide necessary workforce housing to town employees."
Ward 1 Council Member Maureen Curry echoed Abbatiello's statements and thanked developers.
"I could not have said it any better and I thank you for all the same reasons," Curry said. "And I appreciate the Miller (Development Corporation) stepping up and donating $10,000 per unit to our affordable housing fund."

title: Affordable Housing Dilemma at Critical Point in Easton
author: Konner Metz
content:
Affordable housing dilemma at critical point in Easton

 August 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 1041
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Charlotte Brown has lived in Easton since 1996. The "peacefulness" of the town is one of many reasons she's been a longtime resident, but she's worried her time in Easton may end soon.Brown, 70, aims to downsize from her current two-bed, two-bathroom apartment once she retires. She knows she will likely have to move out of Easton to do so.
She points to a lack of affordable senior housing and extensive waitlists that make staying in the town unreasonable.
"I think that is such a disservice," Brown said of seniors having to wait years for housing units to open up.
The roadblocks seniors face to obtain affordable housing are only a portion of the town's current housing dilemma. Home prices are rising, and multiple potential housing developments have been met with pushback from residents.
Brown sees reason for concern not just for seniors, but low-income and middle-class people in search of housing.
"Everybody's not a doctor, everybody's not a nurse, everybody's not a lawyer," Brown said.
SENIOR WAITLISTSMultiple low-rent apartment complexes in town meant for seniors are at capacity. On Bay Street, the 93-unit St. Mark's Village has a waitlist of 262 people, which projects to be six-and-a-half years, director Wendy Dyott said.
"We've always had a waitlist," Dyott said. "It's never been this long. But it's been consistently, six, six-and-a-half years probably for the past three to four (years)."
Brown, who is on the waitlist, could envision herself living there. All of the 93 units are one-bedroom, one-bathroom, and tenants pay 30% of their income in monthly rent. All units used to be for seniors only, but Dyott noted that now the complex also serves those with a "handicap or disability."
Dyott said it's a popular place for seniors to downsize and in a prime location near downtown.
"I think one is affordability, and two is location," Dyott said of the two main factors that limit the options for seniors. " … Folks not only downsize their home, but then the next transition is they give up their driver's license. And (St. Mark's is) downtown pretty much, it's local, it's within walking distance to a bank, to a grocery store."
The 26-unit Asbury Place apartments off of Dover Road have a waitlist of two to three years, Don Bibb, the executive director of the Talbot County Housing Commission, said. Bibb said there's a lack of housing supply in Easton or single people and seniors, though "the demand is there."
Bibb, who serves on the Easton Attainable Housing Task Force, has attended international conference calls to discuss housing problems at a larger level. The struggles aren't just in Easton or the mid-Atlantic region, he said.
"Globally, we're all dealing with the same problem," Bibb said.
HOUSING INITIATIVESAt the local level, home prices in Talbot County are rising. According to the Mid-Shore Board of Realtors' second quarter report, the average home price in the county is just over $900,000, up 27% from the second quarter of 2023.
Realtors Property Resource data provided by Mid-Shore Board of Realtors shows the average estimated property value for single family homes, condos, apartments and townhomes in Easton is up 7.5% from one year ago. June data has shown the market is leaning towards sellers.
Jim Bent, a realtor at Benson & Mangold Real Estate, is working to address housing market problems as chair of Easton's Affordable Housing Board. Two affordable housing programs that he oversees have yielded different results.
The town's purchase program — meant to help provide affordable options for first-time home buyers — "just hasn't been feasible," Bent said. " ... There just isn't any property available to do anything significant," he added.
According to Bent, as of July 23, only six homes in Easton under $350,000 were listed for sale: three between $300,000 and $350,000, two between $250,000 and $300,000, and one under $250,000.
The town's renovation program has been more successful. Bent said there's been 38 renovations completed since 2014, and most of those have been for people that rely on social security as a main source of income.
COUNCIL MOVEMENTBent said of approximately 900 units under or nearing construction across Easton, he expects around 35 to be affordable. It's a reason he has supported potential projects brought to the Easton Town Council in recent weeks.
"A big part of moving this forward is education," Bent said, adding that many residents are often confused or misinformed on the goals of the Affordable Housing Board. Housing costs should not exceed approximately 30% of gross monthly income, Bent said, in order to be affordable.
A potential affordable multifamily housing development on the east side of Ocean Gateway moved forward last month, when the Easton Town Council approved an annexation request of around 17 acres of land between Royal Farms and Unitarian Universalist Fellowship. The annexation agreement included language that 50% of the units must be "attainable." Developers have said they are committed to reaching the 100% mark.
With a lack of land available to be developed without annexation, Bent sees it as one of the town's best opportunities to add a significant number of affordable units.
The annexation was met with mixed feedback from the public, with worries about congestion, safety and whether the project developer would actually commit to the affordability aspect surfacing during town meetings and on social media.
Residents have also voiced concerns about a proposed 33-unit development at the site of the former Safeway on North Washington Street. Resident Charlotte Brown doesn't think 33 townhomes should be packed into that downtown spot, especially if they're not helping local residents in need. Thus far, there has been no commitment from developers to make any of the units affordable.
"What about those that are here?" Brown said. A public hearing on that proposal from Lane Engineering and Miller Development Corporation will continue at Monday's Town Council meeting.
Ward 2 Council Member Don Abbatiello and Ward 4 Council Member the Rev. Elmer Davis previously suggested that the council consider requiring the developers of that project make financial contributions to other affordable housing projects.
Brown hopes that push to require a sizable percent of affordable units is realized. She wants the town to prioritize projects that will help current residents in need rather than projects that are geared towards the upper-class.
"It's like playing Monopoly," Brown said of the town's housing outlook. "Turn a wheel and see who comes up."

title: Port Street Housing Project Nearing Completion
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Port Street housing project nearing completion

 August 1, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 675
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Nine affordable housing units and a new headquarters for a local nonprofit organization are nearing completion on Port Street. The Port Street Commons, a project led by The Arc Central Chesapeake Region, is slated to finish construction in October.The project includes nine apartments — seven two-bedroom units and two three-bedroom units — and approximately 10,000 square feet of space for The Arc's new regional headquarters, featuring offices and a behavioral health suite.
On Tuesday afternoon, Jonathon Rondeau, president and CEO of The Arc, gave a tour of the 24,000-square-foot space to Jake Day, Maryland's secretary of housing and community development.
Construction workers were in action on the site, and drywall and insulation was installed on the first and second floors of the three-story building. Day called it a "great looking building."
Rondeau pointed out the importance of bringing immediate assistance to those in need of housing in the Easton area, which is why his team has worked to aim for completion in under four years. The site was identified in July of 2021, and construction began last June. "We want to move quickly," Rondeau said.
$6.5 million of the project's approximate $11-million price tag has been raised, and The Arc is nearing the end of its capital campaign. Rondeau told Day that The Arc is financing the gap of around $4.5 million.
"If we wanted to raise the full $11 million, that would've taken us about eight years," Rondeau said.
Day was impressed with the pace of the Port Street project, asking Rondeau, "can we set you up with lots of other developers to help guide them through the process as speedily as The Arc has gotten through?"
A ribbon cutting is planned for Nov. 7. Rondeau said the first batch of tenants will move in Dec. 1, with a second batch coming in on Jan. 2. The Arc's headquarters will open in January.
Eight of the nine units will accept tenants based on a public lottery system. The ninth unit is designated to the Talbot Interfaith Shelter to house someone transitioning out of the shelter.
"Because of the site plan, all nine units are slightly different," Rondeau said, "which was not the most economical, but it was the only way we could maximize getting nine units into the available square footage."
All of the units will feature free Wi-Fi and appliances including a microwave, along with "solid surface countertops" and carpet in bedrooms to save money in the back end for property management. The units will be managed by Chesapeake Neighbors, a housing subsidiary of The Arc.
Rondeau said two of the units on the first floor are "universally designed," with accessible bathrooms and appliances meant to accommodate those with disabilities.
As Day and other members of the Department of Housing and Community Development toured the space, Rondeau pointed out how the office spaces will support The Arc's overarching goal of providing counseling and assistance to those with intellectual and developmental disabilities.
The headquarters are expected to add around 35 jobs to the area. Rondeau said employees at the Easton site will have health insurance. A full-time nurse will also be in the building.
"Three years ago, The Arc decided to self-insure our health insurance for our employees," he said. "And we have a partnership. We provide free urgent and primary care to all of our employees."
Rondeau is excited for The Arc's services to continue expanding outside of Anne Arundel County, which is where the organization was founded and has the largest presence.
"We've grown significantly over the last 25 years here in Easton," Rondeau said. "We wanted to have an Eastern Shore headquarters."
The project is the first building in Easton to fall under the town's mixed-use waterfront zoning district regulations, Rondeau said. Passed in 2019, the zoning code emphasizes connecting the Easton Point waterfront to the town's downtown area. Rondeau said The Arc made sure to have the front doors of the project facing Port Street as part of the zoning expectations.
After the tour, Day thanked Rondeau and expressed his support for The Arc's fast-moving efforts.
"It's an awesome project, it's an incredible project," Day said.

title: Council Approves Annexation of Land for Potential Affordable Housing Project
author: Konner Metz
content:
Council approves annexation of land for potential affordable housing project

 July 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 742
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A potential affordable multifamily housing development project on the east side of Ocean Gateway took a step forward at Monday night's Town Council meeting.Council members approved a resolution for the town to annex around 17 acres of land following multiple public hearings.
The land is to be annexed from Talbot County and into the town of Easton. It contains vacant property east of U.S. Route 50, between the Royal Farms and Unitarian Universalist Fellowship. Council members approved the annexation request 4-1.
Ward 4 Council Member the Rev. Elmer Davis was the sole no vote, stating that he wanted to see a plan from the developers, Corrigan & Trippe Ventures.
"If this project has a plan, present the plan, present it now," Davis said. "And then we should look at it, not just piecemeal us, and something turns into something we totally did not think was coming our way."
Earlier in the meeting, attorney Zach Smith spoke on behalf of Corrigan & Trippe, saying that upon successful annexation, developers will conduct designs and traffic analysis before presenting a planned unit development project to the council.
"We don't yet know what the ultimate project will be," Smith said. "But … we will propose a project that provides multi-family apartment rentals, and specifically partnering with the Talbot County Housing Authority to propose units at rental rates … for the folks that organization serves."
Davis, though, was not ready to vote yes without a plan or a guarantee that the project will contain 100% affordable housing.
Developers have said they are committed to the 100% mark. The annexation agreement says at least 50% of the project must be attainable, defined as housing attainable to households "making 60% or less of the Easton Median Family Income adjusted by household size."
"If we're going to do a project, it should be 100%," Davis said. "That's where I'm at."
Ward 3 Council Member David Montgomery expressed full support for the annexation at Monday's meeting.
"If anyone is serious about affordable housing and has meant what they've been saying over the last year, two, five years," Montgomery said, "I don't see how they could possibly vote against this annexation."
Council President Frank Gunsallus, Ward 1 Council Member Maureen Curry and Ward 2 Council Member Don Abbatiello joined Montgomery in approving the annexation.
NUMBER OF UNITS
Despite their approvals, Curry and Abbatiello each stated concerns about the project's density.
Smith said developers initially thought "proposing the maximum density" — around 240 units — "would be well-received" by the council. He said he understands the message that "there needs to be balance" in the project.
"We still don't yet have a density to present, and I think that will really be determined through the design process," Smith told the council. Determining the number of units will depend on what the site can "reasonably accommodate" and "what's needed for a feasible project," Smith added.
Abbatiello said he would have preferred a "concrete number from Mr. Smith," and that he's "closer to 100 than 240" based on town zoning limits. However, he voted yes while stressing that the guarantee of 50% attainable housing must be kept.
The Ward 2 council member said his yes vote on the annexation does not guarantee he'd support a planned unit development proposal. Curry agreed with the density concerns.
"When the PUD comes, I want to see 100% attainable (or) workforce … housing, and no more than 150 (units)," Curry said.
OTHER INPUT
Jim Bent, chair of the town's Affordable Housing Board, and Don Bibb, executive director of the Talbot County Housing Commission, both spoke to support the annexation request during the public hearing.
"The need is here," Bent said, noting that he calculates around 37 current attainable housing units in progress in the town. "And the other thought that comes to mind as far as annexing property: If not this location, where?"
Matt Pluta, Choptank riverkeeper for ShoreRivers, said he hopes developers and the town can take a closer look at who would be responsible for maintaining a wetland east of the property. That wetland serves as a buffer for the Tred Avon River.
"Our experience is that once development goes that close to a waterway, you tend to see negative impacts on water quality and erosion," Pluta said.
Other commenters asked that the town address abandoned downtown buildings or lead affordable housing projects. Davis echoed that sentiment.
"We do, I believe as the town, have resources to deal with affordable housing," Davis said. "I think personally, that we should go buy a piece of land and build affordable housing."

title: Noise Ordinance May Change Live Music Scene in Easton
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Noise ordinance may change live music scene in Easton

 July 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 675
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Residents and business operators are raising concerns about a new noise ordinance that will prohibit commercial establishments from playing amplified outdoor music in the town from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m.The Easton Town Council approved the ordinance by a unanimous vote on July 1. It goes into effect July 21.
Austin Smale, general manager of the Tiger Lily restaurant on North Washington Street, said it will affect how his business accommodates live musicians.
"We might not be able to support the same acts we have in the past, with larger-sized bands as well," Smale said. "And then night entertainment with DJs or any type of musician will be indoors now."
While Smale said the restaurant's entertainment is secondary to its food and drinks, he emphasized that live entertainment has brought in both locals and tourists, even from out of state.
The ordinance defines amplified music as "any music that is played outside of enclosed structures and is amplified through speakers or other electronic means." It also states that if doors or windows are open for an "extended period," then music from indoors will be considered as outdoor music and thus be prohibited.
Businesses can apply to Town Council for a permit to play amplified music beyond the permitted hours. "Government-sponsored events or ceremonies" are exempt from the rule.
Ward 2 Council Member Don Abbatiello said the council received many complaints from residents about noise levels around 11 p.m. and midnight.
"I'm a firm believer if you buy a house next to a bar, you know what you're getting into," Abbatiello said in an interview. "But these weren't complaints from somebody who was across the street. These were complaints from people who were blocks away, and they were still hearing it late into the night."
The 10 p.m. mark was chosen since it falls in line with county regulations, Abbatiello said.
The Town Council held a brief discussion last week prior to voting on the ordinance. Two residents that live on Goldsborough Street spoke during the public hearing to express frustration with noise coming from the nearby Tidewater Inn.
"I'd only moved in for a couple of months when the Tidewater hosted a wedding," resident Helen Houseman told the council. "And that music was so loud that I couldn't hear my TV. … When they host an event in that tent, it is so irresponsibly loud that it's profoundly affecting my quality of life."
"I do think that Tidewater and any other business should be good neighbors," Ward 4 Council Member the Rev. Elmer Davis said at the meeting. "If they're having something outside, they should talk to the neighbors and make them aware of what's going on. It's about being neighborly."
Some residents, though, expressed frustration with the ordinance under a Facebook post by the town on Thursday.
One commenter, Quinn Parsley, is a musician who has played at Tiger Lily before. He's worried the new law will have a negative impact on both local businesses and the town's music scene.
"It's already pretty tricky to do much live music in Easton," Parsley said in an interview with the Star Democrat. "Especially considering how supportive of the arts Easton makes itself out to be, doing something like this, this doesn't do anything to help any musicians."
Don Reedy, director of operations at the Tidewater Inn, said in rare instances, weddings request to use the outdoor tent area on the property. He said the Tidewater Inn will cut off those gatherings at 10 p.m. moving forward compared to what had been a 10:30 p.m. cutoff.
Reedy's main frustration stems from a lack of communication with the town.
In an interview, Reedy said the Tidewater Inn was not notified by the Town Council ahead of July 1's meeting and hasn't heard from the town since. He believes "it could have been a lot better handled."
Smale also said he wished a "different approach" was taken to address noise concerns.
"We've been always respectful and trying to work with the town and the residents," Smale said. " … I wish the Tidewater and ourselves would've been involved in the conversation a little bit more."

title: Residents Share Ideas, Concerns at Easton Crossing Development Community Meeting
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Residents share ideas, concerns at Easton Crossing development community meeting

 July 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 613
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — On Wednesday evening, dozens of people attended a meeting held for the sole purpose of allowing community members to express their concerns and collaborate ideas for the future of Easton Crossing, a planned residential mixed-use development in Easton.During the meeting, attendees raised concerns and hopes for the new development including ideas on parking, accessibility for people with disabilities and accessible affordable housing.
It's unusual for a developer to seek community input so early, said Chris Wheedleton, a consultant and facilitator from River and Roads, a community development firm supporting the development of Easton Crossing.
According to Wheedleton, most developments around the Easton community are done somewhat backward. The first time community members get to share ideas is usually when the development is in front of the town council, and by then essential parts of the plan are difficult to change, he said.
Easton Mayor Megan Cook, Easton Town Council President Frank Gunsallus, members of the Easton Affordable Housing committee, area residents and representatives of the Mid-Shore Board of Realtors were in attendance Wednesday.
Wheedleton said as an Eastern Shore native, he felt proud to help bring people together to share their ideas for this property.
"We understand how important this site is for this town and for the East End neighborhood in general and for the greater community, which is why we're here today," he said.
Two mixed-use developments will be built on the former Perdue grain facility on Brookletts Avenue. The developments will provide affordable housing opportunities and commercial space for the town, the developer said in a May 28 statement.
The project's developer is Chesapeake Community Development, a subsidiary of The Arc focused on creating equitable, accessible and inclusive committees, according to the Chesapeake Community Development website.
Attendees at the Wednesday meeting sat in groups of seven and answered questions about the development's future.
The questions included:
What are key residential elements needed for the community?What challenges do you see for the property?What would success look like for the development?
Every table had large post-it notes for attendees to write down their ideas. Once they moved on to the next question, the meeting leaders would come by each table, take the large note and stick it to the walls for all to see.
As the meeting progressed, attendees shared their hopes and concerns, including wanting active commercial use of the property, playgrounds, proper security and accessible buildings.
Carolyn Jaffe, an advocate for the East End Association, shared her concerns about parking with her table.
"We had a lot of discussion about the difficulty with the streets that surround (the site). The site itself has three very narrow streets," Jaffe said. "They're not expandable … So you've got parking, you've got traffic, which is already a problem. There's a lot to swallow in that."
Other attendees requested restaurants, open space for residents, and a diverse mix of residents from different incomes, ages and ethnicities.
Jonathon Rondeau, president and CEO of The Arc Central Chesapeake Region, said this event was essential to the organization, and he was happy to see a mix of excitement and some well-founded concern.
"Any development that we're doing, whether it's housing or mixed development, is reflective of the communities we serve," Rondeau said. "Before we are fully done with the development process of designing the space. We wanted to hear what the community wants to see as part of that so we can make sure that it's integrated into the plans."
When closing out the meeting, Wheedleton urged everyone to continue to share their ideas through an online feedback form at ccdmaryland.org.
A second community meeting will be hosted in September, with details to be announced soon, according to Wheedleton. That meeting will feature information and plans based on the comments from Wednesday's meeting.
