title: Easton Residents Chime in on Proposed Housing Developments
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Easton residents chime in on proposed housing developments

 July 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 599
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — At a packed Easton Town Council meeting Monday, many attendees took to the podium to show frustration with the current state of housing and development in the town.Two projects were the subject of much discussion: a proposed 33-unit development at the site of the former Safeway on North Washington Street and a plan to annex around 17 acres of land on the east side of Ocean Gateway for a potential affordable multifamily housing development project.
DOWNTOWN PROPOSAL
Miller Development Corporation and Lane Engineering are proposing to the Town Council to build 24 partially-connected townhomes and nine standalone units at the downtown property, which has been vacant since Safeway left it in 2017.
Multiple residents brought up parking as a concern, since the empty space accommodates vehicles.
"If people can't park when they come here, we're going to lose the heart of our town," resident Helen Houseman said.
At the June 17 meeting, Ward 1 Council Member Maureen Curry said she "would hate to not have a project like this because (the town hasn't) done (its) due diligence on creating parking downtown." She said it's been a problem in Easton for 20 years.
"What is going to be done if you haven't done it in 20 years?" resident Brandi Whiting asked Monday. "Are we going to just continue to let developers come and overtake the town?"
Steve Mangasarian provided a different view, saying he thinks "the parking problem's been overstated a little bit." Mangasarian said he conducted his own parking study last week, finding "an excess of 500 parking spaces in various lots around town."
He complimented the developer's plan and warned the council of ramifications if it's denied.
"It could set a dangerous message to anyone, whether they're adding onto their residence or building a housing complex," Mangasarian said, "that you can do everything right, jump through all the hoops that you put before them, and still be denied."
The developers were not at Monday's meeting. Council left the public hearing open for an Aug. 5 meeting.
ROUTE 50 ANNEXATION
East of U.S. Route 50 and between the Royal Farms and Unitarian Universalist Fellowship at Easton, Corrigan & Trippe Ventures is proposing the annexation of county land for an estimated 240-unit housing project.
"Is it ideal to have another 240 cars entering Route 50 where it is already heavily congested?" Easton resident Becky Allen asked. "Do we really want people walking on the shoulder of Route 50?"
Allen, who lives right next to the property, said she still has not heard from developers, even after council previously suggested reaching out to nearby residents. Other residents also indicated worries about traffic and walkability.
"I don't see that we have any benefits to this other than we're packing them in," Connie Knopp said. "We know what benefits it is to the developer, the realtor and the lawyer. They get the benefits."
Corrigan & Trippe's attorney was out of town Monday, deferring a potential vote to July 15.
AFFORDABLE HOUSING
A lack of affordable housing was a common theme from residents who spoke Monday.
"I love this town, but I can't live here," Rudy Reyes said. "I can't afford to live here."
"There is none," resident Charlotte Brown said of affordable housing. "Especially for the seniors. You have senior citizens that are sitting on waiting lists for ten years to get a spot in a place that they can afford."
Stephanie Chester, who currently resides in Trappe, brought up her concerns to council members and the Affordable Housing Board at a meeting on Tuesday.
"The infrastructure of Easton is changing," Chester said Monday evening. "But I don't see people of middle class or lower class getting anywhere. They're not getting houses."

title: Reactions Mixed for Proposed Housing Development at Former Safeway Site
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Reactions mixed for proposed housing development at former Safeway site

 June 30, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 684
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Following a June 17 town council hearing, mixed reactions have poured in concerning a 33-unit development proposal at the site of the former Safeway on North Washington Street.Miller Development Corporation and Lane Engineering are proposing to the Town Council to build 24 partially-connected townhomes and nine standalone units at the property, which has been vacant since 2017.
Some residents have called for a grocery store to occupy the lot ever since 2017. However, Ryan Showalter, an attorney representing Miller Development, told council that hopes for a grocery store will not be fulfilled.
"It's become abundantly clear that there's no circumstance in which Safeway will sell this property in a manner that allows it to be occupied or redeveloped as a grocery use," Showalter said June 17.
Safeway still owns the property. Safeway's parent company, Albertsons, also owns ACME, which has an Easton location on Marlboro Avenue.
Tom Alspach has an office on Bay Street, and is "sympathetic" towards the need for a grocery store, as he often watches downtown residents trek to ACME.
"There's a constant brigade of grocery cart pushers going back and forth there," he said. "People are having to go walk over to the ACME and push grocery carts back from there in order to shop if they are downtown and don't have transportation."
Ward 3 Council Member David Montgomery said he understands that a replacement grocery store will likely not happen at the site based on what the council has been told.
"There's not necessarily a market downtown that would sustain a grocery store," Montgomery added.
He and other council members praised the planned unit development proposal and its designs at the June 17 meeting. The council is expected to discuss the proposal again Monday, which may lead to a vote.
"I think it's a well-thought out plan," Montgomery said in an interview with The Star Democrat. "This was conceived by the architect, designed … thinking about the surrounding buildings in the neighborhood."
PARKINGDesigns of the PUD proposal include two parking spaces per unit, with most of those in townhome garages. Ward 4 Council Member the Rev. Elmer Davis expressed concern about having enough parking for visitors at the proposed development.
During the June 17 public hearing, Ward 1 Council Member Maureen Curry and Montgomery each vowed that the town has its own issues with creating sufficient downtown parking.
"If we're thinking about the downtown as a place where we want to promote denser development like this … it's going to have to be tight," Montgomery said in an interview. " … Parking is going to be an issue across the board. But I think two parking places per townhouse or single-family house here should be ample."
"It would've been nice to have the town buy the property, and just pave it, turn it into some sort of public parking," resident Bobby Cordes said. While Cordes feels the proposal is a solid idea for the currently empty lot, he believes "33 townhouses is probably a bit much for that area."
AFFORDABLE HOUSINGAnother point of discussion at the last council meeting came from Davis and Ward 2 Council Member Don Abbatiello, who each suggested the council consider requiring developers to make affordable housing or open space contributions.
Montgomery, however, feels it's better for the town to focus on encouraging affordable housing projects instead of adding requirements for other developers.
"I just don't think it's worth it, trying to convince this builder to give us enough money to build one, maybe two affordable units somewhere else," Montgomery said. "We keep hearing from developers, especially on our affordable housing task force, what a pain it is to come into Easton and try to do something, because everybody keeps throwing new requirements into what the developer's expected to do."
During the June 17 meeting, Miller Development principal Robert Miller said his team is "threading some really close needles" on the project.
Meanwhile, resident Harriett Page says she would prefer something to "benefit everybody, not just the 2%." She pointed out that this development will likely not fix housing problems for teachers and first-time workers.
"I don't mind change, but I'm a realist on what this town can handle," Page said.

title: Mixed-Use Residential Development Planned in Easton
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Mixed-use residential development planned in Easton

 June 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 492
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Two mixed-use developments will be built on the former Perdue grain facility on Brookletts Avenue. These developments will provide affordable housing opportunities and commercial use for the town of Easton, developers said.The project's developers are Chesapeake Community Development, a subsidiary of The Arc focused on creating equitable, accessible and inclusive committees.
Jonathon Rondeau, president and CEO of The Arc Central Chesapeake Region, said the project will be a thriving neighborhood that will support the various housing needs of the community by offering quality affordable and market-rate rentals.
"When you look at a six-and-a-half-acre site, there's a real opportunity to think more broadly, but also to say, 'how do you really affect the community rather than just building something that's part of the community?'" Rondeau said. "But how can it be a foundation of the community?"
The Arc is a nonprofit organization with a mission to support people with intellectual and developmental disabilities.
About 15 years ago, The Arc decided to create housing opportunities for people with disabilities, which is how Chesapeake Community Development and Chesapeake Neighbors were created.
Though the focus was to establish affordable housing for people with disabilities, the need for affordable housing became so essential that the organization changed its mission to create affordable housing opportunities for all.
Rondeau said they manage about 70 units in Anne Arundel County and the Eastern Shore, including the Primrose and Port Streets Commons. The Arc's subsidiaries seek to create opportunities for people from disadvantaged backgrounds to access services.
Rondeau said mixing affordable and market-rate housing makes development financially viable by allowing subsidies for affordable units through market-rate rents.
He said though Talbot County has a high median income, there are a lot of families that live significantly below the average income. Rondeau said that there is a range of people who have a full time job but make less than $30,000 a year.
workers like baristas and education professionals are people who do important work in the community and should be given the access to live in the area as well, Rondeau said.
Ross Benincasa, a consulting partner and vice president of community development, said the need for affordable housing was great in the area.
"Our vision is to bring a vibrant multi-purpose space to the community that incorporates a wide range of amenities and resources, including much-needed housing," Benincasa said in a press release earlier this month.
Rondeau said they will be hosting a community meeting at the Brookletts Place Senior Center on July 10 at 5 p.m. to hear the concerns and ideas from the local community. He emphasized that community involvement is crucial to addressing any concerns and helping design a development that can meet the people's needs.
"We, The Arc and Chesapeake Neighbors and Chesapeake Community Development want to be part of the community and be part of making Easton an inclusive and equitable community," Rondeau said. "And projects like this allow us to do that, and we hope that the community can help be part of that."

title: Proposed Housing Development at Former Safeway Site Reaches Town Council
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Proposed housing development at former Safeway site reaches town council

 June 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 632
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A proposed 33-unit housing development at the site of a former Safeway was presented to Easton Town Council Monday evening and met with both praise and questions surrounding its design.The proposal comes from Lane Engineering on behalf of NAI Saturn Eastern and Safeway, which still owns the property, along with Miller Development Corporation, the potential developers of the project.
The property, which has been vacant since 2017, sits at 139 N Washington St.
Ryan Showalter, an attorney representing Miller Development, said that designs were presented and passed by the town's planning and historic district commissions.
"I think it's fair to say that the Historic District Commission members were very complimentary and appreciative of the level of design and detail," Showalter said Monday.
Lane Engineering planner Brett Ewing and project architect Maurice Walters showed the council renderings and sketches of the units and surroundings.
Each unit has two parking spaces — most of them in garages — and access to an open walkway in the center of the homes, renderings showed. There are 24 townhomes connected in the middle of the lot, with nine standalone units.
"It is an outstanding, outstanding project," Ward 1 Council Member Maureen Curry said. "I'm excited it's in my ward. Thank you for choosing Easton. That's the plus side."
CONCERNS DISCUSSED
Multiple drawbacks of the project, however, were discussed by the council and the applicants. Parking was one of those concerns, with Ward 4 Council Member the Rev. Elmer Davis suggesting developers purchase additional parking across the street in a public lot.
"I know that you have two parking spaces, but I don't think that's enough parking if you have visitors," Davis said. " … I'd like to see you purchase some of those public parking spaces so that we can assure that you have overflow parking in your proposal today."
Curry said the council has a "bigger problem with parking" than just this one potential development, to which Ward 3 Council Member David Montgomery agreed, calling the two spaces per unit mark "pretty generous."
"Twenty years ago, I was sitting in the same seat, talking about the same thing, that we need parking downtown," Curry said. "But now it's critical. I would hate to not have a project like this because we haven't done our due diligence on creating parking downtown."
Davis and Ward 2 Council Member Don Abbatiello each expressed worries about open space at the property. General planned unit development proposals require at least 30% of a development area be open space, but Miller Development's proposal falls under the town's PUD infill subdistrict.
"Open Space shall be that which is deemed adequate by the Town Council," the town's code states for PUD infill projects.
Davis and Abbatiello suggested that the council consider requiring the developers to make financial contributions to open space areas downtown, affordable housing projects or parks and recreation.
Ewing said he and his team will review parking possibilities and additional contributions. Robert Miller, principal of Miller Development, told the council that "there is a point where we push too far" in terms of finances.
"We are threading some really close needles on this project. I want to be upfront with that," Miller said.
Council President Frank Gunsallus said public comment would remain open at the next meeting on July 1.
NO GROCERY STORE
While the site of the former Safeway has been unoccupied for nearly seven years, hopes from residents for another grocery store remain. Showalter told the council that those hopes will not come to fruition.
He referenced Safeway's parent company, Albertsons, also owning subsidiary ACME, located on Marlboro Avenue in Easton. Albertsons also merged with Kroger, which owns subsidiary Harris Teeter across Route 322 from ACME.
"It's become abundantly clear that there's no circumstance in which Safeway will sell this property in a manner that allows it to be occupied or redeveloped as a grocery use," Showalter said.

title: Easton Town Council Holds Off on Annexation Vote
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Easton Town Council holds off on annexation vote

 June 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 717
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Although the Easton Planning Commission recommended the annexation of land on the east side of Ocean Gateway for a potential affordable multifamily housing development project, the Easton Town Council was not ready to make a move on the recommended legislation at its meeting Monday evening.At the meeting, Zach Smith spoke on behalf Corrigan & Trippe Ventures, the company proposing the project. Smith said the company would like the Town of Easton to annex about 17 acres of Talbot County land.
The now-vacant property lies east of U.S. Route 50, between the Royal Farms and Unitarian Universalist Fellowship at Easton. It is designated as a priority one growth area in the town's comprehensive plan, which means the land is most likely "deemed appropriate for consideration for annexation," according to the plan.
Before Smith spoke, Town Planner Lynn Thomas said that after two meetings, the Easton Planning Commission voted to recommend the annexation request be approved, finding it consistent with the Comprehensive Plan. Thomas said the commission also recommended the Town Council apply the R10A zoning classification to the property, which is for medium-density residential use, according to the town zoning code.
Thomas said the Maryland Department of Planning believes a zoning waiver from the county will be necessary because of the difference in the proposed and existing zoning. Currently, the property is zoned as town conservation, according to the county website.
Although annexation is the only thing on the table right now, Smith went over rough plans for the project, making the argument that it will address Easton's need for more affordable housing.
While there is no definitive plan for the project, the drafted annexation agreement states that, at a minimum, the project will need to have at least 25% affordable housing for any developers that end up taking over the annexed property.
Smith said the company is committed to making 100% of the units affordable housing units.
During the meeting, Ward 4 Council Member the Rev. Elmer Davis Jr. asked Smith what affordable housing means to him.
"We have a lot of people that come before us and say that this is affordable housing," he said. "And I'm not quite sure anyone has fully defined what affordable housing is."
Smith said he believes affordable housing is making units available to people who make 50% to 60% of the community's median household income at a rent that does not exceed 30% of their income.
During a public hearing on the proposed legislation, Tom Alspach, who spoke on behalf of the Talbot Preservation Alliance, said that if they really wanted an estimated 240 affordable units, it should be explicitly written in the annexation agreement. He said that without those "definitive terms," all they have is hopes and plans.
"Hopes and plans are not enforceable," he said. "Hopes and plans change all the time."
Alspach also brought up the project's consistency with the town's comprehensive plan, saying that the comprehensive plan calls for the area to be a commercial developed area, not residential.
Ward 1 Council Member Maureen Curry asked Smith if Corrigan & Trippe Ventures would consider increasing the project's minimum percentage of affordable housing up from 25%. Smith said he thought they would.
"But no matter what, if that fails, any development there, if we build four houses, one of them has to be affordable," he said.
Easton resident Becky Allen, who lives right next to the vacant property, said there are better places in town for this kind of housing project. She said the proposed location is isolated from the town.
"Affordable housing has vulnerable residents," she said. "A lot of times they need pedestrian walkways, they need areas for public transportation."
Allen also brought up congestion. She said that a lot of vehicles driving onto Route 50, which is already "heavily congested" would just be difficult.
Town growth rate was also brought up during the meeting. Ward 2 Council Member Don Abbatiello said he is in favor of affordable housing but, considering the town has a set amount of resources, more than 200 new units seems like "an awful lot."
Ward 3 Council Member David Montgomery pointed out that a project like this could bring more affordable housing to Easton than an inclusive zoning ordinance could. He said that he would like the council to try to vote on this legislation at the next council meeting.
Reporter Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado contributed to this article.

title: Trappe Commission Recommends Changes to Cannabis Zoning
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Trappe Commission recommends changes to cannabis zoning

 May 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 242
 Words 

 Read News Document

 TRAPPE — On Tuesday evening, the Trappe Planning Commission discussed proposed amendments to the zoning ordinance regarding cannabis dispensaries.The commissioners decided to recommend allowing dispensaries in commercial zones C-1 and C-2 by special exception, as they had originally intended.
Throughout Talbot County, towns are establishing cannabis zoning ordinances as they prepare for cannabis businesses to open following the state's legalization of recreational cannabis that took affect in June of last year.
Lyndsey Ryan, Trappe's attorney, stated that the zoning ordinance, which was initially approved by the Planning Commission in March, was returned to the commission due to changes established by the state of Maryland during the 2024 General Assembly, which ended in April.
The Trappe Town Council wanted a clear recommendation from the planning commission before they voted on the cannabis zoning ordinance.
"I think they wanted your opinion because the law had changed from the time you considered it to the time now," Ryan said.
Included in the changes were the additional changes to the zoning ordinances for cannabis dispensaries including adding a 500 foot buffer from schools, childcare centers, playgrounds, recreation centers, libraries, places of worship and public parks. There is also an additional requirement that no licensed dispensary may be located within 100 feet of an area zoned for residential use.
These changes were made to comply with legislation that changed what is considered unduly burdensome for cannabis regulations compared to alcohol regulations.
The planning commission voted to approve their recommendation with the given changes.

title: Easton Planning Commission Approves Recommendation to Annex Property
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Easton planning commission approves recommendation to annex property

 May 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 749
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — On Thursday afternoon, the Easton Planning Commission voted to approve a recommendation to annex land on the east side of Ocean Gateway for a potential affordable multifamily housing development project.This recommendation was controversial to some Easton residents, who expressed concerns about to its location and safety at the meeting and on social media.
Corrigan & Trippe Ventures, an engineering firm based in Easton, issued the proposed plan. Zachary Smith, an attorney representing the business, explained to commissioners that the 17 acres in question are under Easton's Priority 1 annexation area.
Smith said that if annexed, the owners will seek out approval to develop the property as a multifamily residential development, specifically apartments that would be made available to people with lower incomes.
Smith mentioned there was a hope to partner with the public county housing authority in a public-private partnership. The packet that they had given to the planning commission included a letter of support from the Talbot County Housing Authority.
An annexation agreement was drawn that ensured the roads functioned properly, that intersection approval was required and that the developers paid for those requirements. The agreement also ensures pedestrian safety and conductivity at the intersection at Dutchmans Lane and a connection to the town's pedestrian sidewalk.
"If the property is annexed, then the next step is for us to formalize a plan that's consistent with those requirements in the annexation agreement, then bring that forward," Smith said.
Smith reminded the commissioners that this is an application for annexation and not an official application for a site plan for the development. He said the main question the commissioners would need to answer is whether or not this application of annexation is consistent with the town's Comprehensive Plan.
The annexation agreement has language that mentions the developers' intention to have the housing developed at this location be majority affordable. At a minimum, the project will have at least 25% affordable housing for any developers that end up taking over the annexed property.
Public hearingDuring the public hearing, residents near the annexed property voiced their concerns about the potential development.
Drake Ferguson, a nearby resident, said he heard that there was a plan to connect the high-density area to the Stoney Ridge area by means of a walking path, and the residents of the affordable housing development would end up using Stoney Ridge Park, a public park, as a recreational area.
"This sounds like a really bad idea," Ferguson said. "You got a development that is essentially majorly low-income housing, and you're dropping it into an area where the house prices run from $200,000 to $400,000. It's not gonna make anyone on this council real popular with the folks from that area when it comes to their resale value."
Becky Allen, a resident, said she works in the affordable housing industry and had concerns over the lack of accessibility that this property would have to the rest of Easton.
"I know to have a successful, affordable community, you need to have access to the town areas," Allen said. "The resources, the grocery stores. They need to be able to walk safely, ride their bikes safely and get in and out of the community safely, and unfortunately, that area, that piece of land, though I know it's in the town's number one priority for annexation, it's just not the spot for it."
After the public hearing, Commissioner Phillip Toussaint clarified that this approval would simply be the first step of this development project.
"This again is the first step, and legally, I don't know how much we'll be bound by going forward," Toussaint said. "It's been said by the public that this (meeting) is our last chance to look at it, and I don't believe that that's the case. It has to go as a PUD, and we have a lot of discretion as a PUD to request changes to things. It's a whole process."
Commissioner William Ryall raised concerns about the location of the development.
"To me, it doesn't seem like it would be a sustainable community," Ryall said. "Or it will be, but it will be inside itself; it's not going to be part of the town. It's going to be isolated, and that strikes me as being an isolated pocket, which I don't think we want, and it's keeping the lower income out of the town in an isolated area, and I don't like that."
The motion passed 3-1 with Ryall as the sole nay. The application will go before the Easton Town Council for approval with the recommendation of the Planning Commission.

title: Trappe Council Introduces Cannabis Zoning Ordinance
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Trappe council introduces cannabis zoning ordinance

 May 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 288
 Words 

 Read News Document

 TRAPPE — On Wednesday evening, the Trappe Town Council met and unanimously approved the introduction of a cannabis zoning ordinance with amendments based on new state legislation allowing towns more authority in restricting dispensaries.According to Attorney Carly Landolfi, House Bill 805 "clarifies and expands some of the local government authority to regulate where cannabis businesses can be located." The bill was recently passed by the General Assembly and signed by Maryland Gov. Wes Moore.
Trappe Commissioner Brian Schmidt, president of the council, said that HB 805 has helped restrict dispensaries from Trappe's downtown area. Schmidt referred to the downtown area as the area where Momma Maria's Mediterranean Bistro and the Coffee Trappe are located.
Since HB 805 specifies that dispensaries can not be within 100 feet of residential areas, potential dispensaries would not be allowed in one of Trappe's most active business areas.
"Special exemption or not. I think that would help us kind of keep dispensaries out of town," Schmidt said.
Landolfi specified four points that Trappe Attorney Lyndsey Ryan highlighted in an email sent to commissioners about the new legislation. The first is that the local government may establish a distance limitation for dispensaries up to 100 feet from an area of residential use.
The second is that local governments may increase the distance for dispensaries from another dispensary to half a mile.
The third point is that local governments may prohibit licensed dispensaries from locating within 500 feet of pre-existing schools, licensed childcare centers, playgrounds, recreational centers, libraries, public parks or places of worship.
Finally, local governments are prohibited from adopting zoning requirements that are more restrictive for cannabis dispensaries than zoning requirements for alcohol sales stores.
The Trappe Planning Commission will hold a public hearing for the ordinance on June 5.

title: Talbot Planning Commission Approves Lakeside Resolutions
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Talbot Planning Commission approves Lakeside resolutions

 May 2, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 901
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — On Wednesday, the Talbot County Planning Commission reconsidered two resolutions pertaining to the Lakeside at Trappe development that it previously found to be inconsistent with the county's comprehensive plan.This time, both Resolution 347 and Resolution 348 were found to be consistent with the comprehensive plan, as was Resolution 353, which also was reconsidered Wednesday despite the Planning Commission's April 2 finding of consistency.
The Planning Commission's findings follow the recent Talbot County Council approval of Resolution 338, a long-pending resolution amending the Talbot County Comprehensive Water and Sewer Plan and requiring county oversight of any future expansion of the new Lakeside wastewater treatment plant. Resolution 338 passed with a 4-1 vote at the council's April 9 meeting.
Planning commissioners said 338's passage caused them to reevaluate their previous decisions on Resolutions 347, 348 and 353. They decided to reconsider the measures "based on the fact that 338 did pass," Commissioner Phillip Councell said.
All four resolutions attempt to provide clarifications on the housing development's plans and wastewater discharge permit, which were requested by the Maryland Department of the Environment.
Before the introduction of the recently approved resolutions, attempts were made to amend Talbot County's comprehensive plan to reclassify certain portions of the development's property for immediate priority for water and sewer service. This was done through a resolution created called Resolution 281.
The MDE approved the resolution in November 2020. However, a month later, the agency sent a letter stating that Resolution 281 did not provide the number of equivalent dwelling units for the different phases of Lakeside's construction — information needed for further development.
In December 2020, MDE issued a final wastewater discharge permit for Lakeside's new wastewater treatment plant, approving a flow of 540,000 gallons per day — the number the developer requested in its application.
Following public outcry, the Talbot County Planning Commission rescinded its approval of an amendment to Resolution 281, which split the property into two sections for differences in water and sewer classifications. In late October 2022, MDE issued a revised discharge permit for Lakeside, approving a significantly smaller wastewater treatment plant.
Letters were sent by MDE seeking clarification on some specifics of the development. The county debated the best way to address MDE's requests last summer, eventually settling on tackling them via comprehensive plan amendments via introduced resolutions 347, 348 and 338.
Resolution 348 addresses incorrect water and sewer classifications shown in two exhibits — maps displaying updates to Trappe's proposed water and sewer service areas — to Resolution 281.
Resolution 347 provides the number of equivalent dwelling units across all six phases of the Lakeside development's construction. A later amendment to 347 incorporates wording from Resolution 338.
Resolution 353, introduced by council Vice President Pete Lesher and council member Lynn Meilke at a Feb. 27 meeting, "combines Resolutions 338, 347 and 348 into a single resolution," according to County Attorney Patrick Thomas. It was found to be consistent with the county's comprehensive plan on April 2.
At the April 2 meeting, Resolutions 347 and 348 were deemed by commissioners to be confusing on their own, and 348 and 347 were voted to be inconsistent with the Talbot County Comprehensive Plan.
However, at the meeting Wednesday, Planning Commission members said that the recent approval of 338 by the County Council caused them to feel 347 and 348 deserved another look.
The commission made a motion to reconsider Resolutions 347, 348 and 353 during its May 1 meeting.
When reconsidering Resolution 353, Talbot County Attorney Patrick Thomas said the council was essentially looking for clarification in the motion and recommendation that the Planning Commission provided initially and whether or not they found 353 in its current configuration as consistent with the comprehensive plan "not subject to conditions."
The commission found the resolution to be consistent with the Talbot Comprehensive Plan and approved it unanimously.
The commission then moved on to Resolution 347. Vice Chairman Phillip Councell said he feels better about 347 since 338 passed. He said he doesn't have the same "heartburn" about it anymore.
"We're not going to control what happens in 20 years," Councell said. "We're just not going to rule from the grave; it's not going to happen. Therefore, I would support finding 347 and 347 Amendment 1, and leave it up to the council to choose whichever one they like to be consistent, given that 338 did pass."
Councell made a motion to find Resolution 347 and its amendment as consistent with the Talbot County Comprehensive Plan "based on the fact that Resolution 338 did pass."
The motion was passed 3-1, with Commissioner William Boicourt voting against it.
The commission then discussed Resolution 348 and its amendment. They came to the conclusion that Resolution 348 is consistent with the comprehensive plan, but not its amendment.
Councell clarified that the amendment was at the request of the Public Works Advisory Board to "kind of clean some things up."
"I think (the County Council) weren't completely satisfied with the way that came out," Councell said. "So my motion is going to be in regard to 348 only, not 348 Amendment 1. Therefore, I would move that resolution 348 is consistent with the Talbot County comprehensive plan and seven relevant standards based on the fact that Resolution 338 has passed."
"... I still think Resolution 353 is a better solution," Councell added.
The motion passed unanimously.
These resolutions will appear before the Talbot County Council on May 14. If approved by the council, the measures will go to MDE, which can approve, modify or reject them.

title: Easton Town Council passes cannabis ordinance
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Easton Town Council passes cannabis ordinance

 April 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 532
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Nearly two months since opening a public hearing on the topic, the Easton Town Council has passed an ordinance revising the Town Code to regulate zoning for cannabis-related uses.At its meeting Monday, the council voted to pass Ordinance 809 with amendments.
The amended ordinance permits the use of dispensaries through special exception in the central business commercial zoning district and the general commercial district. It also permits, through special exception, cannabis growing and processing facilities in the industrial zoning district and the business commercial zoning district.
On-site cannabis consumption establishments are prohibited in all of Easton's zoning districts under the ordinance.
The passing of the ordinance comes about nine months after the state's approval of various recreational cannabis uses took effect. In November, the council passed a six-month moratorium on businesses looking to produce or sell cannabis within the town limits, which expires May 9.
"If we don't vote today, we must at the next meeting in order to be handled before our moratorium expires," Council President Frank Gunsallus said at the meeting Monday.
The council waited to vote on the topic while the General Assembly discussed the topic in Annapolis. At the council meeting April 1, Easton Town Planner Lynn Thomas said the Maryland Senate had passed a bill that is different from the House of Delegates. He said said that, considering the General Assembly would be adjourning, the town should have the information it needs to vote at April 15's Town Council meeting.
At the meeting Monday, Easton Director of Planning and Zoning Miguel Salinas said that House Bill 805, which deals with cannabis restrictions, had gone through the Senate and House of Delegates and is now awaiting Gov. Wes Moore's signature.
Salinas listed the amendments to Easton's ordinance, including a separation requirement of a half mile between dispensaries. Salinas said that is in House Bill 805.
Salinas said other amendments to the ordinance include the addition of parking standards for dispensaries and the addition of a requirement that a professional engineer or equivalent qualified professional certify that that the proposed odor measures established effectively eliminate outdoor odors.
Before voting on the ordinance, Ward 2 Council Member Don Abbatiello asked that they change the ordinance to permit cannabis growing and processing facilities in the industrial zoning district through special exception, rather than just permitting it.
"There's one industrial area in particular that is off of Dover Road that backs right up to an entire neighborhood," Abbatiello said. "I'm sure that those individuals would at least like the opportunity to share their concerns or joy that a growing facility is going in that area."
Abbatiello said this change would not prohibit growing and processing facilities from the industrial zoning district, it would just give residents "an extra opportunity" to voice their thoughts.
Gunsallus made a motion at the meeting to approve the ordinance with the amendments from the town and the amendment requested by Abbatiello, which passed.
At the end of the meeting, Abbatiello thanked Thomas, Salinas and Town Attorney Sharon VanEmburgh for their work on the ordinance.
"This has been a long process," he said. "It's been a difficult process. And I really do appreciate all their effort to give us the best information so that we can make a decision."

title: Lakeside Resolution 353 Gets Planning Commission's OK
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Lakeside Resolution 353 gets Planning Commission's OK

 April 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 1294
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — On Tuesday morning, the Talbot County Planning Commission approved, with some revisions, a pending resolution clarifying aspects of the often contentious Lakeside at Trappe development. This has been long awaited, and the process of developing and approving the resolution, Resolution 353, began over a year ago.The approval of Resolution 353 allows the Talbot County Council to vote on the measure at its April 9 meeting.
If approved by the council, this portion of the Lakeside development would finally complete the Maryland Department of Environment's requests for further information and correcting mapping errors, which had been roadblocks for the project.
Background
Talbot County Council President Chuck Callahan has described Lakeside as a "complicated matter with a lengthy history."
This residential development project has been 20 years in the making and has been a hot topic for residents in Trappe and throughout the county. Lakeside is a planned 2,501-unit development spanning more than 850 acres off of U.S. Route 50.
According to Erin Braband, Trappe's town clerk, 114 building permits have been issued, and 109 connections have been made to the town's existing wastewater treatment plant.
Trappe's existing plant accommodates wastewater from the development's first 120 homes. Then the flow will eventually be diverted to a new wastewater treatment plant serving the development. The plant is expected to be operational by the beginning of June, according to Ryan Showalter, an attorney representing Lakeside's developers who spoke to commissioners at the April 2 meeting.
Before the introduction of Resolution 353, attempts were made to amend Talbot County's comprehensive plan to reclassify certain portions of the development's property for immediate priority for water and sewer service. The resolution created was called Resolution 281.
The MDE approved the resolution in November 2020. But a month later, the agency sent a letter stating that Resolution 281 did not provide the number of equivalent dwelling units for the different phases of Lakeside's construction — information needed for further development.
In December 2020, MDE issued a final wastewater discharge permit for Lakeside's new wastewater treatment plant, approving a flow of 540,000 gallons per day — the number the developer requested in its application.
There was a wave of public outcry over the development's environmental, pollution and water quality issues during a public hearing in October 2021. A month later, the issue was made more complicated when the Talbot County Planning Commission rescinded its approval of an amendment to Resolution 281, which split the property into two sections for differences in water and sewer classifications.
Lawsuits and petitions soon followed. In late October 2022, MDE issued a revised discharge permit for Lakeside, approving a significantly smaller wastewater treatment plant.
The revised permit allows for an average flow of 100,000 gallons per day — a sharp decrease from the 540,000 gallons per day initially requested by the developer. The limited flow will allow for only 400 residential units to be built, only a small portion of Lakeside's planned development. Any future expansion of the facility will require a significant permit modification.
Letters were sent by MDE seeking clarification on some specifics of the development. The agency re-emphasized the need for the county to provide the number of equivalent dwelling units in each phase of Lakeside to assess the adequacy of the water and sewer system to accommodate and serve the development.
The county debated the best way to address MDE's requests last summer, eventually settling on tackling them via comprehensive plan amendments via introduced resolutions 347, 348 and 338.
Resolution 338 would amend the county's comprehensive plan to be consistent with the provisions of Lakeside's wastewater discharge permit.
An amended version of Resolution 338 was found by the Talbot County Planning Commission to be consistent with the county's comprehensive plan in December, but the County Council has delayed voting on it, awaiting the Planning Commission's recommendations on 347, 348 and 353.
Resolution 348 addresses incorrect water and sewer classifications shown in two exhibits — maps displaying updates to Trappe's proposed water and sewer service areas — to Resolution 281.
Resolution 347 provides the number of equivalent dwelling units across all six phases of the Lakeside development's construction. A later amendment to 347 incorporates wording from the still-pending 338.
The original version of Resolution 347 provides the number of equivalent dwelling units — 2,874 in total across all six phases, with just over 1,200 designated for immediate water and sewer service.
It specified that the phases only represent land uses, not timing or sequence of development, and any changes in phasing or allocation will need to be included in amendments reclassifying any phase's water and sewer service.
Voting and a public hearing were delayed as the commissioners attempted to resolve any issues that may potentially arise from the resolutions being introduced.
Resolution 353
On April 2, the Talbot County Commission found Resolution 353 to be consistent with the Talbot comprehensive plan and will move it toward approval by the County Council.
Resolution 353, introduced by Council Vice President Pete Lesher and Council member Lynn Meilke at a Feb. 27 council meeting, "combines Resolutions 338, 347 and 348 into a single resolution," according to County Attorney Patrick Thomas.
Alone, Resolutions 347 and 348 were deemed by commissioners to be confusing, and 348 and 347 were voted to be inconsistent with the Talbot County Comprehensive Plan at the April 2 meeting.
Resolution 353 stood out to many commissioners on the Planning Commission as an avenue to correct issues from Resolutions 338, 347 and 348.
The commission decided to revise aspects of Resolution 353 before finding it consistent with the comprehensive plan, fixing wording to make it compatible throughout the resolution. The revision also includes the removal of language pertaining to the initial flow for the units.
Resolution 353 specifies that 37,500 gallons will be used daily by the first 120 dwelling units. The commission decided to strike the language providing specific numbers and replace it with "the initial flow necessary to serve no more than 120 dwelling units and a community center and pool complex."
However, not everyone was in agreement. Commissioner William Boicourt said that the general confusion is why it should be labeled as non-consistent.
Talbot County Planning Commissioner Chip Councell said his biggest concern was the mapping of the southern portion of the Lakeside property. Resolution 353 changes the water and sewer services designation from W-2/S-2 to W-3/S-3, extending the amount of time the county would have to introduce future legislation on the project.
The reclassification of W-2/S-2 portions of Lakeside to W-3/S-3 would allow for an extension to existing or potential construction of a new community, multi-use or shared sanitary facilities to progress within a six- to 10-year period rather than a three- to 5-year period.
The commission voted to find Resolution 353 to be consistent with the Talbot County Comprehensive Plan 4-1, with Boicourt voting against it.
Backlash
Though it is a feat to have a resolution approved by the Planning Commission, not everyone agrees with the resolution proposed.
During a lengthy public comment, several people expressed concerns surrounding potential harms to the environment and the oversight efforts by the county on Trappe.
Bob Flower, a Talbot County resident, said he is worried what Lakeside development would do to Talbot County's lakes, forests and air.
Lyndsey Ryan, attorney for the town of Trappe, said that the town of Trappe is opposed to the amendments on Resolution 347, 348 and 353.
"I think it treats Trappe differently than other municipalities in Talbot County to put this restriction on Trappe," Ryan said. "It sets a bad tone between the two entities … which is why Trappe is opposed to 353."
Under the amendment, any expansion of the new wastewater treatment plant would require a new change to the county's comprehensive plan.
Attorneys for Trappe and the developer opposed the requirement for the developer to come back before the county for future expansion.
Resolution 353 is scheduled for a public hearing during the Talbot County Council meeting on April 9 at 6:30 p.m.

title: Easton Town Council Waits on Annapolis to Vote on Cannabis Ordinance
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Easton Town Council waits on Annapolis to vote on Cannabis ordinance

 April 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 354
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Easton Town Council has still not voted on an ordinance that would revise the Town Code to regulate cannabis-related uses in light of the state's approval of various recreational cannabis uses, which took effect July 1.At the meeting Monday, Town Planner Lynn Thomas gave an update on what is going on with related legislation in the State Senate and House of Delegates. He said the Senate has passed a bill that is different from the House of Delegates.
"As best (as) I can read it, the differences deal with a couple of the separation requirements," he said.
Thomas said the Senate version of the bill includes a 100-foot-separation between cannabis dispensaries and residentially zoned properties. He said the Senate version of the bill also allows for an increase to a half mile, or 2,640 feet, in the separation between dispensaries. He said that separation is 1,000 feet in the House version of the bill.
Thomas said a House of Delegates committee had "reviewed and recommended approval with amendments."
"Now I'm not sure if that is referring to the amendments that were in the Senate version or they themselves had proposed further amendments," he said. "But one way or another, it's still playing out."
According to council documents, the ordinance on the table in Easton would permit the use of dispensaries in the commercial general and commercial limited zoning districts and through special exception in the central business commercial zoning district. It would also permit cannabis growing facilities and processing facilities in the industrial zoning district and through special exception in the business commercial zoning district.
On-site cannabis consumption establishments would be prohibited in all of Easton's zoning districts under the proposed ordinance.
Thomas said that considering the General Assembly adjourns next week, the town should have the information it needs to vote on this ordinance at the next Town Council meeting on March 15.
After Thomas spoke, Council President Frank Gunsallus said the council will leave the public hearing on this ordinance open until the next council meeting.
"Hopefully we'll have an update from Annapolis and we'll have some direction regarding what we are able to do," he said.

title: Resolutions Face Vote Tuesday
author: Staff Writer
content:
Resolutions face vote Tuesday

 March 31, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 289
 Words 

 Read News Document

 On Tuesday, April 2, the Talbot County Planning Commission will at long last act on three resolutions (and also three amendments) all involving Lakeside.These matters include fixing the all-important sewer service map improperly approved by the county in 2020 that was the green-light for Lakeside.
A year ago, the Maryland Department of Environment recognized that the sewer service map was wrong, and instructed the county to correct it as the county deems necessary, "including Lakeside." And since then, the county engineer, the county attorney, and the Town of Trappe itself have all acknowledged on the record what MDE had come to understand: that prior to that 2020 approval, Lakeside had always been "unprogrammed" and, contrary to what was told to the Planning Commission and everyone else, had never been previously reviewed and slated for development by the county at all, ever.
The three resolutions before the Planning Commission (R347, R348 and R353) are all deeply flawed for reasons long discussed, and should all be found by the commission to be "not consistent" with the county's comprehensive plan — which is the question the commission must answer under Maryland law.
(The Public Works Advisory Board reviewed them in detail and unanimously recommended rejection of R347 and R348, standing alone and as amended; similarly, they did not recommend R353 as presently drafted.) The language of all three is about as confusing as possible, and misleading. R348 includes a starkly untrue recital. It and R347 are clearly designed not to "fix" the maps as they affect Lakeside, but to assure that that the developer's interests in that billion-dollar subdivision are not disturbed in any way.
The public hearing is scheduled for 9 a.m. on Tuesday, April 2, at the Bradley Room of the Courthouse.
DAN WATSON
Easton

title: Trappe Planning Commission Approves Phase 1D Lakeside Plans
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Trappe Planning Commission approves Phase 1D Lakeside plans

 March 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 414
 Words 

 Read News Document

 TRAPPE — On Tuesday evening, the Trappe Planning Commission met and approved a minor amendment and Phase 1D subdivision revision plat for the Lakeside development. By approving this, they have cleared the way for the Trappe Town Council to vote on this phase of the Lakeside development.The commissioners approved Phase 1D of the subdivision revision, with the notation that the areas identified as public open space on the plat would be clearly labeled as such.
Trappe Attorney Lyndsey Ryan stated that open space is defined as active and passive open space for public use and enjoyment.
Robert Rauch, president of Rauch Inc., the engineering, architecture, and environmental firm constructing the Lakeside development, told the commission that there may be some confusion about the distinction between public open space and private space.
Rauch wanted to ensure that the areas labeled as public open spaces were properly understood to be used by the public.
The open space would not be within stormwater management. Rauch explained that the areas in the exhibit will be green open areas for "throwing frisbees." The exhibit has two parks: Lakeside Public Park and Wooden Public Park. There is public access to the sidewalks between the two areas by trails.
Open space areas would be under the homeowner's association's mandate and management, regardless of whether they are designated as public or private. Rauch clarified that for any areas designated as public open space, the HOA would have the obligation to provide a permanent and perpetual public easement for access and use.
The development agreement states that the public shall have a permanent and perpetual easement to use and enjoy the open space, which may not be limited by the petitioner or any HOA.
The commission voted to approve the revisions of the subdivision to make sure that all designed public spaces were clearly labeled.
Cannabis
Ordinance 1-2024, an ordinance for the town of Trappe to establish reasonable zoning regulations for cannabis businesses, was also approved by the Planning Commission and will be recommended to the Town Council for approval.
Margaret English, a resident of Trappe, was a vocal advocate against approving the zoning regulations for cannabis businesses.
"I don't think you should recommend it," English said. "I don't want drugs in my town, and I ain't moving."
Commissioner Edgar Harrison noted regardless of whether or not he agreed with her; he didn't think the state would permit the town to outlaw the introduction of cannabis businesses into town. After the meeting, he sat down with English and listened to her concerns regarding cannabis.

title: Talbot Planning Commission Plans to Draft Memorandum for New Farms
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Talbot Planning Commission plans to draft memorandum for new farms

 March 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 519
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Wednesday morning, the Talbot County Planning Commission met to approve local requests and discuss the potential of refining the language for farm-based recreational use properties.The Planning Commission voted to approve the major site plan for Brad and Lisa Bebbe's farm-based recreation use. The Bebbes plan to rent out their farm as a venue for weddings and other events. This was the second time Bebbe representatives met with the Planning Commission.
The first time, they were told to "do more," which Zack Smith, a representative for the Bebbes, described as vague.
"We felt at that time and still feel today we demonstrated compliance with technical requirements of the code for that use," Smith said. "... If you feel like what's in the code today isn't consistent with what that intent was, then maybe, like you discussed last month, (this may be) reason to revisit it and perhaps make some modifications."
The commissioners expressed uneasiness with having a farm's primary function be solely an event venue. The commission wanted the owners to view the farm less as a venue and lean more into agriculture.
Smith shared the Bebbes' plan to add bee colonies to the property.
Smith said that Lisa Ghezzi, a master beekeeper from the Maryland State Beekeepers Association, would establish two bee colonies on the property and invite members of the public to learn about beekeeping and raise awareness of bees' role in pollination agriculture. Smith added that there would be potential to market honey, beeswax and other beekeeping products from the colonies.
The commission voted to approve the application; they saw the beekeeping and education component as positively supplementing the farm-based recreation application.
The commission concluded that this application brought up an essential topic regarding language and intent to the commission. Commissioner Paul Spies expressed concern about setting a precedent by allowing recreational-use farms under the current language of the ongoing code and not focusing on agriculture farms.
The other commissioners agreed that the code should prioritize agriculture as the primary use and profit driver rather than supplemental activities like weddings.
The Planning Commission plans to draft a memorandum summarizing the discussion at the Wednesday morning meeting about refining the language for farm-based recreational uses in the zoning code. The commissioners will forward the memorandum to the County Council for consideration, with recommendations to strengthen language ensuring supplemental uses are genuinely ancillary to the primary agricultural use.
The commissioners said they want to help support working farms and young farmers in the agricultural industry, which can be financially challenging. Spies felt concerned that setting a precedent where the supplemental uses could become the main primary income rather than agricultural could lead to more properties being used primarily for non-agricultural events rather than actual farming over time.
Spies said allowing supplemental income was meant to help farming families, not replace farming as the leading enterprise for these businesses.
"It's hard to be a young farmer, it's hard to start out in the industry, it's hard to maintain organic, but if we gave them (farmers) an opportunity to supplement that income with something, then I could see more opportunities in the industry that I love and support," Spies said.

title: Town Council Leaves Public Hearing Open for Cannabis-Related Ordinance
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Town Council leaves public hearing open for cannabis-related ordinance

 March 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 476
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Easton Town Council resumed and kept open a public hearing on a proposed zoning code amendment regarding cannabis businesses at its meeting Monday evening.Before continuing the public hearing, Town Planner Lynn Thomas spoke to the council about concerns regarding the ordinance that were raised at the previous council meeting on Feb. 19, including parking requirements, odors and state limitations and requirements.
Because Ward 3 council member David Montgomery was absent from the meeting, Town Council President Frank Gunsallus said the council would leave the public hearing on this ordinance open. Gunsallus said Montgomery wanted to be able to vote on this legislation.
The proposed cannabis ordinance would revise the Town Code to regulate cannabis-related uses in light of the state's approval of various recreational cannabis uses, which took effect July 1.
According to council documents, the ordinance would permit the use of dispensaries in the commercial general and commercial limited zoning districts and through special exception in the central business commercial zoning district.
It would also permit cannabis growing facilities and processing facilities in the industrial zoning district and through special exception in the business commercial zoning district.
On-site cannabis consumption establishments would be prohibited in all of Easton's zoning districts under the proposed ordinance.
In November, the council passed a six-month moratorium on businesses looking to produce or sell cannabis within the town limits. The moratorium will expire May 9.
Monday night, Thomas called the limitations and requirements at the state level "the biggest unknown."
"Some of this is being ironed out as we speak with proposals for additional clarification or refinement to the regulations, such as the question of how far we can go to regulate cannabis uses," he said. "Frankly, I'm not sure if they're making it clearer or less clear in some cases."
At a previous council meeting on Feb. 19, Thomas called the proposed town ordinance a "relatively conservative approach," making it clear that the suggested approach was recommended under the belief that further guidance and restrictions may come down from the state.
During the public hearing, resident Greg Zimmerman asked if the Easton Rails-to-Trails was considered a park, as the proposed ordinance does not permit dispensaries within 500 feet of a park.
Town Manager Donald Richardson said Easton's Parks and Recreation Department maintains it as a greenway trail but said it is not listed as a park on the town website.
Town attorney Sharon VanEmburgh said that she would have to look, but thinks Rails-to-Trails is considered a park.
"It falls under park rules under the Parks and Rec Department," she said. "I think we consider it a park for our purposes, whether it's designated as a park or not."
Gunsallus said he thinks Rails-to-Trails is something that should be considered.
"Park or not, if we have a well-trafficked area for kids that walk to school, I think that's something that we should also factor into this zoning process," he said.

title: Council Introduces a New Lakeside Resolution
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Council introduces a new Lakeside resolution

 March 1, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 469
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Faced with a bewildering number of resolutions and amendments on the water and sewer plans for Lakeside at Trappe development, the Talbot County Council introduced a new resolution at its meeting Tuesday, Feb. 27.Resolution 353, which was introduced by council Vice President Pete Lesher and council member Lynn Meilke, "combines Resolutions 338, 347 and 348 into a single resolution," according to County Attorney Patrick Thomas.
The resolution also changes the designation for water and sewer services from W-2/S-2 to W-3/S-3, essentially extending the time that the county would have to introduce future legislation on the project.
Resolutions 338, 347 and 348 are pending pieces of legislation that have been long discussed by county officials in an effort to clarify some aspects of Lakeside and ensure county oversight over the project and its impacts on the county as a whole.
Resolution 338 is meant to amend the county's comprehensive plan to be consistent with the provisions of Lakeside's wastewater discharge permit.
Resolution 347 provides the number of equivalent dwelling units across all six phases of the Lakeside development's construction. A later amendment to 347 incorporates wording from the still-pending 338.
Resolution 348 addresses incorrect water and sewer classifications shown in two exhibits to Resolution 281, the original legislation that approved changes to water and sewer service status and a new wastewater treatment plant for Lakeside.
The resolutions were the subject of a joint work session between the county's Public Works Advisory Board and the county's Planning Commission on Feb. 7, which yielded no decisions.
The boards concluded more discussion on the resolutions was needed before they could offer recommendations or findings of consistency with the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan, which would be necessary before the County Council could take the resolutions up for a vote.
"I directed council to draft (Resolution 353) in response to feedback from the Public Works Advisory Board for perceived flaws in Resolutions 347 and 348 from both their meeting and from the joint workshop between the Public Works Advisory Board and the Planning Commission," Lesher said.
The reclassification of W-2/S-2 portions of Lakeside to W-3/S-3 would allow for an extension to existing or potential construction of a new community, multi-use or shared sanitary facilities to progress within a six- to 10-year period rather than a three- to five-year period.
While this doesn't change the timeline of the construction of Lakeside, Lesher said in an interview that it does allow new legislation to be added prior to any construction, should the country determine it is needed.
Resolution 353 is scheduled for a public hearing on April 9 at 6:30 p.m.
"That will allow us to go to the Planning Commission before coming back for our public hearings," Lesher said.
The resolution will require the Planning Commission's finding of consistency with the county's comprehensive plan prior to the council being able to grant its approval.

title: Easton Considering 'Conservative Approach' to Cannabis Business Regulation
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Easton considering 'conservative approach' to cannabis business regulation

 February 22, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 427
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — During a Monday night public hearing, the Easton Town Council considered a conservative approach to regulating cannabis-related zoning ordinances.The discussed Ordinance Number 809 proposes amendments to revise the Town Code to regulate cannabis-related uses in light of the State of Maryland's approval of various recreational cannabis uses, which took effect July 1.
Town Planner Lynn Thomas presented the revised ordinance to the commission, characterizing it as having a "relatively conservative approach."
The revisions to the regulations are similar to those that are in place for medicinal cannabis. Thomas noted that there have been changes to the language, including changing some of the uses from special exceptions to outright permitted and vice versa.
Thomas made clear that the suggested conservative approach was recommended under the belief that further guidance and restrictions may come down from the state.
"So whatever we come up with, if we go too far, we might have to turn around and revise further or outright repeal," he said.
Following the guidance of the state of Maryland, Thomas stressed that the town must allow dispensary growing facilities and processing facilities in some place within the town. However, there is flexibility concerning the standards that the commission can apply.
Council members raised concerns about the need for parking requirements, odor regulations, hours of operation and other standards in the proposed ordinance. The commission considered adding stronger regulations and enforcement mechanisms for odor from growing facilities.
Council Member Rev. Elmer Neal Davis Jr. voiced his support for the conservative approach to the cannabis ordinance.
"If the state of Maryland wants this, they should give us more concrete direction," Davis said, "so we can be inside on the right side of the ball, not going back to court to defend what we're doing."
Easton's moratorium on cannabis businesses could end earlier than planned if the Town Council can agree on regulations promptly.
The Council passed the six-month moratorium in November for businesses looking to produce or sell cannabis within the town limits.
The moratorium, introduced initially this summer as a nine-month ban on cannabis businesses, pauses applications, approval, construction, expansion, processing or issuance of building permits for businesses that grow, process or sell cannabis within the Easton town limits.
If the Council approves the changes to Ordinance 892 before the moratorium expires May 9, they could consider simultaneously passing an ordinance that would end the moratorium early.
The Council ended the Feb. 19 meeting with a suggestion for proposed printed maps to better understand the areas that would potentially have growing facilities or dispensaries.
They are expected to continue discussion of the matter at their next meeting, March 4.

title: County Council Decisions on Lakeside Resolutions Delayed Further
author: Natalie Jones
content:
County Council decisions on Lakeside resolutions delayed further

 February 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: News 
 
 450
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — As happens every time the Lakeside at Trappe development is on the Talbot County Council agenda, the meeting room was packed Tuesday. They left without a deciding vote, which remains weeks away.Public hearings for all three pieces of legislation — Resolution 338, Resolution 347 and Resolution 348 — and their amendments were held, giving residents a chance to voice support or grievances.
But in spite of some support from the council and community members, no votes were taken as the council awaits recommendations from the Talbot County Planning Commission on two of the resolutions.
Most of the discussion centered on Resolution 338 and its amendment, which the Planning Commission deemed consistent with the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan in December.
The legislation proposes amending the county's comprehensive plan to be consistent with the provisions of Lakeside's wastewater discharge permit. Any expansion to the new plant would require a change to the plan and a certification of consistency from the Planning Commission.
Representatives from the Talbot Preservation Alliance and the Chesapeake Bay Foundation voiced support for the legislation requiring review by the county. An attorney representing the Town of Trappe maintained the town's opposition to it, saying it impedes the town's authority to control growth within its boundaries.
Council member Lynn Mielke, who championed Resolution 338 when it was first introduced nearly a year ago, emphasized that the legislation isn't solely about what Trappe wants or needs; it's about the whole county.
"The problem with Trappe is the infrastructure isn't like the other municipalities in the county," she said. "It's developing as this development is going on and that's a concern, and that's why we need to have a review at every stage."
Resolution 347 and Resolution 348 and their respective amendments drew less discussion, but some objections remained. Neither resolution has received a finding of consistency from the Planning Commission yet.
Resolution 347 provides the number of equivalent dwelling units at Lakeside across all six phases of the development. A second amendment to the resolution, which drew more scrutiny, would add language from the still-pending Resolution 338.
Attorneys for the Town of Trappe and Lakeside's developer expressed continued opposition to the second amendment, citing similar reasons to Resolution 338.
Resolution 348 addresses incorrect water and sewer classifications of parcels shown in two exhibits to Resolution 281, the original legislation that approved changes to water and sewer service status and a new wastewater treatment plant for Lakeside. An amendment clarified the purpose of Resolution 281.
Ryan Showalter, the attorney representing Trappe East Business Holdings Trust, which owns the development, said they did not object to the original resolution or its amendment.
The public record on all three pieces of legislation will remain open until the council meets in March.

title: Oxford Votes on Two Items at Commissioners Meeting
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford votes on two items at Commissioners meeting

 February 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 612
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — At a Commissioners of Oxford meeting Tuesday evening, the Commissioners approved an ordinance that establishes zoning regulations for cannabis businesses as well as an application for FEMA technical assistance.CANNABIS BUSINESSES ZONING ORDINANCE
The Commissioners approved an ordinance on zoning regulations for cannabis businesses that would permit cannabis dispensaries and processing facilities as a special exception in Oxford's general commercial zoning districts (C-2).
The ordinance would also permit growing facilities as a special exception in Oxford's commercial industrial district.
A nine-month cannabis moratorium, which temporarily blocked applications, site plans, permits, construction, processing and approval for businesses looking to manufacture or sell recreational or medicinal cannabis in Oxford, will run its course at the end of month.
Town Attorney Lyndsey Ryan said that Oxford must establish reasonable zoning regulations for cannabis businesses and not be more burdensome than the town's regulations on similar businesses.
Under this ordinance, each applicant will have to come to the Board of Appeals to prove the business meets the criteria of a special exception, which includes the most appropriate use of land building and structure, adequate ingress and egress, and adequate utilities.
FEMA ASSISTANCE
The Commissioners also voted to apply for the FEMA Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities Direct Technical Assistance application.
This program provides a wide range of non-financial support to communities that may not have the resources to begin climate resilience planning.It will deliver up to 36 months of technical assistance for the town.
Identified hazards for Oxford include erosion, flood, hurricane winds, rising sea levels and storm surge.
PUBLIC COMMENT
Transparency was a theme throughout public comment at the town meeting Tuesday. Residents asked questions about the town's stormwater management and how the town receives and uses grant monies.
At the beginning of public comment, resident Deborah Pulzone read a letter addressed to the Commissioners of Oxford and the town's citizens. In her letter, Pulzone said that for 2021 and 2022, there was only one Maryland Public Information Act filed. In contrast, from Jan. 1, 2023 to Jan. 30 of this year, Pulzone said 30 PIAs were filed.
"It is obvious that these PIAs have become weaponized," she said. "It appears they were made for the sole purpose of keeping our town employees preoccupied with busy paperwork, thereby making it extremely difficult to function in a productive and cost-effective manner."
After Pulzone received an applause from some residents for her comments, resident Jan Greenhawk said that although she has never written a PIA, the people who have filed them have done so for a reason.
"We don't have anything against our employees," she said. "In fact, our employees do a great job. But the problem is, when you don't have transparency, and when decisions are made that no one understands or knows about, then people will ask questions. And if they don't think they can get the answers, then they file PIAs."
Greenhawk said it is the right of town residents to ask questions.
While Greenhawk was speaking, a moment of tension between her and Pulzone caused Commission President Tom Costigan to say, "Please keep it civil."
Like Pulzone, Greenhawk also received an applause from some residents for her comments.
LIVING SHORELINE
During the meeting Tuesday, Town Manager Cheryl Lewis said resident Jennifer Stanley will be installing a living shoreline to prevent erosion across the front of her property. Lewis said Stanley is willing to extend the living shoreline to include the end of First Street, which is owned by the town.
Lewis said Stanley knows the end of First Street is used to take out kayaks and other small boats, and so Stanley would incorporate that into the design.
Stanley is asking the commissioners if they would like her to extend the shoreline, Lewis said. This would not be a cost to the town.
