title: Talbot County Council Approves Purchase of Poplar Hill Farm
author: Natalie Jones
content:
Talbot County Council approves purchase of Poplar Hill Farm

 February 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Local News 
 
 520
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — An unsuspecting item on the Talbot County Council's Tuesday evening meeting agenda yielded a significant surprise — the council's unanimous approval for the county to purchase Poplar Hill Farm.Placed on the agenda as a nonspecific request from the county manager to approve a contract of sale to acquire property, the request asked the council to agree to purchase the 120-acre property for $6 million.
The newly approved purchase will take the long-proposed Poplar Hill housing development off the table.
The property is slated for future county use, including preservation of open space in the critical area, according to County Manager Clay Stamp.
The property is bounded to the north by Route 333 (Oxford Road) and to the southeast by Route 322 (Easton Bypass). It's near the Easton Club development, the small Papermill Crossing community and 197 acres owned by the Town of Easton for the Easton Woodland Park.
Council President Chuck Callahan said the council began the process of looking into the opportunity to purchase the property in mid- to late December.
The land was appraised in January, listing with a market value of $6,990,000, Stamp said. Funding for the acquisition will come from the county's fiscal year 2024 capital project enabling legislation, which authorized the county to spend up to $6.1 million on property for county purposes.
Stamp called the council's action to acquire the property "visionary," saying it opens up possibilities to address future needs, including facilities and open space. It also maintains critical areas.
Council Vice President Pete Lesher said the previous County Council had eyed a piece of the property for future county facilities, of which there is a "huge need." The property's acreage and proximity to downtown Easton also made it a key purchase.
"I think that this is a really significant and unique opportunity, and I want to express my gratitude for the sellers for approaching us with this opportunity," he said. "This is a really, really significant deal."
One possibility for the site is future county schools, Lesher said after the meeting.
"This leaves the county in the driver's seat for that kind of decision," he said.
Original plans for the property, currently owned by 5001 SHR L.C., were a source of concern for Talbot County residents last year when a developer proposed turning the parcel into a mixed-use development with 456 residential units.
Most concerns stemmed from the developer's request for a critical area growth allocation to reclassify just over half of the property from a resource conservation area to an intensely developed area due to its location within the town's critical area.
The application for the 456-unit development was rescinded last August. A sketch plan for a smaller 119-unit subdivision in the same location was conditionally approved by the Easton Planning Commission in September.
Callahan said the opportunity to purchase the property was a decision the county would be proud of for years to come.
"It's phenomenal," he said. "It's something that we're all going to be proud of, and I'm glad this council chose to do that, that's for sure."
This story may be updated as information becomes available.

title: A Long Way to Go: No Decisions Made on Pending Lakeside Legislation
author: Natalie Jones
content:
A long way to go: No decisions made on pending Lakeside legislation

 February 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Local News 
 
 1211
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Although the Talbot County Planning Commission and Public Works Advisory Board have yet to make final decisions on the pending Lakeside resolutions, a joint work session Wednesday showed that uncertainty still remains.Both bodies stressed that the work session would not yield any final or binding decisions — it served only as an opportunity to work out lingering issues with Resolution 347 and Resolution 348 prior to separate recommendations from each board in future meetings.
But from the cross-table conversation in the Bradley Meeting Room, it was clear that more discussion remains before the boards can make a recommendation or finding on consistency with the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan.
While the lack of action won't impede the Talbot County Council's planned public hearings on the legislation and its amendments at its Tuesday, Feb. 13, meeting, it will delay the council's consideration and vote.
The delay further extends the nearly yearlong process of answering the Maryland Department of the Environment's requests for clarification on some specifics of the Lakeside at Trappe development.
RESOLUTION 347Resolution 347 provides the number of equivalent dwelling units at Lakeside. Across all six phases of the development, 2,874 equivalent dwelling units are planned, with just over 1,200 designated for immediate water and sewer service.
In October, the Public Works Advisory Board voted against recommending the adoption of Resolution 347. The board declined to reconsider that decision in December.
But at a January meeting, the board was asked if they would be in support of the second amendment to Resolution 347.
The amendment would add language from the still-pending Resolution 338, which proposes amending the county's comprehensive plan to be consistent with the provisions of Lakeside's wastewater discharge permit.
Expansion of the development's new wastewater treatment plant would require a change to the county's comprehensive plan.
Public Works Advisory Board Chairman Tom Lane referenced the board's previous recommendation that the council adopt Resolution 338, saying if the language from that resolution was incorporated into Resolution 347, it would give the county a chance to review the new wastewater treatment plant.
"It's a great chance to take a breath," he said. "...Knowing that going ahead, we can start working with what this is going to be, and really looking at the impacts and everything so we won't have a big problem five years from now … so it just seemed like a logical thing."
But to Brian Schmidt, the acting president of the Trappe Town Council, Resolution 338 and Resolution 347 should stand on their own, separately. And in his view, MDE's requests to the county were just addressing clerical errors, he said.
"Honestly, I don't understand how 347 has quite gotten to where it is," he said.
Lyndsey Ryan, Trappe's town attorney, emphasized the town's position against both Resolution 338 and the amendment to Resolution 347, saying they treated Trappe differently than any other community.
"The Town of Easton has had 1,700 residential units developed since 2002 without a comprehensive water and sewer plan amendment and could have another 2,500 without a comprehensive water and sewer plan amendment," she said. "But you're telling Trappe to come back at every 400 to review those things that Easton would have the same impact on?"
Planning Commission member William Boicourt agreed that verbiage in regard to the county reviewing the development was in the wrong resolution, but still stressed its importance.
"I think that the ability to bring it to the county to review at the various phases of the MDE permit at 100,000 gallons is so important; if that's the only place we can get it, I'll take it," he said. "But I agree, there's an apples to oranges aspect."
Ryan said the lengthy process with approving the resolutions was a part of Trappe's concerns.
The town provided information on the number of equivalent dwelling units in the development, along with the maps attached to Resolution 281 — the original legislation approving a wastewater treatment plant for the Lakeside development — to the county last July, and the legislation still isn't approved, she said.
Countering her, Planning Commission Vice Chair Chip Councell said confusion still remains with the southern portion of Lakeside's property, which has made the process longer. And the Commission needs to be sure of its decision, he said.
"Once the Planning Commission finds it consistent and the county council adopts it, there's no turning back," he said. "So, I think that's where we are."
To Ryan, the town not being required to come back at every 100,000-gallon expansion would be enough for the town to be on the same page as the county, considering MDE's review of the discharge permit and authority.
RESOLUTION 348The initially introduced version of Resolution 348 addresses incorrect water and sewer classifications of parcels shown in two exhibits to Resolution 281.
In early January, the Public Works Advisory Board voted against making a recommendation to the County Council to adopt Resolution 348, though it did say it would consider a revised version correctly explaining the differences in the property classifications from Resolution 281 to Resolution 348.
The Planning Commission has yet to make a finding on Resolution 348 or its amendment.
Most of the concerns with Resolution 348 stemmed from confusion with Resolution 281 regarding the classification of the southern portion of Lakeside's property.
To clarify that, the recently introduced amendment to Resolution 348 explicitly states that Resolution 281's "clear and unambiguous" purpose was to reclassify the northern parcels of Lakeside as immediate priority, while the southern portion would be S-2 and W-2 — priority for service in the next several years.
More specifically, the amendment clarified that prior to adoption of Resolution 281, the comprehensive plan depicted a portion of Lakeside's property as immediate priority for water service, with the remainder designated as unprogrammed.
However, Resolution 281 actually stated that some parcels within that portion were being redesignated from their "current" classification of W-2 to W-1, or immediate priority for water service.
And according to the amendment, prior to Resolution 281's approval, maps of sewer service areas in Trappe showed Lakeside's parcels as unprogrammed.
At Wednesday's work session, County Engineer Ray Clarke confirmed that prior to the resolution's adoption, Lakeside's parcels were unprogrammed for sewer.
Ryan did not dispute Trappe's existing land use map as showing the parcels as unprogrammed, but she said it was "clear" that Resolution 281's intent and purpose were to designate the northern part of the development as S-1, immediate priority for sewer service, and the lower portion as S-2.
Public Works Advisory Board member Cory Buxton maintained that ambiguity remained in Resolution 281's language.
"I think an argument can be made that it remains unprogrammed to this day," he said.
Boicourt said he had a tough time being comfortable with the amendment's assertion on the "clear and unambiguous" purpose of Resolution 281.
The text of the resolution overrode the maps, according to the county's legal team.
Planning Commission member Paul Spies said the commission had never been presented with the option to leave the southern portion of Lakeside as unprogrammed — a statement Ryan countered strongly.
"You could have decided (the map) wasn't consistent, you could have declined it, you could have changed the bottom portion," she said.
Public Works Advisory Board member Ed Sclichter noted the extensive amount of time both boards had spent hashing out the Lakeside resolutions.
"It gets more confusing all the time," he said. "The amount of time — it's extraordinary what we've done for this whole program."

title: Easton Town Council Approves Changes to Zoning Code
author: Natalie Jones
content:
Easton Town Council approves changes to zoning code

 February 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Local News 
 
 425
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Easton Town Council voted Monday to approve an ordinance making several changes to the town's zoning code.Although Town Planner Lynn Thomas characterized a majority of the amendments as "housekeeping" at a public hearing last November, one particularly notable change concerning middle housing types was ultimately removed from the approved version of the ordinance.
The final ordinance removed a previously proposed amendment, which would have changed some missing middle housing types from permitted via special exception to outright permitted uses in two residential districts, the R-7A and R-10A districts.
Middle housing units are multi-unit or clustered types of housing that bridge the gap between single-family homes and garden apartment building complexes, according to the existing code.
Duplexes, triplexes, fourplexes and townhouses, among others, are defined as middle housing in the town.
The decision to remove that amendment came after a number of comments in November and a workshop with the town's planning commission in January.
Residents who commented in the fall expressed worries about increasing density and keeping the historic nature of the area intact.
At the Jan. 16 workshop, planning commission members requested the change to use classification for middle housing types be removed to allow for the development of a more comprehensive proposal for addressing a range of housing issues, including missing middle housing types.
Considerations that remain to be addressed include infrastructure needs and ways to work with developers to build more diverse housing, in terms of size and price points, according to Jennifer Dindinger, the chair of Easton's planning commission.
Though most middle housing types are only permitted by special exception in the two residential districts, cottage courts are already allowed by right in the R-7A district. Duplexes, either side by side or stacked, are allowed in both districts.
Contentions were also raised in November about the ordinance changing how quickly planned unit developments must begin construction after final approval, raising the time limit from two years to three years.
Extensions on PUD approval can be granted by the planning commission if requested at least 60 days prior to the PUD's expiration date.
Expired PUDs could also be considered for reinstatement by the planning commission with further documentation and analysis, and reinstated developments will expire two years after the approval of the reinstatement.
At Monday's meeting, council members asked for clarification on the reason to increase the time.
Further developing and receiving approval for engineering plans, along with lining up financing, can make the progress of a planned unit development take close to, if not more than, three years, Thomas said.
The final approved ordinance did raise the limit to three years.

title: San Domingo Park Project Plans Move to Board of Zoning Appeals
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
San Domingo Park project plans move to Board of Zoning Appeals

 February 2, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 513
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — The Town of St. Michaels Planning Commission has found that plans for San Domingo Creek Park are consistent with the town's comprehensive plan.At a meeting Thursday, the Planning Commission voted unanimously on this.
The 7.6 acre property at 201 Boundary Lane was purchased for $2.9 million by the town last year.
The town plans to use the existing building on the property for a new town office. The remainder of the property will be a public park, complete with nature trails, expanded wetlands, a living shoreline, a fishing pier, a comfort station and associated parking.
In late January, the Commissioners of St. Michaels voted to approve a final master plan for the park, as well as a $1.7 million open space grant application to help fund the project.
With the Planning Commission's vote Thursday, the Board of Zoning Appeals will now be able to vote on a request made by the Commissioners of St. Michaels to allow town administration offices and parks and recreation facilities on the property as a special exception.
At the meeting, Town Planner Steve Ball said that in order for this request to go to the Board of Zoning Appeals, the Planning Commission needed to determine that the proposed plans for the property are consistent with the town's comprehensive plan.
Ball gave a brief overview of his findings in reviewing the town's current comprehensive pan.
He said that although there is nothing in the comprehensive plan that specifically addresses the Boundary Lane site — as the project wasn't anticipated when the comprehensive plan was last updated — there were four chapters within the comprehensive plan that he believes prove the project is consistent with the comprehensive plan.
Specifically, Ball pointed to the chapters on municipal growth, environmental resources, climate resistance and parks and recreation.
He said the project is consistent with municipal growth because a part of the property will be annexed into the town.
When it comes to environmental resources in the town, Ball said the park will provide buffers, create stormwater filtration and protect and enhance wetland areas. For climate resistance, he said the park will have a living shoreline to help with sea level rise.
With parks and recreation, Ball said the master plan for the park will give residents the opportunity to enjoy the natural environment. He said the park will enhance the existing town park facilities.
"It also allows for the town's trail system to be expanded for the community," he said.
After Ball presented his findings, Planning Commission Chair Christopher Thomas said he wanted to make it clear that the Planning Commission wasn't voting on the specifics of the master plan, but on whether the project plans, overall, are consistent with the town's comprehensive plan.
"I think that's important to note," he said.
Before making the motion to acknowledge the project plans are consistent with the comprehensive plan, Planning Commission Vice Chair John Novak said he didn't see any contradictions, adding that the project makes economic sense for the town too.
"Using an existing building instead of building an entire new town office for $2 million plus, I think it makes economic sense," he said.

title: Second amendment introduced for Lakeside unit resolution
author: Natalie Jones
content:
Second amendment introduced for Lakeside unit resolution

 January 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Environment 
 
 764
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A second amendment to previously introduced legislation relating to the number of equivalent dwelling units in each phase of development at Lakeside at Trappe was introduced Tuesday by two Talbot County Council members.The amendment, requested by council Vice President Pete Lesher and introduced by him and council member Lynn Mielke, would modify the still-pending Resolution 347 to incorporate provisions of separate, but related, Lakeside legislation — Resolution 338 and its amendment — into its language.
The original version of Resolution 347, first introduced last September, would amend the county's comprehensive plan to include the number of equivalent dwelling units for each phase of development at Lakeside, though the numbers for Phases 2 through 6 are estimated.
It also provides the current water and sewer classifications for each phase. A total of 2,874 equivalent dwelling units are planned at Lakeside.
The language to be incorporated from Resolution 338 proposes amending the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan to be consistent with the Maryland Department of the Environment's discharge permit for Lakeside's wastewater treatment plant.
The permit, issued in October 2022, is limited to the project's first phase and allows for an annual average flow of 100,000 gallons per day, or roughly 250 gallons per day per equivalent dwelling unit, only allowing for roughly 400 residential units to be built.
A major permit modification approved by the Maryland Department of the Environment is required for any future expansion of the wastewater treatment plant.
Resolution 338's provisions also would mandate any future expansion of the new plant to require a comprehensive water and sewer plan amendment.
The resolution's amendment, introduced in November, adds language requiring a certification from the Talbot County Planning Commission of the amendment's consistency with the county's comprehensive plan.
At Tuesday's council meeting, Lesher emphasized that none of the language proposed to be added to Resolution 347 via its second amendment is new. It's a different way to help the county's Planning Commission come to a finding of consistency, he said.
Resolution 347, though considered in a multi-hour Planning Commission meeting last October, has yet to receive any final determination of consistency, which is required when amending the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan.
Multiple postponements of discussion on the legislation have lengthened the process, though the amended language of Resolution 338 was found consistent by the Planning Commission in December.
"This simply gives an alternative for the Planning Commission to say, 'Yes, with this language, if you combine it, we can find this consistent,'" Lesher said. "They may find Resolution 347 consistent without this amendment, they may find it consistent both without and with this amendment. If we get those alternatives, we then have that option to act at the council level."
The need for Resolution 347 stems from a request from the Maryland Department of the Environment last spring.
The agency asked the county to submit updated phase information and figures for water and sewer services with corrected classifications for all parcels within Trappe, including Lakeside, in a comprehensive water and sewer plan amendment.
Related legislation, Resolution 348, addresses the incorrect water and sewer classifications of parcels shown in two exhibits to Resolution 281, the original legislation approving a wastewater treatment plant for Lakeside under a draft discharge permit.
"Without that finding of consistency though, this resolution doesn't reach our desk," Lesher added, "and we don't have that way of bringing closure to the outstanding issues from MDE that will allow us to finish that Report of the Review."
Council Member Keasha Haythe questioned the need to add language from Resolution 338 into Resolution 347, saying the addition seemed to be the opposite of what the Maryland Department of the Environment requested.
The Town of Trappe is not on the same page as the county regarding the resolutions, she pointed out. Later, Haythe confirmed that the initial resolutions proposed were in line with what the agency wanted from the county.
The county's Planning Commission and the Public Works Advisory Board are set to discuss the two pending resolutions and amendments in a joint meeting on Wednesday, Feb. 7, at 11 a.m.
A public hearing on all three Lakeside resolutions and amendments will be held at 6:30 p.m. at the Tuesday, Feb. 13, County Council meeting.
Following Tuesday's meeting, council President Chuck Callahan issued a statement on the pending legislation.
"We understand that the resolutions regarding the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan and the Town of Trappe can be difficult to follow. It is a complicated matter with a lengthy history," he said in the statement. title: Oxford Introduces Ordinance to Establish Cannabis Business Regulations
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford introduces ordinance to establish cannabis business regulations

 January 25, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 486
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — With a nine-month cannabis moratorium set to end in Oxford at the end of February, the Commissioners of Oxford introduced an ordinance that would establish regulations for cannabis businesses at a town meeting on Tuesday.A resolution establishing the moratorium — which temporarily blocked applications, site plans, permits, construction, processing and approval for businesses looking to manufacture or sell recreational or medicinal cannabis in Oxford — was passed May 9, two months before adult use of recreational cannabis was legalized in Maryland.
The ordinance that commissioners introduced at the town meeting on Tuesday would amend the Oxford Zoning Ordinance.
Specifically, the proposed ordinance would permit cannabis dispensaries and processing facilities as a special exception in Oxford's general commercial zoning districts (C-2).
Town Attorney Lyndsey Ryan said that general commercial zoning districts already include greenhouses and retail as special exception uses, so dispensaries and processing facilities are consistent with those uses.
The ordinance would also permit growing facilities as a special exception in Oxford's commercial industrial district. Ryan said this zoning district includes other uses for growing crops.
It also includes the provision that "a particular use may not create excessive noise, smoke, odor and glare." An applicant has to prove this when they to get the special exception with the Board of Appeals."
The proposed ordinance would not allow for on-site consumption of cannabis, like smoke lounges. Ryan said that penalties would be applicable to a property owner if they were to operate an on-site consumption business.
The Oxford Planning Commission recommended the Commissioners of Oxford introduce and adopt the ordinance.
Ryan said that she and Oxford's former Town Planner Maria Brophy had worked with the Planning Commission to draft the ordinance. They based the ordinance on applicable regulations in the Maryland Alcoholic Beverages article in the Code of Maryland Regulations.
A public hearing on the proposed ordinance is set for the beginning of the next Commissioners of Oxford meeting on Feb. 13.
Before voting to introduce the ordinance, Commission President Tom Costigan asked where Oxford was in comparison to other nearby towns regarding cannabis moratoriums.
Ryan said many local municipalities had issued a year-long moratorium. She said she believed Oxford was the only municipality to be drafting an ordinance on cannabis businesses at the moment.
Commissioner Katrina Greer asked if Ryan had heard anything about locations for dispensaries, micro-processing facilities and processing facilities in the county.
Ryan said she hadn't heard anything yet. She said licenses are supposed to roll out in the next few months.
According to the Maryland Cannabis Administration, there are two standard dispensary licenses available in Talbot County.
There are also four standard growers, six micro-growers, eight standard processors and six micro-processors licenses available in the Eastern Region of the state, which includes Caroline, Dorchester, Kent, Queen Anne's, Somerset, Talbot, Wicomico and Worcester counties.
According to a breakdown of business license applications submitted to the Maryland Cannabis Administration, there were 25 applications submitted in Talbot County for standard dispensaries.
Reporter Natalie Jones Contributed to this article.

title: Talbot County Seeking Housing Coordinator to Create Workforce Housing Program
author: Natalie Jones
content:
Talbot County seeking housing coordinator to create workforce housing program

 January 24, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Local News 
 
 670
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — In an effort to address housing needs in the community, Talbot County is seeking a housing coordinator within the county's planning and zoning department.The housing coordinator, who would report to the county's assistant planning officer, would be responsible for creating a critical workforce housing program for individuals seeking safe and affordable housing, according to the job description.
The county-funded role is not a new one. It was a full-time position prior to 2020, with the job focusing on providing technical and administrative assistance to the county related to development and implementation of housing initiatives, said Bryce Yelton, the county's assistant planning officer.
Previous responsibilities included assisting county residents with access to applicable housing services and grant opportunities, along with preparing grant applications, reports and coordinating with federal, state and local housing programs and commissions, Yelton said.
Former housing coordinators also assisted the public with housing program applications as needed.
The role was filled "briefly" in 2020 in a part-time capacity, Yelton said. That year, the county saw widespread housing insecurity due to the COVID-19 pandemic.
But after a period of vacancy in 2020 and 2021, the housing coordinator role was removed and restructured into other positions within the county's department of planning and zoning.
A "pressing need" for housing still exists within Talbot County today, Yelton said, though its effects are not as severe as they were during the pandemic.
Efforts to alleviate housing needs in the county aren't only falling on the planning and zoning department — Talbot County Council Member Keasha Haythe has played a significant part in revitalizing the position into a full-time role.
Haythe, who's just over a year into her first term on the council, advocated for the need for the position to fellow council members at the start of last year's budget cycle.
Having worked with housing coordinators in her previous economic development roles, Haythe was familiar with the job's functions and responsibilities, and she drafted the job description for Talbot County's position.
The role was approved as a full-time position in the county's fiscal year 2024 budget cycle.
While Haythe's career experience aided in her knowledge of the need for the role in the county, prioritizing the search for a housing coordinator also comes from a personal place.
When she was looking into buying her first house in Talbot County 15 years ago, Haythe took advantage of the services offered by a previous county housing coordinator.
Haythe was able to purchase her first home with the help of the United States Department of Agriculture's direct home loan program, which provides a path to homeownership for low-income families in eligible rural areas, including Talbot County.
"Having used those resources before I purchased my home, when I was running for county council, that was the one thing that I said that I wanted to make a priority … to have that housing coordinator position come back, and expand it a little bit to stand up some type of housing program, not only for the purchase of a home, but some type of program that helps with rentals as well," she said.
The lack of affordable housing is affecting all demographics in the county, Haythe said, from younger residents looking to purchase their first home to older individuals on fixed incomes looking for affordable homes to rent.
But for residents in need, ensuring resources like the USDA program are communicated is another key step in addressing housing issues, she said.
Haythe's ultimate goal is for the county to eventually enter a public-private partnership to help with affordable housing and ensure that housing isn't more than 30% of a person's income — a solution she called the "real" and "true" way to achieve affordable housing.
"Home ownership may not be a fit for everyone," Haythe said. "However, if that is the American dream, if that is your dream, we want to make sure that, specifically for Talbot County, that we put tools and resources in place to get people to their dreams of homeownership."
The county is still seeking applicants for the position. The full job description can be found online at talbotcountymd.gov/job_openings.

title: St. Michaels Commissioners Choose Boundary Lane Park Master Plan
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
St. Michaels Commissioners choose Boundary Lane park master plan

 January 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 711
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — With time ticking to submit a grant application to the state, the Commissioners of St. Michaels concluded a nearly three-hour meeting Wednesday with a vote to move forward with a master plan for a new park on Boundary Lane.The master plan for the park that town staff recommend be named San Domingo Creek Park — as the 7.6-acre property is adjacent to the creek — includes nature trails, expanded wetlands, a living shoreline, a fishing pier, a comfort station and a pollinator meadow.
The property was purchased by the town in September for $2.9 million. Formerly owned by nonprofit Environmental Concern, the property has an existing administrative building, which the town plans to use for a new town office.
At the meeting, Town Planner Steve Ball told commissioners that the town intends to submit a grant application to the state for Program Open Space funds in order to offset the cost of the park.
With the grant application due Feb. 10, he said the commissioners would need to decide if any changes need to be made to the master plan at the Jan. 11 meeting so the plan can be brought back for final adoption at the Jan. 24 meeting and then submitted to the state.
After Ball spoke, Scott Scarfone, an associate principal at Mahan Rykiel Associates, gave a presentation on two master plan options.
Following the presentation, commissioners discussed aspects of both plans and whether certain parts should be included. They considered the possibilities of including a dog park and a viewing mound as well as different parking options.
Commissioner Tad DuPont said the town has spent a large chunk of its savings to purchase the land and that the town should maximize the amount of open space in the plan to get as much grant money as possible.
"It's my feeling that the town has this one shot to maximize as much open space, unencumbered as possible, to be able to be able to get the most money we can from Program Open Space to cover our costs," he said, causing residents at the meeting to applaud.
Program Open Space is a state program under the Department of Natural Resources that administers funding for open and recreational space in local communities.
DuPont said he didn't think the dog park was appropriate on the land and didn't like the viewing mound — a 10-foot hill with an ADA-accessible path that visitors could walk up to get a view of the creek from above.
The inclusion of a dog park has been a point of contention when it comes to proposed plans for the park.
In February, town commissioners passed a resolution supporting a dog park location within the town, though no location was specified.
At a joint meeting in December between the St. Michaels Planning Commission and the town's Parks and Recreation Advisory Board, Ball said the inclusion of a dog park would not be consistent with the open space funding program.
DuPont also voiced his concerns with the plans for a parking lot off Boundary Lane. He said that 12 parking spaces outside the town office building would be enough — eight spots for employees, two spots for visitors and two handicap spots.
During public comment, resident Langley Shook said if there is no dog park on the property, there is no need for more parking. He said adding more parking could affect how much funding the town gets from the state.
"All the parking would do would be to draw people who would have to drive at a distance," he said. "Which I think you generally don't want."
Shook made a suggestion to not include the additional parking lot to the plan, and if there is a need for more parking down the line, it can be added to the park later on.
Commission President David Breimhurst said not everyone who uses the park is going to be able-bodied.
"We'll have senior citizens and others who are not going to enjoy (the walk to get to the park)," he said. "They're going to want to be able to park, maybe walk to one of the pavilions and sit and enjoy the view."
Ultimately, the commissioners voted to not include the dog park or viewing mound in the master plan.
The master plan they voted on does include the parking lot off Boundary Lane.

title: Easton Approves Supplemental Growth Allocation at Commerce Park
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
Easton approves supplemental growth allocation at commerce park

 January 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 344
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - The Easton Town Council approved a supplemental growth allocation Tuesday to reclassify just over eight acres of land within the county's critical area on a lot at Talbot Commerce Park.The council granting the supplemental growth allocation is a step in redesignating the lot from a resource conservation area to an intensely developed area - a change in classification for land within the state's critical area, or land within 1,000 feet of tidal waters and tidal wetlands.
However, it is not approval for future development site plans.
Additional reviews will be done by the planning commission and town staff.
Applicant Thomas R. Cohee first requested the growth allocation for the two lots off of Mary's Court in 2020. The lots are zoned agricultural and business commercial, and office buildings already exist on one of the lots.
Several other developments, though residential, have gone through the supplemental growth allocation process since the state's critical area law was passed in 1984, including Easton Club, Cooke's Hope, Easton Village and Londonderry, said Town Attorney Sharon Van Emburgh.
After the critical area law passed, local jurisdictions, including Talbot County, established critical area programs.
The county provided a portion of its growth allocation to Easton, but the town has already used all of its 155 acres originally allotted, meaning that any new growth allocation must come from Talbot County.
Cohee's request was reviewed by both the town and county planning commissions.
Proposed development for the commerce park lots includes an addition to the existing office building, several new office buildings, a mixed use office and warehouse building and stormwater management infrastructure.
Although the property's stream buffer, non-tidal wetlands and wetland buffers are being designated as intensely developed areas with the allocation, no development activity will occur in those areas, said Ryan Showalter, an attorney representing Cohee.
The project received a favorable recommendation from the town's planning commission, though its conditions included rezoning the critical area lot to a zoning district permitting the proposed uses.

title: Doverbrook Apartments Redevelopment Project Begins
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Doverbrook Apartments redevelopment project begins

 December 21, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: A3 | Section: News 
 
 641
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - Work is underway at the Dover brook Apartments, located off Dover Street in Easton.Last week, the apartment complex officially closed its doors to residents for the redevelopment project to begin. When complete, the property's seven buildings will be torn down and replaced with five new buildings.
Although there will be two fewer buildings when complete, there will be an increase in 14 units, bringing the total to 64 units, confirmed Don Bibb, director of the Talbot Housing Commission.
"We're beginning the remediation," he said about where they are in the project.
"Probably in January they'll start tearing buildings down." Rather than a public housing program, the new units will be a part of a housing choice voucher program known as Section 8 housing.
"Both programs are structured such that a program participant pays no more than 30% of their adjusted household income toward the rent," Bibb said about the public housing and voucher programs.
Along with new, energy-efficient units, the redevelopment project will create a playground in the center of the community. Bibb said he believes the basketball court that is already on the property will stay there.
The Easton Housing Authority building located on the property will receive a facelift to create a better space for the community as well as new office space. An addition of 1,000 square feet will be constructed on the back of the building.
Bibb said that it was time for these renovations.
"I mean, this property's close to 51, 52 years old," he said. "It's been fairly well maintained, but it's outlived it's lifetime. So it's time to give something back to the community and the residents." The project, which will take about 14 months (barring any delays, Bibb said), is estimated to cost close to $25 million. Bibb said somewhere around $24 million has been raised so far.
Last year, the Easton Town Council and Talbot County Council each voted to award the project $250,000 - totaling $500,000.
Last Wednesday, Gov. Wes Moore announced $63.7 million in awards through Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development programs, including $400,000 to the Dover brook Apartments project through the department's Community Legacy program.
"To win the decade, we must be intentional about building sustainable, vibrant communities that lift all Marylanders," Moore said in a news release. "These investments will support local and county leaders in their vital work to drive economic growth and create stronger pathways to prosperity in all parts of the state.
Together, we will continue to revitalize our communities and reveal Maryland's full potential." Bibb said the award from the state was great.
"We had that small gap (between cost and money raised), and that's why we applied to the state for that legacy," he said.
Since work on the apartments began last week, some residents have been moved to Housing-Commission-owned properties in St.
Michaels. Bibb said a few of the units in St. Michaels are still being worked on, and so some Doverbrook residents are being put up in a hotel until those renovations are finished.
The Housing Commission of Talbot hired a relocation specialty company to help find Doverbrook's residents relocation units. Bibb said that those who didn't get relocated to the Housing Commission's properties in St. Michaels were given vouchers for other properties.
"It's been tough with the relocation because the rental market is so tight," he said.
"But we did get everyone relocated." Those living at the apartments before renovations will have first right of refusal to come back.
Adding 14 more affordable housing units in Easton is significant, Bibb said.
"There's always a high demand for affordable housing," he said. "Nationwide, it's a problem I mean we could build another 200 (units), and it still wouldn't meet the need."

title: Easton to Take Next Steps in Approving New Apartments - Town Council Reaches Consensus to Move Forward with More Units for Elliott Road Complex
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
Easton to take next steps in approving new apartments - Town Council reaches consensus to move forward with more units for Elliott Road complex

 December 20, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 535
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - The Easton Town Council reached a consensus to move forward with drafting an ordinance to approve a planned unit development amendment, which would add 16 units to an already-approved 120-unit apartment complex on Elliott Road.The apartment complex, first approved as a planned unit development by the council in March 2022, is now proposed to have 136 units in two four-story buildings and two three story buildings - a change from the original plan of four three-story buildings.
Parking requirements under the town's planned unit development overlay district were revised, which spurred the change in the proposal, said Brendan Mullaney, an attorney representing Mallard Construction Group Inc. and Elliott Road LLC, the project's developers.
Under current regulations, a minimum of one parking space per unit is required. The apartment complex is proposed to have 178 parking spaces, more than what's needed.
Though no additional changes are being made to the number of parking spaces, the developer was able to increase the number of units due to the revised regulations, Mullaney said.
Each three-story building is set to include 12 one-bedroom units, 12 two-bedroom units and six three-bedroom units. The four-story buildings will contain 16 one-bedroom units, 16 two-bedroom units and six three-bedroom units.
The new proposal eliminates a pool and adds a dog run and a pickleball court, Mullaney said.
Twenty-eight of the units will be designated as affordable. Those units will be identical to other units in the complex, said Victoria Hoffman of Mallard Construction Group.
Prices for all of the units available for rent have not been finalized, but rent for one-bedroom apartments in other Mallard Construction Group developments fall between $1,250 and $1,450 depending on their location, Hoffman said.
As for traffic, Mullaney said the impact of the 16 additional units would be "negligible" on traffic on Matthewstown Road and intersections in the area. A traffic study indicated a minor impact with the additional units.
Residents have previously raised concerns about extensive traffic congestion along Matthewstown Road. The State Highway Administration is currently studying a 1.6-mile corridor of the road. The study is expected to be completed by next spring.
Ward 2 Councilman Don Abbatiello, who drives down Matthewstown Road every day to go to work, disagreed on the impact being minor, saying he wasn't thrilled about the increase in traffic, but acknowledged the need for the project in town.
"But when we look at the fact that this is an apartment complex that is going to provide somewhat affordable housing for people in town it's worth the increase to provide some affordable, attainable housing in town for professionals," he said.
Ward 4 Councilman Rev. Elmer Davis Jr. agreed.
"I've never seen a traffic study give insight and foresight on the reality of sitting there for 10 to 15 minutes in my perception, but I'm like council member Don Abbatiello - I think it's worth the sacrifice involved to at least have an opportunity for individuals that work in the Town of Easton to live in the Town of Easton, and this is an opportunity for that," he said.
At the council's direction, the town attorney will draft an ordinance for approval at a future meeting.

title: Amended Lakeside Resolution Found Consistent with Comprehensive Plan
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
Amended Lakeside resolution found consistent with comprehensive plan

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News

 EASTON - The Talbot County Planning Commission on Wednesday found an amended version of a resolution, which would ensure some county oversight in future expansion of the Lakeside at Trappe wastewater treatment plant, to be consistent with the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan.The unanimous finding of consistency comes after several months of discussion on the legislation.If passed by the Talbot County Council, Resolution 338 would amend the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan to be consistent with the Maryland Department of the Environment's discharge permit for a wastewater treatment plant serving the Lakeside at Trappe development.The discharge permit at the center of the legislation was issued in October 2022. It's limited to the first phase of the project and allows for an initial annual average flow of 100,000 gallons per day, or 250 gallons perday per equivalent dwelling unit.A major permit modification approved by MDE is required for future expansion of the wastewater treatment plant.The resolution, which was introduced by County Council member Lynn Mielke in February, would also mandate future expansion of the new plant to require a comprehensive water and sewer plan amendment.In October, the resolution was found inconsistent with the comprehensive plan due to a map needing to be reviewed, though planning commission members endorsed the legislation's basic principles.That endorsement led to a chance for reconsideration of the finding in November and into December.The amendment to the resolution considered Tuesday by the planning commission was introduced by Mielke and Council Vice President Pete Lesher on Nov. 28. It adds language requiring a certification from the Talbot County Planning Commission of an expansion amendment's consistency with the comprehensive plan.To Chip Councell, chairman of the planning commission, the amended resolution would be the county's only chance for a review of potential expansion.Councell said it would be "irresponsible" of the county to not look at social factors, including hospitals and schools, when reviewing future expansion, especially considering changes from just the last three years."The world is different, and we don't know what it's going to look like in eight to 10 years, and I just don't see how we can write a blank check," he said. "I trust the Town of Trappe when it comes to their development and what it does. I don't think it's reasonable to put that burden of these other services on all the citizens of Talbot County." The planning commission was also set to consider Resolution 347 and its amendment, along with Resolution 348 - legislation related to Lakeside - on Tuesday, but the five-member board unanimously voted to postpone discussion until they receive a recommendation from the county's Public Works Advisory Board.The two resolutions, introduced in September, address updated information on equivalent dwelling units for all phases of the Lakeside development, along with clarifying Trappe's water and sewer service maps.The Public Works Advisory Board's next meeting is set for Thursday, Dec. 21.No agenda has been made available yet.

 EASTON - The Easton Town Council is considering amendments and updates to two chapters of the town code concerning zoning and subdivisions.The two ordinances, which separately amend several aspects of the town's zoning code and update its existing subdivision code, were up for public hearings at the council's Monday, Nov. 6, meeting, where a number of town residents opposed some changes.Ordinance 803, which concerns changes to zoning code, drew a number of questions and prompted the council to continue its public hearing to the first meeting in January.The public hearing on Ordinance 804, which would update the town's subdivision code, will be continued at the council's Monday, Nov. 20, meeting.ORDINANCE 803: ZONINGThe town approved and adopted a comprehensive revision of its zoning code in December 2021, but after evaluation and monitoring of the code, the planning commission determined that certain amendments were appropriate to better guide and regulate development activities, according to the text of the ordinance.In response to the evaluation, the planning commission proposed 12 amendments to the zoning code, which were recommended for adoption in March. If passed, Ordinance 803 would enact the amendments.At the Nov. 6 meeting, Town Planner Lynn Thomas characterized a majority of the amendments as "housekeeping." But she noted two more important aspects: changing the ways in which middle housing types are created and changing five of those subtypes from a special exception use to a permitted use in three Easton districts: R-7A, R-10A and central business.Lynn Mielke, a Talbot County Council member who spoke at the meeting only as a resident of the Easton Club neighborhood, raised concerns about the "inadequate" amount of time residents had to read through the 250-page agenda packet and research before attending the meeting to make a comment.Mielke also objected to a revision of the language detailing how quickly planned unit developments must begin construction after final approval and language extending the expiration dates of those projects.The proposed revision extends the length of time owners or developers have to begin construction on a project from two years to three years after final approval. If no action is taken within three years, the site's zoning will revert to its previous classification.Mielke pointed to the proposed Maryland Health Club project within the Easton Club neighborhood as an example, asserting that residents have been "living in limbo and uncertainty" about the development's status.Easton Club resident Pamela Reynolds voiced concern with several housing types currently classified as special exception uses being permitted by right in the R-10A district - a residential area."I find most of them charming names, but they can have a considerable impact on the density (of the) development," she said.Reynolds also questioned if the recently approved and scaled-back neighboring Poplar Hill development could increase its density under the amendment and if the Maryland Health Club's PUD application would be impacted.Speaking on behalf of the East-End Neighborhood Association, president Joseph Minarick expressed worries about trash removal the number of additional cars on the streets if middle housing structures were added in the neighborhood, The association recommended and requested that no change be made to the special exception requirements for all middle housing structures in the three districts in question.Kelly Pezor, who serves on the town's historic district commission, said she and other commissioners were concerned about preserving the area's historic nature and keeping new developments within guidelines.In an Oct. 30 letter to the town council and mayor, the planning commission expressed support for limiting special exceptions to address the town's need for more affordable and diverse housing types. Commissioners also supported revising the expiration of PUD approvals to three years.Council members also raised concerns and questions about the complexity of the proposed amendments.The public record will remain open until the council's first meeting in January.ORDINANCE 804: SUBDIVISIONSSpeaking on revisions to subdivisions within the town code, Thomas said there were not a "tremendous" number of proposed changes.To Thomas, the most significant changes include the elimination of a street hierarchy system, which was dictated by average daily trips; adding new nonresidential street types and standards for commercial and industrial roads; revised standards for residential street types, including street widths; and requiring that at least 50% of park space in a subdivision must be provided in the form of one centrally located neighborhood park.No public comments were shared at the Nov. 6 meeting, though council members voiced positive feedback for the revisions.The two ordinances and details of the proposed changes to the town code can be found on the Town of Easton's website under pending zoning legislation.

title: Planning Commission to Reconsider Lakeside Resolution
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
Planning commission to reconsider Lakeside resolution

 EASTON - The Talbot County Planning Commission on Wednesday voted to reconsider an earlier finding of inconsistency on a comprehensive water and sewer plan amendment relating to the Lakeside at Trappe development.Resolution 338, introduced in late February by Talbot County Council member Lynn Mielke, would amend the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan to be consistent with the Maryland Department of the Environment's discharge permit for Lakeside's wastewater treatment plant.The permit, issued in October 2022, is limited to the project's first phase and allows for an annual average flow of 100,000 gallons per day, or roughly 250 gallons per day per equivalent dwelling unit, allowing only 400 residential units to be built.The resolution would mandate that any future expansion of the new wastewater treatment plant require a comprehensive water and sewer plan amendment.In a 3-2 vote in early October, the planning commission found the resolution to be inconsistent with the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan because it referred to a map that needed to be reviewed.However, commissioners endorsed the idea of a phased review and determined its consistency with the comprehensive plan.The maps in need of review are water and sewer service maps for the Town of Trappe.Earlier this year, the Maryland Department of the Environment requested the county submit updated figures for water and sewer service in Trappe with correct classifications for all the town parcels, along with corrected exhibits to Resolution 281 - the original legislation approving water and sewer for Lakeside - to address certain parcels that were inadvertently shown on those maps.At Wednesday's meeting, planning commission member William Boicourt, who initially moved to find the resolution inconsistent with the comprehensive plan at the Oct. 4 meeting, said that while he recognized the issues with the maps, the commission still endorsed the resolution's basic principles.Given that the planning commission would be talking with the county council about other pending Lakeside legislation, Boicourt said he thought it was appropriate to reconsider the resolution's consistency in discussions with the council - a sentiment others agreed with.A joint work session with the county council and county planning commission on all of the Lakeside comprehensive water and sewer plan amendments is scheduled for Monday, Nov. 20 at 4 p.m.The planning commission will hold a special meeting with its attorneys and county staff on Wednesday, Nov. 8, at 9 a.m. to formulate and clarify its questions ahead of the Nov. 20 workshop.

title: Traffic Concerns Derail Proposed Apartment Complex - Board of Zoning Appeals Denies Aspire Apartments' Special Exception Request
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
Traffic concerns derail proposed apartment complex - Board of Zoning Appeals denies Aspire Apartments' special exception request

 October 26, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 1093
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - After four and a half hours of testimony and deliberations, the Easton Board of Zoning Appeals denied Aspire Apartments' request for a special exception to use a property off of Mathewstown Road as a multifamily apartment complex.Almost every seat was full in the meeting chambers Tuesday evening as supporters and opponents waited for a chance to weigh in on the contentious proposed complex - and to hear the long-awaited decision on the project's requests.Brought forth by Aspire Outdoors LLC, a company owned by Easton resident Derick Daly, the project proposed a six-building, 162-unit apartment complex with 27 units in each building.The property is situated on the south end of Camac Street, southwest of the existing Hunters Mill neighborhood and adjacent to the Gannon Range, previously known as the Estates at Gannon Farm, planned unit development. It's also located within the R-10A zone, a residential district within the Town of Easton.A multifamily apartment complex within the district requires a special exception granted by the Board of Zoning Appeals, which prompted Daly's request.Daly also requested a variance to allow reduction of the rear setback dimension for the apartment buildings and parking area to be reduced from the town zoning code's required 75 feet to 50 feet due to the unusual size and configuration of the area.The project first came before the town planning commission last December, where Hunters Mill residents voiced concerns about traffic and accessibility.The proposal was initially slated to be heard by the Board of Zoning Appeals in April, but was delayed by 180 days to address ongoing concerns.Within the last few months, both town planning staff and the planning commission recommended approval of Daly's application with conditions, which included project phasing, addressing traffic mitigation and ensuring adequate wastewater capacity.The proposed phasing suggestion, which was incorporated into plans shown at Tuesday's meeting, indicated that access to the first phase of buildings would be via Camac Street.The second phase of construction would include access to the complex via Gannon Range and Camac Street. An additional entrance for the third phase of development was yet to be determined.To Daly, inspiration for the apartment complex was drawn from the opportunity to provide "much-needed housing" to Easton. About 25% of the profits are going to another one of Daly's ventures: Polaris Village Academy, a free private school located in the Port Street area.Daly said the complex was intended to be a higher-end property to serve employees of the new regional medical center, which has yet to begin construction.Board of Zoning Appeals member Gary Molchan questioned why Aspire Apartments couldn't have its own entrance like other complexes instead of running through residential neighborhoods. Daly said he was limited by wetlands, which would require a different set of approvals.Questions were also raised about the number of parking spaces for the entirety of the complex, the possibility of parking spilling over onto Camac Street and adequate public facilities.A significant portion of the meeting was spent discussing traffic - a primary concern of Hunters Mill residents.Betty Tustin, a senior project manager for The Traffic Group, said once fully developed, the apartment complex would generate 875 average daily trips. The number was one she deemed as sufficient for what was permitted under town standards.But to Troy Brestel, a professional engineer and project manager with Traffic Planning and Design, Inc. who testified on behalf of the project's opponents, said that he agreed with the number of average daily trips listed in the developer's traffic study, but disagreed with amount of average daily trips on Camac Street once the apartments were developed.John Franczak, the vice president of the Hunters Mill Homeowners' Association, led opposition to the apartment complex on behalf of the neighborhood."We feel that the town comprehensive plan should be followed, no variances or exceptions," he said. "The rules are there to protect people."The Town of Easton is also installing a long-promised park in the neighborhood, which means more young children and families out walking - a dangerous situation if there's heavy traffic flow from an apartment complex, Franczak said.Several members of the public took the opportunity to comment at the end of each side's presentation.The board's discussion on the variance request was brief, with members acknowledging its minimal impact - the property's use was more important. Approval of the variance request was unanimous.More detailed deliberations ensued on the special exception request.Molchan voiced concerns about the change in character of the surrounding area and traffic congestion."I would support that the Town of Easton needs apartments like this, but these apartments should not affect a community that already exists," he said. "What we're doing to the people on Camac we're turning a quiet residential neighborhood into a bustling thoroughfare for cars and delivery trucks and contractor vehicles, and that's after the apartments are built, that's not while they're being built. Who knows what that will be?"Board member Zakary Krebeck raised similar points, speaking about the "unrealistic" provision of parking spaces and the impact it would have on Hunters Mill.To board chairman Peter Cotter, traffic and congestion were the two main issues he was grappling with."I don't see how it's currently configured, how I can get to a yes using Camac Street," he said, "because I just think that regardless of how the plan is, that's going to be what is used."A motion to deny the special exception was promptly voted on, earning a unanimous consensus.In a phone interview Wednesday afternoon, Daly said he was "disheartened" by the special exception's denial, but understood why the board chose to do so. Looking forward, he plans to make adjustments to his proposal and come before the board again.Because the board denied the application, Daly must wait a full year before returning with the same proposal, per the town's zoning ordinance. A revised plan could be heard in less than a year if it's substantially different from the previous application. The denial can also be appealed in the county circuit court.In spite of the denial, Daly expressed gratitude to the board for hearing him out, along with thanks for positive recommendations from the planning commission, Easton Utilities and town staff.Franczak said while he didn't think the apartment proposal was bad, the project didn't go well with the adjacent single-family house neighborhood. The opposition wasn't personal; Franczak felt he was allowed to defend his house, neighborhood and the safety of both."Bottom line: no hard feelings," he said.

title: Planning Commission Debates Resolutions on Lakeside Development
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
Planning Commission debates resolutions on Lakeside development

 October 6, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 1198
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON-A multihour meeting of the Talbot County Planning Commission on Wednesday tackled a trio of comprehensive water and sewer plan amendments relating to the Lakeside at Trappe development, concluding with one finding of inconsistency and two postponements.The benches in the Bradley Meeting Room were packed as the five-member planning commission mulled numerous public comments on the three resolutions proposed by the Talbot County Council over the last several months.Because the legislation amends the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan, the council sought recommendations on Resolutions 338, 347 and 348 from the public works advisory board and the planning commission. The council's own public hearings on the resolutions are scheduled for its Oct. 24 meeting.Over a dozen letters commenting on the three resolutions were submitted to the planning commission prior to Wednesday's meeting, with more comments unfolding over the course of the morning.Concerns with the long-contested development centered on Lakeside's size, the capacity of its new wastewater treatment plant, negative environmental impacts, preservation of Talbot County's rural character and Trappe's sewer service maps. Planning commissioners raised their own contentions with the resolutions as well.RESOLUTION 338Introduced in late February by Talbot County Council member Lynn Mielke, the resolution would amend the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan to be consistent with the Maryland Department of the Environment's discharge permit for Lakeside's wastewater treatment plant.The resolution would mandate that any future expansion of the new wastewater treatment plant require a comprehensive water and sewer plan amendment.The discharge permit, issued last October, is limited to the project's first phase and allows for an annual average flow of 100,000 gallons per day, or roughly250 gallons per day per equivalent dwelling unit (EDU), allowing only 400 residential units to be built.But according to the development's attorney Ryan Showalter, who testified at Thursday's meeting, the 250 gallon per day flow is a presumed flow for initial allocation of capacity and treatment. Once the plant is operational, the 100,000 gallon capacity is more likely to serve 500 to 600 houses, he said.A total of 2,501 residences are planned for the development.Showalter expressed opposition to the requirement for the developer to come back before the county for future expansion."The developer understands the requirement to go through a major permit modification; that process involves public hearings, public input, the County Council certainly can weigh in and comment on that, but the notion that every time the Lakeside wastewater treatment plant is required to expand, (and) should come back before the county for a water and sewer plan amendment-which is maybe another four-year process - is not acceptable to the developer," he said, adding: "We would not oppose 338 if that sentence was stricken."Alan Girard, the Chesapeake Bay Foundation's Eastern Shore director, said the nonprofit was supportive of the resolution's intent, but questions remained as to whether the intent could be achieved as it related to the timing of development criteria."The resolution rightly requires an amendment to the sewer plan when a major permit modification is sought, but it's mostly silent on other timing key elements, like the sewer service area maps, the 540,000 gallon per day discharge quantity and phasing, the automatic change to 'immediate priority service status' when the land is annexed," he said. "These timing elements are significant because they're linked to the major concerns the public has with this project."Girard urged the Planning Commission to work with the County Council to ensure the legislation's full intent was realized by updating the sewer service classifications in ways that best serve the community and environmental health.Lyndsey Ryan, Trappe's town attorney, raised similar concerns to those voiced by Showalter."The town feels that this is overly cumbersome and would impede their ability to smartly manage growth and orderly provide adequate public facilities for development within the Town of Trappe," she said.RESOLUTION 347Resolution 347, introduced on Sept. 12, was spurred by MDE's request for the number of equivalent dwelling units for all phases of the Lakeside development.The legislation provides the number of EDUs - 2,874 in total -for all six phases of the development, though the numbers for Phases 2 through 6 are estimated. The legislation includes the current water and sewer classifications.Points of concern voiced by members of the public centered on confusion with timing of the phases and water and sewer classifications for each phase.Ryan, again speaking for the Town of Trappe, said she thought there was a lot of misunderstanding about phases and planning of phases. The town never intended to require that each phase be developed before moving to a later phase; the phases were not intended to be sequential, she said.Ryan also confirmed that 81 residential units within Lakeside are being served and are connected to Trappe's existing wastewater treatment plant.On Monday, the county's public works advisory board voted 5-0 to recommend that the resolution not be adopted as written.RESOLUTION 348Resolution 348, introduced Sept. 12, was also drafted in response to MDE's request for clarification on Trappe's water and sewer service maps. The legislation addresses incorrect water and sewer classifications of parcels shown in two exhibits to Resolution 281, the original legislation approving a wastewater treatment plant for Lakeside under a draft discharge permit.The parcels that were incorrectly shown on the exhibits are unrelated to Resolution 281. The parcels' classifications were not changed, making the resolution's purpose solely to clarify and confirm the water and sewer classifications.To Easton resident Lisa Ghezzi, a former county planning commission member, the resolution signified continued confusion on Trappe's water and sewer service maps. She pointed out that the lack of updates to the county's comprehensive plan is the source of the frustration."We're just spinning our wheels, and we cannot make any decisions until everyone, staff included, knows the facts behind this," she said. "I found confusion in staff's presentation at the outset of this discussion. (The) public works advisory board raised questions earlier this week. How can we operate like this?"Talbot County resident Mike McConnel urged the Planning Commission to consider a revised sewer service map for Trappe that only identifies one small section of Lakeside as an immediate priority and to revert all other sections of the development to unprogrammed."That will mean that as Lakeside progresses, they will have to come back to the Planning Commission and establish that the consequences of the development are consistent as it goes forward," he said.The county's public works advisory board reviewed the resolution on Monday, but tabled a decision until the board's next meeting on Oct. 19.DECISIONSAfter significant back and forth, the Planning Commission voted 3-2 to find Resolution 338 inconsistent with the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan because it refers to a map that needs to be reviewed, but the commission endorsed the idea of a phased review, per the motion made.The commission voted unanimously to postpone its determination on Resolution 347 for further discussion.As for Resolution 348, the commission also voted unanimously to postpone consideration due to ongoing uncertainty that has not been addressed. 
 
 Caption: NATALlE JONES/STAR DEMOCRAT
 
Talbot County Planning Commission Chairman Chip Councell, center, speaks about the Lakeside comprehensive water and sewer plan amendments during a meeting Wednesday, Oct. 4.

title: Reduced Poplar Hill Plans OK'd by Planners
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
Reduced Poplar Hill plans OK'd by planners

 September 28, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 829
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - After the application for the proposed 456-unit Poplar Hill development was rescinded last month, the developer's team returned to the Easton Planning Commission last Thursday seeking approval for a now-much smaller subdivision sketch plan - and received it.At the Sept. 21 planning commission meeting, attorney Ryan Showalter, who represents property owner 5001 SHR L.C., introduced the specifics of the new Poplar Hill sketch plan and sought a waiver request for the length of a proposed alley.The new plan is a significant downsize from the developer's former application, which proposed 456 residential units of various housing types, along with a commercial area, a park and open space, community clubhouses and a satellite fire department building.The former application also sought a supplemental growth allocation to reclassify just over half of the 120-acre Oxford Road property from a resource conservation area to an intensely developed area due to its location in the town's critical area.The growth allocation request was the subject of significant outcry from Easton and Talbot County residents over the last five months, who raised concerns about the development's size and benefits to the greater community, increased traffic and water quality. The request was withdrawn in early August.According to Showalter, the new Poplar Hill sketch plan includes 119 single-family detached homes in a subdivision. Three of the single-family homes are located within the resource conservation area and will be accessed by a shared driveway using the existing critical area density, he said.The resource conservation area designation permits one residential unit per 20 acres. The property has almost 66 acres located within the critical area.As for the waiver request of the alley length, the developer asked the planning commission to permit a 616-foot block, a minor deviation from the 600-foot standard in the town's subdivision regulations.In terms of the rest of the parcel, Showalter said that an area of land along the southern portion of the property is zoned for governmental and institutional uses and can't be used for housing, but it can be used for community parks and facilities.The portion of that land that isn't within the critical area has been set aside as an active park area and is likely to include a community-maintained swimming pool and bathhouse, he said.A question on what would be done with the parcel's remaining agricultural land was raised.Showalter said the developer's intention was to continue to farm that land. It's not clear yet if the homeowner's association will own the land or if the land will be sold to the farm, but whoever the owner is will be responsible for managing the land, he said.Speaking on traffic, Planning Commissioner Paul Weber raised questions on the right-in/right-out entrance and exit to the development along Oxford Road.The main access point to Poplar Hill under the new sketch plan is located at the intersection of Tristan Drive and the Easton Bypass, or Route 322. Most of the houses in the community are located near that proposed entrance.However, the proposed right-in/right-out on Oxford Road would allow future residents to only enter the development from the eastbound lane on Oxford Road and to exit into the same travel lane on Oxford Road.In crafting the right-in/right-out, Showalter said the developer had looked at previous public concerns with traffic volume on Oxford Road and considered the possibility of people attempting to pass through the Poplar Hill community via Tristan Drive to get to Oxford without hitting the light on the bypass.Prior to allowing public comment, Planning Commission Chair Jennifer Dindinger said she appreciated the developer's original proposal for different housing types and price points."I realize that this is what you're allowed to do, and I think it's a perfectly reasonable proposal, but I am sad that our friends and neighbors were so opposed to allowing for more multi-family housing," she said, "but I appreciate that you took the community's comments into consideration and came back with something that met your needs and the needs of the community." Tom Ledvina, president of the Papermill Crossing Homeowners Association, thanked property owner and developer Kevin Sills for listening to the community, acknowledging that it was a difficult process for all involved."We think that this new proposal protects water quality better than the former proposal, protects the scenic Oxford Road corridor, which is important, and I think it helps with the traffic - if nothing else, there's fewer cars coming out of there," he said.Ledvina added that the small community still had concerns about traffic, but the town will be working to fix and mitigate the issues for a long time to come.Following additional discussion, the Planning Commission voted 3-0 to approve the sketch subdivision plan and the block length waiver, with conditions that the State Highway Administration and the Town of Easton decide the best course of action for the right-in/right-out intersection and that the developer meets other staff conditions.

title: County Council Gets New Lakeside Resolutions
