 EASTON - The Talbot County Council on Tuesday introduced several pieces of legislation amending the comprehensive water and sewer plan, including two resolutions concerning the Lakeside at Trappe development.Introduced by council members Keasha Haythe and Dave Stepp, Resolutions 347 and 348 address updated information on equivalent dwelling units for all phases of the Lakeside development, along with clarifying Trappe's water and sewer service maps.Earlier this year, the Maryland Department of the Environment requested that the county submit updated phase information to the agency in a comprehensive water and sewer plan amendment.The county council voted 4-1 in early August to submit the information as part of the county's draft 2023 Report of the Review but changed direction two weeks later to introduce the information through standalone resolutions.Resolution 347 provides the number of EDUs for all six phases of the development, though the numbers for Phases two through six are estimated.The legislation includes the current water and sewer classifications.The phases only represent defined land uses, not the timing or sequence of development, according to the resolution.All phases of Lakeside that aren't classified as immediate priority will need to be reclassified through another comprehensive water and sewer plan amendment before receiving water and sewer service from Trappe.According to the resolution, there are 2,874 total EDUs for the development, and 1,226 of those EDUs are within the S-1 and W-1 classification - areas that exist or are under construction that are of immediate priority for water and sewer service.The number of EDUs for community uses in the first phase and for all in the last five phases are only estimates, per the resolution.Approximately 126 lots in the Lakeside development have already been platted and approved for community water and sewer systems.Resolution 348 addresses incorrect water and sewer classifications of parcels shown in two exhibits to Resolution 281, the original legislation approving a wastewater treatment plant for Lakeside under a draft discharge permit.The parcels that were incorrectly shown on the exhibits are unrelated to Resolution 281. The parcels' classifications were not changed, making the resolution's purpose solely to clarify and confirm the water and sewer classifications.Now that the resolutions have been introduced, they will be referred to the county's public works advisory board and planning commission.The two resolutions are on the public works advisory board's Thursday, Sept. 14, agenda for review and recommendation to the county council.Public hearings for all legislation introduced at Tuesday's council meeting are set for 6:30 p.m. Tuesday, Oct. 10. The full text of each resolution can be found on the Talbot County government website.

title: Updated Lakeside Info Going in Draft Report
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
Updated Lakeside info going in draft report

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: 3 | Section: News

 EASTON - The Talbot County Council voted 4-1 to submit updated information on phases of development for Lakeside at Trappe and Trappe's water and sewer service maps as part of the county's draft 2023 Report of the Review.After significant discussion Tuesday evening, the council reached the deciding vote to submit the information, originally requested by the Maryland Department of the Environment, as part of the draft comprehensive water and sewer plan update, which Talbot County refers to as the Report of the Review.The Report of the Review is "almost like balancing your checkbook," said County Engineer Ray Clarke.The 2023 document will take resolutions, map changes and water and sewer description changes that have been made since the county's previous comprehensive water and sewer plan came out.The council's conversation on certain items to include in the draft report stemmed from a July 21 letter and subsequent email from Dinorah Dalmasy, the program manager for the water and science administration at MDE.The letter and email followed up on letters sent to the county in April and May regarding updated water and sewer maps for the Town of Trappe and a request for equivalent dwelling units (EDUs) for all phases of the Lakeside development, said County Attorney Patrick Thomas.In terms of the maps, Dalmasy said the draft maps the county provided to clarify the existing water and sewer classifications for the town appeared to meet the intent of MDE's classification requests, Thomas said.Dalmasy said MDE was seeking EDUs for all phases of Lakeside, regardless of the existing water and sewer classifications.The number of EDUs of the first phase must be finalized, and remaining phases need to include the best estimates.According to Thomas, the draft water and sewer maps and EDUs need to be submitted to MDE by Aug. 31. The information could be submitted in two ways: as part of the draft 2023 Report of the Review or in standalone amendment resolutions.The draft maps submitted to MDE have already been incorporated into the document, and Thomas and Clarke would be able to incorporate language on the Lakeside EDUs prior to the council's next meeting on Aug. 22.Thomas said the most straightforward approach would be to include the requested information in the draft 2023 Report of the Review.Once the county receives comments on the document from stakeholders, the public and MDE - a process that will take a few months - and is close to finishing the final report, the report will be introduced as a resolution through the county's usual water and sewer amendment process, he said."Either way, we get to the same place and follow the same process, and I think it just makes more sense to incorporate these items into the Report of the Review and do it all at once instead of having a Report of the Review and having these two other resolutions out there that are sort of on parallel tracks," Thomas said.Regardless of the path the council chose to take, either by submitting the full draft report with the Lakeside information or choosing to introduce related resolutions by its next meeting, MDE solely wanted to have the information by Aug. 31, with no expectation for it to be adopted by the deadline, he added.Concerns initially expressed by Council Vice President Pete Lesher and Council Member Keasha Haythe centered on the council's opportunity to fully digest the report before passing the document to MDE for approval.Lesher was the sole council member who voted against including the requested Lakeside information in the report.A digital version of the draft 2023 Report of the Review will be posted to the county's website for public review.

title: Easton Survey Shows Desire for Affordable Housing, Entertainment
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
Easton survey shows desire for affordable housing, entertainment

 August 9, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: 3 | Section: News 
 
 531
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - Young adults in the Easton area want to see more housing options and entertainment, according to results from a town comprehensive plan survey.The survey results, presented by Easton Economic Development Corporation interns Zach Spofford and Dre Brown at the Easton Town Council's meeting Monday, were gathered to get a pulse on what younger adults want to see in the town.The data collected will help with the town's comprehensive plan rewrite.Spofford is a rising sophomore at the University of Maryland. Brown is a ninth grader at St. Michaels Middle High School. Both worked to collect survey results.Seventy-nine individuals, split nearly evenly between male and female respondents, participated in the interns' survey through an in-person interview or online questionnaire.Just over half of survey respondents live within the Town of Easton, with others living in Talbot County, St. Michaels, Denton and Cambridge.The bulk of survey takers were between 20 and 40 years old, Spofford said. About 73% of those surveyed were white, 19% were Black and 3.6% were Asian and Hispanic.Five words - peaceful, welcoming, community, family and home - were the most common words survey takers used in describing Easton, Brown said.As part of the survey, the interns asked young adults which parks and facilities their households utilized most often. The YMCA, Idlewild Park and Rails to Trails were close to the top.Survey takers said the main issues the town is facing include overdevelopment, affordable housing, recreational activities and traffic, Spofford said. About 29% of young adults said they wanted to change Easton's entertainment, and roughly 24% said they wanted to see more housing options. About 13% of survey takers said they wanted to see affordability within the town.As for improvements, survey takers said they wanted more recreational activities, like mini golf, an arcade, batting cages, a driving range, marina improvements and a skate park. More entertainment options, like live music, standup comedy and film festivals, were suggested.In terms of shopping and dining, young adults said they wanted more high-end retail and a grocery store within walking distance of downtown Easton, Spofford said. Bars for younger people, a steakhouse, fast casual restaurants and waterfront dining were on the list.Survey takers also said they would like to see bike lanes, a dog park and a remodel of Easton High School.Ward 4 Councilman the Rev. Elmer Davis Jr. asked the interns what they would like to see in a dream world.Spofford said he'd love bringing a Topgolf to Easton, but didn't think there were enough people in the area for it. A recent graduate of Easton High School, he said he'd also like to see improvements there.Brown said he would like to see affordable housing."because a lot of people, they just can't afford rent of housing in general, and I just think it's a really big struggle right now," he said, also mentioning inflation as prohibitive to housing. "I just want to see more people be able to live here and experience the same joy as living in the Town of Easton, or just in Talbot County in general."

title: In Wake of Fatal Hit-and-Run, Route 50 Safety in Easton a Concern
author: Konner Metz
content:
In wake of fatal hit-and-run, Route 50 safety in Easton a concern

 October 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 826
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Safety concerns for pedestrians and bikers using Route 50 in Easton are being raised after a fatal hit-and-run crash Saturday.Donald Dawson, a 68-year-old Easton resident, was killed riding a bike early Saturday morning in what police said was a hit-and-run crash with a box truck or tractor trailer. Police are still searching for the suspect vehicle.
The crash occurred at U.S. Route 50 and Woodridge Drive.
On Monday, Town Council President Don Abbatiello implored residents to drive safely.
"We already have enough people who come through town speeding. We don't need to add to that," Abbatiello said.
The fatal crash occurred just north of the Immanuel Lutheran Church and across from Saints Peter & Paul High School. Slightly north of the crash location is an overhead sign instruction drivers of the traffic light ahead, reading: "urban area stay alert." The speed limit reduces to 45 mph as drivers funnel toward the Route 50 and Dutchmans Lane intersection.
Saturday's crash is the second fatal collision on that stretch of road this year. In February, a car struck and killed a 35-year-old man near Route 50 and Woodridge Drive.
In response to questions about Route 50 safety in Easton, State Highway Administration spokesman Danny Allman said pedestrian activity near Woodridge Drive "is not encouraged as there are no sidewalks nor shoulders" on that side of the highway.
"We always emphasize visibility for pedestrians and cyclists on any road," Allman wrote in an email statement Tuesday. "Pedestrians and cyclists should always wear reflective apparel, especially in areas with no separation or lighting."
Saturday's fatal crash is also raising the question of whether speed cameras should be placed along Route 50 in Easton. Abbatiello said the cameras are needed.
"I also am pleading with the state to consider adding speed cameras on Route 50," he said during Monday's meeting. "We are talking about adding two crosswalks, one at Dover, one at Goldsborough, hopefully within the next year. We're going to have people walking across Route 50. It needs to be safe for them to do so. And so I hope that the state will seriously consider a request for a speed camera on Route 50."
Easton has its own speed enforcement program to deter speeding in school zones. School zone signs with "photo enforced" written under them indicate where the cameras may be active.
Town Engineer Rick Van Emburgh said speed cameras on town streets and roads have been successful. There are cameras near the YMCA and The Country School, he said.
"I think that speed cameras help change behavior," Van Emburgh said.
While Saturday's crash didn't occur on a town-operated road, Easton engineers are in communication with their counterparts at the state level, he said.
Allman said SHA doesn't have "enabling legislation" to install speed cameras in non-work zones. Per state law, jurisdictions can install cameras in school zones and sometimes residential and other areas, he said.
For a camera to be placed on a state route, Allman said a jurisdiction would have to submit a request to SHA and receive a permit to place the camera.
Abbatiello said in an interview Tuesday that the next step for the town to consider requesting a speed camera permit for Route 50. The precedent is already set in Salisbury Abbatiello noted, pointing to speed cameras on the highway near Wicomico Middle School.
"It's a real issue in Easton," Abbatiello said of Route 50 safety.
Easton Police Chief Alan Lowrey said on Wednesday that the police department is working with a speed camera vendor to assess safety on the highway. "There's a lot of work to be done" before officially submitting a speed camera request to SHA, Lowrey said. Work includes gathering crash data.
"The goal is safety, the goal's not revenue," Lowrey said. "That's how the state looks at it, too."
According to SHA, sidewalks and pedestrian crossings are in the works for two Route 50 intersections — Dover and Matthewstown Roads, or Routes 331 and 328, respectively. Construction will begin in early- to mid-2026, Allman said Tuesday.
For roads maintained by the town, a draft comprehensive "Complete Streets" study is expected to be presented to town officials in the coming weeks. It will outline target speed limits, assess the need for sidewalks or bike lanes and, overall, put "safety first," Van Emburgh said.
"It's gonna tell us what we want our roads to look like," he said.
Talbot Thrive, a local nonprofit that advocates for pedestrian and bicycle safety, said in a statement on Monday that the town's Complete Streets study and similar safety efforts by Talbot County officials are important.
"These efforts need to be, at their core, about saving lives," the statement read.
Talbot Thrive's statement also addressed Saturday's fatal crash.
"This tragedy is a stark reminder of the vulnerability of those who travel by foot, bicycle, or wheelchair in our community — and of the urgent need to make Talbot County's roads safer and more connected for everyone, not just for those in cars," the statement read.
This story has been updated to include comment from Easton Police Chief Alan Lowrey.

title: Trappe Volunteer Fire Company Seeks Funding for Firehouse
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Trappe Volunteer Fire Company seeks funding for firehouse

 July 4, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 396
 Words 

 Read News Document

 TRAPPE — The Trappe Volunteer Fire Company is raising funds to build an up-to-date firehouse. Rep. Andy Harris (R-Md. 1st) wants to secure federal funding to help.The Trappe Volunteer Firehouse was completed in 1951 and has not been updated since. "We probably have the oldest one in the county," Assistant Secretary Treasurer of the Trappe Volunteer Fire Company Cheryl Lewis said.
Lewis said a new firehouse is necessary because the current building is no longer suitable for the modern equipment.
Because Trappe has a volunteer fire company, like many towns on the Eastern Shore, projects like this rely heavily on government and local support, Lewis said.
"We've been in the process of trying to get assistance," Lewis said. "In the last budget year, the federal budget that was just approved, we had successfully worked with Andy Harris's office to be included in the budget. But with the cuts that were done early on this year, it was removed."
Harris said the appropriations bill to provide funding for the project failed due to negotiations in Congress leading to a continued delay, but she said the project has been reapplied for in the current year's legislation.
"We hope the appropriations process has a better outcome, but then that's not up to us because it involves the minority party as well," he said in an interview with the Star Democrat.
In order to qualify for federal grants, the company must match 25% of the projected project cost of $6 million. The company set a goal of $1,500,000 and set aside $450,000 to begin the efforts.
Fundraising efforts include The Trappe Volunteer Fire Company's upcoming annual fair, held on July 31 through Aug. 2 at the firehouse. The event begins at 6 p.m. and ends at 10 p.m. each day and will include fire truck rides, hay rides, food, games and prizes, and live entertainment, according to the fire company's Facebook page. Saturday's event will open with a parade.
Harris said the outcome of federal funding depends on the successful bipartisan negotiations in Congress to pass this version of the appropriations bill.
"In the end, this is going to depend on the minority party. And you know, if they're not willing to negotiate in good faith, that could end up being a problem," Harris said. "The people in Trappe have to know that their member of Congress was working hard to get that money to the fire company."

title: Talbot Sheriff's Office Operating Out of New Facility

Talbot sheriff's office operating out of new facility

 EASTON — The Talbot County Sheriff's Office is operating out of new offices on Mary's Court in Easton.As part of construction of a new Talbot County Public Safety Complex, the sheriff's office relocated in October and early November from its old offices on Glebe Road.
Talbot County Sheriff Joe Gamble said the new offices are "great" and that his department now has "high-tech" filing and storage systems.
"We have an armory in there where we can clean and store firearms, ammunition, which is a very nice space," Gamble added. "All the spaces are very nice. They really did a nice job with the layout of it."

The sheriff says once the Department of Emergency Services fully moves in, there'll be an open house or ribbon-cutting event to celebrate the new building.
"Everybody's really enjoying it," Gamble said. " … Once everything's done, we should be in good shape."

Next phase of Oxford's Strand Beach Project poses funding hurdle

 OXFORD — Phase one of the Strand Beach Project has been completed, but the prospect of phase two is daunting for the town and its residents.The first phase was turbulent. Residents, commissioners and town staff were frustrated with the duration, expense and results of the project.
Funding for phase one came from the state and Department of Natural Resources. Currently, there is no additional funding for future phases of the project.

"We're looking at funding options with the state to mitigate the stormwater on the roadway as well as town internal funds, which it's going to be likely that we're going to have to look at that, especially with mitigating the stormwater on the roadway and that failing bulkhead," Wahl said.

In addition, there's no ADA compliant entrance to the beach area.
These have been hot topics at recent town commissioner meetings. Commissioner Dave Donovan said it has been on the agenda every meeting for the past two months.
Once plans for the second phase of the project are ready, the town will seek permits. Whal said commissioners are unlikely to approve another contract with Underwood & Associates.

title: St. Michaels Commissioners Discuss Sea Level Rise Projects
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
St. Michaels Commissioners discuss sea level rise projects

 September 25, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 384
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — On Wednesday, Roy Meyer of the Climate Change Sea Level Rise Commission and multiple engineers presented key sea-level rise mitigation projects to the St. Michaels commissioners.Meyer said the projects were for the wellbeing of the town of St. Michaels residents and tourists.
"If there's one thing that impacts the town and the Maritime Museum in the same way, it's sea level rise and flooding," Meyer said. "So I mean their campus is going to be flooded, our roads are going to be flooded."
The projects, which will be carried out in two phases, will potentially raise road elevations to five feet. An Advanced Systems grant with FEMA and a state grant will help the town cover the cost of the projects.
Phase one involves raising Mill Street, Burn Street, the Harbor walkway and the end of Cherry Street to an elevation of five feet. It also includes demolishing and rebuilding Honeymoon Bridge at a higher elevation and wider size, rebuilding piers at the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum, installing a larger culvert system where Mill Street meets the tidal area, and adding a north sidewalk along Mill Street.
The cost of Phase one would be more than $5.3 million.
Phase two will address Mulberry Street, Muskrat Park, and Church and Green streets. Phase two features two options, short-term and a long-term solutions.
The short-term would include modifying the parking lot and existing swale in the park to provide immediate relief from flooding by getting water off the streets faster. This solution is expected to be effective for daily high tides until 2050 and cost $708,366.
The long-term approach raises the roads, similar to phase one. It would also move the roads away from the pipe system and allow for overland flow, separating stormwater and tidewater.
Raising to elevation five feet is the ideal solution, but challenges exist with a wall along Church Street near a cemetery and columbarium, engineers said. The long-term approach would cost $896,724.
The commissioners elected to proceed with prioritizing the already advanced Phase one construction plans and will follow up with the Maritime Museum to discuss options.
The commissioners selected the short-term solution for phase two, saying the town will develop a detailed long-term plan for Muskrat Park. The commissioners also said they would defer action on Mulberry Street until more clarity emerges from private development plans.

title: Transportation Officials Tour Eastern Shore to Discuss Funding and Project Statuses
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Transportation officials tour Eastern Shore to discuss funding and project statuses

 September 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: News 
 
 975
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Members of Maryland's Department of Transportation came to the Eastern Shore on Tuesday to meet with county and city officials and give updates on current projects.MDOT officials traveled through the Mid-Shore to discuss the agency's Draft Consolidated Transportation Program for fiscal years 2026 to 2031, which details a $21.5 billion, six-year capital budget investment in the state's transportation network.
Three separate meetings were held with MDOT officials Tuesday, one each in Talbot, Dorchester and Caroline counties. The meetings are part of the department's tour visiting every Maryland county.
TALBOT
Meeting with local officials at the Talbot County Community Center, acting Secretary of MDOT Samantha Biddle presented a draft of the Consolidated Transportation Program, emphasizing efforts to enhance safety, maintain systems and drive economic growth.
Biddle and other MDOT representatives shared status updates for several transportation projects in the county.
The Route 50 corridor project from Dutchman Lane to Lomax Street in Easton is in the final design stages, with construction expecting to begin in 2026, Biddle said. This project includes signalized pedestrian crossings at the Route 50 intersections with Dover and Matthewstown roads.
State Highway Administrator Will Pines reported that the State Highway Administration upgraded and improved 38 crosswalks across Talbot County in fiscal year 2025.
The county will receive a Kim Lanpheir Bikeways Grant for bike racks as part of the Easton Community Bicycle Parking Initiative. Director of Local Transit Support Travis Johnston said that MTA will provide Talbot County with $1 million in operating grants and preventative maintenance for local transit operations.
St. Michaels Town Manager Don Richardson requested the restoration of two crosswalks, which District Engineer Kenny Fender said would be completed in the next two weeks.
Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) raised concerns over a funding issue for the Oyster Recovery Program, which he said is designed to mitigate damage from port activities and has been the backbone of oyster restoration.
Biddle responded to Mautz's concerns with good news, saying funds are secured for this fiscal year to continue that work. But the conversation escalated at the Dorchester County meeting later Tuesday, when Mautz expressed he felt the secretary had presented conflicting answers throughout the day.
DORCHESTER
Mautz worried transportation officials weren't following through on the details of the contract between MDOT and the Department of Natural Resources. That contract outlines that the agencies together will provide $2 million in funding this fiscal year for the oyster program, Mautz said, among other specifics.
Biddle ensured that the departments would hit the $2 million "target," adding that she will "stay very close" on the matter as her agency works with DNR.
Meanwhile, transportation officials told the Dorchester County Council and residents on Tuesday that a long-awaited roundabout project in East New Market is moving forward.
During MDOT'S stop in Dorchester, Pines said the department's six-year capital funding plan fully supports the roundabout design for the intersection of Routes 392 and 14 in East New Market next to Dockins Service Station.
According to the draft plan, estimated cost is $4.65 million for the improvement. Pines said Tuesday the design should be completed in 2026.
Dawn Stanley, who was in an accident at the intersection two years ago and pushed transportation officials on the matter at last year's annual meeting, clapped when Pines spoke and thanked him.
"Knowing that that roundabout is coming is really essential," said Dorchester County Council Vice President Mike Detmer. "Talking with responders from Station 21, this has always, always been a problem. This is gonna be a triumph of making the roads safer."
SHA District Engineer Mark Crampton touched on efforts to fix culverts at Route 336 as it goes over Worlds End Creek. The road is one of limited access points for residents in southern Dorchester County.
Crampton said temporary improvements have been done and estimated a three-week construction timeframe to begin this summer once school is out. State transportation leaders will meet with the county next week to look at the detour route, Crampton said.
Other areas discussed included:
Warwick Elementary School. Biddle said officials have worked to improve safety on the roads in front of the school in Secretary.Route 392 sidewalks. Biddle said the sidewalks on the portion of the state road in Hurlock were completed this year.
CAROLINE
MDOT came to the Health and Public Service Building on Tuesday morning to hear Caroline County's requests for projects and answer questions from the County Commissioners.
The commissioners also listened to MDOT's plans to ensure federal funding possibilities are still available for the county.
"Our team specifically at the State Highway Administration is looking for opportunities to look where we can apply federal funds for critical safety and state of repair projects here in the county," Biddle told the Star Democrat in an interview after the meeting.
"So, as many projects as we can identify that are federally eligible, it allows us to stretch limited state resources even further to be able to do more projects such as, the intersection improvements referenced by the commissioners today or just safety and resurfacing project where those are helpful and necessary parts of keeping our system in a state of good repair," Biddle said.
Here are the current projects in the county under construction, in progress or requested:
Bridge replacement and rehabilitation at Maryland Route 16 and Harmony Road. The project is already under construction.Intersection capacity improvements from Maryland Route 16 and Harmony Road to Greenwood Road. A planning study is underway.Additional striping or re-striping at the intersection of Maryland Route 317 (Burrsville Road) and Maryland 313 (Greensboro Road). This was requested by the county.Signal change for the traffic lane at Maryland Route 16 (Harmony Road) and Maryland 404. This was requested by the county.Additional lighted intersection at Maryland 404 and Gay Street. This was requested by the county.Consideration of the 16 E school in Greenwood and 404 as a major breakout point. The commissioners requested this change, calling the road as a "major disaster."

title: Claiborne Residents, Operating Their Own Well, Look for Water Supply Solution
author: Konner Metz
content:
Claiborne residents, operating their own well, look for water supply solution

 September 13, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 819
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CLAIBORNE — When Rob Todd moved to Claiborne in 2013, he didn't expect to be partially responsible for the village's water services. But it's a role he and others have assumed.From 2015 to 2019, Todd was one of four volunteers for the resident-led Claiborne Water Company, a group that oversees a water system serving about 30 properties.
"I, for one, didn't envision my retirement years being a well operator," Todd said while taking a walk to the community's well on Thursday afternoon.
Todd, 77, volunteered for a relatively short stint. He credits longtime Claiborne resident Renny Johnson — the "water czar" — with the decades-long heavy lifting of maintaining Claiborne's water. Johnson handles the billing, fields questions from residents and arranges testing of the well system.
Johnson moved to his Claiborne house in 1979 and was handed the water company books just a few years later by the outgoing man in charge.
"We had a water company meeting where we invited the people that were on the system to talk about (it), and no one else would take it over," Johnson recalled. "So I said I would, not thinking that I would be doing it for this long."
Johnson, 77, and others are hoping to pass the duties off and find a long-term solution to what's become a multifaceted problem keeping the water system in line with state regulations.
As Claiborne's population ages, attracting volunteers is difficult, Johnson and Todd said. And now more than ever, the Maryland Department of the Environment is pushing Claiborne to meet standards for what the state considers "community water systems."
Community water systems aren't served by a municipal company. They are smaller-scale, like the Claiborne water well. However, MDE requires systems with over 15 properties hooked up to have a licensed operator, according to residents and county officials.
Four Claiborne residents — Johnson, Todd, Jim Richardson and Kirke Harper — explained the issue at a Talbot County Council work session on Sept. 9. While the county doesn't maintain the water system, County Engineer Ray Clarke is willing to help where he can.
"We're grateful that the county was willing to listen to our problem," Todd said.
'WE'RE AGING OUT'
Claiborne, an unincorporated village on the Chesapeake Bay, is a short detour on the drive from St. Michaels to Tilghman Island.
According to residents, a 19th-century railroad company drilled Claiborne's old water well, which was then turned over to the residents when the railroad closed in 1928.
Johnson and Richardson took over in the early 1980s, back when each household paid $18 annually to hook up and just before the railroad's well was replaced. Now, the yearly fee is $200. A second, separate water system serves 14 properties closer to the Bay and past the main Claiborne Road strip. It's not subject to all of the same MDE rules.
Claiborne Water Company's current building is a white structure housing a pressure tank and chlorine pump. It sits a handful of paces away from the well cap a few feet above ground level.
Residents say efforts to find a licensed operator in recent years have come up empty, which is why they're seeking county assistance.
MDE spokesman Jay Apperson said in an email that the state's increased rules on water system operators were implemented in 2001.
"Maryland regulations include requirements for certification, such as passing examinations and continuing education," Apperson wrote.
Claiborne's water company volunteers aren't overly concerned about water quality. MDE's most recent review of the Claiborne water system indicated that it meets state and federal requirements. Low levels of arsenic, while in compliance, was the leading worry.
MDE inspects the water system at least every three years, Apperson said.
Residents' core concern, instead, boils down to meeting MDE's certification requirements, which likely means passing the buck off to a qualified operator.
And for Johnson, who beat cancer a few years ago, juggling the billing, testing and upkeep responsibilities continues to take a toll. "I'm older now, and I don't have as much strength or wherewithal to carry on," he said.
"We're aging out," Johnson added. "Nobody who's retired wants to take on the responsibility of running the water company."
SOLUTIONS
At the county work session, officials agreed to explore options for the Claiborne Water Company through a preliminary engineering report, or feasibility study, which could be authorized at the council's next meeting on Sept. 23.
Clarke, the county engineer, explained that homeowners connected to the community system mostly can't drill individual wells because of necessary setbacks from private septic systems.
Extending sewer services down to the Claiborne village could be a longer-term solution to make private wells a possibility, officials said. But in the short-term, the residents are still seeking a fix.
County Council Vice President Pete Lesher, acting as a liaison to the Public Works Advisory Board, said he understands Claiborne residents have been "clamoring for some assistance" for a long time.
"I'm well aware that, in (this) process, you've already actually explored a lot of options and are coming to us because you've come up empty," Lesher said.

title: Oxford's Strand Beach Frustrations Grow as Fencing is Erected
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Oxford's Strand Beach frustrations grow as fencing is erected

 July 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 455
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — The Strand Beach project has sparked controversy within Oxford since its inception in 2018. Now, a new town manager, a recently elected commissioner and highly invested residents are taking it upon themselves to assess where the project stands.At Tuesday evening's meeting, Oxford commissioner Dave Donovan used his time during the commissioner comment period to say, "I'd hate for a meeting to go by and not talk about the Strand."
Residents sat up a bit straighter and were excited to hear this.
Recently, protective fencing was erected all over the Strand Beach.
"I mean, my god, what an eyesore," Donovan said.
In order for the town to be in compliance with the Maryland Department of Environment, 85% of the Strand must be covered by marsh and vegetation — as seen from an aerial view — for five years.
The protective fencing, which signifies where the marsh and vegetation will go, covers a large portion of the former beach area.
"I think that's a huge change for people to accept because those used to be beach areas," Commission President Katrina Greer said.
Donovan asked if it would be expensive to take the fencing down, and Greer said it would. "It's $25,000, believe it or not," she said.
The fencing will potentially be up for seasons, but commissioners said they hope that will not be the case. Greer said the fencing helps the plants take hold and without it, they could be installing thousands of plants each year.
"It's the project that keeps giving," Greer said, sarcastically.
The town has been urging the Strand Project's contractor, Underwood and Associates, to complete the living shoreline for several months. On Tuesday, commissioners discussed changing contractors from Underwood and Associates, which the town still has the power to do at this stage of the project.
During the open comments period, resident Jan Greenhawk suggested that the town sue Underwood and Associates.
"I'm going to be short and sweet. I know you're going to closed session and you're going to talk about legal issues," Greenhawk said. "I'm going to give you an opinion, and I think a lot of people in town might agree with this: We need to seek legal action against this contractor. I think he pulled a fast one on the town of Oxford."
Underwood and Associates was unable to comment on the situation before The Star Democrat's deadline.
Currently, there is no ADA accessibility at the Strand Beach and the little walking room there is on the street is consumed by an 80-inch standing puddle.
"(The standing water) has been an outstanding problem for this project for years, and years and years," Donovan said.
There will be an update on the Strand's stormwater issues at the next meeting, which will take place Aug. 12 at 6 p.m. at 101 Market Street.

title: As Easton Works on Storm Drains, Future Needs Could Present Challenges
author: Konner Metz
content:
As Easton works on storm drains, future needs could present challenges

 June 6, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 594
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Engineers in Easton are aiming to take a proactive approach to the town's storm drain infrastructure as they look to address flooding in susceptible areas.At an Easton Town Council meeting last month, Town Engineer Rick Van Emburgh and Engineering Director Kody Cario said the town is currently performing video analysis on its storm drains on an as-needed basis. That leaves them in a reactionary position, Cario said.
"We don't know what we don't know right now, and that's concerning to us," he said at the May 19 meeting. "Because we don't know what the next problem could be."
Cario and Van Emburgh explained the town's ongoing storm drain projects and outlined proposals for how to fund future storm drain repair needs. The update to the council comes as experts say storms are putting more of a strain on drain systems.
Easton saw nearly two inches of rain on May 16. Engineers say some storm drain systems were "overwhelmed."
"When we have nights like we did last Friday night (May 16), you see how important it is to make sure that our storm drains are maintained," Van Emburgh said.
Environmental experts say this type of rain event may become more common in coming years.
"That sort of high intensity is what is expected as climate change impacts continue," said ShoreRivers Choptank Riverkeeper Matt Pluta in an interview. "Those storms are different from what we were used to 50 years ago, where a sprinkle or a moderate rain was common."
Pluta said storm drains can't always handle heavy rains and hail.
BEING PROACTIVE
Easton has 351,000 linear feet of storm drain pipe, or around 66 miles. Most of it is concrete, though the town also has plastic, metal, clay and brick pipes. Some of the older infrastructure dates back decades and could present road or water safety challenges according to town officials. But without video analysis done in advance, it's difficult for the town to know what needs to be replaced until it fails.
In hopes of gaining a more complete understanding of the condition of Easton's storm drains, Cario noted a few rough proposals from the engineering department: $500,000 for an emergency storm drain repair fund, $300,000 over six years to assess the town's other watersheds and $25,000 annually for storm drain analysis.
"Eventually we'd like to perform, yearly, a video analysis of our storm drain so that we can start checking through and seeing what the condition of our storm drains are," Cario said at the May meeting.
The proactiveness in video analysis could prevent the town from having to assume unexpected costs when emergency storm drain damages occur. The emergency repair fund would cover "what might be a catastrophic repair on the street," Cario said.
As considerations of future funding are put forward, some of Easton's storm drain systems are receiving attention this summer. Thanks to American Rescue Plan Act federal funding, Easton is forging ahead on two storm drain projects that fall within the Tanyard Branch watershed, a 900-acre area that drains into the Tred Avon River.
First is the mostly-completed Harrison Street effort. The town replaced a lot of brick pipe with reinforced concrete pipe, or RCP, Cario said in an interview. RCP generally has a longer service life compared to clay and brick pipes.
Crews worked Wednesday to repave Harrison Street as part of the project's final touches. Cario said the town appreciates the patience of residents through the multi-month process, which has included road closures.
In a few weeks, the town will embark on its East Avenue project, which is especially meant to address storm drain and flooding issues on August Street.

title: In Visit to Easton, Secretary Day Commends County's Broadband Efforts
author: Konner Metz

In visit to Easton, Secretary Day commends county's broadband efforts

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News

 EASTON — Talbot County's mission to extend broadband to 100% of residents is within reach.During a roundtable discussion Wednesday with Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development Secretary Jake Day, county and broadband leaders said the Connect Talbot broadband initiative has the funding it needs.
"The Connect Talbot project is proof. It's proof that partnerships work," Easton Utilities President and CEO John Horner said. "We're here to say that at this point in time, Talbot County is the first county to be fully funded with enough grant funding to provide service to everyone in the county that does not have service."
Horner said the broadband effort is a "legacy project" and that it is within a year-and-a-half from completion.
Day spoke highly of the county and nonprofit utility company's efforts to connect rural residents with high-speed broadband access.
Day has visited several Eastern Shore counties in recent weeks to tour towns and discuss funding opportunities. Thursday, Day confirmed to Maryland Matters that he's raising money for an "exploratory effort" to challenge U.S. Rep. Andy Harris (R-Md.) in the 1st District that stretches the length of the Eastern Shore.
In Easton Wednesday, Day presented county and Easton Utilities leaders with a $1.1 million check of the grant the department awarded to the project last summer.
"We have been working our tail off to be your partner, to make sure that from Tilghman to Queen Anne to Trappe to Cordova, there is high-speed broadband," Day said. " ... We will make sure you've got the last money you need to get 100%."
According to the Department of Housing and Community Development, Maryland's Office of Statewide Broadband has facilitated $11.1 million in investments for Talbot County.
Talbot County Council Vice President Pete Lesher, who has been a longtime proponent for broadband infrastructure, said he's heard the calls from residents to focus on increasing internet access.
"I have colleagues and constituents who live not too many miles from here, who told me when I was running for office, you need to pay attention to this issue," Lesher said.
As of March, Easton Utilities and its Easton Velocity service had reached 1,900 subscribers since 2021, according to Easton Utilities communications director Kelly Simonsen.
Horner said the county helped the project get off its feet, and a U.S. Department of Agriculture program was an "enormous stepping stone" to begin serving two-thirds of Talbot County residents.
Five grants from the state helped the project forge ahead, Horner said.
"We are on schedule," Lesher said. "We are going to deliver on this, every single address, all those 3,600 addresses. And I am getting the happy calls and happy emails from constituents already all over the county. This is really transformational."

title: Strand Beach Project Not Yet Approved for Completion
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Strand Beach project not yet approved for completion

 April 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 678
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — Small grasses, planted this month, mark something of a turning point for Oxford's Strand Beach, which many residents say has been an eyesore in town since 2023.The new plants are the result of a push by the town for the Strand Beach project's contractor, Underwood and Associates, to finish the job of creating a living shoreline that would prevent erosion and flooding.
Although new grasses have been planted, Oxford Town Manager Holly Wahl said the town has not yet signed off on final completion of the project, which Underwood and Associates was required to finish by April 19.
"We are analyzing all of the work, and we are working with our regulating agencies, the Army Corps of Engineers and the State of Maryland," Wahl said. "They are assessing it as well and making an evaluation."
The grasses were one part of the contractor's job. Other tasks included lowering the islands on the beach, removing temporary access to the islands and installing a grassy strip along the road to prevent sand from flowing into the road.
The work this month comes after Oxford's previous town manager signed off on the project's completion in June 2024.
At a town meeting in December, the Commissioners of Oxford announced the project had not been completed to the specifications Underwood and Associates originally presented. Commissioner Katrina Greer said she had brought together the Maryland Department of the Environment, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Underwood and Associates and the organizations that funded the project to ensure Underwood and Associates would address the town's concerns.
Wahl said there are a "few concerns" that Underwood and Associate's work this month did not fully bring the project into compliance with the project permit. She said she is working with regulating agencies to complete a list of those concerns.
Although the project is still being evaluated to determine everything was completed, Wahl said the town is looking forward to having this phase of the project complete.
"We're doing everything we can to make sure that its purpose of providing stability on that coastal shoreline is adhered to," she said.
CONCERNS FROM RESIDENTS
The Strand Beach project, which was approved in 2021, has stirred up questions and concerns from residents over the years.
Wahl said she has been meeting with residents on the beach to update them on progress. She said residents have raised concerns about the proximity of the dunes and evergreens to the road.
She said she has made a request to relocate the evergreens out of concern they are too close to the road. Regarding the dunes, Wahl said the town is preparing to install sand fencing to stabilize the area.
For resident Mac Sommerlatte, who lives next to the beach, a significant issue with the project remains.
"This is partially completed," he said.
Sommerlatte, who has been involved with the project since before 2021, said he has a contract with the town, which includes that the bulkhead on his property will be fixed as part of the project. He said only some of the bulkhead has been fixed.
Wahl told The Star Democrat the town's engineer examined the bulkhead on Sommerlatte's area and determined the "whole area has been armored.
"And so there is no concern at all about stability of that location," she said.
Sommerlatte said he and his lawyer are reviewing information and considering filing a lawsuit against the town.
"It's not that I'm railing against anyone," he said. "That's not what I'm trying to do. I just want them to complete the work that they agreed to before they started the project."
Wahl said she had no comment on the potential lawsuit.
THE NEXT PHASE
The town sees the shoreline project as the first phase in addressing the Strand. Wahl said once the town has signed off on the completion of the shoreline project, it plans to move on to raising the road and building a water retention area where the parking lot is.
"We definitely have to do some work to address the stormwater that is pooling on the roadway," Wahl said. "So those are additional phases that the commissioners will be talking about here soon in a public meeting."

title: Easton Accepts Transfer of Easton Village Roads, Hears Resident Concerns
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton accepts transfer of Easton Village roads, hears resident concerns

 April 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 502
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Easton Town Council accepted ownership Monday of roads in the Easton Village development, though the transfer of the roads was met with safety concerns from residents.Located off of Easton Parkway and Saint Michaels Road, the neighborhood sits adjacent to the Tred Avon River. Council members unanimously agreed to take on ownership of 28 roads, alleys and rights-of-way, as well as nearly nine acres of open and park space located in the development.
The town will assume responsibility for upkeep of the roads. Town attorney Sharon VanEmburgh said the town is working on a memorandum of understanding to outline how the town and homeowners association will split park maintenance duties.
The conveyance was contingent on the developers, Easton Village LLC, completing a list of work, such as sidewalk, street lights and land restoration improvements. Town officials said most of that work has been done.
But most of Monday's discussion — as well as back-and-forth at a town meeting last month — centered around safety concerns from residents at two Easton Village homes and why a shared driveway between their homes isn't designated as an alley.
Resident Marc Ebersberger said since the lane next to his residence is designated as a shared driveway, his home isn't easily located on GPS systems. He and his neighbors said there have been multiple health emergencies during which response was delayed or they flagged down responders who could not locate the home.
"Twenty minutes could be the difference between permanent disability or recovery, or between life and death," Ebersberger said.
Ebersberger said by sifting through meeting minutes he found the Planning Commission voted not to allow shared driveways to move forward in Easton Village in 2016.
Ryan Showalter, an attorney representing Easton Village LLC, said the two lots and their shared driveway was recorded on a plat in 2015 before the Planning Commission held any discussion of shared driveways.
Town attorney Sharon VanEmburgh said Monday the town believed the issue with Ebersberger was resolved in 2023. She said town staff isn't looking for the shared driveway designation to be changed since "it's not set up to be an alley."
She said shared driveways are still allowed per subdivision regulations.
Town Council members agreed the safety concerns are imminent, though they largely emphasized that approving the road and park transfers was a separate issue from residents' requests.
Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis asked to move forward with the conveyances while noting residents "need to be heard."
"It sounds like to me the can has been kicked down the road and it's been kicked down a little too long," Davis said.
"If we're talking about a life safety issue, this should be a no-brainer," Ward 1 Councilmember Maureen Curry said.
After approving the road and park transfers, the council passed a motion for town engineers to install a street sign and light near the homes in question in the next 60 days. Mayor Megan Cook added she would reach out to Talbot County Emergency Services to discuss how dispatchers can improve response times to the Easton Village homes.

title: Commissioners of Oxford Hear Plans for Portable Pump Stations
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Commissioners of Oxford hear plans for portable pump stations

 March 13, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 481
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — In an effort to address flooding caused by rainy day events, Oxford is looking into setting up portable stormwater pump stations across town.During a Commissioners of Oxford meeting Tuesday, engineer Wayne Newton presented plans to install four temporary, portable pump stations in three locations in town: Two stations near the causeway, one station at Bank Street and one station at Mill Street.
Newton is the president of Messick & Associates, an engineering firm the town has a contract with. He said he expects the pump stations will relieve moderate flooding, which he defined as anything less than storm surge.
"A storm surge comes in, it comes over the bulkhead, it comes over the causeway, that's not what we're planning for here," he said. "We're just planning for rainy day events."
Oxford Wastewater Superintendent Matt Ozman, who has been working closely with Newton, said the pumps will allow the town to drain water faster.
"It's the plan of moving the water where it's not going to take us days, it'll be hours," Ozman said.
Oxford Commission President Norm Bell said the town is trying to take a step back, look at what it would like to see in the future and determine what is needed today in order to build toward that.
"So this is more of a holistic viewpoint than what we've been looking at previously," he said.
Commissioner Tom Costigan said the portable pump stations are more flexible than permanent pump stations in the ground.
"You can take our solution and move it to where the problem is instead of having a problem and saying, 'Oh, well we've got this really neat pump station eight blocks away,'" he said.
Along with placing portable pump stations in the low-lying areas Newton identified, Newton also outlined plans to address the existing drain system on Mill Street that runs through the marina. He said he would like to re-grade and rebuild some of the drain system so water drains toward the water tower and the pump station can be moved to that area.
"We'd prefer (the pump station) to be down there," Newton said about the area where the water tower is. "There's more room for it down there."
Newton said over the next month, his office plans to work on designs and cost estimates for the project that he can bring back to the commissioners for review. He said his goal is to have the project complete by the end of 2025.
The project will be funded using American Rescue Plan Act funds.
Ozman considers this project to be laying the foundation when it comes to addressing flooding issues. He said the town can hone in on these three areas first, then address flooding in other areas.
"We're trying to do the best that we can with the money that's available at the time without having to spend millions on something that can't be moved, can't be touched, can't be retrofitted," he said.

title: 'A Milestone': Demolition of Talbot County Business Center a Big Step for Easton Airport
author: Konner Metz
content:
'A milestone': Demolition of Talbot County Business Center a big step for Easton Airport

 March 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 308
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Wednesday morning, the Town of Easton granted Reynolds Excavating Inc. a demolition permit to begin work on the former Talbot County Business Center.Later that day, demolition had already begun.
The clearing of the property is part of the second phase of Easton Airport's airfield modernization project, a long-term effort to improve the airport's safety and operations.
Micah Risher, Easton Airport's manager, said the demolition is a major step in the modernization efforts, which began in 2006.
"This is a milestone," Risher said. "We've been waiting for 20 years to get to this point."
Once cleared, the site will become a runway protection zone, meant to improve safety in case of an aircraft crash or extended landing.
The business center, previously a Black & Decker facility, saw its tenants move out in 2023 and 2024, all of whom successfully relocated.
Thursday, significant work on the building's southwest end nearest to Glebe Road was underway. The building's exterior and roof were in the process of being torn down.
Risher noted that an environmental report was completed to ensure demolition is handled properly. Testing and mitigation measures were taken to abide by state and federal regulations.
Risher said the site will mostly be made up of open, green space, along with airfield lighting.
"It's a big environmental improvement project," Risher said.
Additionally, scrap materials from the building will be reused, Risher said. Asphalt and concrete will be crushed and repurposed for the new airfield, while aluminum will be recycled by Reynolds Excavating.
Easton Airport will continue operations during demolition. The building is expected to be mostly demolished later this spring, with site work and recycling continuing throughout the year.
Risher expressed excitement that the demolition is underway. He said it's a step forward in swapping one economic driver, the former business center, for a new one, the runway zone and overall airfield upgrade.
"The reality is it's being transformed," Risher said.

title: Trappe, Talbot County Council Discuss Contentious Sewer Connection
author: Konner Metz
content: Trappe and Talbot County officials held a back-and-forth discussion at Tuesday's County Council meeting regarding an industrial property's sewer connection to Trappe's wastewater treatment plant. The discussion centered around whether the connection of Paris Foods Corporation to the treatment plant was done properly. The connection was approved in 2021 and became active in 2022, according to Trappe officials. Lyndsey Ryan, Trappe's attorney, said the town approved that connection with the understanding that Paris Foods sat on a parcel classified as S-1, meaning the connection did not require county approval. But that understanding was based on what officials say were "erroneous maps" attached to Resolution 281, a piece of county legislation. "Recently, it's been brought to Trappe's attention that … the Paris Foods property was actually unprogrammed," Ryan said Tuesday. First introduced in 2019, Resolution 281 amended the county's comprehensive plan to reclassify certain portions of Lakeside — an ongoing 2,501-home development east of U.S. Route 50 in Trappe — for immediate priority for water and sewer service. The resolution's attached maps showed properties not part of the Lakeside development to have incorrect water and sewer classifications. Paris Foods sits on the same side of Route 50 as Lakeside, just south of Lakeside's already-built homes. The map errors came to light in the fall of 2021, county and town officials say. The maps incorrectly showed Paris Foods as S-1, while the resolution's text included correct classifications. As Paris Foods and Trappe now work toward applying for an amendment to the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan to designate Paris Foods as S-1, County Council Vice President Pete Lesher pushed for answers on why it wasn't done sooner. "You were aware that the maps were erroneous, by that time, by November of 2021?" Lesher asked. "I don't believe that it was really brought to our attention," Ryan responded. "I know that there was speculation to the maps being erroneous. But again, at the time, we were focused on Lakeside and the other properties." Ryan emphasized that at the time Trappe approved Paris Foods' connection, there had been "no discussion about the maps of (Resolution) 281 being incorrect." "Certainly, had we been aware of that and looked into the issue, we wouldn't have approved the connection," she said. Lesher later asked Ryan when the town became "aware of this illegal connection." "From our opinion, the connection was not illegal, or there was not an act from the town to make it illegal," Ryan said. Ryan said the town realized last fall that Paris Foods never went through the process to amend the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan. The town informed the county of the Paris Foods situation in December via a letter. Lesher said his main concern was the "long gap between when the erroneous maps came to light in November of 2021 and this report to the county in December of 2024." "We are apologetic for that," Ryan said. "I know that you're a very sharp attorney," Lesher said. "I hope that you'll not disappoint your client next time, and not rely on mere maps and take a sharper look at the text." Council Member Keasha Haythe asked if moving forward, the town and county could better communicate regarding any water and sewer connections. Trappe Town Council President Brian Schmidt said Trappe will "absolutely" work to better that communication.

title: Tunis Mills Bridge Replacement Project Moves Forward
author: Konner Metz
content:
Tunis Mills bridge replacement project moves forward

 January 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 629
 Words 

 Read News Document

 TUNIS MILLS — A beloved bridge in the Tunis Mills community is moving toward reconstruction after months of resident input into the bridge's redesign.In recent years, the 345-foot-long Leeds Creeks Bridge and its wood planks have deteriorated. County engineers consider the bridge structurally deficient, necessitating a replacement.
Tuesday, the Talbot County Council agreed to move forward with the bridge replacement project. County Engineer Ray Clarke recommended the county work toward finalizing rights-of-way acquisitions and necessary permits so construction can be pursued later this year.
As proposed, the replacement would include a wooden deck and a timber wearing surface. The structures below the bridge supporting it, known as piles, would consist of concrete and steel materials.
Clarke told council members that in order to use federal funding for the project, the bridge replacement project cannot use timber piles per the State Highway Administration. He added that trying to build an all-timber replacement will cause significant delays and costs.
"The big disadvantage we have is that if we don't get the federal aid, we're probably going to need to request the council for additional funding for the project, local funding," Clarke said. " … This could be a $3 or $4 million ask."
The project costs around $6.5 million, with $1.5 million coming from the county. The rest is federally funded.
Advocates of a 100% wooden replacement have been in dialogue with the county, including at an August public meeting. Susan McDermott and John Tabori, two of those advocates, have lived in Tunis Mills next to the bridge for four years.
McDermott says the original proposal to rebuild the bridge many years ago "was just unacceptable to the community." The county's recent proposal matches more of what she and some other neighbors had hoped for.
"We're very pleased that the council has shown as much flexibility toward community views as it has," McDermott said.
Residents like McDermott previously expressed concerns that an asphalt wearing surface would encourage speeding across the bridge. The county's plans now include a timber wearing surface. Clarke said that change will amount to around a $250,000 increase.
The other main change based on community feedback is a reduction in the height of the safety railing from 42 to 36 inches.
McDermott, who leads a small group of neighbors called the Tunis Mills All-Timber Bridge Alliance, hopes to find answers to whether an exception can be made for the requirement that piles not be timber.
She adds that the bridge is an integral part of the community.
"I think the town feels that the wooden bridge of Tunis Mills — one of the last wooden-deck bridges in the county — is very much part of the community," McDermott said. "It's not just a bridge that occasional traffic goes across. We've got a lot of walkers in this neighborhood, a lot of kids and people just use that bridge as a foot path."
After a video of the bridge was shown during the meeting, Talbot County Council Member Lynn Mielke said it seems the replacement "needs to be done sooner rather than later."
Talbot County Council Vice President Pete Lesher thanked Clarke and his team for their efforts to advance the replacement project.
"I appreciate the homework that you've done to investigate the alternatives as requested and appreciate that we really can't sacrifice the federal aid," Lesher said. "The economics of this project dictate that we absolutely need to go with the recommended steel concrete pilings and concrete cap."
Lesher motioned to approve the project as presented, and the rest of the council unanimously agreed. Lesher added that he hopes the federal funding for the project comes through, referencing President Donald Trump's temporary pause on federal grants and loans announced earlier this week and rescinded Wednesday.
"And we'll just hope that any suspension of federal grant aid for transportation projects is very short-lived," Lesher said Tuesday.

title: Oxford Commissioners Tackle Strand Project Issues with Meeting
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford Commissioners tackle Strand project issues with meeting

 December 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 527
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — During a Commissioners of Oxford meeting Tuesday, the commissioners talked about the Strand Beach project, acknowledging its bumpy path toward completion."Many of you have asked me (if) the project on the Strand — the beach part of the project — (was) completed," Commissioner Katrina Greer said to residents at the meeting. "And no, it wasn't completed."
Greer said that although contractor Underwood and Associates was paid to create a living shoreline on Oxford's waterfront, the project was not finished to the specifications that Underwood and Associates had originally presented.
The project plan was to create a berm, place hooks along the east and west areas of the Strand to bring in sand, create small islands in the water to reduce waves coming onto the beach and plant low marsh grasses on those islands.
Greer said that to date, not all of the grasses have been planted on the islands and the islands are two feet higher in elevation than they're supposed to be. She said previous Town Manager Cheryl Lewis signed off on the project in June.
"Now we did pay the contractor in June," Greer said. "And so we needed to bring some leverage to the table to be able to have the contractor bring the project back in line with what had been permitted and what we had been owed."
Greer said she made some phone calls and brought together compliance and permitting staff within the Maryland Department of the Environment and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, as well as the organizations that funded the project and the contractor. The meeting with the different groups was held Dec. 10.
"And I will say we came away with exactly what we wanted," Greer said.
Out of the meeting, the town was able to ensure that — at no cost to the town — Underwood and Associates will bring down the elevation of the islands to the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers' specs and take out the sand that goes out to the headlands, which was part of the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers' permitting.
"For us to leave the sand there was a permitting noncompliance issue," Greer said. "It's a very strong word in front of this contractor. He is sitting there looking at his future permitting, his future funding, and they all told him pretty resoundingly that this needed to be done and that the deviation from the permit was unacceptable."
Greer said Underwood and Associates also agreed to put all of the plantings in. The group will need to address all of these issues before April 19, which is the end of the period for installation, to keep the project in compliance.
"So the pressure's on," Commission President Norm Bell said.
Greer said she was glad they were able to have have the meeting and she hopes that in the future, the town won't have to do this with other projects.
Commissioner Tom Costigan expressed hope that it will be smooth sailing going forward.
"There's going to be good discussion after the meeting too, between the actual contractor and the compliance people," he said. "So hopefully there's communication between the two of them and any sort of problems won't rear their ugly heads again."

title: Trappe to Make Changes to Playground and Get a Speed Trailer

 TRAPPE — On Tuesday evening, the Trappe Town Council held a special meeting to discuss the use of over $277,000 in remaining funds from the American Rescue Plan Act. Council members voted to approve using funds for the Lakeview Playground and a speed trailer.During the meeting, Erin Braband, Trappe's clerk, gave a run down of the ARPA funds, pandemic relief money from the federal government. title: Easton Utilities to Join Electric Utility Alliance
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Easton Utilities to join electric utility alliance

 October 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 393

 EASTON — Easton Utilities is positioning to join a municipal alliance with four other electric utility agencies across the state following support from the Easton Town Council on Monday evening.Councilmembers unanimously approved a resolution authorizing Easton Utilities to join in forming the Maryland Municipal Electric Utility Alliance. The other municipalities are Berlin, Hagerstown, Thurmont and Williamsport.
Easton Utilities, a not-for-profit utility and telecommunications company, provides electric, natural gas, water, internet and more to residents of the town ans surrounding areas. Company leaders say the alliance will facilitate a shared voice between the five members on "legislative and regulatory matters."
John Hines, vice president of electric operations and special projects at Easton Utilities, spoke to the Town Council on Monday.
"Formalizing an alliance of these shared interests will strengthen our collective positions in Annapolis during the General Assembly's legislative session," Hines said, "at a time when energy issues continue to be at the forefront of policymakers' agendas."
The alliance's articles of incorporation had already been signed by the mayors of Berlin and Thurmont prior to Monday's approval. Representatives from all five municipalities, including Mayor Megan Cook, gathered in Berlin for a workgroup session to discuss the potential alliance.
"How do you anticipate navigating a vote amongst the alliance that is unfavorable to Easton Utilities and the Town of Easton?" Council President Frank Gunsallus asked Hines.
"There may be issues that don't necessarily help us, but don't hurt us," Hines responded. "And so, at the end of the day, the broader organization and the power that comes from five bodies really will create a bigger impact."
Hines added that Easton Utilities can withdraw from the alliance at any time, and that "it still gives each local government the ability to act autonomously.
Gunsallus called it a "great idea," and all four councilmembers present voted to approve the resolution.
HOSPITAL UTILITIESThe Town Council approved a second resolution Monday evening involving Easton Utilities. Resolution 6201 authorizes the utility company to extend service to what will be Shore Regional Health's new medical center on Longwoods Road in Easton.
The medical center, which held a groundbreaking earlier Monday, is under construction and projected to open in the summer of 2028. It is replacing the current hospital on South Washington Street.
Since Easton Utilities' electric, water and wastewater services to support the project will exceed $2 million, a resolution was necessary. All four councilmembers present voted to approve the resolution.

title: Talbot County Establishes Bike and Pedestrian Committee
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot County establishes bike and pedestrian committee

 September 27, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 409
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A bicycle and pedestrian advisory committee will soon be up and running in Talbot County after the Talbot County Council unanimously approved an administrative resolution on last week.Council Vice President Pete Lesher made the request for the resolution, which will create a committee intended to gather community input regarding bike and pedestrian safety and accessibility in Talbot County.
Lesher said it came in response to a bike and pedestrian trails public workshop held in July.
"I was asked that we put this together to advise council, as we have with other advisory boards, to ensure that we're getting input from representative groups around the county," Lesher said.
He said the committee will be made up of representatives from varying disciplines, including the farming, business, school and police communities.
Heather Grant, executive director of Talbot Thrive, a nonprofit dedicated to outdoor safety and health, said in an interview that it's important for the county to push for a bike and pedestrian master plan. This committee can be a first step in that effort, similar to what she's seen in neighboring Queen Anne's County.
"We really thought that that's needed in Talbot County," Grant said of a master plan. "And the way that Queen Anne's County went about getting that done is they first established a bike and pedestrian advisory committee back in 2008. So we really thought Talbot County was kind of behind the eight-ball on that."
At the July workshop, county officials, employees and community members gathered to discuss plans for a 9.5-mile Frederick Douglass Rail Trail, stretching from the town of Queen Anne to just north of Easton.
Some farmers expressed concerns about safety if that trail is built, referencing potential dangers of farmers using large equipment in such proximity to bikers and walkers.
Grant said the committee will facilitate "perspectives from all different groups" in Talbot County.
"We want them to have a seat at the table, and this is the best way to do that," Grant said.
She is excited for the committee's establishment, not just for the benefit of bicyclists, but also those who walk or use wheelchairs.
"I really think that we can really change our community and make it more friendly and safer for those people," Grant said. "And I think that everyone should be excited about having a more friendly community where we don't totally depend on cars."
After council members granted approval for the committee's creation, Lesher said the next step is working with county staff to recruit committee members.

title: Partial Closure of Route 662 Will Begin in October
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Partial closure of Route 662 will begin in October

 September 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 402
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A portion of Route 662 is expected to temporarily close beginning in October, according to the University of Maryland Shore Regional Health.Shore Regional Health's project on Longwoods Road in Easton is bringing a new medical center to the region. Due to a portion of hospital designs that sit on top of the current Longwoods Road, or Route 662, the roadway is expected to be closed for seven to eight months.
That projected timeframe gives Shore Regional Health time to construct a modified portion of Route 662 slightly eastwards. The closure will ensure there is no delay or interference with construction work on the new hospital.
"While we regret possible inconvenience this may cause to motorists, we want to assure the community that detailed contingency and emergency management plans are in place," Shore Regional Health CEO and President Ken Kozel said in a press release on Friday.
"We have been working collaboratively with the State Highway Administration as well as Talbot County and Easton roads and emergency management officials to plan for safe and efficient management of a wide range of emergency scenarios."
The state's official detour will be Route 50. However, many residents and farmers have raised concerns that the temporary closure will impact traffic on nearby county roads, such as Hiners Lane, Airport Road and Goldsborough Neck Road.
"Our priority is to minimize disruptions while ensuring that essential services remain accessible throughout the construction period," Talbot County Sheriff Joe Gamble said in a press release. "The Talbot County Sheriff's Office is working closely with all partners to maintain safe and reliable transportation routes during this time."
On Wednesday, the Maryland Board of Public Works approved the State Highway Administration to transfer about a half-mile of Route 662 to Talbot County.
That step will allow Talbot County to transfer the road to Shore Regional Health prior to Oct. 1 so relocation work can begin. Last month, the Talbot County Council approved a bill that permits the road can now be transferred to Shore Regional before the new route is completed.
The closure will extend from Airport Road north to Hiners Lane, which is around a mile stretch of the road. On Friday, Shore Regional Health said the closure will begin "on or around" Oct. 1.
Shore Regional Health's medical center is scheduled to complete in the summer of 2028. It is replacing the current medical center on South Washington Street.
To follow construction progress on the hospital, visit umshoreregional.org/rmc.
