 On March 6, the Trappe Town Council met and approved construction bids, an easement agreement and a smoke test for Trappe.BUDGET
The council voted to accept Schumer Inc.'s bid for the pumping station construction project, contingent on the U.S. Department of Agriculture's approval.
The pumping station project is comprised of three out of the seven pumping stations around Trappe. The three that are a part of this phase of the project are located on Rumsey Drive, Main Street and Harrison Circle.
The budget for the pump station construction has increased due to engineering and construction contingencies, according to Lyndsey Ryan, town attorney. The USDA has recommended applying for additional funding to cover the cost of the project.
Due to upcoming grant deadlines, Ryan suggested a resolution allowing Town Administrator Erin Braband to sign loan and grant applications with the USDA.
The resolution limits the signature to this specific project for the additional amount beyond Phase 1 that needs to be funded. It would allow her to execute any application and any necessary documents without having to come back to the council.
The administrator would not be authorized to accept the funding on behalf of the council. Ryan said Braband only would be permitted to submit the application for the funding.
The council approved the motion with all commissioners approving except for Commissioner Rosalee Potter. Potter said she was "unsure" of the information provided.
EASEMENT
The council unanimously approved the easement agreement for a new sewer line serving the Dollar General store. This agreement is contingent on either the agreement being revised to include an easement for the existing line or confirming the town already had an easement for that line.
The agreement would allow the town access under both the new and existing sewer lines located on the Dollar General property in the future if maintenance were required. The sewer main will run along Route 50.
Ryan said they would review whether the town already had an easement for the existing line or revise the agreement as needed before final approval.
SMOKE TEST
The Town of Trappe will schedule a smoke test for the sewer system on April 23. This test will help identify infiltration issues and, by allowing smoke to escape, show where there are holes in pipes and clean-outs.
This smoke test is expected to help determine which sections of town should be prioritized for camera scoping of sewer lines. The public works staff would document the locations of any issues found during the smoke test. The overall cost for the town-wide smoke test was estimated to be between $200 and $300.

title: St. Michaels Issues Update On Marengo Street Pump Station Fire
author: Town Of St. Michaels
content:
St. Michaels Issues Update On Marengo Street Pump Station Fire

 December 15, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Town Of St. Michaels | Page: 5 | Section: News 
 
 420
 Words 

 Read News Document

 On Dec. 3, one of two of the Town of St. Michaels' water treatment plants experienced a major fire, making the facility inoperable. The cause of the fire is still being investigated by the State Fire Marshal but does not appear to be arson-related.Fortunately, the Town has plenty of water capacity to serve the community in the coming months when demand is low during winter and early spring.
Nonetheless, with only a single, operable water treatment plant online, there is some potential of temporary domestic water service interruptions.
Please be assured that Town staff has quickly implemented precautionary and proactive measures to minimize any interruptions in water service to our community. To this end, we have implemented the following measures over the past several days: ¡ Hosted a meeting with Talbot County Emergency Services and other agencies to alert them of the issue.
¡ Coordinated with Town engineers and water treatment equipment suppliers to review all treatment processes in the current operable water plant along with securing back-up equipment if a mechanical failure were to occur.
¡ Worked with St. Michaels Fire Department to establish protocols for the use of alternative water sources if a major fire were to occur.
¡ As lead time for replacement of pump and electronic equipment for the Marengo Station is many months out, the Town is coordinating efforts with our engineers in the development of a temporary water treatment system to be located at the Marengo site creating critical water system redundancy and capacity that will be needed in the coming months.
Engineers have also started to order replacement equipment for the Marengo site.
¡ Costs associated with this fire will be paid for by the Town's insurance carrier minimizing any use of local tax dollars.
With recent emergency planning efforts well underway, the Town is in a much better position than last week. Although there is no mandatory water conservation order at this time, we would appreciate any efforts from the community to voluntarily conserve water in the coming months.
We are optimistic this will be resolved without interruptions in water service. Please be rest-assured that the Town Commission and staff are working diligently to resolve this issue as quickly as possible.
We will keep the community informed with future Constant Contact communications and through updates to our website at www.stmichaelsmd.gov.
If you should have any questions or concerns, please do not hesitate to contact Town Administrator Rob Straebel at 410-745-9535.

title: County Council Approves Vehicle Weight Limit On Black Dog Alley
author: Natalie Jones; Njones@Chespub.Com
content:
County Council Approves Vehicle Weight Limit On Black Dog Alley

 December 14, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; Njones@Chespub.Com | Page: B3 | Section: News 
 
 426
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - The Talbot County Council on Tuesday approved legislation establishing a vehicle weight limit on Black Dog Alley to reduce heavy truck through traffic.Resolution 351, which received unanimous support from council members, will prohibit vehicles over 17,000 pounds from traveling on Black Dog Alley, which runs between Cordova Road and Dover Road.
Some vehicles are exempt from the restrictions, including vehicles owned or operated by government entities and their employees, vehicles involved with agricultural production or operations, emergency vehicles, vehicles belonging to those whose land is located on or is only accessible via Black Dog Alley and vehicles providing services like heating oil delivery, trash pickup or property improvement.
Vehicles over the weight limit can use U.S.
Route 50 as an alternate route, which is better equipped to handle oversized vehicles and higher traffic volume.
The need for the legislation stems from maintenance and safety issues along the narrow roadway.
The concept of a weight limit on the road has previously been considered by the county.
The council introduced similar legislation in late 2019, but the resolution did not progress.
During the legislation's public hearing Tuesday, Talbot County farmer Keith Shortall, who lives off of Black Dog Alley, said while he does utilize the road for agricultural purposes during harvest season, he's noticed many trucks hauling grain from the Port of Baltimore down into Hurlock in Dorchester County year-round.
Shortall emphasized the need for advance signage for the change in vehicle allowance.
He also stressed the need for other improvements on the narrow parts of the road that don't have shoulder lanes.
" Regardless of what you do with this, the work that needs to be done on Black Dog Alley still needs to happen," he said.
Design for improvements to parts of Black Dog Alley is in progress, said Ray Clarke, the county engineer.
Talbot County Sheriff Joe Gamble echoed safety concerns, noting that Black Dog Alley is the most accident-prone road in the county.
Gamble also raised a flag to future traffic problems once the new regional medical center is constructed, saying Black Dog Alley will likely see more emergency vehicles coming from southern Caroline County utilizing the road.
Gamble said the sheriff 's office would start enforcement of the new restriction on Black Dog Alley in an educational way at first.
Citations are more likely to be handed out after an adjustment period.
John Trax, a Talbot County farmer and the "self-proclaimed mayor of Black Dog Alley," expressed full support for the resolution. He adding that he wished more could be added to it, namely ways to further address traffic and speeding.
The resolution took effect upon adoption.

title: Strand Beach Project To Be Completed By Summer
author: Maggie Trovato; Mtrovato@Chespub.Com
content:
Strand Beach Project To Be Completed By Summer

 December 13, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; Mtrovato@Chespub.Com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 839
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD - With the first phase of construction complete, Oxford's Shoreline Improvement project along the Strand is expected to be complete by summer.Oxford Town Manager Cheryl Lewis said the first part of the project, to build the shoreline infrastructure, "touched on nearly all parts of the project."
This part, which was completed before Thanksgiving, included building a berm between the road and the water, placing hooks along the east and west areas of the Strand to help bring sand in and creating small islands in the water to reduce the waves that come onto the beach.
Lewis said these island structures were built using a combination of rock, wood chips and other components.
"(The structures) will sit over the winter months, which allows them to stabilize," Lewis said. "It allows them to go through weather, high tides, we just had a fairly substantial storm, that sort of stuff."
Oxford Police Chief Eric Kellner said the construction brought in extra traffic, particularly with all of the materials that were brought in using larger vehicles like dump trucks.
In order to allow space for workers to do their job and to prevent damage to civilian vehicles, Kellner said that the police department, with the help of Public Works, closed the beach parking lot.
There were some concerns from residents about the large construction vehicles speeding in the area, Kellner said.
"In response to that, we did a few things," he said.
"One was, obviously, we ran radar to enforce the speed limits. And we also deployed our speed sign to remind the vehicles of their speed in hopes of calming any potential speed issues."
Kellner said that in running radar and collecting data from the speed sign, the police department really sees an issue with speeding.
He said that large and loud vehicles driving down a small, narrow street can sometimes give off the perception that the driver is speeding.
"Our findings were that most of those larger vehicles were following the rules of the road," he said.
In the spring, the second part of the project is set to begin.
"We're estimating April," Lewis said. "I mean a lot of this is dependent on weather temperatures, asphalt, plants, a lot of factors."
Lewis said the second part will include adding plants to the new structures, adding signage, elevating land on the far east end and making improvements to the parking lot.
"The whole concept is to build a higher area all along the Strand to protect it from the stormwaters off the river," Lewis said.
The parking lot will be built with storm management areas underneath it so that storm water can enter it and be filtered before going back out. The parking lot will be paved with asphalt, with a cobble layer underneath it.
"There's a lot of - not just tidal water coming from the river - but also stormwater settling along that road in the parking lot," Lewis said.
"So bringing all of that elevation up to prevent that and allowing the water to go under the road and then back out into the creek will basically build resilience for that whole area."
Lewis said that as the sea level rises and the intensity of storms increase, infrastructure along the Strand becomes more vulnerable.
"Keep in mind, this is the only road we really have that runs along the water," she said. "This area here, it's worthy of this type of resilience protection because a breach in any place, especially up near the parking lot, would be so difficult to repair."
Lewis called it a project for the future.
"With the impacts of sea level rise and stormwater and tidal water management that we're seeing currently," she said, "it's necessary to look at how to build in these areas with natural infrastructure that will help to protect it in the future."
David Ghysels, who walks along the Strand every day, said he thinks the project will be nice when it is complete, particularly if it helps with flooding.
Lewis said she has received positive and negative comments from residents on the project.
"I think the closer you are to the project physically, the more involved you may have been over the last five years," she said. "So I think that one of the impacts will be people who don't go there regularly or aren't involved in the government regularly all of a sudden want to know what happened. So it's really just a continued educational process."
Mac Sommerlatte, who lives next to the beach, said he thinks the project should, when finished, positively impact the town by minimizing shoreline erosion and mitigating the impact of sea level rise. He said the project is a complicated one.
"I think one of the problems is that there are several projects here," he said.
"It's not just one. And people don't seem to have the complete information on all of them. And they may disagree with parts of it."

title: MDOT Talks Investments in Talbot County
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
MDOT talks investments in Talbot County

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: 5 | Section: News

 EASTON - State, county and local officials packed the meeting room at the Talbot County Free Library Tuesday afternoon to hear the latest updates on the Maryland Department of Transportation's investments in county projects.The visit to Talbot County capped off another leg of the department's statewide tour discussing its sixyear Draft FY 2024-2029 Consolidated Transportation Program - a $21.2 billion investment into creating a safer, more accessible transportation system.The meeting, hosted by the Talbot County Council, featured Maryland Transportation Secretary Paul J. Wiedefeld and representatives from various state agencies.State Highway Administrator William Pines spoke about his agency's efforts to improve infrastructure and safety at several high-traffic locations within Talbot County.The agency initiated a $1.5 million study of Route 328 to assess safety and capacity improvements along a 1.6-mile stretch between U.S. Route 50 and Black Dog Alley. Delays are seen in this area from turning vehicles and queueing at signalized intersections, and there are limited pedestrian and bicycle facilities, Pines said.A public meeting on the Route 328 project is tentatively scheduled for this winter.Other transportation improvements within Easton include a $600,000 project for new lighting at the intersection of Route 50 and Route 322 (Easton Bypass) to improve visibility and safety, signal improvements and pedestrian upgrades - including a Rails to Trails link - at Route 322 and Glenwood Avenue, and a new signal at Route 50 and Chapel Road that will be activated by the end of November.In 2024, SHA will begin construction on two additional projects: reconstructing the signal at Route 50 and Route 309 and upgrading the flashing signal at Route 331 and Black Dog Alley to a full signal.Two local trail projects are also receiving federal and state grant funding, Pines said.$48,000 will go toward the final design of a 1.25-mile extension of the St. Michaels Nature and Bike Trail, and $30,000 will go toward the study and preliminary design of a rail trail connecting parks in Oxford.Turning to public transit, nearly $1.1 million in operating and capital grants are being allocated to support Delmarva Community Transit.$225,000 of this will fund preventative maintenance and two new small buses, said Travis Johnston, the Maryland Transit Administration's local transit support director.Delmarva Community Services will also receive $123,000 to install a propane filling station for future propane-powered vehicles, enabling DCS to transition to a low-emission fleet.Additionally, $24,000 in highway safety grants were awarded to the Talbot County Sheriff's Office and the Easton Police Department.Turning to the skies, the Easton Airport's runway improvement program is receiving $525,000 from the Maryland Aviation Administration to support the initial phase of construction.THINKING DOWN THE ROADLocal officials also weighed in on a number of priorities and problem areas they hope the transportation agency will address in the future.Discussions on traffic surrounding the proposed new regional medical center site off of Route 50 were top priorities for state legislators, the county and the Town of Easton. Rick Van Emburgh, Easton's town engineer, said he wanted to work with the county and the state on a regional traffic plan to handle the impact on local roads and infrastructure.Cheryl Lewis, Oxford's town manager, raised questions on the agency's response to flooding on the causeway and pedestrian safety in a town with few sidewalks.Queen Anne Mayor Philip Starkey asked if the agency would reevaluate fixing the bridge between the towns of Queen Anne and Hillsboro, which floods every time it rains, he said.Accessibility was raised as an issue in St. Michaels. According to Town Administrator Rob Straebel, all but one of the town's ADA ramps are not in compliance due to poor work from a contractor."I'm not sure what the way forward is, and I'm not here to point fingers or to blame anyone or to place culpability on anyone," he said. "But there really needs to be a sense of urgency to get this project rectified as soon as possible before our tourist season starts in the summer of 2024." Pines said the state was working to develop an "aggressive schedule" to get the project over the finish line.Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-37) further emphasized the need to fix the ramps, noting that Route 33, as the main road running through St. Michaels, doesn't just serve town residents, but residents of Claiborne, McDaniel, Sherwood and Tilghman.Several Royal Oak residents in attendance also raised concerns about the width and safety of Route 329 (Royal Oak Road), asking the transportation officials to lower the speed limit."I wish I could do everything that everyone asked immediately, but we will keep chipping away," Wiedefeld said, closing out the meeting.

 OXFORD - During a Commissioners of Oxford meeting Tuesday, Town Manager Cheryl Lewis gave an update on the Strand Beach project.The project, which was approved in April 2021, is intended to improve the beach shoreline.Lewis said she the project should begin Oct. 15, "give or take a day or two."The project will be completed in two phases, Lewis said. The first phase will take place in the water and on the beach. The second phase will be for the "above ground work.""The paving, the parking lot, that sort of thing," Lewis said.Lewis expects the first phase to be complete before the holidays and the second phase to be complete after the holidays, before spring. She said it will hopefully be completed in a six months."I just want to let everybody know because there will be some activity and you need to be aware of it," Lewis said. "Hopefully it won't be a huge deal because this is not the busiest time of year for that area of town."Along with the update, Lewis gave a breakdown of the project.For the beach, a berm will be created to run along the road between the road and the water. Hooks will be placed along the east and west areas of the Strand to help bring sand in, rather than erode out."The berm, the hooks, that will all be planted," Lewis said. "Typical living shoreline."Along with that, islands will be created in the water to reduce the waves that come onto the beach."Most of the time you won't even see [the islands]," Lewis said. "They'll be underwater, but they'll have grasses on them."To reduce erosion, living shorelines will also be constructed to the right of the ferry dock and behind the beach parking lot."The living shorelines are basically building up your beach," Lewis said. "Incorporating grasses that work well in the water and stabilizing the area."Lewis said the project will include reinforcing some of the areas between the parking lot and the Tred Avon Yacht Club building. These areas will be reinforced as living shorelines and incorporating a hook on the far west end of the Strand to reduce erosion.After that, Lewis said the above ground work will begin. The work will be between Norton Street and the last boatyard on the road. The road will be leveled out so that it doesn't dip down. A permeable layer will be added above the road before asphalt is laid on top of it."What that means is when we have the storm water or the flood water coming in, it will kind of sit under the road as opposed to on top, which is a problem we have now," Lewis said.The parking lot will be built with storm management areas underneath it so that storm water can enter it and be filtered before going back out."All we're really trying to do is to create a higher barrier along the north end of Oxford," Lewis said. "It will not stop flooding, per se. But it will add protection along that north end when it's hit by storms and prevent damage to our actual infrastructure."

title: Talbot County Passes 1-Cent Resolution for 2024 Ballot
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot County passes 1-cent resolution for 2024 ballot

 June 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 424
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Voters in Talbot County will see a familiar question on November's ballot.The Talbot County Council passed a resolution Tuesday to place a question on the 2024 ballot to amend the county's charter to raise residents' taxes for public safety.
The amendment would allow, but not require, the council to add up to 1 cent per $100 of assessed value above the revenue cap for an additional seven years beginning July 1, 2026.
After the council passed a similar 1-cent resolution in 2020, a majority of Talbot County voters in the 2020 general election approved the charter amendment.
Martha Sparks, the county's finance director, said the 1-cent resolution has allowed the county to add 26 public safety positions, including paramedics, EMTs, school resource officers and 911 operators. County Manager Clay Stamp vouched for the 1-cent resolution funding.
"In the last number of years, this additional funding has allowed us to see the best of our services," said Stamp, who is also the county's former emergency services director. "We've stabilized our workforce. We've been able to attract quality individuals as paramedics, correctional officers, deputy sheriffs. We've enhanced our technology, we've enhanced our coverage."
The original resolution from 2020 amended the charter for five years up until July 1, 2026. Resolution 359, which was passed Tuesday, adds an additional seven years.
Originally, Resolution 359 was introduced as extending five years. Council Vice President Pete Lesher proposed an amendment Tuesday to tack on the two additional years.
His reasoning for the amendment was to ensure any future extensions can be voted on by the public during presidential elections, when the ballot is more "uncrowded" than other elections. County council and gubernatorial elections are set to be in 2026 and 2030, meaning that if extended to only 2031, the 1-cent question may have appeared on a crowded 2030 ballot.
"By adding another two years, rather than having this expire in a council election year (or) a gubernatorial election year, this will extend it to the next presidential election year so that should this need to be renewed another time, it can be done when there isn't such a crowded ballot," Lesher said.
Council members unanimously approved the amendment 4-0 before passing the resolution by the same vote, with Council Member Dave Stepp absent.
Sparks said she's seen where the additional tax revenue has been spent, which is in "the areas that the public has supported," noting the new positions and increased funding to volunteer fire departments.
"It's very important for the public to know that they're doing good things to help us," Council President Chuck Callahan said.

title: Oxford Splits General Fund into Three New Funds
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Oxford splits general fund into three new funds

 July 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: News 
 
 385
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — The Town of Oxford has undergone a series of changes over the past year with a new election process, live-streamed town halls and a new town manager, Holly Wahl, who plans on streamlining more of the town's processes.Historically, the town has kept its finances in one general fund and allocated from there. But with the uncertainty of future federal funding, Oxford Town Commissioners, with the guidance of Wahl, and town staff have split the general fund into three separate funds: a general fund, an enterprise fund and the shore maintenance and protection fund.
"We had one budget that was adopted by commissioners each year," Wahl said. "And so the act this year was separating and having an ordinance for each fund being the general fund is one and then the two additional enterprise funds."
According to Wahl, the separation of funds is intended to improve transparency, finance stability and long-term planning for infrastructure projects like the Strand Beach project.
Commissioner Katrina Greer said part of the reasoning behind this decision was to appeal to federal and state grant opportunities, especially at a time when federal funding is uncertain. "Because you're showing that you can support yourself," Greer said. "You're managing the money and you're managing your expenses."
Wahl said commissioners and staff have created five- and 10-year capital improvement plans so the town can prioritize its budgetary needs.
"There may be some movement between fiscal years, but at least if we can prioritize and think about what those expenses are and plug them into a fiscal year so that staff can also prioritize their actions and work towards those projects and seek proposals," Wahl said.
Greer said that throughout the year, the town will start to allocate funds to build up reserves, look at capital and develop a capital plan. "So that means, look at all your infrastructure and all the things you want to do, have a five- or a 10-year plan, and then start to build our revenues accordingly," she said.
The new budget structure allows for proactive rather than reactive management of infrastructure needs, especially for critical systems like water and sewer which require preventative maintenance, Town Commissioners said.
Wahl said there is no plan to further restructure the budget at this time and the town will focus on effective project prioritization and adapting to funding uncertainties.

title: Talbot County OKs $161 Million Budget
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot County OKs $161 million budget

 May 28, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 685
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Talbot County made good on its promise to deliver a flat, conservative budget for fiscal year 2026. The County Council unanimously passed a $161.1 million spending plan Tuesday.It comes in at nearly $3 million under last year's budget amid what County Manager Clay Stamp calls "uncharted waters."
"The economic landscape out there is a bumpy ride right now," Stamp said. "This year, we knew that we needed to flatten the budget out, we needed to live within our means."
Stamp and other officials have emphasized Talbot County's continued financial commitments toward public safety, whether through capital projects such as an EMS station in Cordova or support for correctional officers.
In a draft version of the budget that only received a few adjustments Tuesday, the council is expected to allocate the following funds for public safety:
$11.5 million for emergency medical services.$10.5 million for the Talbot County Sheriff's Office.$7.6 million for the Department of Corrections.$5.4 million for emergency management.$3.3 million for volunteer fire departments.
Council members thanked Stamp, Finance Director Martha Sparks and Assistant Finance Director Kaitlin Foster-Clark for their work during the budget process.
"This was the most challenging budget that I've ever sat through," council member Keasha Haythe said. "The decisions were very hard on some items."
"It was definitely a heavy lift this year, but everyone bucked down, and we made it happen here," council member Dave Stepp said.
The county's property tax rate will remain largely steady at 79 cents per $100 of assessed value, though residents will see a supplemental tax of just over 1 cent per $100 of value on their tax bills.
EDUCATION FUNDING
That supplement stems from education funding OK'd by the county. While most line items were ironed out through deliberations, workshops and meetings, Tuesday's discussion centered on funding amendments for Talbot County Public Schools.
The budget already included $55 million in education funding as required by The Blueprint for Maryland's Future, the state's initiative to fund and improve education. County Council members were left to consider how much the county would contribute above that mark.
In a 4-1 vote Tuesday, the council approved an additional $600,000 in funding for schools, aimed at filling nine positions, including multilingual and special education roles. Council member Lynn Mielke was the sole no vote.
The approved budget change came after an amendment to fulfill the district's entire $1.1 million request — which had been scaled back from $5.5 million earlier this budget cycle — failed narrowly. Vice President Pete Lesher and Haythe favored the $1.1 million, but President Chuck Callahan, Stepp and Mielke did not.
Lesher argued it is "short-sighted" to not fund the full request. He said it'd be prudent for the county to gradually increase its education funding as even higher Blueprint projections loom in future fiscal years.
"This would be a small step in that direction," Lesher said. "And frankly, it will make next year, an election year, a lot easier for all of us up here."
"I think we should be going farther," he said of the $600,000 mark. "But this goes some distance."
Callahan sponsored the amendment to partially OK the district's request, citing the significant need for teachers. The $500,000 not approved by the council was requested by the district to increase teacher and instructional assistant salaries.
"I would ask that the school board use the money that we give you for (hiring) teachers," Callahan said. "I would like to see that, and not for something else."
Mielke said she was initially on board with Callahan's amendment. But she said she needs "more security" that the district will put the $600,000 toward the nine positions.
"I'm not advised that it necessarily would be," Mielke said. "So for that reason I couldn't support it."
A spokesperson for Talbot County Public Schools said in a statement to The Star Democrat that the district stands behind the $1.1 million request but understands the "challenges faced by council and staff in meeting the funding needs of Talbot County in these uncertain times."
"We are grateful for their support for educators' pensions and for the additional staff needed to serve our students," the statement read.
This story has been updated to include a statement from Talbot County Public Schools.

title: Easton Introduces Proposed $28M Budget for FY26

 EASTON — Mayor Megan Cook said Easton's fiscal year 2026 budget focuses on transitioning the town out of an era of one-time funding sources and pandemic-related dollars."That period of growth positioned us well, but now we shift our focus to the responsibility of maintaining what we built," Cook said. "This year's budget is lean, focused on sustaining our progress by investing in the essentials."
At Monday's Town Council meeting, Cook presented a balanced draft budget with $28 million in general funds, nearly even with last year's mark. The capital fund budget came in just above $1 million.
Easton's property tax rate will remain the same as it has been since 2008 — 52 cents per $100 of assessed value. The town is projected to bring in around $13.6 million in real property taxes, according to the draft fiscal year 2026 budget, slightly up from last year.
"When you compare tax rates across the region, Easton stands out," Cook said. "We have the second lowest municipal property tax rate among surrounding towns, but we're also the largest community and provide the most comprehensive range of services."
The budget aims to equip town government departments with the necessary tools and training to do their jobs, Cook said. While "it's not exciting as building new things," she said, it's an important focus.
In the draft fiscal year 2026 budget, just above $1 million is allocated for transfer to capital work. That's down from the around $2.2 million mark in fiscal year 2025.
Cook added that areas of government improvement will include adding safety features to town hall, providing leadership training to Easton employees and hiring a new town manager. The town has been without a permanent employee in that role since last August.
Expenditure categories in the draft general fund budget include:
Public safety (police, fire, code enforcement, etc.): $11.5 million.
Public works: $7.1 million.
General government (financial administration, IT, HR, planning and zoning, executive functions, etc): $5.3 million.
Economic development: $503,000.
Recreation: $192,000.

title: Counties Approve Chesapeake College Budget Request, Shift Cost of Tech Center
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Counties approve Chesapeake College budget request, shift cost of tech center

 April 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 526
 Words 

 Read News Document

 WYE MILLS — In a joint meeting Thursday, officials across Caroline, Dorchester, Kent, Queen Anne's and Talbot counties approved a shift in county cost shares for Chesapeake College's new technical building.During the meeting, which was held at the college's main campus in Queen Anne's County, the five counties approved a total $9.02 million budget request made by the college for fiscal year 2026. The school's budget is $1.31 million higher than its fiscal year 2025 budget.
Part of the $9.02 million budget request included a $952,560 request for the design of a new technical building. Chesapeake College Vice President for Administrative Services Karen Smith said the new building will have areas for a variety of programs, including agriculture, electrical, welding and fabrication, construction trades and advanced manufacturing. She said the cost for the design phase could be lower depending on state approval.
Although the five counties approved the request for funding for the design, the decision came with a shift in contributions toward the project.
Dorchester County's share of costs for the design phase will be taken on by Queen Anne's County. This means Queen Anne's County's responsibility for the project will jump from 28.9%, or an estimated $275,290, to 47.8%, or an estimated $455,324.
During the meeting, Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer and Vice President Mike Detmer outlined their council's concerns regarding paying for the project.
Although other counties hope to use the new technical building for career and technical education at the high school level, Dorchester County has a career and technology center it is still paying off, they said.
Through its budget process, Dorchester County has struggled to eliminate an estimated $6.2 million deficit.
Pfeffer said Dorchester County takes in about $45 million in property and income taxes and will have to give Dorchester County Public Schools $26.6 million for fiscal year 2026.
"So we're trying to run the rest of the county on half of that," he said. "So while in conceptual context, we believe in the project, fiscally our citizens and our staff are saying we don't know how we're going to be able to participate."
At the Chesapeake College meeting, Queen Anne's County Commissioner Jack Wilson Jr. shared his county's decision to cover Dorchester County for the project design costs.
"We all know what happens if we let this money go back to the state," Wilson said. "It's going to go somewhere else in this state, and it's not going to be here. We got this far. And Lenny, listen, I feel for you guys. I know what you're going through. But I think we just need to keep it on the rails at least through the design phase and see what the state's going to help with."
According to documents from the meeting, the state will support 75% of project costs, and the counties will support the remaining 25%.
After the counties voted to approve the amended capital budget, Kent County Commission President Ron Fithian said he understands the position Dorchester County is in, mentioning the Blueprint for Maryland's Future and "unfunded mandates" by the state.
"I think we all understand any one of us could be in your same position very easily," Fithian told the Dorchester County Council members.

title: Talbot County Introduces $161M Budget with a Focus on Conservatism
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot County introduces $161M budget with a focus on conservatism

 April 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 718
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Talbot County officials introduced a $161 million budget proposal Tuesday, emphasizing their intention to flatten spending after multiple years of significant increases.Tuesday's proposal is balanced at around $2 million below last year's total budget.
"This year, you are introducing a budget that is flat from last year at this point in time, which was a hard task, and I commend you for doing that," County Manager Clay Stamp told County Council members.
Three fiscal years ago, the county's budget was $112 million before it rose to $128 million one year later and $163 million last year. The county is continuing to focus on building a stable fund reserve, an effort that has peaked in the last three years, Stamp said.
In addition to smoothing out recent hikes, Stamp said this year's budget considers threats it faces from federal and state government spending cuts.
"There's some severe federal policy shifts going on right now," Stamp said. "The state of Maryland is passing funding obligations down to (county) governments."
One obligation Talbot County will assume, pending an amendment to the proposed budget, is $440,000 in teachers' pension payments. Finance Director Martha Sparks noted the county worked with state legislators to add language to the law "in the eleventh hour" during this year's General Assembly.
Talbot County would cover that $440,000 through an education supplement tax. The supplement to the property tax would be less than half a cent per $100 of assessed value.
Overall, the real property tax rate is proposed at 79 cents per $100 of assessed value, nearly even with last year's total rate. The tax bill on a home valued at $300,000 would increase by $4.80 from last year, county officials said.
The county will bring in a projected $67 million in property tax revenue in fiscal year 2026, up from $60 million last year (not including the education supplement tax). That's a 12.3% increase, which stems from rising property value reassessments.
"As undesirable as it is to raise taxes, our tax increases by our charter's design are moderate increases and are reflected in our standing as the county with the lowest property tax rate in the state of Maryland," Sparks said.
The proposed budget includes $55 million in funding for Talbot County Public Schools, a mark required by the state's funding plans in its expansive education initiative, The Blueprint for Maryland's Future.
The county did not include the district's request for $5.7 million in additional funding to help with teacher salary increases and new positions, among other requests. Vice President Pete Lesher urged the council to do so at a previous workshop, but the rest of the council opted to hold off. The budget ordinance could be amended to include some or all of that request.
Stamp said despite the flattened budget, capital upgrades aren't stalling. He pointed to projects such as the St. Michaels library branch upgrade, moving the county's public safety complex and continuing renovations at Chapel District Elementary School.
Sparks noted the county is in a "healthy financial position" thanks to fiscal year 2025 revenues exceeding projections by around $8 million. The added revenue is largely due to income tax distributions from the state coming in higher than expected, Sparks said.
A similar situation with the income tax revenue isn't a guarantee for next fiscal year, she said.
Tax hikes to the state's most wealthy, part of Gov. Wes Moore's plan to close an over $3 billion state budget deficit, were enacted by the General Assembly this month. Those increases could drive wealthy residents out of Talbot County to surrounding states and reduce income tax revenue, county officials say.
"The last time this type of tax was implemented, Talbot County's income tax revenues decreased by 40% within one year," Sparks said.
Amid looming uncertainty, County Council members thanked Stamp and the financial staff for their work to present a balanced budget ordinance Tuesday.
"Clearly we've still got some storm clouds on the horizon, both from the federal and state budgets (and) impacts on local budgeting." Lesher said. "… We're going into this, as you outlined, in a strong position. I think that this is a sound approach."
Public budget hearings will be held May 6 at 2 p.m. in the Talbot County Courthouse Bradley Meeting Room and 7 p.m. in the Easton High School Cafeteria. The final budget is expected to be passed by the County Council May 27.

title: How ARPA Funds Shaped Maryland's Mid-Shore
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
How ARPA funds shaped Maryland’s Mid-Shore

 March 20, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 884
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Delegate Jay Jacobs, who represents Maryland's District 36 — encompassing Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil and Caroline counties — has seen the region through economic peaks and valleys. But the COVID-19 pandemic presented a crisis unlike any other.At the same time, it brought a rare opportunity.
Through the American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA), Maryland received $3.7 billion in federal relief funds. Jacobs estimated that roughly $88 million of that flowed into his district over the past five years.
"The money gave counties and municipalities a chance to get things done when they normally might not have had that opportunity," Jacobs said.
Across the district, more than 200 projects were funded through ARPA, aimed at bolstering local infrastructure, supporting nonprofits and modernizing essential services.
Rock Hall to Queen Anne's: Local Needs, Local SolutionsEach town took a unique approach, reflecting ARPA's flexible framework.
In Rock Hall, the town's aging wastewater system was a priority. Mayor James Cook said of the $1.3 million received, $300,000 went toward replacing the headworks at the sewer plant — a key filter that removes debris such as grease and rags from wastewater.
Chestertown formed a task force led by Ward 2 Council member Tom Herz to ensure transparency and community input. Of the $4.25 million allocated, local nonprofits were invited to align funding requests with the town's comprehensive plan.
In Galena, $570,000 supported road improvements designed to make parks more accessible and attract visitors.
Betterton directed its $311,000 toward modernizing its website to be ADA-compliant, enabling online payments, purchasing an air purifying unit, and upgrading pump stations with generators for resilience.
Millington received $504,821, though specific projects were not detailed.
Queen Anne's County saw one of the largest allocations: $16.3 million. Projects included installing 3,300 feet of water line at the Old Towne Shopping Center, investing $900,000 to upgrade affordable housing units, and expanding broadband access with $1.5 million. Six new consoles were also added to the county's 911 backup center, and cell phone boosters were installed in public schools to strengthen communication in rural areas.
Countywide Efforts and Broadband ExpansionIn Cecil County, where municipalities received a greater share of ARPA funds than the county itself, a major initiative focused on expanding high-speed internet. A $16.2 million broadband project combined $12.8 million in state funds, $2.5 million from internet service providers, and $900,000 in ARPA funds contributed by the county.
According to county officials, additional ARPA investments went toward two emergency medical services paramedic stations and a new training center for the Cecil County Sheriff's Office.
Rising Sun used $2,300 for infrastructure repairs, while the Town of North East applied its share to enhance police department operations.
In Caroline County, which received just under $6.5 million, part of the funding was used for infrastructure, while a portion supported reentry programs and post-release case management for individuals leaving the Ordnance Road Detention Facility.
Jacobs noted that ARPA's flexibility was one of its most valuable aspects.
"It was not one size fits all," he said. "Municipalities could use the money to meet their specific needs — with the only caveat being it must be spent by Dec. 31, 2026."
As ARPA Winds Down, Financial Pressure MountsNow, with the funding window closing, local governments are bracing for its absence. Jacobs said the drying up of ARPA funds is intensifying pressure on the state as the General Assembly works to pass the FY 2026 budget — which currently faces a $3.5 billion shortfall.
"Certain services were being relied on and now are cut off," Jacobs said. "ARPA funds possibly would have kept some of these programs afloat."
A notable cut is the reduction in senior care funding by the Maryland Department of Aging. Jacobs said the proposed $2.5 million budget — an 18% reduction — could translate to about $28,000 less per county. He warned this could destabilize staffing and services for vulnerable seniors, such as in-home care, transportation and meal delivery.
"These cuts will be felt, not by the lawmakers, but by ordinary hardworking folks who have to make decisions about affording food or putting gas in the car," he said.
Talbot County: Planning for LongevityTalbot County took a strategic approach. Officials distributed surveys to identify community priorities, which included broadband access, public health, and household assistance.
According to Cassandra Vanhooser, director of Talbot County Economic Development and Tourism, the county received about $7.2 million in ARPA funds. The goal, she said, was to ensure that projects wouldn't falter once federal dollars were gone.
"These are largely capital items, these are one-time items... a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity," said then Talbot County Council Vice President Pete Lesher. "We need to be very careful about how this is done."
Among Talbot's allocations:
- $1.75 million to Easton Utilities' Connect Talbot project to expand broadband to rural residents.
- $105,000 to the Chesapeake Center in Easton to replace a failing septic system and connect to county sewer.
- $500,000 in grants for volunteer fire company equipment upgrades.
"People recognize that this is transformational money," Vanhooser said at the time of the funding discussion, "It's a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to be a driving force for change and to impact the lives of our citizens."
Looking AheadAs the Dec. 31, 2024 obligation deadline nears, and the Dec. 31, 2026 expenditure deadline looms, local leaders are focused on maximizing remaining funds while grappling with what comes next.
Jacobs is urging urgency from lawmakers.
"With less than 20 days in session," he said, "the Assembly needs to come up with solutions — and fast."

title: Mid-Shore Counties Advocating Against State Cost Shifts
author: Konner Metz
content:
Mid-Shore counties advocating against state cost shifts

 March 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 371
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Talbot County Council sent a letter this week to the Maryland General Assembly expressing its concerns regarding more than $1 million in county money impacted by the state's Budget Reconciliation and Financing Act."The proposal to shift costs onto counties by sending invoices simply places the State's fiscal problem into other hands and threatens local services," reads the letter, which was unanimously approved by the council Tuesday.
Cost shifts are expected as the state aims to balance a budget with a nearly $3 billion deficit. Specific costs include contributions to teacher pensions and the state Department of Assessments and Taxation.
Council Vice President Pete Lesher said it's "simply a poor and inappropriate strategy for resolving the very real state budget crisis."
Lesher noted Tuesday that Talbot County isn't seeing the worst of the cost shifts — Dorchester County may be looking at more than $3 million affected, he said.
Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer said he testified at a Senate budget committee meeting in Annapolis and talked with members of the governor's staff.
Pfeffer says Department of Legislative Services recommendations to double the costs for counties to pay toward teacher pensions is particularly alarming. For Dorchester, it would cost $1.1 million compared to the previously estimated $550,000.
Gov. Wes Moore has said solving the budget crisis is an "enormous task" only made more difficult by constraints from the federal government. At a Feb. 28 Senate budget committee hearing, he emphasized that the budget bill is nowhere near final.
"While I still remain locked in on the destination, I come in moving in partnership to be flexible on the journey," Moore said.
Caroline County Commissioners President Travis Breeding said the county may lose $1.1 million in income tax revenue if Moore's tax cut plan is approved.
Moore has maintained that giving middle-class families tax relief is a critical component to the budget and state's economic growth plan.
"Marylanders are being squeezed. They're being squeezed by rising prices," Moore said Feb. 28. "They're being squeezed by the rising cost of groceries, they're being squeezed by the rising cost of energy."
As session continues, Breeding says Caroline County has representatives in Annapolis fighting for relief from the potential cost shifts.
"We have a lot of heartburn with the proposed budget," Breeding said.

title: Talbot County Provides First Look at Draft Budget for FY26
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot County provides first look at draft budget for FY26

 March 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 474
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Talbot County Manager Clay Stamp said one aspect was clear when drafting the county's fiscal year 2026 budget: it needed to remain flat.Speaking with the Talbot County Council at a workshop Tuesday, county employees presented a balanced draft budget coming in at $163.3 million. It comes in slightly below last year's budget of $163.8 million.
The county's total budget has ballooned in recent years. In fiscal year 2023, it was $112 million, and one year later, it rose to $128 million. It took a sharper jump to the $163 million mark last year.
Stamp said the increases were for good cause. "You've made incredible and important investments in public safety and education," he told council members.
But Stamp emphasized that given federal uncertainties, state cost shifts and recurring county costs, it is important to curb that recent upward trend.
"That was a mandate as we put this budget together," Stamp said of the belt-tightening.
Stamp said the draft fiscal year 2026 budget currently proposes no additional job positions. The county's capital improvement plan is also trimmed back, he said. He hopes the county can focus on finishing projects already underway, such as Chapel District Elementary School renovations and a new EMS station in Cordova.
When drafting the budget, Stamp and Finance Director Martha Sparks said they initially came in $6 million over their target. To remedy that, they're proposing delayed payments for postemployment benefits and correctional officers' retirements, respectively — the latter of which is to be expected to be included in fiscal year 2027.
Sparks mentioned that tax hikes proposed at the state level for wealthy individuals may have an impact on Talbot County revenues. Sparks said last time a similar tax increase was levied in 2009, it made a significant dent, partly due to the recession.
"We had an exodus of the wealthy in our county as a result of that," Sparks said. "And it took us approximately 10 years to recover."
Sparks added, however, that the county looks OK for fiscal year 2026 in terms of those tax proposals. She said she's "not sure what that will look like for us moving forward."
As for policy and funding shifts at the federal level, Stamp said "it's reasonable" to expect impacts will trickle down to Talbot County.
"We are cognizant of that," Stamp said. "Radars are up, antennas are up. We're watching closely."
The draft budget shows $55 million in funding for the Talbot Board of Education. Stamp said the county must contribute that mark since it's required by state funding formulas. Any additional education funding is left for the County Council to consider in the coming weeks.
Council members and staff will hold a number of workshops this month and in April before a budget proposal is officially introduced April 15.
Public budget hearings are scheduled for May 6, and the County Council is expected to enact a budget ordinance May 27.

title: MACo Officials Say Cost Shifts from State to Counties Are 'Absurd,' Unfair
author: Konner Metz
content:
MACo officials say cost shifts from state to counties are 'absurd,' unfair

 March 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 647
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Representatives from the Maryland Association of Counties minced no words when speaking to the Eastern Shore's state legislators Friday morning about the expected cost burdens being placed on counties this budget cycle."Shifting these costs onto counties at this point is absurd," said Kevin Kinnally, the association's legislative director.
Earlier this month, the Department of Legislative Services told the Eastern Shore Delegation that local governments across the state may have to pick up around $144 million in costs as the state legislature and Gov. Wes Moore grapple with tackling a near $3 billion deficit.
The governor's proposed fiscal year 2026 budget would shift costs in a number of areas, including teacher pensions and property assessments, according to MACo officials.
In Caroline and Talbot counties, projected local cost shifts are in the $700,000 range, per legislative services projections. Dorchester County is at $830,000, while Queen Anne's County leads the pack for the Mid-Shore at $970,000. Kent is the lowest of the five counties with a $300,000 projection.
Friday at the Eastern Shore Delegation meeting, Kinnally said the Shore's poorer counties, like Caroline and Dorchester, are being "railroaded."
Kinnally claims the state budget leaves counties with no choice but to raise property tax rates, going so far as to deem it a "state-mandated property tax increase."
"Two-thirds of Marylanders live in counties at the maximum local income tax rate, so the only place to go is to the property tax," Kinnally said. "Which is regressive, which everybody hates. But they're pushing us into a corner here, and that's not fair."
Michael Sanderson, executive director of MACo, said the organization took a closer look at how cost shifts would impact Dorchester County's fiscal situation.
After running the numbers, Sanderson said he believes Dorchester County may have to raise property taxes, a result he called "absolutely bonkers."
"I have no idea how Dorchester County manages this year's budget," Sanderson said.
SOLAR COMPROMISEAs legislators and industry leaders have eyes on a joint hearing Friday regarding the state's solar legislation, MACo is opposing Senate Bill 931 and its paired House bill.
The legislation is designed to expand solar energy across the state, a measure intended to work toward accomplishing Moore's clean energy goals for Maryland. If passed, the bill would give the state authority to approve solar energy projects — a significant harm to local siting authority, critics say.
Dominic Butchko, MACo's intergovernmental relations director, said the association opposes the legislation based on five impacted areas: safety, livability of rural areas, concerns for local taxpayers, affordable housing opportunities being stripped and inefficiencies in the legislation's requirements.
Butchko said the legislation strays from compromises MACo thought it reached last November.
But through recent discussions with solar industry leaders and environmental advocates, Butchko still sees a path to compromise.
"Those efforts have started to yield some fruit," Butchko said. "We believe we actually have amendments that revert the legislation back to where we were at or pretty close to where we were at in November."
MUNICIPAL LEAGUE
Friday, the Eastern Shore Delegation heard a brief update from the Maryland Municipal League, an organization representing local municipal governments.
The group has two legislative priorities this session: Senate Bill 390, which would allow local governments to have trained civilians issue speed camera citations instead of police officers; and House Bill 991, which would allow local governments to institute food and beverage fees.
Justin Fiore, the league's deputy director of advocacy and public affairs, said House Bill 991 could give flexibility to governments that are "heavily dependent on property taxes as (their) only revenue."
"We have 43 million visitors annually to the state of Maryland, and while they do pay a hotel tax if they stay, we really don't capture revenue from the services that they utilize," Fiore said.
The food and beverage fee bill is still waiting committee review and House approval before it moves to the Senate, while the speed camera citation bill was passed by the Senate earlier this month and currently sits in the House.

title: Talbot County Council denies raise in accommodation tax
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Talbot County Council denies raise in accommodation tax

 December 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 879
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A controversial proposal to raise the accommodation tax was voted down by the the Talbot County Council Tuesday.During an impromptu public comment period, lodge owners and community members expressed concerns over the increase in the accommodation tax saying it would hurt profits and tourism in the county. Additional comments concerning a lack of information were shared resulting in the proposal not passing.
The rise of the accommodation tax was presented by Cassandra Vanhooser, director of the department of Economic Development and Tourism, on Tuesday who gave an overview of the steps taken by her department to get a proposal in front of the council including approval for the Tourism Board of Talbot County and receiving support from Easton, Oxford, St. Michaels and Trappe.
"(Talbot County Council is) being called on to balance the effects on tourism businesses with the benefits to the towns and the county," Vanhooser said. "The Tourism Board has weighed the evidence, and they believe that the benefits outweigh the disadvantages."
Talbot County's current public accommodations tax rate, or hotel tax rate, is 4%, the lowest of any county in the state. The tax is levied on those staying in hotels and short-term rentals, collected by the business and then paid to either the county or to the towns.
Easton, Oxford and St. Michaels collect revenues from such properties within one mile outside town limits. The county collects revenue from all other properties.
A potential increase to 6%, which would raise annual revenue by around $1 million, requires approval from lawmakers in Annapolis.
Despite voting down an increase, the council voted to strengthen the existing accommodation tax.
Martha Sparks, financial director for Talbot County, suggested removing the 120-day grace period for owners of short-term rentals to provide accommodation tax collected to the county before the county can impose a 10% penalty. Sparks proposed that the council approve a request to the legislature to reduce that period of time.
The council unanimously approved the proposal.
Prior to voting on a letter of support for the accommodation tax increase, several people began to raise their hands in order to get their opinions on record. Commission President Chuck Callahan opened the floor for public comment.
PUBLIC COMMENTDuring public comment, business owner Scott Wagner expressed concern on raising taxes saying that though the accommodation tax has not been raised in 20 years, prices of rooms for rentals have, which in turn provides more funds from accommodation tax.
Wagner said room rates have "ridden the wave of inflation" and described raising the accommodation tax to "feeding the monster."
"This is feeding the monster, and the monster is asking for a million dollars more next year, so when the monster is going to get fatter. I've never seen the tax go down, quite frankly."
In contrast, Jessica Bellis, a member of the Talbot County Tourism Board, expressed concern over the negative connotation with the accommodation tax.
"We can use words like the monster that you're feeding, but the monster is making sure that we do have the roads and the infrastructure and the police department and the marketing to be able to promote and sustain tourism, which is a major industry in Talbot County," Bellis said.
Included in public comment were concerns over information. Kevin Hartmann, Easton resident, said lodging providers were not asked for comment at the time of the town's vote. He said the towns were "significantly under-educated as to the ramifications."
According to Hartmann, two surveys were conducted to gather the opinions of lodging operators. One was done by the Talbot County Tourism Board and the other was conducted by Hartmann. The board's survey, he said, showed 75% of operators did not support the increase in tax. For the survey done by Hartmann it was over 84%.
The survey by the tourism board was released on Dec. 5 and the last town to vote on supporting the raise was on Dec. 4.
"You have in your package, letters from your five towns of Talbot County, each one of those voted for the increase," Hartmann said. "But the significant difference is this: None of those towns heard what you're hearing tonight, none of those towns have the results of the survey at the time of their vote. None of those towns held a public hearing on the matter."
After hearing the comment given by Hartmann, Easton Council President Frank Gunsallus, spoke and shared his thoughts on the information provided.
"Our vote already occurred, but after hearing all the testimonies tonight, and especially Mr. Hartmann's … perhaps we could have been better educated before we voted," Gunsallus said. "I believe that people reserve the right to change their mind, and I know our votes were cast, but I am, on your record, withdrawing my support for this accommodation tax."
After much deliberation from the council, the motion was denied in a 3-2 vote with Councilmembers Pete Lesher and Keasha Haythe voting in support of the proposal.
Vanhooser, director of Economic Development and Tourism, said Wednesday that the proposal failed and will not move forward this state legislature period.
"The Tourism Board obviously supports this, because they see it as a way to fund my department and tourism marketing and promotion, and the towns, you know, were in favor, despite what was said last night, because it raises their revenue, which they need for the various things they spend the money on."

title: Trappe Approves Accommodation Tax Increase
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Trappe approves accommodation tax increase

 December 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 574
 Words 

 Read News Document

 TRAPPE — Talbot County is moving forward in support of a countywide accommodation tax increase. On Dec. 4, the Trappe Town Council approved a 2% increase for all short-term rentals in the area.The accommodation tax has been a hot topic issue among residents of the county over the last year. Though an accommodation tax raise would immediately benefit towns with large tourism traffic such as St. Michaels and Easton, Trappe does not have an influx of tourism.
However, Trappe voted in favor of the increase with hopes of establishing a strong foundation for tourism growth. The motion was passed with four votes in favor. Commissioner Jeremy Newnam abstained.
Talbot County's current public accommodations tax rate, or hotel tax rate, is 4%, the lowest of any county in the state. The tax is levied on those staying in hotels or short-term rentals, collected by the business and then paid to either the county or to the towns.
Easton, Oxford and St. Michaels collect revenues from such properties within one mile outside town limits. The county collects revenue from all other properties.
A potential increase to 6%, which would raise annual revenue by around $1 million, requires approval from lawmakers in Annapolis.
According to Trappe Commissioner Brian Schmidt, there are currently no short-term rentals in Trappe. The town had recently suspended the only short-term rental in town due to the operators not giving accommodation tax funds to the town.
Although there is a lack of rentals, over the past few months Trappe has prepared for potential growth by updating regulations for short-term rentals.
Cassandra Vanhooser, director of economic development and tourism, said even though, at the moment, Trappe does not have short-term rentals to collect funds from, there is growing potential especially with the increase in population due to the Lakeside residential property.
"It's not outside the question that you could someday have a Route 50 hotel or even an inn or an Airbnb," Vanhooser said. "You have some beautiful homes here. Someone might come along someday and buy one of these beautiful homes and make it an inn, and then you have 10 rooms generating some significant income. And that would be income and revenue to your bottom line."
During the meeting, Commissioner Jeremy Newnam raised questions concerning use of marketing from the county. Newnam said Trappe currently does not have the clientele base to benefit from tourism but in the future when the town has grown, he asked how Trappe could be represented in the county when it is up against towns such as St. Michaels and Easton.
Vanhooser said she seeks to represent all towns in the county fairly "because all the county paid my salary."
Later in the meeting, Vanhooser brought up the public meeting at the Talbot County Free Library on Dec. 5 where a number of business owners and managers pushed back on the proposed increase to the county's accommodation tax rate.
According to Vanhooser, the approval of the increase would provide additional revenue for the towns. Furthermore, the towns can spend their money anyway they want to offset the cost of tourism.
Vanhooser mentioned that tourists who stay in the towns use local services such as roads, police and garbage collection. She said during the previous public meeting participants had issues with fund usage going toward offsetting the cost of tourism.
"Some people don't see it that way. … Some people want all the money for themselves and none of the money for the people providing the services, which I find disingenuous."

title: Legislators Talk State Budget Before Heading Back to Annapolis in January
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Legislators talk state budget before heading back to Annapolis in January

 December 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 557
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The state of the state's budget took up a large part of the conversation at a Dorchester Chamber of Commerce luncheon with state legislators on Dec. 4.The Lower Shore delegation answered questions from chamber members regarding concerns about Maryland's fiscal health, with a looming $2.7 billion state budget deficit predicted in fiscal year 2026.
"The reality is that if you continue to do the things that have gotten us into this deficit, it's only going to take us back there again," Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) said. "There needs to be a structural, fundamental change."
Mautz and Dels. Sheree Sample-Hughes (D-Dorchester, Wicomico), Chris Adams (R-Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) and Tom Hutchinson (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) all spoke at the chamber lunch. They, along with the rest of the state's legislators, will head back to Annapolis in January for the 447th session of the Maryland General Assembly.
In talking about the state's budget, Mautz also said there should be incentives in place to try to drive state agencies to save money.
Sample-Hughes said the state should do its fiscal homework and find out what it "really (has) to work with."
"But I do believe that we can still address and attack some of these goals that we have, whether it's education, whether it's climate, whether it's criminal justice," she said. "We can do it in a pragmatic way."
Adams said to solve the budget problem, the state has to leverage and grow its private sector.
"You do not do what we've done for the past two years," he said. He said the state and its leadership need to stop spending so much, own up to the problem and stop blaming it on COVID-19.
Hutchinson expressed his concerns with the transportation budget and the lack of funding for many infrastructure projects across the state.
"We've got to pay attention to our transportation budget," he said.
BLUEPRINTThe legislators also talked about the Blueprint for Maryland's Future, a plan passed by the Maryland General Assembly in 2021 that aims to improve student outcomes and the quality of education across the state through increasing education funding by $3.8 billion over a 10-year period.
Sample-Hughes said although Blueprint's goals are important, the General Assembly's decision to pass the plan has contributed to the state's budget deficit. She later advocated for giving more resources to the nonprofits that already serve 3 and 4 year olds, rather than putting money toward expanding early childhood education in the state's public school systems.
Mautz said he thinks the project needs to be paused so that the plan's strengths and weaknesses can be better evaluated.
JUVENILE CRIMEThe legislators also talked about the state of juvenile crime in Maryland, with Sample-Hughes calling for the removal of Department of Juvenile Services Secretary Vincent Schiraldi.
Hutchinson said that with recent juvenile justice reforms going into effect Nov. 1, he doesn't think a lot of legislators are going to want to discuss juvenile crime this upcoming session.
"Because they'll say, 'We just put that in place. We haven't even been able to see the results,'" he said.
Adams said law enforcement is needed now more than ever and officers need to be able to do their jobs.
"If you want a society, if you want a City of Cambridge, if you want an Eastern Shore (or) State of Maryland, if you want a United States that is civil, there have to be consequences," he said.

title: Talbot's 1-Cent Amendment Passes by Slim Margin
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot's 1-cent amendment passes by slim margin

 November 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 396
 Words 

 Read News Document

 By a razor thin margin, Talbot County voters approved a charter amendment extending the county's ability to raise residents' taxes for public safety funding.According to Maryland Board of Elections data, 10.968 Talbot County ballots approved the measure, 400 more than voted against the measure. Ballot canvassing was completed by the local Board of Elections on Friday.
The 1-cent amendment authorizes the Talbot County Council to raise property taxes one cent per $100 of assessed value each fiscal year. The council already had the authorization to do so through fiscal year 2026 thanks to a previous charter amendment.
This year's charter amendment passing means the county, if it deems necessary, can raise revenue derived from those taxes through fiscal year 2033.
County Council Vice President Pete Lesher, a vocal proponent of the amendment, said he hopes the council does not have to enforce the additional tax hike, acknowledging that "nobody wants to pay higher taxes."
"We don't want to do that anymore than the public wants it," Lesher said in an interview on Monday. "And I think my hope is that we will not have to do that, that inflation will be under control (and) will be under 2%."
However, if inflation does not decrease, Lesher says, then the county may elect to collect additional tax revenue to fund public safety measures. While it hasn't always been collected, it has contributed to areas such as sheriff's deputy salaries and retirement for correctional officers when the county did choose to collect it, Lesher said.
"If inflation does not come down as we're expecting, (then) we may need this tool, just to keep up, just to be able to fill those positions," Lesher said.
Martha Sparks, the county's finance director, said at a July county meeting that the 1-cent measure has helped the county in adding 26 public safety positions, including paramedics, EMTs, school resource officers and 911 operators.
In 2020, voters approved the original 1-cent amendment by a wider margin. Just over 10,000 voters approved it, with around 7,200 voting against it at the time.
Lesher said he understands why Talbot County voters may have voted against the measure in 2024. He emphasized that the county has followed through on using any of the additional tax revenue to improve public safety.
"All of the funds that we've raised through that extra penny and more have gone toward public safety," Lesher said. " … We've kept our word."

title: County Discusses Regulation Enforcement on Short Term Rentals
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
County discusses regulation enforcement on short term rentals

 October 31, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 430
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — At a Tuesday evening meeting between the Talbot County Council and incorporated towns within the county, concerns were raised over the enforcement of the county's accommodation tax on short-term rentals.Martha Darling Sparks, finance director for Talbot County, shared future plans to better regulate short-term rentals with a platform already used by the county called Granicus. Granicus owns a software called Host Compliance, which uses artificial intelligence and machine learning to provide data on short-term rentals and track them as they appear online.
The software will be able to help towns know of unlicensed rentals in their area so local officials can better enforce rental regulations.
Currently, enforcement of the accommodation tax on short-term rentals relies on what Sparks describes as an "honor system."
Sparks said the law requires owners of short-term rentals to collect an accommodations tax from patrons. Owners are then required to remit the funds to the county on a monthly basis. Then, on a quarterly basis, the county remits 95% of the tax collected back to the towns and keeps 5% as an administrative fee.
According to Sparks, because the tax requirement not more strictly enforced, there are rentals operating in Talbot County that may not adhering to the regulations.
Alfred Mercier, St. Michaels commission president, said short-term rentals have become a challenge to the town. Mercier said on a monthly basis there could be 30 different Airbnbs in operation but that they are hard to track because the rentals can be open one weekend and closed the next.
Sparks said if towns have a permitting process or an approval process for these rentals, it is important to emphasize to owners that short-term rentals are subject to the accommodation tax in Talbot County.
According to Sparks, historically, the county does not involve itself in regulation or the monitoring of the towns because that is done through planning and zoning committees to make sure that short-term rentals are properly licensed.
Sparks said that when the county moves toward this new system of collecting accommodation tax online, there is a request from the county to see the number of short-term rentals in towns.
Sparks plans to discuss with Bryce Yelton, assistant planning officer of Talbot County, about a new process where the county communicates with the towns when new unlicensed rentals appear online.
"We were going to talk about a process where we'd like to communicate with the towns when something comes up on our radar, to pass it along to (towns), because we already have that software," Sparks said. "So it might be a good way for us to partner and (give an) information exchange."
