title: Easton Outlines Plan to Use Excess ARPA Funds
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Easton outlines plan to use excess ARPA funds

 October 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 390
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — As the deadline to obligate pandemic-era federal funds nears, the Town of Easton is moving toward an agreement that will allow for flexibility in allocating that money to different public works projects.The Easton Town Council held a workshop Monday to discuss a memorandum of understanding that will allocate up to $735,270 of American Rescue Plan Act funds to the town's public works department. The American Rescue Plan Act of 2021 awarded funds to local governments in the wake of the pandemic.
Funds must be obligated by Dec. 31 and spent by the end of next year.
There are currently $664,350 in ARPA dollars that still need to be obligated. In that total, the council previously approved the reallocation of $225,000 for Rails to Trails work on Port Street.
Town Attorney Sharon VanEmburgh said the U.S. treasury department allows for interagency agreements in obligating the ARPA funds, such as the one drafted for Easton.
Town Engineer Rick Van Emburgh said the MOU, which would be between Mayor Megan Cook and the public works department, will provide flexibility in making sure excess funds are used.
"To the dollar is hard to predict," Van Emburgh said of the fluctuating costs of projects. "And so that's why we are asking for the flexibility of having the MOU."
In addition to the Port Street trails, projects around town that may receive this funding include: impervious surface removal at Easton Point Park, sidewalk accessibility improvements, storm drain work on Harrison Street and East Avenue, and traffic signal intersection improvements.
A schedule of project timelines was shared with council members on Monday. Interim Town Manager Alan Lowrey said the town is aiming to complete projects by September, 2026 in order to have a "three-month buffer" with the Dec, 31, 2026 deadline.
"It's investments in hard infrastructure improvements in the town that we need and will have to be paid for at some point to be done, which I think is great," Lowrey said. "If we can knock some of this stuff that we need to do with these residual dollars and not give money back to the federal government, that's a win-win."
An ordinance to amend the ARPA budget and make the memorandum of understanding possible was introduced at Easton Town Council later Monday evening. A public hearing for that ordinance will be held at the town's next council meeting on Nov. 4.

title: Talbot County Proposes Hotel Tax Increase to Local Delegation
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot County proposes hotel tax increase to local delegation

 October 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 589
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Talbot County leaders met with the local delegation Tuesday afternoon to discuss creating legislation during the upcoming General Assembly to raise the county's hotel taxes.Talbot County's current public accommodations tax rate, or hotel tax rate, is 4%, the lowest of any county in the state. The tax is levied on those staying in hotels or short-term rentals in the county, collected by the business and then paid to either the county or one of three towns.
Easton, Oxford and St. Michaels collect revenues from such properties within one mile outside town limits. The county collects revenue from all other properties not within those boundaries.
A potential increase to 6%, which would increase total revenue collected by around $1 million in fiscal year 2024, requires approval from lawmakers in Annapolis.
Cassandra Vanhooser, the county's director of tourism and economic development, along with Talbot County Council members briefed Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico), Del. Christopher T. Adams (R-Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) and Del. Tom Hutchinson (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) on the proposed increase.
"I'm anticipating that this is going to be our principal legislation request for the delegation this year," council Vice President Pete Lesher said.
Adams and Mautz explained that state lawmakers will be tasked with addressing significant budget problems in the upcoming session. Adams said it's likely lawmakers will try to pass the budget by voting for state tax increases that were not passed last year.
He said it's probably the first year he will vote against the budget. Any tax bill will require his careful consideration, Adams noted, saying he'd like to hear the council's opinions on potential hotel tax legislation.
Council Member Keasha Haythe said the spike would help "level the playing field" for the county, as well as increase funding for the tourism and economic development department. Revenue the county collects from the accommodations tax goes to that department.
"This particular tax I do believe is necessary for Talbot County and tourism and (the) hospitality industry," Haythe said.
Mautz agreed with Haythe's points but brought up the benefits of Talbot County's low accommodations tax rate.
"I also agree with the perspective that would say, if your accommodation tax is lower than the neighboring county, then you have an advantage as far as attracting (people)," Mautz said. He added that the council should take into consideration that it may make the area more attractive for investors.
Jessica Bellis, CFO at the Avalon Foundation and a member of the Talbot County Tourism Board, expressed her support for the increase. She said the taxes benefit her organization since they are cycled back into Talbot County's and Easton's respective economic development and tourism departments.
"We can't market in the big world, as tiny little Avalon Foundation or as a small Airbnb in Talbot County," Bellis said. "We really rely on that tourism office for its marketing power."
Hutchinson said the county should ensure business owners are on board and lay out to the delegation how the taxes collected cycle back into the local economy.
Council President Chuck Callahan said it's important for the county to do its "due diligence" and gather feedback from businesses before voting on the topic as a council. While the bill could be pre-filed by the local delegates in November, January was agreed upon as a deadline for the county to have a draft bill ready for the legislators.
"This is a really important issue," Mautz said. "We definitely don't want to be in a situation where we go up to Annapolis and are not prepared."
"It's a different discussion when you go across the bridge," he said.

title: St. Michaels Approves Accommodation Tax Increase
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
St. Michaels approves accommodation tax increase

 October 2, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: General Assembly 
 
 727
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST MICHAELS — The accommodation tax has long been a topic of controversy in the town of St Michaels, and some residents expressed concerns about a proposed 2% increase in the tax during a Sep. 25 commissioners meeting.The tax increase endorsement was approved by a majority of the town's commissioners at the meeting following months of discussions.
Since August, Talbot County has made moves for a 2% increase in accommodation tax countywide. The county has the lowest hotel tax rate in the state at 4%, which has been in place since 2005.
According to council Vice President Pete Lesher, in order to enact the tax increase, the county would need to ask state delegates this month to bring the proposed change to the General Assembly next year.
Prior to legislative submittal, Oxford, Easton and St. Michaels would need to approve an endorsement for the increase. St. Michaels' approval was the last the county needed to move forward.
The county attempted to raise the accommodations tax in 2021, but St. Michaels' commission at the time was not on board.
In town, discussion of a potential increase of accommodation tax has been in the works since the commissioners' race in May, when the three newly elected commissioners, David Wojciechowski, Alexis Roiter and Jay Hudson, all showed support for the increase.
According to St. Michaels Commissioner Alfred Mercier, the tax would increase the cost of rooms by around $2 to $8.
Mercier said because the increase in tax is minimal, it "really doesn't have any impact" in terms of the number of people who stay over in a destination site.
Additionally, Mercier said the increase in tax would have a larger impact if the incremental rate, the total change in tax, is "fairly significant," meaning if the increase was above 10%.
"I just wanted to get rid of the misconceptions on this because this is not a tax on the hotel," Mercier said. "This is truly a way to tax, if you will, visitors that come into town, and there has been other discussions on how we can generate money, and I know they're out there."
Commissioner Alexis Roiter said she agreed with the points made by Mercier and made clear her support for the raise in tax, especially since it will be paid by tourists.
"2% is very small," Roiter said. "And this isn't passed down to the actual people coming to town who use our garbage cans, park their cars illegally, throw their trash out and increase the cost of our own services like water. The fact that we are the lowest in the state doesn't make any sense."
Commissioner Katrina Whittington reminded commissioners that if they voted against the endorsement, it would be taking away the opportunity for Easton and Oxford to get the additional money, since all three towns would have to agree to raise the accommodation tax.
Although there seemed to be unanimous support among commissioners, business owners and residents in town were concerned of the potential harm the increase would have on businesses.
George Wilson, owner of the Old Brick Inn, shared that occupancy is down for lodging in town, and an increase could have negative effects for businesses like his. Wilson said the tax increase should be met with more scrutiny due to lingering unanswered questions.
"Where is the accommodation tax going? Because I don't think we have done our due diligence," Wilson said. "We know what we need, I understand that, but what are we doing with what we have?"
Wilson said the town was ignoring other potential revenue sources, like entertainment taxes on restaurants and stores.
During the public hearing Sep. 25, former St. Michaels Commissioner Tad DuPont brought up concerns involving the loss of smaller inns in the area within the last two years. Along with those concerns, DuPont mentioned the negative affect that undocumented Airbnbs are having on inns.
Whittington said undocumented Airbnb rentals have been a longstanding issue among the town and encouraged residents to report addresses they may suspect of hosting Airbnbs so the town could investigate.
After the public comment, Mercier requested the commissioners move the vote for a later meeting to obtain more information.
Wojciechowski said delaying the vote would interfere with the county's deadline to bring the issue to state legislators.
A motion was passed for the endorsement of the tax increase with a 4-1 vote. Mercier, who previously supported the increase, voted against the motion, stating there were "a lot of unanswered items."

title: MACo and Talbot County Council Discuss Fiscal Pressures Facing State
author: Konner Metz
content:
MACo and Talbot County Council discuss fiscal pressures facing state

 September 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 490
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — When entering last year's General Assembly, the fiscal situation Maryland faced needed serious attention. In some ways, that fiscal pressure has increased since.Michael Sanderson, the executive director of the Maryland Association of Counties, briefed the Talbot County Council on those financial troubles and more during a special meeting Tuesday.
He told council members a budget shortfall of potentially $600 to $800 million could be facing lawmakers in Annapolis. Fixing that is "not easy, but not impossible," he said.
"There are a couple of years of that in our forecast, and then it gets really serious," Sanderson said.
When fiscal year 2028 arrives, Sanderson warned that the state will run out of money in its trust fund that's been used for The Blueprint for Maryland's Future, the state's expansive and optimistic education initiative.
Many counties have been under significant financial pressure due to state requirements stemming from Blueprint. Sanderson says the state will be feeling that level of pressure soon.
"The counties are feeling it now," he said. "The state doesn't really feel it for a couple years down the road, and that has been a meaningful disconnect."
Without significant timeline adjustments for Blueprint from the state, MACo feels there will continue to be that disconnect between the fiscal situation of the state versus the situation counties are facing. State funding for transportation, though, is already causing serious impacts, Sanderson said.
"The canary in the coal mine that's already chirping is in transportation," he told the council members. " … The conversation in the summer time is sometimes ambiguous and hazy and that sort of thing. But this year, not so much. They were just saying, 'If there aren't already shovels in the ground, we can't afford the next thing.'"
The Maryland Department of Transportation has been forced to delay many statewide projects amid a significant budget deficit. Earlier this month, the department released a draft plan that showed $1.3 billion in cuts from the state's six-year transportation plan.
Sanderson noted the "state's transportation challenge is not a function of the Key Bridge" rebuild, which is set to begin next year.
At the county level, council Vice President Pete Lesher said Talbot County is "finding itself in a slightly different place" than others.
"We are going through a number of capital construction projects, our health department, our sheriff's office, our 911 center," Lesher said, emphasizing some of those projects are receiving "pandemic-era related funds" from the federal government.
"The pinch that a lot of counties are feeling right now, the income tax, is not yet being felt in Talbot County," Lesher said. "We can look around at our neighbors and see what is coming, even though we are not yet in that position now."
Lesher thanked Sanderson and MACo President Johnny Olszewski Jr. for their work to represent the counties at the state level year-round.
"We know that we are stronger together in Annapolis," Lesher said. "And we see every year what a powerful voice MACo is for all of us jointly."

title: Easton Council Supportive of Potential Spike in Hotel Tax Rate
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Easton council supportive of potential spike in hotel tax rate

 September 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 415
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A plan to increase the accommodation tax rate in Talbot County was presented to the Easton Town Council at Tuesday night's meeting.Cassandra Vanhooser, the county's director of economic development and tourism, recommended the increase to the council. It would raise the accommodation tax, or hotel tax, from 4% to 6% in the county.
"Anybody who's renting a room to someone for less than four months who's considered a 'transient' would be required to collect accommodations tax," Vanhooser said.
Vanhooser pointed out that Talbot County's rate is the lowest in the state. Around $2 million was collected throughout the county in accommodation taxes in fiscal year 2024. If the rate had been 6%, that total would have increased to just above the $3 million mark.
She noted the success of the county in the tourism industry. Despite the rate remaining stagnant since 2004, Talbot County has more than doubled its accommodation tax revenue.
"We consider this as an indicator of our success as a tourism destination," Vanhooser said. "We know people are coming here. We know we're commanding a premium price, and people are willing to pay that."
In order to raise the rate, the county needs to ask state delegates this October to bring the proposed change to the General Assembly next year. The county is looking for support from three towns, including Easton, in order to move forward.
The towns of Easton, St. Michaels and Oxford collect revenues from the 4% tax on all hotels and short-term rentals within respective town limits or within a mile of those limits. The county collects the tax from lodgings that don't fall in or within a mile of town limits.
"The county would like to hear a vote from you on whether you would support this or not, because obviously, we don't want to go to the state legislature and ask for something that you do not support," Vanhooser said.
Ward 2 Councilmember Don Abbatiello asked if the county reached out to hotels in the area for feedback on the spike. Vanhooser said the county's tourism board has hotel representation, adding that the county is aiming to reach out to all hotels as a courtesy.
After a short discussion, the council voiced support for the proposed increase, unanimously voting in favor. No formal resolution was required for the agenda item.
"Talbot County obviously is not unique," Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery said. "But we have attractions that are not matched by our neighbors, and for that reason, I fully support raising this to 6%."

title: Talbot County Considering Raising Hotel Tax Rates for Visitors
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Talbot County considering raising hotel tax rates for visitors

 August 29, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 482
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Talbot County Tourism Board is asking county officials to consider raising its accommodations tax rates from 4% to 6%.The Talbot County Council held a work session Tuesday to discuss the possibility of raising its accommodations tax, or hotel tax, on visitors to the county. The county has the lowest hotel tax rate in the state at 4%, which has been in place since 2005.
Around $2 million was collected throughout the county in accommodation taxes in fiscal year 2024. If the rate had been 6%, that total would have increased to just above the $3 million mark.
Harold Klinger, a member of the tourism board since its inception, relayed the history of the county's hotel tax rate to council members. He noted that the law was first passed in 1986, updated once in 2005 and has remained flat at 4% since.
"The person who pays an accommodation tax are visitors when they come to Talbot County, it's not the residents who pay the accommodation tax," Klinger told the council.
Cassandra Vanhooser, the county's director of economic development and tourism, said the portion of the accommodations tax the county collects goes towards tourism marketing and economic development.
"I think we can all agree that the cost of serving our visitors has increased," Vanhooser said. "The cost of policing, the cost of roads, sidewalks, trash collection, all of that. An accommodations tax is merely asking your visitor … to help offset the costs."
The towns of Easton, St. Michaels and Oxford collect the 4% tax on all hotels and short-term rentals within respective town limits or within a mile of those limits. The county collects the tax from lodgings that don't fall in or within a mile of town limits.
Council Vice President Pete Lesher said the county would need to be prepared to ask state delegates this October to bring the proposed change to the General Assembly next year.
"What has to happen on our part between now and Oct. 1 to make this happen?" Lesher asked.
Vanhooser said the three towns would need to be on board for the spike and added that there needs to be public meetings and votes in each town.
Klinger said the county attempted to raise the accommodations tax in 2021, but St. Michaels was not on board. Vanhooser said she has already presented the proposed change to the three towns.
If approved by the towns and county, the tax rate could be introduced at the upcoming legislative session and take effect Jan. 1, 2026, upon approval from the state.
"It's not a guarantee that it'll pass when it gets to the state legislature," Vanhooser said. "Worcester (County) raised their accommodations tax in the last legislative session, but the previous one they failed, in spectacular fashion. We will have to do quite a bit of work to make sure that we have laid all the groundwork at the state legislature once it leaves our hands."

title: Trappe Council Considers Uses for Remaining ARPA Funds
author: Konner Metz
content:
Trappe council considers uses for remaining ARPA funds

 July 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 328
 Words

 TRAPPE — Town leaders held a workshop on Wednesday afternoon to discuss potential ways to allocate outstanding funds from the American Rescue Plan Act in Trappe.The town has about $758,000 in ARPA funds that must be obligated by the end of 2024 and used by the end of 2026. While no formal decisions were made, the Trappe Town Council did agree to look into securing two new trucks for its public works department.
Town Administrator Erin Braband said that the town's current two trucks are "at their last leg." Council President Brian Schmidt estimated that the costs for two trucks could be around $150,000.
Braband also presented the idea of buying new water meters for the town since the current ones are about 20 years old. This would allow the city to directly receive reports, along with allowing residents to track hourly water usage and receive usage emails.
Council members were open to using ARPA funds for new meters and radio-read transmitters. Braband estimated the cost may be around $175,000.
Much of Wednesday's discussion centered around the town's roads. Town Attorney Lyndsey Jones Ryan warned the council about using ARPA funds to pave roads due to a lack of "clear guidance" at the federal level on whether it falls under allowed uses.
Though she said towns like Federalsburg have allocated ARPA money towards paving, she pointed out that there is a risk the town would end up responsible.
Council Member Jeremy Newnam also expressed concern about beginning work to pave roads before a lead lining initiative this October that may necessitate tearing up the roads for repair.
"I just really worry about paving roads and then possibly having to tear them all up in a couple months," Newnam said. Schmidt agreed, saying "it would be an awful shame" to have newly-paved roads and then tear and patch parts of the road.
Another workshop is planned for early August. No ARPA funds will be officially allocated until the council takes a vote at a council meeting.

title: Trappe Council Holds Special Meeting Monday to Approve USDA Loan
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Trappe council holds special meeting Monday to approve USDA loan

 June 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 558
 Words 

 Read News Document

 TRAPPE — After an in-depth discussion on financial alternatives, the Trappe council unanimously voted to approve a 40-year, potentially low-interest loan from the U.S. Department of Agriculture to help fund the first phase of its pumping station project.Monday morning, a letter from the USDA informed town leadership they had until the end of the day to agree to the conditions of the loan. A special meeting was called to discuss the matter that afternoon.
The town's pumping station project began in 2017. Trappe Attorney Lyndsey Ryan said the town had initially received funding from the USDA for $2,002,000 to cover phases one and two of the project, which aims to repair and replace seven pumping stations in town.
Ryan said after the designs were complete for the project, Trappe received construction bids exceeding the expected budget of $1,396,000.
The lowest bid received, which they awarded the contract to, was from Schumer for a total of $2,195,850.
"Not only did we not have enough funding for the whole project, but we also didn't even have enough funding to complete phase one," Ryan said.
Ryan and Town Administrator Erin Braband spoke to the Department of Agriculture about more funding to fill the gap. The USDA agreed to give Trappe an additional $1,141,000 as a loan, not a grant.
According to Ryan, the USDA said applications for grant funding were highly competitive this cycle. Trappe's pumping stations did not qualify as one of the highest-scoring projects, so the town was automatically bumped into the loan award only category.
Ryan referenced a USDA scoring sheet that took into account socioeconomic status, environmental justice index and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data. Ryan said that the Department of Agriculture took into account the entire Census block, which includes properties outside of incorporated Trappe. This block brought down the score of need for the project, she said.
The terms of the loan require that the town use the new loan funds before they can use the grant funds they had already secured. The USDA also requires that the project be completed and funds fully disbursed, meaning that construction has to meet substantial completion, within three years.
The town will enter into a 40-year loan agreement. The interest rate will not be determined until the end of the project, but the USDA told Ryan that the town should use 2.125% as an interest placeholder.
After Ryan shared the information with the council, members went back and forth trying to find an alternative way to gain the necessary funding.
Several council members asked if it would be possible for the town to reapply for USDA funding next year. Ryan explained that though it is possible Trappe would receive additional funding next year, the town would risk receiving less funding or even no funding if it chose to reapply.
"This is a cycle Trappe's been in for a decade at this point," Commissioner Jeremy Newnam said. "... I don't think we have much of a choice, it just kind of is what it is at this point in time. I don't think it's worth vetoing the whole entire project to possibly be in the exact same position next year or worse."
The council approved the loan with a 4-0 vote. Commissioner Walter Chase did not attend the meeting.
The council said it would take time out of its July meeting to explain the loan to the residents of Trappe.

title: Trappe Council, Developers Address Questions
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Trappe council, developers address questions

 June 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 806
 Words 

 Read News Document

 TRAPPE — Trappe residents recently used a Town Council meeting to voice concerns over fee increases.In the public comments during the meeting, town officials said residents offered misinformation about Lakeside that the council and Lakeside developers attempted to clear up.
The public hearing was held during a June 5 meeting on Ordinance 3-2024, an ordinance to increase the monthly water and sewer fees. Many residents asked why there was a fee increase for the residents of Trappe and why the Lakeside development hasn't offset the cost of living in Trappe.
Brian Schmidt, Trappe council president, told residents that the rise in sewer and water fees has nothing to do with Lakeside but rather with the rise in the cost of living in the area as a whole.
Schmidt reminded residents that in 2017, the town was almost bankrupt, and it couldn't sustain itself without increasing water bills. Additionally, the cost of chemicals and the cost of running the plant as a whole has risen. He said he was confused as to why residents saw a correlation between the rise in water and sewer fees and the Lakeside development.
"We haven't put out a single dime for the Lakeside's treatment plant," Schmidt said. "We are responsible for ours (treatment plant) and the water tower that we have over here also servicing Lakeside, and they (Lakeside residents) are paying toward that water bill, that water bill that Lakeside is paying towards our treatment, toward our water tower."
In a separate interview, Schmidt mentioned that the developer of Lakeside is investing in Trappe and has made plans to continue to invest in Trappe, including a new town hall, water system expansion and funding for the fire department.
"The volunteer fire department is close to receiving a $450,000 check from the developer," Schmidt said. "Each one of those houses is responsible for a $100 donation to the fire department as well. So, at this point, it is $1,200 from the 120 homes."
In a separate interview, Robert Rauch, Lakeside's engineer, explained the economic benefits the development brings to not only the town but the region as a whole.
"The planning, design, studies, permitting and construction have supported dozens of local companies and hundreds of people employed by the companies that have worked on the project for over 20 years," Rauch said. "Taxes, impact fees, and developer contributions have and will continue to benefit town and county residents."
Rauch said the Gov. Wes Moore and the state of Maryland have publicly recognized the housing shortage in Maryland. The Lakeside development will provide a wide range of housing types and price points to help address the housing needs. Lakeside provides a regional growth center that will ease the pressure of sprawl development on other areas in the county.
Rauch mentioned that the residents of Lakeside will support local restaurants and businesses, use locally provided services and support the many local charities, non-profit organizations and arts and entertainment venues.
For Rauch, there are people who misunderstand that the approved Lakeside Planned Neighborhood is a large development of 2,501 residential units with a mix of commercial use on the property. However, it has had a slow start to growth in a way that many surrounding communities have not.
"Over the 20-plus years since Lakeside was approved, fewer than 150 homes have been built in Lakeside, while more than 1,900 homes were approved or built in Easton," Rauch said.
Schmidt told residents at that Wednesday evening meeting that the benefits and profits from the development would come later when the Lakeside development has grown more.
Eventually, the Lakeside wastewater treatment plant will be transferred to Trappe. Agreements for this transfer were mentioned at Wednesday's meeting and tabled for a future meeting.
Ryan Showalter, attorney for Lakeside, explained the developer's responsibilities after the plant is transferred.
"The developer is responsible for providing all of the wastewater collection and treatment infrastructure necessary to serve the full build-out of the Lakeside project," Showalter said in a separate interview. "Once the initial phase of the wastewater treatment plant is complete and turned over to the town, the developer remains responsible for any deficiencies between the costs of operation and maintenance and the sewer revenues collected by the town from Lakeside residents."
Additionally, once the transfer is completed, the developer remains responsible for incrementally expanding the wastewater treatment plant as the capacity is utilized.
Toward the end of the meeting, the council unanimously voted to adopt Ordinance 3-2024. Council member Rosalee Potter commented to the residents of Trappe prior to the vote.
"It's hard for you, but it's also hard for us because whatever we do, it affects you, but it also affects our pocketbooks as well," Potter said. "We're not doing these things because we want to, but we do these things because we have to, in order to see that the town itself continues to thrive, continues to operate, continues to be a town of Trappe."

title: Easton Budget Projects More Than $100K Saved in Overtime Pay
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton budget projects more than $100K saved in overtime pay

 June 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 604
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — In what was a difficult process, Easton officials worked all spring to finalize the $28 million fiscal year 2025 budget, which included a sizable decrease in overtime pay, an area of much discussion in previous council meetings.According to figures provided by Town Manager Donald Richardson, the town is budgeted to save $127,250 in overtime pay to employees in FY25.
The decrease comes after Mayor Megan Cook reworked the budget, which was approved at a June 3 Town Council meeting, to switch the status of 13 department heads from non-exempt to exempt. Exempt employees do not receive overtime pay.
"It was a lot of negotiation, because it's not an easy transition," Ward 1 Council Member Maureen Curry said. "But in my opinion, it was the right thing to do."
While $430,320 was budgeted for overtime in FY24, Richardson said the current expenditures are about $498,000 as the July 1 fiscal year end approaches. FY25's budget allots $303,070 for overtime pay.
Notably, there is no overtime budgeted in FY25 for the town manager, building inspections and engineering departments. Those three areas combined for a total of more than $90,000 in projected overtime in FY24's budget, with engineering coming in second-highest overall at $72,000.
The highest department in overtime budgeting was police patrol, which will decrease from $256,700 in FY24 to a projected $209,000 in FY25, still the highest amount.
IT, police administration and parks and recreation will all receive overtime decreases compared to last year's budget. Police special operations, meanwhile, is budgeted for an increase of more than $25,000 in FY25 overtime pay.
"Shifting select administrative staff to exempt status has reduced overtime costs and aims to prevent potential budget overruns," Council President Frank Gunsallus wrote in a statement. "... I commend everyone involved in this budget process for their hard work to ensure financial responsibility and transparency."
The Town Council held a workshop in April to discuss shifting department heads to exempt status. Cook presented a plan of action, including a 3% salary increase for those moving to exempt status to offset the losses in overtime pay.
Council members expressed concern with this increase during the workshop, and those increases were reduced by the time the final budget was passed early June.
In June 7 interviews with the Star Democrat, Curry and Ward 2 Council Member Don Abbatiello both praised the mayor for working to reduce those increases during the budget process.
"She came back, and many of those increases that we thought were a little excessive were reduced by the mayor to make it a little bit more palatable for the council to accept," Abbatiello said.
Cook and Chief Human Resource Officer Rick Farr vouched during the April workshop that this was a much-needed change for the town. While council members largely agreed, it took some tinkering and adjustments.
Abbatiello is pleased with the status change for select employees and sees it continuing for years to come.
"We're talking about department heads," Abbatiello said. "We're not talking about the guys who work outside in public works. We're not talking about the office staff."
While Abbatiello and Curry each expressed satisfaction with this year's budget, next year's will be no easy task.
Both mentioned that federal funds from the American Rescue Plan Act will run dry. Abbatiello noted the council must keep its eye on the balance of the budget's allocation toward salaries and benefits versus capital projects
"You do not want salaries and benefits far (exceeding) operations and capital projects, because then you're not going to get anything accomplished around town," he said.
"Next year is going to be even more of a challenge," Curry said. "And some belt-tightening may be in order."
Maggie Trovato contributed reporting to this story.

title: Council Introduces One-Cent Resolution Question for 2024 Ballot
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Council introduces one-cent resolution question for 2024 ballot

 June 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 427

 EASTON — Five years ago, Talbot County residents had the opportunity to vote on a one-cent resolution that would increase residents' taxes for public safety over five years. Last week, Talbot County Council members introduced the same resolution to appear on the 2024 general election ballot.During a May 28 meeting, the council unanimously introduced a resolution to place a question on the ballot at the 2024 general election to amend section 614 of the charter of Talbot County to allow the council to add up to one cent per $100 of assessed value above the revenue cap for an additional five years beginning July 1, 2026.
According to the resolution document, the original resolution was adopted by a 5-0 vote of the Talbot County Council on July 21, 2020. The resolution was approved by the majority of Talbot County voters at the 2020 general election.
This resolution would "allow but not require" the Talbot County Council to add up to one cent per one hundred dollars of assessed value above the revenue cap for an additional five years.
Talbot County Attorney Patrick Thomas said that as of July 1, 2021, revenues derived from property taxes included in the constant yield tax rate certification shall not increase more than 2% from the previous year.
This increase has helped offset the county's costs of maintaining public safety, officials said.
Clay Stamp, the county manager of Talbot County, said he was a public supporter of the resolution when it was initially introduced because it would assist in providing quicker services for the residents of Talbot County.
Over the last fiscal year, the one-cent initiative has provided about $200,000 for the county to offset the public safety budget, which includes law enforcement, fire departments and other emergency services.
When reintroduced in May, Council Member Dave Stepp said over half of Talbot County voters supported this resolution in 2020. The funds generated from this resolution have solved many problems Stepp has seen in neighboring counties, he said.
"It would benefit our public services here in Talbot County," Stepp said. "The names of the departments that would make it to the ballot question would be the Sheriff's department, Department of Emergency Services as well as the Department of Corrections. We've seen a lot of positive things that have happened in those departments over the years."
Stepp asked his fellow council members to support the resolution and allow residents to decide whether or not they would like to see it implemented for the following five years.
The council unanimously voted to introduce the resolution. A public hearing will be on Tuesday, June 25.

title: Easton Town Council Approves FY2025 Budget
author: Maggie Trovato

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News

 EASTON — The Easton Town Council voted unanimously to approve the town's fiscal year 2025 budget at a council meeting Monday.Before the vote, Town Manager Donald Richardson said the proposed $28 million working budget took months to get to the finish line. title: Talbot County Council Approves 2024-2025 Budget
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Talbot County Council approves 2024-2025 budget

 May 30, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 587
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — On Tuesday evening, the Talbot County Council approved the 2024-2025 annual budget with a 4-1 majority.Council member Lynn Mielke was the sole nay, citing increased taxes for residents as her reason for voting against the proposal.
Martha Sparks, finance director for Talbot County, presented the budget and gave an overview of an additional amendment introduced in April that would allow the movement of expenses between categories in the budget. It has been described as a "formality" by Clay Stamp, manager for Talbot County, and would have no impact on the total revenues and expenditures for the general funds, Stamp said.
Sparks opened the floor so the council could ask final questions. Mielke asked Sparks about the excess funds that were developed through the increase in taxes.
Mielke noted that in the last few years, there has been a noticeable excess of funds from income tax revenues, yet the council continues to raise taxes through 1 cent increase initiatives and educational supplement tax rate raises.
Local income tax revenue for the new budget is based on a rate of 2.4 percent of the Maryland taxable income.
"My question is, why continue an increase in the taxes if we're sitting on these reserves," Mielke asked. "I'm just looking at the state of the economy as it presently is and how necessary that is."
Sparks explained that income tax revenues are volatile, and the main reason for that is the "few" number of high-income earners in Talbot County.
"We budget conservatively on income tax because we are unsure of the levels, and we're not the only county that struggles with budgeting the correct levels of income tax during budget time," she said.
Sparks explained that the excess of those revenues goes to reserves, and this budget up for vote includes those reserves for capital improvement projects and capital outlay items.
County Manager Clay Stamp said that this year, the council made adjustments in the budget assumptions, basically diverting the income tax revenues into capital to build reserves.
"What we're seeing and what we will continue to see is an increase in costs, especially to provide public safety services," Stamp said. "We expect that we will not see the revenue this year that we've seen in the past because we're applying to operational needs, which are recurring needs."
Sparks added that the finance department conservatively budgeted income tax for the county because of potential uncertainty. When budgeting this way, the county receives income tax revenues that are higher than budgeted, she said.
Sparks called it a "really good policy to have."
Mielke said that after three years of building reserves, the council should consider doing something different.
"I'm not suggesting that we use all of the reserves; I'm just suggesting that we have considerable reserves," she said. Mielke explained that given the current state of the economy, inflation and the burden carried by taxpayers, the council should consider not raising taxes this year.
Sparks responded that the county has not raised the income tax rate since 2013, and it has only increased what has been allowed by charter. This includes 2% over the revenues certified by the state Department of Assessments and Taxation, a penny increase authorized by voters in 2020 and 4 cents to the tax rate for the educational supplement to help cover increased school costs.
The approved budget set a real property tax rate 79.1 cents for $100 of assessed value for all properties outside the incorporated limited of the towns of Easton, Oxford, Queen Anne, St. Michaels and Trappe, where tax differentials have been established. This includes an educational supplement.

title: Talbot County Council Holds Public Hearings on Budget

 EASTON — On Tuesday, the Talbot County Council reviewed the 2024-2025 county budget with a 4.76 cent increase in the property tax rate, a 6.4% increase.The council held two public hearings for the annual fiscal year budget Tuesday, the first at the Talbot County Courthouse and the second in the Easton Elementary School cafeteria.
Martha Sparks, finance director of Talbot County, said Talbot County has a conservative approach to proposed budgets that prioritizes public safety and education for the county.
The increase 4.76 cent property tax rate increase includes a 1-cent raise previously approved by voters to support public safety and a 4-cent "education supplement" to increase funding for Talbot County Public Schools.
The 2025 fiscal year budget allocates $54.6 million to Talbot County Public Schools. This is an increase of $3.65 million from last year's budget and $2.8 million above the required local share funding. The budget exceeds the state-mandated funding level for Talbot County Public Schools, which is proposed at 43.3% of the county's 2025 operating budget.
The Capital Improvement Project budget included funding for Talbot County Public Schools, which includes $16.9 million for capital projects. Capital projects included in the 2025 budget include an expansion of the Talbot County Free Library in St. Michaels and renovation of the Chapel District Elementary School in Cordova.
Sparks told the council that during a review by Moody's Investors Service of the county's budget, Talbot was given rave reviews. Sparks said Moody's Investors Service described the budget as "very strong, and the management team is generally conservative in its budgeting."
PUBLIC HEARINGDuring the public hearing, Dana Newman, director of the Talbot County Free Library, thanked the council for funding the expansion of the Talbot County Free Library and supporting education for the county.
"The St. Michaels library is just a wonderful place. I was there this morning, there were people from the Benedictine school, their staff were just making them laugh, it was a really joyful experience to see that. That happens in county libraries every day; we just have two libraries," Newman said. "... We just want to make sure that the spaces are adequate and that they serve the public in the best way possible."
Cliff Coppersmith, president of Chesapeake College, and Karen Smith, CFO of Chesapeake College, appeared before the council representing Chesapeake College. Coppersmith thanked the council for its support of the college in the 2025 budget.
"It's because of the support of you as leaders in our regional county setup that we have posted five county institution, the only one of its kind in the state of Maryland," Coppersmith said. "But we do appreciate the unanimous support we have from all of you, which I can say all of you have some connection to the college."
Susan Sherman, president of the Public County Library Board of Trustees, and Charles Yonkers, member of the Board of Trustees, spoke during the public hearing. Sherman began by thanking the council for its support.
"I want to thank you for your support of the St. Michael's expansion," Sherman said. "I think it's such a wonderful example of community involvement and responsibility as community members. So, thank you. I think your response to our community is just amazing, and it feels so much appreciated.

title: Easton Town Council Hears About Proposed Budget, Approves EPD Vehicle Purchase
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Easton Town Council hears about proposed budget, approves EPD vehicle purchase

 May 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 579
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — At a regular meeting Monday, the Easton Town Council heard from Mayor Megan Cook about the proposed fiscal year 2025 budget, approved the purchasing of seven police vehicles and talked about communication with residents regarding a proposed ordinance.BUDGET PRESENTATION
During the proposed fiscal year 2025 town budget presentation, Mayor Megan Cook talked about the various amenities and services that "(make) Easton Easton."
She also talked about the difficulties of drafting this year's budget compared to years past. She said the fiscal year 2024 budget still had "the major effects" of American Rescue Plan Act funds and 2020 bond funds.
"One of the main reasons this year's budget has been so difficult is due to the completion of those projects and the allocation of the ARPA funds," she said.
ARPA funds need to be obligated by the end of calendar year 2024 and spent by the end of calendar year 2026.
Cook said they were able to get the draft budget down to $28 million from about $31 million. The tax rate is proposed to stay the same as it has been since 2008 at 0.52 cents per assessed $100 of value.
Looking into the future, Cook said rising costs will come with the growth of the town. That could result in a need for reevaluating the tax rate, she said.
"We have to consider the balance between maintaining what we have and our projected future growth," she said.
A public hearing on the budget is set for the next council meeting on May 20.
POLICE VEHICLES
The Town Council approved the purchase of seven vehicles for the Easton Police Department and radios for those vehicles.
Town Manager Donald Richardson said the police department was able to find seven vehicles on lots in Howard County and in Pennsylvania.
Richardson said the total cost of the vehicles is $307,425. This will be paid for using ARPA funds, which were reallocated by council from a $390,000 stream restoration project in early March.
Richardson said the the police department also requested new radios be purchased for the vehicles. He said the cost of this, which is $52,756.41, would come out of the remaining ARPA funds allocated for the purchasing of the police vehicles. He said there was a remaining balance of $516,000 after the vehicles were purchased.
ILLICIT DISCHARGE ORDINANCE
A proposed ordinance that would define what illicit discharges into stormwater drains are and provide for enforcement actions brought discussion from council members about the town's communication with residents.
Town Engineer Rick Van Emburgh said illicit discharge is essentially anything that isn't stormwater. While there are some exemptions, he said anything other than stormwater — such as petroleum, industrial waste or hazardous waste — shouldn't go into the town's storm drains.
Van Emburgh said the ordinance is necessary for Easton's participation in Maryland Department of the Environment's Municipal Separate Storm Sewer Systems, or MS4, program.
The town's goal with this program is to educate and work with the community on what can and cannot go into the storm drains.
"Ultimately, we're just trying to keep the Bay clean," Van Emburgh said.
Ward 4 council member the Rev. Elmer Davis Jr. asked what the town would do to ensure the community is aware of this new enforcement. He said transparency is key, and this addition would enhance the policy. Ward 1 council member Maureen Curry said some kind of an outreach plan would be beneficial.
Van Emburgh said he would make a revision to include communication with residents in the ordinance. A public hearing for the ordinance is set for June 17.

title: Talbot Council Introduces 2025 Budget
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Talbot Council introduces 2025 budget

 April 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 511
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — On Tuesday evening, the Talbot County Council voted unanimously to introduce the proposed fiscal year 2025 general fund budget of $163,970,000.The budget will include an education increase of $3.65 million from the 2024 budget.
Talbot County Public Schools will receive $54.6 million in total funding, according to the proposed budget. This increase will go toward the capital project request for planned Chapel District Elementary School renovations and other capital projects.
The increase in the education budget is due, in part, to the implications of the Maryland Blueprint for Education plan. Blueprint is a plan passed by the Maryland General Assembly in 2021 that aims to improve student outcomes and the quality of education across the state by increasing education funding by $3.8 billion each year over the next 10 years.
"Maryland Blueprint required local share funding to increase by $1.053 million for FY2025 budget," Martha Sparks, finance director for Talbot County, said at the Tuesday meeting. "In addition to the mandated funding, the county has included an additional appropriation of $2.6 million. Funding to support Talbot County Schools increased overall by $3.65 million above FY24 levels."
Education spending represents 37.7% of the county's total proposed budget. These numbers include Talbot County Public Schools, Chesapeake College and the Talbot County Free Library expenses.
The budget also allocates an additional $1.5 million in capital improvement project funding for Talbot County Public Schools to prioritize other projects.
The budget discussion included the option to expand the amendment of the 1-cent increase in property tax rates for public safety.
In November 2020, Talbot County voters approved an amendment allowing a 1-cent increase to the property tax rate to support public safety spending. This increase began in the FY2022 budget and will continue until the FY2026 budget.
Revenues from the 1-cent increase have been used to fund 26 new public safety positions across departments, such as deputies, paramedics, emergency medical technicians and 911 operators. The funds from the amendment have allowed for inclusion of sheriff's office, paramedics/EMTs and correctional officers in enhanced retirement programs for public safety employees.
Sparks noted that the county has used more than the funds provided by the 1-cent increase to public safety.
"The county has used more than the revenues generated from the 1 cent to enhance public safety personnel serving the citizens and visitors of Talbot County," she said.
The council has the option to allow county residents to extend the 1-cent increase beyond FY2026 through a ballot initiative for voters in the November 2024 general election.
Clay Stamp, county manager for Talbot County, expressed his admiration for the county's finance team for their work on the budget.
"There's a lot of hard work that went into drafting the FY 25 proposed balanced budget," Stamp said. "While we're here tonight, I want to thank the council for your cooperation and support over the last number of months."
Two public hearings will be held to gather community input before final approval.
A public hearing will be held on May 7 at 2 p.m. in the Talbot County Courthouse and at 7 p.m. in the Easton Elementary School cafeteria, located at 307 Glenwood Avenue.

title: Easton Works Toward Approval of Fiscal Year 2025 Budget
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Easton works toward approval of fiscal year 2025 budget

 April 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 546
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Easton Mayor Megan Cook said there isn't a lot of fluff in the $28 million proposed overall budget for fiscal year 2025."We continue to fund salaries and all training and safety," Cook said in an interview. "That's our No. 1 priority."
Cook said some tough decisions needed to be made to get that number down to $28 million.
"The original asks for the proposed budget might have been $34 million," she said. "We've had to cut back. And each department has been really good about helping to identify areas where we could cut to save some money."
According to town documents, the combined general fund and capital fund budget for fiscal year 2024 was $36.2 million.
Council President Frank Gunsallus said one of the biggest changes to the budget this year is the change in overtime.
"That's a very big step, and it's long overdue," he said.
At an Easton Town Council workshop on exempt and non-exempt employment status April 1, the council discussed the possibility of switching some employee statuses from non-exempt to exempt. Cook said in an interview April 3 that around 13 department heads would be affected.
"Adjusting the classification of specific employees from non-exempt to exempt status is not a routine practice," Gunsallus said. "Therefore, we will carefully consider this allocation of related funds."
Budget workshops have begun. Two were held this week — one on Tuesday and one on Wednesday. Another budget workshop is scheduled for next Wednesday, April 17.
Cook said the town has presented a balanced budget to the council.
"So anything that we're adding back in, we're going to have to take something back out," she said about the process ahead.
The council plans to approve a budget June 3 so that there is enough time for the budget ordinance to go into effect on July 1, the first day of fiscal year 2025.
Cook said she plans to have a first reading of a budget ordinance and presentation for the council on May 20.
"That'll give them that meeting to discuss any changes," she said.
Cook said the budget workshops have gone well so far.
"The department has done a great job presenting and answering questions from the council," she said.
Because there are three new members on the council, there have been a lot of questions, Cook said.
"There are a lot of questions about where the numbers come from and things like that because it's the first time they've been through the process," she said. "But department heads have done a great job presenting their priorities."
Gunsallus called the proposed budget a rough draft, saying that it's now a matter of deliberating on certain allocations, scrutinizing potential purchases and discussing what should take priority.
"Once you get out of the core essentials of what each department needs to operate, that's when you really get into the splitting of the remaining funds," he said.
Cook said she will sit down with the finance department and Town Manager Don Richardson, as well as department heads, after the next budget workshop to make any changes to the proposed budget based on comments from the council.
Gunsallus said Easton is in a good position, where it is able to fulfill all departments' needs.
"But then you get into the requests beyond basic needs," he said. "And then that's where the hard work and the group collaboration comes in."

title: Talbot County Council Approves Hog Neck Golf Course Renovation
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Talbot County Council approves Hog Neck Golf Course renovation

 March 27, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 454

 EASTON — The Talbot County Council's Thursday evening to discussion of the county's enterprise funds budgets for the upcoming fiscal year included a lengthy talk about the renovations of the Hog Neck Golf Course.Richard Settler, general manager at Hog Neck Golf Course, came to the council with a plan for the future of this golf course.
The plan includes improvements such as driving range enhancements, venue operations and a new kitchen so the golf course can generate significantly higher revenues in the future.
Settler focused on the need for funds for kitchen improvements. This project would require $405,000, including items like a flat-top grill, oven, fryer and hood unit.
Settler provided financial projections to the council, showing that with the new projects, revenues could increase to around $3 million annually once the new facilities are open and fully operational.
The goal, Settler said, would be for the golf course, which is owned and operated by the county, to become more financially self-sufficient over time and generate enough revenue to pay for its capital projects and operations without needing as much subsidy from the Talbot County general fund.
"We're basically creating a whole new business," said Settler of the golf course's renovations, many of which are already underway.
Including Settler's $405,000 ask, the project will cost about $2.3 million.
Council members Lynn Mielke and Dave Stepp supported the changes to the golf course.
"I'm the only one that has seen one of these driving ranges and how popular and successful it is," Mielke said. "That makes an impact on me in terms of my view on proceeding on this and making an investment."
Council members Chuck Callahan, Keasha Haythe and Pete Lesher were more hesitant about investing further into the project.
Haythe said it was essential to treat this as a new business and take a more conservative approach to the revenue produced during its first fiscal year. Funds have already been provided for other capital projects, like the driving range enhancements.
Callahan suggested that they wait a bit longer before approving the decision. Haythe and Lesher agreed with this statement.
"It's a business decision that we have to make with the taxpayers' money," Callahan said. "I would feel a bit more comfortable waiting to see."
Stepp and Mielke protested.
"My theory on this is if we're going to do it, let's do it right," Stepp said. "Let's get everything in place because we're going to have an opportunity here for a lot of first impressions."
Settler stressed that revenue would drastically decrease if the business were unable to sell hot food, which ultimately changed the minds of Callahan, Haythe and Lesher. The council approved fully funding the kitchen improvements at the golf course.
Settler said they hope to complete kitchen renovations before the "true grand opening" in May 2024.

title: Commissioners of Oxford introduce FY2024 amended budget
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Commissioners of Oxford introduce FY2024 amended budget

 March 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 749
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — The time to approve budgets is right around the bend for the Commissioners of Oxford.At a town meeting Tuesday, the commissioners introduced an amended fiscal year 2024 general budget and heard from Town Manager Cheryl Lewis on a preliminary draft budget for fiscal year 2025.
At the previous town meeting on Feb. 27, Lewis said she always starts this time of year with going over amendments to the current budget.
"It's almost like a training session for the real budget for the public and commissioners," she said.
According to an amended budget document posted on the town website, the town's revised income for fiscal year 2024 is $5.57 million The original budget listed $6.33 million for income.
The town's revised expenses for fiscal year 2024 was $5.76 million. The original budget listed $6.59 million for expenses.
The revised net income is negative $183,560. On the original budget, the town's net income was listed as negative $252,465.
For fiscal year 2023, the town's revenues were $2.61 million and its expenses were $2.79 million.
At the meeting Tuesday, Commissioner Katrina Greer noted that the town had $120,000 more in investment income this year.
Commissioner Susan Delean-Botkin said she was concerned that legal fees were $30,000 higher in the amended budget than the original budget for fiscal year 2024.
Lewis said legal fees are always estimated in the budget.
"When you have more legal needs than any other year, it's going to happen," she said. "In the last nine months, we've had more legal needs."
After introducing the amended budget, the commissioners scheduled a public hearing for April 23.
PRELIMINARY DRAFT
The Commissioners of Oxford also heard from Lewis about a preliminary draft budget for fiscal year 2025. Lewis went through different capital expenditures that the commissioners will need to consider as they begin the budget approval process.
"Those are the things you really need to pick through and decide what items you think you want to do," she said.
One budget item Lewis pointed out was $20,000 for improvements to the Community Services Building, where the Oxford Town Office, commissioners meeting room and Oxford Police Department are located. Lewis said these funds would go toward replacing the deck on the back of the building and painting parts of the building.
For the police department, Lewis pointed out $68,000 that would go toward replacing or purchasing a new truck for the department and toward furnishings needed for the office.
Lewis said she put $10,000 in the preliminary draft budget to purchase two AED units — one to be placed outside the Community Services Building and one to be placed at the ferry dock.
Lewis said the Public Works Department would like to trade in and upgrade one of its tractors. She said the cost would be between $70,000 and $80,000. Along with the tractor, she said public works has asked to get the shop painted.
Lewis said she added another $10,000 to the budget for public works that could be used to purchase a trailer or to purchase a few smaller items.
For the Roads Department, $150,000 is currently earmarked for a paving project that would include the post office and bank parking lots. Although this project was originally a part of the fiscal year 2024 budget, Lewis said the town would not be able to go out to bid, get a contractor and pay for the project before fiscal year 2025 begins.
Lewis said the Oxford Community Center — which is owned by the town — also asked to be included in this paving project so its back parking lot, which is currently gravel, could be paved.
Lewis mentioned a $100,000 optional budget item to replace water lines under the street. She said the town could earmark money for this in the event that it identifies a real problem.
For wastewater, Lewis highlighted a $200,000 budget item for a backup pump. Lewis also suggested incorporating $100,000 into the budget every year to pay for water lines and sewer lines on an alternating basis. She said this had been set up before the COVID-19 pandemic, but hadn't been continued.
Lewis said she will come back to the commissioners with a date for a budget workshop so that the budget can be adopted by May 31.
In a text, Lewis said the goal is to adopt the budget 30 days before the start of the new fiscal year, July 1.
"It is always possible to have the process carry past that date," she said. "I try to set it up so the commissioners understand their target dates far enough in advance to keep things on schedule."

title: Budget and County Leadership Worries Shared with Eastern Shore Delegation
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Budget and county leadership worries shared with Eastern Shore delegation

 March 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 379
 Words 

 Read News Document

 With the state facing a budget shortfall in coming years, Maryland counties may see an increase in unfunded mandates.That was the message Maryland Association of Counties Executive Director Michael Sanderson delivered to the Eastern Shore Delegation Friday morning.
He began the presentation by saying that as the counties face many different issues, a state agency is "just never going to have the on-the-ground view" that local governments have connecting with the community and getting input from the people who live there.
Among the causes of concern for straining county budgets, Sanderson said, is the Blueprint education plan, an education bill passed in 2021 that increases annual education funding by over $3.8 billion over the next ten years.
Del. Christopher Adams (R-Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico), delegation chair, later commented that the budgets could be similar to what happened in the 2007-2008 financial crisis when teacher pension costs were shifted to counties.
Sanderson warned that the projected state budget shortfalls over the next few years could squeeze county budgets, especially as the costs of fully implementing the Blueprint education plan begin taking effect a couple of years from now.
He said that local governments "don't have a bunch of money" like the state does to push this problem out and call it a "future problem." He said it is urgent for county budgets, mainly because of an existing transportation funding crisis.
Adams expressed his own concerns, saying that the budget that's coming up over the next two to three years will not only be stressful for local officials but may also put them in a position to handle an unfunded mandate.
"The state may or may not have any other choice but to take these education shortfalls, and that's what this budget shortfall is going to be in two to three years. It's all about education," Adams said.
Sanderson warned that the coming economic difficulties will be the first exposure for many local leaders to a situation where their county budget is in trouble.
"About 40-something percent of our local elected leaders only have experienced in the last three or four years with this kind of paper over the economy, healthy state budgets and surpluses and so forth," Sanderson said. "And this will be the first exposure for a lot of them, for suddenly their county budget is in crisis."

title: Easton Town Council Amends Proposed ARPA Fund Ordinance Ahead of Public Hearing

Easton Town Council amends proposed ARPA fund ordinance ahead of public hearing

 EASTON — The Easton Town Council amended a proposed ordinance that deals with the distribution of American Rescue Plan Act funds.The Town Council voted to remove a $390,000 stream restoration project from the list of fiscal year 2024 ARPA-funded projects and reallocated those funds for the purchasing of police cars for the Easton Police Department.
Before voting on this, Ward 2 council member Don Abbatiello asked if the town would be able to fund the restoration project another way.
Town Engineer Rick Van Emburgh said the project could be funded through a capital request in the budget or through applying for grant funding.
"We've done three stream restoration projects since I've been here," he said. "The first two we did with grant funding and the third one we did with the ARPA funding."
Town Manager Donald Richardson said that although both projects are important, the city has an "outstanding commitment" to Easton police to fund take-home vehicles.
Mayor Megan Cook said the reallocated ARPA funding would cover the cost of purchasing and outfitting nearly four vehicles.
Richardson said eight police vehicles are needed in the next fiscal year and said putting ARPA money toward this could alleviate the town's budget.
"The budget is going to be challenging this year," he said.
Richardson said that ARPA funds, federal funding used to aid economic recovery from the COVID-19 pandemic, must be allocated by December.
A public hearing on the amended ordinance is set for the next Town Council meeting on March 18.

title: Oxford audit brings question of how to strengthen internal controls in small town
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford audit brings question of how to strengthen internal controls in small town

 January 25, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 512
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — After a presentation on the Town of Oxford's fiscal year 2023 audit, commissioners received suggestions on how the town could address a material weakness for its segregation of duties.During a Commissioners of Oxford meeting Tuesday evening, Roy Geiser, a partner at the accounting firm UHY, went through the highlights of the financial report. For fiscal year 2023, Oxford received an unmodified opinion, the highest level of assurance that can be given by an auditor.
"And what that means is (that) these financials as presented, in our opinion, are free of any material misstatements," Geiser said.
Toward the end of his presentation, Geiser detailed a material weakness that was found regarding the town's segregation of duties — meaning that there aren't enough town employees to separate financial duties.
"A lot of towns your size have this exact comment," Geiser said about the finding.
There are three levels of of control deficiencies that auditors can find, Geiser said. These are: a deficiency, a significant deficiency or a material weakness.
Geiser said that material weakness is the most severe of these deficiencies. If found, a material weakness needs to be communicated by the auditor via a letter.
This is not the first year the Town of Oxford has received this comment about the lack of internal controls in its audit. According to the financial reports posted on the town website, this has been a finding in town audits going back to 2016.
Geiser suggested that commissioners ask questions if they ever notice something "out of line" when it comes to town finances.
After Geiser's presentation, Commissioner Katrina Greer asked him how other towns handle this material weakness issue.
Geiser said that while some towns don't do anything, others use a third-party consultant.
"They maybe bring them in quarterly just to have another set of eyes looking around," he said.
Some other towns, Geiser said, will have council member involved or set up an audit committee. He said an audit committee is "very rare" for a town the size of Oxford.
Greer said this is something the commissioners will be talking about more in the future.
At the previous town meeting on Jan. 11, Greer said she would like to discuss the possibility of hiring someone with a finance or accounting background to take on some of the town's financial duties in order to address this issue with internal controls.
"This would take some burden off the manager and enable us to comply with the audit recommendation of having multiple people performing financial roles," she said at the meeting.
Town Manager Cheryl Lewis said she had shared originally this idea with the commissioners because hiring more employees is the way to solve this problem.
"Admittedly most towns our size can't afford more staff," Lewis said at the Jan. 11 meeting. "Oxford is not in that situation, per se."
At the meeting Tuesday, one resident asked Geiser if hiring a part-time employee could solve the issue.
"In a perfect world, you want at least three people in your accounting function," Geiser said. "There are ways to get around it with other checks and balances. So a part-time person could help that situation."

title: Oxford To Create Investment Opportunity Task Force
author: Maggie Trovato; Mtrovato@Chespub.Com
content:
Oxford To Create Investment Opportunity Task Force

 December 14, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; Mtrovato@Chespub.Com | Page: B3 | Section: News 
 
 582
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD - After months of discussion, the Commissioners of Oxford passed a resolution to create an Investment Opportunity Task Force at a meeting on Tuesday.Both Commission President Tom Costigan and Commissioner Katrina Greer voted in favor of the resolution.
Commissioner Susan Delean-Botkin voted against it.
The resolution for the task force, previously named the Investment Advisory Committee, was introduced by Costigan at a commissioners meeting on Oct. 24.
The task force, made up of three members, will be charged with reviewing the town's investments quarterly, providing recommendations to the commissioners on investment opportunities, responding to other commissioner requests, and annually reviewing and providing recommendations on the town's investment policy.
The task force will receive a packet of documents, which are listed in the proposed resolution, by the town manager.
Members of the task force must be registered to vote in the Town of Oxford and have "experience and training in municipal investment policies and implementation."
Members cannot hold a paid, appointed or elected position in Oxford's government.
At the October meeting, Costigan's resolution was introduced alongside a competing proposed resolution to create a Financial Advisory Committee by Greer.
In Greer's proposal, the committee would be tasked with providing recommendations to commissioners "in matters and issues related to town finances and financial topics" and responding to recommendation requests from commissioners regarding issues related to town finances and financial topics.
The committee would not exercise financial powers of the town. It would have the authority to access any financial information available to the public via the Maryland Public Information Act.
Members would need to be a registered voter, renter, resident or property owner in the town and have "demonstrable, professional experience in finance." Members would not be able to hold a paid, appointed or elected position in Oxford's government.
The commissioners waited to vote on whether to enact one of the two resolutions, or neither of them, until the meeting Tuesday, in order to give residents time to look at both resolutions and share their thoughts and feedback.
Greer's resolution was voted on before Costigan's. Greer voted in favor of it. Costigan and Delean-Botkin voted against it. Greer then voted in favor of Costigan's resolution.
"I want to take the time to thank everyone who took the time to write in and express your opinions on this matter," Costigan said at the meeting.
"Your thoughts have certainly helped me and, I'm sure, the other commissioners, come to a conclusion."
At October and November meetings, some residents shared their support for Greer's proposal, some shared support for Costigan's proposal and others questioned why the town needed a committee or task force in the first place.
Delean-Botkin spoke before both votes to say that, having read letters from residents as well as heard many opinions and comments from residents, she had concerns about both proposals. She said that for this reason, she would be voting against the resolutions.
"My guiding principal is what is the best for the town of Oxford now and in the future," Delean-Botkin said. "On that basis, I don't believe an independent citizen advisory committee is in the best interest of the town."
After the vote, Greer said she was pleased with the result.
"I'm glad that we have come to the legislative process and produced something," she said.
"I think it will be a great benefit."

 Oxford Commission President Tom Costigan (left) and Commissioner Katrina Greer discuss their respective committee proposals at a Commissioners of Oxford meeting Oct. 24. At a meeting Dec. 12, the commissioners passed a resolution to create Costigan's proposed Investment Opportunity Task Force.
