title: Local State Legislators Discuss Predicted State Revenue Shortfall
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Local state legislators discuss predicted state revenue shortfall

 December 7, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 5 | Section: News 
 
 759
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - Local state legislators gathered at the Chesapeake Grove Intergenerational Center Tuesday afternoon to share their expectations for the 2024 Legislative Session with constituents.At the event, hosted by the Dorchester Chamber of Commerce, attendees were served lunch before getting the opportunity to ask questions to District 37 legislators Sen. Johnny Mautz (R, Talbot County), Del. Chris Adams (R, Wicomico) Del. Tom Hutchinson (R, Dorchester) and Speaker Pro Tem Sheree Sample-Hughes (D, Wicomico) regarding the 446th session of the Maryland General Assembly that will commence in Annapolis on Jan. 10.The legislators answered questions on topics ranging from the Blueprint for Maryland's Future to economic development to juvenile crime.Matthew Teffeau, manager of government affairs and economic development at Choptank Electric Cooperative, asked the first question of the event. He asked for ways in which the estimated state revenue shortfall of more than $460 million could be addressed.Sample-Hughes, who spoke first, said that this situation with the budget is challenging."There have been many task forces that have taken place this interim to address issues," she said about the shortfall.When it comes to the Blueprint for Maryland's Future, for example, Sample-Hughes said the state won't have enough money in the budget to cover what has been proposed until 2027.Sample-Hughes also brought up fuel tax funds, which have decreased in the state due to the increase in electronic vehicles."That requires a whole other level of structure and planning to see what that looks like for the state," she said. "Do we put in fees for these electric vehicles and hybrid vehicles so we can come out into somewhat of a balanced budget?" New legislation regarding this could come out of the upcoming General Assembly session, she said.Adams followed Sample-Hughes in answering the question. He said the budget will be the "number one topic" of discussion going into Legislative Session this year.He said that COVID-19 emergency funding has helped the state's budget in the past couple years, but said he has noticed many municipalities and county governments using these funds for programs that move into the future, not just one-time appropriations."Many of the budget problems that we're going to have are going to come down to this: Ongoing spending of dollars for social programs for which there are no tax revenue sources to derive those from," he said.Adams said this could lead to fee and tax increases as well as cuts to spending "in places where we should not be cutting."Adams concluded his answer by saying that the state's budget deficit could reach $1.8 billion by 2027."So we're talking $400 million next year," he said, "In a couple years, if we don't right this ship, we're talking about multiple billions of dollars of revenue shortfall.That's going to hit hard."Mautz spoke next, saying that there is no simple answer to fixing the predicted budget shortfall."I think everything is going to be on the table this session," he said. "There's going to be all kinds of maneuvering."Mautz said that it's important to make sure that the burden of the budget shortage isn't left on local governments. He said that the best solution to the problem is to drive investment."The budget depends on revenues, and the way you do that is you try to get capital investment and you try to fuel small business," he said. "And that's the backbone of the Eastern Shore."Mautz said that lessening the economic burden on independent businesses and constituents at a statewide level is important to drive economic activity."Anything we can do statewide to loosen that burden, to drive economic activity, I think will be a fundamental policy that will help change that budget imbalance," he said.Hutchinson answered the question last, saying that government can only make money by raising taxes, raising fees or cutting spending."I'm sure - based on what I've heard from the chairman of appropriations - we'll see a number of bills about taxes and fee increases," he said.Hutchinson brought up the recent announcement from the Maryland Department of Transportation that it will be reducing funding for its six year capital budget for transportation projects."We'll probably start seeing that across the other departments as well," he said. "But there's a lot of projects that, if they're not announced by the end of January, won't be seeing the light of day next year."

title: St. Michaels Talks Tax Rates at Commissioners Meeting
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
St. Michaels talks tax rates at commissioners meeting

 November 10, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 3 | Section: News 
 
 848
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS - At a meeting Wednesday, the Commissioners of St. Michaels spoke about gathering stakeholders to discuss the town's tax rates.The discussion followed an issues brief sent to the commissioners from the St. Michaels Historic District Residents Association.The issues brief argues that St. Michaels, "a small tourist town with a tourism economy," is largely supported by its residents, rather than its businesses."The infrastructure needed to support Talbot County's and the town's tourism economy imposes a heavy tax load on St. Michaels homeowners, while those who benefit most are taxed the least, or not at all in the case of the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum," the issues brief states.At the meeting, Commission President David Breimhurst said he was glad that the Historic District Residents Association is offering to be part of the solution. He suggested getting all stakeholders from every aspect of the community together to talk and see what they can come up with."I don't think it needs to be 'us against them' or adversarial in any way," he said. "Just to have a calm, adult discussion about where we stand." Dan Spiegel spoke on behalf of the St. Michaels Historic District Residents Association at the meeting Wednesday.He summarized some of the points made in the issues brief and named the four steps the group hopes the commissioners will take:▪ Begin a period of study and assessment of the tax options other towns use to raise revenue from business activities.▪ Engage with the Maritime Museum to urge they make a payment in lieu of taxes to the town.▪ Hold public hearings to discuss any plans that may develop.▪ Look at current residential property rates to determine whether they are "fair and appropriate," in the case that the town raises additional revenue from businesses.Spiegel said that most of the money the town uses to fund services and maintain its infrastructure comes from property taxes.He said that, based on data gathered from the state, there are 81 business structures that pay property taxes in town, compared to 796 homes and non-business structures."In other words, only 9% of the property taxes are paid by businesses," he said.Spiegel said that although Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum is the "crown jewel" of the town's tourist economy, it is tax exempt and does not make any voluntary payments directly to the town. These types of payments are known as payments in lieu of taxes, or PILOTs."Many universities and colleges pay PILOTs to towns because of their use of the infrastructure and other things that impact the town," he said. "The museum makes no PILOT payments." Spiegel also said money generated by businesses does not stay in the town. He said that 97% of the town's commercial buildings are owned by non-residents and more than 90% of the business operators who rent the buildings are also non-residents."So non-resident landlords, business operators and employees spend their money elsewhere because there are very few normal types of businesses that they can spend money on that would attract their dollars," he said.After Spiegel spoke, Commissioner Tad DuPont said this conversation has already begun."You're stimulating a conversation, but it has started," he said.DuPont said that with the changing tourist economy, St.Michaels needs to change with it and be ahead of it.Commission Treasurer Al Mercier said he could envision multiple areas where the town could generate more revenue, including a tourism tax, an alcohol tax, an accommodations tax and parking meters."These are nine or 10 things that I think we need to put on the agenda going forward," he said.During public comment, Kristen Greenaway, president and CEO of the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum, talked about what the museum pays the town, including an annual event fees tax, and what services it offers residents.She said the museum offers free after school and summer programming for local and Talbot County youth, free museum membership for St. Michaels' youth and free entry for locals with passes that can be obtained at the library.Greenaway said the taxes on The Crab Claw restaurant property, which the museum is purchasing, will still be paid, as it will remain zoned as maritime commercial.Spiegel said the Historic District Residents Association is not anti-museum or anti-business."This is an informal group of residents that were organized, that live in the historic district, that are concerned about the future of St. Michaels," he said.John Marrah, a property owner in St. Michaels, said he enjoyed the Historic District Residents Association presentation."It's important that people think they're treated fairly from a taxation standpoint," he said.Marrah added that business and property owners are taxed "with no representation" in St.Michaels. He said that might be something the town should look into."I own properties in town, but since I don't live in town, I can't vote," he said. "I pay property taxes like everybody else."

 OXFORD - A decision to keep a decades-old financial investment policy, which the town didn't know about until recently, in place was met with applause at a Commissioners of Oxford meeting Tuesday.Commission President Tom Costigan said that while the existing policy might not be perfect, it's what the town can work with for the time being."I think there's consensus from a lot of people in the room and a lot of people at this table that our existing policy is a good one. We should keep it and we should follow it," he said, which was followed with claps from residents in attendance.The policy features three sections that are unique to Oxford.One section states that each commissioner and the clerk treasurer must disclose "any substantial personal investment or management role in any financial institution which conducts business in Talbot County." Another section states that no more than half of the town's investment should be in a stable financial institution.Lewis said that other municipalities didn't necessarily state this the same way.The last section states that the length of maturity on an investment should not exceed one year.At the previous town meeting Sept. 26, Town Manager Cheryl Lewis said that Oxford has had a financial investment policy since the 1990s, which the current town officials and commissioners had not been made aware of.Lewis said that after learning about the policy, she created an updated version.She gave commissioners copies of the original policy as well a policy with her updates at the Sept. 26 meeting.After Costigan said the town should keep the existing financial policy at the Tuesday meeting, Commissioner Susan Delean-Botkin asked if they would consider looking at the small updates that Talbot County had made to its financial policy."Would we consider looking at that and seeing (if) there (is) anything we need to address?" she asked.Costigan said the commissioners could look at "anything," but said that right now, the plan is to stick with what is already in place.Commissioner Katrina Greer said she was thrilled to keep the existing policy in place.During the meeting, commissioners briefly discussed whether to create a Budget and Finance Committee.During the last meeting, Greer had asked to discuss a resolution to create the committee, which she drafted.Commissioners agreed to discuss it at the meeting Tuesday.However, because Greer wanted to go through the language, Costigan suggested the commissioners hold a workshop next week to discuss the resolution.Greer said she would be happy with that, as long as the meeting was in the evening, rather than in the afternoon, so that more residents can attend.Town Attorney Lyndsey Ryan said she envisions that commissioners would discuss what they anticipate the committee would do at the workshop so that she can draft something to be put on the agenda for the next regular town meeting.Delean-Botkin said the first question the commissioners have to decide is whether the committee is necessary."Having gone through 40 phone calls of other entities on the Shore, Rockville, Frederick Annapolis, Anne Arundel County, Talbot County, Easton, Trappe, Salisbury, Cambridge, Denton, all the school boards - none of them have a citizens budget advisory committee," Delean-Botkin said. "When I asked the aldermen, councilmen, committee members and board members why not, it is because it is the duty of the sworn officials to manage the budget and finances is in every entity's charter." In response, Greer said Annapolis does have a Finance Committee.Costigan said the commissioners should first decide what the committee would be."Let's first define what it is and then we'll decide whether we need it or not," he said. "And we can vote on whether we want it or not." The commissioners workshop will be held Thursday, Oct. 19, at 5 p.m. in the Commissioners of Oxford meeting room.

title: Oxford Uncovers Investment Policy - Policy Was Not Considered by Commission in Recent Votes on Investment Changes
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Oxford uncovers investment policy - Policy was not considered by commission in recent votes on investment changes

 September 29, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 961
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD - Unknown to current town officials and commissioners, Oxford has had a financial investment policy in place since the 1990s."In the 90s, the state of Maryland asked all municipalities in the state to create an investment policy and file it with them," Town Manager Cheryl Lewis said during a commissioners meeting Tuesday.Lewis said she had not been made aware of this policy when she was hired. She said she didn't believe the commissioners at the time she was hired, nor the person whose role she replaced, knew of the policy."The policy, I assume was written and filed away in the archives," she said. "That seems to be where it was at."Commissioner Katrina Greer said that when she emailed Town Attorney Lyndsey Ryan last week to ask if an investment policy existed, Ryan said the policy had not been attached to the ordinance it was supposed to be attached to."I'm embarrassed for us and for Cheryl that we didn't know about it," Greer said during the meeting. "And so we are in the unfortunate position as commissioners and as a manager of not being in compliance with our own law. So this is serious, and I apologize and we will all apologize to you for that."In a text message Wednesday, Greer said it was "unacceptable" for town administration to say they did not know about the policy."Knowing the town laws and comporting with them is the primary function of an administrator," she said. "This is deeply concerning that a highly compensated long-term employee did not know about a town investment policy."During the town meeting, Lewis said that after learning about the policy, she created an updated version."So I've provided you with a resolution and then also [the original] investment policy," she said. "This is just being provided for this evening. This is not something that I expect anybody to act on."Lewis said she took the state's recommendations and spoke with Talbot County's finance manager to create the updated policy.Lewis listed three sections of the original policy that are "unique to Oxford," which commissioners could consider changing if they desired to.One section states that each commissioners and the clerk treasurer must disclose "any substantial personal investment or management role in any financial institution which conducts business in Talbot County."Another section states that no more than half of the town's investment should be in a stable financial institution. Lewis said that other municipalities didn't necessarily state this the same way.The last section Lewis mentioned states that the length of maturity on an investment should not exceed one year."Obviously, which many people in the room are aware of, we did not follow these as they were written because it's pretty hard to follow a policy that you don't know exists," Lewis said.While the town has one certificate of deposit that is longer than 12 months, Lewis said it is in compliance with the section that states no more than half of investments should be in a financial institution.At the previous town meeting Sept. 12, the commissioners voted to temporarily move $2 million from an account with BayVanguard Bank to the investment bank, Maryland Local Government Investment Pool, until Lewis could come back with a report on alternative investment options.During the most recent meeting, Lewis reported on her review of three banks: BayVanguard Bank, Shore United Bank and Queenstown Bank. No decision has been made yet on where to keep that $2 million.After Lewis shared information on the investment policy and possible update, Greer said she wanted to wait before any action is taken."We are going to fix it," she said. "But we don't want to act hastily."Greer added that she feels a finance advisory committee is necessary so that the town can make "sound judgements" about its investments.In response to this, Commissioner Susan Delean-Bot-kin brought up the importance of having a paid adviser."They don't have the same responsibility if we are not paying them," she said. "They do not have the same fiduciary responsibility to the town. And that is very important for us to think about."Earlier in the meeting, Greer asked to discuss a draft resolution to create a financial advisory committee, which she drafted for the consideration of the commissioners."The idea is to advise the commission so that they may instruct the town administrator on the best options for investments," Greer said.Committee members would be required to have certain certifications, Greer said."This would be a very high-level, high-functioning committee and there are people here in town that have those certifications," she said.Delean-Botkin said she thinks the draft resolution should be discussed, but said it was not on the agenda for the meeting."You're trying to move through a resolution that none of us have seen," Delean-Bot-kin said. "I would like to stick to the agenda."Greer said she didn't expect the resolution to be voted on at the meeting and said she had sent a memo to the commissioners and Lewis to put it on the agenda.Commission President Tom Costigan said he would like time to reflect on the draft resolution."I would also like some time for our town attorney to review it and give us an opinion on it as well," he said. "And then we can revisit it at our next date."Later in the meeting, Ryan said that if the commissioners vote in favor of creating a committee, they might consider having the committee review the financial investment policy yearly."So that the policy is constantly being refreshed within the town government," she said.

title: Newcomers Win Talbot County Board of Education Seats
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado valvarado@chespub.com
content:
Newcomers win Talbot County Board of Education seats

 November 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado valvarado@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 455

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Talbot County Public Schools is looking at new leadership, according to uncertified vote totals from the Maryland Board of Elections.Cynthia Marrah Jurrius, Karla Wieland-Cherry and Ann O'Connor, none of whom have prior experience on the Talbot County Board of Education, won seats for their districts.
The elected board members said they plan to bring their campaign priorities to the forefront of their terms, which begin Dec. 1 and will last for four years.
Talbot County's Board of Education is made up of seven members from different districts in the county and two student board members. Districts 2, 5 and 6 were on the ballot in the November election.
For district 2, O'Connor won with 52.7% of the vote, according to the State Board of Elections, beating out incumbent Board Member Candace Henry. O'Connor said her campaign provided the opportunity for her to get a better understanding of leading a campaign, school board responsibilities and Blueprint, Maryland's 10-year plan to improve the state's education system.
O'Connor said she has just skimmed the surface and is ready to learn more.
She said she will be prioritizing academics and discipline. With academics, she said she would like to see elementary students reading every night and working on more book reports, and for schools to provide summer reading lists.
For discipline, O'Connor said she has noticed a lack of consistency, or "different rules for different people."
"We need a plan for all the schools that this is the way we're going to, you know, this is the dress, this is the behavior when you walk in the building. If you veer from that, there's going to be this consequence, and you got to, I mean, it's the follow through," she said.
For District 5, Karla Wieland-Cherry won with 54.6% votes, according to the State Board of Elections. Wieland-Cherry, who defeated incumbent Board Member Anna Howie, said she appreciated the support she received from her campaign, though she did mention she "got a lot of negativity." She hopes she can work through any negative sentiments to have a productive four years on the board.
Wieland-Cherry said she will be prioritizing open communication for everyone she works with and promoting the Career and Technology Education Program, which offers job training in various fields.
She said it's important to encourage kids to look at career alternatives for those not interested in college, whether that be training to become a firefighter, plumber or welder.
"I think (the CTE program is) under encouraged, under utilized," Wieland-Cherry said. "And that's where jobs are."
For District 6, Jurrius won with 51.9% of the vote, defeating Kerry Gunshenan, according to the State Board of Elections. Current District 6 Board Member Mary Wheeler did not seek reelection.
Jurrius did not answer calls from reporters in time for publication.

title: Easton Approves Restrictions on Campaign Donations
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton approves restrictions on campaign donations

 October 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 472
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Candidates in future campaigns will face new fundraising restrictions and reporting requirements thanks to a new law passed by the Easton Town Council.After nearly six months of fine-tuning, Easton passed its first campaign finance ordinance on Monday.
It will limit campaign contributions to $1,000, ban contributions from political committees and organizations, and require campaign treasurers to submit detailed financial reports before and after the election.
Council members said the ordinance is a win for transparency in Easton's elections. All five voted in favor of the new regulations.
"I think that (we) have done an excellent job of putting together an ordinance which achieves our goals of providing transparency in elections," said Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery, who sponsored the ordinance alongside Mayor Megan Cook.
The ordinance was introduced in April, amid a heated and politically charged race between current Town Council President Don Abbatiello and former President Frank Gunsallus.
There were largely no requirements for candidates to report specific contributions made to their campaigns during this year's election. Financial disclosures submitted by candidates when they filed for candidacy didn't include campaign donations. Montgomery, Cook and others argued that there should be more transparency on which organizations and people make donations to candidates.
Now, future candidates must name a campaign treasurer, who is responsible for sending the town office documentation of each donation, whether from an individual, business or organization.
The council has made several edits to the campaign ordinance since April, including raising the maximum donation mark from $250 to $1,000 and exempting spouses or domestic partners of candidates from the $1,000 limit.
Ward 2 Councilmember Robert Rankin said Monday that concerns he had about a political committee donation ban in the ordinance breaching First Amendment standards were quelled after discussion with Town Attorney Sharon VanEmburgh.
Rankin said individuals involved in political organization can still donate on behalf of themselves. And the ordinance doesn't stop political committees from making "independent expenditures" supporting a candidate, as long as the money doesn't go to the candidate directly.
Political groups will be required to file reports to the town if their expenses for an election cycle are $100 or more.
Town elections are nonpartisan.
Resident Lance Simon, a vocal advocate for the ordinance, thanked council members for supporting the new restrictions and said he hopes it can be "up and running" soon to allow enough time for it to be properly implemented. The town's next election is scheduled for May 2027.
Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis, who expressed concerns with the first draft of the ordinance potentially blocking some residents from running for office due to fiscal limits, said Monday that the final version is in a better place.
Davis thanked Cook and Montgomery for sponsoring the ordinance and bringing transparency to future town elections.
"I think the work has been done," Davis said. "I think we have really mulled it over a lot."

title: Donovan Wins Oxford Commissioner Seat
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Donovan wins Oxford commissioner seat

 June 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 518
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — Dave Donovan won the Oxford town commissioner election by 44 votes Tuesday after a sometimes tense race.Residents cast their ballots for either Donovan or incumbent Tom Costigan between 8 a.m. and 8 p.m. or by absentee ballot. On Tuesday, 326 voters showed up, and 71 voters cast absentee ballots.
"It's quite gratifying," Donovan said after hearing the results. He said it was hard to tell if the news was good when he initially received the phone call from Oxford's Board of Elections Supervisors Tuesday night. "They're very matter of fact. They have a form they read to you, so you don't really know what the punch line is until the end."
Donovan will serve a three-year term as an Oxford commissioner.
The town's elections took a new shape this year, with the Board of Elections overseeing the process after residents voiced concerns over transparency.
The board instituted two new rules that chair Debbie Krolicki said went smoothly during Tuesday's voting process. Krolicki said residents now have to bring proof of domicile and identification, measures taken in order to prevent "temporary residents" who do not live in the town year-round from voting.
"About 95% of our voters have brought their IDs," Krolicki said. "They're very happy about our new process, but it's a new process."
According to Costigan, the past three elections have become increasingly "ugly" and contentious. "People should treat each other with a little bit of respect and a little bit of courtesy, you know?" he said Tuesday afternoon.
Donovan and Costigan both referenced separate "smear campaigns" that have spread throughout the town during campaigning.
"I was surprised that they waited until the last minute when they knew there was no opportunity for me to address it, which I thought was underhanded," Donovan said in reference to emails sent to town residents Sunday questioning Donovan's motivations.
Though tension was building between candidates, the atmosphere on Election Day was relatively light. The Board of Elections livestreamed the vote count inside the Oxford Community Services Building.
Resident Carol Griggs said she came out to vote in this election because of pressing issues at hand, particularly town finances and the Strand Beach project.
"You know, we need a little change here," she said. "We need things to move forward."
Griggs said this election has drawn more community attention than previous elections due to all the "hot button issues" at hand like town finances and the Strand project.
Costigan said he was disappointed with the results of the election and in some ways disappointed with the people of Oxford. "I've served in this town for 15 years, and they decided to bring on somebody new. I understand that, that's their choice," Costigan said.
Donovan will be sworn in as the new town commissioner on July 3. "Honest to God, I think this is a win for everybody in Oxford," he said. "There's still a small number of people that may be upset by this, but I also believe that those people are just as important to the outcome as anybody else in town, and I will represent them as if they voted for me. I hope that I can earn their trust."

title: Oxford town commissioner election Q&As
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Oxford town commissioner election Q&As

 June 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 1203
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — On June 17, the Town of Oxford will choose someone to fill one of three town commissioner seats. The race is between incumbent Tom Costigan and resident Dave Donovan. The winner will serve a three-year term.The Star Democrat sent a questionnaire to candidates running in the election to allow them to share their perspectives on various town issues in their own words.
Tom CostiganAge: 67.
Family: Married 39 years.
Occupation: Oxford Town Commissioner; retired realtor.
Political Experience: Three years as Oxford Town Commissioner.
Why are you running for office?
I am now, and have been for many years, dedicated to the town of Oxford. I devoted 12 years serving on our Historic District Commission (10 of those as chair) in the interest of preserving and protecting our architectural and cultural heritage. I've also spent countless hours volunteering within our community.
We're in the midst of progressing on many important challenges and projects, and I am determined to see them through. The institutional knowledge I've acquired in service to our town covers every facet of our government.
What are your priorities if elected?
My priorities are to fully staff and equip our police department; attract, retain and support our town staff; complete Oxford's comprehensive plan (our road map to the future); continue our progress on flood and stormwater control (pumps and check valves); complete our infrastructure projects (water upgrades, shoreline protection); hold the line on property taxes and water/sewer fees; limit the growth trajectory of short-term rental properties; explore new technologies to defray escalating utility costs; support our local businesses and civic organizations and help them thrive; continue to resist Oxford Road development/sprawl; and ensure that Oxford's future is determined by full-time residents.
How should Oxford address the flooding and infrastructure concerns in the town?
We are addressing these issues. I have personally visited other coastal jurisdictions, where they shared their knowledge, challenges and solutions. Here in Oxford, we have successfully installed check valves and tide gates to limit tidal inundation in vulnerable areas. We have procured ARPA funding, which will allow us to purchase mobile pumps. I will continue to lobby the state government to resolve flooding issues at the Causeway (a choke point that can cut our town off from emergency services). In addition, I'll continue to seek new solutions such as cisterns to collect stormwater and appropriate plantings to further mitigate flooding.
How would you as an Oxford commissioner ease tensions between residents and the commission?
It all starts with effective communication. One recent example relates to our FY2025/26 budget planning, where we hosted citizen workshops to explain our financial projections and to garner the public's input. During my tenure, I've initiated live streaming of all town meetings. I instituted the Constant Contact platform to inform residents of helpful messages relating to meeting agendas, board openings, weather alerts, events, etc. In addition, we've implemented a new, more user-friendly website for ease of locating information. I will always welcome and respect new voices and ideas to enhance transparency.
What is your vision for the Strand Beach project?
Most importantly, I want to see the Strand project succeed. When the next major storm hits, I want to provide the most resilient protection possible. Did you know that the east end of the Strand was once an island? This project, which has been discussed in public workshops and presentations since 2010, is being done with grant funding, not costing local taxpayers a single dollar. As for the logs, discussions should continue as to their disposition — It's a question of aesthetics vs. ecological benefit. Bottom line: the project is working, the beach area is expanding and plantings are taking root.
Dave DonovanAge: 67 years old in June.
Family: I have been married to my wife Rose for 44 years this August. We have three children and two grandchildren.
Occupation: I retired at the end of 2018 from my partnership in a large law firm in Washington, D.C.
Political Experience: I have not previously sought to hold any public elective office or played any role in a political campaign other than as a low-level volunteer.
Why are you running for office?
For the past three years, the town has made needless mistakes that have created and exacerbated deep frustration among our residents. These errors include mishandling the termination of a long-time police chief; appointing a candidate to fill the balance of the term of a resigning commissioner rather than holding an election as the voters demanded; failing to manage completion of the Strand project; and utterly botching the hiring of the previous Town Manager last summer. We have serious issues that need to be addressed. I have the experience to help us make needed improvements, minimize damage already done and avoid repeating errors.
What are your priorities if elected?
We need to correct and complete the Strand project and get it behind us. Sound financial management is also a top priority. We need sensible management of our substantial cash reserves. I also will prioritize open and candid communications about all our issues, engaging the community to discuss potential solutions, and leveraging the incredible reservoir of talent and expertise we have in Oxford. We need to take advantage of the skills and experience of our residents and not shut them out, as has happened far too often in the last three years.
How should Oxford address the flooding and infrastructure concerns in the town?
We have had a plan in place for nine years to address flooding and infrastructure and done next to nothing to implement it. Addressing the Strand was the lowest priority in that plan, yet it has almost completely swallowed our attention. We need to work with our engineers and our residents to confirm our priorities, restart stalled initiatives, and identify and execute work that is in line with the priorities in that plan. With federal grants now drying up and our own tight budget, our options are limited, but we can still make meaningful progress.
How would you as an Oxford commissioner ease tensions between residents and the commission?
Rebuilding trust is essential, and it starts by electing new leadership that is not tied to and responsible for past mistakes. Much of our tension is due to poor communication by the commissioners. We need more open and candid discussions by the commissioners about matters that come before them so that residents can understand what the commissioners are thinking and why (and vice versa). Commissioners need to provide actual answers to questions that are asked. Too often, questions are acknowledged but never answered. With new leadership and better communication, we can rebuild the trust between our residents and the commissioners.
What is your vision for the Strand Beach project?
We must get this project behind us. We don't have the money to redesign or rebuild it, and it appears we waived many of our legal rights when the commissioners prematurely signed off on its completion last year. The only course now is to figure out what needs to be done to finish it, including restoring public and ADA access and minimizing the hazards created by the "natural" features in the islands. We should never again embark on a project of this magnitude just because we found a funding source, especially one for which there was no clear design at the outset.
Candidate responses may be edited for length and clarity.

title: Record Voter Turnout, Margins of Victory Highlight Easton Election
author: Konner Metz
content:
Record voter turnout, margins of victory highlight Easton election

 May 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 727
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — In an election with record voter turnout, two of every three Easton voters cast ballots for current Ward 2 Councilmember Don Abbatiello, giving him a landslide victory over incumbent Frank Gunsallus in the race for Town Council president.Easton also elected Robert Rankin to fill Abbatiello's Ward 2 seat and reelected incumbent the Rev. Elmer Davis in Ward 4.
More than 3,200 residents cast ballots, a record high for a municipal election, according to town officials. Abbatiello earned 2,215 votes, or 69%, to Gunsallus' 1,012.
Abbatiello said he was "amazed" and "grateful" when the results were announced.
"To get over 2,000 of those 3,000 votes was amazing and humbling," Abbatiello said. "But then it very quickly set in, over 2,000 people have put a lot of faith in me to make sure that I do the right things for the town. So there's that as well in the back of your mind."
Abbatiello said Gunsallus congratulated him when the results were announced Tuesday night and that the two shook hands.
In a statement Wednesday, Gunsallus thanked his supporters and said he "will always be grateful for the opportunity" to serve the community. Gunsallus' term ends after less than two years on the council, as he won a special election in September 2023.
"While this election didn't go our way, I'm incredibly proud of the honest and transparent campaign we ran — and deeply thankful to those who stood beside our team throughout it," Gunsallus wrote.
"My hope moving forward is that the Easton Town Council listens closely to all voices in our community, and that we continue building a future rooted in respect and shared purpose," he later added.
The election cycle was heated and political, especially the Abbatiello and Gunsallus contest. Republican-endorsed candidates sent mailers calling out Mayor Megan Cook. Campaign signs were stolen and vandalized. And council held tense debates over campaign finance transparency.
Wednesday morning, Abbatiello said his goal during the campaign was to be nonpartisan. He thinks the vote outcome shows Easton residents agree.
"I think that that's what that vote yesterday showed, is that the residents of Easton want the town to remain nonpartisan, to focus on town issues first," he said.
Rankin shared a similar sentiment.
"A lot of resources were put into a lot of billboards and mailers and robocalls, and I think some of the turnout was due to folks who saw through some of that and don't want big party politics in local elections," Rankin said.
"I think that stood out yesterday and the town of Easton, the people of Easton, had their chance to speak and they did so with a resounding voice."
Once absentee ballots were counted Wednesday, Rankin held a 528-237 advantage over opponent Lynn Keefe. Rankin, winning 69% of the vote, said the result was humbling.
"Local government works best when the community is engaged and involved, and to have so many people from the town of Easton participate in the election is just so important and so rewarding," Rankin said.
In a statement, Keefe said the campaign cycle was an experience she won't forget. "I pray that the Lord will lead the newly election to do the right thing for all the citizens of the town," she wrote.
In Ward 4, incumbent the Rev. Elmer Davis earned 54% of the vote 287 ballots cast for him. Cameron Keefe was second with 129 and Moonyene Jackson-Amis third with 117.
Davis said it was a challenge to run a successful campaign in the crowded Ward 4 field.
"It's one thing to have one opponent, but it's another thing to have two opponents," Davis said. "In my mind, I had to do double the work."
In a statement, Cameron Keefe wished Davis the best, and added: "It was an absolute blast running and I urge the people of Easton to keep those on the council in our prayers."
Moonyene Jackson-Amis thanked her supporters for voting for values such as affordable housing and cultural offerings.
"In less than two weeks of campaigning, Elmer Davis and his supporters got their wake-up call," she wrote. "Yes, he won the election, but my team and I won the victory. Over 100 voters stood up for values that matter."
The Board of Canvassers certified the election results Wednesday. The elected council members will be sworn in at the Town Council's next meeting on May 19.

title: Easton Election Cycle Has Been Charged, Political in Nature
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton election cycle has been charged, political in nature

 May 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 869
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Easton saw a heated election the last time the council president seat was up for grabs. This year's race is no different.Since campaigns for the three open Town Council seats began this winter, there have been stolen and vandalized campaign signs, tense debates on campaign finance transparency and, most recently, political mailers from Republican-endorsed candidates calling out Mayor Megan Cook.
The tenor of the election cycle — which culminates with voting Tuesday — is largely influenced by the race for Town Council president between incumbent Frank Gunsallus and current Ward 2 representative Don Abbatiello.
At a town hall Tuesday, both candidates offered thoughts on civility.
"In the past two years, the council members overall, have been almost always conducting themselves in a civil manner," said Gunsallus. "There are times where debate may get heated. That is the nature of democracy."
"Arguing is fine, I get it. Disagreements occur," Abbatiello said. "But it needs to be done in a respectful manner."
Ward 1 Councilmember Maureen Curry, who has endorsed Abbatiello, said the charged nature of this election isn't normal for Easton. And it's hurting the town, she says.
"Anytime you create an environment based on animosity, it becomes counterproductive, fairly quickly," Curry said. "And I think that's sort of where we are today."
Talbot County Republican Central Committee vice chair Shari Wilcoxon believes a reason the race is so intense is that it's a fight to preserve Easton's charm.
"People love our little town. It's a jewel," she said. "And we had a lot of people move here during COVID because they wanted to get out of the crud to come to this little town. A lot of us want to preserve that."
ENDORSEMENTS
As Gunsallus and Abbatiello square off, they have racked up endorsements from local politicians and even fellow council members.
Abbatiello received endorsements from Curry and, in a surprise to some, Ward 3's David Montgomery, who had sided with Gunsallus on several contentious matters discussed by the council in the past year.
"It would be very hard for us to move forward productively for the next four years under that kind of leadership," Montgomery said of Gunsallus.
Curry says Abbatiello's experience and knowledge make him the best candidate. "He has the right temperament," she said.
Meanwhile, Gunsallus' main endorsements come from Republican leaders — the Republican Central Committee, Sheriff Joe Gamble, Sen. Johnny Mautz and Dels. Chris Adams and Tom Hutchinson.
Wilcoxon said the committee looked at values — not necessarily party affiliation — when endorsing Gunsallus and mother-and-son newcomers Lynn and Cameron Keefe, who are running in Wards 2 and 4, respectively.
"To me he's a phenomenal leader," Wilcoxon said of Gunsallus, citing his thoughtfulness and transparency.
"He's not afraid to ask questions," Mautz said. " ... Sometimes, the questions may seem silly. And other times, they may reveal things that most people aren't aware of."
Abbatiello and his supporters have denounced the involvement of political parties in the town's election, which is nonpartisan and doesn't list candidates alongside a party.
"I do not think that the Republican Party platform has anything to do with the issues that we face here in Easton, and so I don't understand why the party has decided to intervene so strongly in a local election," Montgomery, a Republican, said.
Mautz said while the election is performed as nonpartisan, it is political in nature. "Every election has got politics baked into it," he said.
"I think that everybody fools themselves if they say it's nonpartisan," Wilcoxon said. "Everybody knows. Everybody knows everybody's party. We can just cut the pretending, right?"
Flavio Hickel, an associate professor of political science at Washington College, sees both sides of the argument.
"Broadly speaking, I don't think it's a good idea to allow for local party endorsements or to make nonpartisan elections partisan, because you are allowing partisanship to interfere in local town government," Hickel said.
However, Hickel said knowing which parties candidates align with is informative for voters, especially at a local level.
"Most voters probably aren't familiar with the candidates running," he said. " ... What party identity does at all levels of elections is it provides a very quick information shortcut for voters."
Curry and Montgomery's endorsements have raised questions, too.
Wilcoxon said she views Montgomery's opposition to Gunsallus as personal and said she believes Montgomery and Cook's sponsorship of a campaign finance ordinance was "100%" an attack on Gunsallus' campaign.
At the town hall Tuesday, Gunsallus spoke of council endorsements: "I would not want an endorsement from a fellow council member because I believe that that is out of bounds," he said. Then he made a remark seemingly concerning Montgomery.
"And especially one of them, I would not accept it."
Montgomery disputed that claim, telling The Star Democrat Friday that Gunsallus asked for his endorsement a few months ago, but that he declined.
Curry said she hadn't before made an endorsement as a sitting council member, but that she gave a "great deal of thought" in endorsing Abbatiello.
In her eyes, the discourse around endorsements and political sides are making the campaign heated, instead of what she'd rather the election be centered on: issues such as growth and housing.
"There's too much of the 'he said,' 'he said,' and he's backed by this guy and he's backed by this guy," Curry said. "The issues have taken a back seat, and that's wrong."

title: Political Mailers Stir Discourse; Mayor Says Gunsallus Claims Are 'Flat-Out False'
author: Konner Metz
content:
Political mailers stir discourse; mayor says Gunsallus claims are 'flat-out false'

 May 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 764
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Two political mailers from Town Council President Frank Gunsallus and the local Republican committee are stirring discourse, including from Mayor Megan Cook, who said claims made on the flyers are "flat-out false" and insulting.The mailers, which many residents received Thursday, list the Talbot County Republican Central Committee on the authority line. The committee has endorsed Gunsallus in his race against Don Abbatiello for president, as well as candidates Lynn and Cameron Keefe in the Ward 2 and Ward 4 races, respectively.
Both Gunsallus flyers call out the mayor, one stating, "Don't let our out-of-town Mayor and her supporters change the character of Easton." They home in on draft inclusionary zoning legislation — which Cook and town planners have advocated for and Gunsallus opposes — that has not yet been introduced as an ordinance.
Cook told The Star Democrat Friday that multiple statements made by the Gunsallus campaign are false, including the claim Cook recruited three candidates to run in Tuesday's election. Cook said she did not recruit anyone.
"I just think all the claims are ridiculous," Cook said. "They're all misleading or flat-out false."
One sentence states that Cook "and her staff quietly usher in new developments—with little to no public input." The mayor disputed that assertion.
"It's an insult to our staff, who are excellent, and the many volunteers that we have serving on boards and commissions," she said.
Neither Gunsallus nor the Republican Central Committee responded to The Star Democrat's requests for interviews.
This year's council president race is the second in a row during which mailers were sent to residents. In 2023, during a four-person race for the seat, mailers targeted former mayor and then-candidate Bob Willey.
Flyers during that campaign were paid for by Scott R. Wagner, a former Pennsylvania state senator and Talbot County business owner. One featured an image of a diaper and said both politicians and diapers need to be changed.
In an interview Thursday, Abbatiello said this year's flyers are "full of misstatements."
"They are meant to instill fear in residents," Abbatiello said. "They are meant to divide the community. All so that they can win an election."
INCLUSIONARY ZONING
In Thursday's flyers — as well as flyers sent to Ward 4 mail boxes this week by Cameron Keefe and the Republican committee — inclusionary zoning is prominent.
Presented to the Town Council at a February workshop, draft legislation would require residential developers to allocate 15% of their units as affordable. For ownership developments, the legislation would require inclusionary units meet an affordable price for households making up to 100% of area median income.
The legislation would grant developers that provide inclusionary units on the same site as market-rate units with a 20% density bonus. But the ordinance hasn't been formally introduced. Its next step is a potential recommendation to the council from the town's housing task force.
In an interview earlier this week before the flyers were received, Republican Central Committee Vice Chair Shari Wilcoxon said inclusionary zoning is the "number one thing in this whole race." She said if passed, it could hurt property values.
"In my opinion, every single person who owns property in this town, Republican or Democrat, ought to be concerned," she said.
"I am of the full belief that the mayor, it's her bill," Wilcoxon said. "She tried to get it through before, but didn't have the votes, so it somehow got tabled until after the election."
Gunsallus has made clear his opposition to inclusionary zoning. In an interview with The Star Democrat's editorial board last week, he said defeating inclusionary zoning is one of his top three priorities.
Regarding the legislation, a Gunsallus mailer reads: "I am the only Councilmember who has vocally opposed the current Inclusionary Zoning bill, which will allow (and effectively require) high-density housing in each and every neighborhood."
In a fact check post on the town's website Friday afternoon, the town clarified the bill would only affect new developments or redeveloped properties with seven or more residential units. It also addressed other claims made by candidates during this election cycle.
Councilmember David Montgomery has also expressed his opposition publicly. Montgomery has endorsed Abbatiello and cited Abbatiello's concerns over the legislation as a reason for supporting him.
"I think neither of us sees the inclusive zoning ordinance as the best way of going out and providing affordable housing," Montgomery said last month.
Abbatiello, who was questioned at a candidate town hall Tuesday about his unclear stance on inclusionary zoning, said Thursday he doesn't think it's the answer.
"I think there's other things that we can do, and I've said that repeatedly," he said. "But again, I wasn't going to make a decision without hearing all the information."

title: Ward 4 Candidates Talk Property Taxes, Housing
author: Konner Metz
content:
Ward 4 candidates talk property taxes, housing

 April 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 734
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Candidates for the Ward 4 seat on the Easton Town Council have offered varying opinions on the town's property tax rate.Incumbent the Rev. Elmer Davis, Moonyene Jackson-Amis and Cameron Keefe are squaring off in the town's election May 6. Each discussed their views on property taxes, housing and more in interviews with The Star Democrat's editorial board last week.
Currently, the town levies a tax on real property at 52 cents per $100 of assessed value. That mark hasn't changed since 2008. It's higher than Talbot County's other towns, but relatively low compared to Eastern Shore towns such as Cambridge, Denton and Salisbury.
Property values, though, have increased significantly in recent years. The state's 2025 reassessments showed the value of Group 1 residential and commercial properties in Talbot County increased by 22.1% from 2022. The town's proposed fiscal year 2026 budget projects $13.6 million in real property tax revenue, slightly up from last year. It was a tight and "lean" budget, Mayor Megan Cook has said.
Davis, who's been on the council since 2020, said the property tax rate should be increased.
"I think the mayor's playing around a little bit. … They're not fiscally responsible," Davis said. "We have not raised taxes, and here's the problem. We got that COVID money. We've been living high on the hog, and now we have to pay the piper."
Jackson-Amis, Ward 4's representative from 2001 to 2008, says the Town Council should have conversations with professionals about potential tax breaks.
"I think the property tax is a little steep," Jackson-Amis said. "It seems like the idea is to get, to have a money funnel. A funnel as opposed to exacting what's necessary to support the budget."
Keefe in his interview emphasized fiscal responsibility, while adding he understands new initiatives cost money.
"They make a lot of decisions that don't affect their wealth, but it affects everybody else's wealth," Keefe said of the council. " ... We need to dismantle this ivory tower thing."
HOUSING
The Ward 4 hopefuls each touched on plans to improve Easton's affordable housing stock. Keefe said "we need to make Easton not just survivable, but livable."
"We can say all the buzz words we want, but I would love to see specifically starter homes in Easton, things that draw young families here," Keefe said.
He said he hopes to sit down with town planners to discuss their proposed inclusionary zoning ordinance that would require residential developers to allocate 15% of their units as affordable.
Jackson-Amis says she's "all for inclusionary zoning." She hopes to revisit the requirement that developers include 25% low or middle-income units in projects, an effort she supported in her prior stint on the council.
"If you're getting a benefit from the town, we need to be able to exact a benefit from you," Jackson-Amis said. "If you're creating housing, we ought to know what our housing needs are, and that it shouldn't just be for the financial gain of wealthy people."
Davis said he's "not 100% sure" current housing legislation in the works will answer all of Easton's housing needs. He advocated for the town to buy a piece of land and work with nonprofits.
"The town should buy a piece of land," Davis said. "And the town should partner with Habitat (for Humanity) or some other organization to … ensure that we deal holistically with the person and the property."
EXPERIENCE
The Ward 4 candidates bring different experience levels to the table.
Davis, 58, said he focused on constituent representation during his time on the council, such as when he supported a seafood odor ordinance last year.
"I'm in the position as the council member because of the people," he said. "I represent those individuals in my ward. I'm not the end-all, be-all. So if my constituents say that this is what they want, then I represent them well."
Jackson-Amis, 77, said "we should look toward wisdom."
"Right now you need people with some seasoned ability to ferret out issues and help bring solutions to problems," she said. "So I don't think age really should be that important, but I think the experience is what should matter."
Keefe, 25, said he wants more youth involvement in the town.
"I know I'm young. That is by no means any reason to take this lightly," Keefe said. "I think this is important. I think there's a lot of potential for good that can happen from this. And above all of those things, I want to be a representative who listens."

title: Easton Town Council Candidates Make Their Cases at Town Hall
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton Town Council candidates make their cases at town hall

 April 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 756
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — With the election less than a week away, voters had the chance Tuesday to ask Town Council candidates a number of questions about issues facing Easton, including fiscal responsibility and housing.During a town hall hosted by The Talbot Spy and the Avalon Foundation Tuesday night, all seven candidates for three spots on the council made their pitches to voters.
For the council president seat, incumbent Frank Gunsallus and current Ward 2 representative Don Abbatiello will square off.
With Abbatiello opting to run for president, a new resident will assume the Ward 2 seat. In that race, Lynnette Keefe and Robert Rankin will face off.
The Ward 4 race will present voters with three options: incumbent the Rev. Elmer Davis, who has served in the seat since 2020; Moonyene Jackson-Amis, previously Ward 4's representative from 2001 to 2008; and newcomer Cameron Keefe.
Gunsallus and Abbatiello, along with other candidates, spoke about the town's budgetary outlook. The town's proposed budget for fiscal year 2026 is $28 million and includes a real property tax rate of 52 cents per $100 of assessed value. That mark hasn't changed since 2008.
One resident asked whether the candidates would consider a property tax rate cut given increasing property values, which have caused residents' tax bills go up.
Gunsallus said he would consider it and that it has been discussed by the council. He said the town could work on increasing the number of business to bring in more commercial tax revenue.
He added that since joining the council in 2023, he's pushed for detailed reviews of the town's budget.
"Through my direction, this council has done something that it hasn't done in at least 30 years," Gunsallus said, "and that is go line by line, every single line, in the $28 million budget to be just that: responsible stewards of the town's money."
Abbatiello said during this year's budget discussions, he was against a property tax rate hike. He said a tax break is dependent upon the town's fiscal need.
"If we can afford to reduce taxes, great. I'm all in favor of that," Abbatiello said. "I don't think we should just automatically say we're cutting taxes. We need to also look at other revenue sources."
Abbatiello said he's focused on keeping the Easton Volunteer Fire Department a volunteer organization — since a shift to paid would be "one of the biggest tax increases this town will ever see."
Ward 4's Cameron Keefe advocated for the town to continue funding its police department at a high level. He said he's "absolutely immovable" on fiscal transparency.
"I would like to — and I might be shooting myself in the foot — strike fear into the hearts of our representatives and let them know, the money we're spending is not ours," Keefe said. "We have to have the people of Easton's best interests in mind."
HOUSING
During both the moderated and open question portions of the town hall, the need for more affordably priced homes was mentioned. Candidates offered different ideas to tackle the dilemma.
Jackson-Amis said the town should "hold the developers responsible" by requiring a percentage of units be affordable. She vouched for smart growth, and said the Town Council should have more say in approving housing projects.
"We need to be very strategic in what it is we desire, and then how that can be implemented," Jackson-Amis said. "But the council is accountable for that. We're responsible. It's not the Planning Commission."
Davis has lobbied for that same increase in council involvement. Tuesday, he told residents the town should buy land and partner with a housing developer or nonprofit.
"So, therefore, the people who work at Wawas can get a house that's around $200,000 because the town has purchased property," Davis said. "I think we need to make that kind of investment for affordable housing in the Town of Easton, and we will meet the needs of the individuals in the community."
Ward 2 candidate Lynn Keefe emphasized the town should be thinking "outside of the box" when it comes to addressing housing and infrastructure problems.
"I really feel like we need to work on our green space here," she said. "We need to look at different parts of housing, not just affordable housing through the government, but also sustainable neighborhoods."
Rankin, Lynn Keefe's opponent, said development is the most common issue he hears from residents. Rankin said it's important to attract health care professionals and young people to Easton while also keeping an eye on growth.
"It's really important that we properly manage these developments that are coming on to make sure that those potential concerns are mitigated," Rankin said.

title: Easton Election: Gunsallus, Abbatiello Weigh in on Housing, Growth and More
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton election: Gunsallus, Abbatiello weigh in on housing, growth and more

 April 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 749
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Town Council president candidates Frank Gunsallus and Don Abbatiello both recognize the need to monitor and manage Easton's growth, but they each indicated different strategies on how to do so in editorial board interviews with The Star Democrat this week.Gunsallus, the incumbent, is being challenged by Abbatiello, the current Ward 2 councilmember. Voters head to the polls May 6 to decide the council's next leader, as well as representatives for the second and fourth wards.
During the interviews, both candidates were asked how to tackle Easton's affordable housing issue.
Gunsallus noted one of his priorities is to vote down an inclusionary zoning ordinance town leaders have expressed mixed opinions on. Instead, he said methods like removing impact fees or marking down land should be considered.
"It's a lot simpler than it's being made out to be," Gunsallus said. "Those are very straightforward, simple ways that can be done very soon to make that happen."
Abbatiello said the main issue with the lack of affordable homes is the rising price of land. He said incentivizing developers to build "middle housing" options is a solution.
"How do you get that price of land out of the equation? You have townhouses," Abbatiello said. "And townhouses become your starter home for people."
The current Ward 2 representative added that his vote against the Gannon Range project on Matthewstown Road in 2022 stemmed from the high prices of those homes.
"It was bringing us $450,000, $500,000 homes, which is not something that we needed," he said.
Gunsallus pointed out he's asked for the Town Council to have more say in approving housing projects. At a February workshop, Gunsallus and others led a discussion of how the council has only approved 37% of the town's 1,000 housing units in the pipeline at the time.
ENVISIONING THE FUTURE
The town is in the early process of revising its comprehensive plan for the first time in 15 years. The Planning Commission is currently reviewing drafts of the new plan, which lays out a vision for how the town should prioritize its growth.
Abbatiello said that in 2010, Easton was aiming to draw developers into town, but now the focus has changed.
"Tap the brakes, we need to slow down," he said of the current thought process.
The town's current comprehensive plan calls for 1% year-to-year growth. Gunsallus says he's "of the school of thought that that 1% is the ceiling, and we should not be exceeding that."
"When I graduated high school here in 2006, the town was literally half the size population-wise that it is now," he said. "So if we continue that same rate of growth, in 20 years, we'll have almost 40,000 people here."
REPRESENTING RESIDENTS
Candidates were asked questions concerning constituent representation. Gunsallus said he's given underrepresented groups a voice since being elected, such as when he voted to remove a 10-cent paper bag fee, a measure that narrowly fell short.
"That stemmed directly from a conversation with a room full of people about, 'I count my pennies when I go shopping so I can buy bags because my food stamps don't cover the cost of bags,'" Gunsallus said.
Abbatiello said if elected, he would push for each ward to have quarterly meetings. He said follow-up is critical, such as when he helped Ward 2 residents who raised concerns about safely walking to Walmart and Giant.
"I was annoying in saying, 'There needs to be a sidewalk on Elliott Road,'" Abbatiello said.
LEADERSHIP
With an election cycle that's become increasingly heated, both candidates offered thoughts on the responsibility of the council president and the disagreements that come with serving on the council.
"You can be the most amazing council president in the world, but if you can't get there with the rest of the council members, then you're going to lose every single vote that comes up," Abbatiello said.
"Sometimes you are not even part of the issue, but you still have to mediate or at least navigate the conversation," Gunsallus said. " ... Let's find common ground and go from there."
Gunsallus said it's been an honor to serve in the role since 2023.
"I'm happy with what has occurred under my administration, and I am looking forward to continuing the good work for another four years," Gunsallus said.
Abbatiello acknowledged serving on the council isn't an easy job, but he said it's an enjoyable one.
"You wonder if you're making the right decision," Abbatiello said. "But at the same time, I am still glad that over the last six years I've had the opportunity to make those decisions. And I wouldn't trade it for anything."

title: As Easton Election Nears, Campaign Finance Transparency Discussion Sparks
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
As Easton election nears, campaign finance transparency discussion sparks

 April 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 621
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — With a little less than a month until Easton residents elect their next council president, incumbent Frank Gunsallus said he is voluntarily reporting his campaign finances.Gunsallus' announcement came after Easton Mayor Megan Cook and Councilmember David Montgomery shared their efforts to draft a town ordinance related to campaign finances.
The ordinance would require campaign contributions be reported and would limit the amount someone can contribute to a campaign. The town doesn't currently have any campaign finance-related laws in place.
In an interview with The Star Democrat Monday, Cook said they hope to introduce a draft ordinance at the next Easton Town Council meeting April 21.
"We've been receiving questions from residents and neighbors," Cook said, "and here's a way that we can move forward and better the election process for the community."
Although Cook said this effort is an attempt to address an "overall general concern" that isn't specific to any one campaign, Montgomery raised concerns with the upcoming town election, which is set for May 6.
"In my opinion, the elections before this have largely been financed by the candidates themselves," he said. "The candidates have gotten out knocking on doors, sometimes through media, frequently in forums that are put on. ... Nobody before this has tried to flood the town and the roads all over the county with signs and other ways of publicizing their name."
"We don't want that to determine who wins," he said.
GUNSALLUS' STATEMENT
Gunsallus' statement, which he sent to The Star Democrat Monday afternoon, says he "agrees with and joins hands with" Cook and Montgomery in their efforts to ensure there is more transparency surrounding campaign finances.
"Transparency builds trust, and that's why I have made the conscious decision to voluntarily report my campaign finances annually through the Maryland Campaign Reporting Information System (MDCRIS)," the statement says. "All citizens are welcome to go to this public website at (https://campaignfinance.maryland.gov/Public/ViewCommittees) and review all elected officials' financial reporting. Open, consistent financial disclosure is essential to maintaining public confidence in our local government."
Gunsallus said he has been reporting campaign finance information on the website for years.
As of early Monday evening, the Friends of Frank Gunsallus page showed campaign activity from Jan. 11, 2024, through Jan. 8, 2025. Gunsallus announced his reelection campaign in December.
As of Jan. 8, the committee had paid $639 to APG Chesapeake, which owns The Star Democrat, for political advertising. The website showed only two contributions, each under $50, from individuals.
Current Ward 2 Councilmember Don Abbatiello, who is running against Gunsallus for the council president seat, said he thinks transparency with campaign finances is important at every level of government.
"I think it's important that the residents, the voters know exactly who's donating to the candidates that they're thinking about voting for," he said.
Abbatiello said he wouldn't have a problem sharing his campaign finances with the public.
"I don't have any political party support in this race or any kind of political action committee," he said, "so it's all been from individuals donating to the campaign."
Abbatiello said he hasn't heard concerns from voters specific to campaign finances in the town's upcoming election.
"I know there were some people questioning about the number of signs around town," he said. "But nobody questioning specifically, 'Where'd the money come from?'"
Along with the council president seat, candidates are vying for Ward 2 and Ward 4 council seats. In Ward 2, Lynnette D. Keefe and Robert J. Rankin will go head to head. In Ward 4, the race is between incumbent the Rev. Elmer Davis, Moonyene S. Jackson-Amis and Cameron Keefe.
If the council votes to introduce a campaign finance ordinance, a public hearing will need to be scheduled before the council can pass it. As a result, it is unlikely to take effect before the May 6 election.

title: Oxford Residents Share Thoughts on Who Should Be Allowed to Vote in Town Elections
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford residents share thoughts on who should be allowed to vote in town elections

 February 27, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 731
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — At a Commissioners of Oxford public hearing Tuesday evening, it all boiled down to the question of who should have the right to vote in town elections.The public hearing was held for a resolution that would amend the town's charter to clarify a person must register with the Talbot County Board of Elections to qualify as a voter in the town. This means a resident would not be able to vote in Oxford town elections if they aren't registered with the county board.
The commissioners opted not to vote on the resolution during the meeting.
"Listening to this conversation, it seems like we're putting the cart before the horse," Resident Warren Davis said during the public hearing. "What we really want to do is figure out who we want to vote in our elections."
Oxford Town Attorney Lyndsey Ryan said registering with the Talbot County Board of Elections means an Oxford resident is declaring their home in Oxford as their domicile, or primary residence. She said that when a person registers in Talbot County, they are removed from any voting registry they may have been on elsewhere.
Currently, the town charter states a person should register in the town office. The charter says it is the duty of Oxford's Election Board to keep registration lists up to date.
When it comes to eligibility, the charter states a person is able to vote if they are a U.S. citizen, are at least 18 and have resided in the town for at least 30 days prior to any town election.
At the outset of the public hearing, Ryan said the commissioners could choose to take a different path than the resolution presented.
Commissioner Katrina Greer brought up her concern that the list of registered voters in Talbot County is not always updated.
"As residents in a very small town, I know who lives here, I know who died this year," she said. "And so it's much easier for our own board of elections to clean up those voter logs."
Residents who spoke at the public hearing brought up scenarios and shared thoughts on who should and shouldn't be able to vote in town elections.
After confirming Oxford commissioners serve all proprietors and renters in town, Dan Kordell said anyone who owns or rents property in town should have a say in who is serving them.
"It's about representation," he said.
Jim Wilcox asked the commissioners to focus on who should vote based on "who has skin in the game." He said property owners and people with leases for more than 30 days should be able to vote in town elections.
"I would say somebody who has maybe a six-month lease," he said. "Something that shows a substantial term commitment to Oxford rather than just landing here for 30 days."
Warren Davis brought up that there are multiple residents in town with more than one residence. He included himself in the category, saying he usually goes to Maine in the summer.
"Should I be allowed to vote in Oxford because I'm not here for 30 days before the election?" he asked.
Multiple residents spoke to the issue of whether residents away at college should be able to vote in town elections. David Donovan said he doesn't think these students should be able to vote in town elections.
"They don't have any skin in the game," he said. "They don't have any intention to move back here. ... So I don't think those people should be allowed to vote here."
Chris Maynard said that could be considered disenfranchisement.
"We should keep in mind that 18-year-olds, we're referring to them as children, but they're really adults," she said, later adding, "It's not that the parents drive them over to the voting place and tell them what to do."
Donovan said he has an alternative to the town's proposed resolution. He proposed the town instead amend the voting eligibility section in the charter to say that voters should be physically present in their Oxford residence 30 days prior to the election unless they are absent due to vacation or circumstances beyond their control.
He said residents absent from town for those 30 days due to "voluntary enrollment in any education program" should not be considered eligible to vote.
Donovan said the town should add an application for absentee voting that requires absentee voters to affirm they are eligible to vote.
After the public hearing, the commissioners agreed to schedule a work session to discuss the issue further.
