title: Oxford Election Board Makes Recommendations for Future Town Elections
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford Election Board makes recommendations for future town elections

 November 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 399
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — The Oxford Election Board discussed ways it believes the town's election process could be improved during a Commissioners of Oxford workshop Tuesday.At the meeting, Election Board members and town's commissioners went through a list of different recommendations from the Election Board. Some of those recommendations would need to be addressed by the commissioners.
The board is recommending some changes to the charter. Pam Baker, who is on the board, asked that the voter registration process be clarified in the town charter. She said the board uses a list of registered voters from the county when it comes to verifying voter registrations.
Commissioner Katrina Greer said the town charter does not say anything about registering to vote with the county. Baker said that is why they are recommending the process be clarified in the charter.
Baker said the charter also needs to be cleaned up and corrected when it comes to the election process.
"It's probably worth going through it carefully and picking up all those changes at one time," she said. "A lot of things have been done piecemeal in the past. It's a little bit hard to follow."
Along with charter changes, Baker talked about the board's interest in requiring candidates in town elections to disclose campaign finances.
"We felt that transparency was talked about an awful lot in the last several campaigns, but one area that remains totally opaque is finances," she said. "And I think it's worthwhile for voters in Oxford to understand where the financial support is coming from for candidates."
When it comes to transparency in the voting process, Baker said the board prefers livestreaming the election rather than allowing poll watchers. She said having board members as well as poll watchers in the room could be intimidating for voters.
Before the last town election in June, resident Josh Coder requested poll watchers be present. At a town meeting that month, the commissioners voted to recommend livestreaming, which was implemented.
Other recommendations the board made at the workshop Tuesday include setting up a locked mailbox in the town office for absentee ballots and limiting political signage.
Commissioner Tom Costigan said limiting signage could raise an issue with the First Amendment.
Baker also talked about procedural changes the Election Board can implement itself, including getting better signage and rearranging the voting room.
Moving forward, Baker said she would like to sit down with Town Attorney Lyndsey Ryan to look through the charter for errors.

title: Republicans Continue to Push Talbot Board of Elections on Election Judge Breakdown
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Republicans continue to push Talbot Board of Elections on election judge breakdown

 October 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 775
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — County Republicans continued to push the Talbot County Board of Elections to equal its selection of election judges during the board's monthly meeting on Wednesday morning.The breakdown by party was 62 Democratic judges, 50 Republican judges and 11 unaffiliated judges in September, according to Election Director Tammy Stafford. Local officials have indicated at meetings that the number of judges for each party may now be closer to equal, but this has not been confirmed by the Board of Elections.
Election officials have said the makeup is "fluid" and will change up until Election Day. During Wednesday's meeting, Stafford said "judges are always needed" and that her office "continuously" accepts interest forms.
According to Sept. 18 meeting minutes read aloud Wednesday, staffing for the election began in June of 2023. Training for those who filled out interest forms began in early 2024.
In the last month, concerns have circulated regarding a party imbalance of election judges, or those who staff polling places on Election Day.
Local officials, including Talbot County Sheriff Joe Gamble and Talbot County Council Member Dave Stepp, have cited that the board is not in compliance with state law.
Maryland election code states "each polling place shall have an equal number of election judges" from "the majority party" and "the principal minority party."
State election law permits judges not affiliated with either party for precincts with six or more judges, as well as "one or more election judges who are minors." The number of unaffiliated judges "may not exceed the lesser of" the majority or minority party, law states.
These concerns led to a flurry of responses from state agencies emphasizing the security of the electoral process. In an Oct. 2 statement responding to a letter sent by Gamble to the Talbot Board of Elections, State Board of Elections Administrator Jared DeMarinis said voters should feel "confident" in the state's election security and "compliance with the law."
Attorney General Anthony Brown weighed in as well, writing a letter to Gamble on Oct. 7.
"Even at the individual polling place level, while all local boards make best efforts to achieve exact party balance, this is not always possible for reasons outside the local board's control, including the number of judges from each party who volunteer," Brown wrote.
Stafford stated at the Sept. 18 meeting that the training for election judges can no longer be done after Oct. 8 since the room used for training is also used for canvassing.
During Wednesday's public comment, Gary Judy, a member of the Talbot County Republican Central Committee, said he's heard from Republicans who applied to be an election judge but were not told there are no vacancies for this year's general election. He said the fact that the board did not achieve exact party balance is "extremely alarming to Talbot County voters."
"We decided to keep close track on it this year," Judy said, "and can confirm that there were more than enough Republicans who signed up to be election judges to fill the available Republican positions of the equal representation required by Maryland election law."
On Wednesday, Judy provided board members with copies of a letter written by the Maryland Republican Party addressing election judge concerns in Talbot County. Adam Wood, executive director of the Maryland Republican Party, later told the Star Democrat that the letter was a "draft" letter and had not been sent to the state board.
Shari Wilcoxon, also a member of the Republican central committee, spoke during public comment, asking the board to ensure "parity" of election judges.
"I think that it is an actual embarrassment that this board is allowing the executive director free rein to break the law," Wilcoxon said. "It is your duty to hold her feet to the fire, and that she does what is Maryland law."
Wilcoxon questioned why election judge applications were denied in February and March.
"February and March had to do with the primary," Stafford responded. "Let's be specific here. That was the primary. Those were the first people who were contacted for the general (election)."
This led to tense back-and-forth between Wilcoxon and Stafford.
Board President Susan MacKinnon stepped in, asking Wilcoxon to stop speaking.
"You have had the opportunity to speak, you are now being disruptive," MacKinnon said to Wilcoxon. "You are being disruptive, and if you continue being disruptive, I will call a recess and have you removed."
Wednesday's meeting was the board's last regularly scheduled meeting before the election Nov. 5. During Stafford's report to the board, she said "logic and accuracy testing on the electronic equipment was completed" on Sept. 16. The Board of Elections will have its logic and accuracy testing documentation available for public inspection Friday at 10 a.m. at 215 Bay Street in Easton.

title: Attorney General Weighs in on Election Judge Imbalance, Sheriff's Role at the Polls
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Attorney general weighs in on election judge imbalance, sheriff's role at the polls

 October 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 676
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Maryland Attorney General Anthony Brown has weighed in on the equality of election judges, the topic of sometimes tense back-and-forth between the Talbot County Board of Elections, The Talbot County Sheriff and local elected officials in recent weeks.A letter from Brown was read out loud by Tammy Stafford, election director for Talbot County, during an Oct. 7 Board of Elections special meeting.
The letter, addressed to Talbot County Sheriff Joe Gamble, details the "limited role of local law enforcement, including our sheriff's office, in the electoral process." Although the letter is not an official opinion of the attorney general, Brown said he hopes the letter is helpful in setting forth the roles of law enforcement officers during elections.
Brown's letter responds to a letter sent by Gamble to the Board of Elections on issues concerning the upcoming election, in which Gamble "strongly" urged the board to follow state law.
In Brown's letter, he addresses the role of law enforcement, security, authority on election law violations and concerns involving election judges.
"State law does, specifies and carefully circumscribes the authority of local law enforcement and polling places while conferring primary responsibility for election law enforcement on other agencies," Brown said. "I understand that local law enforcement agencies do provide assistance to local boards of elections in some jurisdictions, including deploying personnel to provide security and transporting election materials. But importantly, this is done at the request and under the direction of the local Board of Elections itself."
Gamble's letter came in the midst of intense discussions centering concerns over the partisan breakdown of election judges ahead of the Nov. 5 General Election.
According to the most recent breakdown from the Talbot County Board of Elections, 62 judges are Democrats, 50 are Republicans and 11 are unaffiliated.
Maryland election code states "each polling place shall have an equal number of election judges" from "the majority party" and "the principal minority party."
State election law permits judges not affiliated with either party for precincts with six or more judges, as well as "one or more election judges who are minors." The number of unaffiliated judges "may not exceed the lesser of" the majority or minority party, law states.
Discussion about the imbalance of election judge political party affiliations surfaced after Talbot County Council Member Dave Stepp raised it in a council meeting Sept. 24. He voiced concerns the county Board of Elections was not following state law for election judges, though his motion for the council to send a letter to the elections board failed by a 3-2 vote.
In his letter, Brown emphasized State law "does not require equality in the total number of judges" recruited and trained by the local Board of Elections.
"Even at the individual polling place level, while all local boards make best efforts to achieve exact party balance, this is not always possible for reasons outside the local board's control, including the number of judges from each party who volunteer," Brown said.
Toward the end of Brown's letter, he advised that opening a polling place, even if the number of judges from each party is not exactly equal, is preferable to "closing the polling place and disenfranchising all the voters who would have voted there."
After the reading of the letter, the county board of elections weighed whether to release its own letter or statement to the public addressing the election judge concerns.
Denise Lovelady, a member of the board of elections, said the issue with Brown's letter is it is still subject to "clarification." She said the letter speaks more to security issues than election judge equality.
After a bit of discussion, board members voted 3-1 to sent out Brown's letter instead of drafting their own. Lovelady voted against sending Brown's letter.
"I don't feel that it services the public, that it's giving them the full information that they need," Lovelady said. "The board is kind of skirting the issue that it needs to be defined better than what it has been in these meetings."
According to Stafford, election judge assignments are on the agenda for a second special meeting Tuesday, Oct. 8 at 9:30 a.m.

title: State Board of Elections Weighs in on Election Judges Amid Concerns in Talbot County
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
State Board of Elections weighs in on election judges amid concerns in Talbot County

 October 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 802
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — After some Talbot County officials and residents raised concerns about the partisan breakdown of election judges, the Maryland State Board of Elections is telling voters that election judge affiliations will not bring about disenfranchisement at the polls in November.Discussion about the imbalance of election judge political party affiliations surfaced last week after Talbot County Council Member Dave Stepp raised it in a council meeting Sept. 24. He voiced concerns the county Board of Elections was not following state law for election judges, though his motion for the council to send a letter to the elections board failed by a 3-2 vote.
One week later, Talbot County Sheriff Joe Gamble sent a letter to the Talbot County Board of Elections, "strongly" urging the board to follow state law.
The following day, Jared DeMarinis, the state administrator of elections, released a statement regarding the assignment of election judges. In it, he emphasized that Maryland voters should feel "confident" in the state's election security and "compliance with the law."
"An election judge's partisan affiliation does not impact or determine the outcome of the election," DeMarinis wrote. "Voters decide the outcomes of elections. The party affiliation of an election judge does not stop them from casting their ballots or disenfranchise a voter. And to say otherwise is disingenuous."
DeMarinis noted in his statement the strict rules election judges must follow, bounding them "to conduct the election in a nonpartisan manner and fashion."
Maryland election code states "each polling place shall have an equal number of election judges" from "the majority party" and "the principal minority party."
State election law permits judges not affiliated with either party for precincts with six or more judges, as well as "one or more election judges who are minors." The number of unaffiliated judges "may not exceed the lesser of" the majority or minority party, law states.
According to the most recent breakdown from the Talbot County Board of Elections, 62 judges are Democrats, 50 are Republicans and 11 are unaffiliated.
Following a closed session meeting on Friday for legal advice, the Talbot Board of Elections is set to meet Monday at 1 p.m. to discuss of a statement to send to the public, according to Talbot County Election Director Tammy Stafford. She said election judge assignments are on the agenda for a second special meeting Tuesday at 9:30 a.m.
Stafford did not respond to questions from the Star Democrat rabout the election judges and whether legal counsel has advised if the board is in compliance with law or not.
Election judges are appointed 13 weeks prior to the primary elections, DeMarinis said, and recruiting judges is an ongoing process local boards of elections undertake.
"There are never enough election judges on call to serve," the statement read. "Individuals get sick, have emergencies, have transportation issues, and a whole list of other things that might prevent them from serving on an assigned day. Having election judges assigned to being on call is the only way to mitigate this problem and ensure smooth election operations."
LETTER FROM SHERIFFIn Gamble's letter sent to the board and Election Director Tammy Stafford, the sheriff stated he's received more than 25 complaints regarding the election and "feelings of disenfranchisement."
"Complaints received highlight a clear disparity among one party over another and in this current instance, registered Republican voters are not being equally represented," Gamble wrote.
In an interview, Gamble, a Republican, explained the reasoning for his concerns and why he sent the letter.
"We provide security at the polling places," Gamble said. "We also escort ballots back. The election judges, we follow them back and make sure that the election's not tampered with by outsiders, however they might do that. I think to have free and fair elections, you need to be transparent, and you need to follow the law."
DeMarinis' statement addressed the role of local sheriff's offices in elections.
"The Sheriff's office does not have any legal authority to conduct security checks or a role in securing the ballots in a polling place," DeMarinis wrote. "Nor does the Sheriff enforce the requirements of the Election Law Article. The legal authority to keep the peace, to preserve the integrity of the voting process and maintain order in the polling place is entrusted to the election judge. In fact, a police officer must obey the order of the election judge at the polling place."
Gamble said he's not heard back from the county or state elections boards. In an interview, he expressed worry that the election judge controversy may affect safety during the election process.
"It causes me security concerns, too, because people are going to get frustrated," Gamble said. "We've already seen violence associated with this election cycle with two assassination attempts of the former president.
"And we don't want any issues here in Talbot County with people getting frustrated and then taking their frustrations out in some criminal manner," he said.

title: Election Judge Imbalance Stirs Concerns in Talbot County
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Election judge imbalance stirs concerns in Talbot County

 September 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 1009
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Concerns over election judge appointments made by the Talbot County Board of Elections are being raised by residents and local officials.Adding an unexpected agenda item to the Talbot County Council's Tuesday meeting, Council Member Dave Stepp voiced such concerns, which deal with the party makeup of Talbot County's election judges for the November election. He said the elections board is not following a state law that requires an equal number of election judges from the two political parties.
"I feel like there's certain aspects of election law that are trying to be skirted here, from both an elections director from Talbot County as well as the majority of members of our Talbot County elections board," Stepp said.
According to Election Director Tammy Stafford, current judges consist of 62 Democrats, 50 Republicans and 11 unaffiliated, though that makeup is "fluid" and will change up until Election Day. Currently, she says there are no vacancies.
The 123 election judges, people who are responsible for running polling places and verifying voters, will work at 10 different polling places in the county.
Maryland election code states "each polling place shall have an equal number of election judges" from "the majority party" and "the principal minority party."
Stafford told the Star Democrat that election judge selection is "based on recruitment numbers," which has been a challenge for the county and something the board is "committed" to fixing. "Even if we use everyone on our list, it would be hard pressed to be 50-50," Stafford said.
"Our recruitment levels are still low, and the interest of certain parties is low," Stafford added. She said the board's goal is to "be as party balanced as possible."
Richard Osborne, chair of the Talbot County Republican Central Committee, says he's heard from many Republicans over the past two years that they had applied to be an election judge but were never selected.
This year, the central committee began to document those who were not accepted, Osborne said.
"We have a backlog of almost 30 Republicans who have applied to be an election judge over the last three to four months," Osborne said. "They have not been able to do any of the training. They have been turned down."
Stafford said since canvassing of mail-in ballots begins on Oct. 15, the county's elections board "will not have space for training" or the resources to train individuals who have applied to be judges but have not been accepted yet.
"We have a window of time when we train individuals," Stafford said. Those that have applied will be "one of the first groups of people that we contact for 2026," she said.
Other factors, such as prior experience, play a role. Stafford said the board is also "looking to diversify the age of the election judges throughout the county."
The five members of the Board of Elections are appointed by the governor to four-year terms, with approval from the House of Delegates. The election director is appointed by the county board.
Osborne said the issue boils down to the state code not being followed.
"It's just incredible to me that you have state employees and people that have been appointed to the state board knowingly agree to break the law," Osborne said. "Our committee is not done with fighting this battle."
COUNCIL DEBATETuesday's County Council meeting came after a special meeting held Tuesday morning by the Board of Elections to discuss election judges. Stepp and Council President Chuck Callahan attended that morning meeting and brought forth their worries to council members, leading to tense discussion.
In an agenda item added at the start of the council meeting, Stepp asked the council to send a letter reminding Stafford and the elections board to follow state law, garnering support from Callahan.
The council's three other members, who did not attend the elections board's special meeting that morning, were not immediately willing to send a letter to the election director.
"I understand your concern," Council Vice President Pete Lesher said to Stepp. "That's a serious allegation. But I'm not sure that I could substitute my lower level of expertise here for the judgment and command of the data that the Board of Elections has to take action."
Council Member Keasha Haythe said, "I cannot sign onto a letter that I haven't received any type of information regarding this going on or any constituent complaint," adding that council members typically have a draft of the letter to view prior to signing it.
Stepp said he's heard of citizen complaints and was aware of the Republican Central Committee's efforts to provide judge applications to ensure an even distribution between the two parties.
"I believe it's very timely that we do this because if we miss the opportunity today, I feel like it's going to be a totally missed opportunity," Stepp said of sending the letter.
"Witnessing what was going on this morning was concerning," Callahan said. "There's one thing us five don't want to do, is meddle into an election. That's not what we're here for."
"I think that's what you're doing," Mielke said to Callahan.
"With all due respect to the two councilmen, I think it's sort of based on hearsay and interpretation (of) what they saw," Mielke later stated, saying she didn't have enough information to sign the letter. "And you're tainting the public's view of this election."
"So we just don't bring it up at all then?" Callahan responded. Mielke followed, "No, we don't bring it up in the letter. We have other options."
Callahan and Stepp voted in favor of sending the letter, while Lesher, Haythe and Mielke all voted no.
After Stepp's motion to send a letter failed, he provided additional comment at the end of Tuesday's meeting, emphasizing that the Board of Elections is not in compliance with Maryland law.
"He's just tainted our elections," Mielke said. As Stepp continued, Mielke asked County Attorney Patrick Thomas, "is this appropriate to make accusations as a comment of council?"
Stepp finished his comment asking the Board of Elections to balance its selection of judges.
"Follow the law, do your job, be transparent and train more Republican election judges immediately, and have them ready to work our general election," Stepp said.

title: 'We Need to Get Along' - Many Speak Out About Negative Tone of Council President Campaign
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
'We need to get along' - Many speak out about negative tone of council president campaign

 September 8, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: A1 | Section: News 
 
 671
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - As the election for the Easton Town Council's next president draws closer, current council members, candidates and town residents are speaking out about the negative campaigning seen this election cycle.The special at-large election is set for Tuesday, Sept. 12. Four candidates are running for council president: former Easton Mayor Robert Willey, former Ward 1 council member Al Silverstein, Frank Gunsallus and Kevin Bateman.But as election day fast approaches, many have noticed a difference in the spirit of this year's campaigning.At Tuesday's Town Council meeting, sitting council members raised concerns with negative political mailers targeting one candidate and complex questionnaires sent to all four candidates.Ward 1 Councilwoman Maureen Curry said she was appalled and offended by a political flyer she recently received in the mail.The flyer - one of at least four that hit mailboxes this week - specifically addressed Willey's lengthy service to the town, his loss in the May mayoral race and his current candidacy for town council president, stating: "Easton doesn't need any more career politicians. After 30 years, Easton needs a new voice." "This is a derogatory piece to a candidate for town office, someone who has served this community for over 30 years," Curry said.A second flyer mailing sent earlier this week featured an image of a diaper and said that both politicians and diapers need to be changed.The flyer repeated allegations about the town wrongly paying employees overtime, giving certain town officials special exemptions from contributing to health insurance coverage and misusing taxpayer dollars to benefit Willey and his family.The flyers were paid for by Scott R.Wagner, a former Pennsylvania state senator and Republican gubernatorial candidate.The information detailed in the second flyer was similar to points made by Silverstein in an Aug. 23 letter to the editor, which was published in the Talbot Spy.On Thursday, Silverstein told the Star Democrat he was "absolutely not" connected to Wagner's mailers and had not seen them until they arrived in his mailbox.To Willey, the political attacks are mean-spirited, especially when they bring his family into it, he said."(It's) not something we're used to in town," he said, later adding that the accusations are not valid. Bringing family into politics is something that crosses the line, Willey added.Nearly a dozen Easton residents have submitted letters to the editor of the Star Democrat denouncing the mailers. Others have spoken out on social media.Tom Duncan, who served on the Talbot County Council for 19 years and as the county sheriff for eight years, said the attacks on Willey and other candidates were "uncalled for." "(It) upsets me that we've stooped to this level in the county," he said, likening the negativity to what's seen in the national political arena.Willey isn't the only candidate who's been targeted leading up to the election.Gunsallus said he's recently experienced multiple attempts to damage his campaign.Gunsallus, who ran for the Ward 1 seat on the council in the spring, said while he's disappointed in the negativity in the current race, he's focusing on the positive."In every election, it's crucial that we focus on the issues that matter most to the residents of Easton, rather than resort to negative tactics," he said in a statement. "I firmly believe in running a campaign based on vision, solutions and a genuine commitment to bettering our community." Gunsallus encouraged other candidates to rise above the noise and maintain integrity as well.Closing out Monday's council meeting, Don Abbatiello, the town council's acting president, encouraged voters to look into each of the four candidates and decide for themselves who to support."I am asking that everybody in the community choose civility over negativity," he said. "Negative politics, regardless of who they're done by, should have no place in our town, because whatever happens next Tuesday, come next Wednesday, we're all still going to be neighbors, so we need to get along."

Ward 1 Councilwoman Maureen Curry criticizes a political flyer attacking former Easton Mayor Robert Willey at the Easton Town Council meeting Tuesday, Sept. 5.

title: Master Plan, Grant Application Approved for St. Michaels Park
author: Natalie Jones
content:
Master plan, grant application approved for St. Michaels park

 January 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Environment 
 
 676
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — Months of work came to a happy conclusion Wednesday evening with the Commissioners of St. Michaels' unanimous approval of a final master plan for San Domingo Creek Park and a $1.7 million open space grant application.The final master plan for the park, previously referred to as the Boundary Lane Waterfront Park, includes nature trails, expanded wetlands, a living shoreline, a fishing pier, a comfort station and associated parking.
A long-wanted dog park was initially included in draft park plans, but following extensive debate, it was ultimately removed to extend the area of the park's pollinator meadow, said Scott Scarfone, an associate principal at Mahan Rykiel Associates who worked on the park design.
Leashed dogs will still be allowed to walk through the new park.
Plans for a defined dog park are still in the works, according to Town Manager Rob Straebel. A 2.4-acre parcel next to Bradley Park was identified as a likely location, and the town is working on a purchase or lease agreement for the site.
A viewing mound, a 10-foot hill with an accessible path to give visitors an elevated view of the creek, was also eliminated from the new park's final master plan.
The viewing mound will be replaced by a circular loblolly pine grove, with views of the creek still visible. The expansive pollinator meadow will extend into the center of that space.
Scarfone called the town's decision to buy the property and develop it into a park "wise" and "visionary."
"I can tell you that generations of people who visit this park are going to enjoy it in the future, so congratulations to the town for acquiring an amazing piece of property," he said. "I think it was a very smart decision."
The town purchased the 7.6-acre property on Boundary Lane, which is adjacent to San Domingo Creek, for $2.9 million last year. Formerly owned by nonprofit Environmental Concern, the property also includes an administrative building, which is slated for use as the town's new office.
Because most of the park is intended as open space, opportunities to receive state grant funding through Program Open Space are available to help offset the purchase price.
Nearly six acres of the property were designated by Talbot County as potential open space.
Appraisals of the open space acreage came in at $1.6 million and $1.8 million, according to Town Planner Steve Ball, leading to town staff seeking approval to apply for a $1.7 million grant for reimbursement of acquisition costs.
The request was approved unanimously. The grant application, due in the next few weeks, was set to be submitted Thursday.
Though master plan approval and the submittal of the grant application mark important steps forward in bringing San Domingo Creek Park to reality, more regulatory work remains to be done.
While the town owns the property, and over half of it is located within town limits, nearly three acres remain under the county's zoning jurisdiction.
The town is seeking to annex the remainder of the property into its limits, including Boundary Lane itself, which includes the property in front of the park's entrance. St. Michaels Police Chief Jeff Oswald also requested to include the road in the annexation, Ball said.
Neighboring resident Langley Shook and Commissioner Tad DuPont raised concerns about bringing Boundary Lane into the annexation.
"I'm leery about taking on the expense of maintaining a road when we are really pinched on every single front," DuPont said.
If the annexation is approved, the new portion will also need a town zoning designation.
St. Michaels doesn't have designated zoning for parks, and the part of the park property already within the town limits is zoned residential, Ball said.
The remaining area would need to be zoned as residential, and that's in part due to many state grants requiring the property to be in a priority funding area, an urban area where the state will invest money for infrastructure, Ball said.
The annexation request will be heard by the St. Michaels Planning Commission next month.
The town's board of zoning appeals will also consider a special exception to use the existing offices on the property as town administrative offices in February.

title: Residents Eager as St. Michaels Considers Dog Park Locations
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Residents eager as St. Michaels considers dog park locations

 September 6, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 384
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — A dog park in St. Michaels has been in discussion for almost four years. Now, with a special meeting planned, the town and commissioners are turning their attention to finding a location where the dog park can properly serve the community.The commissioners want to take into account multiple factors when decided the location of the dog park, including cost of building and maintenance, liability concerns, who is allowed to use the park, and limiting the amount of people affected by the noise and traffic.
While a date is still being chosen for the special meeting, some dog owners in town said they were excited that the town is looking to get the ball rolling.
"It's exciting," said Jonathan Dietrich, St. Michaels resident and owner of two dogs, as he was walking his dogs through town. "It's exciting as long as the location is right and everybody approves of it. I know it's been a very long journey, and it's pretty complicated, but it would be great. It would be great if we could get one but we'll see what happens."
When dog park discussion started in St. Michaels four years ago, a group of lawyers in St. Michaels came together and created a group called "The Friends of St. Michaels Dog Park."
Member Devon Hewitt spoke at the August town meeting about donors for the dog park and potential locations.
According to Hewitt the group of lawyers did research and came up with multiple locations, but the conversations fell through. After the new commissioners were elected, conversations began again.
While determining the master plan for San Domingo Creek Park construction at the August Town Council meeting, discussion arose about a dog park being included in the master plan. The town commissioners decided not to include a dog park in the plan.
One of the reasons brought forward at the meeting was that if dog park plans were added to the master plan, the grant received from the Maryland Department of Natural Resources could be pulled back.
While the location for the potential dog park is unclear, St. Michaels residents say they are ready to see movement.
When Stacy Sass, a resident of St. Michaels, was asked how soon she would hope to see a dog park in St. Michaels for her dog Ginger to play in, she said, "tomorrow."

title: Talbot County Approves Senior Task Force

Talbot County approves senior task force

 EASTON — The Talbot County Council passed a resolution to create a Senior Citizens Task Force amid calls to address a rise in senior homelessness.Council OK'd the task force 5-0 at its meeting Tuesday after hearing from senior care and housing experts at a work session last month. Council member Lynn Mielke originally brought forth the resolution earlier this summer.
Mielke said she's pleased the task force was established and looks forward to serving on the body. Council Vice President Pete Lesher thanked Mielke for leading the effort.
"I look forward to working with the folks that we'll be calling together for that," Lesher said.
The task force will make recommendations to the County Council on housing, health care, transportation and meal services for homeless seniors.
It will consist of representatives from the following entities, among others: Commission on Aging, Delmarva Community Services, Talbot Interfaith Shelter, Neighborhood Service Center, Talbot County Health Department, Easton Town Council and County Council.
At the July 29 work session, Talbot Interfaith Executive Director Julie Lowe cited an increase in calls from seniors as evidence that homelessness is growing.
In 2023, the shelter received 15 calls from men 55 and older and 14 calls from women 55 and older. One year later, those marks increased to 30 and 23, respectively.
This year, the Easton-based shelter has already received 19 calls from men and 13 calls from women in that age range, Lowe said.
Other nonprofit and health care leaders advocated for the task force's creation at that meeting. They said it's especially needed to help align local nonprofits, county boards and the health department.
"There isn't anybody who is behind all of these organizations pushing to keep everybody connected," said Rachel Smith, chair of the county's Commission on Aging. "And that's what we found is one of the biggest problems. We have all these organizations out here that are doing so much great work, but then we've got to figure out a way to connect so we can help all these people."

title: 'Only Going to Get Worse': Talbot Officials Discuss Rise in Senior Homelessness
author: Konner Metz
content:
'Only going to get worse': Talbot officials discuss rise in senior homelessness

 July 31, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: News 
 
 648
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Talbot County officials and senior care leaders met Tuesday to discuss creating a task force to address senior homelessness, a rapidly accelerating problem, experts say.The request for the task force comes from Talbot County Council member Lynn Mielke. Based on council feedback, a resolution to create the task force seems poised for approval at the council's Aug. 12 meeting.
Members of the county's Commission on Aging and other health and housing experts spoke on mounting challenges faced by area seniors, from housing costs and food insecurity to mental health struggles.
Rachel Smith, chair of the aging commission, said a task force would help align local nonprofits, county boards and the health department. There's currently a "disconnect," she said.
"There isn't anybody who is behind all of these organizations pushing to keep everybody connected," Smith said. "And that's what we found is one of the biggest problems. We have all these organizations out here that are doing so much great work, but then we've got to figure out a way to connect so we can help all these people."
Mielke said there's no single solution to help the homeless senior population.
"Each agency would bring solutions or suggestions, but not one agency can deal with all of the issues," Mielke said.
As drafted, the senior citizens task force would consist of representatives from the following entities: Commission on Aging, Delmarva Community Services, Talbot Interfaith Shelter, Neighborhood Service Center, Talbot County Health Department, Easton Town Council and County Council. Members from Mid-Shore Behavioral Health and law enforcement agencies may also be added based on Tuesday's discussions.
The task force would make recommendations to the County Council on housing, transportation and meal services for homeless seniors.
Homelessness is growing
Julie Lowe, executive director of Talbot Interfaith Shelter, cited jumps in calls from seniors as evidence that homelessness is on the rise.
In 2023, the shelter received 15 calls from men 55 and older and 14 calls from women 55 and older. One year later, those marks increased to 30 and 23, respectively.
This year, the Easton-based shelter has already received 19 calls from men and 13 calls from women in that age range.
Talbot Interfaith has limited capacity, Lowe said. It runs a multi-year program to transition people into paying for partial rent before moving out on their own. But even when shelter residents move out, Lowe said finding a financially viable apartment in the area isn't an easy task, especially for seniors who can't work.
"Most of the people who we work with will never get to that point with the market-rate housing and where it is now," Lowe said.
Lee Newcomb, a Talbot County social worker for 26 years and the aging commission's secretary, said she's never seen senior need at such a high level.
Newcomb said the Days Inn in Easton is home to many unhoused individuals. Smith said seniors especially suffer in the winter months since Talbot County doesn't have a low-barrier homeless shelter.
Smith noted an incident at the Days Inn last December as a wake-up call. According to police, an unhoused man who was living in the woods behind the hotel was found dead on Dec. 14, 2024.
"I feel like we missed something there," Smith said. "We shouldn't have our senior residents — some of them have worked in our community — die."
Cambridge-based Delmarva Community Services has served many homeless people from Talbot County down in Dorchester, according to president and CEO Andy Hollis.
Hollis said a low-barrier, overnight shelter is a gap in Talbot County, and something that a task force could work on. Many others at the meeting on Tuesday emphasized the need for a physical location to consolidate services for the senior homeless population.
'We don't have this issue in Talbot,' we thought for so long," Hollis said. "And we truly do. It's something that is long overdue in terms of being addressed."
"The challenge is not leveling out and it's only going to get worse," he added.

title: Talbot Council Discusses a Senior Citizens Task Force
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot Council discusses a senior citizens task force

 July 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 469
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Talbot County Council is set to consider creating a senior citizens task force to address the needs of the county's older residents, including those without stable housing.Council member Lynn Mielke asked for the council to approve the task force by way of a resolution last week, but council members largely preferred holding off until a work session is held.
"We do have a growing problem with homeless senior citizens," Mielke said at the July 1 council meeting. "They are in need of services, particularly in the Easton area but throughout the county."
Council President Chuck Callahan said he liked the idea.
"But the first thing that came to my mind was, do we get these groups and we have a work session and kind of get a game plan," he said.
The council introduced Mielke's resolution but did not approve it, opting instead to hold the work session with local senior care leaders.
As Talbot County's average age grows, nonprofit organizations like Upper Shore Aging and groups like the health department's senior care program aim to address senior housing and health needs. The county has a Commission on Aging which meets monthly; Mielke is the council's liaison to that commission.
According to census data, people 65 and older account for 30% of Talbot County's total population. The county's average age was 50.9 in 2023 and has slightly increased each year since 2020. The national average is just under 39 years old.
The task force, if created, would provide recommendations to the County Council on how to implement services for homeless senior citizens in the county.
Mielke said after talking to leaders at Upper Shore Aging, the Talbot Interfaith Shelter and the aging commission, it's clear homelessness is a problem for seniors. She said the groups are aware of 52 seniors in the area dealing with homelessness.
"I think it's extremely important that we form this task force and move forward to address those special needs," Mielke said.
Council member Keasha Haythe said a work session could be a "starting point" so the entire council can gather information and data from senior care experts.
Mielke reluctantly agreed to a work session but said it'd be "redundant."
"So because, I guess, they're senior citizens, you're putting another level of delay by having a work session rather than moving forward with the task force," Mielke said. "I hear you."
All five council members introduced the resolution, though a vote to approve was not held at the meeting. As currently written, the task force would include: a Commission on Aging member; a board member each from Delmarva Community Services, Talbot Interfaith Shelter, Neighborhood Service Center; a person working in Talbot County Health Department's senior care program; an Easton Town Council member; and a Talbot County Council member.
A work session to discuss the potential senior citizens task force has not yet been scheduled.

title: Residents Soon Will Move in to Renovated Doverbrook Apartments
author: Konner Metz
content:
Residents soon will move in to renovated Doverbrook Apartments

 May 6, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 339
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The revitalized Doverbrook Apartments were shown off to state, county and town leaders last week as final touches are completed before residents move in.Don Bibb, executive director of the Housing Commission of Talbot, said the 64-unit redevelopment project will benefit the community.
"You can see the tremendous improvement this has made to the community and the opportunity for much improved, long-term sustainable housing for the program participants that we have that are going to be living here," Bibb said April 30 during a tour of the complex.
Bibb said Thursday that move-in for returning residents is imminent and is likely to begin within seven to 10 days.
The commission and construction company Pennrose began redevelopment of the Doverbrook Apartments in late 2023. The $26 million project replaced the apartment complex's seven old buildings with five new buildings, adding 14 units to its original 50-unit setup.
"It's good utilization of open space that provides the opportunity for the growth to add more units in," Bibb said.
Located on Dover Street, the complex will accommodate households earning between 30% and 80% of the area median income, or between $21,000 and $58,000 for one-person households.
It includes one-, two-, three- and four-bedroom apartments. Project leaders said the complex was designed to bring original residents — who were assisted in finding temporary housing during construction — back once completed.
Bibb said of the original 50 tenants, around 30 will return — a relatively high percentage for a redevelopment project during which residents move elsewhere temporarily.
Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development Secretary Jake Day toured the apartment complex April 30. He applauded the redevelopment efforts and lightheartedly pointed out how close residents will be to Rise Up Coffee across the street.
"Do your marketing materials for the remaining (units) talk about how many steps it is to the Rise Up?" Day said with a smile.
Bibb praised the public-private aspect of the project, which included state and local funding and low-income housing tax credits for the 14 new units.
"It was well worth the blood, sweat and tears," Bibb said.

title: Neighborhood Service Center in $300,000 hole amid federal funding uncertainty
author: Konner Metz
content:
Neighborhood Service Center in $300,000 hole amid federal funding uncertainty

 April 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 686
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — In her 15 years at the Neighborhood Service Center, Marilyn Neal has never faced a financial obstacle like the one the nonprofit is up against now.A delayed grant reimbursement is leaving the organization $300,000 in the hole. The center's leaders say the financial uncertainty has caused panic, sleepless nights and fear.
"Fear that we close the doors and our staff can't work," Neal said, "fear that we can't give food to a family."
Located on Port Street, the Neighborhood Service Center is a go-to for low-income residents, seniors and families. It lends emergency financial support on electric and rent bills. Staff run a daily food pantry and mobile food pantry. The nonprofit provides case managers to work directly with the county's most vulnerable populations.
The center is designated as Talbot County's community action agency, meaning its most consistent federal funding comes from a Community Services Block Grant.
That grant is administered by the federal Administration for Children & Families, a division of Health and Human Services, along with the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development at the state level.
Neighborhood Service Center leaders say they've been working around that "fully executed grant," which hasn't been reimbursed yet. They expected to start receiving funds for this year's first two quarters by the end of December. That didn't happen.
In a statement Friday, the Department of Housing and Community Development said it received payment from the federal government this week for its first and second quarter block grants. First quarter funds were delayed, and payments to local agencies are in the process of approval. Second quarter funds will be on time, DHCD stated.
In the meantime, the service center says the holdup is leaving it $302,000 short, forcing it to pull from contingency funds.
Sitting across from one another late Thursday morning, Neal and fiscal officer Kathy Taylor discussed which cost-saving strategies are being implemented and the additional belt-tightening that might be on the way.
The nonprofit's 13-member staff is already trimming its hours. Full-time staff are down from 40-hour to 32-hour weeks, and part-time stuff have cut back from five to two days a week.
There's been discussion around how the nonprofit would operate with only three staff members and whether after-school offerings or programs for formerly incarcerated fathers have to shut down.
"Everything we do stabilizes a household," Neal said. "And when we don't have those funds and we don't have the Neighborhood Service Center in Talbot County, I don't know what this county looks like."
ASKING FOR HELP
Earlier this week, Neal, Taylor and many staff members attended a Talbot County Council meeting to request $150,000 in county assistance to fill the gaps presented by the reimbursement delay.
"The money's tightening down now," County Manager Clay Stamp said. "But the need is not tightening down. They run everything on a shoestring."
Council members were largely supportive of the center's work, but they remained steadfast in keeping fiscal responsibility at top of mind. Council members Keasha Haythe and Lynn Mielke preferred the council hold off on any promises until it came to understand how town governments may be helping the center financially.
Haythe asked if the center has a long-term sustainability plan or money in savings. Neal said the center operates by drawing on its available funds to help families in poverty at any given moment, making it hard to save a specific amount.
"We're scaling back," Council President Chuck Callahan, who also serves as chairman of the service center's board, said at the meeting. " … I think we also need a plan for the future on how we stabilize the Neighborhood Service Center."
The council partially fulfilled Neal's request, giving the center $50,000, which won't put the county's budget in any danger, Stamp noted.
Despite the shortened hours and growing uncertainty, Neighborhood Service Center staff have remained dedicated to their work.
To Neal, it all starts with the staff members and how their compassion spreads into the community. Taylor feels that now more than ever.
"We struggle with that balance of, 'OK should we leave?'" Taylor said. "But we don't want to because we love what we do and the impact on the community that we have."
To learn more, visit https://nsctalbotmd.org/.

title: Idlewild Park's Cherished Tile Wall to Remain Up Until the Spring
author: Konner Metz
content:
Idlewild Park's cherished tile wall to remain up until the spring

 October 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 572
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Town of Easton's plans to tear down an Idlewild Park walkway adorned with hand-painted tiles has brought back cherished memories for many Easton residents.Like many others, Easton resident Michael McCormack remembers painting his tile around 17 years ago. He was eight years old, and it included trees and grass, which fit with his then-involvement in Boy Scouts and camping outdoors.
His tile is one of hundreds that make up a winding path next to the playground at Idlewild Park — some include handprints, names or school classes. While the tiles remain, they are weathered and damaged from the time that's passed.
After the town initially announced on Sept. 25 that the tile walkway would be taken down in October, many town residents asked to retrieve their tiles, with others suggesting a new community art project go in its place.
The town has said the tiles have too much wear and tear to be retrieved without damaging the wall entirely. But the outpouring of community input led town officials to delay the removal of the tiles to the spring of 2025.
"It has been truly heartwarming to see all of the community response regarding the tile wall at Idlewild Park," the town wrote in a Facebook post on Sept. 27. " … Hopefully this way everyone who wishes to visit will have a little more time to make the trip and take photos before the tiles are gone."
McCormack said he's reconnected with old friends in recent weeks after going to Idlewild Park to look at the tiles.
"You bring back these memories that aren't necessarily attached to the tile, but they're attached to the person," McCormack said. "Just seeing their name and seeing what they did makes you laugh."
Mayor Megan Cook was a driving force behind Idlewild Park's construction in 2006. As co-chairman of Project Idlewild at the time, Cook helped spearhead a community-led effort to fund and build the park that opened in the summer of 2007.
"The whole thing from start to finish was a massive undertaking with so many volunteers," Cook said, "and then so many people came to build it over a two-week period."
Cook said hundreds of people showed up to help construct the park. There was even a dedicated team in charge of watching over the kids so parents could come chip in.
The hand-painted tiles cemented the park as a community-driven project, the mayor said.
"The hope had always been that, as a community project, … there would always be that link back in community," Cook said.
She said the town is considering ideas to incorporate the tiles into a new design once the tile wall is taken down. The town's Parks & Recreation department is "all ears" on ideas from residents, it said in a Facebook post.
McCormack hopes to see the piece of Easton history commemorated, even if all of the tiles cannot be saved.
"It would be cool to save the ones they can," McCormack said. "People my age are starting to have kids, so it'd almost be cool to have their kids paint it. And then you could connect two generations together out there."
"You can see the weather, you can see the time has taken its toll on those things for sure," he said. "So you can see why they need to be taken down. It's just one of those things that I don't think people in the town really appreciated until they realized it was going to be gone."

title: Talbot County Nonprofit Says Heating Cost 'Crisis' Looms Amid Gaps in Funding
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Talbot County nonprofit says heating cost 'crisis' looms amid gaps in funding

 October 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 441
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Representatives from the Neighborhood Service Center spoke during an Easton Town Council meeting Monday evening, requesting funding from the town for what's been deemed a potential heating cost "crisis" this winter.The nonprofit assists families in Talbot County with heating costs during cooler weather. Marilyn Neal, executive director of the Neighborhood Service Center, told council members that a "drastic change" in funding will limit the assistance provided by the organization to residents in the form of kerosene, heating oil, propane and electric.
"I fear we are going to have a crisis," Neal said. " … I'm worried that our seniors and some low-income individuals in Talbot County, as well as the town of Easton, may not be able to keep warm this winter, and it keeps me up at night."
Neal said the nonprofit provides financial assistance to local residents and is then reimbursed by the Maryland Energy Assistance Program, a state program under the Department of Housing and Community Development that is federally funded.
Cardeaner Robinson, the Maryland Energy Assistance Program director, said the number of customers for the energy assistance program statewide has doubled. She said Gov. Wes Moore "wanted to see more people use the program," which led to changes in eligibility requirements.
Increased eligibility and funding cuts for the Maryland Energy Assistance Program will impact how much financial assistance the Neighborhood Service Center can provide to county residents, Neal and Robinson said.
"It sounds like really, really bad policy making and planning on the part of the state," Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery said.
Neal said it happens "with every administration," but that she's "not seen a crisis as large" as what may come this winter.
Neal asked for "at least $50,000" from the town to aid the center's energy assistance efforts. Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis and Montgomery each asked for Neal to bring a breakdown of how many Easton residents are served by those efforts.
Ward 2 Councilmember Don Abbatiello asked that the council and town employees take a look at where the money may come from if the town contributes to the Neighborhood Service Center's program.
Following the presentation and questions from councilmembers, Council President Frank Gunsallus said the council will put follow-up questions together requesting further information and details from the Neighborhood Service Center.
"I don't see how our seniors living on a fixed income will be able to sustain," Neal said. "Normally, the subsidy would take them through the winter. Well this year, it won't fill their propane tanks up, it won't give them a full tank of kerosene.
"And the Neighborhood Service Center has expended 85% of our funding. … By December, all the funding will be gone."

title: St. Michaels Proposed Dog Park Must Find New Location
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
St. Michaels proposed dog park must find new location

 September 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 489
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — The long-desired dog park for St. Michaels has faced yet another barrier in its journey to becoming reality. Friends of St. Michaels Dog Park, a volunteer group advocating for the park, have decided to move away from the proposed Bradley Parks location due to concerns from residents.During the Aug. 14 Commissioners of St. Michaels meeting, members of Friends of St. Michaels Dog Park spoke up and suggested Bradley Park as the location for the future park. According to Mitch Ettinger, the founder of Friends of St. Michaels Dog Park, the one-acre park was "underutilized" with few residential homes located nearby and had the added bonus of already being maintained by the town.
But last week, St. Michaels residents were sent a message from Ettinger stating the group had requested the commissioners remove the planned dog park discussion from the Sept. 11 meeting.
Ettinger said the decision came after hearing concerns from those living adjacent to Bradley Park. These concerns included noise from barking and the effect the park would have on the property value of their home, Ettinger said.
"Quite frankly, I just couldn't see myself standing up and saying, 'disregard these neighbors.' That's not the way that I think. That's not the way that my committee thinks," Ettinger said. "And so we withdrew the proposal for Bradley Park and asked the commissioners to take it off the agenda for this week."
The effort to have a dog park built in St. Michaels has been ongoing for more than three years. Ettinger said the dog park has been volunteer-led since its origins and is widely supported by residents of the town, according to a survey conducted when an architect was coming up with a master plan for seven acres at San Domingo Park. The site did not work for a dog park due to grant requirements that would prohibit fencing.
Moving forward, Ettinger said he would like to see commissioners of St. Michaels to take initiative and assist with the finding of a new property.
"It's time for the commissioners to step up, and they've been supportive of this concept, but they have yet to propose a location," Ettinger said.
Ettinger said his group would continue to work behind the scenes to assist commissioners in picking a location, and currently there are a couple of options that are under consideration.
Dan Conway, a member of Friends of St. Michaels Dog Park, said he and the committee are still committed to the dog park project. For him, it is more than just a place for dogs to run around. It is a community building area and would benefit owners and dogs alike in St. Michaels.
"Dog parks aren't really for dogs ... They're for people, and they help make a municipality, a community," Conway said. "In my experience, it's where townspeople can get together and renew acquaintances and make friends and share experiences. And so that, to me, is the beauty of a dog park."

title: Bradley Park Suggested for Future Dog Park in St. Michaels
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Bradley Park suggested for future dog park in St. Michaels

 August 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 679
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — A group of St. Michaels residents want a dog park in what they call an "underutilized park," but the town administrator and some commissioners seemed reluctant to commit to it at a Wednesday night meeting.The Commissioners of St. Michaels did not vote on the issue, and the item was moved to the next meeting in September.
Mitch Ettinger, founder of Friends of the Dog Park, came dressed for the occasion — a shirt decorated with dog drawing and a folder covered with dogs wearing sunglasses.
For over three years, Friends of the Dog Park, a group of St. Michaels residents and dog owners, have been advocating for a park to bring their dogs and create community.
Now in front of a new commission, Ettinger recommended Bradley Park for the dog park. According to Ettinger, the one-acre park is underutilized; there are few residential homes located nearby. Bradley Park is also already unkempt by the town, and it would not require additional acquisition funds.
Ettinger said the overall cost of the park would be approximately half a million dollars to remove the old playground equipment, create a fence and renovate the park to better fit a dog park. The Friends of the Dog Park has filed to become a nonprofit and will plan to raise the funds through donations and grants so the cost would not fall on St. Michaels residents.
Ettinger asked commissioners to tentatively approve Bradley Park as the future St. Michaels dog park and to direct town staff to retain an engineering firm to prepare a site plan that will be submitted to the Parks and Recreation Advisory Board and Planning Commission.
The group asked for about $7,000 for the site survey because all efforts up until now have been completed and paid for by residents.
"[Friends of the Dog Park] might feel that the town has skin in the game," Ettinger said. "That we don't have to go out and raise $7,000 in our pockets to have a site plan that ultimately could be shut down."
Rob Straebel, town administrator, raised concerns he had with the park, stating a need for more public comment from residents before moving forward.
"I know that this community, they take their parks very seriously," Straebel said. "And unfortunately, this is going to be a fair amount of people that are opposed to it, and there's probably going to be a fair amount of people that would love to see a dog park there."
Commissioner Katrina Whittington raised questions over the town's prioritizes when it comes to supporting projects. According to Whittington, the town was deciding whether to pay over $200,000 for a small plan for a dog park and yet there is concerns over funding a site plan for Bradley Park.
Straebel said the $200,000 would have been a "policy decision" by commissioners for a different property.
More questions and potential ideas were raised by commissioners. Some suggesting bifurcating Bradley Park and updating the playground equipment, others sharing concern for the price of the park and public opinion of the park.
Ettinger reminded commissioners that he had offered to do a survey the last time he was in front of the council and he was told not to.
Additionally, he said, when the town hired an architect to come up with a master plan for the seven acres at San Domingo Park, a survey of the entire town was done and from the residents who participated, their No. 1 request was a dog park.
A few resident commented that there is a responsibility from the new commissioners to work toward a dog park since during the commission election last spring they had said they would approve it.
Whittington suggested the commissioners move the subject to the next meeting but noted that the idea of a dog park has not seen much progress in years.
"This seems like Groundhog Day all over again," Whittington said. "... This is ridiculous just to get a dog park here at St. Michaels."
After a bit of back and forth from commissioners and town residents, the council decided to delay further discussion on the park until the September meeting.

title: County, state leaders break ground on St. Vincent de Paul expansion
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
County, state leaders break ground on St. Vincent de Paul expansion

 August 1, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 585
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — County and state leaders joined together Thursday morning to ceremonially break ground on the expansion and remodeling of St. Vincent de Paul, a nonprofit organization that provides food, shelter and clothing assistance to Talbot County residents in need.Though the project still needs a town permit to begin actual construction, stakeholders gathered to celebrate the progress the nonprofit has made toward growing its space and offerings.
The expansion and remodeling will increase the current 7,200-square-foot building on Canvasback Drive by 2,560 square feet. It will grow the organization's space for its food pantry, thrift store and advisory offices.
Alex Handy, president of the Easton Chapter of St. Vincent de Paul, spoke at the ceremony about the building's growth since he joined the organization.
"We have an incredible facility here," Handy said. "We're about to expand it even larger. And we have hundreds of volunteers. And all I can say (is) that God must've had a vision for where we were going, because I can tell you 22 years ago, we had no idea we'd be here today."
Willow Construction has designed a floor plan for the remodel, which attendees could look at on Thursday. St. Vincent de Paul Vice President John Plaskon says Willow Construction's general contracting service will cost about $898,000. Additional costs for engineering, plumbing and architecture may put the total mark over $1 million, Plaskon said.
To help with funding, St. Vincent de Paul is receiving a $625,000 grant from the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development. The department's assistant secretary, Carol Gilbert, attended Thursday's ceremony.
"You guys are doing something right, I'm sure," Gilbert said. "I'm really impressed by the volume of support of services that you give to your community."
Talbot County Council Member Keasha Haythe also talked to the crowd about the organization's importance to Talbot County, calling it an "exciting day" for the county. Last month, the council allocated $100,000 in American Rescue Plan Act funds for the nonprofit's expansion project.
Plaskon said the project may take around eight to nine months once a permit is issued and work commences. He hopes that all sections of St. Vincent de Paul will remain operational for as much time as possible during construction.
Part of the added-on space will include a new food pantry. Plaskon said that if they can move the pantry from its old area to the new one between its normal Tuesday and Saturday distribution days, no services will be affected.
The thrift store, though, will have to close down for a short period.
"The thrift store generates half the revenue that we need to operate. The other half comes from donations," Plaskon said. "We want to minimize how long it's shut down. But there's no way around it, it's going to have to happen, it's just a matter of how many weeks."
In addition to a larger space for the pantry, thrift store and meeting rooms, Plaskon said the site's parking situation will be improved. Plaskon said the "parking lot gets really jammed up" on Saturday mornings when the pantry distributes and the thrift store and boutique are open.
During the ceremony, Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) spoke to the crowd, emphasizing the current economic struggles residents are experiencing and thanking the St. Vincent de Paul volunteers.
"Being able to have this resource in the community is a life-saver for so many, so many that can't afford anything, and there's some that can afford some, but they still need some help," Mautz said. "And this has become just a critical part of the Mid-Shore community."

title: Easton Dedicates Trail to Former Mayor Willey
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Easton dedicates trail to former Mayor Willey

 July 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 418
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Bob Willey, Easton's former mayor, was honored Friday morning with a plaque describing his instrumental work in expanding Easton's Rails to Trails.The East-West section of the rail trail, which was dedicated to Willey, opened in April 2023. It connected the existing North-South trail to Port Street, the culmination of work by the town and the state.
Current Mayor Megan Cook said Willey carried the vision to expand the town's trails.
"Mayor Willey played an important role in turning the abandoned rail line into a thriving bike trail," Cook said. "Not only was he instrumental in the creation of the original North-South trail, but he recognized the benefits of extending the trail system throughout the community."
Town Manager Donald Richardson said expanding Rails to Trails became a priority of Willey's around 2016.
"It was a plan that had been sitting on a shelf for quite a long time," Richardson said. "And if any of you know Mayor Willey, he does not like plans to be sitting on the shelf. So we dusted it off, it already had some funding in place through Maryland State Highway Administration, and we went to work. By no means was this trail an easy endeavor."
Easton's North-South Rails to Trails path, completed in 1998, is nearly three miles long, connecting North Easton Park and Idlewild Park. It is a popular stretch for walkers, runners and bikers, as well as the newer East-West path.
There is still about half a mile left to be finished of the East-West expansion. Cook said once completed, the East-West section will add 1.5 miles of additional trail for residents. She emphasized that the Rails to Trails project helps public health, recreation and the economy.
Willey and his family attended the ceremony on South Hanson Street, with more than 60 town employees and residents in attendance. The former mayor celebrated his retirement this past winter after more than 30 years of service to the town, which included his time as mayor from 2003 to 2023.
"You get electeds like myself that come up with these hair-brained ideas of a rail trail and all the other stuff that needs to be done," Willey said Friday morning to the crowd. "Then the engineers worry about how it's going to fit in. And then we have a very talented public works crew, that really guys, I haven't seen anything you haven't been able to do and do very well."
The stone and plaque honoring Willey can be seen next to the East-West trail on South Hanson Street near Station Lane.

title: Easton Residents Look to Jumpstart Discussion of Soon-to-Be Vacant Lot
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Easton residents look to jumpstart discussion of soon-to-be vacant lot

 June 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 532
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Two Easton residents are seeking feedback on the prospects of a soon-to-be vacant one-acre lot on South Hanson St, which will be left when the Talbot County Health Department moves to a new location on Cadmus Lane later this month.Residents Greg Zimmerman and Joyce DeLaurentis created a survey to collect opinions of town residents on what the space could turn into. In the survey, it states that "with community support, there may be an opportunity for the Town of Easton to acquire this property" from the county.
Zimmerman, who has a background in business development and has lived in Easton for six years, feels this is a chance for community members to "lead on an issue rather than react to something later."
"The survey gives the community members a voice in the decision making process," Zimmerman said. "It'll also help the public officials understand community priorities."
The survey includes a list of multiple-choice questions measuring respondents' thoughts on potential uses for the space, such as a community pocket park, housing and small business startups. It also has open feedback questions for residents to fill out.
Thus far, Zimmerman has noticed many responses indicating residents would support a new community center, a multi-use park or a courtyard with small shops.Throughout his time in Easton, he also has noticed that the public's opinions are not always known, adding that the survey can "create a conduit between residents and public officials."
"When I have attended some of the meetings, I'm always wondering, 'What does the majority of the population feel about this?' Zimmerman said. "I don't know. And I don't really know if the town officials know either."
The property, which is owned by the county, is still operational and will be through most of June. County Manager Clay Stamp said the council will discuss the future prospects of the building and surrounding land "in the coming months."
"It's going to be a process that the County Council goes through," Stamp said. "I'm sure it's going to be a fairly open process. I'm sure they're going to be interested in getting input … That's going to be on their agenda in the coming months."
Stamp said the primary focus will be on moving the department into its new building, which will better house the department that has outgrown its current location.
"We're laser-focused on trying to get them into their new building, where they'll be able to better serve the community," Stamp said.
Talbot County Health Department spokesperson Justin Beall said a ribbon-cutting is set for the end of this month. The department's goal is to re-open at the new location by early July.
Results of the survey will be presented to Easton Town Council and Talbot County Council once county discussions concerning the property begin, according to Zimmerman. However, the survey will remain open for the foreseeable future to gather "as many responses as possible."
"We're not advocating for a specific outcome or on behalf of any interest group," Zimmerman said. "This is a grassroots effort to promote a process that encourages public input. Tell us what you think and we'll help amplify the collective voice of the community."
Residents can fill out the survey by emailing {span}eastoncommunitysurveys@gmail.com and filling out the anonymous form.
