title: Community Development Block Grant Projects Celebrated
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Community Development Block Grant projects celebrated

 May 22, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 573
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — On Friday morning, community members and partners gathered to celebrate two Community Development Block Grant recipients: Family Support Center and Chesapeake Multicultural Resource Center's Community and Commercial Kitchen Space.The Community Development Block Grant Program assists in strengthening Maryland's communities by funding projects generally falling into three types: housing, public facilities and economic development projects.
Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development Assistant Secretary Carol Gilbert was also present for the tour.
Family Support Center, a recipient of the grant, held an open house for its Early Head Start center. This center offers year-round comprehensive early care, education and family support to children from birth to 3 years of age, as well as their families.
Mary Kay Verdery, grants administrator for Talbot County, gave opening remarks outside of the center.
Verdery told community members the renovated space, including classrooms for up to 65 infants and toddlers, office space, kitchen and laundry facilities for the program, was possible due to the grant the center received.
Maria Maguire, health officer for the Talbot County Health Department, gave a speech noting the significance of Head Start programs for the community, including research showing that children enrolled in Early Head Start programs have better social-emotional language and cognitive development.
"All babies and toddlers need positive early learning experiences to foster their intellectual, social and emotional development and to lay the foundation for later school success," Maguire said. "Talbot County Health Department's Early Head Start program offers daily, year-round services to families and young children in Talbot County. It provides a comprehensive array of services, including mental health, education, housing, referrals and linkages to health services."
Community partners and members were given a tour of the center, where they were greeted by staff and children enjoying the care and benefits of the program.
Afterward, people enjoyed refreshments and baked goods before heading to the next stop on the grant project tour, the Chesapeake Multicultural Resource Center Kitchen and Community Space.
This full restoration of a brick warehouse provides the resource center with a much-needed space for small groups, class opportunities and community gatherings.
Adding a full commercial kitchen will allow small food businesses to expand their economic impact on the community and provide an appropriate space to create meals and food options for the community.
Talbot County Councilmember Pete Lesher, vice president of the council, shared the council's enthusiasm and gratitude for the community space and renovations made by the Chesapeake Multicultural Resource Center.
"This is an organization that has an important mission to a growing part of our population in this community," Lesher said. "Thanks to all of you who are already doing that. Thanks to the rest of you who have helped to make this project possible."
Attendees were welcomed to a feast of Pakistani food created by Veronica Guevara, who used the kitchen to help launch her catering business. People enjoyed a delicious array of lentils, fresh strawberry salad, seasoned chicken and fluffy naan. Guevara explained each dish and showed the best way for attendees to eat it.
Matthew Peters, director of Chesapeake Multicultural Resource Center, described this project as a "labor of love."
"So we've got that whole new growth take, and all really thanks to having a little bit more space to breathe and to get people together like this provided to the community," Peters said. "And hopefully, we keep finding more and more of our clients that are those secret gems so that I can create an amazing mission to share. So thank you all."

title: Ribbon Cut for St. Michaels Community Center Renovation
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Ribbon cut for St. Michaels Community Center renovation

 May 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 464
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — On Monday morning, many community members gathered for the ribbon cutting ceremony for an approximately $4.5 million renovation project to help serve the community of St. Michaels.The St. Michaels Community Center has been operating for over 30 years and has provided various supports through community pantries, events, senior and adult programs, youth programs and community gardens.
Lori Morris, the center's board chair, said she is excited to continue serving the community 2,500 meals a week and distributing groceries to neighbors in need.
"The outstanding center staff, both past and current, many of whom are here, not only provided ongoing input to the design and construction process but kept as many of our programs running as possible while we were out of the building," Morris said.
The approximately 5,700-square-foot building now houses a modern commercial kitchen, two classrooms, a technology center, a gallery and upstairs offices for staff. The main level of the building will serve multiple uses, including cafe seating, a space for speakers or performances and a place where people can pick up items from the center's community pantry.
The 800-square-foot commercial kitchen will serve the new Culinary Arts & Hospitality Workforce Development Program and the center's Community Cafe, which serves chef-made meals free of charge to anyone experiencing food insecurity.
The two classrooms on the other side of the gallery will be used primarily for children's programming but also for adult programs.
A technology center will have desks and computers for different organizations and nonprofits.
During the ribbon cutting ceremony, Morris praised her predecessor Langley Shook, former chair of the board of directors.
Morris said that Shook's leadership was the foundation of the project. The renovation was his vision, and he and his wife, Karen Shook, threw themselves into the fundraising, representing the committee before the town commissioners and the Historic District Committee.
Shook spoke about the work that many put into the project and thanked everyone involved in making the community center what it is today.
"The programs have been expanded, the staff has been strengthened," Shook said. "Our fundraising has made this platform possible and successful, and I think our greatest days are yet to come."
One of the speakers, State Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico), requested that all people who had attended St. Michaels Middle or High School come to stand with him as he presented the St. Michaels Community Center board of directors a citation in recognition for the work that was put into the community project.
"Because we do citations and we do projects, and it's part of the government doing something, but this is the will of the people," Mautz said. "This is what the town needed. This is what the town wanted, and by golly, this is what the town was going to get. So it's a great day for everybody."

title: Housing Commission, Developers Break Ground on Doverbrook Apartments
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Housing Commission, developers break ground on Doverbrook Apartments

 April 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 475
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Although some foundations have already been laid for the new Doverbrook Apartments in Easton, the Housing Commission of Talbot and project developer Pennrose hosted a ceremonial groundbreaking at the site off Dover Street Thursday morning."Try to ignore the fact that we've got building foundations in place," Pennrose Regional Vice President Patrick Stewart said, "because this is a groundbreaking."
Those in attendance for the event included Stephanie Staats, a field office director for the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development; Gregory Hare, assistant secretary for the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development; Easton Mayor Megan Cook and members of the Easton Town Council and Talbot County Council.
The $25 million redevelopment project is to replace the apartment complex's seven buildings — which had been around since the 1970s — with five new buildings. Project partners estimate apartment doors will open to new and returning residents in spring 2025.
Although there will be two fewer buildings when complete, the new complex will have 14 additional units, bringing the total to 64 units. There will be a mix of one-, two- and three-bedroom energy-efficient apartments, all of which will be a part of a housing choice voucher program known as Section 8 housing.
In December, Housing Commission of Talbot Executive Director Don Bibb said the project includes the creation of a playground in the center of the community and a facelift and addition to the Easton Housing Authority building located on the property.
At the groundbreaking, Bibb spoke about the importance of realizing the effects of this project, and not just talking about "the bricks and sticks."
"It's about the people," he said. "We can build buildings all the time. But giving the quality of life and living in an environment that's conducive to what people should have is what this is all about today."
Staats said the groundbreaking memorializes the beginning of a project that will create 14 new affordable units.
"Those 14 units symbolize 14 families who will now have safe, stable, desirable housing," she said, later adding that at the core, "that's what it's really all about."
According to a press release from Pennrose, the project is being funded through state and local proceeds, Low-Income Housing Tax Credits and a loan from M&T Bank. This funding includes a $350,000 grant from the Town of Easton and a $350,000 grant from Talbot County.
In mid-December, the apartment complex officially closed its doors to residents so the redevelopment project could begin. In a December interview, Bibb said residents of the previous apartments were relocated or given vouchers for other properties.
At the groundbreaking, Hare talked about the addition of units to the redevelopment project.
"But we're not just making more housing," he said. "We're making it better. ... When it's complete next year, Doverbrook will become a fantastic accomplishment and a great example of how public and private partnerships work to benefit the community."

The brightly-lit space can be used for more than sports, too — the community center has already received an inquiry for a wedding and plans to host a trade show, along with job and college fairs, Peper said.
Davis, Bowen & Friedel Inc, a local architectural and engineering firm, completed the architectural work before handing over the reins to Easton-based Willow Construction, who built the gymnasium.
Talbot County Council President Chuck Callahan commended all who were involved in making the new gym a reality, with special thanks to former council members, the county's park board and the Parks and Recreation department staff who were present Wednesday evening.
Callahan also thanked community members, from gym users to youth sports coaches, for their excitement about the project.

title: Long-Awaited Easton Dog Park Officially Opens
author: Natalie Jones
content:
Long-awaited Easton dog park officially opens

 January 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Local News 
 
 467
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Not even sub-freezing temperatures and bits of ice laying on the turf grass Thursday morning could stop over a dozen dogs — and their owners — from celebrating the grand opening of Easton's long-awaited dog park.Dogs of all ages, sizes and breeds were pulling at their leashes with energetic anticipation, waiting for the ceremonial red ribbon to be cut by Easton Mayor Megan Cook.
Thursday's ribbon cutting was a welcome sight for local dog owners and dog lovers, many of whom had waited years for the project to come to fruition.
A voiced interest in a dog park first came seven or eight years ago, said Rick Van Emburgh, the town engineer.
But in 2019, Easton residents David Ferraris and Noah Matten restarted the efforts, working with Rauch Inc., a local engineering firm, to prepare concept plans for a dog park near the downtown area.
And in fall 2020, the town received $7 million in bond funding, a majority of which was required to be allocated to parks.
Almost three years later, in March 2023, the Easton Town Council voted to fully fund the dog park on Brewers Lane and to add a restroom there, Van Emburgh said.
With the legislative work completed, construction of the dog park required a true group effort from the town's public works, parks and recreation, IT, buildings and finance departments.
Willow Construction, Easton Utilities and Chester River Landscaping also lent a hand with a number of other efforts to make the park a reality.
"I believe this is a wonderful example of teamwork," Van Emburgh said. "I believe it's a wonderful example of our community working together to build something beautiful for our town residents and our dogs."
Cook kept her comments brief, acknowledging a number of excitedly yapping dogs waiting to enter the park and play.
"I really want to give an extra shoutout to all the departments," the mayor said. "Pretty much every department in the Town of Easton played a role in getting this park up and running."
Once the ribbon was cut, the dogs were unleashed and off to play.
The new park, open dawn to dusk, includes two separate play areas for the pups based on weight, with a larger area allocated to dogs over 35 pounds.
A turf grass layer on top makes for a comfortable surface for dogs to run, jump and roll around, and underneath, there's an anti-microbial infill material and an irrigation system for cooling the turf.
It was clear that the dogs were excited as they raced in circles and made new friends, and the smiles on owners' faces told a similar story.
Easton resident Scott Cohen, who stopped by the park with his two Australian Shepherd-poodle mixes Scruffy, 4, and Casey, 3, said the dogs had a great time playing Thursday morning.
"I think it's a terrific add to the community," he said.

title: New Park Seeks to Welcome Public to Easton's Waterfront
author: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com
content:
New park seeks to welcome public to Easton's waterfront

 November 1, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com | Page: 1A | Section: News 
 
 704
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - Turning a former industrial site into a public park takes a lot of vision, according to officials from the Town of Easton.But as the Easton Point Park nears its completion, more than three years of planning are beginning to take shape."Before it was a dump and a highway you couldn't cross," said Kody Cario, project manager for the Town of Easton. "Now we are going to have a traffic light. We are going to have the trail. We are going to have the park, boat ramp. It is really incredible progress down here, and we are planting trees." The land used to take oil delivered by boat. Now, it is the home of Easton's only public waterfront park on the Tred Avon River, thanks to bond money secured by the town in 2020.The park spans 12 acres of waterfront at the end of Glenwood Avenue. Over 150 trees have been planted, and benches were installed to invite visitors to take in the surroundings. The new gate marks the main entrance at Flood Avenue.Easton Point Park is just one part of a series of projects costing the city $6.75 million in bond funding, which needed to be spent by the end of October, a goal the town was confident they would meet as the month drew to a close.The projects under the bond also included improvements to the Rails to Trails, the North Easton Sports Complex, access to John Ford Park, underground infrastructure for Port Street and several land acquisitions, among others."We were able to do a lot of different things. So there is everything from a new skate park to new field lights for the existing soccer, lacrosse and football. There is a new dog park down Brewers Lane behind the farmer's market. There is Rail to Trails work," said Town Engineer Rick Van Emburgh.Though the Easton Point Park was been designed to make the town's waterfront more visitor-friendly, it has not completely lost touch with its roots.Much of the project involved taking old industrial buildings down as part of the bond, said Easton Mayor Megan Cook, but not all of the existing structures were demolished."There is the partnership with Phillips Wharf," Cook said. "So originally in the park design, that building was supposed to come down, but an opportunity to have them here and keep the building, it kind of fell in our laps a few years ago." "Phillips, for one, wanted to come closer towards Easton, where the schools are. They are a water-focused conservation nonprofit that has students." Along with the conservation organization, the new park is home to metal signs displaying environmental messages, courtesy of Jessica Hammond, a senior at Gunston School."We had a Girl Scout project.She just put up signs for a gold award. We worked with her. It is like an Eagle Scout," said Van Emburgh.Down the road, the park will feature a boat ramp that is based on the Town of Newcomb's dual boat access model. There will be more parking here than the boat ramp at Easton Point, officials said.The town is also going to stabilize the shore further with a living shoreline."A living shoreline uses natural marsh grasses to filter water quality - not only the existing water but water runoff. So it filters nutrients and pollutants in two ways then stabilizes the shoreline. It creates habitat," said Cario.Surveying the park's progress, the town officials couldn't help but comment on how much the site had changed in just a few years."So we are going from this to a park. Open space," said Easton Mayor Megan Cook, pointing to a before and after map of the project.She made a point of thanking all the engineers and skilled labor that helped to build it all."This is one of the things we are doing good for the environment and all of that is to the (Town) Council's credit for that as well," said Cario.

Standing in front Easton's only waterfront public access is Kody Curio, project manager for the Town of Easton; Rick Van Emburgh, town engineer; and Easton Mayor Megan Cook.

Informal committee to plan beautification of 'eyesore'

 October 13, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 OXFORD - Following direction from a Commissioners of Oxford meeting on Tuesday, a resident has moved forward with creating an informal committee to beautify the area surrounding the water treatment facility on Jl Thompson Drive.The committee will formulate a plan to be brought to the Commissioners of Oxford for consideration.Nick Papson, the resident tasked with creating the informal committee, submitted a petition, signed by more than 180 residents, to the town to "accelerate a beautification campaign along the fence surrounding the water treatment facility" on Jl Thompson Drive."For years, this has been an eyesore, which those of us who live nearby and pass daily have been asked to tolerate as higher priority facility and beautification projects have taken place," the petition said, which Commission President Tom Costigan read at the meeting.Since the meeting, Papson said he has assembled a committee of six residents.He said the committee will meet next week to begin the process of putting together a plan and getting quotes for potential projects. title: Talbot County Passes DAF Restrictions
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot County passes DAF restrictions

 July 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 303
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Talbot County Council passed new regulations on food processing residuals Tuesday.County leaders said the approved legislation helps Talbot fall in line with neighboring counties on restricting the residuals, also referred to as dissolved air flotation, or DAF, materials.
The materials often come in the form of animal waste from food processing, which then can be spread as fertilizer. State rules took effect last summer cracking down on DAF residuals, but some counties have since enacted local legislation to quell further resident concerns.
Jurisdictions like Caroline County saw tense debate over the matter. Many Caroline County residents complained of noxious odors from operations storing food processing residuals in open-top storage containers. Last year, Caroline County banned the open-top method.
Similarly, Talbot's legislation requires closed-top storage of food processing residuals. In addition to the open-top storage ban, Talbot's regulations require the storage applicant to:
Receive site plan approval from the county.Obtain an approved nutrient management plan from the state.Remain at least 500 feet from any residential property lines. If all affected property owners consent to a setback reduction, it can be decreased as far as 200 feet.
"We certainly don't want to be the only jurisdiction on the Shore that neglects to regulate this material," County Council Vice President Pete Lesher said.
Lesher, Council President Chuck Callahan and council members Lynn Mielke and Dave Stepp voted in favor of the legislation. Keasha Haythe, who was absent from Tuesday's meeting, did not vote.
Talbot's Planning Commission and planning officers Brennan Tarleton and Bryce Yelton ironed out the specifics of the regulations since it was drafted last year. Lesher thanked them for their efforts.
"This is one of the more technical issues that we've dealt with," Lesher said, "and I just want to express my appreciation for the staff and for the Planning Commission in working out the details of this."

title: Planning Commission Recommends Against Seafood Odor Amendment
author: Konner Metz
content:
Planning Commission Recommends Against Seafood Odor Amendment

 May 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 613
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Planning Commission Thursday provided an unfavorable recommendation on a recently proposed amendment to a seafood odor ordinance.The ordinance, which came after a multi-year push from Ward 4 residents, aims to address complaints of odor emanating from Chesapeake Brand Seafood, a facility located on Maryland Avenue near many homes. The legislation was passed in December, but a final resolution hasn't been reached.
The business recently requested an amendment to the already-approved ordinance, citing that industry experts consider legislation's requirements unachievable.
It requires the business to install odor control technology so "that no odor ... can be detected outside the building on the same property or on adjacent properties or public rights-of-way." The deadline to install is July 1.
Owner Mitch Hughes, attorney Zach Smith and the vendor of an odor control system explained Thursday that the ordinance isn't feasible as written.
Their amendment proposes a new standard — that engineers or industry experts confirm odor control equipment uses "best control technologies and methods designed to mitigate odor before it leaves a building."
Commission members agreed the proposed change was too vague. But they also acknowledged that the original ordinance doesn't create a clear path to compliance.
"I feel like we're trying to put a round peg in a square hole here," member Tom Klein said.
Chairperson Philip Toussaint said the business, which was legally permitted to operate by the town beginning in 2019, should've never been OK'd at that site.
"That's tough to hear when we, again, followed the town zoning codes," Smith said. "It's tough to hear that position from the Planning Commission."
Smith said the amendment is not an attempt by Hughes to avoid addressing the odor complaints. Hughes noted he's fully willing to install the odor control system, but he doesn't want to foot the cost if his efforts won't meet the ordinance.
Smith said if the "no odor" requirement isn't changed, it leaves only two options: Chesapeake Brand goes out of business or involves the town in "some sort of protracted legal battle."
Commission members, along with some residents, criticized the business for proposing the amendment so soon before the July 1 deadline.
"If we had another month or two, it could've been doable," said William Ryall, the commission's chair pro tem.
The commission voted 4-0 to advise the Town Council to reject the amendment. But in that same motion, the commission directed the council to incorporate an "enforceable standard" into the already-approved legislation. Despite much discussion Thursday, it's not yet clear exactly what that standard might be.
The Town Council will still review the proposed amendment, likely considering the commission's advice to find a middle ground on a standard that can be met and enforced.
PUBLIC INPUT
Public comment was mixed Thursday, with many of the residents affected by the odor in attendance to oppose Chesapeake Brand's amendment. Some suggested alternative ways to reach a compromise.
Shawn Nuthall said the amended wording has "no teeth, no data, no standards."
"We've been going through this for years and years and years," he said. "It's way, way too long. They should've done something before now."
Others, including some fellow business owners and seafood processors, spoke in support of Hughes and Chesapeake Brand Seafood.
"Mitch got a permit," Donna Bramble said. "He did not hide what kind of business he was having. He told you what it was going to be. It's a signed, legal document, and now the town is trying to take that away."
Joe Spurry, owner of Chesapeake Landing Seafood in St. Michaels, said Hughes has good intent and that the town should be wary of not driving the business away.
"He started a business that nobody starts," Spurry said. "Processing seafood is a dying business. I'm one of the last in Talbot County. He's the newest."

title: Eastern Shore Legislators Push for Gov. Moore to Veto Solar Bill
author: Konner Metz
content:
Eastern Shore legislators push for Gov. Moore to veto solar bill

 May 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 626
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Eastern Shore legislators, House Republicans and agricultural advocacy groups in Maryland are making one last effort to nix controversial solar energy legislation by asking for a veto from Gov. Wes Moore.Senate Bill 931, the Renewable Energy Certainty Act, was passed by the General Assembly in April. It aims to increase the state's solar generation by streamlining the regulatory process for solar projects. Fencing, setback and vegetation requirements would be standardized.
House Republicans and the Eastern Shore Delegation both wrote letters to the governor urging him to veto the bill. While Moore (D) hasn't publicly signaled whether or not he's considering a veto, some believe it could be in play given he hasn't yet signed the legislation.
"I've heard it is possible," said Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) in an interview Wednesday. "I'm hopeful that he would see the opportunity and the wisdom and just say, 'No, not yet.'"
Qualms with the solar legislation largely relate to a reduction in the control local governments would have over solar project approvals, and the increase in Public Service Commission authority.
The legislation outlines a cap on how much land the Maryland Public Service Commission can grant to solar projects in each county — 5% of land designated for agriculture and forests.
Republicans attempted but failed during session to lower that cap.
Del. Chris Adams (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) said Thursday that Eastern Shore counties could have thousands of acres up for solar development even with the 5% cap.
At a legislative wrap-up discussion in Easton Wednesday, Mautz said solar interests came into Annapolis and "cleared the decks."
"They wanted to set up their own regulatory system, they wanted to set up their own siting system," he said. "And they wanted to run this through the Public Service Commission."
"It puts an X on the Eastern Shore," Mautz added. "We are the prime target for solar investment."
The Chesapeake Climate Action Network, an environmental nonprofit that's one of the bill's many advocate groups, encouraged supporters to contact Moore's office and lobby for no veto. Brittany Baker, the organization's Maryland director, said rumors of a veto were floating.
"The rumor mill was churning, and no one had a concrete answer here or there," Baker said.
Baker said in addition to streamlining processes that otherwise vary greatly across the state, the bill is set to codify best practices. And it could help local farmers who are looking to remain economically viable, she said.
"It provides another way for people to be able to stay on their farms and make revenue," Baker said.
PUSH TO VETO
The governor's office didn't comment specifically on whether Moore is considering a veto, but did provide a statement.
"As Governor Moore reviews the hundreds of bills put forward this session, he will continue to work with the State Legislature, local leaders, and all partners involved to ensure that we are signing legislation that will make Maryland safer, more affordable, more competitive, and the state that serves," the statement read.
Baker said despite rumors, the Chesapeake Climate Action Network believes Senate Bill 931 will become law.
"We're pretty sure at this point that the governor will not be vetoing this bill," she said.
Mautz acknowledged a veto is a tricky, party-line situation. He said it would be messy, but "less messy" than what happens down the line if the bill becomes law.
"For the governor to veto it, he's going to cross his own party," Mautz said. "He's going to cross some of his own advocates. It's going to be extremely controversial."
Adams acknowledged that vetoes are rare. But he said the bill not yet being signed may signal "at the minimum, that the governor's paying attention."
If Moore doesn't sign the Renewable Energy Certainty Act by May 27, it automatically becomes law. The governor's next slate of bill signings is scheduled for May 20.

title: Talbot Planning Commission Sends DAF Legislation to County Council
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot Planning Commission sends DAF legislation to County Council

 April 4, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 380
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Talbot County Council will soon be considering new restrictions on the storage of food processing residuals.Wednesday, the Talbot County Planning Commission unanimously voted to send a piece of legislation up to the council, deeming it consistent with the county's comprehensive plan.
The legislation aims to help Talbot County fall in line with neighboring counties on restricting the residuals, which are animal waste from food processing that are often applied to farmland as fertilizer.
Under state law, the residuals cannot be applied to land between Dec. 15 and March 1, requiring them to be stored during the winter months.
Last year, Caroline County restricted storage of food processing residuals, often referred to as dissolved air flotation, or DAF, residuals. It came amid significant resident complaints of the noxious odors and bugs that stemmed from farming operations keeping the product in open storage tanks.
Talbot's legislation would ban open-top storage of DAF or food processing residuals. Closed-top storage would be permitted provided it follows the following conditions, among others:
The storage applicant receives site plan approval from the county.The applicant has an approved nutrient management plan from the state.The applicant has at least a 500-foot setback from residential properties, or at least a 200-foot setback if all affected property owners consent.The applicant applies the materials on the same property where they are being stored.The applicant stores and applies the materials in a permitted zoning district.
The legislation would not ban storage of food processing residuals in a temporary storage unit — such as a "mobile, closed container" — near where they are being applied. Such temporary storage would be capped at 90 days.
Before the commission approved the legislation, the body set forth a few minor conditions to be amended.
"The one thing that we do want to make sure is that we exempt food processing residuals that are used for livestock feed," commission member Chip Councell said.
Bryce Yelton, assistant planning officer, said that would be an easy amendment to make, simply by adjusting the definition for food processing residuals in the legislation.
Councell added that the county discussed the DAF legislation with the Talbot County Farm Bureau last August. The farm bureau was supportive, he said.
While the commission is recommending approval to the County Council, the bill will still require a council vote to be enacted.

title: Easton Passes Ordinance to Mitigate Seafood Processing Odors
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Easton passes ordinance to mitigate seafood processing odors

 December 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 577
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Easton Town Council approved an ordinance Monday that aims to crack down on odors from seafood processors by requiring the installment of odor control technology.In a 4-0 vote, the town passed Ordinance 835, which was drafted following resident concerns about the odor emanating from Chesapeake Brand Seafood on Maryland Avenue.
Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis was outspoken Monday evening about bringing his constituents relief from the odors they smell during crab season.
"Constituents in the neighborhood should not have to go through another season of having to endure that kind of odor," Davis said. "And if the business is friendly and working with the community, something of this nature should have been worked out prior to now."
The ordinance, which will go into effect later this month, requires that seafood processing operations install odor control technology "in such a manner that no odor from any product or by-product can be detected outside the building on the same property or on adjacent properties or public rights-of-way."
Zach Smith, an attorney representing Chesapeake Brand Seafood, said the business' concerns center the spray application system it plans to install — which will cost around $20,000 and may not fulfill the town's new requirements of "no odor" being detectable.
"We're confident it will address the issue, at least to some extent," Smith said. "But we're not confident, not necessarily confident, it'll meet that standard."
Smith requested a compromise, stating he thinks the ordinance should not retroactively apply to "existing, lawful seafood processing uses" such as his client. He submitted proposed revisions to the ordinance that were read aloud Monday evening.
Following a lengthy council discussion, Ward 2 Councilmember Don Abbatiello said he was ready to pass the ordinance as written, without Smith's proposed changes. Council President Frank Gunsallus agreed those changes were "overly specific."
Abatiello made a motion to approve the ordinance, which was seconded by Ward 1 Councilmember Maureen Curry. Gunsallus and Davis joined in voting yes. Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery was absent from Monday's meeting.
TIMELINE DEBATEIn the approved ordinance, businesses must comply with odor control and storage requirements by July 1, 2025. Prior to Monday, the compliance date on the draft ordinance was Jan. 1, 2026. The change stirred discussion Monday evening.
Davis pushed for that date to be even sooner — Jan. 1, 2025 — though he was outnumbered by Gunsallus, Abatiello, and Curry, who all voted in favor of amending the ordinance to the July date.
Curry maintained that it's important the town be fair to the business since it's planning to pay up for the new odor control system to address the problem.
Town Attorney Sharon VanEmburgh said she had legal concerns about shortening the period, saying that "even January (2026)" is pushing it.
"They've had time to comply," Davis said.
"But they didn't have this ordinance," VanEmburgh responded. "The ordinance is what would be challenged."
"I mean the worst case scenario is that we go to court, and is that the end result? Then so be it," said Davis. " … If you say comply by 2026, just think about this for a moment. The same people who live in Ward 4 have to suffer through this this year again until January 2026."
"I have to stand on what I believe in, and I believe that they've already had enough time to do it," Davis later stated. "It seems to me that we're more worried about going to court than listening to the people. And I think we should listen to the people."

title: Oxford Commission Approves Changes to Floodplain Management
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Oxford commission approves changes to floodplain management

 October 24, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 333
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — The Commissioners of Oxford approved an ordinance to amend the town's floodplain management ordinance. The changes would loosen requirements for residents seeking to make significant improvements to buildings.Commission President Norm Bell opened the public hearing for Ordinance 2416 and shared additional information on the changes made.
Previously for buildings in Oxford, owners were required to track and calculate the costs of any construction made since July 1, 2013 prior to making changes to the structures.
If all those improvement costs equal or exceed 50% of the market value of a building prior to the start of the construction, it would require the building to be up to code and raised in elevation.
The amended ordinance revises the definition of "substantial improvement," removing the 2013 date and substituting "the previous five (5) years."
Bell said the revision allows for a lean way for owners to make improvements on their buildings.
"What this is saying is we're only going to go back five years, or 1,825 days," Bell said. "So it's shortening the period that you can take a look at the 50% requirement. It's liberalizing it."
An additional change in the ordinance was the revision of the "agreement to submit an elevation certificate."
An elevation certificate is a form on which applicants for a permit to construct a building or structure show compliance with floodplain management legislation.
Previously people looking to make substantial improvements to buildings would need to submit an elevation certificate with a building permit application upon the construction of the foundation and prior to further vertical construction; and prior to the final inspection and moving in.
The revision removes the requirement of submitting the form prior to placement of the foundation and further vertical construction.
According to Bell, the changes would make it cheaper for owners to have engineers/surveyors certify that the floor of buildings seeking improvements is above the mean high water mark and it lowers costs of the certification by a "couple of hundred dollars."
After answering clarifying questions from the public, commissioners unanimously approved the ordinance.

title: Talbot County Looks into Restrictions on Food Processing Residuals
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Talbot County looks into restrictions on food processing residuals

 September 27, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 370
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Restrictions on the storage of food processing residuals are in the works for Talbot County.The county's Planning Commission and County Council held a preliminary work session Tuesday to discuss regulations for the residuals, which are animal waste from the food processing process.
Earlier this month, Caroline County passed a bill to restrict the storage of the residuals, which are often referred to as dissolved air flotation, or DAF, residuals. It came amid significant resident complaints of the noxious odors and bugs that stemmed from farming operations keeping the product in storage tanks.
Talbot County is looking to the neighboring county and hoping to be proactive.
"We think we need to get ahead of it," Planning Commission Vice Chairman Chip Councell said. He noted that Caroline and Wicomico counties were "behind the eight ball" in enacting legislation.
Councell said he met with the Talbot County Farm Bureau regarding potential restrictions.
"I think they would like to see some restrictions put on it, one being that any type of food residuals storage would have to be enclosed, so it couldn't be open-air," Councell said. "The storage of it would have to be used in that agricultural operation. A farmer couldn't store it for everybody in the neighborhood. He could store it for his operation only, so there wouldn't be commercial storage."
Councell clarified the county would focus on the storage of the residuals, not the land application. State legislation that went into effect July 1 created a formal permitting process for the usage of food processing residuals.
"There's a few bad actors out there that, frankly, I think see profit potential with handling the material," said Alan Girard, advocacy director at the Chesapeake Bay Foundation, during Tuesday's meeting.
While Wicomico County banned the storage of residuals, temporary storage for 45 days is allowed. In Caroline County, storage is allowed once a permit is acquired, as long as the storage tank has a closed top.
Councell said the 45-day allowance may be adjusted once the legislation begins to be drafted.
"I think 45 days might be a little bit tight," Councell said.
At the end of the work session, Planning and Zoning Director Brennan Tarleton said discussion of potential DAF legislation will be added to the Planning Commission's agenda in November.

title: Solar Energy Discussed at MACo Summer Conference
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Solar energy discussed at MACo Summer Conference

 August 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 543
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OCEAN CITY — Solar energy was one topic of discussion that captured the attention of multiple Mid-Shore counties at the Maryland Association of Counties Summer Conference.Caroline County Commission President Travis Breeding said solar energy came up a lot at the four-day conference, which went from Aug. 14 to Aug. 17 in Ocean City. Breeding said there are elected officials from different Maryland counties who feel that solar lobbyists are pushing the state to take away local authority when it comes to where solar energy system sites can go and how close those sites can be from roads and neighboring structures.
Caroline County currently has a 2,000-acre cap on solar projects. Once that limit is reached, the county will stop permitting new solar energy system projects on county land, Breeding said.
Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer said his fellow council member Ricky Travers asked about solar site acreage caps in a MACo session with the Maryland Public Service Commission. Specifically, Travers asked about how the commission feels about these caps.
Pfeffer said that after the session, the Dorchester County Council members had a conversation with Public Service Commissioner Kumar Barve, and the council was able to explain its concerns about increasing solar sites in the county. Pfeffer said the only part of the county that can host these sites is the north part of the county, and that is where the council hopes to grow the county's tax base.
"They were very interested and didn't realize some of the demographics and logistics of Dorchester County," Pfeffer said about the Public Service Commission. "So I'm hoping that is successful for us, they'll take a look at it and they won't establish any legislation that's one-size-fits-all."
Talbot County Council Vice President Pete Lesher called the conference one of the best he's been to. He said it ran smoothly and was well put together.
Breeding said that MACo's summer and winter conferences give Maryland counties an opportunity to get together, discuss and "try to come up with a unified message."
"It was a good conference," Breeding said. "We got to talk to all of our partners in other counties, bounce ideas off of them, discuss problems and issues that we're all facing and kind of brainstorm on how to resolve those issues."
Pfeffer, who is the secretary of MACo this year, said that all counties have problems.
Pfeffer said the opportunity to discuss these common problems, no matter how many zeros come after them, can benefit each county.
Breeding said he is taking some ideas on solar power back home to Caroline County this year. He talked about the systems that Talbot and Queen Anne's counties have in place, including Talbot County's point system that is used to help preserve prime farmland for farming and determine where solar sites can go.
Lesher said he didn't attend the solar session at MACo, but said the Talbot County Council tackled legislation dealing with solar energy sites last year when it put the point system in place.
"Which I think is model legislation for other rural jurisdictions," he said. "Right now we're in the testing period for this. Will this hold up? Will this have the desired impact of preserving farmland and channeling solar toward areas where we have more marginal soils that are not the highest priority for cropland?"

title: Town Passes Ordinance Cracking Down on Illicit Discharges
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Town passes ordinance cracking down on illicit discharges

 July 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 512
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — An ordinance that will crack down on the dumping and spillage of certain discharges in Easton is set to take effect in early August.The Easton Town Council unanimously passed an illicit discharge ordinance on Monday following discussions of the item at three public meetings. Town Engineer Rick Van Emburgh worked to put the ordinance together, emphasizing that the only discharge that should end up in the street is rainwater.
"At the end of the day, the only thing allowed in the stormwater system is rainwater, so we need to do our best to keep everything else out," Van Emburgh said.
Due to EPA requirements that were passed down to the Maryland Department of the Environment, the town is required to restrict certain discharges. The restrictions come since Easton is in its sixth year of the Municipal Separate Storm Sewer System program — a program that the state requires the town to follow.
The ordinance authorizes the town to perform inspections at sites where it has "reasonable cause" that an illicit discharge violation is occurring. The town may also fine violators.
However, Van Emburgh stated that the main goal is to make residents aware of the law and how to achieve "best practices" when disposing of substances.
"We're not going to come out and fine anybody," Van Emburgh said at the meeting. "We're just going to come out, and we'll have flyers."
Matt Pluta, the Choptank riverkeeper for ShoreRivers, expressed support for the Municipal Separate Storm Sewer System program. Pluta said foreign material entering the stormwater system negatively impacts the Chesapeake Bay and local waterways. Grease from restaurants and concrete were two materials Pluta pointed out as harmful.
"Those storm drains along the street, those aren't treated," Pluta said. "The water that goes in there isn't treated, it's just a direct conveyance to our local waterways. Here in Easton, that waterway is the Tred Avon River right here at Easton Point."
PROHIBITED DISCHARGESThe town engineer noted some specific examples during Monday's Town Council meeting. Van Emburgh said the town is asking for leaves to be placed "behind the curb" for the public works crew to pick up. He also addressed the example of changing oil.
"We're not going to be out looking for people changing the oil in their cars," Van Emburgh said. "We're looking to make sure it's done in a responsible way, and if there is an accident, we use what's available to us to clean it up."
Some other prohibited discharges outlined in the ordinance include swimming pool water with chlorine levels beyond state regulations, new or used petroleum products, industrial waste and septic tank waste.
Chemicals put down drains in houses are fine, since those go to the sanitary sewer line and a wastewater treatment facility, Van Emburgh clarified at a previous Town Council meeting.
Exempt discharges include discharges from firefighting, irrigation water, dechlorinated swimming pool water in line with state regulations and residential car washing, among others.
While commercial car washers are not exempt, Van Emburgh said that car washing companies in town have proper recycling methods that will fall in line with the requirements of the ordinance.

Easton Town Council discusses discharge ordinance

 June 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News

 A public hearing on an ordinance to update town code regarding illicit discharges brought worries and questions from the Easton Town Council Monday.Town Engineer Rick Van Emburgh discussed the ordinance, which stems from state requirements by the MS4 storm sewer system program.
"What it says is that anything that's not stormwater, rainwater runoff cannot enter into our storm drain system," Van Emburgh said. "This (ordinance) will allow us the enforcement if those are put into our storm drain system."
"What happens when I power wash my house?" Ward 1 Council Member Maureen Curry asked.
Van Emburgh said while there are some exceptions, he would check back on power washing. He added that commercial car washing does not fall under the exceptions.
"Even if we have to approve it, I think somehow before we start enforcing it, we need to make the whole town aware of what's going on," Ward 4 Council Member the Rev. Elmer Davis said.
Van Emburgh said the ordinance is very similar to what the city of Salisbury used a few years back. He said he will contact the state "to see how much we're able to modify the ordinance."
ANNEXATION UPDATE
At its June 3 meeting, council members pushed off a vote for the annexation of land on the east side of Ocean Gateway for a potential affordable multifamily housing development project. It includes about 17 acres of Talbot County land that the town would annex.
One of the council's main hopes was to ensure the annexation agreement included as much affordable housing as possible. Curry asked June 3 if the original 25% guaranteed affordable housing could be increased to around 50%.
"I did speak with my client, and they are certainly agreeable to that," said Zach Smith on behalf of Corrigan & Trippe Ventures at the June 17 meeting. "And again that would be the minimum required. And as we discussed last meeting, the annexation agreement obligates us to pursue in good faith and diligently, a (planned unit development) project that proposes 100% affordable."
The proposed annexation will appear on the council's agenda for its July 1 meeting.
HOSPITAL PROGRESS
Council members unanimously passed a resolution to amend a development rights and responsibilities agreement for a new UM Shore Regional Health medical center, another step towards beginning work on a hospital that's planned to be built off Longwoods Road in Easton.
Shore Regional Health attorney Ryan Showalter thanked the town for its support for the hospital. The county also passed the development rights and responsibilities agreement amendment last week.
"This is an important project (and it) needs to get done," Ward 2 Council Member Don Abbatiello said.

title: Trappe Sends Letter to MDE Calling for Rejection of Resolution 338
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Trappe sends letter to MDE calling for rejection of Resolution 338

 June 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 622
 Words 

 Read News Document

 TRAPPE — The Town of Trappe is calling for the Maryland Department of the Environment to reject Resolution 338.In a letter, the town, along with Trappe East Holdings Business Trust, called on MDE to "disapprove" of the Comprehensive Water and Sewerage Plan amendment proposed by the resolution.
It took the Talbot County Council upwards of a year to approve the measure, which addresses specific issues raised by MDE dealing with the number of equivalent dwelling units in the different phases of the housing development's construction.
Resolution 338, which was approved in April, amends the Talbot County Comprehensive Water and Sewer Plan to be consistent with provisions of Lakeside's wastewater discharge permit and requires an amendment to the comprehensive plan for any future expansion of the new Lakeside Wastewater Treatment Plant.
In the letter, Resolution 338 is described as intended by Talbot County to establish a "county growth control mechanism specific to a single development project located entirely within the town."
The resolution has been sent to MDE for its review, and MDE will make the final decision to approve, edit or deny the resolution.
The Issues
Described as the most significant problem with Resolution 338 in the letter is Table 1, specifying the yearly average flow to be 100,000 gallons per day, and a footnote.
Table 1 states that expansion of the plant will require an amendment, including a certification by the Talbot County Planning Commission that the amendment is consistent with the Talbot County Comprehensive Plan.
The letter's writers said Talbot County's adoption of this language is premised upon a "fundamental misunderstanding of the role and authority of the Talbot County Council."
The letter's writers stated the incorporation of Table 1 infringes on MDE's exclusive authority to regulate groundwater discharge in the state.
Additionally, Resolution 338 states the first 100,000-gallon phase of the plant "will allow approximately 400 residential units to be built." The letter sent to MDE states the 100,000 gallons of capacity in the first phase of the plant will serve more than 400 homes.
In the eyes of the town and developer, it will "constitute an enforceable restriction on the number of homes that can be connected to the (wastewater treatment plant), regardless of actual flows."
The writers stated that MDE should reject this phrase in Resolution 338 because it creates a restriction that is "unduly burdensome on the town, which has the authority to oversee the operation and allocation of capacity within its municipal system."
The letter includes several exhibits, including copies of letters of objections submitted to the Talbot County Council, as well as a detailed historical account of the decisions made within the last 20 years of this development project, titled "Prior County Attempt to Control Timing of Town Infrastructure for Lakeside."
Further down in the letter, the county's envisioned dual approval process was criticized as "practically and legally flawed."
The timeline for a future expansion of the plant will likely take 2.5 to 4 years, according to Trappe and Lakeside's attorneys. Adding eight to 12 months for Talbot County to determine whether it is an "appropriate" time for the town to continue implementing its Comprehensive Plan would require the town to initiate the Comprehensive Water and Sewer Plan amendment four to five years before expanded treatment capacity.
Toward the end of the letter, the writers stated that if MDE is inclined to approve any portion of Resolution 338, "at a minimum, the 100,000 gallons per day daily capacity limit and the footnote requiring a (comprehensive water and sewer plan) amendment for each expansion of the Lakeside (wastewater treatment plant) should be deleted."
However, they also stated that if MDE were to "approve Resolution 338, this would establish a precedent that could result in unintended consequences, including erosion of MDE's authority to regulate the timing, scope and conditions of discharge permits."

title: Caroline Commissioners Discuss Landfill, Solar Batteries
author: Tom McCall
content:
Caroline commissioners discuss landfill, solar batteries

 May 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Life 
 
 568
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — At their May 7 meeting, the Caroline County Commissioners extended a moratorium on solar array batteries and finalized an agreement to retain the regional landfill for another 18 years.Caroline County has agreed to 2042 being the end of life for its landfill. Mid-shore II Regional Landfill is governed by a four-county agreement between Queen Anne's, Kent, Talbot and Caroline counties.
In the late 1980s, due to new federal regulations, the counties had to close their landfills and replace them with new landfills. In response to this new regulation, Talbot, Caroline and Queen Anne's counties engaged with MES to form a partnership where each county would take turns hosting a landfill for a 20-year term. Kent County later joined that partnership.
Caroline County is hosting the current landfill and, under the original arrangement, would be off the hook at the end of 2030 when Queen Anne's County would take over the responsibility of host. However, the partnering counties have agreed to allow the landfill to stay in Caroline County for 12 years longer than initially planned.
Dan Fox, deputy administrator, said the county will receive a revenue increase of around $12.3 million over the duration of the extended agreement. The counties agreed on a $3 per ton post fee until 2030. In 2031 it will rise to $6.
"That is a big number as far as our budget," Fox said.
Commissioner Larry Porter said the increased revenue will be helpful as he looks to the future of Caroline County's finances.
"The tipping point is knowing what is coming down the road to the county from a financial standpoint. The Blueprint numbers for education, the numbers for the budget projections that will start this fiscal year from the state," Porter said. "It has been our goal to have maintained property tax rates. We have done this for eight years and are going to do it again this year. Beyond that we cannot control the additional things that will be mandated by the state of Maryland. To turn away the opportunity to generate revenue without raising property tax rate is something we have to consider."
The next action agenda item was solar energy batteries and the commissioners' belief that they are dangerous.
The commissioners extended a moratorium on the batteries until March 31, 2025. Explaining this decision, they said that the local fire departments and first responders are not equipped and staffed to safely deal with these energy storage systems were they to catch on fire.
"When the electric is generated from the solar panels, if it is not distributed to the grid, it is stored in batteries that are then stored in, like, large storage containers," Porter said. "How would it be addressed if those storage facilities were malfunctioning and caught on fire?"
He said the moratorium will remain in place until these batteries can safely be put in place.
During public comments, James Baker brought up the issue of what to do with a solar energy battery at the end of its 20 year life cycle. He said he thought it would cost taxpayers.
At the May 7 meeting, the commissioners also made two proclamations. The first was to Ken Eaton and Mark Kerzener, who represented the Mid-Shore chapter of A Brotherhood Against Totalitarian Enactments of Maryland. The commissioners proclaimed May a month for motorcycle safety and awareness.
The other proclamation went to Derek Simmons, superintendent of Caroline County Public Schools. It was a proclamation for teacher appreciation month.

title: Caroline Commissioners Hear Options for Landfill After 2030
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Caroline commissioners hear options for landfill after 2030

 April 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 785
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Caroline County could remain the host of the regional landfill for 12 years longer than originally planned.At a Caroline County Commissioners meeting Tuesday morning, Queen Anne's County Administrator Todd Mohn, CPA and Queen Anne's County Consultant Joe Zimmerman and Queen Anne's County Commissioner James Moran came to speak about the possibility of using the Mid-Shore II Regional Landfill in Ridgely through 2042 rather than building a new landfill in Queen Anne's County for 2031.
During their presentation, Mohn said Maryland Environmental Service has been working with county administrators to evaluate the future of Mid-Shore II, and it has concluded that the landfill could "easily provide service" to the citizens of the region through approximately 2042.
The Mid-Shore II landfill, which was opened in 2011, provides services to Talbot, Caroline, Queen Anne's and Kent counties.
Mohn explained that in the late 1980s, due to new federal regulations, the counties had to close their landfills and and replace them with new landfills. In response to this new regulation, Talbot, Caroline and Queen Anne's counties engaged with MES to form a partnership where each county would take turns hosting a landfill for a 20-year term. Kent County later joined that partnership.
Caroline County is hosting the current landfill and, under the original arrangement, would be off the hook at the end of 2030 when Queen Anne's County would take over the responsibility of host. However, if the partnering counties agreed, they could instead extend the lifetime of Caroline County's landfill.
During the presentation, Mohn listed reasons why Queen Anne's County feels this option makes sense. For Caroline County, he said that this option would provide economic stability for Ridgely businesses and that the county would get a host fee for the extension of service.
He said the option would also maximize the value of public infrastructure, defer liability for debt to construct a new landfill, maintain shorter haul routes for Talbot County and avoid the cost of a transfer operation.
Moran said landfills are at a premium.
"We want to maximize that," he said about the space in each landfill. "And if this (provides) us with an extra 30 years of life that we didn't have coming into this 80-year deal, then that's a good thing for the environment, it's a good thing for the Eastern Shore."
If this proposal moves forward, all of the partnering counties would need to come to an agreement on a modified arrangement, including the host fee for Caroline County.
At the meeting, Zimmerman presented three options for host fees and annual tipping fee increases for the Mid-Shore II landfill:
A host fee of $2 per ton of waste growing to $4 after 2031 with an annual increase of 1.15% in tipping fees.A host fee of $3 per ton of waste growing to $5 after 2031 with an annual increase of 1.35% in tipping fees.A host fee of $4 per ton of waste growing to $6 after 2031 with an annual increase of 1.5% in tipping fees.
"We think these are achievable options," Zimmerman said about the three options. "It's really the question of how much risk the counties want to take on in terms of their competitive posture."
He said that historically, tipping fees have, on average, annually increased by 1.42%.
Caroline County Commission President Travis Breeding said he has made it clear to MES that he agrees with keeping the landfill operating in Caroline County for environmental and economic reasons, but he would like to make sure the county retains "any of the savings associated with the extension of the landfill."
He said the county's residents are the ones burdened with the affects of the landfill operations, including truck traffic and bad smells from time to time.
Commission Vice President Larry Porter spoke about the impact of MES operations on the county.
He said that although this proposal is an opportunity to generate more revenue without raising property taxes, having the landfill in the county has affected the condition of the roads where trash is being driven, including trash left on those roads. He said the extension of the landfill's services would be a hard sell to the public.
"For me, anything that we do is going to have to involve MES stepping up to the plate and fulfilling what I think the obligations and responsibilities are," he said, adding that roads would be part of that obligation, in his mind.
Porter asked the presenters if it appears that the other partnering counties are on board with keeping the landfill in Caroline County and paying a host fee. Mohn said everyone seems to be in agreement.
"The question is, what is that host fee going to be?" Mohn said.
Porter said the county will have a public hearing on this in the future. He did not give a date.

title: St. Michaels Mulls Proposed Flood Mitigation Improvements - Coastal Engineer Presents Findings Of Study Investigating Town'S Current, Future Flooding
author: Natalie Jones; Njones@Chespub. Com
content:
St. Michaels Mulls Proposed Flood Mitigation Improvements - Coastal Engineer Presents Findings Of Study Investigating Town'S Current, Future Flooding

 December 15, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; Njones@Chespub. Com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 672
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS - To mitigate increased flooding from sea level rise and stormwater runoff, the Commissioners of St. Michaels are considering investing in improvements to vulnerable shorelines and infrastructure.At the commissioners' Wednesday meeting, BayLand project manager and coastal engineer Anna Johnson presented the San Domingo Creek and West Side stormwater and harbor infrastructure assessment and flood mitigation study.
The study, performed by BayLand, an environmental engineering firm, focused on San Domingo Creek, which hugs the west side of town and opens into Broad Creek. It aimed to examine the town's current flooding sources and investigate what flooding will look like in the future.
The study came as another effort by the town government to address stormwater and coastal flooding. In 2021, the town created the Climate Change/Sea Level Rise Commission, which then worked with the Maryland Department of Natural Resources to obtain a grant for a study.
Much of Maryland, including St. Michaels, is experiencing both global and relative, or local, sea level rise, Johnson said. And according to historic water level measurements taken from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration tide station in Cambridge, sea levels in the lower Chesapeake Bay have risen just over a foot in 80 years.
After the BayLand team assessed existing conditions, current stormwater infrastructure and sea level rise data, further modeling was performed to identify the six most vulnerable areas along San Domingo Creek.
Grace Street was determined to be the highest priority area, Johnson said. The culvert bridging over the creek is undersized, she said, and its low elevation means that by 2050, standing water could occur daily on the road.
A county pump station is also in close proximity to the Grace Street culvert, and that area is also likely to experience daily flooding.
Back Creek Park was ranked as the second highest priority, primarily due to the condition of the bulkhead on its southern shoreline.
West Chestnut Street at Tilden Street, Canton Street at Glory Avenue, the St.
Michaels Nature Trail and Thompson Street were also identified as priority areas.
As for risk mitigation strategies, nature-based, passive solutions are preferred, Johnson said.
"Marshes rebound. A marsh may flood, but then six months later, it's back to being a marsh, whereas if a house floods, it all has to be replaced, or major construction has to be done to fix it," she said.
Nature-based solutions are also grant-friendly, Johnson said.
According to Roy Myers, chair of the town's Climate Change/Sea Level Rise Commission, grant requests are underway for expansion of the living shoreline at Back Creek Park and completion of an assessment and preliminary design for a tide gate under the nature trail bridge.
Once the BayLand team compiled a list of projects based on the needs for mitigation, an implementation plan was developed to determine a timeframe for addressing the needs.
Because of the failing bulkhead, the Back Creek Park living shoreline improvement project was designated as an immediate implementation project.
The project is estimated to cost $204,000.
Installing a tide gate where the St. Michaels Nature Trail bridge crosses San Domingo Creek is another project proposed for immediate implementation.
If installed, the tide gate could prevent coastal flooding in the surrounding area.
However, assessment, preliminary design and implementation for a tide gate come with a hefty price tag - just over $2.4 million.
Johnson recommended the town look into applying for a Federal Emergency Management Agency grant to offset the cost.
Johnson warned of the risk of waiting to implement improvements, pointing out that prices will increase over the next few years.
Improvements to the Grace Street culvert, pipe outfall improvements at the West Chestnut and Tilden Street retention area, stormwater infrastructure replacement along the St. Michaels Nature Trail and raising boating infrastructure at Back Creek Park were listed as shortterm implementation projects.
The total cost for those four projects is estimated at $1.07 million.
Long-term implementation projects, like monitoring flood risk for assessed areas and nourishing living shorelines along Back Creek Park, are designated as such to see if a stronger need develops over time.

title: Easton Town Council Approves Food Truck Pilot Program
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Easton Town Council approves food truck pilot program

 September 4, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 286
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — At a meeting Tuesday evening, the Easton Town Council unanimously approved a resolution that creates a pilot program for food trucks in town.The program allows food trucks to operate on private property with the owners' permission. They will not be allowed downtown or on public property, and they cannot be located within 300 feet of a brick-and-mortar restaurant.
The effort comes as the council discusses potentially revising a 2011 ordinance that limits food trucks to only operating during special events like festivals.
In last month, pushback against Easton's food truck rules has been widespread online. The outcry came after town code enforcement began to more closely enforce the 2011 rules, prohibiting food trucks from operating in the parking lot of the town's hospital.
The pilot program aims to pinpoint where town rules regarding food trucks can be revised in the future, town officials said.
"I worked with staff to try and come up with a strong pilot program for you to look at," Town Attorney Sharon Van Emburgh said at the meeting Tuesday.
The pilot program is set to run for eight months. There will be a one-time $250 fee for each vendor participating.
Permits must be submitted to the town with a map of the location of intention. The map can be an aerial photo, but it must clearly show the food truck is not blocking exits, fire hydrants or entryways.
The food trucks cannot remain in the same place for more than 24 hours, and truck owners' responsibility to get permission from property owners. Vendors must have trash and recycling available and ensure the space is clean before they leave.
Once permits are submitted, it should take around three days for approval or denial. The resolution is effective immediately.

title: Easton Farmers Market Retains Downtown Spot for 2025
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton Farmers Market retains downtown spot for 2025

 March 28, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 540
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Easton Farmers Market is set to remain at its normal downtown spot this season, though the location drew concerns at a recent town meeting.The market's public assembly permit was approved by the Easton Town Council March 18, allowing the market — operated by the Avalon Foundation — to run Saturdays from 8 a.m. to 1 p.m. on North Harrison Street behind Goodwill in the town's parking Lot 5.
But some business owners expressed worry about the farmers market limiting downtown parking on Saturday mornings.
Steve Mangasarian, owner of Breakfast in Easton, said at the March 18 Town Council meeting that there have been parking and trash disposal issues stemming from the farmers market.
In an interview, Mangasarian said while he's not against the market and acknowledged it has "many good actors," he believes the Avalon is not doing enough to police market vendors.
"We feel as if we have a right as taxpayers to be entitled to some parking spaces, to be entitled to the secure use of our dumpsters, and accessibility to our parking lot," Mangasarian said. "And nobody at the farmers market seems to worry about these merchants who are being negatively impacted by the market."
Marie Nuthall, the Avalon's outdoor event coordinator , argued the downtown location is crucial for community connection. The market has been in the same spot for more than 30 years, Nuthall said.
"Over that time, families get to know where to find us, generations, their kids, so forth," she said. "Longevity and consistency is very, very important to us."
"The town has a vested interest in the farmers market being there, because we are part of a tourism draw," she added.
Nuthall said vendors sign memorandums of understanding at the beginning of each season outlining proper garbage disposal standards and parking regulations.
"We do everything that we can to be really good neighbors to all the neighboring businesses," Nuthall said.
The public assembly permit first went through the Easton Police Department before it hit the Town Council desk. While the Easton Police Department recommended approval for the North Harrison Street location, it also suggested an alternative spot at the District Court parking lot on Dover Street.
That lot is larger and would prevent downtown parking from being unavailable on Saturday mornings, according to EPD recommendations.
Easton Sgt. Patrick Sally said while the Harrison Street setup is "as safe as it ever has been," the department explored another option because an unofficial parking lot on Washington Street at the site of the former Safeway is soon to be under construction.
In an interview, Sally said the district court lot may be more of a "long-term" consideration. "It is a safety concern because there (are) a lot of people that do walk there," Sally said of the current downtown location.
Crossing guards are typically stationed at the current location during peak hours to assist pedestrian traffic on Harrison Street and Brewers Lane.
Nuthall said it's a relief to have the market remain in Lot 5 this year. She said "if a move is inevitable" in the future, she hopes the market and vendors "have buy-in" during that decision-making process.
"It should be something that is done thoughtfully and collaboratively," Nuthall said.
The Easton Farmers Market kicks off its 2025 season Saturday, April 12, and runs through December.
