title: St. Michaels Hears Presentation on Houseboat Vacation Rentals
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
St. Michaels hears presentation on houseboat vacation rentals

 February 28, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 575
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST.MICHAELS — Flohom, a company that provides vacationers the chance to stay on houseboats, presented the company's plans for St. Michaels to government officials.Flohom and St. Michaels Marina owner Michael Morgan have discussed putting one or two Flohoms in the marina.
"I run a strict place. Everyone knows my style," Morgan told the town's commissioners at a meeting Wednesday. "I was timid at first, but then a heard their rules and the type of clientele that they have. If I thought this would displease my customer base, I wouldn't even have entertained it. I think it's a neat concept."
The Flohom presentation showed how the boats are built, how the company was started, and what types of rules and regulations are enforced within the company.
Customers are not permitted or allowed to drive the Flohom boats at all, so they remain docked in the same place.
To eliminate excessive noise, Flohom monitors the sound of anyone that stays in the houseboats. If the sound gets too loud, the guest will receive a text message asking them to lower their noise level. Noise monitors do not listen or record conversation but monitor the sound decibels in the home.
Flohom staff members look to dock in places where guests can walk or drive a short distance to get breakfast or lunch and attend different town events.
"I'm new to this as well," Morgan said. "I'm willing to take the chance on it because I think it would be a unique thing for the town, it would be another option for people to come and stay and do something in St. Michaels. Not to mention the accommodation tax"
Commissioners and town residents had multiple questions for the company and for Morgan.
Commissioner David Wojiechowski questioned if Flohom would have to pay accommodation tax, and if so, if all other boats or yacht should pay the same accommodation tax if they stay overnight.
"It is an overnight rental competing against our hotel rooms," Wjiechowski said. "So if this gets approved and pays an accommodation tax, then all 200 slips that are overnight should pay an accommodation tax."
Morgan said that other slips would not be subject to accommodation tax.
Flohom staff confirmed the company does have a plan to bring business to St. Michaels after going through the proper protocols. But the company has an interest in exploring the town and gauging reception first.
"This is just an initial presentation," Jerry South Co-Founder of Flohom said. "Were not sure if this is something that requires a vote. We wanted to be very proactive and come in and say, 'hey, this is what we are doing.'"
Flohom doesn't need a approval from the town council just yet. The company first must go in front of the town's Planning Commission to ensure plans abide by the town's zoning policies.
"The use that they are proposing tonight would not be allowed with our current codes," Town Administrator Rob Straebel said. "So it would require a zoning change that would most likely go in front of the Planning Commission, then come back to the commissioners for discussion.
"So the presentation is just to see if there is enough support to move forward with consideration of a zoning change to potentially allow this."
St. Michaels residents also wanted to know if Flohom can give the houseboat model an historic look instead of a "business look."
Flohom officials confirmed they can remodel the boats to give them a historic look.
This report was updated to clarify how accommodation tax could be applied.

title: St. Michaels Tourism Advisory Board Holds First Meeting
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
St. Michaels Tourism Advisory Board holds first meeting

 January 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 538
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — After months of controversy surrounding its creation, the St. Michaels Tourism Advisory Board held its first meeting at the Boy Scout Cabin in St. Michaels Thursday morning.During this meeting, members of the board, the St. Michaels Business Association and residents of the town came together to discuss the future and current condition of the tourism industry.
The board discussed potential budgets, marketing and branding strategies including combining various websites, and getting a better understanding of the tourists who are visiting and the tourists the board would like to bring to St. Michaels.
Timothy Law, the representative of retail businesses on the board, said as a business owner he is really excited for the work the board will produce.
"I love St. Michaels, and today was a huge stride forward to really understanding tourism and promoting our spectacular destination. I think it's a great group of people and we've got a great diversity of thought and diversity of background. It was just a very positive first step."
The idea of a tourism board was brought forth during a commissioners candidate forum hosted by the St. Michaels Business Association last April, when representatives of the Business Associations stated a need for marketing assistance due to a decrease in revenues within the last year.
The purpose of the board, according to a town memo, would be to assist the town in its efforts to encourage businesses to locate or remain in the town and to make recommendations to the commissioners. The board would also "work closely with the Talbot County Tourism Board on a unified, regional marketing approach."
The board has seven members serving four-year terms, all appointed by the commissioners. Membership includes residents not associated with a business and representatives from the lodging, eating/drinking, retail or service, marinas, museums and nonprofit sectors.
The members of the board were elected by the Commissioners of St. Michaels and include:
Brian Ball, managing director for the Wildset Hotel, to represent lodging.
Chris Agharabi, chief executive officer of Ava's Hospitality Group, to represent restaurants.
Katie Blaha, advancement manager of the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum, to represent nonprofits/museums.
Michael Morgan, owner and president of St. Michaels Marina LLC, to represent marinas.
Timothy Law, owner of American Holiday Shop, to represent retail.
Craig Bertolett, chief operating officer of COLUMBIA Technologies, and Michael McMillan, associate clinical professor of accounting at the University of Maryland, as two representatives for the residents of St. Michaels.
Included in the board is St. Michaels Commissioner Katrina Whittington as acting representative for the commission.
On Thursday, the board discussed the importance of a unified marketing message and the potential benefits of public Wi-Fi for data collection. Board members emphasized the need for a clear target audience and suggested a short-term plan to focus on digital marketing.
Ball said it's important for people to understand how tourism effects all aspects of the town's economy.
"St. Michaels is very much a tourism-based economy and it really affects everything we do from local government to all the businesses and all the restaurants and hotels," Ball said. "I think that this (board) is a very valuable economic tool to use to help the town grow."
Plans were made for the next meeting to include presentations on budget allocation and marketing strategies. The next meeting will be held on Jan. 30.

title: After Months of Debate, St. Michaels Tourism Board Is Approved
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
After months of debate, St. Michaels Tourism Board is approved

 November 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 602
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — After months of heated discussions, revisions and compromises, the St. Michaels Tourism Board was unanimously approved by commissioners on Wednesday evening.According to Commissioner David Wojciechowski, the board will help provide additional resources in case funds from different avenues, including federal funds, are reduced after the election.
"It's a proactive measure to get ahead of the curve," Wojciechowski said. "A lot of things have happened in the past two weeks, we're counting on a lot of grant money coming into this town. There might be an administration in place right now that jeopardizes that grant money. We need to preserve and protect the revenue that's coming into the town."
The purpose of the board, according to a town memo, would be to assist the town in its efforts to encourage businesses to locate or remain in the town and to make recommendations to the commissioners. The board would also "work closely with the Talbot County Tourism Board on a unified, regional marketing approach."
According to the ordinance, the board will be composed of seven members including a mix of business types from the community and residents. The now approved board will recommend to commissions an annual promotional plan and budget that will manage tourism for the upcoming year.
The board would include representatives of several businesses including lodging, food and beverage, retail or service, marinas and nonprofits. The commissioners will appoint the members of the board and appoint one commissioner to participate as a non-voting member of the board.
The idea of a tourism board was suggested during the town election last May. Wojciechowski, Alexis Roiter and Jay Hudson, who were elected as commissioners, said during their campaigns that they would work with business owners to make the town more friendly to their needs.
The tourism board faced pushback soon after its suggestion. During an August commission meeting, residents raised an array of concerns over potential conflicts of interest and a lack of data supporting the board's creation.
PUBLIC COMMENTDuring public comment on Wednesday evening, Daniel Spiegel, a member of Residents Association of St. Michaels, said he and other residents have four issues with the proposed ordinance.
Spiegel said the issues include a lack of adequate data and evidence, an underrepresentation of residents on the tourism board, a "dangerous and unwelcome built-in conflict of interest," and the potential for "managed tourism."
According to Spiegel, managed tourism is a "code word" for moving tourism "upscale," which he has based on previous discussions among commissioners with business representatives.
"I think it's inappropriate for a town, which basically says, 'Bring in the Porsches and keep out the buses and day trips,'" Spiegel said. "I don't think a government policy should be advocating this type of upscale tourism. I think it's not appropriate."
Following comments included a sentiment from residents that St. Michaels is more than a tourism town and a request to focus on already existing institutions.
Debbie Jackson said she is a longtime resident and the town has "always been businesses." Jackson addressed what she described as anti-business sentiment from the residents who said the town was more than just businesses.
According to Jackson, business owners have seen a decline in sales the past two years and support the establishment of a tourism board. Additionally, Jackson said there has been a "wedge" she had seen in town between residents and business owners.
"What prompted all the citizens of St. Michael's to feel this way? Or is this just one little group that's gotten together to hype this up?" Jackson said.
After comments from residents and business owners, Commissioner Alfred Mercier brought the matter up for a vote. The commissioners unanimously voted to approve the tourism board.

title: Urban design consultant presents analysis of Easton's economic potency
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Urban design consultant presents analysis of Easton's economic potency

 August 30, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 564
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Town employees and representatives gathered at the Easton Town Office on Aug. 22 for a presentation of Easton's economic potency for land use planning.Joe Minicozzi, the principal and founder of Urban3, an urban finance consulting group, spoke during the presentation regarding Easton's potential to up its economic potency. He compared the growth of the town to the trajectory of one's DNA.
"Cities all have those moments," Minicozzi said. "They all have a DNA baked into them through their infrastructure, their growth patterns, that will have effects into the future."
Miguel Salinas, the town's director of planning and zoning, helped organize the partnership with Urban3 and last week's presentation.
"We hired Urban3 to model the potential revenue implications of various development scenarios based on different types of land use, … how we build out, … and at what densities," Salinas said.
Minicozzi pointed out the success of Easton's core downtown area. His presentation provided hypothetical examples of how much certain residential developments, businesses and homes could deliver in property taxes per acre.
"As Talbot County taxpayers, you take up 3% of the county's footprint, you're producing 26% of the county's property taxes," Minicozzi said of the town. He encouraged the town to find "opportunities for infill" and "neighborhood growth areas."
Urban3's analysis noted there was a potential $637,000 in property tax revenue from a Poplar Hill housing proposal that never came to fruition.
In August 2023, an application from a developer to build 456 residential units between Easton Bypass and Oxford Road was rescinded. A 119-unit plan was approved by the Easton Planning Commission in September 2023, but this February, Talbot County bought the 120-acre Poplar Hill Farm property.
"That was an opportunity lost," Minicozzi said. "Make sure that you account for that or find a way to learn from this and do it in another place. Maybe that's not the right place, that's cool, your decision. But don't just avoid that."
Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery, who attended the meeting, said he felt it was "inappropriate" for the presentation to mention the canceled Poplar Hill proposal given that it was a "democratically led and made decision."
"The data are perfectly useful in their own way," Montgomery said of the presentation as a whole, "but I was disturbed by the way the presentation made it seem like the only objective we should have … is how we can maximize the amount of tax revenue we can take in. And that's just wrong. There are so many other things that matter, starting with how we preserve the character of the town and maintain our rural character, maintain our open spaces."
During the presentation, Minicozzi raised the topic of sea level rise. He noted Maryland Department of Planning projections that predict Talbot County will lose $817 million in property value due to sea level rise by the year 2100, with $8.1 million of that coming in Easton.
Minicozzi also encouraged the town to ensure underrepresented groups of people — such as those under 45 and the town's non-white population — should be heard in conversations of economic potency.
"Those folks get pushed out of the community and take on more burden in transportation to get here," Minicozzi said, "which is even more painful financially."
Salinas said the analysis and presentation brought information that can serve the town's planning and zoning department moving forward.
"This information can be important for us to add another tool to the toolbox," Salinas said.

 ST. MICHAELS — The Commissioners of St. Michaels is making moves to market the town, including creating a marketing and social media presence and establishing a tourism advisory board.After briefly advertising for bids from marketing firms, the commissioners unanimously approved Madison Enterprises LLC to provide strategic marketing for St. Michaels.
During the firm's June 12 presentation to the commissioners, representatives emphasized their previous experience working with 75 local businesses.
Maya Brandon, a representative of Madison Enterprises LLC, explained that she has been running all of the digital marketing assets, including Stmichaelsmaryland.com, an associated Facebook page called Experience St. Michaels and Instagram account @st.michaelsmd.

He said a tourism advisory board would help prepare an outline of objectives and could consist of representatives from the hotel industry, businesses and nonprofits, and residents of St. Michaels.

title: Lodging Tax Increase Proposed for St. Michaels
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Lodging tax increase proposed for St. Michaels

 May 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 578
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — On Wednesday evening, the Commissioners of St. Michaels discussed a new proposal to address a potential increase to the town's accommodation tax, the tax charged to travelers when they rent lodging.The topic raised controversy during the town election earlier this month.
Commission President David Breimhurst said the reason he added the subject to the agenda was due to concerns brought up during a Talbot County Tourism Board meeting that the town's new commissioners, who will be sworn in next month, "are likely to approve an increase in the accommodation tax."
Breimhurst said the new proposal would "level the playing field in a way that benefits all stakeholders."
The accommodation tax is currently 4% and could potentially increase to 6%, a 50% increase. Based on the town's current budget projections, the fiscal year 2025 budget real property tax revenue will raise about $1.68 million. Breimhurst said over a third of that revenue comes from commercial properties, and almost two-thirds comes from residential homeowners.
The current real estate tax rate is 47 cents per $100 of assessed value. The added accommodation tax revenue could be used to lower that rate to 35 cents per $100 for homeowners, lodging facilities and short-term rentals, while the remaining commercial properties would continue to pay the current rate.
According to Breimhurst, the $425,000 in added accommodation tax revenue would cover a $359,215 shortfall and leave $65,785. Breimhurst said the remaining money could be returned to the town's reserves or used for some other purpose.
"This proposal, I believe, has something in it for all stakeholders and fairly addresses the issue of unequal taxation while supporting a healthy business climate," Breimhurst said.
Commissioner Alfred Mercier raised questions about Breimhurst's proposal. Mercier asked how they are supposed to move forward with this proposal with the restrictions on how the town is supposed to use revenue from the accommodation tax.
"We have to use it for promoting tourism," he said.
Mercier also raised questions about the extent to which giving tax breaks to either residential properties or business owners would affect the town's ultimate goals.
Breimhurst responded that the tax statute states that the money collected would be paid to the municipal corporation's governing body to "alleviate costs associated with tourism." He went on to explain the associated costs taxpayers take to maintain the town such as a tourist attraction, including brick sidewalks, extra police and maintenance of parks.
Mercier proposed using some of the revenue for marketing the town, purchasing banners, replacing street maps or creating transportation to take tourists through major landmarks of the town. Breimhurst said, however, that their current budget already accounts for maintaining the town's infrastructure, and with the potential increase, they will have to figure out where to put that money.
Breimhurst said that no action would be taken at Wednesday's meeting and that he just wanted to record a proposal he came up with so people can review it and consider uses for that increase.
During the recent commissioner election, accommodation tax split candidates, with Breimhurst opposed to raising it.
Breimhurst and Commissioner Joyce Harrod both lost their bids for reelection earlier this month. Three new commissioners, Jay Hudson, David Wojciechowski and Alexis Roiter, will be sworn in in the coming weeks.
Hudson and Roiter did not respond to a request for comment on the issue in time for publication of this article.
Wojciechowski said he was open to the consideration of the raise.
"It needs to be taken under consideration to understand the impact it may have on everyone concerned," Wojciechowski said.

title: Easton Police Chief: Traffic Stops Bill Would Have 'Drastic' Impacts on Police Work
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton police chief: Traffic stops bill would have 'drastic' impacts on police work

 February 20, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 478
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Police Chief Alan Lowrey raised concerns over a proposed bill in the state legislature that would limit police officers' abilities to make traffic stops for certain violations.Senate Bill 292, cross-filed in the House of Delegates, would shift many primary offenses to secondary offenses, including improper use of headlights and taillights, failing to use turn signals, missing or improper license plates, and excessive noise.
That change would mean police officers can only cite a driver for those offenses if they pull over the driver for a different, primary offense.
During an Easton Town Council meeting Monday, Lowrey, also serving as the interim town manager, said the bill's proposed changes would be "drastic" and negatively impact police in detecting crime.
"There's a number of concerns on my part as the chief of police, and I've spoken with my staff about this," Lowrey said.
Lowrey said offenses such as driving without headlights are common signs indicating potential impaired driving. He said all of the offenses that would be reclassified are safety issues.
"I personally have arrested a number of people, based upon traffic stops, for serious crimes," Lowrey said.
As written, the bill seeks to make evidence gathered during traffic stops inadmissible if an officer fails to state their name, identification number, agency and reason for the stop. Lowrey called that measure "drastic" as well.
Sen. Charles Sydnor III (D-Baltimore County) is the bill's sponsor. At a Jan. 28 Senate Judicial Proceedings hearing, Sydnor noted Baltimore County statistics that indicated Black and Hispanic drivers face inequities in the rate of citations issued.
"It is these disparities that spurred me to seek and introduce a legislative remedy," Sydnor said.
Sydnor said he worked with the Maryland Office of the Public Defender on the drafted bill. Moving primary violations to fall under secondary violations make way for technologies such as cameras to detect traffic violations, the senator said.
"Technology that can be modified to do what people do today," Sydnor said. "So really, this bill kicks off a conversation about, I would say, a reimagining of how we deal with traffic offenses on the highways."
At the hearing, though, some legislators and law enforcement officials from around the state spoke unfavorably of the legislation.
Those conversations around Maryland have continued in the weeks since. Last month, the Caroline County Commissioners discussed the bill at a meeting and expressed intent to write a letter in opposition.
Monday in Easton, Ward 2 Councilmember Don Abbatiello said the job of being a police officer is "tough enough as it is."
"We don't need to make it any tougher," Abbatiello said. "So I would support anything that the town would like to do in order to try to prevent this from passing."
Town Council President Frank Gunsallus asked Lowrey how the town could express its concerns regarding the bill. Lowrey suggested drafting a letter.
Following discussion, Easton councilmembers voted unanimously to send correspondence to committees in Annapolis opposing the bill.

title: Talbot Police Accountability Board Releases Inaugural Report
author: Natalie Jones
content:
Talbot Police Accountability Board releases inaugural report

 January 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Crime 
 
 749
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Talbot County Police Accountability Board's first year was marked by challenges in adjusting to citizen oversight in policing, but "reluctant confidence" from law enforcement is believed to be growing, the board said in its inaugural report.The annual report, submitted to the Talbot County Council on Dec. 20, 2023, outlined the board's yearlong struggle in establishing a rapport with the county's four law enforcement agencies, which voiced concerns with the state-mandated legislation that created the board and a committee to review complaints of police misconduct.
Trends in call volume, arrests, struggles with recruitment and retention, use of force and police-community relations within each of the county's law enforcement agencies were analyzed in the report.
The board also asked the County Council to consider a number of recommendations to improve police accountability in Talbot County.
However, the board said most of the concerns from local police agencies centered on the Administrative Charging Committee, which is tasked with determining if officers should face administrative charges following a police agency's own investigation into the allegations. The committee also recommends appropriate discipline.
The committee is composed of five county residents and is helmed by Mitchell Ettinger, who also serves as the chairman of the Police Accountability Board.
Gaining the confidence of the county's law enforcement agencies proved to be the Administrative Charging Committee's great challenge last year, the report said.
Police questioned the wisdom of citizen oversight, the breadth of the committee's role and a lack of experience in law enforcement, which could translate to a gap in understanding the tasks and competing interests police officers face daily, according to the report.
In 2023, 15 complaints were submitted to the Administrative Charging Committee for review: 10 from the Sheriff's Office and five from the Easton Police Department.
Twelve complaints resulted in officer exonerations or were ruled as unfounded charges. Three complaints ended with varying disciplinary actions — two of which involved disagreements on recommended dispositions between the Administrative Charging Committee and the officers' respective agencies, the report said.
In one case, a Sheriff's Office deputy was administratively charged for undue use of force. According to the report, the deputy deployed pepper spray in an attempt to stop a juvenile who was improperly operating a mini-bike on the road.
The Administrative Charging Committee found it was unreasonable for the deputy to do so and imposed charges. The committee recommended two days' loss of pay, which the deputy accepted, according to the report.
The Sheriff's Office also revised its policy to clarify that deploying pepper spray on a moving motorist is inappropriate.
Use of force reports were a particular focus of the Police Accountability Board in 2023, according to its report. Law enforcement agencies now submit those reports quarterly.
The board's report said given the extensive interaction between police and the public, it was "remarkable" that officers only resorted to use of force on 10 occasions — six times by the sheriff's office, three times by the Easton Police Department and once by the St. Michaels Police Department.
Another case was heard against an Easton officer for unbecoming conduct off-duty, along with administrative failures to report conduct and a subpoena to testify. The allegations in that case were sustained, with the committee recommending two days' loss of pay or leave and a letter of reprimand.
The committee heard a third complaint against a sheriff's office deputy for speeding, which the deputy acknowledged. The deputy received a letter of reprimand.
Despite a year of building relationships, some distrust still lingers between the Administrative Charging Committee and local law enforcement.
"...The LEAs most certainly will maintain that they did not (and do not) need citizen oversight to exercise proper review and disposition of citizen complaints," the report said.
Though work remains to be done, the board believes the Administrative Charging Committee has established credibility with police through its "well-reasoned and supported" opinions on each of the complaints.
Easton Police Chief Alan Lowrey acknowledged the lack of consensus between law enforcement and the committee on some case dispositions, but he said there was space for those disagreements.
"I think that we all want to be going in the same direction, and that is to have professional law enforcement in Talbot County," he said. "I've never gotten a sense from either entity, the PAB or the ACC, that they're looking to do in law enforcement like has been the narrative nationally for a few years of some groups — not all groups."
"We understand that it's important to have a rule of law in our community, and we just want it to be done well," Lowrey continued.

 The Easton Police Department announced its first Community Police Academy.The goal of this program, the department said in a press release, is to educate the public about the Easton Police Department and to increase the rapport between community members and police officers.The Community Police Academy will take place from 6 to 9 p.m. on the following eleven evenings: Jan. 17, Jan. 24, Jan. 31, Feb. 7, Feb. 15, Feb. 21, Feb. 28, March 6, March 13, March 20 and March 27.Most of the classes will meet at the Easton Police Department on 106 W.Dover St. in Easton. "We invite Easton residents to apply and learn more about their Easton Police Department. If you are interested in attending, please contact the Easton Police Department. Class size is limited, so don't wait."Questions about this program can be directed to: EPDCareers@eastonmd.gov. Applications can be filled out at: eastonmd.gov/604/Community-Police-AcademyQUALIFICATIONSEligible applicants must meet the following criteria:. Resident of the Town of Easton. title: Ann O'Connor
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Ann O'Connor

 October 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Ann Oconnor 
 
 589
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Ann O'Connor, 55, is a resident of Easton. She is running for the District 2 seat on the Talbot County Board of Education.She is a former teacher and has six children.
Why are you running for office?
I am running for the school board because I am deeply passionate about children's education. As a former teacher and mother of six, I have dedicated my career to helping children reach their highest potential.
Having witnessed my six children go through (Talbot County Public School), I have observed a decline in academic rigor, expectations and accountability, both in behavior and academics. This experience drives my desire to make meaningful changes on the school board. The fact that our students are scoring 18% proficient in math and 55% in reading indicates a pressing need for new perspectives on our educational strategies.
What are your priorities if elected?
My priorities are the ABCs of education: advancing academics, boosting accountability and cultivating character. The focus is on the whole child. We cannot advance academics without discipline.
When students develop self-discipline, good character naturally emerges. This requires daily practice and consistent reinforcement of rules and clear expectations for all students across all buildings. Disruptive behavior must be addressed promptly and effectively.
Regarding academic accountability: A 95% graduation rate when less than ¼ of our students are proficient in math skills, and less than ½ are reading on grade level is inconsistent — something is broken here and we need to fix it.
What is the most important issue that Talbot County Public Schools faces and how do you think the board needs to address it?
The most important issue is the steady decline of academic rigor. We need to make sure we continue to implement early intervention in elementary schools to support those who need that extra push. It's essential to send home books and ensure that our children have access to/and are accountable for reading materials throughout elementary, middle and high school.
We should place greater emphasis on traditional learning — using pencils and paper, cursive writing, fostering reading and critical thinking skills, while reducing reliance on computers. We need to offer pathways for middle school students interested in college or the workforce, including advanced/honors classes.
Talbot County residents have been receiving postcards in the mail criticizing education in the county. What are your thoughts on the postcards and how should these concerns be addressed?
The postcards received in the mail are snapshots of where our schools stand. No one wants these scores, they are abysmal. It's a wake up call to attack the problem and change the way we have been doing education here in Talbot County.
We need to put our focus on reading, writing and math. Our students are distracted. Let's eliminate anything that detracts from our mission as educators and focus on what truly matters — educating the child. Let's get back to basics with my ABCs of education.
What are your thoughts on the Blueprint For Maryland's Future? What concerns or benefits do you see?
Simply changing a name doesn't lead to improvement. Over the last two decades, this initiative has gone through four name changes. Although there are many wonderful proposals in the Blueprint, I don't believe that top-down programs created by education experts would make our local schools better.
The Blueprint is a blanket principle mandated for all 24 counties in Maryland. The counties have no say in how it is implemented. It removes the schools from the control of locally elected school boards and puts control in the hands of unelected officials. I believe we want control over our local schools.

title: Anna Howie
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Anna Howie

 October 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Anna Howie 
 
 511
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Anna Howie, 49, is a resident of Easton and the current District 5 member of the Talbot County Board of Education. She was appointed to the post by Gov. Wes Moore in October, 2023.Howie is the assistant principal at Federalsburg Elementary School. She is married and has three children.
Why are you running for office?
I am running for the District 5 seat of the Talbot County Board of Education to represent students, families and other stakeholders. We are making gains in our school district, and I want to continue to ensure that our students and teachers have access to high quality instructional materials that will have an impact on student achievement and success.
What are your priorities if elected?
My priorities align with the goals set by the members of the Board of Education and the superintendent, Dr. (Shraron) Pepukayi. My two main areas of focus are increasing student achievement in the areas of mathematics and reading, and recruiting and retaining quality teachers.
Having teachers that provide outstanding instruction to our students will ensure that our students will be academically successful.
What is the most important issue that Talbot County Public Schools faces, and how do you think the board needs to address it?
The most important issue that Talbot County Public Schools face right now is providing exceptional education opportunities for all students while being fiscally responsible.
Currently, the curriculum coordinating committee has brought high quality resources to the board for approval in the areas of reading and mathematics. These resources are paid for through educational grants. Utilizing grants is a responsible way of ensuring that we are providing our students with high quality instructional materials while being fiscally responsible.
Talbot County residents have been receiving postcards in the mail criticizing education in the county. What are your thoughts on the postcards and how should these concerns be addressed?
The postcards that have been mailed out focused on student test scores as well as other concerns. In terms of student test scores, we have purchased new high quality instructional materials. Our 2024 data reflects growth in all subgroups as well as certain subject areas and grades.
Student test scores are not just a concern for our district but across the State. Through the Governance and Accountability pillar of the Blueprint, expert review teams will be visiting schools across the state to review literacy and mathematics instruction in our classrooms and provide quality feedback for improvement.
What are your thoughts on the Blueprint For Maryland's Future? What concerns or benefits do you see?
I believe that the pillars of the Blueprint reflect the areas that all Maryland Schools want to address. Those pillars address early childhood education, high quality and diverse teachers, college and career readiness, more resources for students to be successful, and governance and accountability.
The Blueprint identifies and prioritizes the needs that we see in our district and across the state. In order for our students to be college and career ready by 10th grade, we need to start addressing their needs in pre-Kindergarten and ensure that they are receiving the resources they need to be successful in every grade.

title: County Council Introduces Bills to Improve Auditorium Lights, Athletic Fields
author: Konner Metz
content:
County Council introduces bills to improve auditorium lights, athletic fields

 January 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 330
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Talbot County Council introduced three pieces of capital-enabling legislation during Tuesday's meeting that would dedicate funds for school improvements.Bills 1580, 1581 and 1582 were introduced by all five council members. If passed at a future meeting, they will approve a combined $1.5 million in funding for three projects: new auditorium lights at Easton High School ($817,321), light replacements at St. Michaels Middle High School ($556,000) and athletic field improvements across the district ($116,679).
The fiscal year 2025 budget already accounted for the capital costs, County Manager Clay Stamp noted. The three bills would simply authorize the usage of funds for those three projects, respectively.
Talbot County Public Schools Director of Operations Kevin Shafer said Easton High's auditorium lights date back to the school's renovation in 1997.
Talbot County Council Vice President Pete Lesher said he's noticed "how desperately needed this lighting system is."
"In order to put on some of the really quality student productions that we've seen at Easton High School, I believe that some of the lighting directors have been bringing equipment in from … the University of Maryland, Baltimore County and other places to supplement the antiquated equipment that the auditorium itself has," Lesher said.
"We've moved into an era of LED lighting, which didn't exist back in 1997," Lesher added. "This is going to be a huge leap forward."
Shafer said the light replacements and improvements at St. Michaels Middle High School will complete the ongoing LED conversion product across the entire St. Michaels campus. Grant funding allowed for new side lights at St. Michaels Elementary, Shafer said.
The $117,000 for athletic field improvements will help the district move forward with its grass field upgrades.
"Generally speaking, the athletic field improvements are going to be surrounding the current fields that we have, grass fields," Shafer said. "(We are) doing some longstanding improvements related to some issues or concerns that came up."
A public hearing on the three bills will be held during Talbot County Council's Feb. 11 meeting at 5:30 p.m.
